Three Views Compared Protestant (Calvinist) The elect are guaranteed final salvation. True believers may doubt temporarily, but they cannot ultimately fall away. Assurance is available — and expected. (The popular phrase "once saved, always saved" is more Baptist than strictly Reformed.) The inner witness of the Holy Spirit confirms one’s elect status. Departing from faith proves the person was never truly saved to begin with (1 John 2:19). Roman Catholic Salvation can be forfeited through mortal sin. The Council of Trent taught that no one can know with the certainty of faith that he has obtained God’s grace (Session 6, chapter 9), and that absolute certainty of persevering to the end comes only by special revelation (canon 16). Hope of salvation is firm and warranted; certainty is not available to most. Oriental Orthodox Salvation is a living relationship and ongoing process (theosis). It can be forfeited through persistent rejection of God. We have confident, anchored hope — not anxious fear, but also not guaranteed certainty.

This hope rests on God’s faithfulness and mercy, not on our own spiritual achievements. Humility and watchfulness are signs of health, not doubt. The OO position is closer to Rome than to Calvinism on this question, but with a distinctive theological texture: the Catholic emphasis is more legal (mortal sin breaks grace), while the OO emphasis is more relational and transformational (the question is whether one is genuinely oriented toward God and growing).

secs.h: Hope vs. Certainty — A Crucial Distinction
secs.x: Hope vs. Certainty — A Crucial Distinction The Oriental Orthodox tradition insists on a precise distinction that is often collapsed in popular Christianity: the difference between hope and certainty . Hope (Greek: elpis ) in the biblical sense is not wishful thinking. It is confident, anchored expectation based on the character of God and his promises. Paul says that “hope does not put us to shame” (Romans 5:5), not because we are certain of our own spiritual state, but “because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.” The anchor of hope is God, not us. Certainty about one’s final salvation would require either: (a) complete knowledge of one’s future choices and repentance, or (b) a guarantee that those choices no longer matter. The OO tradition accepts neither. We are genuinely free; the future is genuinely open; God’s mercy is genuinely available to the end.

secs.h: Hope vs. Certainty — A Crucial Distinction
secs.x: “We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf.” — Hebrews 6:19 The ground of our hope is not in ourselves, not in our faith, our repentance, or our fasting, but in God, who "is greater than our heart, and he knows everything" (1 John 3:20). What This Looks Like in Practice A Christian living in repentance, receiving the sacraments, praying, and fighting sin with the Church’s weapons has every reason for profound, joyful, stable hope. Not because they have assessed their own spiritual state and found it satisfactory — but because they are in the hands of a God who “is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy” (Jude 24). The hope is in the keeper, not the kept.

secs.h: The Holy Tension — Fear and Love Together
secs.x: The Holy Tension — Fear and Love Together What makes the Oriental Orthodox position genuinely distinctive — and, the tradition argues, genuinely biblical — is that it refuses to resolve the tension the New Testament holds together: profound confidence in God’s mercy alongside honest awareness of human fragility and the cost of discipleship. The Confidence Side “…nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 8:38–39) “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.” (Philippians 1:6) “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.” (John 10:28) “I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.” (1 John 5:13) The Watchfulness Side “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” (Philippians 2:12) “Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.” (1 Corinthians 10:12) “I discipline my body… lest after preaching to others I

secs.h: The Holy Tension — Fear and Love Together
secs.x: myself should be disqualified.” (1 Corinthians 9:27) “But the one who endures to the end will be saved.” (Matthew 24:13) The OO tradition does not resolve this tension by choosing one side. It holds both simultaneously — and considers that the ability to hold both is itself a mark of spiritual maturity. The Calvinist resolves the tension by minimizing the watchfulness texts. The anxious person resolves it by minimizing the confidence texts. The Orthodox path is to live within the tension, trusting God’s faithfulness while remaining genuinely responsible for one’s ongoing choices. “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.” — Philippians 2:12 –13 This passage holds the tension in a single breath: you work it out with fear and trembling — and God is the one working in you. Both are true simultaneously. Your effort and God’s sovereign grace are not alternatives; they are cooperating realities.

secs.h: Against Presumption — Why Certainty Can Be Dangerous
secs.x: Against Presumption — Why Certainty Can Be Dangerous The Oriental Orthodox tradition is firm: presumption on one’s salvation is spiritually deadly. Not because God is stingy, but because the presumption that one is already certainly saved tends to dissolve the genuine conversion and ongoing repentance that salvation requires. Jesus’ most alarming words are addressed not to unbelievers but to people certain of their standing: “On that day many will say to me, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name…?’ And then will I declare to them, ‘I never knew you.’” (Matthew 7:22–23). The presumption here is not that these people were lying about their spiritual experiences — they may have been genuine. The problem is they substituted spiritual activity for genuine relationship and obedience.

secs.h: Against Presumption — Why Certainty Can Be Dangerous
secs.x: “But when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice and does the same abominations that the wicked person does, shall he live? None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered; for the treachery of which he is guilty and the sin he has committed, for them he shall die.” — Ezekiel 18:24 Paul’s Self-Watchfulness The Apostle Paul — who wrote that nothing can separate us from the love of God, also wrote: “I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27). Paul does not write as someone certain of his final destination but as someone running a race with full effort until the finish line. The OO tradition points out: if Paul was uncertain enough about his own final standing to train himself rigorously, what grounds do we have for settled certainty? “So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air.

secs.h: Against Presumption — Why Certainty Can Be Dangerous
secs.x: But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.” — 1 Corinthians 9:26 –27 Abba Sisoes the Great d. c. AD 429 One of the great Desert Fathers of Egypt. On his deathbed, when the brothers told him he had no need to repent, he replied: “I do not think that I have even begun to repent.” This was not false modesty from a saint; it was the deepest spiritual health, measuring oneself against the fullness of God rather than against other people. (Wording as given by OrthodoxWiki.) St. John Chrysostom 347–407 AD “I do not think there are many among bishops that will be saved, but many more that perish: and the reason is, that it is an affair that requires a great mind. Many are the exigencies which throw a man out of his natural temper; and he had need have a thousand eyes on all sides.” ( Homily 3 on Acts ). Chrysostom, the greatest preacher of the ancient church, expressed genuine uncertainty about the salvation of bishops, presumably including himself. Not despair, but honest watchfulness.

secs.h: Against Despair — Why Fear Must Not Become Paralysis
secs.x: Against Despair — Why Fear Must Not Become Paralysis If presumption is one danger, despair is the other — and the Oriental Orthodox tradition is equally firm against it. A God who is genuinely merciful, whose nature is love, who sent his Son to seek and save the lost — this God does not want his children paralyzed by existential anxiety about their standing with him. “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.” — 1 John 4:18 The saints of the Oriental Orthodox tradition are characterized not by spiritual anxiety but by radiant joy and freedom. Precisely because their hope rests in God rather than in themselves, they are free from the frantic self-monitoring of those who must constantly prove their salvation. They can acknowledge sin honestly — because God’s mercy is greater than any sin they can confess. The Prodigal Son — The Pattern Jesus’ parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32) is the master key to the OO understanding of assurance.

secs.h: Against Despair — Why Fear Must Not Become Paralysis
secs.x: The son “came to himself” — genuine metanoia — and turned toward home, not knowing what reception awaited. He did not presume on his father’s love; he turned toward it. And “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him” (Luke 15:20, ESV). The father does not wait for the son to complete his penitential speech before welcoming him. The initiative of grace is entirely from the father’s side. The son’s only role is to turn — and the father does the rest. The Desert Fathers speak of God as the physician of the soul: the sinner comes to Him as a patient, not as a defendant. Abba Moses the Black c. 330–405 AD “The monk must die to his neighbour and never judge him at all, in any way whatever.” (Seven Instructions of Abba Moses, 1). The Egyptian Desert Father, a former bandit turned saint and venerated in all the Oriental Orthodox churches, embodied the paradox at the heart of OO assurance: radical self-condemnation without despair.

secs.h: Against Despair — Why Fear Must Not Become Paralysis
secs.x: When summoned to judge a brother, he came carrying a leaking jug or basket of sand on his back and said: “My sins run out behind me, and I do not see them, and today I am coming to judge the errors of another.” ( Sayings of the Desert Fathers , Moses 2; translations as published by johnsanidopoulos.com.) St. Isaac of Nineveh d. c. 700 AD (Church of the East; beloved in OO and EO monasticism) “Love sinners, but hate their works; and do not despise them for their faults, lest you be tempted by the same trespasses.” ( Ascetical Homilies ). Isaac of Nineveh, a Syriac bishop of the Church of the East tradition, yet read and loved across Oriental Orthodox, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic monastic circles for over a millennium, taught that the sight of one's own sin, rightly perceived, produces not despair but compassion. The person who knows his own need for mercy cannot despise another sinner. St.

secs.h: Against Despair — Why Fear Must Not Become Paralysis
secs.x: Anthony the Great 251–356 AD “I saw the snares that the enemy spreads out over the world and I said groaning, ‘What can get through from such snares?’ Then I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Humility.’” ( Sayings of the Desert Fathers , Antony 7, tr. Ward). Anthony does not name correct doctrine, moral achievement, or certainty of election as the path through the snares. He names humility, the posture of one who trusts in God rather than in oneself, the opposite of both presumption and despair.

Key Scriptures The Confidence of Hope “For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” — Romans 8:38 –39 “Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy… be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority.” — Jude 24–25 “I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.” — 1 John 5:13 The Call to Watchfulness “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.” — Philippians 2:12 –13 “Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.” — 1 Corinthians 10:12 “For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened… and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance.” — Hebrews 6:4 –6 “The one who conquers will be

clothed thus in white garments, and I will never blot his name out of the book of life.” — Revelation 3:5 (implying names can be blotted out if one does not conquer) The Ground of Hope: God's Faithfulness, Not Ours “If we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself.” — 2 Timothy 2:13 “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.” — 1 Thessalonians 5:24 “And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.” — Philippians 1:6

Church Fathers on Assurance St. Anthony the Great 251–356 AD “This is the great work of a man: always to take the blame for his own sins before God and to expect temptation to his last breath.” ( Sayings of the Desert Fathers , Antony 4). The father of monks describes the healthy Christian as one who never settles into complacency, yet whose watchfulness is turned on himself, not on others. The Prayer of St. Ephrem Prayed throughout Lent in the Orthodox churches “O Lord and Master of my life, a spirit of idleness, despondency, ambition, and idle talking give me not. But rather a spirit of chastity, humble-mindedness, patience, and love bestow upon me Thy servant. Yea, O Lord King, grant me to see my own failings and not condemn my brother; for blessed art Thou unto the ages of ages.” (Translation as published by orthodox-europe.org; English versions vary.) The prayer traditionally ascribed to St. Ephrem asks for self-knowledge and repentance, not for assurance of one's standing, and names despondency among the spirits to be driven out. St.

Athanasius of Alexandria 296–373 AD “For He was made man that we might be made God.” ( On the Incarnation 54). Athanasius' framing of salvation as theosis, an ongoing participation in the divine life, makes the question of assurance a different question entirely. The issue is not whether one's ticket has been punched but whether one is genuinely growing in divine life.

FAQ Does 1 John 5:13 not prove we can know we have eternal life? Yes — and the OO tradition does not deny this. John says believers can “know” they have eternal life. The question is what kind of knowing this is. It is not the logical certainty of a deductive proof, nor the guaranteed security of an irrevocable legal contract. It is the relational knowing of one who is genuinely in communion with God — the same knowing John describes elsewhere: “And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments” (1 John 2:3). This knowing is a present, living, relational reality — not a permanent status-certificate that cannot be revoked. Doesn't John 10:28 say no one can snatch believers out of Christ's hand? Yes — and this is a magnificent promise. No external power — no devil, no persecution, no tragedy — can forcibly remove a person from Christ’s care. The OO tradition fully affirms this. What it does not affirm is that the passage eliminates the possibility of voluntary departure. A person cannot be snatched out; they can walk out.

The parable of the Prodigal Son is about a son who left voluntarily — the father did not eject him. John 10:28 protects believers from external compulsion; it does not override human freedom. This reading is consistent with the many NT warnings about apostasy addressed to believers. “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.” — John 10:27 –28 Is the OO view just constant anxiety about salvation? No — and this is the most important misunderstanding to correct. The saints of the Oriental Orthodox tradition are not characterized by anxiety but by profound, unshakeable joy and peace. The difference is the ground of their peace: not a judgment that one’s own spiritual state is satisfactory, but trust that one is in the hands of a God whose mercy is inexhaustible. Watchfulness and joy are not opposites; in the saints they are the same thing.

Can genuine Christians actually lose their salvation? The OO tradition’s answer is: yes, in principle — through sustained, persistent, final rejection of God. Not through individual sins, failures, or even long periods of backsliding (for which repentance is always available). What the tradition describes as genuine final loss is a hardening of the will against God sustained to death — a deliberate, final choice. Hebrews 6:4–6 and Hebrews 10:26–31 describe a state of apostasy after genuine enlightenment. The OO tradition does not identify particular individuals as having reached this state — that judgment belongs to God — but it does not deny the possibility. The same God who does not desire the death of the sinner (Ezekiel 18:23) also will not override the final choice of a creature made in his image.

Glossary Elpis (ελπίς) Greek for “hope.” In the NT, not wishful thinking but confident, anchored expectation based on God’s character and promises. The Christian’s hope is “sure and steadfast” (Heb 6:19) because its anchor is God, not the self. Theosis “Deification” — salvation understood as genuine, ongoing participation in the divine life. Makes assurance a question of present growth, not a one-time status. One can ask “am I growing toward God?” rather than “am I in the elect?” Nepsis (νηψις) “Watchfulness, sobriety.” The vigilant attentiveness to one’s inner life that characterizes hesychast spirituality. Not anxious monitoring but clear-eyed awareness. “Be sober-minded; be watchful” (1 Peter 5:8). Presumption In OO spirituality, the sin of treating God’s mercy as a guarantee that requires nothing in return — treating salvation as a concluded transaction rather than a living relationship. Opposite of despair; equally dangerous. Despair The sin of concluding that one’s sins are beyond God’s mercy — effectively placing limits on God.

Judas represents this: his grief at betrayal turned inward rather than toward God. The OO tradition treats despair as an offense against the nature of God as love. Perseverance of the Saints Calvinist doctrine that the genuinely elect will inevitably persevere in faith to the end. Their final salvation is certain. OO rejects this as eliminating genuine human freedom and undermining the reality of apostasy warnings in scripture.

I. Introduction: The Apostolic The Coptic Church calls him Athanasius the Apostolic . He was the twentieth Pope of Alexandria, and for forty-five years he was the chief defender of the faith confessed at Nicaea, that the Son of God is "of one essence with the Father." He was driven from his see five times by four emperors, and spent about seventeen of those years in exile. This page is the first in a series on the Oriental pillars: Athanasius, Basil and Cyril , the Fathers whose teaching shaped the councils the Oriental Orthodox receive. Athanasius comes first because the others build on him. Basil defended the Holy Spirit along lines Athanasius had drawn. Cyril of Alexandria, his successor two generations later, built his defence of the one Christ on Athanasius' writings. The page lets Athanasius speak for himself: on why God became man, against Arius, on Nicaea, on the Holy Spirit and on the one Christ, on the canon of Scripture, and in his own record of the slanders and exiles he endured.

"For He was made man that we might be made God." St Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54 A Note on Quotations Every quotation marked VERBATIM has been checked word for word against the public domain translation in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, volume 4 (Athanasius) and volume 7 (Gregory the Theologian). Where a work has no public domain English translation, such as Athanasius' Letters to Serapion, the teaching is summarised and marked PARAPHRASE . Scripture follows the NKJV.

II. Glossary of Terms Homoousios ὁμοούσιος: "of one essence" The word of Nicaea: the Son is of the same essence as the Father. Athanasius was its great defender. Ousia οὐσία: "essence, being" What God is. Father, Son and Holy Spirit share one ousia. Hypostasis ὑπόστασις: "subsistence" In Athanasius' day the word could mean either essence or person, which caused real confusion. Later it came to mean the three Persons. Logos λόγος: "Word" The eternal Son, through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3), who became flesh. Arianism after Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria The teaching that the Son was the first and greatest creature, made from nothing, and that "once He was not." Homoiousios ὁμοιούσιος: "of like essence" A middle position of the 350s: the Son is like the Father in essence. Athanasius treated those who held it as brothers who were close to the truth. Theosis θέωσις: "deification" Our sharing in the divine life by grace (2 Peter 1:4). For Athanasius it is the purpose of the Incarnation.

Festal Letter ἑορταστικὴ ἐπιστολή The yearly letter in which the Pope of Alexandria announced the date of Pascha. Athanasius used his thirty-ninth to list the books of Scripture. Meletians after Meletius of Lycopolis A schismatic party in Egypt that allied with the Arians against Athanasius. Pope πάπας: "father" The ancient title of the Archbishop of Alexandria. Letters of his own century already address him by this title.

III. His Life Athanasius was born in Egypt around 296 to 298 and was raised in the Church of Alexandria under Bishop Alexander, who made him a deacon and his secretary. His life cannot be separated from the Arian controversy, which began in Alexandria when he was a young man and outlasted him. c. 296–298 Born in Egypt, probably in or near Alexandria. c. 318 Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, begins teaching that the Son is a creature. Bishop Alexander condemns him. AD 325 The Council of Nicaea. Athanasius attends as Alexander's deacon. Gregory the Theologian later writes that, though not yet a bishop, "he held the first rank among the members of the Council." AD 328 Elected Pope of Alexandria after Alexander's death, at about thirty years of age. AD 335 The Synod of Tyre, packed with his enemies, accuses him of murdering a bishop named Arsenius. Arsenius is found alive. Constantine nonetheless exiles Athanasius to Trier in Gaul. First exile, 335–337. AD 336 Arius dies suddenly in Constantinople on the eve of his planned readmission to communion.

AD 339–346 Driven out again, he takes refuge in Rome with Pope Julius, who receives him as a lawful bishop. Second exile. AD 356–362 The general Syrianus surrounds his church during a night vigil with thousands of soldiers. He escapes and hides among the monks of the Egyptian desert for six years, writing many of his major works. Third exile. c. AD 357 Writes the Life of St Antony, after the great hermit's death. AD 362 Returns under Julian and holds the Council of Alexandria, whose Tome to the Antiochenes reconciles parties divided by words. AD 362–363 Exiled again by Julian the Apostate, who was trying to revive paganism. Fourth exile. AD 365–366 Exiled under Valens. Coptic tradition says he hid in his father's tomb. Fifth exile. AD 367 His thirty-ninth Festal Letter lists the twenty-seven books of the New Testament. AD 373 Departs on 2 May, aged about seventy-five. The Coptic Church keeps his feast on 7 Pashons. AD 1973 Portions of his relics are brought to Cairo on his feast day after Pope Shenouda III's visit to Rome, and are kept at St Mark's Cathedral.

St Gregory the Theologian Oration 21, On the Great Athanasius, 14 (c. AD 380) "And therefore, first in the holy Synod of Nicæa, the gathering of the three hundred and eighteen chosen men, united by the Holy Ghost, as far as in him lay, he stayed the disease. Though not yet ranked among the Bishops, he held the first rank among the members of the Council, for preference was given to virtue just as much as to office." secs.h: IV. On the Incarnation: Why God Became Man
secs.x: IV. On the Incarnation: Why God Became Man On the Incarnation is Athanasius' most famous work and one of his earliest. It asks why the eternal Word took a body, and answers that only the Creator could re-create. Mankind, made by the Word and sharing in Him, had turned away and was sliding back into corruption and death. God could neither let His work perish nor simply set aside the sentence of death. St Athanasius On the Incarnation 6 (c. AD 318–335) "For it were not worthy of God's goodness that the things He had made should waste away, because of the deceit practised on men by the devil. ... So, as the rational creatures were wasting and such works in course of ruin, what was God in His goodness to do? Suffer corruption to prevail against them and death to hold them fast? And where were the profit of their having been made, to begin with?" Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Athanasius On the Incarnation 8 "But He takes a body of our kind, and not merely so, but from a spotless and stainless virgin, knowing not a man, a body clean and in very truth pure from

secs.x: intercourse of men. For being Himself mighty, and Artificer of everything, He prepares the body in the Virgin as a temple unto Himself, and makes it His very own as an instrument, in it manifested, and in it dwelling." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Hebrews 2:14 "Inasmuch then as the children have partaken of flesh and blood, He Himself likewise shared in the same, that through death He might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil," Shared reading: The Word shares our flesh in order to die in it, and by dying to undo death. This is the heart of On the Incarnation. St Athanasius On the Incarnation 54 "For He was made man that we might be made God; and He manifested Himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father; and He endured the insolence of men that we might inherit immortality." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION 2 Peter 1:4 "by which have been given to us exceedingly great and precious promises, that through these you may be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that

secs.h: IV. On the Incarnation: Why God Became Man
secs.x: is in the world through lust." Orthodox reading: "Made God" means this: not that we become God by nature, but that by grace we become "partakers of the divine nature." Athanasius' sentence is the classic summary of theosis. Protestant reading: Many Protestants read this verse as moral renewal rather than participation in God's life. Notice what the argument requires. If the one who became man were a creature, as Arius taught, He could not give us a share in the divine life, because He would not have it to give. Athanasius' whole doctrine of salvation depends on the Son being fully God. That is why he fought Arianism for half a century. See Theosis & Deification .

V. Against Arius Arius set out his teaching in a popular poem called the Thalia . Athanasius quotes it so that readers can see what was really being taught. Arius, quoted by St Athanasius Discourse I Against the Arians 5 (c. AD 340) "'God was not always a Father.' but 'once God was alone, and not yet a Father, but afterwards He became a Father.' 'The Son was not always;' for, whereas all things were made out of nothing, and all existing creatures and works were made, so the Word of God Himself was 'made out of nothing,' and 'once He was not,' and 'He was not before His origination,'..." Condemned Teaching VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION "Once He Was Not" Athanasius' first answer is that Arius' little word "once" gives the game away. "Once" means a time before the Son. But the Son is the Word through whom time and all things were made.

St Athanasius Discourse I Against the Arians 11 "Say then what was once when the Son was not, O slanderous and irreligious men? If you say the Father, your blasphemy is but greater; for it is impious to say that He was 'once,' or to signify Him by the word 'once.' ... And your other, 'The Son was not before His generation,' is equivalent to saying, 'There was once when He was not,' for both the one and the other signify that there is a time before the Word." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION John 1:1-3 "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made that was made." Orthodox reading: "In the beginning was the Word." There was no "once" before the Word, because all things, time included, were made through Him.

Hebrews 1:3 "who being the brightness of His glory and the express image of His person, and upholding all things by the word of His power, when He had by Himself purged our sins, sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high," Orthodox reading: Athanasius' favourite image: the Son is the radiance of the Father's glory. A light is never without its radiance, so the Father was never without the Son. "The Lord Created Me" The Arians' chief proof text was Proverbs 8:22, which in the Greek Bible reads, "The Lord created me a beginning of His ways for His works." Wisdom is speaking, and Wisdom is Christ (1 Corinthians 1:24). So, they said, Christ was created. Proverbs 8:22 "'The Lord possessed me at the beginning of His way, Before His works of old." Orthodox reading: The Hebrew is usually rendered "possessed" (NKJV), but the Greek Bible the Fathers used read "created." Athanasius accepted the Greek and answered the argument on its own ground. Protestant reading: Many modern Protestants read the passage as poetry about God's wisdom, not a direct statement about the Son.

St Athanasius Discourse II Against the Arians 44–45 "...and by Solomon Wisdom says of Itself with cautious exactness, not 'I am a creature,' but only 'The Lord created me a beginning of His ways for His works,' yet not 'created me that I might have being,' nor 'because I have a creature's beginning and origin.' For in this passage, not as signifying the Essence of His Godhead, nor His own everlasting and genuine generation from the Father, has the Word spoken by Solomon, but on the other hand His manhood and Economy towards us." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION "Created" refers to the Word's becoming man, His "manhood and Economy," not to His divine being. The same rule, that some things are said of Christ as God and some of Him as man, runs through all of Athanasius' reading of Scripture, and it is the rule Cyril would later use (Section IX). We Do Not Worship a Creature John 5:23 "that all should honor the Son just as they honor the Father.

He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him." Orthodox reading: The Son receives the same honour as the Father. If He were a creature, worshipping Him would be idolatry. St Athanasius Letter 60, to Adelphius, 3 (c. AD 370) "We do not worship a creature. Far be the thought. For such an error belongs to heathens and Arians. But we worship the Lord of Creation, Incarnate, the Word of God." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The Arians worshipped Christ too. Athanasius pressed the point: either they were worshipping a creature, which is paganism, or Christ is not a creature. For the full scriptural case see The Divinity of Christ and The Holy Trinity .

VI. Nicaea and "One in Essence" Why did Nicaea use a word that is not in Scripture? Athanasius was in the room, and he tells us. The bishops first tried to use Scripture's own words. The Arians found ways to agree with every one of them. St Athanasius De Decretis (Defence of the Nicene Definition) 19 (c. AD 350s) "The Council wishing to do away with the irreligious phrases of the Arians, and to use instead the acknowledged words of the Scriptures, that the Son is not from nothing but 'from God,' and is 'Word' and 'Wisdom,' and not creature or work, but a proper offspring from the Father, Eusebius and his fellows, led by their inveterate heterodoxy, understood the phrase 'from God?' as belonging to us, as if in respect to it the Word of God differed nothing from us..." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Athanasius De Decretis 20 "...were again compelled on their part to collect the sense of the Scriptures, and to re-say and re-write what they had said before, more distinctly still, namely, that the Son is 'one in essence' with the Father: by way of signifying,

that the Son was from the Father, and not merely like, but the same in likeness..." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION "From God" was not enough, because Christians too are "from God" (1 Corinthians 8:6). So the bishops wrote "from the essence of God" and "one in essence." The new word did not add to Scripture; it shut the door on a false reading of it. See Understanding the Nicene Creed . John 10:30 "I and My Father are one.'" Orthodox reading: "One" is neuter in Greek: not one person, but one thing. The Father and the Son are distinct, yet one in what they are. John 14:9 "Jesus said to him, 'Have I been with you so long, and yet you have not known Me, Philip? He who has seen Me has seen the Father; so how can you say, 'Show us the Father'?" Orthodox reading: To see the Son is to see the Father, because the Son is the Father's own image and radiance, not a likeness made from outside.

secs.h: Brothers Who Mean What We Mean
secs.x: VII. Words and Meaning Athanasius is remembered as unbending, and on the substance of the faith he was. But he was also careful not to divide Christians who meant the same thing with different words. This side of him matters greatly for the Oriental Orthodox today. Brothers Who Mean What We Mean In the 350s a large party of bishops would not say "one in essence" but would say "like in essence." Athanasius did not lump them with the Arians. St Athanasius De Synodis (On the Councils) 41 (c. AD 359) "...those, however, who accept everything else that was defined at Nicæa, and doubt only about the Coessential, must not be treated as enemies; nor do we here attack them as Ario-maniacs, nor as opponents of the Fathers, but we discuss the matter with them as brothers with brothers, who mean what we mean, and dispute only about the word." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION One Hypostasis or Three? In 362 the Church at Antioch was split. One party spoke of three hypostases in God, the other of one, and each suspected the other of heresy.

secs.h: Brothers Who Mean What We Mean
secs.x: Athanasius' council at Alexandria questioned both. The Council of Alexandria under St Athanasius Tome to the Antiochenes 5–6 (AD 362) "...they replied, Because they believed in a Holy Trinity, not a trinity in name only, but existing and subsisting in truth, ... and that the Son is coessential with the Father, as the fathers said; while the Holy Spirit is not a creature, nor external, but proper to and inseparable from the Essence of the Father and the Son. ... But they in their turn assured us that they neither meant this nor had ever held it, but 'we use the word Subsistence thinking it the same thing to say Subsistence or Essence;'" Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The Council of Alexandria under St Athanasius Tome to the Antiochenes 8 (AD 362) "...counsel the others also who explain and hold aright, not to enquire further into each other's opinions, nor to fight about words to no useful purpose, nor to go on contending with the above phrases, but to agree in the mind of piety." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Gregory the

secs.h: Brothers Who Mean What We Mean
secs.x: Theologian Oration 21, On the Great Athanasius, 35 (c. AD 380) "He conferred in his gentle and sympathetic way with both parties, and after he had carefully weighed the meaning of their expressions, and found that they had the same sense, and were in nowise different in doctrine, by permitting each party to use its own terms, he bound them together in unity of action." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Athanasius' test was simple: ask what the words mean, and if the meaning is orthodox, do not fight over the words. The Oriental Orthodox have always made the same appeal about Christ. When they confess "one incarnate nature of God the Word," they mean one Christ, God and man, without mixture or change, not a nature in which the humanity is swallowed up. The theological dialogues between the Oriental and Eastern Orthodox in 1989 and 1990 rested on exactly this Athanasian principle. See Eastern & Oriental Orthodoxy and Miaphysite Christology .

VIII. The Holy Spirit Nicaea in 325 said only "And in the Holy Ghost." In the 350s a group in Egypt, whom Athanasius called the Tropici , began teaching that the Son was God but the Spirit was a creature, a kind of higher angel. Bishop Serapion of Thmuis wrote to Athanasius for help. St Athanasius Letters to Serapion on the Holy Spirit (c. AD 358–359) Athanasius answers that the Spirit cannot be a creature, because He sanctifies, gives life and makes us partakers of God, which no creature can do. The Trinity is one and indivisible: whatever the Father does, He does through the Son in the Spirit. To call the Spirit a creature is to break the Trinity apart and to bring a creature into the God in whose Name we are baptized. Coptic Pope & Church Father PARAPHRASE In 362 his council at Alexandria put the point plainly: the Holy Spirit "is not a creature, nor external, but proper to and inseparable from the Essence of the Father and the Son" (Tome to the Antiochenes 5, quoted in Section VII). Athanasius died in 373, before the Council of Constantinople.

But the line he drew, that whoever sanctifies and gives life must be God, is the line St Basil took up in On the Holy Spirit , and the line the Creed of 381 confessed when it called the Spirit "the Lord and Giver-of-Life," who "with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified."

IX. The One Christ Athanasius did not live to see the controversies of Ephesus and Chalcedon. But the way he speaks of Christ is the way Cyril of Alexandria and the Oriental Orthodox speak of Him: one subject, the Word Himself, who does divine things and suffers human things in His own flesh. St Athanasius Discourse III Against the Arians 30 "And He became man, and did not come into man; for this it is necessary to know, lest perchance these irreligious men fall into this notion also, and beguile any into thinking, that, as in former times the Word was used to come into each of the Saints, so now He sojourned in a man, hallowing him also, and manifesting Himself as in the others." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Athanasius Discourse III Against the Arians 31 "And on account of this, the properties of the flesh are said to be His, since He was in it, such as to hunger, to thirst, to suffer, to weary, and the like, of which the flesh is capable; while on the other hand the works proper to the Word Himself, such as to raise the dead, to restore sight to the

blind, and to cure the woman with an issue of blood, He did through His own body. And the Word bore the infirmities of the flesh, as His own, for His was the flesh; and the flesh ministered to the works of the Godhead, because the Godhead was in it, for the body was God's." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The Council of Alexandria under St Athanasius Tome to the Antiochenes 7 (AD 362) "Wherefore neither was there one Son of God before Abraham, another after Abraham: nor was there one that raised up Lazarus, another that asked concerning him; but the same it was that said as man, 'Where does Lazarus lie;' and as God raised him up: the same that as man and in the body spat, but divinely as Son of God opened the eyes of the man blind from his birth..." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION "Not one... another... but the same." This is the single subject that Nestorius would later deny and Cyril would defend. The same Tome insists that "the Saviour had not a body without a soul," against those who would make His humanity incomplete.

St Athanasius Letter 59, to Epictetus, 2 (c. AD 371) "What lower region has vomited the statement that the Body born of Mary is coessential with the Godhead of the Word? Or that the Word has been changed into flesh, bones, hair, and the whole body, and altered from its own nature?" Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Athanasius is just as firm against confusing the two. The Word was not changed into flesh, and His body is not of the same essence as His Godhead. One Christ, without division and without change: this is the faith Cyril received from him and the Oriental Orthodox confess. In the same Discourses he calls the Virgin "Mary Bearer of God" (Discourse III 29). See Mary: Theotokos & Perpetual Virginity . St Athanasius Letter 60, to Adelphius, 3 (c.

AD 370) "And we neither divide the body, being such, from the Word, and worship it by itself, nor when we wish to worship the Word do we set Him far apart from the Flesh, but knowing, as we said above, that 'the Word was made flesh,' we recognise Him as God also, after having come in the flesh." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION

X. Scripture and the Canon Each year the Pope of Alexandria wrote a Festal Letter announcing the date of Pascha. In his thirty-ninth, in 367, Athanasius listed the books of Scripture. It is the earliest surviving list of exactly the twenty-seven books of the New Testament. St Athanasius Festal Letter 39, 5–6 (AD 367) "Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul... And besides, the Revelation of John. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness.

Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Athanasius Festal Letter 39, 7 (AD 367) "But for greater exactness I add this also, writing of necessity; that there are other books besides these not indeed included in the Canon, but appointed by the Fathers to be read by those who newly join us, and who wish for instruction in the word of godliness. The Wisdom of Solomon, and the Wisdom of Sirach, and Esther, and Judith, and Tobit, and that which is called the Teaching of the Apostles, and the Shepherd." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Two honest notes. First, Athanasius' Old Testament list is not identical to any modern one. He includes Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah with Jeremiah, sets Esther among the books to be read, and places Wisdom, Sirach, Judith and Tobit in that second group too. The Coptic Church reads these books in her services, and the Oriental Churches' canons are fuller than Athanasius' list. Second, notice who decides.

The canonical books are those "handed down, and accredited as Divine," and even the books for reading were "appointed by the Fathers." Athanasius does not compile the canon by his own judgement; he records what the Church had received. See The Biblical Canon . St Athanasius Against the Heathen 1 (c. AD 318–335) "For although the sacred and inspired Scriptures are sufficient to declare the truth, while there are other works of our blessed teachers compiled for this purpose, if he meet with which a man will gain some knowledge of the interpretation of the Scriptures, and be able to learn what he wishes to know..." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Protestant writers often quote the first half of this sentence. The second half matters as much: the Scriptures are sufficient, and the Church's teachers are given to interpret them. Athanasius' whole defence of Nicaea was a contest over how to read Scripture, which he won by appeal to "the sense of the Scriptures" as the Fathers had received it. See Scripture and Tradition .

XI. Athanasius and the Desert Athanasius was the first great friend of Egyptian monasticism. During his third exile the monks hid him for six years, and soon after St Antony's death he wrote the Life of Antony , which carried the monastic ideal across the Roman world. Coptic tradition adds that he was the first Pope to wear the monastic habit. St Athanasius Life of St Antony 69 (c. AD 357) "And once also the Arians having lyingly asserted that Antony's opinions were the same as theirs, he was displeased and angry against them. Then being summoned by the bishops and all the brethren, he descended from the mountain, and having entered Alexandria, he denounced the Arians, saying that their heresy was the last of all and a forerunner of Antichrist." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Antony the Great, in the Life Life of St Antony 91 "And divide my garments.

To Athanasius the bishop give one sheepskin and the garment whereon I am laid, which he himself gave me new, but which with me has grown old." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The father of monks left his sheepskin to the defender of Nicaea. The desert and the throne of St Mark stood together against Arius, and that bond between monastery and patriarch has marked the Coptic Church ever since. See Monasticism & the Desert Fathers .

secs.h: The Murdered Bishop Who Was Alive
secs.x: XII. Exile and Endurance The Murdered Bishop Who Was Alive At the Synod of Tyre in 335 Athanasius' enemies accused him of murdering a Meletian bishop named Arsenius, and carried about a severed hand as evidence. Athanasius records the plot himself. St Athanasius Apology Against the Arians 63 (c. AD 357) "...and at last that calumny is invented by them, that Macarius had broken a cup, and that a certain Bishop named Arsenius had been murdered by me. Arsenius they placed in concealment, in order that he might seem made away with, when he did not make his appearance; and they carried about a hand, pretending that he had been cut to pieces." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Arsenius was found alive, and the same Apology preserves letters from bishops who confirmed it. Athanasius was exiled anyway. The charges against him were political, and the emperors who exiled him were, for the most part, the patrons of the Arian party. Why He Fled St Athanasius Defence of His Flight 24 (c.

secs.h: The Murdered Bishop Who Was Alive
secs.x: AD 357) "It was now night, and some of the people were keeping a vigil preparatory to a communion on the morrow, when the General Syrianus suddenly came upon us with more than five thousand soldiers, having arms and drawn swords, bows, spears, and clubs... Now I considered that it would be unreasonable in me to desert the people during such a disturbance, and not to endanger myself in their behalf; therefore I sat down upon my throne, and desired the Deacon to read a Psalm, and the people to answer, 'For His mercy endures for ever'" Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION His enemies called him a coward for hiding. In his Defence of His Flight he answers from Scripture: Jacob fled from Esau, Moses withdrew into Midian for fear of Pharaoh, David fled from Saul, and the Lord Himself "hid Himself, and went out of the temple" when the Jews took up stones (John 8:59). Matthew 10:23 "When they persecute you in this city, flee to another.

secs.h: The Murdered Bishop Who Was Alive
secs.x: For assuredly, I say to you, you will not have gone through the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes." Orthodox reading: Athanasius cites this command. Flight was not cowardice but obedience, and it kept the shepherd alive for the flock. The Pillar of the Church St Gregory the Theologian Oration 21, On the Great Athanasius, 26 (c. AD 380) "Such was Athanasius to us, when present, the pillar of the Church; and such, even when he retired before the insults of the wicked." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Gregory the Theologian Oration 21, On the Great Athanasius, 1 (c. AD 380) "In praising Athanasius, I shall be praising virtue. To speak of him and to praise virtue are identical, because he had, or, to speak more truly, has embraced virtue in its entirety." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION

XIII. Athanasius and the Oriental Orthodox The Twentieth Pope of Alexandria The Coptic Church counts Athanasius as the twentieth successor of St Mark. The title "pope" was used of the Archbishop of Alexandria long before it became usual in Rome, and Athanasius' own Apology preserves a letter from a repentant priest addressed "To the Blessed pope Athanasius" (Apology Against the Arians 64). The Coptic Synaxarium remembers him on 7 Pashons as the Pope who stood before the whole world for the faith of Nicaea. The Father of the Ethiopian Church Athanasius consecrated Frumentius, known in Ethiopia as Abba Salama, as the first bishop of Axum. From that time the Ethiopian Church received its archbishops from Alexandria, until it became autocephalous in the twentieth century. The clearest evidence for the consecration comes from Athanasius' enemy, the Emperor Constantius, who wrote to the kings of Axum demanding that Frumentius be sent to Egypt to be examined by the Arian bishop George. Emperor Constantius II Letter to Ezana and Sazana of Axum, in Athanasius, Apology to Constantius 31 (c.

AD 356) "For of course you know and remember (unless you alone pretend to be ignorant of that which all men are well aware of) that this Frumentius was advanced to his present rank by Athanasius, a man who is guilty of ten thousand crimes..." Imperial Letter VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Ezana is the king remembered in Ethiopia as the first Christian ruler of Axum. The letter shows the Arian emperor trying to pull the young Ethiopian Church away from Athanasius. There is no sign that it succeeded. See History of the Oriental Orthodox Church . The Teacher of St Cyril Cyril of Alexandria, the twenty-fourth Pope, is the theologian of the Oriental Orthodox Christology. His writings appeal again and again to Athanasius as a father of the faith, and his single-subject Christology is Athanasius' own: the Word made flesh is the one who acts and suffers (Section IX). The line from Athanasius to Cyril to Dioscorus and Severus is the spine of the Oriental Orthodox tradition.

In Coptic Worship Athanasius is commemorated in the Coptic liturgy among the great teachers of the Church, and his feast falls on 7 Pashons. In 1973, on that feast day, portions of his relics were brought to Cairo, where they rest at St Mark's Cathedral.

XIV. Objections Answered The objections below come from Jehovah's Witnesses, sceptics and some Protestants. "Constantine and Nicaea invented the deity of Christ." OO Response: Arius himself is the evidence against this. He was condemned by his own bishop, Alexander, years before Constantine called the council, because Alexander saw that Arius' teaching was new. Athanasius says the bishops at Nicaea first tried to use Scripture's own words and only adopted "one in essence" when the Arians twisted every one of them (Section VI). And Constantine did not hold the line. Within ten years he had recalled Arius and exiled Athanasius. Most of Athanasius' exiles were ordered by emperors who favoured the Arians. If Nicene faith had been imposed by imperial power, it would not have survived the emperors. "Athanasius was a violent political operator who won by force." OO Response: The charges against him at the time are known, and the most famous of them collapsed: the bishop he was accused of murdering turned up alive (Section XII).

Some accusations of rough treatment by his supporters may have had substance, and historians still debate them. But Athanasius spent seventeen years of his episcopate in exile, hunted by soldiers. Those with the power to use force were his enemies. "Athanasius taught sola scriptura." OO Response: He taught that the Scriptures "are sufficient to declare the truth," and in the same sentence he commends "other works of our blessed teachers" for interpreting them (Section X). His whole defence of Nicaea appeals to "the sense of the Scriptures" as the Church had received it, against Arians who also quoted Scripture. He receives the canon from "the Fathers." That is Scripture read within the Church, which is the Orthodox position. See Scripture and Tradition . "Proverbs 8:22 says Wisdom was created, so the Son is a creature." OO Response: Athanasius answered this at length. The verse is a proverb and must be read as one.

Wisdom does not say "I am a creature," but "The Lord created me a beginning of His ways," and this refers, he says, to "His manhood and Economy towards us," not "the Essence of His Godhead" (Section V). The Word who made all things cannot be one of the things He made (John 1:3). "The majority of bishops were Arian in the 350s, so Nicene orthodoxy was just the side that won." OO Response: Truth is not decided by numbers, and Athanasius never thought it was. Many bishops signed Arian-leaning creeds under imperial pressure, and many, like the "like in essence" party, were much nearer to Nicaea than to Arius (Section VII). When the pressure lifted, the Church returned to the faith of Nicaea and confessed it again at Constantinople in 381.

XV. Frequently Asked Questions Did Athanasius write the Athanasian Creed? No. The creed that begins "Whoever wishes to be saved" (the Quicunque ) was written in Latin in the West, probably in the fifth or sixth century, and was later attached to his name. It is used in some Western churches. It is not used in the Oriental Orthodox Churches, and it contains the Western teaching that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. What does "Athanasius against the world" mean? Athanasius contra mundum is a later Latin phrase, not his own words. It sums up the years when he seemed to stand almost alone against emperors and councils. It is a fair summary of his courage, but he was never really alone: the monks of Egypt, Pope Julius of Rome and the faithful of Alexandria stood with him. Why is he called "the Apostolic"? Because he defended the apostolic faith when much of the Church's leadership had wavered, and because his teaching was received as a faithful handing on of what the apostles taught. The title is used in the Coptic Church and elsewhere.

Did Athanasius use the formula "one incarnate nature of God the Word"? St Cyril believed he did, and quoted the phrase as Athanasius'. Modern scholars agree that the text Cyril had was written by Apollinaris of Laodicea and circulated under Athanasius' name. This does not affect Cyril's meaning, which he defined carefully: one Christ, with a complete human nature and a rational soul, without mixture or change. That meaning rests on Athanasius' genuine teaching, quoted in Section IX. See Miaphysite Christology . Did Athanasius call Mary Theotokos? Yes. In his third Discourse Against the Arians he speaks of the Son who "took flesh of a Virgin, Mary Bearer of God," and in the second he calls her "Mary Ever-Virgin." How did Arius die? According to a report Athanasius received from a priest in Constantinople, Arius died suddenly in 336, on the eve of the day he was to be received back into communion, in a manner that recalled the death of Judas (Acts 1:18).

Athanasius tells the story in his Letter 54 to Serapion, adding that the Church gave thanks "not as exulting in his death (God forbid!)." Where should I start reading Athanasius? On the Incarnation . It is short, clear and still one of the best books ever written on why God became man. Then the Life of Antony . Both are freely available in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, volume 4.
