I. Introduction: Basil the Great St Basil, Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, died, by the traditional dating, on the first day of 379 (some scholars place his death in 377 or 378), aged about fifty. In those few decades he defended the divinity of the Holy Spirit when even many who accepted Nicaea hesitated, gave the Church the clear distinction between one essence and three hypostases in God, shaped the monastic life of the Christian East, built a whole quarter of his city to care for the sick and the poor, and faced down an emperor. Two years after his death the Council of Constantinople confessed the Holy Spirit "the Lord and Giver-of-Life," who "with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified," in words that echo his. For the Coptic faithful, Basil is above all a name heard every Sunday. The Divine Liturgy most often prayed in the Coptic Church is the Liturgy of St Basil. This is the second page in the series on the Oriental pillars.

Athanasius, the first, defended the Son against Arius; Basil, who wrote to him as the Church's "physician," carried the same defence over to the Holy Spirit. Cyril of Alexandria is the third. "...the honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype." St Basil, On the Holy Spirit 18.45 A Note on Quotations Every quotation marked VERBATIM has been checked word for word against the public domain translation in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, volume 8 (Basil) and volume 7 (Gregory the Theologian). Several of Basil's most famous works, including Against Eunomius , the monastic Rules and the sermons on wealth, have no public domain English translation. Their teaching is summarised and marked PARAPHRASE . Scripture follows the NKJV.

II. Glossary of Terms Ousia οὐσία: "essence" What God is: the one Godhead common to Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Hypostasis ὑπόστασις: "subsistence, person" Each of the Three in their distinct reality: Father, Son, Holy Spirit. Basil fixed the distinction between ousia and hypostasis for later theology. Eunomius Anomoean, d. c. 393 A radical Arian who taught that the Son is "unlike" (anomoios) the Father and that God's essence can be fully known as "unbegotten." Basil wrote three books against him. Pneumatomachi "fighters against the Spirit" Those who accepted that the Son is God but denied that the Holy Spirit is. Basil's On the Holy Spirit answers them. Doxology δοξολογία: "word of glory" The prayer of praise. Basil was attacked for saying "Glory to the Father with the Son together with the Holy Spirit." Economy οἰκονομία: "management, wise handling" Pastoral prudence: Gregory the Theologian uses it of Basil's care in how he spoke of the Spirit in public.

Agrapha ἄγραφα: "unwritten things" Teachings and practices received from the apostles through the Church's life rather than in writing. Hexaemeron "the six days" Basil's nine homilies on the creation account in Genesis 1. Basiliad "the new city" The complex of hospital, hostel and poorhouse Basil built outside Caesarea. Cappadocian Fathers Basil, Gregory the Theologian, Gregory of Nyssa Basil, his close friend Gregory of Nazianzus, and his younger brother Gregory of Nyssa, whose teaching shaped the Council of 381.

III. His Life Basil was born around 329 or 330 into a family of saints. His grandmother, Macrina the Elder, had treasured the teaching of St Gregory the Wonderworker; his sister Macrina the Younger and his brothers Gregory of Nyssa and Peter of Sebaste are all venerated as saints. St Basil Letter 204, to the people of Neocaesarea, 6 (c. AD 375) "What clearer evidence can there be of my faith, than that I was brought up by my grandmother, blessed woman, who came from you? I mean the celebrated Macrina who taught me the words of the blessed Gregory; which, as far as memory had preserved down to her day, she cherished herself, while she fashioned and formed me, while yet a child, upon the doctrines of piety." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION c. AD 329–330 Born in Caesarea in Cappadocia, in what is now central Turkey. c. AD 350–355 Studies in Constantinople and Athens, where he forms a lifelong friendship with Gregory of Nazianzus. c. AD 356–357 Returns home as a rhetorician. His sister Macrina, Gregory of Nyssa records, draws him from worldly ambition to the ascetic life.

He is baptized and travels to see the monks of Egypt, Palestine, Syria and Mesopotamia. c. AD 358 Withdraws to the family estate at Annisi in Pontus, where Gregory joins him. They compile the Philokalia , a selection from Origen. AD 362–364 Ordained deacon (c. 362) and then priest (c. 364) in Caesarea. AD 368–369 During a great famine he spends his own means and organises the feeding of the hungry. AD 370 Elected Archbishop of Caesarea, with authority over the churches of Cappadocia. c. AD 371–372 Confronts the prefect Modestus, sent by the Arian emperor Valens, and refuses to submit. Valens attends his liturgy at Epiphany. c. AD 372 Builds the "new city" outside Caesarea: hospital, hostel and poorhouse. c. AD 375 Writes On the Holy Spirit . AD 379 Departs, by the traditional dating, on 1 January. The Coptic Church keeps his feast on 6 Tobi. AD 381 The Council of Constantinople confirms the faith of Nicaea and confesses the divinity of the Holy Spirit. St Gregory the Theologian Oration 43, Funeral Oration on St Basil, 21 (c.

AD 381) "Two ways were known to us, the first of greater value, the second of smaller consequence: the one leading to our sacred buildings and the teachers there, the other to secular instructors. All others we left to those who would pursue them, to feasts, theatres, meetings, banquets." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION

IV. Knowing God: Against Eunomius By the 360s the most radical Arians, led by Aetius and Eunomius, taught that God's whole essence is captured in the word "unbegotten." Since the Son is begotten, they said, He is of a different essence: "unlike" the Father. Their claim rested on a bold idea, that the human mind can know exactly what God is. St Basil Against Eunomius I–III (c. AD 364) Basil answers that the names we give God, such as "unbegotten," "good" or "eternal," are true, but none of them defines His essence. We form them from His works, by reasoning about what He has done. "Unbegotten" tells us that the Father has no source, not what the Father is. To claim to know God's essence is not a higher theology but pride. And "Father" and "Son" are names of relation: they show that the Son is from the Father and of the same nature, not that He is unlike Him. Church Father PARAPHRASE St Basil Letter 234, to Amphilochius, 1–2 (c.

AD 376) "The operations are various, and the essence simple, but we say that we know our God from His operations, but do not undertake to approach near to His essence. His operations come down to us, but His essence remains beyond our reach. But, it is replied, if you are ignorant of the essence, you are ignorant of Himself. Retort, If you say that you know His essence, you are ignorant of Himself." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 "But God has revealed them to us through His Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, yes, the deep things of God. For what man knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him? Even so no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God." Shared reading: Only the Spirit of God knows the things of God. We know God truly, because He reveals Himself; we do not comprehend Him. Basil's humility before the mystery of God is not vagueness. He is precise about what can be said and honest about what cannot.
This is the spirit of every Orthodox liturgy, where God is praised as beyond all understanding and yet truly known.

V. One Essence, Three Hypostases Athanasius had shown, at the council of 362, that some who said "one hypostasis" and some who said "three hypostases" meant the same faith. Basil gave the Church a settled vocabulary so that the confusion would not return: one ousia , the Godhead the Three share; three hypostases , the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in their distinct reality. St Basil Letter 236, to Amphilochius, 6 (c. AD 376) "The distinction between οὐσία and ὑπόστασις is the same as that between the general and the particular; as, for instance, between the animal and the particular man. Wherefore, in the case of the Godhead, we confess one essence or substance so as not to give a variant definition of existence, but we confess a particular hypostasis, in order that our conception of Father, Son and Holy Spirit may be without confusion and clear." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Basil's analogy has limits, and he knew it: three men are three separate beings, but the Three in God are one God, never separated in will or action.

The analogy shows only how the two words differ. What it secures is that we neither merge the Persons into one, as Sabellius did, nor divide the Godhead into three, as tritheism would. St Basil Letter 52, to the Canonicae, 1 (c. AD 370) "...as being heirs of the same Fathers who once at Nicæa promulgated their great decree concerning the faith. Of this, some portions are universally accepted without cavil, but the homoousion, ill received in certain quarters, is still rejected by some. These objectors we may very properly blame, and yet on the contrary deem them deserving of pardon. To refuse to follow the Fathers, not holding their declaration of more authority than one's own opinion, is conduct worthy of blame, as being brimful of self-sufficiency." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Here are Athanasius' two instincts together: firmness on the faith of Nicaea, and patience with those who struggled over a word because others had misused it. A note for readers of the Christology pages: in the doctrine of the Trinity the Oriental Orthodox use Basil's vocabulary exactly.

In speaking of Christ, St Cyril used the word physis , nature, in a related but distinct sense, which is why "one incarnate nature" does not mean what a later reader might assume. See Miaphysite Christology .

secs.h: Ranked with the Father and the Son
secs.x: VI. On the Holy Spirit Basil's great treatise began with an argument over a single word. At prayer he sometimes said "Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit," and sometimes "Glory to the Father with the Son together with the Holy Spirit." Some objected that the second form was new and ranked the Spirit with God. St Basil On the Holy Spirit 1.3 (c. AD 375) "Lately when praying with the people, and using the full doxology to God the Father in both forms, at one time with the Son together with the Holy Ghost, and at another through the Son in the Holy Ghost, I was attacked by some of those present on the ground that I was introducing novel and at the same time mutually contradictory terms." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Ranked with the Father and the Son Matthew 28:19 "Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," Orthodox reading: One of Basil's decisive arguments. The Lord Himself joined the Spirit to the Father and the Son in the one Name of baptism.

secs.h: Ranked with the Father and the Son
secs.x: To rank Him with creatures is to break the Name in which we were baptized. St Basil On the Holy Spirit 27.68 (c. AD 375) "They must now instruct us either not to baptize as we have received, or not to believe as we were baptized, or not to ascribe glory as we have believed. Let any man prove if he can that the relation of sequence in these acts is not necessary and unbroken; or let any man deny if he can that innovation here must mean ruin everywhere." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Baptism, faith and praise belong together. We are baptized into the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; therefore we believe in all three; therefore we glorify all three together. The doxology is not a liturgical accident. It is the creed sung.

secs.h: Ranked with the Father and the Son
secs.x: The Work of the Spirit St Basil On the Holy Spirit 16.38 "And in the creation bethink you first, I pray you, of the original cause of all things that are made, the Father; of the creative cause, the Son; of the perfecting cause, the Spirit; so that the ministering spirits subsist by the will of the Father, are brought into being by the operation of the Son, and perfected by the presence of the Spirit. ... For the first principle of existing things is One, creating through the Son and perfecting through the Spirit." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Psalm 33:6 "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, And all the host of them by the breath of His mouth." Orthodox reading: The Word and the Breath (Spirit) of the Lord together make the heavens. Basil reads the Spirit's perfecting work in creation in verses like this.

secs.h: Ranked with the Father and the Son
secs.x: St Basil On the Holy Spirit 9.23 "Hence comes foreknowledge of the future, understanding of mysteries, apprehension of what is hidden, distribution of good gifts, the heavenly citizenship, a place in the chorus of angels, joy without end, abiding in God, the being made like to God, and, highest of all, the being made God." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION This is Athanasius' argument carried over to the Spirit. Only God can make us partakers of God. If the Spirit makes us "like to God" and, "highest of all," makes us god by grace, He cannot be a creature. See Theosis & Deification . Acts 5:3-4 "But Peter said, 'Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and keep back part of the price of the land for yourself? While it remained, was it not your own? And after it was sold, was it not in your own control? Why have you conceived this thing in your heart? You have not lied to men but to God.'" Orthodox reading: To lie to the Holy Spirit is to lie to God. The apostle speaks of the Spirit as God without needing to argue it.

secs.h: Ranked with the Father and the Son
secs.x: One Worship, Not Three St Basil On the Holy Spirit 18.45 "Because we speak of a king, and of the king's image, and not of two kings. The majesty is not cloven in two, nor the glory divided. The sovereignty and authority over us is one, and so the doxology ascribed by us is not plural but one; because the honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype. Now what in the one case the image is by reason of imitation, that in the other case the Son is by nature..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Basil's sentence about the image and the prototype is about the Son, the perfect image of the Father, and it shows why worshipping the Son is not worshipping a second God. Four centuries later the defenders of icons took the same sentence as the key to their case: honour shown to an icon passes to the one it depicts. See Icon Veneration .

secs.h: VII. The Reserve of a Shepherd
secs.x: VII. The Reserve of a Shepherd There is a striking fact about Basil. In On the Holy Spirit he gives the Spirit every honour that belongs to God, but he does not, in so many words, write "the Spirit is God." Some of his own friends were troubled by this, and his enemies accused him of heresy or cowardice. Gregory the Theologian wrote to tell him so. St Gregory the Theologian Letter 58, to Basil (c. AD 372) "Many people have condemned us as not firm in our faith; those, I mean, who think and think rightly that we thoroughly agree. Some openly charge us with heresy, others with cowardice; with heresy, those who believe that our language is not sound; with cowardice, they who blame our reserve." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION After Basil's death Gregory explained the reason. Basil was not uncertain. He was guarding his see, and with it the orthodox teaching of a whole region, from an Arian emperor waiting for a pretext to remove him. St Gregory the Theologian Oration 43, Funeral Oration on St Basil, 68 (c.

secs.h: VII. The Reserve of a Shepherd
secs.x: AD 381) "The enemy were on the watch for the unqualified statement the Spirit is God; which, although it is true, they and the wicked patron of their impiety imagined to be impious; so that they might banish him and his power of theological instruction from the city... Accordingly, by the use of other terms, and by statements which unmistakably had the same meaning, and by arguments necessarily leading to this conclusion, he so overpowered his antagonists, that they were left without reply..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION "Statements which unmistakably had the same meaning." Once again a Father puts meaning above a particular word, as Athanasius did with the "like in essence" party and with the Antiochenes. The Church judged him by what he taught, not by whether he used one formula. Two years after his death, the Creed of 381 also confessed the Spirit's divinity without the bare words "the Spirit is God," by calling Him Lord, Giver of Life, and worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son.

VIII. Written and Unwritten Tradition The Pneumatomachi demanded a Bible verse for the doxology "with the Spirit." Basil answered that much of what all Christians do and believe is received through the Church's life rather than written down, and he gave examples his opponents practised themselves. St Basil On the Holy Spirit 27.66 (c. AD 375) "Of the beliefs and practices whether generally accepted or publicly enjoined which are preserved in the Church some we possess derived from written teaching; others we have received delivered to us in a mystery by the tradition of the apostles; and both of these in relation to true religion have the same force. ...

For instance, to take the first and most general example, who is thence who has taught us in writing to sign with the sign of the cross those who have trusted in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ? What writing has taught us to turn to the East at the prayer? Which of the saints has left us in writing the words of the invocation at the displaying of the bread of the Eucharist and the cup of blessing?" Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION 2 Thessalonians 2:15 "Therefore, brethren, stand fast and hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or our epistle." Orthodox reading: Paul himself names two channels of tradition, "by word" and "by our epistle," and asks for both to be held. Basil's distinction is Paul's. Protestant reading: Paul's oral teaching was later written in Scripture, so Scripture alone now carries the apostolic tradition. Every one of Basil's examples is still part of Coptic worship: the sign of the cross, prayer facing east, and the words of the invocation of the Holy Spirit over the bread and cup. Note also what Basil does not say.

He does not set unwritten tradition against Scripture. Both carry "the same force" because both come from the apostles, and he spends most of his treatise proving the Spirit's divinity from Scripture. See Scripture and Tradition .

IX. Baptism and the Eucharist St Basil On the Holy Spirit 12.28 (c. AD 375) "Faith and baptism are two kindred and inseparable ways of salvation: faith is perfected through baptism, baptism is established through faith, and both are completed by the same names. For as we believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost, so are we also baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION See Understanding the Nicene Creed for how this passage illuminates "one baptism for the remission of sins." St Basil Letter 93, to the Patrician Caesaria, on Communion (c. AD 372) "It is good and beneficial to communicate every day, and to partake of the holy body and blood of Christ. For He distinctly says, He that eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life. And who doubts that to share frequently in life, is the same thing as to have manifold life.

I, indeed, communicate four times a week, on the Lord's day, on Wednesday, on Friday, and on the Sabbath, and on the other days if there is a commemoration of any Saint." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION John 6:54 "Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day." Orthodox reading: Basil quotes this verse as the reason for frequent communion. The Eucharist is "the holy body and blood of Christ," and to receive it is to share in life. Protestant reading: Many Protestants read the discourse as a call to believe in Christ, with eating and drinking as images of faith. The same letter records that in Alexandria and Egypt "each one of the laity, for the most part, keeps the communion, at his own house," a practice from times of persecution and from the desert. Basil writes of it as an accepted custom. The Church later regulated it closely, but his letter is a precious glimpse of how highly the Egyptian Church of his day prized the holy Mysteries. See The Seven Mysteries of Christ .

secs.h: X. The Monk and the Community
secs.x: X. The Monk and the Community Basil learned the monastic life in Egypt before he taught it in Asia Minor. St Basil Letter 223, against Eustathius of Sebaste, 2 (c. AD 375) "And many did I find in Alexandria, and many in the rest of Egypt, and others in Palestine, and in Cœle Syria, and in Mesopotamia. I admired their continence in living, and their endurance in toil; I was amazed at their persistency in prayer, and at their triumphing over sleep..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Basil Letter 2, to Gregory, 2 (c. AD 358) "We must strive after a quiet mind. As well might the eye ascertain an object put before it while it is wandering restless up and down and sideways, without fixing a steady gaze upon it, as a mind, distracted by a thousand worldly cares, be able clearly to apprehend the truth." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Basil The Longer Rules 7 (c. AD 370s) Basil prefers the common life to the life of the solitary.

secs.h: X. The Monk and the Community
secs.x: Alone, a man cannot practise the commandments of love: he has no one to serve, no one to correct him, and no one with whom to share the gifts of the Spirit. He asks the hermit, in effect, whose feet he will wash, since the Lord who washed His disciples' feet commanded us to do the same. Church Father PARAPHRASE John 13:14 "If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet." Shared reading: Basil's question to the solitary rests on this command. Love needs a neighbour. Acts 4:32 "Now the multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul; neither did anyone say that any of the things he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common." Shared reading: Basil took the Jerusalem church as the model for his communities: one heart, one soul, and goods held in common. Basil did not invent community monasticism; St Pachomius had founded communities in Upper Egypt a generation earlier.

secs.h: X. The Monk and the Community
secs.x: What Basil did was to write the principles of the common life with such clarity that his Rules became a foundation for monastic life across the Christian East. The Egyptian desert and the Cappadocian monastery speak with one voice. See Monasticism & the Desert Fathers .

secs.h: XI. The New City: Basil and the Poor
secs.x: XI. The New City: Basil and the Poor During the famine of 368, before he became archbishop, Basil used his own means and fed the hungry himself. St Gregory the Theologian Oration 43, Funeral Oration on St Basil, 35 (c. AD 381) "He gathered together the victims of the famine with some who were but slightly recovering from it, men and women, infants, old men, every age which was in distress, and obtaining contributions of all sorts of food which can relieve famine, set before them basins of soup and such meat as was found preserved among us, on which the poor live. Then, imitating the ministry of Christ, Who, girded with a towel, did not disdain to wash the disciples' feet, using for this purpose the aid of his own servants, and also of his fellow servants, he attended to the bodies and souls of those who needed it..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Gregory the Theologian Oration 43, Funeral Oration on St Basil, 63 (c.

secs.h: XI. The New City: Basil and the Poor
secs.x: AD 381) "Go forth a little way from the city, and behold the new city, the storehouse of piety, the common treasury of the wealthy, in which the superfluities of their wealth, aye, and even their necessaries, are stored, in consequence of his exhortations... where disease is regarded in a religious light, and disaster is thought a blessing, and sympathy is put to the test." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The "new city" was a hospital, hostel and poorhouse, with care for lepers, whom others would not touch. It is often called one of the first public hospitals of the Christian world. Luke 12:18-20 "So he said, 'I will do this: I will pull down my barns and build greater, and there I will store all my crops and my goods. And I will say to my soul, 'Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; take your ease; eat, drink, and be merry.'' But God said to him, 'Fool! This night your soul will be required of you; then whose will those things be which you have provided?'" Orthodox reading: Basil preached a famous sermon on this parable.

secs.h: XI. The New City: Basil and the Poor
secs.x: St Basil Homily 6, on "I will pull down my barns" (4th century) Basil tells the rich that what they store beyond their need is not theirs to keep. The bread held back belongs to the hungry, the unused coat to the naked, the shoes rotting in the cupboard to the barefoot, and the hoarded money to those in need. Church Father PARAPHRASE

XII. Bishop Before the Emperor The emperor Valens was an Arian, and he set out to bring the Church of Cappadocia into line. His prefect Modestus summoned Basil and threatened him. St Gregory the Theologian Oration 43, Funeral Oration on St Basil, 49 (c. AD 381) "What are these? said Basil, pray, inform me. Confiscation, banishment, torture, death. Have you no other threat? said he, for none of these can reach me. How indeed is that? said the prefect. Because, he replied, a man who has nothing, is beyond the reach of confiscation; unless you demand my tattered rags, and the few books, which are my only possessions. Banishment is impossible for me, who am confined by no limit of place... As for tortures, what hold can they have upon one whose body has ceased to be? ... Death is my benefactor, for it will send me the sooner to God..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Gregory the Theologian Oration 43, Funeral Oration on St Basil, 50 (c. AD 381) "Amazed at this language, the prefect said, No one has ever yet spoken thus, and with such boldness, to Modestus.

Why, perhaps, said Basil, you have not met with a Bishop, or in his defense of such interests he would have used precisely the same language." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Valens himself then came to Caesarea and attended the liturgy at Epiphany. Gregory describes the emperor overwhelmed by the singing of the psalms and the calm of the archbishop at the altar, so shaken that he staggered as he brought his offering (Oration 43, 52). Basil was not exiled. The emperor left him in his see, and Cappadocia remained Nicene.

XIII. Basil and the Oriental Orthodox The Liturgy of St Basil The Coptic Church prays three anaphoras: those of St Basil, St Gregory and St Cyril. The Liturgy of St Basil is by far the most used, prayed at most Sunday and weekday liturgies throughout the year. Its anaphora gives thanks for creation, the fall, the prophets and the whole saving work of Christ, and calls down the Holy Spirit on the gifts. How much of this anaphora Basil himself wrote is debated. The Coptic form belongs to an Egyptian family of texts that is shorter and simpler than the Byzantine Liturgy of St Basil, and an early Sahidic Coptic manuscript preserves an older stage of it. There is no clear evidence that Basil wrote the Egyptian form. Many scholars think it is older, and that Basil may have known it, perhaps from his visit to Egypt, and expanded it into the longer Byzantine form. The Coptic Synaxarium honours him as the author of the liturgy that bears his name. Either way, Coptic Christians who pray it are praying a text bound up with Basil's name and with Egypt, the land he visited to learn holiness.

His Feast and His Canons The Coptic Church remembers his departure on 6 Tobi. The Synaxarium recalls him as the one who "set down canons that believers still follow": his canonical letters on penance and church discipline (Letters 188, 199 and 217) became part of the Church's canon law in the East. Basil and Athanasius Basil wrote several letters to Athanasius in the last years of the older bishop's life, seeking his help to heal the divisions of the Eastern churches. They show how the second of the pillars looked to the first. St Basil Letter 82, to Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria (c. AD 372) "When I turn my gaze upon the world, and perceive the difficulties by which every effort after good is obstructed, like those of a man walking in fetters, I am brought to despair of myself.

But then I direct my gaze in the direction of your reverence; I remember that our Lord has appointed you to be physician of the diseases in the Churches; and I recover my spirits, and rise from the depression of despair to the hope of better things." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Armenia and Cappadocia Caesarea, Basil's see, was where St Gregory the Illuminator was consecrated as the first bishop of the Armenians early in the fourth century, and Armenian bishops long continued to look to Caesarea. Basil is held in great honour in the Armenian Apostolic Church, which has also preserved an anaphora under his name. The Road to 381 The Oriental Orthodox receive the Council of Constantinople of 381 as the second ecumenical council. Basil died two years before it met, but his brother Gregory of Nyssa and his friend Gregory the Theologian were among its leading figures, and the clauses on the Holy Spirit in the Creed carry his thought. See Understanding the Nicene Creed .

XIV. Objections Answered "Basil never calls the Holy Spirit God, so the deity of the Spirit is a later idea." OO Response: Basil gives the Spirit everything that belongs to God: He is ranked with the Father and the Son in baptism, He perfects creation, He makes us god by grace, and He receives the same glory. Gregory the Theologian, who knew Basil better than anyone, explains that Basil held back the bare phrase for a time to protect his church from an Arian emperor, while teaching "by statements which unmistakably had the same meaning" (Section VII). Gregory himself said it plainly, and the Council of 381 confessed it. The Spirit's deity is also not a fourth-century invention. Peter tells Ananias that lying to the Spirit is lying to God (Acts 5:3-4), and the Lord places the Spirit in the one Name of baptism (Matthew 28:19).

"Basil's appeal to unwritten tradition opens the door to anything the Church wants to add." OO Response: Basil's examples are modest and verifiable: the sign of the cross, facing east to pray, the words of the Eucharistic invocation, the blessing of baptismal water. These were practised by every church of his day, including by his opponents. He gives them weight because they are universal and apostolic, not because a bishop invented them. And Basil does not use tradition to avoid Scripture. Most of On the Holy Spirit is careful exegesis. His point is that Christians have always received the faith through both channels Paul names in 2 Thessalonians 2:15. "Basil's "three hypostases" amounts to three gods." OO Response: Basil rejected this charge directly. The three hypostases share one essence, one will, one operation and one glory: "the sovereignty and authority over us is one, and so the doxology ascribed by us is not plural but one" (On the Holy Spirit 18.45).

The Father creates through the Son and perfects through the Spirit; "the first principle of existing things is One." "The Cappadocians turned the simple faith of the Bible into Greek philosophy." OO Response: Basil used the best language of his education to protect the faith, as Paul used the Greek of his day. But the content of his argument is biblical: the baptismal Name, the work of the Spirit in Scripture, the worship of the Church. It was Eunomius, not Basil, who claimed that the human mind could define God's essence. Basil's answer, that we know God from His works but cannot grasp what He is, is a confession of the limits of philosophy, not a surrender to it. "Letter 93 shows laypeople giving themselves communion, so the priest is unnecessary." OO Response: Basil describes the custom of keeping the consecrated gifts at home, which arose in persecution and in the desert, and he is careful to say that the gifts were first offered and given by the priest: "when once the priest has completed the offering, and given it, the recipient...

is bound to believe that he properly takes and receives it from the giver." The Eucharist still comes from the Church's priesthood. The letter shows how precious the Mysteries were, not that they could be made without a priest.

XV. Frequently Asked Questions Did St Basil write the Coptic Liturgy of St Basil? The Coptic tradition attributes it to him, and the Synaxarium says he "wrote the liturgy that bears his name." Scholars debate how much he composed and how much he received and expanded, especially since the Egyptian form differs from the Byzantine one. What is certain is that it has carried his name in Egypt for many centuries and remains the Coptic Church's main liturgy (Section XIII). Why is he called "the Great"? For the greatness of his work as theologian, bishop, monastic founder and servant of the poor. The title was given to him soon after his death and is used in East and West. Who are the Cappadocian Fathers? Basil, his friend Gregory of Nazianzus (Gregory the Theologian) and his brother Gregory of Nyssa. Their writings shaped the doctrine of the Trinity confessed at the Council of Constantinople in 381. The Coptic Church prays the Liturgy of St Gregory, attributed to Gregory the Theologian, on major feasts.

Did Basil believe in icons? The icon controversy came four centuries after him, so he did not write about it directly. But his sentence "the honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype," written about the Son as the image of the Father, became the foundation of the Church's defence of icons. See Icon Veneration . Did Basil know St Athanasius? They never met, as far as we know, but Basil wrote to him several times between 371 and 373, seeking his help for the troubled churches of the East and calling him the "physician of the diseases in the Churches" (Letter 82). Was Basil's sister really his teacher? Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Macrina says that when Basil came home proud of his learning, their sister Macrina drew him to the life of prayer and poverty. Basil himself credits his grandmother Macrina the Elder with his first teaching in the faith (Letter 204). Where should I start reading Basil? On the Holy Spirit , especially chapters 9, 16, 18 and 27. Then the Hexaemeron , his homilies on creation, and Gregory the Theologian's Oration 43 , the funeral oration on Basil.
All are in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, volumes 7 and 8.

secs.h: Where to Begin: Come and See
secs.x: Where to Begin: Come and See When Nathanael doubted, Philip did not argue with him. He simply said, “Come and see” ( John 1:46 ). That remains the first and best counsel for anyone drawn to Orthodoxy. Before you resolve every question, go to the Divine Liturgy — and go more than once, because the first visit will feel strange, and the strangeness is part of the point. The Oriental Orthodox liturgies — Coptic, Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, Malankara — are long, sung, ancient, and heavy with incense and mystery. You will not understand everything at first. That is normal. Let it work on you. Orthodoxy is learned less like a syllabus and more like a language: by immersion, repetition, and time. “Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.” Psalm 34:8 — the invitation is to experience, not merely to conclude

secs.h: Finding a Parish and a Father
secs.x: Finding a Parish and a Father The single most important practical step is to find a parish you can attend regularly and to introduce yourself to the priest. Tell him plainly that you are an inquirer. Do not lurk anonymously for a year; the Church is a family, and you enter families by being known. Which of the six churches? In practice, geography decides more than theology, since all share one faith. Look for a Coptic, Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, or Malankara parish within reach. Some worship largely in an ancestral tongue; many now weave in English, especially where converts are common. Visit more than one if you can. In time you will have a spiritual father — the priest who guides your repentance, hears your confession, and helps you grow. This relationship is central to Orthodox life. It is not therapy and not mere friendship; it is being apprenticed in the life of Christ by someone accountable for your soul ( Hebrews 13:17 ).

The Catechumenate A catechumen is one being instructed in the faith in preparation for reception into the Church. It is an ancient office — in the early Church catechumens were prayed for by name and dismissed before the Eucharist. Becoming a catechumen is a real step, often marked by prayers, and it begins a period of formation that commonly lasts from several months to a few years. The catechumenate is not merely a reading list. It includes: Learning the faith — the Creed, the councils, the sacraments, the lives of the saints. A rule of prayer — beginning to pray daily, often with the Agpeya (the Coptic book of the hours) or a simple rule your priest gives you. Fasting — gradually entering the Church’s fasting seasons under guidance, not all at once. See Fasting → . Repentance — the real work: turning from sin, examining your life, preparing for confession. Patience — letting formation take the time it takes. Resist the urge to rush. The goal is not to acquire a new identity quickly but to be genuinely re-formed in Christ.

How You Are Received How a person enters the Church depends on their background, and it is decided pastorally, by the priest and bishop — not by a formula you can settle in advance. If you have never been baptized You will be baptized — full immersion, into the death and resurrection of Christ Followed immediately by chrismation (anointing with holy myron) and first Communion This is the normal, complete entry into the Body of Christ If you were baptized in another church The church may receive you by chrismation rather than re-baptism, by the principle of economy Or, by strictness (akribeia), may baptize — practice varies by jurisdiction and case Your priest and bishop will determine the right form; ask, do not assume Baptism is not a mere ceremony of joining. It is union with Christ, death and resurrection with him ( Romans 6:3-4 ), the washing of regeneration, and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Whatever the form of your reception, you are being incorporated into Christ’s own body — that is the reality to keep your eyes on.

Living the Faith Reception is a beginning, not a graduation. Orthodox life is a lifelong rhythm, and the convert grows into it season by season: Prayer A daily rule — morning and evening prayers, the hours (Agpeya), the Jesus Prayer. Prayer is the breath of the Christian life. The Mysteries Regular Communion and confession, the medicine of immortality and the healing of the soul. See The Mysteries → . Fasting The Church's fasting seasons — Great Lent, the Nativity Fast, and others — entered under guidance, training the body to serve the spirit. The Calendar Living by the feasts and fasts of the liturgical year, so that time itself is sanctified around the life of Christ. Almsgiving Mercy to the poor, hospitality, and generosity — the faith made visible in love of neighbour. Community Belonging to a parish: worshipping, serving, and bearing one another's burdens. You are not saved alone. “And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” Acts 2:42 — the four pillars of the Church's life, from the very beginning

Common Obstacles — and Encouragement “It feels like an ethnic club.” Some parishes carry deep ancestral culture, and a newcomer can feel like an outsider. Give it time, learn the essentials, and most communities will embrace you. If one parish is not a good fit, another jurisdiction may be. The faith itself is for all nations ( Matthew 28:19 ). “I still have doubts.” Doubt is not the enemy of faith; unrepented pride is. Bring your questions to your priest honestly. You do not need every question answered before you begin — only enough trust to take the next step. “What about my family?” Conversion can strain relationships. Move with love, patience, and honesty, not with the zeal of a new convert eager to argue. Let the change in your life speak before your words do. “I feel unworthy.” Good — that is where everyone starts. The Church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum for saints ( Matthew 9:12 ). Christ calls the sick, and the door is open. “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” ( Matthew 11:28 ).

FAQ How do I start exploring the Orthodox Church? Begin by attending the Divine Liturgy in person, more than once. Orthodoxy is not primarily a set of arguments to be read but a life to be entered, and worship is its heart. Introduce yourself to the priest afterward and let him know you are inquiring. Read at your own pace, but do not try to settle everything intellectually before you ever step inside a church. Which Oriental Orthodox church should I approach? Usually the most practical answer is whichever has a parish near you where you can actually attend regularly: Coptic, Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, or Malankara. All six share the same faith and sacraments. Some parishes worship largely in an ancestral language; many now include English. Visit, speak with the priest, and let geography and pastoral fit guide you rather than trying to pick the theologically best one. Will I be baptized again, or received some other way? That is decided pastorally by the priest and bishop, and it depends on your background. Someone never baptized will be baptized.

Someone already baptized in a trinitarian church may sometimes be received by chrismation rather than re-baptism, by the principle of economy. Do not assume; ask, and let the church determine the proper form. Do I have to become culturally Coptic, Armenian, or Ethiopian? No. These churches carry deep ethnic heritage, and at first a convert can feel like an outsider. But the faith is catholic, meant for all nations, and converts of every background are received. Give it time, learn the essentials, and most parishes will welcome you warmly. If one community is not a good fit, another parish or jurisdiction may be. How long does becoming Orthodox take? There is no fixed timetable. The catechumenate is a period of learning, prayer, repentance, and gradual entry into the rhythm of the Church, and it commonly lasts many months to a few years. The point is not speed but genuine formation: that you are truly entering the life of the Church, not merely changing labels.

I. Introduction "The Bible has been changed." The sentence is spoken by two very different people. The Muslim says it because the Quran's account of Jesus contradicts the Gospels, and one of the two must give way — this is the doctrine called tahrif , corruption. The skeptic says it as the "telephone game": a whisper passed through centuries of copyists until the original is lost. Both versions of the charge are answerable in the same way, because both are claims about manuscripts — and manuscripts are physical objects that can be counted, dated, and read. That is the quiet strength of the Christian position here: it does not rest on trust. The evidence sits in museums and libraries — the British Library, the Vatican, St. Catherine's at Sinai, the Chester Beatty and Bodmer collections, the Israel Museum — much of it photographed and freely readable online by anyone. This page lays out what exists, what the differences between copies actually look like, and why the Church has never feared the question.

secs.h: II. The Two Forms of the Charge
secs.x: II. The Two Forms of the Charge The Skeptical Form "Copies of copies of copies — errors compounding for centuries, doctrine invented along the way. We cannot know what the originals said." This is an empirical claim about transmission quality. It is tested by comparing early manuscripts against later ones and measuring what actually changed. The Islamic Form (Tahrif) "The Torah and the Gospel were genuine revelations, but Jews and Christians corrupted the text, removing prophecies of Muhammad and inserting the crucifixion and divine sonship." This is a historical claim with a date attached: the corruption must have happened before the seventh century (or the Quran's own affirmations become a problem), yet after the manuscripts we possess were written — which is the difficulty. Note what both charges require: not the existence of copying differences (every ancient text has those, and Christians have catalogued them openly for centuries), but differences of the right kind — systematic, doctrinal, and early enough to erase the original.

secs.h: II. The Two Forms of the Charge
secs.x: Keep that standard in view through the next four sections.

secs.h: III. The Old Testament — The Dead Sea Scrolls Test
secs.x: III. The Old Testament — The Dead Sea Scrolls Test Until 1947, the oldest complete Hebrew manuscripts of the Old Testament were medieval — the Masoretic codices of roughly the tenth and eleventh centuries. A skeptic could reasonably ask what a thousand years of copying had done to the text. Then the Dead Sea Scrolls were found at Qumran: biblical manuscripts copied between roughly the third century BC and the first century AD, including the Great Isaiah Scroll — the entire book of Isaiah, about a thousand years older than the medieval copies. The comparison could have destroyed the Bible's credibility. Instead it became a celebrated vindication of the copyists: across a millennium of hand-copying, the text of Isaiah proved remarkably stable — the differences overwhelmingly matters of spelling and minor wording, with the message of every passage intact. The fifty-third chapter — "He was wounded for our transgressions" — reads in the scroll, centuries before Christ, substantially as it reads in your Bible tonight.

secs.h: III. The Old Testament — The Dead Sea Scrolls Test
secs.x: Two further witnesses corroborate from independent directions: the Septuagint, the Greek translation made by Jews beginning in the third century BC — a snapshot of the Hebrew text long before Christianity or Islam existed — and the Samaritan Pentateuch, preserved by a community estranged from the Jews since deep antiquity. Communities that distrusted each other transmitted recognizably the same books. A conspiracy to alter the text would have needed the cooperation of bitter enemies across continents and centuries.

secs.h: IV. The New Testament — An Embarrassment of Riches
secs.x: IV. The New Testament — An Embarrassment of Riches Ancient works survive, as a rule, in handfuls of late copies. The New Testament is the great exception — by manuscript count and by closeness to the events it is commonly judged the best-attested text of antiquity, and the margin is not narrow: Greek Manuscripts Several thousand Greek New Testament manuscripts survive — commonly numbered above five thousand — from scraps to complete Bibles, alongside thousands more in early translations (Coptic, Syriac, Latin, Armenian, Ethiopic — the languages of the Oriental churches among the earliest). The Earliest Papyri Fragments and substantial portions copied within roughly a century of composition — the John Rylands fragment of John (P52) is commonly dated to the second century, and the Chester Beatty and Bodmer papyri preserve large runs of the Gospels and Epistles from around the third. Complete Bibles Before Islam Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus — essentially complete Greek Bibles from the fourth century, some three hundred years before the Quran.

secs.h: IV. The New Testament — An Embarrassment of Riches
secs.x: Both are photographed online; anyone can check that John 14 reads parakletos and that the crucifixion narratives stand. Patristic Citations The Church Fathers quoted Scripture so extensively that their citations form a further check on the manuscripts, from writers spread across the whole Mediterranean. The popular claim that the entire New Testament could be rebuilt from them alone goes further than the evidence allows, since the Fathers often quoted loosely or from memory, but they show which text was being read in their cities, and where. For comparison: the works of Tacitus, Caesar, or Thucydides — texts no historian doubts we essentially possess — survive in far fewer copies, typically written many centuries after their authors. If the New Testament's text is unknowable, then no text from the ancient world is knowable, and the libraries of classics departments should close. No one proposes this, because the standard is being applied selectively. The men closest to the sources treated the apostolic writings as fixed and public. Writing around AD 180, St.

secs.h: IV. The New Testament — An Embarrassment of Riches
secs.x: Irenaeus regards the fourfold Gospel as already settled beyond revision: "It is not possible that the Gospels can be either more or fewer in number than they are." Direct Quote (Against Heresies 3.11.8). A generation later Tertullian could still send a skeptic to read the apostles' own manuscripts in the churches that held them: "Run over the apostolic churches, in which the very thrones of the apostles are still pre-eminent in their places, in which their own authentic writings are read." Direct Quote (Prescription Against Heretics 36, c. AD 200). This is a Church checking its text against apostolic exemplars within living memory of the authors — not a rumor mutating down a chain.

secs.h: V. What the Variants Actually Are
secs.x: V. What the Variants Actually Are Skeptical presentations cite large numbers of "variants" among the manuscripts. The number is real; what it measures is misunderstood. A "variant" is counted every time any manuscript differs from any other in any word — so the count grows with the number of manuscripts. The New Testament has an enormous variant count because it has an enormous number of copies; a text surviving in three manuscripts has few variants and far less certainty. What kind of differences are they? Overwhelmingly: spelling, word order (highly flexible in Greek), the presence or absence of articles, and the substitution of a name for a pronoun ("Jesus said" / "he said"). A small remainder are meaningful and a smaller subset both meaningful and hard to decide — and these are catalogued, published, and printed in the footnotes of any serious Bible. The crucial fact, acknowledged across the scholarly spectrum, is that no article of the Christian faith rests on a disputed reading.

secs.h: V. What the Variants Actually Are
secs.x: The divinity of Christ, the crucifixion, the resurrection, the Trinity — each is taught across so many undisputed passages that no textual decision touches it. Even Bart Ehrman — the most-read skeptical textual critic — has acknowledged, in the question-and-answer material appended to Misquoting Jesus , that essential Christian beliefs are not affected by the textual variants in the manuscripts. Paraphrase The man whose books popularized the variant count concedes the point that matters.

VI. The "Telephone Game" Answered The telephone game corrupts a message for three reasons: the message passes in a single chain ; each whisper destroys the previous one; and the game is played for laughs , with no one checking. Manuscript transmission differs on every point: It is a tree, not a chain. Copies were made in parallel across Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor, Greece, Italy, North Africa — independent lines that can be compared against each other. An error entering one line is exposed by the others; that comparison is the entire discipline of textual criticism. The originals' early copies were not destroyed by later ones. We are not limited to the end of the chain — we can read the second-, third-, and fourth-century links directly. The game would be no game at all if you could walk back and ask the third whisperer what he heard. The copyists believed they were handling the words of God. Jewish scribal culture counted letters; Christian scribes copied under the eye of churches that publicly read these texts every Sunday and would notice alteration.

Reverence does not prevent slips of the pen — but it is the opposite of a careless whisper. The conclusion is not that copying was perfect — it was not, and the footnotes in your Bible say so. The conclusion is that the transmission is reconstructable : with thousands of early, independent, comparable witnesses, the original text is recoverable to a degree unmatched by any other ancient book.

secs.h: VII. The Islamic Version — Tahrif's Dilemma
secs.x: VII. The Islamic Version — Tahrif's Dilemma The Islamic charge faces a problem the skeptical one does not: the Quran itself testifies to the Bible's integrity in Muhammad's own day. It calls the Torah and the Gospel guidance and light, instructs the People of the Book to judge by what God revealed in them, and directs doubters to ask those who read the earlier Scripture (see the fuller treatment, with the passages, on The Islamic Dilemma ). The Quran nowhere says "the books in their hands are forgeries"; it argues with Jews and Christians for failing to follow books it treats as present and authoritative. Now add the manuscripts. The corruption — to do the work the doctrine needs — must have removed the prophecies of Muhammad and inserted the crucifixion, the resurrection, and the divine sonship. But complete Greek Bibles from the fourth century (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus), papyri from the second and third, the Dead Sea Scrolls from before Christ, and the citations of the Fathers all contain the crucifixion and the sonship and lack any prophecy of Muhammad.

secs.h: VII. The Islamic Version — Tahrif's Dilemma
secs.x: So the corruption must predate all of them — predating, in some cases, the apostles' own lifetimes — while the Quran simultaneously affirms the uncorrupted scriptures as present in the seventh century. The two requirements cannot both be met. Either the seventh-century scriptures were sound (and they read as ours do — we have them), or the Quran affirmed corrupted books. It is also worth saying plainly: the Christian scriptures were already translated into Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Latin, and Ethiopic, and spread from Britain to India, centuries before Islam. A global, simultaneous, undetected revision of all of them — agreed upon by churches that were excommunicating each other over single words — is not a historical hypothesis; it is the abandonment of history.

secs.h: VIII. The Honesty of Modern Bibles
secs.x: VIII. The Honesty of Modern Bibles Open a serious modern Bible to Mark 16 or John 8 and you will find a footnote: the longer ending of Mark (16:9–20) and the account of the woman taken in adultery (John 7:53–8:11) are absent from some of the earliest manuscripts, and the editions say so on the page. Skeptics sometimes present these notes as damaging admissions. They are the opposite: they are the proof that nothing is hidden. A tradition that had corrupted its text would not print the evidence in its own margins. The Church's scholars catalogue every variant, publish the apparatus, photograph the codices, and put them online. The two famous passages are the largest textual questions in the New Testament — and neither adds or removes a doctrine: Christ's resurrection is proclaimed throughout the undisputed text, and His mercy to sinners likewise. That these are the worst cases is itself the strongest evidence of how sound the whole is.

secs.h: VIII. The Honesty of Modern Bibles
secs.x: The Orthodox Church receives the Scriptures within Holy Tradition — the same Church that wrote, copied, canonized, and liturgically proclaimed them (see The Canon of Scripture and The Authority of the Church ). The manuscripts are not a problem the Church manages; they are the paper trail of her faithfulness.

IX. FAQ Q: Weren't the Gospels written long after Jesus, by people who never met Him? That is a different question from corruption — it concerns composition, not copying — but briefly: the Gospels were written within the first century, within living memory, while hostile witnesses could contradict them; and Paul's letters, earlier still, already contain the creed of the death and resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). See Did Jesus Exist? and The Resurrection — Answering the Skeptics . Q: What about the "lost gospels" — Thomas, Judas, Barnabas? The second-century gnostic texts (Thomas, Judas, and the rest) were never hidden by the Church — the Fathers discussed and rejected them publicly, and their late dates and alien theology are why no ancient community of the apostles' heirs received them.

The "Gospel of Barnabas" sometimes cited in Muslim apologetics is a different matter entirely: it survives in two manuscripts of the late sixteenth century, one Italian and one Spanish, contains anachronisms of late medieval Europe, and is regarded across scholarship — including by a number of Muslim scholars — as a medieval composition. See The Canon of Scripture . Q: Doesn't the Quran have a cleaner transmission history? The Quran's transmission was standardized early — Islamic tradition itself records that the caliph Uthman had an official text compiled and ordered variant codices destroyed. Standardization by authority produces uniformity, but uniformity is not the same as preservation of the original; it removes precisely the independent witnesses by which an original is verified. The Christian tradition kept its thousands of messy, comparable, datable copies — which is why its text can be checked . The two histories are different strategies, and the open one is the auditable one.

In fairness, Muslims answer that the Quran was preserved above all by memorisation, recited by many people from the start, and that is a real strength. The point here is narrower: the written witnesses that would let a historian check the earliest text independently were deliberately reduced. One of the few to survive, the lower text of the Sana'a palimpsest, differs in places from the standard text. Q: If the text is fine, why do translations differ? Translation differences (NKJV vs. ESV vs. an Arabic Bible) are choices about rendering the same underlying text into another language — synonyms, word order, formal versus dynamic style. They are not evidence of different originals, any more than two English translations of the Quran prove the Arabic is corrupt. Q: Where can I see the manuscripts myself? Codex Sinaiticus has a dedicated website with full photographs and transcription; the Vatican Library has digitized Vaticanus; the Israel Museum presents the Great Isaiah Scroll online; and the Center for the Study of New Testament Manuscripts hosts images of papyri and codices.
An afternoon with these sites is worth more than any debate video.

secs.h: Why Many Translations Doesn't Mean Many Bibles
secs.x: Why Many Translations Doesn't Mean Many Bibles Every mainstream English Bible is translated from the same body of ancient manuscripts — Hebrew and Greek for the Old Testament (with the Church favouring the Greek Septuagint), and Greek for the New Testament. A translation is simply the act of carrying that fixed, inspired message from one language into another. The words on the English page differ; the revelation behind them is one. Think of it the way the Church has always thought of the Gospel itself: one truth proclaimed in many tongues. At Pentecost the Apostles spoke and “each one heard them speaking in his own language” (Acts 2:6) — the same message, many languages, no contradiction. The Coptic Church has read the scriptures in Greek, Coptic, Arabic and now English for nearly two thousand years, and her Ethiopian sister in Ge'ez, without ever supposing there was more than one Bible. A helpful test: open any three reputable translations side by side at John 1:1. Every one of them says the Word was God, was in the beginning, and was with God.

secs.h: Why Many Translations Doesn't Mean Many Bibles
secs.x: The vocabulary shifts — word order, punctuation, a synonym here or there — but the doctrine is identical. Translations vary in wording , not in the faith they deliver . So Why Do Any Differences Exist At All? Three honest reasons, none of them sinister. First, English changes: “thee” and “thou” were plain speech in 1611 and are archaic now, so revisions modernise the language. Second, translators must choose how literally to render idioms and figures of speech — this is the real dividing line, covered in the next section. Third, translators occasionally weigh manuscript evidence differently for a handful of verses. These are matters of craft and clarity, not competing revelations. “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever.” Isaiah 40:8

The Three Translation Philosophies Almost every difference you will ever notice between two Bibles comes down to how literally the translators chose to work . There are three broad approaches, and knowing them lets you read any version wisely. Word‑for‑Word Formal Equivalence KJV • NKJV • ESV NASB • RSV Stays close to the original Thought‑for‑Thought Dynamic Equivalence NIV • NAB • NJB NEB • REB Prioritises readability Paraphrase Free Retelling Living Bible • The Message Good News (GNT) Loosest — use with caution Formal Equivalence — Word-for-Word The translator tries to render each word and grammatical form of the original as closely as English allows, even at the cost of some smoothness. The great strength is fidelity: when the Greek is ambiguous, a formal translation tends to preserve the ambiguity and let the reader (and the Church) interpret, rather than deciding for you. This is why serious study, doctrine and liturgy lean on word-for-word versions.

Dynamic Equivalence — Thought-for-Thought The translator asks “what did this sentence mean?” and then says that meaning in natural, flowing English. The strength is readability — excellent for a child, a new reader, or reading aloud. The weakness is that somebody has already interpreted the text for you . Where the original is deliberately layered or ambiguous, a thought-for-thought version often flattens it into a single reading, and that reading reflects the translators' judgement. For casual reading this is fine; for pinning down doctrine it can quietly mislead. Paraphrase — A Free Retelling A paraphrase is not really a translation at all but one person’s restatement of the Bible in his own words. The Message and the old Living Bible can be vivid and moving, but they should never be used to settle a question of doctrine or to study a passage closely. Read them, if at all, alongside a faithful translation — never instead of one.

The rule of thumb: the more literal the translation, the more the interpreting is left to you and the Church ; the freer the translation, the more the interpreting has already been done for you by the committee. For the Orthodox reader, who receives scripture within the Church's Tradition, that is a strong reason to keep a word-for-word Bible as the main text.

Which Translations Are Trustworthy? No English translation is perfect, and none is “forbidden.” But some are markedly more reliable than others for an Orthodox Christian who wants both accuracy and a text compatible with the Church's Tradition. The table below rates common versions on three things that matter: how faithful (literal) they are, how readable they are, and whether they make a good main study Bible.
