The one version to genuinely avoid is the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ New World Translation, which deliberately alters key verses (most infamously John 1:1, rendered “the Word was a god”) to deny the divinity of Christ. That is not a translation choice but a doctrinal corruption. See our page on the Divinity of Christ .

secs.h: A Closer Look at the NIV
secs.x: A Closer Look at the NIV The New International Version deserves its own section because it is the most popular modern Bible in the English-speaking world, and because its strengths and weaknesses are widely misunderstood. A fair Orthodox assessment is this: the NIV is fine for children and new readers, but it muddies things once you dig into the details. This is the view held across many — if not all — of the Oriental Orthodox churches, and it holds up under examination. What the NIV Does Well The NIV reads clearly and naturally. For a child, a catechumen, or anyone reading Scripture for the first time, its plain English removes needless obstacles, and it is far more accurate than any paraphrase. As a first Bible or a reading Bible, it does real good. Where It Muddies the Details Because the NIV is a thought-for-thought translation, its committee frequently decides for the reader what an ambiguous verse means, and then prints only that meaning. Three examples that matter to Orthodox doctrine: 1. Holy Tradition (2 Thessalonians 2:15).

secs.h: A Closer Look at the NIV
secs.x: Paul tells the Thessalonians to hold fast to what they were taught “by word” and “by letter.” The Greek is paradosis — “that which is handed down,” traditionally rendered “traditions.” The NIV renders it “teachings,” a softer word that blunts a verse plainly supporting the Church's Holy Tradition alongside Scripture. 2. Flesh vs. “sinful nature” (Romans 8, Galatians 5). The Greek sarx (“flesh”) carries a rich range of meaning the Fathers explored deeply. Older NIV editions repeatedly replaced “flesh” with the interpretive phrase “sinful nature,” committing the text to one theological reading and obscuring the patristic understanding. (The 2011 revision restored “flesh” in many places — itself an admission that the earlier choice had been an interpretation, not a translation.) 3. Readability over precision. In smoothing the text for easy reading, the NIV frequently resolves a deliberate ambiguity into a single sense. That is a gift to a beginner and a hazard to anyone building doctrine on the exact words.

secs.h: A Closer Look at the NIV
secs.x: The pattern: none of these is a “lie” — each is a defensible interpretive choice. But that is exactly the problem. A study Bible should hand you the text and let the Church interpret; the NIV often hands you the interpretation and hides the text. Fine for a child; not what you want when the details matter. “Therefore, brethren, stand fast and hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or our epistle.” 2 Thessalonians 2:15 (NKJV) The practical counsel that follows is simple: keep the NIV, if you like it, as a readable companion — but study, memorise doctrine, and settle arguments from a word-for-word Bible.

secs.h: What the Coptic Orthodox Church Recommends
secs.x: What the Coptic Orthodox Church Recommends The Coptic Orthodox Church has never bound the faithful to a single English translation the way it holds to the Greek Septuagint and the Coptic texts for its liturgy. But its guidance to English-speaking Copts has been consistent and clear. Pope Shenouda III of Alexandria 117th Pope • 1971–2012 Under Pope Shenouda III the Coptic Church consistently pointed English-speaking faithful toward the New King James Version as the most suitable everyday English Bible: faithful and word-for-word, based on the traditional Byzantine / Received Text underlying the Church's New Testament, yet readable in modern English. Coptic parishes and Sunday-school materials across the English-speaking diaspora overwhelmingly use the NKJV for exactly this reason. The Orthodox Study Bible The fullest recommendation for a serious English reader is the Orthodox Study Bible (St. Athanasius Academy / Thomas Nelson, 2008).

secs.h: What the Coptic Orthodox Church Recommends
secs.x: Its Old Testament is translated from the Septuagint — the Church's Old Testament — rather than the later Hebrew Masoretic text, and its New Testament is the NKJV. Crucially it includes the deuterocanonical books the Church has always read, and its notes draw on the Fathers rather than modern Protestant commentary. For an Orthodox Christian it is the single best English study Bible available. In short: for daily reading and study, the Coptic Church's practical counsel is the NKJV ; for the fullest Orthodox text with the Septuagint Old Testament and patristic notes, the Orthodox Study Bible . Both are word-for-word and both carry the Church's tradition faithfully.

secs.h: Why the Septuagint Matters for the Old Testament
secs.x: Why the Septuagint Matters for the Old Testament Choosing a translation is not only about English style; for the Old Testament it is also about which ancient text is being translated. Here the Orthodox position is distinctive and important. The Church's Old Testament is the Septuagint (LXX), the Greek translation used by the Apostles themselves, not the later Hebrew Masoretic text that most Protestant Bibles follow. This is not a minor preference. When the New Testament quotes the Old Testament — roughly 300 times — it most often follows the Septuagint, though some quotations follow the Hebrew instead (Matthew 2:15 and John 19:37, for example). The most famous case is the prophecy of the Virgin Birth. Isaiah 7:14 — “Virgin” or “Young Woman”? The Septuagint renders Isaiah 7:14 with parthenos — “virgin.” Matthew 1:23 quotes it in exactly that form to announce the birth of Christ.

secs.h: Why the Septuagint Matters for the Old Testament
secs.x: But some modern translations, following the Hebrew almah and modern critical fashion, render it “young woman.” The RSV famously did this and caused an uproar; a young-woman reading quietly weakens the Messianic prophecy that the Gospel itself depends on. A translation that keeps “virgin” is standing with Matthew and the Church. “Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and shall call His name Immanuel.” Isaiah 7:14 (LXX) / Matthew 1:23 This is why an Orthodox reader benefits from a Bible whose Old Testament rests on the Septuagint — above all the Orthodox Study Bible — and why, among ordinary translations, the ones that preserve the traditional readings (KJV, NKJV) are preferred. For the full story see our page on the Biblical Canon .

secs.h: Scripture Came Through the Church — Why Tradition Matters
secs.x: Scripture Came Through the Church — Why Tradition Matters Once you understand how the Bible was translated, copied and handed down, a deeper point comes into view — one that is among the most useful things an Orthodox Christian can raise with a Protestant friend. The Bible did not drop from heaven as a finished, bound book. It came to us through the Church , and that fact quietly undoes the idea that Scripture can stand entirely alone, apart from Tradition. The Church Came First For the first decades of Christianity there was no New Testament at all. The Apostles preached, taught and celebrated the Eucharist; the faith was living and complete before a single Gospel was written. When the New Testament letters and Gospels were finally set down, they were written within the Church, by her members, to her congregations — not handed to outsiders as a rulebook. The community existed first; the text was born inside it. The Bible's Own Table of Contents Is Tradition Here is the argument that stops many a discussion: nowhere does the Bible list its own books.

secs.h: Scripture Came Through the Church — Why Tradition Matters
secs.x: No verse names the twenty-seven books of the New Testament. The canon — the very decision about which writings are Scripture and which are not — was discerned and settled by the Church over several centuries, through her bishops, councils and Fathers. So to hold the Bible at all is already to trust a decision of Holy Tradition. A Protestant who says “the Bible alone” is relying, for the contents of that Bible, on the very Church authority he means to set aside. Sola scriptura cannot even tell you what “scriptura” is. Scripture Itself Commands Holding to Tradition Far from opposing Tradition, the New Testament explicitly commands it. St. Paul tells the faithful to hold fast the traditions they were taught “by word” as well as “by epistle,” and praises those who keep them. The written word never claims to be the whole of the deposit; John says as much when he notes that not everything Christ did was written down (John 21:25).

secs.h: Scripture Came Through the Church — Why Tradition Matters
secs.x: “Now I praise you, brethren, that you remember me in all things and keep the traditions just as I delivered them to you.” 1 Corinthians 11:2 (NKJV) “Therefore, brethren, stand fast and hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or our epistle.” 2 Thessalonians 2:15 (NKJV) St. Basil the Great c. 330–379 AD In his work On the Holy Spirit , Basil teaches that the Church holds her faith from two sources — the written Scriptures and the unwritten Tradition handed down from the Apostles — and that both carry the same force for true religion. Practices as basic as facing east to pray, the words of the Eucharistic blessing, and the sign of the cross, he observes, are nowhere written in Scripture but come from Apostolic Tradition. The Church never lived by the text alone. St. Irenaeus of Lyon c. 130–202 AD Writing against the Gnostics, Irenaeus argued that the true faith is guarded in the Church through the unbroken succession of bishops from the Apostles.

secs.h: Scripture Came Through the Church — Why Tradition Matters
secs.x: He pointed to whole nations of believers who held the faith rightly by Tradition, “without paper or ink” — proof that the Gospel lived in the Church's teaching before, and beneath, the written page. ( Against Heresies 3.4) The whole point: the same Church that preached the Gospel, discerned the canon, copied the manuscripts and translated the text is the Church whose living Tradition guards its meaning. Text and Tradition flow from one source. You cannot keep the book while discarding the community that wrote, chose and preserved it — which is exactly why the Bible is read most safely within the Church. See Scripture & Tradition and The Biblical Canon .

secs.h: The King James Version — A History, and Why It Is Reliable
secs.x: The King James Version — A History, and Why It Is Reliable The King James Version of 1611 is one of the most influential books in the English language — and one of the most misunderstood. A claim heard often today runs like this: because King James I was a man, and a king, the Bible he commissioned was slanted to make women submit and subjects obey. It is a memorable charge. It is also historically false, and the record is public and checkable. Here is what actually happened. How the KJV Was Made King James authorised the translation at the Hampton Court Conference in 1604, and it was published in 1611. The work was done not by one man but by roughly 47 scholars organised into six committees — two each at Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge. They translated from the Hebrew of the Old Testament and the Greek Received Text of the New, and they leaned heavily on the earlier English Bibles, above all the work of William Tyndale. Each company's draft was reviewed by the others and by a final revising committee.

secs.h: The King James Version — A History, and Why It Is Reliable
secs.x: The whole structure was built to make sure no single person — least of all the king — could quietly insert his own agenda. It Was a Revision, Not a Royal Invention The KJV was not composed from scratch in 1611. Scholars estimate that roughly 80 to 90 percent of its New Testament wording is taken directly from William Tyndale , whose translation appeared in 1526 and who was strangled and burned for it in 1536 — decades before James was even born. The English Bible the KJV gives us is essentially Tyndale's, polished through three generations of revisers (the Great Bible, the Geneva Bible, the Bishops' Bible). The supposedly “biased” passages were already fixed in English long before James, and they stood in Latin, Greek and Syriac for more than a thousand years before that. What James Actually Cared About James did give the translators rules, drawn up by Archbishop Richard Bancroft. His one genuine political concern was marginal notes .

secs.h: The King James Version — A History, and Why It Is Reliable
secs.x: The Geneva Bible, beloved of the Puritans, carried study notes, some of which questioned the authority of kings — one famous note on Exodus praised the Hebrew midwives for disobeying Pharaoh. James considered such notes seditious. So Bancroft's sixth rule forbade doctrinal margin notes, permitting only brief explanations of Hebrew and Greek words. His other preferences were matters of church government , not sex: keep the old church vocabulary, render the Greek as “church” rather than “congregation,” “bishop” rather than “elder.” Nowhere in the rules, the translators' records, or the finished text is there a single instruction touching the status of women. That part of the story is simply an anachronism. Why this makes the KJV reliable: its trustworthiness rests on public, verifiable history — a large committee that checked one another, a known Hebrew and Greek textual base, a documented chain of descent back to Tyndale and the ancient manuscripts, and a set of royal rules whose one political edge concerned anti-monarchy footnotes, not women.

secs.h: The King James Version — A History, and Why It Is Reliable
secs.x: The KJV is a faithful English rendering of the same Scriptures the Church has always read. That is precisely why the Coptic Church is at home with its careful modern descendant, the NKJV.

secs.h: How to Choose a Bible Translation
secs.x: How to Choose a Bible Translation Put the pieces together and the decision becomes simple. Start with your purpose, then pick accordingly. 1. Decide what the Bible is for For study, doctrine and liturgy , choose a word-for-word translation — the Orthodox Study Bible or the NKJV first of all. For a young child or a brand-new reader , a readable version such as the NIV is a reasonable starting point, with the plan of moving to a fuller translation as they grow. For devotional reading aloud , readability matters more, but never let a paraphrase be someone's only Bible. 2. Prefer a text the Church can stand behind Favour translations whose Old Testament respects the Septuagint readings and whose New Testament rests on the traditional Received Text — the NKJV and KJV both do. The Orthodox Study Bible does this most completely and adds the deuterocanonical books the Church reads. 3.

secs.h: How to Choose a Bible Translation
secs.x: Match the reader to the version An honest, practical ranking for an Orthodox home: keep the Orthodox Study Bible as the anchor; use the NKJV as the everyday text (this is the Coptic Church's counsel); let a child begin with a clear version like the NIV and grow into the NKJV; treat paraphrases as devotional extras, never as the main Bible; and avoid the New World Translation entirely. 4. Read it within the Church, not alone The deepest safeguard is not the translation but the community. Scripture was written in the Church, canonised by the Church, and is rightly read within the Church's Tradition and the mind of the Fathers. No translation, however good, is a substitute for reading with the Church. See Scripture & Tradition . The one-line answer: get the Orthodox Study Bible if you can; otherwise the NKJV. Use the NIV for children as a first step. Skip the paraphrases for study, and avoid the New World Translation altogether.

Frequently Asked Questions Is it a sin to read the NIV? No. The NIV is a real translation of Scripture, not a corruption, and reading it is no sin. The counsel is simply to prefer a word-for-word Bible for study and doctrine, because the NIV's thought-for-thought method sometimes settles interpretive questions for you. Is the King James Version the only true Bible? No. The “KJV-only” position is a modern Protestant idea the Orthodox Church does not hold. The KJV is an excellent, faithful translation resting on the traditional text, and Orthodox readers love it — but the NKJV carries the same textual tradition in modern English, and the Church has never taught that salvation depends on one English version. Which Bible should I buy first? If you can get one Bible, get the Orthodox Study Bible: Septuagint Old Testament, NKJV New Testament, the deuterocanonical books, and notes from the Fathers. If you want a plain, affordable everyday Bible, the NKJV.

Why do Orthodox Bibles have more books? Because the Church's Old Testament is the Septuagint, which always contained the deuterocanonical books — Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, and others. These were read in the Church from early times, though some Fathers such as Jerome and Athanasius ranked them below the books of the Hebrew canon. In the 16th century Protestant Bibles moved them into a separate section (the 1611 King James Version still printed them), and most Protestant printings dropped them altogether in the 19th century. The full account is on our Biblical Canon page. Are modern translations trying to change Christianity? Mostly no. Most differences are honest questions of English style and manuscript weighing. A few choices — “young woman” for “virgin,” “teachings” for “traditions” — do carry doctrinal weight, which is exactly why an Orthodox reader keeps a faithful, word-for-word Bible as the main text and reads within the Church.

Canon at a Glance Book totals vary significantly across traditions. The Protestant Old Testament follows the rabbinic Hebrew list that settled in the generations after the fall of the Temple (AD 70). Every other major tradition uses a larger canon rooted in the Septuagint. 66 Protestant 39 OT + 27 NT Luther 1534; Westminster 1647 73 Roman Catholic 46 OT + 27 NT Council of Trent 1546 76–79 Eastern Orthodox 49–52 OT + 27 NT Varies by jurisdiction 73–76 Oriental Orthodox 46–49 OT + 27 NT Coptic, Armenian, Syriac 81 Ethiopian Orthodox 54 OT + 27 NT, or 46 OT + 35 NT Largest canon 22–27 Syriac NT (Peshitta) NT originally 22 books Lacked 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude, Revelation Key insight: Most Old Testament quotations in the New Testament follow the wording of the Septuagint (LXX), the Greek translation used by Diaspora Jews and early Christians, and the Christian copies of the Septuagint contain the deuterocanonical books. The shorter Protestant Old Testament follows the Hebrew list kept by the rabbis after the rise of Christianity.

The Septuagint — The Church's Bible The Septuagint (LXX) is the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, begun in Alexandria in the 3rd century BC with the Law and completed over the following two centuries, for Jewish communities who no longer spoke Hebrew. The Christian manuscripts of the Septuagint carry the deuterocanonical books (Tobit, Judith, Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach and Baruch) among the other books, not as appendices. We have no complete Jewish copy from before Christ, so exactly which books pre-Christian Jews counted in it is debated. Most of the roughly 300 Old Testament quotations in the New Testament follow the Septuagint wording. The New Testament does not quote a deuterocanonical book with a formula such as “it is written,” but it echoes them in many places (see the objections section below). The Isaiah 7:14 Problem This verse is a decisive example of why the LXX matters. The Hebrew text uses almah (young woman). The Septuagint translates this as parthenos (virgin).

Matthew 1:23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 specifically using parthenos — the LXX word, not a fresh translation from the Hebrew. Matthew’s Messianic prophecy depends on the Septuagint text. It shows that the apostles were content to use the Greek translation as Scripture. It does not by itself show which books they counted, a point Protestants rightly press. “Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; behold, a virgin [ parthenos ] shall conceive in the womb, and shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name Emmanuel.” — Isaiah 7:14 (LXX, tr. Brenton; quoted in Matthew 1:23) Why the LXX Included More Books The LXX canon reflected the broader scriptures in use among Diaspora Jewish communities. Wisdom was written in Greek, probably in Alexandria. Sirach was written in Hebrew in Jerusalem and translated into Greek in Egypt by the author’s grandson. 1 Maccabees was written in Hebrew and translated into Greek. These books were read by Greek-speaking Jews before Christianity and passed into the Church’s use, where they were read from the beginning.

The Codices The three great manuscripts of the early Christian Bible — Codex Vaticanus (4th c.), Codex Sinaiticus (4th c.), and Codex Alexandrinus (5th c.) — contain the deuterocanonical books mixed among the protocanonical texts (Vaticanus lacks the books of Maccabees). No ancient Christian Bible gathers them into a separate section called “Apocrypha.” That arrangement became standard with Luther’s Bible of 1534. Origen of Alexandria c. 185–253 AD In his Letter to Africanus , Origen defended the Greek additions used in the churches (such as the story of Susanna in Daniel) against Julius Africanus, who rejected them as absent from the Hebrew. He asks mockingly whether, on noticing such differences, “we are immediately to reject as spurious the copies in use in our Churches, and enjoin the brotherhood to put away the sacred books current among them.” Though he elsewhere gives the Hebrew enumeration, his own homilies and commentaries cite Wisdom, Sirach, Tobit, and Judith as scripture. Irenaeus of Lyon c.

130–202 AD Irenaeus treats the books of the wider Greek Old Testament as Scripture without qualification. In Against Heresies IV.38.3 he echoes Wisdom 6:19 (“immortality renders one near unto God”), and in V.35.1 he quotes Baruch under the name of Jeremiah (see below).

secs.h: The Jamnia Dispute — A Post-Christian Jewish Decision
secs.x: The Jamnia Dispute — A Post-Christian Jewish Decision Protestants often argue that the Church should follow the “Hebrew canon” — the canon defined by rabbinical Judaism. But this argument rests on a historical reversal: the Hebrew canon in its final closed form was settled after Christianity began, and some scholars think partly in reaction to it. Yavneh (Jamnia) c. AD 90 Around AD 90, after the destruction of the Temple, rabbinic gatherings at Yavneh (Jamnia) in Judea took up questions of practice and scripture for a post-Temple world. Note: the older scholarly term “Council of Jamnia” — popularized in the 19th century — has been largely abandoned in modern scholarship. There was no single formal council issuing canon decrees; rather, ongoing rabbinic discussions gradually produced consensus over decades. The functional result of this process was a narrower Jewish canon that excluded Greek-language books, including Wisdom, Sirach, and others already in continuous use in LXX Christianity.

secs.h: The Jamnia Dispute — A Post-Christian Jewish Decision
secs.x: The critical problem: The Christian Church had already been using the Septuagint for 50–60 years before Jamnia. Asking the Church to adopt a Jewish canon finalized after Christ, and, some scholars think, partly in reaction to Christianity, is asking the Church to submit to a post-Christian, non-Christian authority on which books are divinely inspired. The Protestant reply, in fairness: Protestant scholars answer that the shorter list was not invented at Yavneh but was already the Scripture of Palestinian Judaism in Christ’s day. They point to Josephus ( Against Apion 1.8, c. AD 95), who counts twenty-two books, to the threefold division “the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms” in Luke 24:44, and to Christ’s phrase “from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Luke 11:51), which they read as spanning the Hebrew Bible from Genesis to Chronicles. Orthodox reply that the evidence for a closed list before Christ is thin, and that the apostolic Church read the wider Greek collection.

secs.h: The Jamnia Dispute — A Post-Christian Jewish Decision
secs.x: What the Early Church Said The Councils of Hippo (AD 393) and Carthage (AD 397), with Augustine taking part, listed the deuterocanonical books as canonical scripture, and the list sent by Pope Innocent I to Exsuperius of Toulouse in 405 agrees with them. This was a formal recognition of what was already read. The East was less uniform: the Synod of Laodicea (c. 363) gave a shorter list, and several Greek Fathers followed the Hebrew count, but no council condemned these books. “But the Canonical Scriptures are as follows: Genesis. Exodus. Leviticus. Numbers. Deuteronomy. Joshua the Son of Nun. The Judges. Ruth. The Kings, iv. books. The Chronicles, ij. books. Job. The Psalter. The Five books of Solomon. The Twelve Books of the Prophets. Isaiah. Jeremiah. Ezechiel. Daniel. Tobit. Judith. Esther. Ezra, ij. books. Macchabees, ij. books.” — Code of Canons of the African Church, Canon 24 (Carthage 419, repeating the list of Hippo 393 and Carthage 397; the canon adds that it is to be sent to Boniface of Rome “that they may confirm this canon”) St.

secs.h: The Jamnia Dispute — A Post-Christian Jewish Decision
secs.x: Augustine of Hippo 354–430 AD “Now the whole canon of Scripture on which we say this judgment is to be exercised, is contained in the following books: Five books of Moses, that is, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy; ... Judith, and the two books of Maccabees, and the two of Ezra.” ( On Christian Doctrine II.8.13). Of Maccabees he also writes that these books “are held as canonical, not by the Jews, but by the Church” ( City of God XVIII.36). For Augustine the Church’s reception, not the synagogue’s list, settles the matter. St. Cyril of Jerusalem c. 313–386 AD “Read the divine Scriptures, the twenty-two books of the Old Testament...But have nothing to do with the apocryphal writings. Study earnestly these only which we read openly in the Church.” ( Catechetical Lectures 4.35). Cyril is, in fact, a witness for the shorter Hebrew list: he counts twenty-two Old Testament books (grouping Baruch and the Epistle of Jeremiah with Jeremiah) and warns catechumens away from books outside it.

secs.h: The Jamnia Dispute — A Post-Christian Jewish Decision
secs.x: He is cited here in fairness — the patristic record is genuinely mixed, and not every Father favored the broader canon.

The Deuterocanonical Books — Individual Profiles Each of these books was read in the early Church, several are echoed in the New Testament, and all are in the lists of Hippo and Carthage, which the Byzantine Council in Trullo (692) later received for the Greek East. Here is what each contains and why it matters. Tobit OO EO RC Eth. A narrative about a righteous Jew in exile, his son Tobias, and the angel Raphael who heals blindness and drives away a demon. Rich in teachings on prayer, almsgiving, and marriage. Contains one of the most beautiful wedding prayers in scripture. The angel Raphael is named here (Tob 3:17; 12:15), one of only three angels named in the Septuagint Old Testament and New Testament, with Michael and Gabriel. “Prayer with fasting is good, but better than both is almsgiving with righteousness. A little with righteousness is better than wealth with wrongdoing. It is better to give alms than to lay up gold. For almsgiving saves from death and purges away every sin.” — Tobit 12:8–9 Judith OO EO RC Eth.

A heroic narrative about a pious Jewish widow who saves her city by assassinating the Assyrian general Holofernes. Theologically it emphasizes trust in God over military might, the power of prayer and fasting, and God’s use of the weak to shame the powerful — themes echoed in the New Testament’s Magnificat (Luke 1:52). Clement of Rome already holds up Judith’s courage as an example to the Church (1 Clement 55). “The Lord is a God who crushes wars; he sets up his camp among his people; he delivered me from the hands of my pursuers.” — Judith 16:2 1 Maccabees OO EO RC A historical account of the Maccabean revolt against Seleucid Greek oppression (175–134 BC), including the desecration and re-dedication of the Temple — the origin of Hanukkah. Essential historical background for understanding the New Testament world. Written in Hebrew (now lost), translated into Greek. Josephus used it as a primary historical source.

“They decreed by public ordinance and vote that the whole nation of the Jews should observe these days every year.” — 2 Maccabees 10:8 (the Feast of Dedication, whose founding 1 Maccabees 4:59 records; cf. John 10:22) 2 Maccabees OO EO RC A theological companion to 1 Maccabees, covering the same period from a different angle. Doctrinally the most significant deuterocanonical book: it explicitly teaches bodily resurrection (ch. 7 — the martyrdom of seven brothers), prayer for the dead (ch. 12), and the intercession of the saints (ch. 15, the vision of Onias and Jeremiah interceding). These are the clearest Old Testament witnesses that Orthodox and Catholics cite for these teachings, which the Church also holds from its liturgy and tradition. “He [Judas] also took up a collection, man by man, to the amount of two thousand drachmas of silver, and sent it to Jerusalem to provide for a sin offering. In doing this he acted very well and honorably, taking account of the resurrection.

For if he were not expecting that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead.” — 2 Maccabees 12:43–44 Wisdom of Solomon OO EO RC Eth. Written in Greek in Alexandria, probably 1st century BC, Wisdom presents divine Wisdom as a hypostatic figure who participates in creation. Many scholars see the prologue of John’s Gospel (John 1:1–18) as deliberately engaging Wisdom’s language. The book also contains the most explicit pre-Christian reflection on individual immortality in the Jewish scriptural tradition and a lengthy critique of idolatry that Paul echoes in Romans 1. “She is a reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness… She reaches mightily from one end of the earth to the other, and she orders all things well.” — Wisdom 7:26; 8:1 Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) OO EO RC Eth. The longest deuterocanonical book, written by Jesus ben Sirach of Jerusalem around 180 BC and translated into Greek by his grandson.

A comprehensive wisdom text covering ethics, family life, prayer, and the praise of famous men (ch. 44–50). The title “Ecclesiasticus” means “Church book” — a name given by the Latin West because it was so widely used for moral instruction in the early Church. James, Hebrews, and Matthew contain numerous echoes of Sirach. “With all your heart honor your father, and do not forget the birth pangs of your mother. Remember that through your parents you were born; and what can you give back to them that equals their gift to you?” — Sirach 7:27–28 Baruch (with Letter of Jeremiah) OO EO RC Eth. Attributed to Baruch, the scribe of Jeremiah, and circulated as an appendix to Jeremiah in the Septuagint. Contains a confession of Israel’s sin, a poem on divine Wisdom (chapter 3–4 closely parallels Proverbs 8 and Job 28), and an encouragement to exiles. Cyprian quotes the line “After this He was seen upon earth, and He conversed with men” under Jeremiah’s name as a prophecy of Christ ( Testimonies II.6), and Irenaeus likewise cites Baruch as Jeremiah ( Against Heresies V.35.1).
“Afterward she [Wisdom] appeared upon earth and lived among men.” — Baruch 3:38

Additional Books — Eastern & Oriental Orthodox Beyond the seven deuterocanonicals accepted by Rome, the Eastern and Oriental Orthodox traditions receive several additional texts, though practice varies somewhat by jurisdiction. 1 Esdras EO OO (Var.) RC (devotional) A Greek retelling and expansion of material from Ezra, Chronicles, and Nehemiah, plus a unique section — the Contest of the Three Guardsmen (1 Esd 3–4) — which concludes that truth is mightiest of all. The Eastern Orthodox Church treats it as canonical and the Ethiopian Church includes it; Rome printed it in the appendix of the Clementine Vulgate without canonical status. “But truth endures and is strong forever, and lives and prevails forever and ever. With it there is no partiality or preference.” — 1 Esdras 4:38–39 (NRSV) Prayer of Manasseh EO OO (Var.) RC (devotional) A short, beautiful penitential prayer purportedly spoken by King Manasseh of Judah — the most wicked of Judah’s kings (2 Kings 21) who repented in captivity (2 Chronicles 33:12–13).

The Chronicles account mentions Manasseh’s prayer but does not record it; this text fills that gap. Found in the Didascalia and the Apostolic Constitutions, and prayed in the Byzantine service of Great Compline. “I have sinned, O Lord, I have sinned, and I know my transgressions. I earnestly beseech thee, forgive me, O Lord, forgive me! Do not destroy me with my transgressions!” — Prayer of Manasseh 12–13 Psalm 151 OO EO RC (devotional) A short psalm in the first person attributed to David, describing his anointing and victory over Goliath. Found in the Septuagint manuscripts (marked “outside the number” in LXX) and found in Hebrew among the Dead Sea Scrolls (11QPs a ), confirming its antiquity. Canonical in both Eastern and Oriental Orthodoxy and in the Syriac Psalter; not part of the Catholic Bible. “I was small among my brethren, and youngest in my father's house: I tended my father's sheep. My hands formed a musical instrument, and my fingers tuned a psaltery. And who shall tell my Lord?” — Psalm 151:1–3 (LXX, tr.

Brenton) 3 Maccabees EO OO (Var.) RC: No Despite its name, 3 Maccabees has nothing to do with the Maccabean revolt. It describes events under Ptolemy IV Philopator of Egypt (3rd century BC): an attempt to force Jews into the cult of Dionysus, miraculous deliverance, and the institution of a feast of thanksgiving. Accepted in the Greek and Slavonic Bibles of the Eastern Orthodox Church and found in some Syriac manuscripts. Its Jewish-Egyptian setting resonates particularly with the Coptic tradition. “King of great power, Almighty God Most High, governing all creation with mercy, look upon the descendants of Abraham, O Father.” — 3 Maccabees 6:2–3

The Ethiopian Canon — 81 Books The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church preserves the largest biblical canon of any Christian tradition — reckoned as 81 books. It preserves ancient texts that were lost elsewhere. Ethiopia received Christianity in the 4th century through Frumentius, and its Bible was translated into Ge’ez from Greek in the following centuries, which is how Jewish writings such as Enoch and Jubilees, read by early Christians, survived there. Two Ways of Counting 81 The total of 81 is reached in two ways. The large printed Ge’ez and Amharic Bibles have 54 Old Testament books and the usual 27 New Testament books. The older reckoning in the traditional commentary on the Fetha Nagast counts 46 Old Testament books and 35 New Testament books, adding eight books of church order (the Sinodos, the Book of the Covenant, Clement and the Didascalia). Western writers call these the “narrower” and “broader” canons. 1 Enoch (Henok) Ethiopia Only One of the most remarkable canonical inclusions: the Book of Enoch, an extensive Jewish apocalyptic text (c.

300–200 BC) preserved in full only in the Ethiopian Ge’ez language. It was widely read in early Christianity — found in the Dead Sea Scrolls, cited by multiple Church Fathers, and explicitly quoted in the canonical New Testament book of Jude (vv. 14–15). Tertullian defended it as scripture. It was lost to other traditions and only recovered for Western scholarship when James Bruce returned from Ethiopia with manuscripts in 1773. “It was also about these that Enoch, in the seventh generation from Adam, prophesied, saying, ‘See, the Lord is coming with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all…’” — Jude 14–15, NRSVUE (quoting 1 Enoch 1:9) Jubilees Ethiopia Only Also called “Lesser Genesis,” Jubilees retells the narrative of Genesis and Exodus organized around a 49-year jubilee calendar. It was highly regarded at Qumran (15+ manuscripts found in the Dead Sea Scrolls), was cited by early Christian writers, and has been in continuous canonical use in Ethiopia. Gives expanded accounts of creation, the fallen angels, and patriarchal history.

Argues for a solar-based liturgical calendar, which distinguishes it from rabbinic tradition. “And there shall be no Satan nor any evil destroyer; for all their days shall be days of blessing and healing.” — Jubilees 23:29 (tr. R. H. Charles) 1–3 Meqabyan Ethiopia Only Despite being called “Maccabees” in some translations, the Meqabyan books are completely distinct from 1–4 Maccabees. They are Ge’ez works dealing with martyrdom, the power of God and persecution, and are not translations of any known Hebrew or Greek book. Unique to the Ethiopian canon and deeply embedded in Ethiopian theological identity. Broader NT Books Ethiopia Only The broader reckoning of the Ethiopian NT adds four works (counted as eight books) to the 27 shared NT books: Sinodos (Apostolic Canons, church order), Kidan (Book of the Covenant, liturgical law), Qalementos (Clement — a version of the Clementine literature), and Didaskalia (Apostolic teaching). These govern church practice, worship, and ethics.

They are treated as having normative authority for church life even if distinguished from the narrative books of the NT. Tertullian of Carthage c. 155–220 AD “Enoch had preceded, predicting that the demons, and the spirits of the angelic apostates, would turn into idolatry all the elements, all the garniture of the universe…” ( On Idolatry 4, ANF). Tertullian vigorously defended the authority of 1 Enoch in On the Apparel of Women I.3, arguing that it could have survived the Flood and that it is cited in Jude. St. Frumentius (Abba Salama) c. 300–380 AD The apostle of Ethiopia, consecrated by Athanasius of Alexandria, brought Christianity to Aksum. Under his influence the Aksumite kingdom became Christian under King Ezana. The Ethiopian canon was shaped in this Alexandrian theological environment, and the Ge’ez Bible translated from Greek in the following centuries kept Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch and Jubilees that the early Church had read.

secs.h: The Syriac Peshitta — An Ancient Variant NT
secs.x: The Syriac Peshitta — An Ancient Variant NT The Peshitta is the standard Bible of the Syriac-speaking churches (Syriac Orthodox, Maronite, Church of the East, Chaldean). The name means “simple” or “straight.” Its OT was translated largely from Hebrew, probably in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD, so it is younger than the Septuagint but an important independent witness. Its NT reflects a distinctive textual tradition. The Original Peshitta NT: 22 Books The original Peshitta New Testament contained 22 books — the 27 universal books minus 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude, and Revelation. These “five missing” books were not in the earliest Syriac canon and entered Syriac use only gradually, with some jurisdictions adding them by the 6th century and others later still. The Peshitta text tradition is one of the most ancient NT witnesses. Significance: The fact that the original Syriac NT lacked Revelation — the most disputed NT book in the Greek East — shows that Revelation’s place was genuinely uncertain there for a long time.

secs.h: The Syriac Peshitta — An Ancient Variant NT
secs.x: The canon was discerned by the Church over centuries, not settled at once. The Peshitta OT The Peshitta OT was largely translated directly from Hebrew, making it a distinct textual tradition from the LXX. It includes many deuterocanonical books (Sirach, Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, 1–2 Maccabees) though the precise canon varies by jurisdiction. Aphrahat the Persian Sage c. 280–345 AD One of the earliest Syriac Church Fathers, Aphrahat quotes Scripture extensively in his 23 Demonstrations . The early Syriac New Testament (the Peshitta) lacked Revelation and four of the shorter Catholic Epistles, and this shorter canon long remained standard in the Syriac-speaking churches. He shows that Syriac Christianity had its own ancient scriptural formation. Philoxenus of Mabbug 440–523 AD A Syriac Oriental Orthodox bishop under whom a new Syriac translation of the New Testament (the Philoxenian version, 508) was made. It included the minor Catholic Epistles missing from the Peshitta (2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude), and Revelation was translated into Syriac in the same period.

secs.h: The Syriac Peshitta — An Ancient Variant NT
secs.x: This shows both openness to the wider canon and an honest acknowledgment that these books were not in the earliest Syriac tradition.

New Testament Canon Development The New Testament canon was not handed down complete from the apostles — it developed through the life of the Church over three centuries. This is not a problem for Orthodox Christianity, which understands the Church as the guardian and authenticator of scripture, but it is a problem for Protestant theories of scripture that make the Bible prior to and independent of the Church. Protestants answer that the Church recognised a canon it did not create, since the books carried their authority from the start. c. AD 50–100 The Writings Appear Paul’s letters circulate among churches. The Gospels are composed. Revelation is written. These texts have authority from the start, but no “New Testament” as a collection exists. c. AD 140 Marcion’s Challenge The heretic Marcion of Sinope publishes his own truncated canon: only a version of Luke and 10 Pauline letters, rejecting the entire Old Testament. His challenge forces the Church to begin articulating criteria for recognizing authentic apostolic scripture. c.

AD 170 Muratorian Fragment The earliest known list of NT books, from Rome. Lists most of what would become the NT canon but includes the Apocalypse of Peter and the Wisdom of Solomon, and omits Hebrews, James, and 1 and 2 Peter. It also notes that some would not have the Apocalypse of Peter read in church. Most date it to the late 2nd century, though some scholars argue for the 4th. Either way it shows the canon was still in formation. c. AD 325 Eusebius' Categories Church historian Eusebius of Caesarea classifies NT books into three categories: accepted (Gospels, Acts, Paul’s letters, 1 John, 1 Peter, Revelation “if it seem right”), disputed (James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2–3 John), and spurious (Acts of Paul, Shepherd of Hermas, Apocalypse of Peter, Epistle of Barnabas, Didache). His disputed category includes books that remain in our NT today. AD 367 Athanasius' 39th Festal Letter Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria sends his annual Festal Letter listing the 27 books now in every NT. This is the first known complete list matching the modern NT exactly.

For the Old Testament he follows the Hebrew count (with Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah inside it) and sets Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith and Tobit, with the Didache and the Shepherd, “not indeed included in the Canon, but appointed by the Fathers to be read” by catechumens. He does not mention Maccabees. Protestants cite this distinction; Orthodox note that he still commends these books and reads them in the Church. AD 393 & 397 Councils of Hippo & Carthage The North African councils, with Augustine present and influential, list the 27-book NT and an OT that includes the deuterocanonical books. Pope Innocent I gives the same list in 405, and it becomes the common list of the Western church, though Jerome’s shorter view was never forgotten there. The Eastern church arrives at the same NT list through parallel development. AD 692 Quinisext Council (Trullan) The Byzantine council ratifies the canon decisions of Laodicea, Carthage, and Athanasius.

Notably, it endorses several lists that differ (Laodicea’s lacks Revelation and the deuterocanonicals, Carthage’s has both) without resolving them. The Oriental Orthodox did not take part in this council and do not receive it. AD 1546 Council of Trent In response to the Protestant Reformation, Trent formally defines the Roman Catholic biblical canon, including all 46 OT books. The Council of Florence had already listed the same books in its 1442 decree of union with the Copts, but Trent was the first to bind the list under anathema. The Eastern Orthodox answered the Protestant challenge at the Synod of Jerusalem (1672), which named Wisdom, Judith, Tobit, Sirach, Maccabees and the additions to Daniel as genuine Scripture. The Oriental Orthodox have never issued such a definition.

secs.h: NT Disputed Books — What the Fathers Debated
secs.x: NT Disputed Books — What the Fathers Debated Several books now in every edition of the New Testament were disputed, doubted, or questioned by major Church Fathers. Far from undermining the canon, this history shows that the canon was discerned carefully by the Church over time — not simply invented or inherited without reflection. Hebrews Authorship disputed from the beginning The Letter to the Hebrews was disputed not over its content — everyone valued it — but over its authorship. It does not name its author, and stylistic differences from Paul’s other letters led many to doubt Pauline authorship. Origen famously said: “But who wrote the epistle, in truth, God knows.” Yet he still used it as scripture. Clement of Rome (c. 96 AD) draws heavily on Hebrews (1 Clement 36), making it one of the earliest-used NT texts. Origen of Alexandria c.

secs.h: NT Disputed Books — What the Fathers Debated
secs.x: 185–253 AD “If I gave my opinion, I should say that the thoughts are those of the apostle, but the diction and phraseology are those of some one who remembered the apostolic teachings, and wrote down at his leisure what had been said by his teacher. Therefore if any church holds that this epistle is by Paul, let it be commended for this. For not without reason have the ancients handed it down as Paul’s. But who wrote the epistle, in truth, God knows.” ( apud Eusebius, HE 6.25.13–14) Revelation The most disputed NT book in the East Revelation (Apocalypse) was the most controversial NT book in the Eastern churches. Cyril of Jerusalem omitted it from his canon list. Gregory of Nazianzus left it out of his list. Eusebius placed it in both his “accepted” and “spurious” categories. The Syriac Peshitta originally excluded it, and the Syrian church doubted it for centuries. The Byzantine lectionary still has no readings from it. The Coptic Church, by contrast, reads the whole book on the night of Bright Saturday (Apocalypse Night).

secs.h: NT Disputed Books — What the Fathers Debated
secs.x: It was eventually accepted as canonical throughout all Orthodox traditions. St. Cyril of Jerusalem 313–386 AD “Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous… Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank.” ( Catechetical Lectures 4.36, NPNF). Cyril’s New Testament list does not include Revelation. St. Gregory Nazianzus 329–390 AD Gregory’s famous poem on the scriptural canon ( Carmen 1.12) lists 26 NT books — omitting only Revelation. His list ends by saying, in substance, that the reader now has them all, and whatever lies outside these is not among the genuine books. Yet Gregory’s judgment on this point was not final: the Church ultimately received the book. James Luther's “epistle of straw” James was among the “disputed” books in Eusebius’ list.

secs.h: NT Disputed Books — What the Fathers Debated
secs.x: Luther famously called it an “epistle of straw” because its emphasis on works seemed to contradict his doctrine of sola fide (faith alone). He placed James at the end of his German New Testament, unnumbered in the table of contents, along with Hebrews, Jude, and Revelation, books he considered of lesser authority. While Luther did not finally exclude them, his ranking introduced a Protestant tradition of questioning the universal canonical authority of these books. James stood in the Syriac Peshitta from the start and was accepted across the East by the fourth century. “You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.” — James 2:24 2 Peter / Jude Catholic Epistles disputed in multiple traditions Both 2 Peter and Jude were widely disputed in antiquity. 2 Peter was doubted by Eusebius, absent from the original Syriac canon, and questioned by Jerome. Jude was problematic because it explicitly quotes 1 Enoch (vv. 14–15) and the Assumption of Moses — non-canonical texts — as authoritative.

secs.h: NT Disputed Books — What the Fathers Debated
secs.x: This created a circular problem: if Jude quotes 1 Enoch as prophecy, does that make 1 Enoch canonical? The Ethiopian Church says yes. For the other Orthodox churches, the Jude quotation is treated as citing an early tradition without implying full canonicity for 1 Enoch.

secs.h: Church Fathers on the Biblical Canon
secs.x: Church Fathers on the Biblical Canon The Fathers quote the deuterocanonical books freely and often call them Scripture. Several of the formal lists, however, follow the shorter Hebrew count (Melito, Origen, Athanasius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome), while the African councils and Augustine give the larger list. The record is mixed, and the cards below show both sides. St. Clement of Rome c. 35–99 AD In his letter to the Corinthians ( 1 Clement , c. 96 AD), Clement holds up Judith as an example of heroic faith: “The blessed Judith, when her city was besieged, asked of the elders permission to go forth into the camp of the strangers; and, exposing herself to danger, she went out for the love which she bare to her country and people then besieged; and the Lord delivered Holofernes into the hands of a woman.” ( 1 Clement 55, ANF). He uses Judith as he uses the other Scriptures, as a model for Christians. St. Polycarp of Smyrna c.

secs.h: Church Fathers on the Biblical Canon
secs.x: 69–155 AD Polycarp’s letter to the Philippians echoes Tobit 4:10 and 12:9 as part of his moral teaching: “When you can do good, defer it not, because alms delivers from death.” ( Philippians 10, ANF). He shows no awareness that the book might be considered non-canonical. St. Irenaeus of Lyon c. 130–202 AD Irenaeus quotes Baruch 4:36–5:9 as a prophecy of Jeremiah: “And Jeremiah the prophet has pointed out, that as many believers as God has prepared for this purpose, to multiply those left upon earth, should both be under the rule of the saints to minister to this Jerusalem, and that [His] kingdom shall be in it, saying, Look around Jerusalem towards the east…” ( Against Heresies V.35.1, ANF). Tertullian of Carthage c. 155–220 AD Tertullian quotes Wisdom and Sirach and also appeals to 1 Enoch. He wrote five books against Marcion’s truncated canon, defending the Old Testament and the full Gospel. His defence of 1 Enoch ( On the Apparel of Women I.3) is the most vigorous patristic argument for that book. Origen of Alexandria c.

secs.h: Church Fathers on the Biblical Canon
secs.x: 185–253 AD Origen gave a list of twenty-two OT books following the Hebrew count, adding “besides these there are the Maccabees” (Eusebius, HE 6.25.2). In practice, his commentaries and homilies often cite Sirach, Wisdom, Judith, and Tobit as scripture. Origen represents the scholarly tradition of awareness of the Hebrew-Greek distinction without excluding the larger canon. St. Jerome of Stridon c. 347–420 AD Jerome is the Father most cited by Protestants because he expressed preference for the Hebraica Veritas — the Hebrew truth — and noted that Judith, Tobit, Wisdom, and Sirach “are not in the canon.” Yet his practice was looser than his theory: he translated Tobit and Judith at the request of bishops, the Vulgate kept all these books, and he still quotes Sirach and Wisdom in his letters and commentaries. Augustine objected to his preference for the Hebrew text over the Septuagint. St. Augustine of Hippo 354–430 AD Augustine was the most forceful patristic defender of the larger canon. For him the Church’s long reading of these books was itself evidence of their authority.

secs.h: Church Fathers on the Biblical Canon
secs.x: Of Maccabees he writes that they “are held as canonical, not by the Jews, but by the Church” ( City of God XVIII.36). He also defended the LXX as inspired, arguing that the Holy Spirit guided the translation just as he guided the original authors. St. Athanasius of Alexandria 296–373 AD Athanasius’ 39th Festal Letter (367 AD) is the first document to list the exact 27 NT books we have today. For the OT he lists 22 books (following Hebrew enumeration) but immediately adds: “But for greater exactness I add this also, writing of necessity; that there are other books besides these not indeed included in the Canon, but appointed by the Fathers to be read by those who newly join us, and who wish for instruction in the word of godliness. The Wisdom of Solomon, and the Wisdom of Sirach, and Esther, and Judith, and Tobit...” Protestants read this as a clear line between canon and edifying reading; Orthodox stress that he still sets these books apart from the heretics’ apocrypha and appoints them for the Church’s use. Both are true to the text. St.

secs.h: Church Fathers on the Biblical Canon
secs.x: Cyril of Alexandria 376–444 AD Patriarch of Alexandria and the great defender of Theotokos, Cyril regularly cites Wisdom and Sirach as inspired scripture in his Christological writings. His commentary on John often draws on Wisdom. As the leading theologian of the Alexandrian tradition that gave us the Coptic Church, his acceptance of these books is foundational for Oriental Orthodox canon tradition. St. John Chrysostom 347–407 AD Chrysostom quotes Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) often in his homilies, alongside the other books of Scripture and in the same way, as a source of moral teaching for the faithful. Clement of Alexandria c. 150–215 AD Clement quotes many of the deuterocanonical books, especially Wisdom and Sirach, alongside the other Scriptures, and cites 1 Enoch as well. He taught in the catechetical school of Alexandria after his teacher Pantaenus, and that Alexandrian tradition, which produced Origen, Athanasius and Cyril, inherited this broad use of the Greek Old Testament.

secs.h: How the Protestant Canon Was Formed
secs.x: How the Protestant Canon Was Formed The Protestant Old Testament canon took its final shape in the 16th century, when the Reformers adopted the Hebrew list against the common use of the Church. They could appeal to Jerome and to some medieval scholars who had kept his view, but the Church at large had read these books as Scripture for fifteen centuries. Understanding how this happened is essential for evaluating Protestant canon arguments. 1517–1520 Luther's Reformation Begins Martin Luther begins his reform movement. His key doctrines — sola scriptura (scripture alone) and sola fide (faith alone) — place him in conflict with teachings that have scriptural support only in the deuterocanonicals. Prayer for the dead (2 Macc 12) and purgatory (2 Macc 12:43–44) are the most direct conflicts. At the Leipzig Debate (1519) Johann Eck cited 2 Maccabees for purgatory, and Luther replied that the book was not canonical. 1534 Luther's German Bible Luther publishes a complete German Bible.

secs.h: How the Protestant Canon Was Formed
secs.x: He places the deuterocanonical books in a separate appendix between the Old and New Testaments, labeled: “Apocrypha: These are books which are not held equal to the Holy Scriptures, and yet are profitable and good to read.” This became the pattern for Protestant Bibles. 1546 Council of Trent (Catholic Response) The Roman Catholic Church responds to Luther by formally defining its canon for the first time, including all seven deuterocanonicals as fully canonical. This is the first dogmatic canon definition in Western Christian history. 1611 King James Bible The original 1611 King James Bible included the Apocrypha between the Testaments — the deuterocanonical books. The KJV without the Apocrypha is a later omission.

secs.h: How the Protestant Canon Was Formed
secs.x: Many Anglicans continued using these books for devotional reading under Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles (1563), which distinguished them from canonical scripture but permitted their use “for example of life and instruction of manners.” 1647 Westminster Confession of Faith The Westminster Confession formally defines the Protestant canon as 66 books, explicitly stating: “The books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture, and therefore are of no authority in the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved, or made use of, than other human writings.” Earlier Reformed confessions (French 1559, Belgic 1561) say the same, but Westminster became the most influential statement for modern evangelical canon views. 1827 British & Foreign Bible Society The British and Foreign Bible Society decides to print and distribute Bibles without the Apocrypha.

secs.h: How the Protestant Canon Was Formed
secs.x: This decision, taken under pressure from Scottish supporters who objected to the Apocrypha on theological grounds and not by any council, is largely responsible for the fact that most Protestant Bibles today do not include the deuterocanonicals even as an appendix. Luther’s and the KJV compilers’ intention to include them (even if demoted) is forgotten. The decisive question: Luther’s argument was that the deuterocanonicals were not in the Hebrew Bible. But which Hebrew Bible? The Hebrew canon was itself not fixed in pre-Christian Judaism. Different Jewish groups (Pharisees, Essenes, Alexandrian Jews) used different collections. And the decision to follow post-Christian rabbinic Judaism rather than the Septuagint used by Christ and the apostles is itself a theological choice, not a neutral appeal to historical fact.

Doctrinal Implications of the Deuterocanon The canon question is not merely academic. Removing the deuterocanonical books removes the primary scriptural basis for several important doctrines. Protestants say Luther simply followed Jerome and the Hebrew canon. Critics note the timing: 2 Maccabees had just been used against him at Leipzig in 1519. Prayer for the Dead 2 Maccabees 12:43–45: Judas Maccabeus collects money to offer sacrifice for the sins of fallen soldiers so they might be freed from sin at the resurrection. This passage is the direct biblical foundation for prayer for the dead and, in Catholic theology, purgatory. Removing 2 Maccabees removes this foundation. Most Protestant churches correspondingly reject prayer for the dead. Resurrection of the Body Alongside Daniel 12:2, 2 Maccabees 7 is one of the clearest Old Testament statements of individual bodily resurrection. The seven brothers who are tortured and killed declare their confidence that God will raise them, and one even speaks of receiving back his hands.

Hebrews 11:35 alludes directly to these martyrs: “Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release.” Intercession of Saints 2 Maccabees 15:12–16: Judas sees a vision of the high priest Onias (who had died) and the prophet Jeremiah (long dead) interceding for Israel. Jeremiah is described as “a man who loves the brethren and prays much for the people.” This text directly supports the Orthodox doctrine of the saints’ intercession. Without it, Protestant arguments against intercession of saints lose a major counter-text. Angelology Tobit 12:15: The angel Raphael reveals himself as “one of the seven angels who stand ready and enter before the glory of the Lord.” This is the only biblical text naming Raphael and speaking of seven angels who stand before God. Orthodox angelology — which venerates Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, and the other archangels — is grounded in this passage. Revelation 8:2 echoes it.

Wisdom Christology Wisdom of Solomon 7:26 calls divine Wisdom “a reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God.” Hebrews 1:3 calls Christ “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature” — almost certainly echoing Wisdom. John 1:1–18’s Logos prologue draws on Wisdom’s personified Wisdom theology. The Christological use of Wisdom provides rich theological grounding that is diminished when Wisdom is removed from the canon. Almsgiving & Salvation Tobit 12:9: “Almsgiving delivers from death and purges away every sin.” Sirach 3:30: “Water extinguishes a blazing fire: so almsgiving atones for sin.” These texts ground the Orthodox theology of almsgiving as a spiritual practice with salvific significance — part of the broader Orthodox understanding that salvation involves genuine transformation of life, not merely forensic declaration. Luther kept these books in his Bible but denied them authority to establish doctrine.

Protestant Objections & Oriental Orthodox Responses Protestant “Jesus and the apostles only quoted from the Hebrew Old Testament, not the Apocrypha.” OO Response It is true that the New Testament never quotes a deuterocanonical book with a formula such as “it is written.” But it never quotes Esther, Ecclesiastes or the Song of Songs either, and most of its quotations follow the Septuagint, the collection in which these books were read. Specific NT allusions and echoes to deuterocanonicals include: Matthew 27:43 echoing Wisdom 2:18–20; Hebrews 11:35–38 alluding to 2 Maccabees 6–7; Romans 1:18–32 extensively paralleling Wisdom 13–14; Hebrews 1:3 echoing Wisdom 7:26; James 1:19 paralleling Sirach 5:11; John 10:22 referencing the Feast of Dedication from 1 Maccabees 4; and Jude 14–15 directly quoting 1 Enoch (canonical in the Ethiopian Church). The argument that Jesus never cited the Apocrypha ignores the fact that he never explicitly “cited” most canonical books either — allusion and echo are the standard forms of scriptural engagement.

Protestant “The Jews rejected these books — we should follow the Jewish canon.” OO Response The relevant question is: which Jews, and when? Pre-Christian Alexandrian Jews used the LXX and its included books. The Qumran community valued 1 Enoch and Jubilees highly. The rabbis after Yavneh (c. AD 90) kept a narrower canon, and some scholars think the Christian use of the Greek books hardened their position. Protestants reply that Josephus already counts twenty-two books (c. AD 95) and that the list was older than Yavneh. Even granting that, the apostolic Church read the wider collection, and the rabbis are no authority for Christians. Moreover, Christians do not follow Judaism on the question of whether Jesus is Messiah — why would we follow Judaism on which books are scripture? Protestant “Jerome preferred the Hebrew canon — he is the greatest biblical scholar of the Fathers.” OO Response Jerome’s preference for the Hebrew text is a valid scholarly position about textual transmission — but it is not the same as a theological argument for excluding books from the canon.

Jerome himself translated Tobit and Judith (at the request of bishops), and the Vulgate that served Western Christianity for a thousand years kept all these books, the rest in their Old Latin form. He also quotes them in his letters and commentaries. Furthermore, Augustine, Jerome’s contemporary and the more influential theologian in the Western tradition, objected to Jerome’s preference for the Hebrew over the Septuagint and defended the larger canon. The tradition chose Augustine’s position in the Councils of Hippo and Carthage, not Jerome’s. Protestant “These books contain errors — Judith's geography is wrong; 2 Maccabees contradicts 1 Maccabees.” OO Response Historical and geographical anomalies in Judith are understood by many scholars as deliberate — the book signals its own theological character by mixing eras (Nebuchadnezzar reigning over Nineveh) to indicate it is a didactic narrative, not a chronicle.

The same hermeneutical charity applied to Genesis, Jonah, and Job — all of which contain features that cannot be read as straightforward historiography — should be applied here. As for 2 Maccabees, the differences from 1 Maccabees reflect different theological purposes and sources, not errors. This argument, applied consistently, would eliminate far more canonical books than it solves. Protestant “The early Church Fathers sometimes distinguished these books from the canon.” OO Response True — but the patristic evidence is far more complex than Protestant canon apologists typically acknowledge. (1) Fathers who note a distinction (Jerome, Athanasius) still include the books in their Bibles and cite them as scripture in practice. (2) The distinction they draw is typically not “these are false” but “these are for catechumens / for reading / of secondary status” — exactly how many Eastern churches still categorize Psalm 151 or the Prayer of Manasseh. (3) The councils that formally determined the canon in the West, Hippo 393 and Carthage 397, included the deuterocanonicals.

In fairness, the shorter lists were not rare in the Greek East (Athanasius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory of Nazianzus, Epiphanius), and some of the same lists also left out Revelation. The Church’s settled practice, East and West, went on reading these books as Scripture.

Frequently Asked Questions Why does the Oriental Orthodox Bible have more books than the Protestant Bible? Because the Oriental Orthodox tradition preserved the Septuagint (LXX) canon — the Greek Old Testament of the apostolic Church, from which the Latin, Coptic, Syriac (in part), Ethiopian and Armenian Bibles were made. The Protestant canon was reduced in the 16th century when Luther and the Reformers adopted the rabbinic Hebrew list, following Jerome. Critics note that this also removed the clearest text for prayer for the dead (2 Maccabees 12). “Now the whole canon of Scripture on which we say this judgment is to be exercised, is contained in the following books: Five books of Moses... and the two books of Maccabees.” — St. Augustine ( On Christian Doctrine II.8.13, c. AD 397) Did the apostles use the deuterocanonical books? Yes. The New Testament authors quote, echo, and allude to the deuterocanonicals frequently. Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch directly. Hebrews 11:35–38 alludes to the Maccabean martyrs.

Romans 1:18–32 parallels Wisdom 13–14 so closely that scholars debate whether Paul is quoting or echoing. Hebrews 1:3 echoes Wisdom 7:26. The LXX — which included these books — was the Bible the apostles used and cited. Why does the Ethiopian Bible have 81 books? The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church received Christianity in the 4th century through Frumentius (consecrated by Athanasius of Alexandria) and translated its Bible from the Greek. This preserved ancient texts — especially 1 Enoch and Jubilees — that were lost to other traditions. 1 Enoch was widely used in early Christianity (cited by Jude, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria) and survived complete only in Ge’ez. The Ethiopian canon is best seen as a preservation of writings the early Church read, not as an expansion. Does the Oriental Orthodox Church have an official, definitive canon list? The Oriental Orthodox churches have never issued a single formal canon definition comparable to Trent.

The canon is received through tradition: the liturgy, the patristic citations, the ancient manuscripts, and the practice of the churches. The core 73 books (39 + 7 deuterocanonicals + 27 NT) are universally accepted. Additional books like Psalm 151, 1 Esdras, and Prayer of Manasseh are received in some OO churches, such as the Coptic and Syriac; the Ethiopian canon extends further to 81. This diversity is not a weakness but reflects the conciliar, distributed nature of Orthodox authority. What is the difference between “deuterocanonical” and “apocryphal”? “Deuterocanonical” (second canon) is the Catholic and Orthodox term for the books accepted as canonical that are not in the Hebrew Bible — recognizing that they entered the canon’s formal definition slightly later or through different channels than the protocanonical books, but affirming their full scriptural authority. “Apocryphal” means “hidden” and is the Protestant term for these same books — implying they are non-canonical additions.

Protestants and Catholics also speak of “Pseudepigrapha,” Jewish writings outside every Western canon such as 1 Enoch and Jubilees (both canonical in the Ethiopian Church). Early Christian works never received as Scripture, such as the Gospel of Thomas, are called New Testament apocrypha. If the canon was disputed for centuries, how can we trust any of it? This question assumes that divine inspiration requires immediate universal recognition, which is not a biblical or patristic principle. The Orthodox answer is that the Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, discerned the canon through its life, worship, and theological reflection over time — exactly as it discerned the doctrines of the Trinity and the nature of Christ. The canon debates demonstrate serious, careful engagement with the scriptures, not casual acceptance. The books that were disputed (Hebrews, Revelation, James) were doubted precisely because they were scrutinized seriously; their eventual acceptance reflects the Church’s Spirit-guided confidence, not arbitrary decision.

Glossary Septuagint (LXX) The Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, begun in Alexandria in the 3rd century BC and completed over the next two centuries. Used by the New Testament authors and the early Church. Includes the deuterocanonical books. Deuterocanonical “Second canon.” The seven books (Tobit, Judith, 1–2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch) included in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles but not the Protestant Bible. Fully canonical in OO, EO, and RC traditions. Protocanonical The 39 Old Testament books accepted by all traditions and corresponding to the Hebrew Bible. Also called the “first canon.” Apocrypha Protestant term for the deuterocanonical books, implying non-canonical status. From Greek apokryphos (hidden). Also used technically for books that no tradition accepts as canonical (e.g., Gospel of Thomas). Peshitta The standard Syriac Bible, meaning “simple.” The Peshitta OT was translated from Hebrew; the original Peshitta NT contained 22 books (lacking Revelation, 2–3 John, 2 Peter, Jude). Jamnia / Yavneh Rabbinic gatherings at Yavneh c.

AD 90 where post-Temple Jewish scholars worked toward canon consensus, excluding Greek-language books. The older term “Council of Jamnia” (a 19th-century scholarly construction) is now largely abandoned; the canon settled through gradual rabbinic discussion, not a single formal council. Protestants argue the shorter list was already fixed before Christ; Orthodox reply that the evidence for this is thin. Canon From Greek kanon (measuring rod). The list of books recognized as divinely inspired scripture by a given tradition. Different Christian traditions have different canons. Hebraica Veritas “Hebrew truth.” Jerome’s principle that the Hebrew text of the OT is more authoritative than the Greek Septuagint. Adopted by Reformers to justify using the shorter Hebrew canon. Muratorian Fragment The earliest known list of NT books (c. AD 170, Rome). Lists most of the NT but includes non-canonical texts and lacks several books, demonstrating the canon was still developing. Sola Scriptura “Scripture alone.” The Protestant principle that scripture is the only authoritative source of doctrine.

Orthodox point out that the list of books itself was received through the Church’s tradition; Protestants answer that the Church recognised the canon rather than conferring authority on it. 1 Enoch (Henok) An ancient Jewish apocalyptic text quoted in Jude 14–15. Canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Churches. Preserved complete only in the Ethiopian Ge’ez language. Cited by Tertullian, Clement, and other early Fathers. Tewahedo “Being made one.” The Ge’ez name of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches, referring to the complete union of divinity and humanity in Christ (miaphysitism). The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church holds the largest biblical canon of any Christian tradition.
