Luke 1:43 St. Cyril of Alexandria (d. 444) "If anyone will not confess that the Emmanuel is very God, and that therefore the Holy Virgin is the Mother of God [Theotokos], inasmuch as in the flesh she bore the Word of God made flesh ... let him be anathema" (First Anathema, Third Letter to Nestorius ). Was Mary really ever-virgin? Yes — the Oriental Orthodox affirm Mary’s perpetual virginity before, during, and after the birth of Christ.

The "brothers of the Lord" mentioned in the Gospels (Matt 12:46; Mark 6:3) are understood in the OO tradition (following Epiphanius) as sons of Joseph from a prior marriage, or as cousins — the Greek word adelphos covers both relations, as does the Aramaic word achim. Tertullian thought Mary had other children after Jesus, but by the 4th century the Church’s teaching was settled, and when Helvidius denied it Jerome answered him. The Gospel of Matthew says Joseph "knew her not until she had given birth to a son" (Matt 1:25), using "until" idiomatically — not implying a change afterward, just as "the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool" does not imply he ceases to sit afterward. "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel." Matthew 1:23 (citing Isaiah 7:14) St. Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373) Against the Arians, Athanasius speaks of the Son who "took true human flesh of Mary Ever-Virgin" ( Against the Arians II.70). Why is Mary honored so highly? Because Scripture commands it.

The Holy Spirit inspired Elizabeth to say "Blessed are you among women" (Luke 1:42), Gabriel to address her as "favored one" (Luke 1:28), and Mary herself to prophesy "henceforth all generations will call me blessed" (Luke 1:48). To refuse to call her blessed — out of Protestant anxiety about excess — is to disobey a Spirit-inspired prophecy. The Oriental Orthodox honor Mary because she is the Theotokos, the greatest of all human beings, the most perfect cooperator with God’s grace, the first to receive Christ into herself. She is also the mother of every Christian — "Behold, your mother" (John 19:27). For a full treatment see The Theotokos → "For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name." Luke 1:48-49 St. Ephrem the Syrian (d. 373) "Blessed be Mary, who without vows and without prayer, in her Virginity conceived and brought forth the Lord of all the sons of her companions, who have been or shall be chaste and righteous, priests and kings" ( Hymns on the Nativity 6).

Is venerating saints a form of worship? No. The Eastern tradition carefully distinguishes latreia (worship, adoration due to God alone) from dulia and proskynesis (honor, veneration given to saints). When an angel appears in Revelation and John falls at his feet, the angel refuses: "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you… Worship God" (Rev 19:10) — the refusal of divine worship by a creature, not of all reverence. The Church gives saints the highest human honor precisely because they are filled with God — and honoring them is, ultimately, honoring the grace of God working in them. The same Greek word for "venerate" (proskuneo) is used for honoring earthly kings in the Old Testament without implying idolatry. "You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve." Matthew 4:10 — worship (latreia) is God’s alone; honor of holy persons is a different act St. Basil of Caesarea (d. 379) "The honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype" ( On the Holy Spirit 18.45). St.
John of Damascus quotes these words of Basil in defending the icons ( Exposition of the Orthodox Faith IV.16).

Icons Why use icons? The Incarnation made the invisible visible. Before Christ, no one could depict the face of God — "no one has ever seen God" (John 1:18). But "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). God took a human face. To refuse to depict that face is, paradoxically, to deny that the Incarnation was real. An icon of Christ is a confession: the eternal Word truly became a specific, visible, depictable human being. Paul calls Christ "the image (eikon) of the invisible God" (Col 1:15) — Christ himself is the first icon, the perfect image of the Father. Our icons are images of that image. For a full treatment see Icon Veneration → "He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation." Colossians 1:15 St. John of Damascus (d. c. 749) "Of old, God the incorporeal and uncircumscribed was never depicted. Now, however, when God is seen clothed in flesh, and conversing with men, I make an image of the God whom I see" ( On Holy Images I.16, tr. Allies).

Isn’t venerating icons a violation of the Second Commandment? The Second Commandment forbids making idols to worship as gods — not the making of sacred images as such. God himself commanded the making of sacred images: the golden cherubim on the Ark of the Covenant (Exod 25:18-20), the bronze serpent that prefigures Christ (Num 21:8-9), the embroidered figures of cherubim in the Temple curtains (Exod 26:31). The issue was never images — it was treating images as gods. After the Incarnation, when the invisible God took a visible face, the theological situation changed: now we can and should depict his face. The Seventh Ecumenical Council (Nicaea 787) explicitly addressed this, distinguishing veneration of icons from idolatry. "And you shall make two cherubim of gold; of hammered work shall you make them, on the two ends of the mercy seat." Exodus 25:18 — God commands sacred images St. John of Damascus (d. c. 749) "For as Basil, that much-versed expounder of divine things, says, the honour given to the image passes over to the prototype.

Now a prototype is that which is imaged, from which the derivative is obtained" ( Exposition of the Orthodox Faith IV.16). What’s the difference between worshipping an icon and venerating one? Worship (latreia) is offered to God alone — it means total submission, adoration, and ultimate dependence on a being as the source of one’s existence. Veneration (proskynesis, dulia) is honor given to a holy person or object that points beyond itself. When you venerate an icon, the honor passes through the image to the person depicted. Nicaea 787 defined this precisely: the icon receives veneration (proskynesis) but not worship (latreia). It is the same distinction as kissing a photograph of someone you love — you are not worshipping the photograph; you are expressing love for the person. The material object is the medium, not the end.

"God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth." John 4:24 — true worship is directed to God; reverence for holy things is a different act Seventh Ecumenical Council, Nicaea II (787) "For the honour which is paid to the image passes on to that which the image represents, and he who reveres the image reveres in it the subject represented." Icons receive "due salutation and honourable reverence ..., not indeed that true worship of faith [latreia] which pertains alone to the divine nature" (Definition of the Council). Why kiss icons? The kiss is one of the oldest human gestures of love, greeting, and reverence — "greet one another with a holy kiss" (Rom 16:16). To kiss an icon is a physical act of love toward the person depicted — Christ, the Theotokos, a saint — because we are embodied beings and our faith must involve the body. The Incarnation itself is God’s statement that the physical is not beneath holiness; matter can carry grace.

The woman in Luke 7:38 kissed the feet of Jesus as an act of love and devotion — the Church continues that gesture toward his holy image. The kiss does not transfer power from the icon; it expresses love toward its subject. "She began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment." Luke 7:38 St. Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373) "And we may perceive this at once from the illustration of the Emperor's image. For in the image is the shape and form of the Emperor, and in the Emperor is that shape which is in the image" ( Against the Arians III.5). The Fathers who defended the icons built on this same picture of the king and his portrait.

Salvation Are we saved by faith alone? The phrase "faith alone" appears exactly once in the New Testament — in James 2:24: "a man is justified by works and not by faith alone." The OO understands salvation as theosis — a process of participation in the divine life — which is entered by faith and lived out in the whole person. We are "saved through faith" (Eph 2:8), not by our own merit — the OO agrees entirely. But the faith that saves is not an intellectual assent or a moment of decision; it is a living trust that necessarily produces love, obedience, and cooperation with grace. "Faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead" (Jas 2:17). Faith is the door; the whole life of sacrament, prayer, and virtue is what lies beyond it. "You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone." James 2:24 St. John Chrysostom (d. 407) On Romans 2: "it is not right to trust in faith only. For it is deeds also into which that tribunal will enquire" ( Homily 5 on Romans ).

What is theosis (union with God)? Theosis is deification — the process by which the human person genuinely participates in the divine nature and becomes, by grace, what God is by nature. It is not absorption into God (that would be pantheism) but transformation by union with him — the human person retaining their identity while being thoroughly penetrated by divine life and light. Athanasius’ summary is the classic: "He was made man that we might be made God." Peter calls this "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Pet 1:4). Theosis is the goal of the Christian life — not merely forgiveness of sins, not merely a ticket to heaven, but genuine transformation into the likeness of God, beginning now and consummated in the resurrection. For more see Salvation → "He has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature." 2 Peter 1:4 St. Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373) "The Word was made flesh in order to offer up this body for all, and that we partaking of His Spirit, might be deified" ( De Decretis 14).

Can salvation be lost? Yes. The OO does not teach the Reformed doctrine of the perseverance of the saints, or the popular "once saved, always saved." Salvation in the OO framework is not a one-time forensic transaction but an ongoing relationship and process of theosis. Relationships can be broken. Paul warns explicitly: "if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off" (Rom 11:21-22). The prodigal son was the father’s son; he left; he returned. The possibility of falling away is the very reason the New Testament is full of calls to persevere, to run the race to the end, and to work out salvation with fear and trembling. "Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness." Romans 11:22 St. John Chrysostom (d.

407) On Romans 11:22 to 23: "For it was not God that cut them off, but they have broken themselves off and fallen" ( Homily 19 on Romans ). What role do works play in salvation? Works do not earn salvation — we are saved by grace through faith, "not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Eph 2:8-9). But the very next verse says: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them" (Eph 2:10). Works are not the cause of salvation but its necessary fruit and arena. A person genuinely united to Christ will produce his fruits — not to earn union but because union produces them. The absence of works reveals that faith is not alive (Jas 2:17). In the OO framework, works are also the concrete expression of theosis — acts of love, fasting, prayer, and mercy are the means by which the divine life grows in us. "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them." Ephesians 2:10 St. Cyril of Jerusalem (d.

386) "For the method of godliness consists of these two things, pious doctrines, and virtuous practice: and neither are the doctrines acceptable to God apart from good works, nor does God accept the works which are not perfected with pious doctrines" ( Catechetical Lecture 4.2). What happens to people who never hear the Gospel? The OO teaches with humility here, refusing to draw God’s boundaries more narrowly than he has drawn them. God is just and does not condemn people for what they could not have known. Paul writes that those without the written law "are a law to themselves" because the law is written on their hearts (Rom 2:14-15). The economy of salvation is entirely Christ’s — but his mercy is not mechanically limited to those who have received the explicit Gospel. Justin Martyr spoke of the logos spermatikos — seeds of the divine Word scattered in all human reason. What the OO will not say is that everyone is automatically saved regardless; what it will not say either is that God damns the sincerely seeking. The rest is God’s mystery, and it is in good hands.

"For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves." Romans 2:14 St. Justin Martyr (d. c. 165) "Those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; as, among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus, and men like them" ( First Apology 46).

Sacraments Why are sacraments necessary? Because we are embodied beings. God does not save us as disembodied minds — he saves us in our whole persons, through physical means, because the physical is what we are. The Incarnation is the principle: God used matter — a body, water, bread, oil, the laying on of hands — to convey his presence and grace. When Jesus said "unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you" (John 6:53), he was not speaking metaphorically — he was naming a specific, physical, sacramental requirement. The sacraments are not rituals that symbolize a grace obtained elsewhere; they are the means through which the grace of Christ’s Incarnation, death, and resurrection is applied to each person. "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you." John 6:53 St. Cyril of Jerusalem (d.

386) "Consider therefore the Bread and the Wine not as bare elements, for they are, according to the Lord's declaration, the Body and Blood of Christ; for even though sense suggests this to you, yet let faith establish you" ( Mystagogical Lecture 4.6). What actually happens in baptism? Baptism is death and resurrection with Christ. Paul’s teaching is explicit: "all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death… we were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life" (Rom 6:3-4). It is also new birth — "unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God" (John 3:5). In the OO, baptism is by triple immersion, death and resurrection enacted in the body, conferring adoption as children of God, forgiveness of personal sins, and entry into the Body of Christ. Chrismation immediately follows, conferring the seal of the Holy Spirit.

"We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life." Romans 6:3-4 St. Cyril of Jerusalem (d. 386) "And at the self-same moment you were both dying and being born; and that Water of salvation was at once your grave and your mother" ( Mystagogical Lecture 2.4). Why baptize infants? Infants need what baptism gives. The OO does not baptize infants to remove inherited guilt (the Eastern tradition does not teach inherited guilt — see Original Sin → ), but to give them union with Christ, the healing of the fallen nature, adoption as children of God, and the indwelling Holy Spirit. If an infant is fully a human being in need of salvation, why would we withhold the means of salvation? Paul explicitly links baptism to Old Testament circumcision (Col 2:11-12) — which was given to eight-day-old infants as the covenant sign. The household baptisms in Acts (Acts 16:15, 16:33) almost certainly included children.

Origen states plainly that the Church received from the Apostles the tradition of baptizing infants, and Cyprian’s council (c. 253) ruled that infants need not wait until the eighth day. "In him also you were circumcised… having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him." Colossians 2:11-12 Origen (d. c. 253) "The Church received from the apostles the tradition of giving baptism even to infants" ( Commentary on Romans 5.9). He goes on to say the apostles knew that all are born with the stains of sin that must be washed away through water and the Spirit. This work survives only in Rufinus' Latin translation. Is the Eucharist really Christ’s Body and Blood? Yes — this is the unambiguous and universal teaching of the early Church. Jesus said "This is my body… this is my blood" (Matt 26:26-28) at the Last Supper and then said in John 6 that unless you eat his flesh and drink his blood, you have no life in you — so literally that many disciples left and Jesus did not call them back to explain it was metaphorical.

Paul warns that eating and drinking unworthily is eating and drinking judgment on oneself, "not discerning the body of the Lord" (1 Cor 11:29). The Eucharist is the center and summit of OO worship because it is not a memorial ceremony — it is the real, living presence of the risen Christ, offered and received. "For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread… ‘This is my body which is for you.’" 1 Corinthians 11:23-24 St. Ignatius of Antioch (d. c. 107) Of the heretics of his day: "They abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father, of His goodness, raised up again" ( Smyrnaeans 7). Why confess sins to a priest? Because Christ gave the apostolic ministry the authority to forgive sins. On the evening of the resurrection, Jesus breathed on the disciples and said: "Receive the Holy Spirit.

If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld" (John 20:22-23). This is a real commission, not a metaphor — an authority exercised through the apostolic succession of bishops and priests. Confession is not telling your sins to a man as though he were the judge; the priest is a witness and a minister. The words of absolution are Christ’s words through him. James commands "confess your sins to one another" (Jas 5:16) as part of the healing ministry of the Church. Regular confession is essential to the life of theosis — it clears the mirror of the soul. "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld." John 20:23 St. Ambrose of Milan (d. 397) "For this power has been entrusted to priests alone. Rightly, therefore, does the Church claim it, which has true priests" ( On Repentance I.2.7). Why receive Chrismation immediately after baptism? Because the gift of the Holy Spirit has always been inseparable from baptism in the Apostolic pattern.

Peter at Pentecost proclaimed: "Repent and be baptized… and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:38) — one action, two dimensions. The OO (along with Eastern Orthodoxy) maintains this ancient, integrated initiation: Baptism, Chrismation (anointing with the Holy Myron), and first Eucharist are administered together, even to infants. The Western practice of delaying Confirmation to adolescence is a medieval innovation — a pastoral accommodation that became separated from its sacramental context. The Apostolic pattern is a single, complete initiation into the full life of the Church. "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit." Acts 2:38 St. Cyril of Jerusalem (d. 386) "And to you in like manner, after you had come up from the pool of the sacred streams, there was given an Unction, the anti-type of that wherewith Christ was anointed; and this is the Holy Ghost" ( Mystagogical Lecture 3.1).

Worship and Liturgy Why are services so long? The Eucharistic liturgy is not designed for efficiency — it is an entering into eternity. The early believers "devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers" (Acts 2:42) and "spent the whole night in prayer" (Luke 6:12, following Jesus’ own pattern). The worship described in Revelation 4-5 is unceasing and unhurried — the four living creatures cry "Holy, holy, holy" without pause. Long liturgies are not a failure of planning; they are a refusal to let urgency substitute for depth. They are also a countercultural act — they insist that meeting God is not something to be squeezed into a convenient slot. You do not set a timer on an encounter with eternity. "And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, ‘Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty.’" Revelation 4:8 St. Cyril of Jerusalem (d.

386) On the Holy, Holy, Holy of the Liturgy: "For the reason of our reciting this confession of God, delivered down to us from the Seraphim, is this, that so we may be partakers with the hosts of the world above in their Hymn of praise" ( Mystagogical Lecture 5.6). Why is worship so structured and repetitive? Structure is not the enemy of spirit — it is its container. The Psalms are structured and repetitive (Psalm 136 repeats "his steadfast love endures forever" twenty-six times). The seraphim cry "Holy, Holy, Holy" without ceasing (Isa 6:3). Jesus himself "went to the synagogue, as was his custom" (Luke 4:16) — structured, weekly, liturgical worship. Liturgical forms protect the faith against individual distortion, unite the worshipper across centuries with the same words, and provide a vessel into which the heart can pour itself without having to reinvent the prayer from scratch each Sunday. Familiarity is not staleness — it allows the words to sink deeper over decades, revealing inexhaustible depths.

"Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever." Psalm 136:1 — refrain repeated 26 times in one psalm St. Basil of Caesarea (d. 379) "Thus we all look to the East at our prayers ... We pray standing, on the first day of the week" ( On the Holy Spirit 27.66). Basil gives these, with the words of invocation over the Eucharistic bread and cup and the blessing of the baptismal water, as practices received by unwritten tradition. Why do people stand so much? Standing is the posture of the resurrection. We stand because Christ has risen and we share in his victory — "rise, let us go" (Matt 26:46). Kneeling expresses penitence and humility; standing expresses the joy and freedom of those for whom Christ has won. The Council of Nicaea (325, Canon 20) explicitly prohibited kneeling on Sundays, recognizing that Sunday — the day of resurrection — calls for the posture of the risen. Standing is also the posture of readiness and watchfulness — "stand firm in the faith" (1 Cor 16:13), "having done all, to stand" (Eph 6:13).

The body participates in worship, and the posture of the body is a theology in itself. "Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm." Ephesians 6:13 Council of Nicaea, Canon 20 (325) "Forasmuch as there are certain persons who kneel on the Lord's Day and in the days of Pentecost, therefore, to the intent that all things may be uniformly observed everywhere (in every parish), it seems good to the holy Synod that prayer be made to God standing." Why are ancient languages sometimes used? The ancient liturgical languages — Coptic, Ge’ez, classical Armenian, classical Syriac — serve two purposes simultaneously. First, they provide continuity: the same syllables that shaped the worship of the earliest Christians in each community still shape it today, creating an acoustic thread across fifteen centuries. Second, they mark worship as a register distinct from ordinary speech — the encounter with the holy has traditionally been approached with a language set apart.

In practice, most OO churches use both the ancient tongue and the vernacular together, so comprehension is not sacrificed. The ancient language is not a barrier to participation; it is an invitation into the depth of time. "…addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart." Ephesians 5:19 Note Coptic is the last stage of the language of ancient Egypt, written in an alphabet drawn from Greek. It remains a liturgical language of the Coptic Church, used alongside Arabic and the local language of each country. Why is there so much chanting? Because Scripture is meant to be sung. The Psalms are songs — the Hebrew word mizmor means "song." Paul commands "psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs" (Eph 5:19; Col 3:16). The Temple worship, which Jesus himself attended and participated in, was musical. Chanting slows the text, forces attention to each word, elevates speech into prayer, and carries the voice into a different state of attention.

The monotone of Coptic chant, the polyphony of Ethiopian praise, the ancient modes of Syriac hymnody — these are not decorations on the liturgy. They are the liturgy in its most concentrated form, shaped over centuries into vehicles for the praise of God. "Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works!" Psalm 105:2 St. Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373) In his Letter to Marcellinus (27 to 29), Athanasius explains that the Psalms are chanted with melody not for the sake of pleasant sound, but so that the harmony of the voice may bring the soul into harmony and order. (Summary, not a quotation.) Why doesn’t the sermon take center stage? Because the Eucharist is the center of Christian worship, not the homily. The Apostles’ practice was centered on "the breaking of bread" (Acts 2:42), with teaching as one element among four. In much of Evangelical Protestantism the sermon is the climax of the service and the Eucharist (if celebrated at all) is an addendum. In the OO the order is reversed: everything — readings, psalmody, homily — leads toward the Eucharist.

Words about God, however excellent, are subordinate to encounter with God. The homily prepares the heart; the Liturgy delivers what the heart is prepared to receive. This is not anti-intellectual; it is a statement about what kind of thing Christian worship ultimately is. "For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes." 1 Corinthians 11:26 St. Ignatius of Antioch (d. c. 107) "For there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and one cup to [show forth] the unity of His blood; one altar; as there is one bishop, along with the presbytery and deacons" ( Philadelphians 4).

Fasting Why does the Church require so much fasting? The OO calendar includes approximately 180-210 fasting days per year — more than most Christian traditions. Fasting is not dietary discipline for its own sake; it is the training of the whole person — body and soul together — in self-mastery, simplicity, and longing for God. The body’s hunger, redirected toward prayer, becomes a physical expression of the soul’s hunger for God. Jesus said "when you fast" (Matt 6:16-18), not "if you fast" — he assumed his disciples would fast. The OO fasting seasons (Lent, Apostles’ Fast, Advent, Dormition Fast, Wednesdays and Fridays) follow the rhythm of the liturgical year and orient the whole life of the Christian toward the mysteries of salvation. "And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces that their fasting may be seen by others… And your Father who sees in secret will reward you." Matthew 6:16, 18 St. Basil of Caesarea (d.

379) "It was the first commandment that Adam received: 'Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil ye shall not eat.' ... Since we did not fast, we fell from Paradise; let us, therefore, fast in order that we might return thither" ( On Fasting , Homily 1.3 to 4). Is fasting biblical? Thoroughly. Moses fasted forty days at Sinai (Exod 34:28). Elijah fasted forty days in the wilderness (1 Kgs 19:8). David fasted in penitence (2 Sam 12:16-23). The entire nation fasted on the Day of Atonement (Lev 23:27). John the Baptist and his disciples fasted (Matt 9:14). Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness (Matt 4:2) and taught his disciples the proper way to fast — assuming they would (Matt 6:16-18). The Apostles fasted before appointing elders (Acts 14:23). Paul fasted frequently (2 Cor 11:27). Fasting is not a pious extra — it is one of the three pillars of the inner life that Jesus addresses in the Sermon on the Mount alongside prayer and almsgiving (Matt 6). "Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.

And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry." Matthew 4:1-2 St. John Chrysostom (d. 407) "Fasting is a medicine; but a medicine, though it be never so profitable, becomes frequently useless owing to the unskilfulness of him who employs it" ( Homily 3 on the Statues ). Why avoid animal products during fasts? The OO fast — abstinence from meat, dairy, fish (in stricter seasons), oil, and wine — is rooted in the Daniel fast (Dan 1:8-16; Dan 10:3) in which Daniel abstained from the king’s rich food and ate only vegetables and water. The principle is simplicity and the subduing of the appetites. Rich foods stimulate the body and distract the mind; simple food quiets them. Paul says "it is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble" (Rom 14:21), acknowledging the spiritual weight of food choices. The strict OO fast also expresses solidarity with the poor, who eat simply by necessity, and reminds the Christian that they are stewards, not masters, of creation.

"Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king’s food, or with the wine that he drank." Daniel 1:8 St. John Chrysostom (d. 407) "For the honour of fasting consists not in abstinence from food, but in withdrawing from sinful practices" ( Homily 3 on the Statues ). What if I cannot keep the fast? Economia — pastoral accommodation — applies in full force here. The sick, the pregnant, the nursing, the elderly, young children, and those with medical conditions are exempt, without guilt or spiritual loss. The purpose of fasting is spiritual growth, not legal compliance; a fast that destroys health is not a holy fast. Jesus himself said "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" (Matt 12:7) when the Pharisees criticized his disciples for a technicality. The spirit of fasting — simplicity, restraint, increased prayer, redirection of appetite toward God — can be maintained even when the full letter cannot. A spiritual father or confessor guides the practice according to each person’s condition and capacity.

"And if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless." Matthew 12:7 Apostolic Canons (c. 4th century) "If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or reader, or singer, does not fast the holy Quadragesimal fast of Easter, or the fourth day, or the day of Preparation, let him be deposed, unless he be hindered by some bodily infirmity" (Canon 69). Even this strict canon makes room for the sick.

Christology What is Miaphysitism? Miaphysitism is the Christological teaching of the Oriental Orthodox churches: that Jesus Christ has one united nature (Greek: mia physis) that is both divine and human, joined without separation, confusion, mixture, or alteration. The "one" is not a simple arithmetic one (which would be Monophysitism — see below) but a composite one: the Incarnate Word is a single, undivided subject who is both fully divine and fully human. The formula comes from St. Cyril of Alexandria: "one nature of the Word of God Incarnate" (mia physis tou Theou Logou sesarkomene). The Oriental Orthodox maintain that this formulation faithfully expresses the Nicene and Ephesian faith, and that Chalcedon’s language of "two natures" risked the Nestorian error of dividing Christ’s person. For a full treatment see Christology → and The Chalcedonian Schism → "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God… And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." John 1:1, 14 St. Cyril of Alexandria (d.

444) "We, therefore, confess one Christ and Lord, not as worshipping a man with the Word (lest this expression with the Word should suggest to the mind the idea of division), but worshipping him as one and the same" ( Second Letter to Nestorius ). Are Oriental Orthodox Monophysites? No — this is the most persistent and most damaging misrepresentation of OO theology. Monophysitism (properly: Eutychianism) teaches that Christ has only one nature, with his humanity absorbed into or swallowed by his divinity — like a drop of honey in the ocean. This was explicitly condemned by the Oriental Orthodox as a heresy. The OO condemned Eutyches and rejected Monophysitism just as firmly as any other church. The OO formula — one composite nature, fully divine and fully human, united without confusion — is the precise opposite of Monophysitism.

Modern ecumenical dialogue (including the 1973 Common Declaration of Pope Paul VI and Pope Shenouda III, and the 1989–1990 Agreed Statements with the Eastern Orthodox) has confirmed that the OO and Chalcedonian churches hold the same essential Christological faith despite different technical terminology. "For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily." Colossians 2:9 Pope Shenouda III of Alexandria (d. 2012) Pope Shenouda taught that the Coptic Church is not Monophysite in the Eutychian sense, that it anathematizes Eutyches, and that it confesses Christ as perfect God and perfect man in one incarnate nature (see his book The Nature of Christ ). (Summary, not a quotation.) What’s the difference between Miaphysitism and the Catholic/Protestant view? The Council of Chalcedon (451) defined Christ as "one person in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation." The OO accepts the substance of all four adverbs — Christ’s divine and human realities are not confused, not changed, not divided, not separated — but rejects the phrase "two natures"

as liable to Nestorian misreading (as if Christ were a human person joined to a divine person). The OO prefers Cyril’s formula: "one nature of the Word Incarnate," in which the "one" is not arithmetic but signifies the complete, undivided unity of the divine Son who has fully assumed human nature. The modern ecumenical consensus is that the difference is terminological rather than substantial: both sides confess the same Lord, fully God and fully man, undivided. For a full treatment see The Chalcedonian Schism → "There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." 1 Timothy 2:5 Common Declaration — Pope Paul VI and Pope Shenouda III (1973) "We confess that our Lord and God and Saviour and King of us all, Jesus Christ, is perfect God with respect to His divinity, perfect man with respect to His humanity.

In Him His divinity is united with His humanity in a real, perfect union without mingling, without commixtion, without confusion, without alteration, without division, without separation." Did the Church reject Chalcedon for theological or political reasons? Both — but the theological concern was primary. The OO Fathers who rejected Chalcedon — above all Dioscorus of Alexandria and Timothy Aelurus — objected that the council’s language of "two natures" echoed Nestorius, whom Ephesus had condemned. They also objected to the deposition of Dioscorus, who was condemned on procedural grounds rather than for heresy, and to the growing power of the imperial capital at Alexandria’s expense; Canon 28 gave Constantinople privileges equal to Rome’s. Many modern scholars, and the official dialogues of 1989 and 1990, conclude that the theological difference was largely terminological: both sides confessed one Christ, truly divine and truly human. If so, the tragedy is that a difference of vocabulary, compounded by imperial politics, produced a schism that has lasted fifteen centuries.

Some on both sides, including the monasteries of Mount Athos, still hold that real differences remain. For a full treatment see The Chalcedonian Schism → "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will recognize them by their fruits." Matthew 7:15-16 — the criterion of fruits, not just formulas His Holiness Pope Shenouda III (d. 2012) Pope Shenouda held that the division after Chalcedon was in large part a matter of terminology and of history, and he worked for reconciliation with the Chalcedonian churches, signing the 1973 Common Declaration with Pope Paul VI. (Summary, not a quotation.)

Scripture How was the Bible compiled? The Bible did not compile itself. The New Testament canon was debated and discerned over three centuries — letters circulated, some were disputed (Hebrews, Revelation, James), and the Church tested them against the apostolic rule of faith. It was the Council of Carthage (397), under the guidance of Augustine and the African bishops, that confirmed the twenty-seven-book canon that most Christians use today. The Old Testament question is even more complex: the earliest Christians used the Septuagint — the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, which includes the deuterocanonical books (Tobit, Judith, 1-2 Maccabees, Sirach, Wisdom, Baruch). The Protestant Reformation rejected these books, following the rabbinic Hebrew canon and Jerome. The OO, faithful to the early Church’s use of the Septuagint, retains the larger canon. "…knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation." 2 Peter 1:20 St. Augustine of Hippo (d.

430) "For my part, I should not believe the gospel except as moved by the authority of the Catholic Church" ( Against the Epistle of Manichaeus 5). Why trust Church Tradition? Because the Church predates the Bible, produced it, and was entrusted by Christ to transmit it faithfully. Tradition is not man-made addition; it is the living stream of the Apostolic faith — of which Scripture is a part. Paul commands the Thessalonians to hold fast to the Traditions he delivered both by letter and by spoken word (2 Thess 2:15), making clear that the written and unwritten transmission are equally apostolic. The Tradition is the context that makes Scripture intelligible. Without the Church’s Tradition you do not know which books belong in the Bible, you do not know that the Trinity is taught in it, and you do not know what baptism and Eucharist mean. Scripture and Tradition are not rivals; they are the two dimensions of a single Apostolic deposit.

See Church Authority → "So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter." 2 Thessalonians 2:15 St. Basil of Caesarea (d. 379) "Of the beliefs and practices whether generally accepted or publicly enjoined which are preserved in the Church some we possess derived from written teaching; others we have received delivered to us in a mystery by the tradition of the apostles; and both of these in relation to true religion have the same force" ( On the Holy Spirit 27.66). Why are some books included that Protestants reject? The books Protestants call Apocrypha and Catholics call Deuterocanonical (Tobit, Judith, 1-2 Maccabees, Sirach, Wisdom, Baruch) were part of the Septuagint — the Greek translation of the Old Testament used by the earliest Christians, quoted in the New Testament, and used in the Church’s worship for fifteen centuries. The New Testament itself reflects the theology of 1-2 Maccabees (Hebrews 11:35 alludes to 2 Maccabees 7).

The Protestant Reformers set these books apart in the 16th century (Luther printed them in a separate section, and the 1611 King James Version still included them), choosing to follow for the canon proper the Hebrew list kept by the rabbis after the fall of the Temple. Most Protestant Bibles dropped them altogether in the 19th century. Protestants argue this list was already fixed before Christ; Orthodox reply that the apostolic Church read the larger Greek collection. See The Biblical Canon page. The OO retains the canon of the early Church, which is the larger, Septuagint canon. "Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life." Hebrews 11:35 — alluding to 2 Maccabees 7, a deuterocanonical book St. Cyril of Jerusalem (d. 386) "Read the Divine Scriptures, the twenty-two books of the Old Testament ... And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself" ( Catechetical Lecture 4.35 to 36).

Who has the authority to interpret Scripture? The Church, guided by the Holy Spirit. Peter explicitly says "no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone’s own interpretation" (2 Pet 1:20). When Philip asked the Ethiopian eunuch "Do you understand what you are reading?" the eunuch replied "How can I, unless someone guides me?" (Acts 8:30-31) — the principle is plain: Scripture requires authoritative interpretation. The OO does not say individuals should not read Scripture (the OO strongly encourages Scripture reading). It says that when an individual’s interpretation conflicts with the consistent, universal teaching of the Church Fathers across all the ancient churches, the individual should reconsider. The Church that produced and authenticated the canon holds the authority to interpret it. "‘Do you understand what you are reading?’ And he said, ‘How can I, unless someone guides me?’" Acts 8:30-31 St. Vincent of Lérins (d. c.

445) "Owing to the depth of Holy Scripture, all do not accept it in one and the same sense, but one understands its words in one way, another in another; so that it seems to be capable of as many interpretations as there are interpreters" ( Commonitory 2.5). His answer is to read it by the rule of the Church's faith.

Prayer and Spiritual Life Why use written prayers? The Psalms are written prayers — 150 of them, inspired by the Holy Spirit and used in Jewish and Christian worship for three thousand years. The Lord’s Prayer is a written prayer that Jesus himself gave us (Matt 6:9-13). The Apostles used the structured, written prayers of the Temple liturgy (Acts 3:1 — "the hour of prayer"). Written prayers do not prevent sincerity; they train the mind and heart into the right channels, correct our disordered impulses, and unite us with the whole Church praying the same words across centuries. A Christian who has prayed the Psalms daily for decades does not find them empty — they find them inexhaustible, each reading revealing new depths. The problem Jesus warned against (Matt 6:7) is vain babbling — empty repetition without thought — not structured prayer as such. "Pray then like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name…’" Matthew 6:9 The Didache (c. 100 AD) After giving the Lord's Prayer in full: "Thrice in the day thus pray" ( Didache 8).

Why repeat prayers? Jesus himself prayed the same prayer three times in Gethsemane (Matt 26:44) — "praying the same words again." The seraphim in Isaiah 6 cry "Holy, Holy, Holy" without ceasing. Psalm 136 repeats "his steadfast love endures forever" twenty-six times without apology. The Jesus Prayer ("Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner") is prayed hundreds of times daily in the hesychast tradition — not as vain babbling but as the beating heart of the soul. The warning against "vain repetitions" (Matt 6:7) is directed at pagan babbling — multiplying words as a magical technique to get attention. Repetition born of love is different: it deepens, not empties. A mother does not stop saying "I love you" to her child because she has said it before. "And going a little farther he fell on his face and prayed, saying, ‘My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me’… Again, for the second time, he went away and prayed, saying the same words again." Matthew 26:39, 44 St. John Climacus (d. c.

649) "Let your prayer be entirely simple." "One word was enough for the publican and for the prodigal son to obtain God's forgiveness." "Prolixity in prayer often fills up the spirit with images and dissipates it" ( Ladder , Step 28). Why ask for the prayers of departed Christians? Because they are alive. "He is not God of the dead, but of the living" (Matt 22:32). Those who have died in Christ are alive to him, alive to us, and alive to our prayers. Paul asks living people to pray for him; the same logic applies to those more perfectly alive in Christ. The specific saints we ask to intercede are not independent powers — they are members of the Body of Christ who bring our prayers before God as Rev 5:8 depicts. Praying with and through the saints is not bypassing Christ; it is participating in the communion of the whole Body. The alternative — that death ends the ability to intercede — contradicts the entire Biblical witness that the saints are alive, aware, and with God. "He is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him." Luke 20:38 St. John Chrysostom (d.

407) "Let us not then be weary in giving aid to the departed, both by offering on their behalf and obtaining prayers for them" ( Homily 41 on 1 Corinthians ). What is the Jesus Prayer? "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner." It is one of the simplest and most concentrated prayers in the Christian tradition. It compresses the entire Gospel into one sentence: the Lordship of Jesus, his identity as the Son of God, the petition for mercy, and the sinner’s humble self-knowledge. It draws on the publican’s prayer ("God, be merciful to me, a sinner" — Luke 18:13) and the blind man’s cry ("Lord, have mercy" — Matt 20:30-31). In the hesychast tradition, the prayer is synchronized with the breath until it becomes the ongoing, wordless prayer of the heart — the prayer Paul commands when he says "pray without ceasing" (1 Thess 5:17). Its roots are in the Egyptian desert, where the monks taught short prayers repeated all day, and forms of it are prayed across the Orthodox world, Oriental and Eastern.

"But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’" Luke 18:13 St. John Climacus (d. c. 649) "Let the remembrance of Jesus be present with your every breath. Then indeed you will appreciate the value of stillness" ( Ladder , Step 27, tr. Luibheid and Russell). Why pray facing east? The East is where the sun rises — a universal symbol of Christ, "the Sun of Righteousness" (Mal 4:2), the "Dayspring from on high" (Luke 1:78). Eden was in the east (Gen 2:8) — praying east is a longing for paradise, our lost homeland. Christ will come again "as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west" (Matt 24:27). The early Church prayed facing east from at least the second century, as Origen and Tertullian attest. It is an orientation of the whole body — not merely the mind — toward the coming Lord. In the OO, the altar faces east, the priest faces east at the central moments of the liturgy, and the faithful pray east. The body’s orientation is itself a theology.

"For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man." Matthew 24:27 St. Basil of Caesarea (d. 379) "Thus we all look to the East at our prayers, but few of us know that we are seeking our own old country, Paradise, which God planted in Eden in the East" ( On the Holy Spirit 27.66).

The Afterlife What happens immediately after death? The soul separates from the body and encounters Christ — the particular judgment. The OO does not teach soul sleep (unconsciousness until the general resurrection); the souls of the righteous are with God immediately. Jesus told the repentant thief: "today you will be with me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43). Paul writes: "we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Cor 5:8), and says that "to die is gain" (Phil 1:21) — not something you would say about unconsciousness. The state of the departed is not the final state; the full resurrection of the body awaits Christ’s return and the general judgment. The particular judgment is the soul’s encounter with God in its own condition, without the body, anticipating the final verdict. "Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise." Luke 23:43 St. Polycarp of Smyrna (d. c. 155) Of Ignatius, Paul and the other apostles: "they are [now] in their due place in the presence of the Lord, with whom also they suffered" ( Philippians 9).

Why pray for the dead? The practice of praying for the dead is ancient, apostolic, and present in OO liturgy from the beginning. 2 Maccabees 12:46 ("it is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins") has informed Christian practice throughout. The Church is one Body — those who have died in the faith remain members of the Body, and we remain in communion with them through prayer. The OO does not define precisely what prayer for the dead achieves — that belongs to God’s mercy. But it knows that the whole Church prays together, the living for the departed, and that God hears and acts. This is not purgatory as a system of punitive debt; it is the expression of love and unity in the one Body of Christ. See Roman Catholic Dogmas → "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." 2 Maccabees 12:46 St. John Chrysostom (d.

407) "For if the children of Job were purged by the sacrifice of their father, why do you doubt that when we too offer for the departed, some consolation arises to them?" ( Homily 41 on 1 Corinthians ). Does Oriental Orthodoxy believe in purgatory? No — not in the Roman Catholic sense. The OO prays for the dead, as all ancient Christian traditions do. But it does not accept the Latin doctrinal framework of purgatory: a third distinct place of punitive suffering, a debt of temporal punishment owed to divine justice after forgiveness, a Treasury of Merit, and indulgences administered by the Church. These are medieval Latin theological constructions unknown to the Eastern Fathers. What happens to the departed — exactly — the OO entrusts to God’s mercy without drawing up a detailed map. Prayer for the dead flows from love and the unity of the Body, not from a theology of debt-satisfaction. For a full treatment see Roman Catholic Dogmas → "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints." Psalm 116:15 St. Cyril of Jerusalem (d.

386) "Then on behalf also of the Holy Fathers and Bishops who have fallen asleep before us, and in a word of all who in past years have fallen asleep among us, believing that it will be a very great benefit to the souls, for whom the supplication is put up, while that holy and most awful sacrifice is set forth" ( Mystagogical Lecture 5.9). What is heaven like? Heaven is the full and unhindered vision and union with God — theosis consummated. "We shall see him as he is" (1 John 3:2). Not merely a pleasant place with pleasant company but the complete fulfillment of human nature: what we were created for, what we have always been moving toward, the deepest desire of the human person which no created thing can satisfy. In the resurrection, body and soul are reunited — the body itself glorified and transfigured, as Christ’s body was after the resurrection. John’s vision speaks of the New Jerusalem in which "God himself will be with them as their God… and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore" (Rev 21:3-4).

But the heart of it is not the absence of suffering — it is the presence of God. "Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is." 1 John 3:2 St. Irenaeus of Lyon (d. c. 202) "For the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God" ( Against Heresies IV.20.7). What is hell? Hell is the ultimate privation: eternal separation from God — the only source of life, joy, and being. It is the state of a person who has definitively chosen themselves over God and has thereby forfeited the only thing that could satisfy them. Paul describes it as "everlasting destruction, away from the presence of the Lord" (2 Thess 1:9). The OO avoids literalistic geography — what matters is the theological reality. Jesus uses the imagery of fire and outer darkness — not as a precise map but as the most vivid possible language for absolute loss. The God who made us for himself does not impose hell on anyone; it is the consequence of the definitive refusal of God.

St. Isaac the Syrian, a bishop of the Church of the East whose writings are loved and read in the Oriental Orthodox churches, speaks of hell as the torment of love refused, and some of his writings express hope that God’s love may reach even there. The Church has not made that hope a dogma. "They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might." 2 Thessalonians 1:9 St. Isaac the Syrian (d. c. 700) "As for me I say that those who are tormented in Gehenna are tormented by the invasion of love. What is there more bitter and violent than the pains of love?" ( Ascetical Homilies ).

Church Practices Why do men and women sometimes sit separately in some churches? The practice of men and women sitting on opposite sides of the nave is ancient, described in church orders such as the Apostolic Constitutions, and still maintained in many Ethiopian, Coptic, and Eritrean congregations. The reason is not a statement about the spiritual inferiority of women (the OO venerates the Theotokos above every male saint) but a commitment to sobriety and recollectedness in worship. The Liturgy is an encounter with God, not a social occasion, and the physical arrangement signals that. It also has practical roots in cultures where mixed seating would be an unfamiliar distraction. The practice is not universal in the OO — many parishes do not observe it — and it is a custom, not a binding canonical requirement. "Let all things be done decently and in order." 1 Corinthians 14:40 Apostolic Constitutions (c. 4th century) "Let the younger women also sit by themselves, if there be a place for them; but if there be not, let them stand behind the women ...

but let the virgins, and the widows, and the elder women, stand or sit before all the rest" ( Apostolic Constitutions II.57). Why are babies allowed to receive communion? Because they are fully baptized members of the Body of Christ, and the Body of Christ does not withhold itself from its own members. "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you" (John 6:53) — this is said without age restriction. If an infant is fully incorporated into the Body of Christ through baptism and Chrismation, what theological principle excludes them from the Eucharist? In the OO, the complete initiation — Baptism, Chrismation, Eucharist — is administered together from infancy, following the Apostolic pattern. The practice of delaying first communion to an age of reason is a late Western development with no apostolic precedent. "Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God." Mark 10:14 St. Cyprian of Carthage (d.

258) Of baptized infants carried by their parents to pagan sacrifice in the persecution, he imagines them saying at the judgment: "We have done nothing; nor have we forsaken the Lord's bread and cup to hasten freely to a profane contact" ( On the Lapsed 9). Cyprian assumes that infants received the bread and cup. Why do Orthodox Christians make the sign of the cross? The sign of the cross is a physical confession: "I have been crucified with Christ" (Gal 2:20), a marking of the body as belonging to him who died on the cross for us. It traces the cross from forehead to chest, from shoulder to shoulder — from mind to heart, across the full breadth of the person — signifying that the cross of Christ covers all of us: our thinking, our feeling, our body. The practice is already found in Tertullian (c.

200 AD): "At every forward step and movement, at every going in and out, when we put on our clothes and shoes, when we bathe, when we sit at table, when we light the lamps, on couch, on seat, in all the ordinary actions of daily life, we trace upon the forehead the sign." It is a brief, bodily liturgy of the faith. "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Galatians 6:14 Tertullian (d. c. 220) "At every forward step and movement, at every going in and out ... in all the ordinary actions of daily life, we trace upon the forehead the sign" ( The Chaplet 3). Why are there so many feast days and fast days? The liturgical calendar is the sanctification of time itself. Every day of the year is given a theological meaning: a feast of the Lord, a commemoration of a saint, a fasting season that re-enacts the Church’s longing for God. The year tells the whole story of salvation — the Incarnation, the Epiphany, the Lenten journey, the Passion, the Resurrection, Pentecost — and then begins again.

Time is not a neutral container; it is the arena of God’s action in history, and the Church year redeems it. The saints commemorated daily are not honored because they are dead heroes; they are models of what salvation looks like in concrete human lives — proof that the grace of God actually transforms people. Each saint is an invitation: this could be you. "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman." Galatians 4:4 St. Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373) "We duly proceed, my brethren, from feasts to feasts, duly from prayers to prayers, we advance from fasts to fasts, and join holy-days to holy-days" ( Festal Letter 5.1). Why is confession encouraged regularly? Because theosis is not a one-time event but an ongoing process, and sin interrupts it. Regular confession — monthly, or before major feasts — is the OO norm not as a legal requirement but as a spiritual discipline. Confession brings sin out of darkness into light, allows it to be named and released, and provides the practical pastoral guidance of a confessor who knows the person over time.

John says "if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9) — the verb is present tense, ongoing. The mirror of the soul becomes dusty with accumulated sin; confession cleans it. Regular confession is one of the primary means by which theosis progresses. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." 1 John 1:9 The Didache (c. 100 AD) "In the church you shall acknowledge your transgressions, and you shall not come near for your prayer with an evil conscience" ( Didache 4).

Modern Issues Why doesn’t the Church change its teachings with modern culture? Because the Church’s teaching is not a human construct that can be updated with cultural trends. "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever" (Heb 13:8), and the faith "was once for all delivered to the saints" (Jude 1:3). The Church is not obligated to be acceptable to every generation; it is obligated to transmit the truth faithfully to every generation. Cultural norms change; the nature of the human person, the character of God, and the moral structure of reality do not. Adapting doctrine to culture is the opposite of the Apostolic mission — the Apostles were sent to transform cultures, not to be transformed by them. What does change in the Church is the expression, the language, and the application of the teaching — never the teaching itself. "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings." Hebrews 13:8-9 St. Vincent of Lérins (d. c.

445) "To preach any doctrine therefore to Catholic Christians other than what they have received never was lawful, never is lawful, never will be lawful" ( Commonitory 9.14). Yet knowledge "ought, in the course of ages and centuries, to increase and make much and vigorous progress; but yet only in its own kind; that is to say, in the same doctrine, in the same sense, and in the same meaning" (23.54). How does the Church view science and evolution? The Church has never defined how the days of Genesis are to be read, and the Fathers differed. St. Basil, in his Hexaemeron, took the days as days of twenty-four hours and refused allegory, while Origen and Augustine read the days non-literally (Augustine thought God made all things at once). The OO has no defined teaching on the age of the earth or on evolution. Some Orthodox accept evolution as the way the body came to be; others, including respected modern Orthodox teachers, reject it. Both sides hold firmly what follows.

What the Church insists on — and what no scientific theory can contradict, because it is not in the same domain — is: that humanity is created in the image of God (Gen 1:26-27), that each human soul has a unique dignity, that the world is created and sustained by God’s will. How the biological body came to be is a question for science; why we exist, who we are, and where we are going are questions for theology. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them." Genesis 1:27 St. Basil of Caesarea (d. 379) "Now twenty-four hours fill up the space of one day" ( Hexaemeron 2.8). "I know the laws of allegory ... For me grass is grass; plant, fish, wild beast, domestic animal, I take all in the literal sense" ( Hexaemeron 9.1). Why does the Church oppose abortion? Because human life from its beginning bears the image of God and is therefore inviolable. "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you" (Jer 1:5).

The Didache, one of the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament, dated to around 100 AD, lists "you shall not murder a child by abortion" among the commandments of the Way of Life, showing that the early Church regarded abortion as homicide from the beginning. Every human being at every stage of development is a person created in the image of God; to end that life is to destroy what God is forming. The OO offers pastoral compassion to those who have had abortions — the sacrament of confession and God’s mercy are never withheld. But the moral teaching is clear and ancient. "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you." Jeremiah 1:5 The Didache (c. 100 AD) "You shall not murder a child by abortion nor kill that which is begotten" ( Didache 2). What is the Orthodox view of marriage? Marriage is the union of one man and one woman, blessed by God from creation, elevated by Christ to a sacrament, and patterned on the union of Christ and the Church. "What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate" (Matt 19:6).

Marriage is not merely a legal contract or a social arrangement — it is an icon of the divine love: the self-giving of Christ for his Bride is mirrored in the mutual self-giving of husband and wife. Its purpose is the sanctification of the spouses, the bearing and raising of children in the faith, and the creation of a domestic church. The OO, like all ancient Christian churches, holds that marriage is between a man and a woman — not because of cultural conservatism but because the sacramental icon itself requires the two poles of human nature: male and female, created in complementarity. "Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh." Ephesians 5:31 St. John Chrysostom (d. 407) "For there is no relationship between man and man so close as that between man and wife, if they be joined together as they should be" ( Homily 20 on Ephesians ).

Why are only men ordained as priests? The Oriental Orthodox ordains only men to the priesthood and episcopate — following the unbroken practice of the Apostles, the entire pre-schism Church, and the universal patristic Tradition. This is not a statement about the spiritual worth, intelligence, or holiness of women. Mary the Theotokos is honored above every bishop and patriarch who has ever lived. The reason is iconographic and theological: the priest at the Eucharist acts as an icon of Christ the Bridegroom — and Christ, in freely choosing to take male flesh and to choose twelve male apostles, set the pattern. The OO also has an immensely rich tradition of women monastics, deaconesses (in the ancient sense), confessors, and saints. The exclusion from ordination is not exclusion from holiness; the Theotokos herself was never ordained. "And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve." Mark 3:13-14 — the Twelve were all male; this was deliberate, not cultural accident St. John Chrysostom (d.

407) On 1 Timothy 2:12 he holds that the Apostle "wishes the man to have the preeminence" in teaching in the Church ( Homily 9 on 1 Timothy ). Yet of Junia he writes, "How great is the devotion of this woman, that she should be even counted worthy of the appellation of apostle!" ( Homily 31 on Romans ).

The Heart of the Matter The dispute over fasting turns on two questions. First, is fasting commanded for the Christian, or is it an optional private devotion the gospel left behind? And second, does the Church have the authority to appoint set seasons of fasting — Lent, Wednesdays and Fridays — or is any such calendar a return to the Law? The Orthodox and many Protestants answer both differently. Orthodox Christ said " when you fast," assuming His followers will He foretold that the Church would fast once the Bridegroom was taken up The apostles fasted and ordained with fasting (Acts 13–14) The Church may appoint common seasons, as she did from the first century Fasting is ascesis — medicine for the passions — not a means of earning salvation Common Protestant view Fasting is permitted but never commanded; it is private and spontaneous Fixed fasting seasons are man-made rules (Colossians 2; Romans 14) Mandatory food-laws are the "doctrine of demons" of 1 Timothy 4 Such discipline easily becomes works-righteousness and legalism The believer is free; "the kingdom of God is not eating

and drinking" The Orthodox case is not that fasting earns God’s favour, nor that food is unclean — both ideas the Church explicitly condemns. It is that the Lord who fasted forty days, who taught His disciples how to fast, and who promised they would fast in His bodily absence, left the Church a discipline she has kept unbroken. The argument that follows rests on four pillars: the words of Christ, the witness of all Scripture, the unanimous practice of the early Church, and the Fathers’ insistence that the true fast is inward.

Why the Church Fasts Fasting in the Orthodox tradition is never an end in itself, and never a hunger strike to bend God’s arm. It is ascesis — spiritual training, as an athlete trains the body. Its purposes are several and they work together: To master the body and weaken the passions. The appetite for food is the most basic of the bodily appetites; the one who cannot say "no" to the stomach will not easily say "no" to anger, lust, or greed. By learning to govern the simplest hunger, the Christian trains the will to govern the rest. Fasting "subdues the body and brings it into subjection" (cf. 1 Corinthians 9:27). To free the soul for prayer. Scripture again and again joins fasting to prayer — Anna in the Temple, the church at Antioch, the Lord in the wilderness. A lightened, disciplined body prays more readily than a sated and drowsy one. Fasting clears a space; prayer fills it. To give to the poor. The Fathers insist that the food and money saved by fasting are owed to the hungry.

A fast that merely shifts the rich man’s diet from meat to costly delicacies, while the poor go unfed, is no fast at all. Fasting and almsgiving are two hands of the same mercy. To repent. Throughout the Bible, fasting is the language of repentance and mourning for sin — Nineveh in sackcloth, Joel’s call to "return with fasting and weeping." The Church’s fasts are seasons of return, drawing the soul back toward God. To remember Paradise. The Fathers saw in the fast a return to the diet of Eden, where Adam ate only the fruit of the garden and no flesh was killed. Fasting is a brief recovery of that first innocence — and a foretaste of the Kingdom, where the appetites of this fallen body will be no more.

Fasting Throughout Scripture Fasting is not a relic of the Old Covenant that the gospel abolished. It runs from Sinai to the Apostles, and the Lord Himself both practised it and taught His followers how to do it rightly. First, Christ assumes His disciples will fast. He does not say "if," but "when": "And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites… But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret." Matthew 6:16 –18 (ESV) Second, He foretold that His Church would fast — precisely in the age that began at His Ascension: "Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast." Matthew 9:15 (ESV) Third, the apostolic Church did exactly that — fasting at the great moments of decision and ordination: "While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said… Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off." Acts 13:2 –3 (ESV) "And when they had

appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord." Acts 14:23 (ESV) The prophets call God’s people to fast as the very form of repentance, and Daniel models the abstinence from rich food that the Church’s fasts imitate: "Yet even now," declares the LORD, "return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning." Joel 2:12 (ESV) "I ate no delicacies, no meat or wine entered my mouth, nor did I anoint myself at all, for the full three weeks." Daniel 10:3 (ESV) And the holiest figures of the New Testament are marked by fasting: Anna the prophetess "worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day" (Luke 2:37), and St. Paul "in fastings often" (2 Corinthians 11:27). The pattern is unbroken — fasting is the normal posture of the people of God before their Lord.

secs.h: The Forty Days & the Lord’s Example
secs.x: The Forty Days & the Lord’s Example At the centre of the Christian fasting year stands the Great Fast — the forty days that imitate the Lord’s own fast in the wilderness, where He overcame the tempter not by power but by abstinence and the word of God. "And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry." Matthew 4:2 (ESV) The number forty is woven through salvation history as the measure of testing and preparation. Moses fasted forty days on the mountain before receiving the Law; Elijah journeyed forty days on the strength of one meal to the mountain of God; Israel was tested forty years in the desert. "So he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights. He neither ate bread nor drank water." Exodus 34:28 (ESV) "And he arose and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mount of God." 1 Kings 19:8 (ESV) The Church, following her Lord, keeps a Holy Forty before Pascha (Easter) so that the faithful may walk with Christ into the wilderness and emerge with Him to the Resurrection.

secs.h: The Forty Days & the Lord’s Example
secs.x: This is no late invention: by the fourth century the forty-day Lenten fast was universal, and St. Athanasius of Alexandria — the great Coptic father — announced its dates each year to the churches of Egypt in his Festal Letters , urging all the faithful to keep it. The Lenten fast is thus among the oldest common observances of the whole Church, East and West alike.

secs.h: The Fasts of the Coptic Year
secs.x: The Fasts of the Coptic Year The Coptic Orthodox Church keeps more fasting days than any other apostolic church — over two hundred a year. Each fast has its own length, its own commemoration, and its own degree of strictness. (Gregorian dates are approximate, since the Coptic calendar runs on its own months and some fasts move with the date of Pascha.) The Great Fast (Great Lent) — 55 days The strictest and greatest fast, before Pascha. It joins a week of preparation, the Holy Forty (in imitation of Christ’s wilderness fast), and Holy Week. No animal products and no fish; the faithful also abstain from all food and drink until a set hour. Preceded by the joyful pre-Lenten weeks. The Fast of Nineveh — 3 days A short, strict fast about two weeks before Great Lent, recalling the repentance of Nineveh at the preaching of Jonah (Jonah 3). A foretaste and rehearsal of the Great Fast. The Nativity Fast (Advent) — about 43 days Before the Feast of the Nativity (celebrated 7 January). Forty days recall Moses’ fast before receiving the Law, with additional days added in later centuries.

secs.h: The Fasts of the Coptic Year
secs.x: Fish is generally permitted. A season of preparation for the coming of Christ in the flesh. The Apostles’ Fast — variable length Begins the Monday after Pentecost and ends on the Feast of the martyrdom of Sts. Peter and Paul (about 12 July). Its length changes each year with the date of Pascha. It commemorates the apostles fasting before they went out to preach (Acts 13). Fish is generally permitted. The Fast of the Theotokos (St. Mary’s Fast) — 15 days In August, ending on the Feast of the Dormition (Assumption) of the Virgin (about 22 August). A beloved and well-kept fast in honour of the Mother of God. Fish is generally permitted. Every Wednesday and Friday — year-round Kept throughout the year (apart from the joyful fifty days from Pascha to Pentecost and a few feast exceptions). Wednesday recalls the council that resolved to betray Christ; Friday recalls His crucifixion. Observed strictly, like Lent — no animal products and no fish. This is the very practice attested in the Didache around AD 100.

secs.h: The Fasts of the Coptic Year
secs.x: The Paramoun (vigil) fasts Strict fasting on the eve of the great feasts of the Nativity and Theophany (Epiphany), preparing the faithful to receive the feast. Beneath the variety lies a single rhythm: the Church’s year breathes in and out between fasting and feasting. Every great joy is preceded by a fast, and every fast is crowned by a feast — so that the body and soul together pass from preparation to celebration, from the wilderness to the Kingdom.

How the Copts Fast Coptic fasting has two dimensions, and both belong to it. The first is abstaining from food and drink altogether for part of the day — traditionally from midnight until a set hour, often the ninth hour (about three in the afternoon) or until the Divine Liturgy has ended. The second is, when one does eat, keeping a strict vegan diet : no meat, poultry, eggs, milk, butter, cheese, or any other animal product. The degree of strictness varies by season. During the lighter fasts — the Nativity Fast, the Apostles’ Fast, and the Fast of the Theotokos — fish is permitted . During the strict fasts — Great Lent, the Fast of Nineveh, Holy Week, and every Wednesday and Friday — even fish is set aside, and the diet is entirely plant-based. Why a vegan diet in particular? The Fathers saw in it a return to the food of Paradise. Before the Fall, God gave humankind only the fruit of the earth: "Behold, I have given you every plant yielding seed that is on the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit.

You shall have them for food." Genesis 1:29 (ESV) The eating of flesh was permitted only after the Flood — a concession to a fallen world: "Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you" (Genesis 9:3). To fast from animal products, then, is to step briefly back behind the Fall, to eat as Adam ate, and to loosen the grip of an appetite that entered the world with death. It is not that meat is unclean — the Church blesses and gives thanks for it on every feast — but that abstaining from it for a season disciplines the body and recalls Eden. Two cautions the Church herself insists upon. First, the fast is adjusted for the weak: the sick, the elderly, young children, expectant and nursing mothers, and those doing heavy labour are not bound to its full rigour. Fasting is medicine, and medicine is dosed to the patient. Second — and far more important — the bodily fast is worthless without the inward one. To abstain from meat while feasting on anger and gossip, the Fathers say, is no fast at all.

Voices of the Fathers The witness to fasting runs from the earliest Christian manual through the great preachers of the fourth century. Two themes recur: that fasting is an ancient and binding part of Christian life, and that its whole worth lies in the change of heart it serves. The Didache (c. AD 80–100) "But let not your fasts be with the hypocrites; for they fast on the second and fifth day of the week; but fast on the fourth day and the Preparation (Friday)." Didache 8 ( ANF, Roberts-Donaldson ) — the Wednesday & Friday fast, attested c. AD 100 Direct quote St. John Chrysostom (d. 407) "The honour of fasting consists not in abstinence from food, but in withdrawing from sinful practices… let not the mouth only fast, but also the eye, and the ear, and the feet, and the hands, and all the members of our bodies." Homily 3 on the Statues §11 ( NPNF 1st Series, Vol. 9 ) Direct quote St. Basil the Great (d. 379) He taught that fasting is as old as Paradise: the first command God gave Adam — "you shall not eat" of the tree — was itself a law of fasting and self-restraint.

We fell, he said, because we did not fast; let us fast now that we may return. First Homily on Fasting — summary of his argument Paraphrase St. Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373) In his annual Festal Letters the great Coptic father announced the dates of the Holy Forty Days to the churches of Egypt and urged all the faithful to keep the Lenten fast, binding the whole Church to the discipline in imitation of the Lord’s forty days.
