Festal Letters ( NPNF 2nd Series, Vol. 4 ) — summary Paraphrase Chrysostom’s words are the Church’s own answer to the charge that fasting is empty ritual: the food-fast is nothing if the eyes, ears, hands, and tongue do not fast from sin. And the Didache shows that the Wednesday-and-Friday rhythm Copts keep to this day was already the Christian custom within living memory of the Apostles.

Objections & Answers The Protestant case against mandatory fasting rests on a handful of texts. Read in context, none of them condemns the fasting Christ commanded; each targets something quite different. Romans 14 — "One person esteems one day above another" Paul is settling a quarrel between Jewish and Gentile believers who were judging and despising one another over private observance of days and foods (Romans 14:3–4). His point is pastoral: do not condemn a brother over disputable matters of conscience. This is not a ruling that the Church may never appoint a common fast; it is a warning against contempt and division. Indeed Paul, who wrote this, was "in fastings often" himself (2 Corinthians 11:27, NKJV) and ordained with fasting (Acts 14:23). The Church’s fasts are kept in love and freedom, not to despise the weak. Colossians 2:16 — "Let no one pass judgment on you… in regard to food" The whole chapter is aimed at false teachers binding the Colossians to the Mosaic ceremonial law and to a strange asceticism tied to "the worship of angels" and visions (Colossians 2:18).

Paul tells the believers not to let these Judaizers condemn them for failing to keep the old shadows — "a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath… a shadow of the things to come" (2:17). He is dismissing the obligatory observance of the Old Covenant calendar, not the gospel discipline of fasting that the Lord Himself instituted. Colossians 2:20–23 — "Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch" These "regulations" have "an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism… but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh" (2:23). Paul is condemning a proto-Gnostic asceticism that treated matter itself as evil and sought righteousness by rule-keeping apart from Christ. Orthodox fasting is the opposite: it honours the body as God’s good creation, eats every food with thanksgiving outside the fast, and is rooted in Christ, not in self-salvation by abstinence. 1 Timothy 4:1–5 — "doctrines of demons… abstinence from foods" This is the sharpest objection, and the context answers it precisely.

Paul condemns those who "forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving … for everything created by God is good" (4:3–4). The error is teaching that certain foods or marriage are intrinsically evil or unclean — the doctrine of the Gnostics and later the Manichaeans. The Orthodox hold the exact opposite: all food is good, marriage is holy, and the fast is a voluntary, temporary abstaining from good things, after which they are received again with thanksgiving on the feast. To fast from a good gift for a season is not to call it evil. "Fasting is legalism — works-righteousness." Fasting earns nothing and saves no one; the Orthodox confess that salvation is the gift of God’s grace. Fasting is not payment but training — ascesis, the discipline of an athlete (1 Corinthians 9:25–27). It weakens the passions, frees the soul for prayer, and funds almsgiving. The Pharisee who boasted "I fast twice a week" went home unjustified (Luke 18:12); the danger is real.

But the remedy for proud fasting is humble fasting, not no fasting at all — exactly as Christ taught when He said to fast in secret, before the Father alone (Matthew 6:18). "Jesus’ own disciples didn’t fast." (Matthew 9:14) Jesus answered that very objection Himself. The disciples did not fast while the Bridegroom was present — a wedding is no time to mourn — "But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast" (Matthew 9:15, NKJV). That time is now: the age of the Church between the Ascension and the Lord’s return. Far from excusing the Church from fasting, the verse commands it for precisely this age. "Fasting is just an empty external ritual." The Fathers say this more forcefully than any critic.

"The honour of fasting consists not in abstinence from food, but in withdrawing from sinful practices," says Chrysostom; let the eyes, ears, hands, and tongue fast too, for "what does it profit if we abstain from birds and fishes, and yet bite and devour our brethren?" The bodily fast is the outward scaffold for an inward repentance joined to prayer and mercy. Kept that way, it is not empty at all; kept as mere diet, it condemns itself — which is exactly the Orthodox teaching.

Fasting in the Living Tradition For the Copts, fasting is not an idea in a book but the texture of ordinary life. A Coptic household keeps the strict fast through the whole of Great Lent, cooking from a deep repertoire of vegan dishes — ful (stewed fava beans), koshari , lentils, vegetables, tahini and pickles — that the cuisine itself has shaped over centuries of fasting. Children grow up knowing which days are "fasting days," and the Wednesday-and-Friday rhythm marks the week as surely as Sunday does. The fast is bound tightly to the sacraments. The faithful fast before receiving the Holy Communion — keeping the eucharistic fast from the night before — so that the first food of the day is the Body and Blood of Christ. The great fasts climax in the feasts they prepare: the Nativity Fast in the joy of Christmas, the Great Fast in the Resurrection, the Theotokos Fast in the feast of the Virgin’s Dormition. Fasting and feasting are inseparable; the one makes the other sweet. It is also a fast kept with the whole Church, and often with the wider community.

In Egypt the long fasting seasons are publicly known; restaurants and shops offer "fasting" (vegan) food, and the rhythm of abstaining and feasting is woven into the shared life of an ancient Christian people who have kept it under every kind of pressure for nearly two thousand years. What holds it all together is the conviction that the body and the soul are saved together. The Copt does not fast to punish the body or to earn heaven, but to offer the whole person — appetite and all — back to God, and to walk, in some small bodily way, the road the Lord walked into the wilderness and out again to the empty tomb.

FAQ Isn’t fasting trying to earn salvation by works? No. The Orthodox confess that salvation is God’s gift, received by grace through faith and lived out in love. Fasting earns nothing; it is spiritual training — discipline for the body, fuel for prayer, and a source of alms for the poor. Christ commanded it ("when you fast"), so to keep it is obedience, not merit. The proud fast of the Pharisee is condemned; the humble fast in secret, before the Father alone, is what the Lord asked for. Why do Copts fast from animal products rather than from all food? They do both. There is a daily abstaining from all food and drink until a set hour, and then, when one eats, a vegan diet. The plant-based diet recalls the food of Paradise (Genesis 1:29), where no flesh was eaten; the eating of meat came only after the Flood (Genesis 9:3). To fast from animal products is to step briefly back behind the Fall — not because meat is unclean, but to discipline an appetite and remember Eden.

Doesn’t 1 Timothy 4 call forbidding foods a "doctrine of demons"? It condemns teaching that certain foods or marriage are intrinsically evil — the error of the Gnostics, "who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving" (1 Timothy 4:3). The Orthodox teach the opposite: all food is good and is received with thanksgiving on every feast. Fasting is a voluntary, temporary abstaining from good things — the very reverse of calling them unclean. What if I’m sick, pregnant, elderly, or doing hard labour? The Church relaxes the fast for those who cannot bear its full rigour — the sick, the elderly, young children, pregnant and nursing mothers, and those in heavy work or travel. Fasting is medicine, and medicine is dosed to the patient. Anyone unsure of how to fast should speak with their priest or father of confession, who applies the rule with discernment rather than rigidity. Where does the Wednesday-and-Friday fast come from? From the earliest Christian generations.

The Didache , a manual from around AD 100, already directs believers to fast on "the fourth day and the Preparation" — Wednesday and Friday. Wednesday recalls the plot to betray Christ; Friday recalls His crucifixion. The Copts have kept this weekly fast unbroken ever since, which is why it is observed as strictly as Lent itself. Do other Orthodox and ancient churches fast like this? Yes. The Eastern Orthodox, the other Oriental Orthodox churches (Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, Indian), and the ancient liturgical churches all keep substantial fasting seasons built on the same biblical and patristic foundations — the Forty Days, the weekly fast, and seasons before the great feasts. The Coptic Church keeps the fullest calendar of all, but the practice itself is the common inheritance of the undivided early Church.

Glossary Fasting (Coptic: ṣawm ) Abstaining from food and drink for part of the day and, when eating, keeping a vegan diet — undertaken for spiritual training, prayer, repentance, and almsgiving. Ascesis From the Greek for an athlete’s training. The spiritual discipline — fasting, prayer, vigil — by which the Christian trains the will and weakens the passions. The Great Fast Coptic Great Lent: a 55-day fast before Pascha, joining a preparation week, the Holy Forty, and Holy Week. The strictest fast of the year. The Holy Forty The forty days of Lent that imitate Christ’s forty-day fast in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2), echoing Moses and Elijah before Him. Fast of Nineveh A three-day fast before Great Lent recalling the repentance of Nineveh at Jonah’s preaching (Jonah 3). Apostles’ Fast A variable-length fast after Pentecost, ending on the feast of Sts. Peter and Paul, commemorating the apostles fasting before they preached (Acts 13). Fast of the Theotokos A 15-day fast in August honouring the Virgin Mary, ending on the Feast of her Dormition (Assumption).

Nativity Fast The roughly 43-day Advent fast before the Feast of the Nativity (7 January), preparing for the coming of Christ in the flesh. Paramoun The strict vigil-fast on the eve of the great feasts of the Nativity and Theophany (Epiphany). Eucharistic fast The fast kept before receiving Holy Communion — abstaining from food and drink from the night before — so that the Body and Blood of Christ are the first food of the day. Didache "The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles," a Christian manual of about AD 100 that already prescribes the Wednesday-and-Friday fast. Festal Letters The annual letters of the Patriarch of Alexandria (notably St. Athanasius) announcing the date of Pascha and the start of the Lenten fast to the churches of Egypt.

I. Introduction The filioque controversy is one of the most important and least understood theological disputes in Christian history. The Latin word filioque means "and from the Son" — and the dispute concerns whether these three words should be added to the Nicene Creed's description of the Holy Spirit's procession. The original Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (AD 381) states that the Holy Spirit "proceeds from the Father." The Western (Latin) Church gradually added "and from the Son" — the filioque — so that the Creed read that the Spirit "proceeds from the Father and the Son ." This addition was the primary theological cause of the Great Schism of AD 1054, which divided Western (Roman Catholic) and Eastern (Orthodox) Christianity — a division that persists to this day. The Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian, Malankara) never accepted the filioque, maintaining the original Nicene Creed and the Eastern theology of the Spirit's procession from the Father alone. The issue is not merely a matter of a few words.

At stake is the eternal nature of the Holy Trinity — specifically, the eternal relationships between the three Persons of the Godhead. The question "from whom does the Holy Spirit eternally proceed?" touches the deepest mysteries of the divine life and has profound implications for prayer, worship, and the entire experience of God in the Christian life.

secs.h: II. The Nicene Creed — Original and Altered
secs.x: II. The Nicene Creed — Original and Altered Original Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (AD 381) "And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the Giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who together with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified, who spoke through the prophets." Used by: Oriental Orthodox, Eastern Orthodox, and originally all of Christendom. Never altered by any Ecumenical Council. Western Version with Filioque (from c. AD 589) "And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the Giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son , who together with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified, who spoke through the prophets." Used by: Roman Catholic Church, most Protestant denominations (who inherited it from the Latin West). The Council of Nicaea (AD 325) and the Council of Constantinople (AD 381) established the Creed.

secs.h: II. The Nicene Creed — Original and Altered
secs.x: The Council of Ephesus (AD 431) — one of the councils the Oriental Orthodox accept — explicitly forbade any addition to the Nicene Creed: "…it is unlawful for any man to bring forward, or to write, or to compose a different (ἑτέραν) Faith as a rival to that established by the holy Fathers assembled with the Holy Ghost in Nicæa." (NPNF) The filioque addition violates this explicit conciliar prohibition.

secs.h: III. What Is the Filioque? — The Theological Question
secs.x: III. What Is the Filioque? — The Theological Question The filioque concerns the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit — not his temporal mission into the world (which both East and West affirm involves the Son), but his eternal relationship to the Father and Son within the immanent Trinity. The Eastern tradition, following the Cappadocian Fathers and Cyril of Alexandria, holds that the Father alone is the mone archē (sole principle/source) of the Trinity — the one from whom the Son is eternally begotten and the Spirit eternally proceeds. The Father is the font of divinity; the Son and Spirit derive their personal existence from the Father (while being fully equal in divine nature). This preserves the monarchy (single-source unity) of the Father. The Western tradition, beginning especially with Augustine of Hippo (AD 354–430), emphasizes the unity of the divine essence shared by Father and Son — and concludes from this that the Spirit proceeds from the divine essence (which both Father and Son equally possess) or from both Father and Son as a single principle.

secs.h: III. What Is the Filioque? — The Theological Question
secs.x: This "double procession" is what the filioque expresses. The Oriental Orthodox reject the filioque primarily for three reasons: (1) it contradicts the explicit text of John 15:26; (2) it was added unilaterally by one part of the Church without an Ecumenical Council; and (3) it distorts the Eastern understanding of the Trinity by introducing a "double principle" for the Spirit's existence.

IV. Biblical Evidence John 15:26 OO "When the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me." The key text in the entire filioque debate. Christ himself says the Spirit "proceeds from the Father" (Greek: para tou Patros ekporeuetai ). He does NOT say "from the Father and the Son." He says he will "send" the Spirit — but the procession is from the Father. The Oriental Orthodox distinguish: temporal mission (Christ sends the Spirit into the world) from eternal procession (the Spirit's eternal origin from the Father alone). The filioque conflates these two distinct relationships. John 14:16–17 OO "And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth." Christ asks the Father to give the Spirit — the Father is the source of the Spirit's coming. Christ is the one who asks; the Father gives.

This distinction of roles within the Trinity — Father as source, Son as mediator — does not support the Western view that the Son is a co-equal source of the Spirit's procession alongside the Father. John 20:22 CTX "And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.'" Christ breathes the Spirit on the Apostles after the Resurrection — this is the temporal mission of the Spirit by the Son. Western theologians cite this as evidence that the Spirit proceeds "from the Son." The Eastern response: the temporal mission (Christ breathing the Spirit in time) does not establish the eternal procession (the Spirit's origin within the immanent Trinity). The risen Christ can send the Spirit in time without being the eternal source of the Spirit's hypostatic existence. Romans 8:9 CTX "You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you.

Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him." The Spirit is called both "Spirit of God" (the Father) and "Spirit of Christ" — suggesting a close relation to both Father and Son. The West uses this language to support the filioque. The East responds: the Spirit is the Spirit of Christ in the sense of belonging to Christ and being sent by him — not in the sense of eternally proceeding from him. The Spirit belongs to both Father and Son; this does not mean the Spirit originates from both. Galatians 4:6 CTX "And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!'" The Father sends "the Spirit of his Son" — another close association between Spirit and Son. The East: "Spirit of his Son" denotes the Spirit's mission and relationship to Christ in the economy of salvation, not the Spirit's eternal origin. In the temporal economy, the Spirit is sent by the Father through the Son; in the eternal immanent Trinity, the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone.

1 Corinthians 2:12 OO "Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God." Paul names the Spirit's origin directly: He is "the Spirit who is from God" (Greek: to ek tou Theou ) — from the Father, the fountain of divinity. When Scripture states the Spirit's source, it names the Father alone; it never says "from the Father and the Son." The East holds Scripture to its own precision on this point. John 16:14–15 CTX "He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you. All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you." The strongest Western prooftext: the Son says "all that the Father has is mine," so the Spirit's taking "what is mine" is read as procession from the Son too. The East answers that Christ is speaking of the Spirit's revealing work in the economy — the Spirit declares and glorifies the Son to us — not of the Spirit's eternal origin.
What the Son shares with the Father is the one divine essence; but being the cause of the Spirit is a property of the Father's person (hypostasis) alone, not of the shared essence.

secs.h: V. Historical Origins of the Filioque
secs.x: V. Historical Origins of the Filioque c. AD 400–430 Augustine of Hippo — In his treatise On the Trinity , Augustine develops a Western Trinitarian theology emphasizing the unity of the divine essence. He concludes that the Spirit proceeds principally ( principaliter ) from the Father, but also from the Son, laying the theological groundwork for the filioque. This is a genuine theological development, not apostolic tradition. AD 447 Pope Leo the Great — Uses filioque language in a letter (Letter 15, to Turribius, whose authenticity some scholars question), though not in the Creed itself. The Western theological tradition is moving toward filioque as a received teaching. AD 589 Third Council of Toledo (Spain) — The filioque is formally inserted into the Nicene Creed for the first time in the Visigothic Spanish Church, to combat Arianism. This is the first official addition of filioque to the Creed — a local, regional decision, not an Ecumenical Council. c. AD 800 Charlemagne and the Frankish Church — The Frankish church adopts the filioque and begins pressuring Rome to include it.

secs.h: V. Historical Origins of the Filioque
secs.x: When Eastern monks in Jerusalem complain that Frankish monks are singing the filioque, the dispute becomes international. Charlemagne commissions theologians to defend the filioque against Eastern critics. AD 809 Pope Leo III refuses the filioque — Pope Leo III explicitly refuses to add the filioque to the Creed, stating that while the doctrine may be orthodox, the addition is inappropriate. He has the Creed without filioque engraved on silver shields in St. Peter's Basilica. This is the last time Rome officially opposed the filioque. AD 867–880 The Photian Schism — Patriarch Photius of Constantinople writes his famous encyclical condemning the filioque on theological grounds, leading to a major schism between Rome and Constantinople. Though temporarily healed, this establishes the filioque as the central theological point of East-West division. AD 1014 Rome formally adopts the filioque — Pope Benedict VIII, under pressure from Holy Roman Emperor Henry II, officially inserts the filioque into the Creed at Rome.

secs.h: V. Historical Origins of the Filioque
secs.x: This is the final step — over 400 years after its first insertion in Spain, Rome officially adopts what will become the primary theological cause of the Great Schism of 1054. AD 1054 The Great Schism — Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius exchange mutual excommunications, an event later remembered as the formal division of Eastern and Western Christendom (the separation itself hardened gradually, above all after the sack of Constantinople in 1204). The filioque is among the central theological disputes. The Oriental Orthodox, already separated after Chalcedon in 451, were not party to it, though they share the Eastern rejection of the filioque.

VI. Eastern Theological Objections St. Maximus the Confessor (c. AD 580–662) Letter to Marinus of Cyprus — c. AD 645 "…they showed that they themselves do not make the Son Cause (Aitia) of the Spirit. They know, indeed, that the Father is the sole Cause of the Son and of the Spirit, of one by generation and of the other by ekporeusis — but they explained that the latter comes (proienai) through the Son, and they showed in this way the unity and the immutability of the essence." Direct quote — PG 91, 136, as translated in the Pontifical Council's 1995 clarification Significance: Maximus, defending the Latins two centuries before the schism, gives the Eastern reading of the Western "from the Son" language: it is admissible only if it means the Spirit is manifested through the Son, never that the Son is a cause . The Father alone is the one cause. This is the very distinction the later filioque, made into dogma, blurs — which is why the East, which honours Maximus as a confessor and martyr, rejects the addition to the Creed while affirming the "through the Son" of the economy. St.

John of Damascus (c. AD 676–749) Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, I.8 — c. AD 743 "And we speak likewise of the Holy Spirit as from the Father, and call Him the Spirit of the Father. And we do not speak of the Spirit as from the Son: but yet we call Him the Spirit of the Son… And we confess that He is manifested and imparted to us through the Son." Direct quote Significance: The last of the Greek Fathers states the rule flatly: the Spirit is from the Father, never from the Son; He is the "Spirit of the Son" only in that He is manifested and given through the Son. This is the settled patristic grammar the East preserves — procession (from the Father) and mission (through the Son) are two different things, and the creedal Filioque collapses them. St. Photius of Constantinople (c. AD 820–893) Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit — c. AD 886 Summary: Photius argues that if the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, either the Father is not the sole principle of divinity or there are two principles in the Trinity.

Either way the monarchy of the Father is lost, and the logic of the filioque would invite the absurd question why the Son should not also proceed from the Spirit. SUMMARY Significance: Photius's theological argument against the filioque is the classic Eastern critique: the filioque undermines the monarchy of the Father (the Father as the sole source and principle of the Trinity) and introduces two principles into the Spirit's eternal existence. If both Father and Son are sources of the Spirit, the unity of the Trinity is threatened. This argument has never been satisfactorily answered by Western theologians. St. Gregory Palamas (c. AD 1296–1359) Apodictic Treatises on the Procession of the Holy Spirit — c. AD 1335 Summary: Palamas denies that the Spirit has His eternal, hypostatic existence from or through the Son, while affirming that the Spirit is given, manifested, and shines forth through the Son. Eternal procession and temporal mission are different things, and the filioque, he argues, confuses them.

SUMMARY Significance: Palamas draws the crucial distinction that underlies the entire Eastern position: the Spirit's eternal hypostatic procession (from the Father alone) vs. the Spirit's temporal manifestation and mission (through the Son). The Eastern tradition consistently accepts that Christ sends the Spirit in the economy of salvation — this is not disputed. What is disputed is whether this temporal mission implies an eternal double procession.

VII. The Council Prohibition — Ephesus 431 Beyond the theological objections, the Oriental Orthodox have a canonical/ecclesiological objection to the filioque: it was added to the Creed in violation of an explicit prohibition by an Ecumenical Council that the Roman Catholic Church itself accepts. The Council of Ephesus (AD 431) — accepted by Rome and by the Oriental Orthodox — declared in its Seventh Canon: "…the holy Synod decreed that it is unlawful for any man to bring forward, or to write, or to compose a different (ἑτέραν) Faith as a rival to that established by the holy Fathers assembled with the Holy Ghost in Nicæa. But those who shall dare to compose a different faith, or to introduce or offer it to persons desiring to turn to the acknowledgment of the truth… if they be bishops or clergymen, they shall be deposed… and if they be laymen, they shall be anathematized." (NPNF) Whether the canon, which speaks of the faith of Nicaea, also binds the text of 381 has itself been debated between East and West.

The filioque is an addition to the Creed defined by the Fathers at Nicaea and Constantinople. It was added unilaterally — first by a regional Spanish council (589), then gradually by the Frankish church, and finally by Rome (1014) — without an Ecumenical Council. Even if the filioque theology were correct (which the Oriental Orthodox deny), its insertion into the Creed is a canonical violation of the Ephesian prohibition. The Oriental Orthodox point to Pope Leo III (c. AD 809) as evidence: even the Bishop of Rome refused to add the filioque to the Creed, on the grounds that the Fathers who framed the Creed had not included it. The later reversal by his successors does not change the canonical fact.

VIII. Theological Implications The filioque dispute is not merely an abstract scholastic debate. The Oriental Orthodox theologians have consistently argued that it has profound practical implications for the understanding of God, salvation, and the Church. Trinitarian Structure: The Eastern understanding — Father as sole source, Son eternally begotten, Spirit eternally proceeding from the Father — maintains a clear monarchical structure within the Trinity without compromising the equality of the three Persons. The filioque introduces a structural asymmetry: the Spirit's existence depends on two Persons (Father and Son together) while the Son's existence depends only on one (the Father). The Spirit is thus relationally subordinate to both, while the Son is subordinate only to the Father. This asymmetry troubles Eastern theologians. The Western Reply: In fairness, Catholic theology does not teach two sources in God.

The Council of Florence (1439) taught that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son "as from one principle", and that the Son receives even this from the Father, so the Father remains the source without source. The Vatican's 1995 clarification adds that the Latin procedit is a broader word than the Greek ekporeuetai used in the Creed, which the West agrees is said of the Father alone. Western theologians also note that Greek Fathers such as Cyril of Alexandria and Maximus spoke of the Spirit as being from or through the Son. The Oriental Orthodox answer is that "through the Son" describes how the Spirit is sent and shines forth, not how He eternally has His being, and that a disputed theological opinion still had no place in the common Creed. The Spirit's Role in Salvation: In the Eastern tradition, theosis (the deification and transformation of the human person) is accomplished by the Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father and rests on the Son. The Spirit is the Gift of the Father given through the Son — arriving directly from the Father's "paternal bosom" to the believer.

In the Western filioque tradition, the Spirit proceeds from the Father-Son unity and is essentially the Love that binds Father and Son — which, critics argue, subordinates the Spirit to the Father-Son relationship rather than allowing the Spirit to be distinctly the "Gift of the Father" (as Jesus calls him in Luke 24:49 and John 14:26). Ecclesiological Implications: St. Photius argued that the filioque was not merely a theological error but a symptom of the papal ecclesiology — the claim that one bishop (Rome) can unilaterally change the universal faith without conciliar agreement. The same spirit of unilateral authority that allowed Rome to add the filioque to the Creed is the same spirit that claims papal infallibility and universal jurisdiction. The two issues are connected at their root.

secs.h: IX. Western Arguments for the Filioque
secs.x: IX. Western Arguments for the Filioque Western Argument: Augustine's theology demonstrates the double procession from Scripture The Western Claim Augustine in On the Trinity demonstrates from multiple Scripture passages that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as the Father. John 20:22 (Christ breathing the Spirit), Romans 8:9 ("Spirit of Christ"), and Galatians 4:6 ("Spirit of his Son") all show the Spirit's intimate relation to the Son that amounts to procession. Eastern Response The Oriental Orthodox accept Augustine as a theologian of the Western tradition worthy of respect but not as a universal Father binding on Eastern theology. Augustine's Trinitarian theology, shaped by Neo-Platonic categories, represents a distinctly Western development not shared by the earlier Alexandrian, Antiochene, or Cappadocian schools. The scriptural passages cited describe the Spirit's temporal economy of salvation (the Spirit as sent by Christ, belonging to Christ, working through Christ) — not the Spirit's eternal hypostatic procession within the immanent Trinity.

secs.h: IX. Western Arguments for the Filioque
secs.x: The distinction between the immanent Trinity (God as God is in himself) and the economic Trinity (God as he reveals himself in salvation history) is crucial and is consistently maintained by the Eastern Fathers. Western Argument: The Fathers of the West support the filioque theology The Western Claim Ambrose of Milan, Hilary of Poitiers, and other Western Fathers use language implying the double procession before it was formally inserted into the Creed. The filioque is not an innovation but the articulation of a theology already present in Western Christianity. Eastern Response Even granting that some Western Fathers used filioque-adjacent language (which Eastern theologians dispute or interpret differently), this is a regional Western development, not the universal apostolic tradition. The Eastern Fathers — Athanasius, the Cappadocians, Cyril of Alexandria, John Chrysostom — all speak of the Spirit proceeding from the Father, with the Son as the mediator through whom the Spirit is sent to the world.

secs.h: IX. Western Arguments for the Filioque
secs.x: The universal tradition (East and West through Nicaea and Constantinople) confesses procession from the Father. The specifically Western development of filioque theology represents a divergence from this universal tradition, not its clarification.

secs.h: X. The Oriental Orthodox Position — A Summary
secs.x: X. The Oriental Orthodox Position — A Summary The Oriental Orthodox position on the filioque can be summarized in four points: 1. Scriptural: John 15:26 says the Spirit "proceeds from the Father" — not "from the Father and the Son." Christ's own words are the supreme authority, and they do not support the filioque. The passages cited in favor of it (John 20:22; Romans 8:9; Galatians 4:6) describe the Spirit's temporal mission and relationship to Christ in the economy of salvation — not the Spirit's eternal procession within the immanent Trinity. 2. Patristic: The Eastern Fathers — Athanasius, the Cappadocians, Cyril of Alexandria, and all the major Alexandrian and Antiochene theologians — speak of the Spirit proceeding from the Father, often adding that the Spirit is sent through the Son or manifested through the Son. None of them affirm a double procession in the eternal Trinity. The filioque is a Western theological development, not the universal apostolic tradition. 3. Conciliar: The Council of Ephesus (AD 431) explicitly forbade additions to the Nicene Creed.

secs.h: X. The Oriental Orthodox Position — A Summary
secs.x: The filioque was added in violation of this prohibition — first regionally (Spain, AD 589), then universally by Rome (AD 1014) — without an Ecumenical Council. Even Pope Leo III (c. AD 809) refused to add it, on the grounds that the Fathers had not put it there. The insertion is canonically irregular regardless of its theological content. 4. Theological: The filioque threatens the monarchy of the Father (his role as the sole source of the Trinity) and introduces a "double principle" for the Spirit's existence — a problem that Western theologians have never satisfactorily resolved. The Eastern theology — Father as sole source, Son as eternally begotten, Spirit as eternally proceeding from the Father through the Son in the economy — maintains the unity and monarchy of the Trinity without subordinating any Person.

XI. FAQ Q: Do most Protestant churches use the filioque? Yes. Most Protestant denominations inherited the Nicene Creed from the Western (Latin) Catholic tradition, including the filioque. When Protestants recite the Nicene Creed, they typically use the Western version with "and the Son." This is not a conscious theological decision for most Protestants but a historical inheritance from the Latin Church they came from. The filioque is rarely a point of active theological reflection in Protestant churches — it is simply received as part of the traditional Creed. Some ecumenically minded Protestant theologians have expressed openness to removing the filioque in the interest of East-West Christian unity. Q: What do modern Catholic-Orthodox dialogues say about the filioque? Modern ecumenical dialogues have made significant progress on the filioque.

The Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity issued a clarification in 1995 ("The Greek and Latin Traditions Regarding the Procession of the Holy Spirit") acknowledging that the East and West may be expressing the same truth in different ways — and that the filioque was an unauthorized addition to the Creed. Pope John Paul II recited the Nicene Creed without filioque in joint celebrations with Eastern Orthodox patriarchs on several occasions. However, Rome has not officially removed the filioque from the Creed for Latin Rite Catholics, and the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox consider its removal a prerequisite for any meaningful reunion. Q: Is the filioque the only reason for the East-West Schism? No — the Great Schism of 1054 had multiple causes: the filioque was the primary theological dispute; papal primacy and jurisdiction was the primary ecclesiological dispute; and various cultural, political, and liturgical differences (use of unleavened bread in the Latin Eucharist, clerical celibacy rules, etc.) contributed.

The 1054 schism was also the culmination of centuries of growing estrangement — the Photian schism of 867–880 being an earlier rupture that was healed but left scars. The filioque, however, is consistently identified by Eastern theologians as the most fundamental theological issue — because it touches the eternal being of God himself.
