I. Introduction No aspect of Oriental Orthodox practice provokes more immediate suspicion among Protestants — and, in some contexts, among Muslims — than the veneration of icons. Walk into a Coptic church and you will find every wall covered with images of Christ, the Theotokos, the Apostles, and the saints. The faithful kiss these images, bow before them, burn incense before them, and keep them in their homes. To the uninitiated, this looks uncomfortably like the idolatry condemned throughout the Old Testament. The OO tradition insists that this reaction, however understandable, rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of what an icon is and what happens when it is venerated. An icon is not an idol. The veneration given to it is not worship. And the theological justification for sacred images rests not on pagan tradition or medieval corruption but on the Incarnation of the Son of God — the most radical claim in Christian theology.

This site traces the full biblical, patristic, and historical case for icon veneration: from the Old Testament's own sacred images, through the early Church's practice, through the great iconoclast crisis of the eighth and ninth centuries, to the definitive articulation of icon theology at the Second Council of Nicaea (AD 787). It also engages fully with Protestant and Islamic objections. "When the Invisible One becomes visible to flesh, you may then draw a likeness of His form." — John of Damascus, First Apology Against Those Who Attack the Divine Images (tr. Allies)

II. Glossary of Key Terms Icon Greek: eikōn — "image, likeness" A sacred image of Christ, the Theotokos, angels, or saints, written (not painted) according to a theological and liturgical tradition. An icon is a window into the presence of the one depicted, not a portrait of an absent person. Iconoclasm Greek: eikon + klaō — "image-breaking" The movement that rejected the veneration of icons as idolatry. Two major periods: 726–AD 787 (resolved at Nicaea II) and 814–AD 843 (resolved at the Triumph of Orthodoxy). Iconodule / Iconophile Greek: eikon + douleia/philos — "image-servant / image-lover" Those who defended the veneration of icons as legitimate Christian practice. Their opponents called them "idolaters"; they called themselves defenders of the Incarnation. Prototype Greek: prōtotypon — "first type, original" The person depicted in an icon. The honor given to the icon passes through it to the prototype. Veneration of the image is veneration of the person, not of the wood and paint.

Proskynesis Greek: "prostration, reverence, bowing" The act of bowing or prostrating before an icon. Used in secular contexts for honor to emperors; used in sacred contexts for veneration of icons. Distinguished from latreia (worship). Theotokos Icon Hodegetria, Eleusa, Blachernitissa types Icons of the Virgin Mary, of which several classic types exist. The Hodegetria ("She Who Shows the Way") depicts Mary pointing to Christ. The Eleusa ("Tenderness") shows mother and child embraced. Both are found in all OO traditions. Pantocrator Greek: "Ruler of All" The most common icon type of Christ: enthroned, holding the Gospels, right hand raised in blessing. Found in the dome of every Orthodox church, above the congregation, signifying Christ's lordship over all creation. Triumph of Orthodoxy First Sunday of Great Lent The feast commemorating the restoration of icon veneration on March 11, AD 843, after the Second Iconoclasm. Celebrated as one of the most important feasts in both Eastern and Oriental Orthodox traditions.

Acheiropoieta Greek: "not made by human hands" Icons believed to have been miraculously created without human hands — most notably the Image of Edessa (Mandylion) and the Veil of Veronica. These played a significant role in the iconoclast debates as evidence of divine approval of images.

III. What Is an Icon? The word eikōn (εἰκών) means "image" or "likeness." It is the word used in Genesis 1:26–27 (in the Septuagint) to describe humanity as bearing the "image" of God. It is the word Paul uses in Colossians 1:15 to call Christ "the image of the invisible God." And it is the word used for the sacred images venerated in the Church. An icon is not a painting in the ordinary sense. It is "written" — iconographers use the word "write" rather than "paint" — according to a theological tradition that determines its content, composition, and spiritual intention. The gold background represents the uncreated light of the Kingdom. The elongated figures represent bodies transfigured and spiritualized. The flat perspective (rather than three-dimensional) signals that the icon opens onto a spiritual reality beyond ordinary space and time. Most importantly: an icon is a window, not a wall. It does not enclose a reality; it opens onto one. When an Orthodox Christian stands before the icon of St. Antony, they do not imagine they are looking at a picture of someone absent.

They believe they are in contact with a person alive in God — present in a mode different from, but not less real than, physical presence. This understanding explains the full range of devotional acts: kissing the icon (greeting a person), bowing (honoring a person), burning incense (a liturgical act of honor), and praying before it (addressing the person depicted, asking for intercession). None of these acts are directed at the wood and paint — they pass through the image to the prototype.

IV. The Incarnation as the Foundation of Icon Theology The deepest theological argument for icons is not pragmatic or aesthetic — it is Christological. The Incarnation of the Son of God is the foundation on which the entire theology of the icon rests. John 1:14 "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth." OO: "We have seen his glory" — Christ was seen. The eternal invisible God became visible. This is the premise of icon theology. Colossians 1:15 "The Son is the image (eikōn) of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation." OO: Christ is himself the eikōn — the icon — of the invisible God. Every icon of Christ is an icon of the Icon. The word "icon" is Scriptural and Christological before it is devotional.

1 John 1:1–3 "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked at and our hands have touched — this we proclaim concerning the Word of life… We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard." OO: The Apostolic proclamation is rooted in physical sight and touch. John insists on the physical visibility of Christ — the same physicality that makes icons possible. To deny that Christ can be depicted is implicitly to deny that he truly became visible flesh The Iconoclast Heresy as Crypto-Docetism The OO and Eastern Orthodox traditions argue that iconoclasm, however well-intentioned, smuggles in a form of Docetism — the heresy that Christ only appeared to have a human body. If Christ truly became flesh and was truly seen, then his visible human nature can be depicted. If you deny that his face can be shown in an icon, you are implicitly suggesting that his human nature was not truly visible — that he did not really become flesh in the full sense. John of Damascus First Apology Against Those Who Attack the Divine Images (c.

AD 730) "Therefore I venture to draw an image of the invisible God, not as invisible, but as having become visible for our sakes through flesh and blood. I do not draw an image of the immortal Godhead. I paint the visible flesh of God…" VERBATIM tr. M. H. Allies, 1898 In the Orthodox view, the iconoclasts never found a satisfying answer to this argument. If you accept the full Chalcedonian (or Miaphysite) Christology — that Christ is truly God and truly human in one person — then you must accept that his human nature is depictable. The invisible God became visible. The icon depicts the visible.

V. Old Testament Precedents for Sacred Images The charge that icons violate the Old Testament's prohibition of images founders immediately on the Old Testament's own sacred images, commanded by God himself. Exodus 25:18–22 "And make two cherubim out of hammered gold at the ends of the cover… The cherubim are to have their wings spread upward, overshadowing the cover with them. The cherubim are to face each other, looking toward the cover. Place the cover on top of the ark… There, above the cover between the two cherubim that are over the ark of the covenant law, I will meet with you." OO: God commands golden images of heavenly beings to be placed in his sanctuary — and promises to meet with his people between them. Images of holy beings are not inherently idolatrous.

The cherubim were also embroidered on the inner curtains of the Tabernacle (Exodus 26:1) and carved throughout Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6:23–35) Numbers 21:8–9 "The LORD said to Moses, 'Make a snake and put it up on a pole; anyone who is bitten can look at it and live.' So Moses made a bronze snake and put it up on a pole. Then when anyone was bitten by a snake and looked at the bronze snake, they lived." OO: A material image, commanded by God, through which physical healing is obtained. Christ himself interprets this as a type of his own Crucifixion (John 3:14–15). The image was later destroyed by Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:4) only when it was being worshipped as a god — the problem was idolatry, not the image itself 1 Kings 6:23–29 "For the inner sanctuary he made a pair of cherubim out of olive wood, each ten cubits high… On the walls all around the temple, in both the inner and outer rooms, he carved cherubim, palm trees and open flowers." Solomon's Temple — the House of God — was covered with images of cherubim and natural forms.

God dwelt in a house full of sacred images and showed no displeasure. The Key Distinction in Deuteronomy 4 The classic prohibition in Exodus 20:4 says: "You shall not make for yourself an image in the form of anything in heaven above or on the earth beneath…" The key clarification comes in Deuteronomy 4:15–19, where Moses explains the reason for the prohibition: "You saw no form of any kind the day the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the fire. Therefore watch yourselves very carefully, so that you do not become corrupt and make for yourselves an idol, an image of any shape, whether formed like a man or a woman, or like any animal on earth…" The prohibition is against making images to worship as gods — specifically because Israel saw no form of God at Sinai. The issue is not images per se but the worship of images as gods. And the entire argument collapses with the Incarnation: now God has shown his face. The reason for the prohibition (God has no visible form) has been answered in the most radical way possible — by God himself taking on visible, human form in Jesus Christ.

VI. The Early Church and Images — Archaeological Evidence The claim that early Christianity was entirely imageless — and that icons developed later as a pagan corruption — does not survive archaeological scrutiny. The evidence for Christian images in the early centuries is extensive and unambiguous. c. AD 232 Dura-Europos house church — the oldest known Christian worship space, discovered in Syria. Contains painted images of Christ healing the paralytic, the Good Shepherd, the Women at the Tomb, and other biblical scenes. This is pre-Constantinian, pre-any-supposed-pagan-corruption. c. 200–AD 400 Roman catacombs — the underground burial chambers of the early Roman Christians are extensively decorated with images of Christ (as the Good Shepherd), biblical scenes, and symbols. These were made by Christians living under a pagan empire, often in times of persecution. 6th Century The earliest surviving icon panel — the encaustic (wax) icon of Christ Pantocrator at St.

Catherine's Monastery, Sinai — dates to the 6th century, but the iconographic tradition it represents is considerably older. c. 300–AD 400 Eusebius of Caesarea (c. AD 313) mentions seeing painted portraits of Christ, Peter, and Paul. He records that the woman healed of the issue of blood (Luke 8:43–44) erected a bronze statue of Christ at Caesarea Philippi. The Significance of Dura-Europos The Dura-Europos house church is the single most important archaeological refutation of the claim that early Christianity was imageless. Discovered in Syria in the 1920s and dated to approximately AD 232, it contains painted images of biblical scenes covering its walls — in a small, persecuted Christian community in a frontier town far from Rome. These images predate Constantine by nearly a century. They were created by Christians whose primary concern was survival, not accommodation to pagan aesthetics. The idea that icons represent a later corruption by paganism cannot be sustained in the face of Dura-Europos.

VII. The First Iconoclasm (726–AD 787) According to later iconophile sources, the first systematic assault on Christian images began in AD 726 when Emperor Leo III ordered the removal of a prominent icon of Christ from the Chalke Gate of the imperial palace in Constantinople. (Some modern historians, such as Leslie Brubaker and John Haldon, think these sources exaggerate Leo's actions and that firm imperial policy against icons began under his son Constantine V.) What followed was a seventy-year crisis that shook the Byzantine Empire and the Church. The Origins of Byzantine Iconoclasm The causes of the First Iconoclasm were complex. Byzantine military defeats — particularly to the Arab Muslim armies — were interpreted by Leo III as divine punishment for idolatry. Islamic and Jewish criticism of Christian image-veneration may have influenced his thinking. There were also genuine theological questions in circulation about the proper limits of image-veneration. AD 726 Emperor Leo III orders removal of the Christ icon from the Chalke Gate. Riots in Constantinople.

Pope Gregory II protests from Rome. AD 730 Leo III, by the traditional account, issues an edict against icons and deposes Patriarch Germanos. John of Damascus (in Muslim-controlled Jerusalem, safely beyond imperial reach) writes his three Treatises Against Those Who Attack the Divine Images. AD 754 Iconoclast Council of Hiereia — 338 bishops condemn icon veneration. Germanos of Constantinople, George of Cyprus, and John of Damascus are anathematized. The council claims ecumenical authority but is later rejected. 754–AD 775 Emperor Constantine V (Copronymus) intensifies persecution of iconodules. Monks and clergy tortured, blinded, exiled. Icons burned, monasteries dissolved. AD 780 Death of Leo IV (Constantine V had died in 775). Empress Irene becomes regent for her son Constantine VI. She moves toward restoring icon veneration. AD 787 Second Council of Nicaea — Seventh Ecumenical Council. Icon veneration restored. Iconoclasm formally condemned.

The OO Position During the First Iconoclasm The Oriental Orthodox churches — Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian — had already separated from the Byzantine communion after Chalcedon (AD 451). They were therefore not subject to the Byzantine imperial decrees. The Coptic church continued venerating icons throughout this period without interruption. The most powerful theological defender of icons, John of Damascus, lived in Muslim-controlled territory and was entirely free of Byzantine imperial pressure — making his defense of icons a purely theological, not political, statement.

VIII. John of Damascus — Defender of Icons John of Damascus (c. 675–AD 749) is the greatest theological defender of icon veneration in Christian history. A monk and priest of the Monastery of Mar Saba near Jerusalem, living under Muslim rule and therefore immune to Byzantine imperial pressure, he wrote three definitive treatises against iconoclasm that remain the foundational texts of icon theology. John of Damascus Third Apology Against Those Who Attack the Divine Images (c. AD 730) "Every image is a revelation and representation of something hidden. For instance, man has not a clear knowledge of what is invisible, the spirit being veiled to the body, nor of future things, nor of things apart and distant, because he is circumscribed by place and time." VERBATIM tr. M. H. Allies, 1898 John of Damascus First Apology Against Those Who Attack the Divine Images "Of old, God the incorporeal and uncircumscribed was never depicted. Now, however, when God is seen clothed in flesh, and conversing with men, I make an image of the God whom I see.

I do not worship matter, I worship the God of matter, who became matter for my sake, and deigned to inhabit matter, who worked out my salvation through matter. I will not cease from honouring that matter which works my salvation." VERBATIM tr. M. H. Allies, 1898 John's Threefold Argument John of Damascus advances three interconnected arguments that together form the complete theological defense of icons: The Incarnational argument : The eternal invisible God became visible in the flesh. What has become visible may be depicted. To deny this is to deny the Incarnation. The Prototype argument : Honor given to an image passes to its prototype. Venerating an icon of Christ honors Christ; it does not dishonor him. The image and the person are distinct but related. The Tradition argument : The Church has always used images. The practice is not innovation but inheritance — from the Apostles and their successors, documented in the Church's continuous life.

John of Damascus First Apology Against Those Who Attack the Divine Images "We proclaim Him also by our senses on all sides, and we sanctify the noblest sense, which is that of sight. The image is a memorial, just what words are to a listening ear. What a book is to the literate, that an image is to the illiterate. The image speaks to the sight as words to the ear; it brings us understanding." VERBATIM tr. M. H. Allies, 1898

IX. The Second Council of Nicaea (AD 787) The Second Council of Nicaea — the Seventh Ecumenical Council — was convened in AD 787 under Empress Irene and formally restored icon veneration, condemned iconoclasm, and provided the definitive theological framework for the doctrine that has been held ever since. The Council's Definition "…define with all certitude and accuracy that just as the figure of the precious and life-giving Cross, so also the venerable and holy images, as well in painting and mosaic as of other fit materials, should be set forth in the holy churches of God, and on the sacred vessels and on the vestments and on hangings and in pictures both in houses and by the wayside, to wit, the figure of our Lord God and Saviour Jesus Christ, of our spotless Lady, the Mother of God, of the honourable Angels, of all Saints and of all pious people.

For by so much more frequently as they are seen in artistic representation, by so much more readily are men lifted up to the memory of their prototypes, and to a longing after them; and to these should be given due salutation and honourable reverence (ἀσπασμὸν καὶ τιμητικὴν προσκύνησιν), not indeed that true worship of faith (λατρείαν) which pertains alone to the divine nature; but to these, as to the figure of the precious and life-giving Cross and to the Book of the Gospels and to the other holy objects, incense and lights may be offered according to ancient pious custom. For the honour which is paid to the image passes on to that which the image represents, and he who reveres the image reveres in it the subject represented." (NPNF translation) Key Theological Points of the Definition Two kinds of honor are distinguished : proskynesis timetike (veneration of honor) given to icons versus latreia (worship) given to God alone The prototype principle : Honor given to the image passes to the person depicted — the locus of the honor is always the person, not the material The continuity

of tradition : The Council explicitly frames its decision as restoration of ancient custom, not innovation Universal scope : Icons of Christ, the Theotokos, angels, and all saints are included The Second Council of Nicaea is the Seventh Ecumenical Council, accepted in full by the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches. The Oriental Orthodox churches (who reject councils after Ephesus as non-binding) nonetheless hold the same theology of icons independently — as evidenced by their continuous uninterrupted practice throughout the iconoclast period.

X. The Second Iconoclasm (814–AD 843) After the death of Empress Irene, Byzantine iconoclasm was revived under Emperor Leo V in AD 814 — a second assault that lasted nearly thirty years. This second crisis produced its own martyrs and its own theological defenders before being definitively ended on March 11, AD 843. AD 814 Emperor Leo V revives iconoclasm. Patriarch Nikephoros deposed and exiled. Theodore the Studite leads monastic resistance. 815–AD 843 Persecution of iconodule monks, clergy, and laypeople. Theodore the Studite imprisoned and flogged. Icons destroyed throughout the empire. AD 842 Death of Emperor Theophilos. Empress Theodora becomes regent. She convenes a council and restores icon veneration. March 11, AD 843 The Triumph of Orthodoxy — icons are solemnly restored in the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. The Eastern Orthodox celebrate it on the First Sunday of Great Lent. The Oriental Orthodox, who were not in communion with Constantinople, do not keep this feast, though they venerate icons in their own traditions.

Theodore the Studite Theodore the Studite (759–AD 826) was the most important defender of icons during the Second Iconoclasm. His theological contribution was to deepen and systematize the Christological argument, drawing especially on the logic of the hypostatic union to argue that because Christ's human nature is inseparable from his divine Person, any depiction of his human nature necessarily depicts the divine Person — and thus icons of Christ are intrinsically Christological confessions of faith. Theodore the Studite Antirrhetici Against the Iconoclasts (c. 815–AD 820) Summary: Theodore argues that to deny that Christ can be circumscribed and depicted is to deny the reality of His human nature, so that iconoclasm collapses into Christological error. The icon is therefore a confession of the Incarnation. SUMMARY No public-domain English translation of the Antirrhetici is available to quote

secs.h: The Analogy of the Emperor's Image
secs.x: XI. The Theology of the Prototype The central principle of icon theology — stated definitively at Nicaea II and rooted in John of Damascus — is the doctrine of the prototype: honor given to the image passes to the person depicted. This principle is not invented by the Church Fathers — it is borrowed from philosophy and applied to theology. The Neoplatonist philosopher Porphyry (c. 234–AD 305) articulated a version of this principle in a pagan context. Basil the Great applied it to the Christian context before the iconoclast controversy even began: Basil the Great On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 18 (c. AD 375) "Because we speak of a king, and of the king's image, and not of two kings. The majesty is not cloven in two, nor the glory divided… because the honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype. Now what in the one case the image is by reason of imitation, that in the other case the Son is by nature." VERBATIM On the Holy Spirit 18.45 (NPNF).

secs.h: The Analogy of the Emperor's Image
secs.x: Basil uses the emperor analogy, universally understood, to explain how honor to the image reaches the person The Analogy of the Emperor's Image In the ancient world, the emperor's image — on coins, statues, and official portraits — was treated as a kind of extension of the emperor's presence. To honor the image was to honor the emperor; to desecrate it was to commit treason. This was not considered idolatry (worship of the image) but normal political honor (reverence for the person represented). The OO tradition uses exactly this analogy: the icon of Christ is the image of the King of Kings. Honoring it honors him. What the Prototype Principle Does Not Mean The prototype principle does not mean that the material of the icon is holy in itself. The icon is not a magical object. The wood and paint have no power of their own. If an icon is damaged or destroyed, the person depicted is neither harmed nor dishonored — the icon was a vehicle, not a vessel.

secs.h: The Analogy of the Emperor's Image
secs.x: When Hezekiah destroyed the bronze serpent (2 Kings 18:4), the serpent itself had become an object of false worship; its destruction was righteous. The same logic applies if icons are treated as magical objects rather than windows to the prototype.

XII. The Image of God in Man — Theological Anthropology The theology of icons connects directly to the theology of the human person. Humanity is made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27) — we are, in a sense, living icons of the divine. The icon written on wood is a reflection of the icon that God wrote in human flesh. Genesis 1:26–27 "Then God said, 'Let us make mankind in our image (eikōn), in our likeness (homoiōsis)…' So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them." OO: Humanity is God's icon in creation — the living image of the invisible God. If God himself made living images of himself, he cannot be opposed to the making of images in principle. 2 Corinthians 3:18 "And we all, who with unveiled faces contemplate the Lord's glory, are being transformed into his image (eikōna) with ever-increasing glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit." OO: The Christian life is a process of becoming more fully the image of God — theosis. The icon depicts the saint as already fully transformed, already fully the image.

It is an eschatological portrait. The Icon as Eschatological Vision One of the most profound aspects of Orthodox icon theology is that an icon does not depict the saint as they were on earth — fallen, limited, subject to decay — but as they are now in the Kingdom of God: transfigured, glorified, fully bearing the divine image for which they were created. The gold background is not decorative — it is the uncreated light of the Age to Come. The elongated figures are not poor anatomy — they are bodies no longer subject to gravity and entropy. The icon is a window into the eschatological reality of the Kingdom. This is why the OO tradition (and the Eastern Orthodox) insists that iconographers must be people of prayer, fasting, and spiritual preparation — the icon is a theological statement, not an artistic one, and requires a person in tune with the spiritual realities it depicts.

XIII. Relics — The Extension of Icon Theology The veneration of relics — the physical remains of saints — flows from the same theological root as icon veneration. If the bodies of the saints are temples of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19) in life, they retain a sacred dignity in death. 2 Kings 13:21 "Once while some Israelites were burying a man, suddenly they saw a band of raiders; so they threw the man's body into Elisha's tomb. When the body touched Elisha's bones, the man came to life and stood up on his feet." OO: The bones of the prophet Elisha — his relics — effect a miracle of resurrection. The OT precedent for the sanctifying power of the saints' physical remains is explicit. Acts 19:11–12 "God did extraordinary miracles through Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick, and their illnesses were cured and the evil spirits left them." OO: Physical objects that touched an Apostle transmitted healing grace.

This is the NT foundation for the veneration of relics — the principle that holiness communicates through material contact. The Martyrs' Tombs From the earliest centuries, Christians gathered at the tombs of the martyrs for prayer and Eucharist. The Martyrdom of Polycarp (c. AD 156) records that the Christians of Smyrna collected Polycarp's bones after his martyrdom, calling them "more precious than gold," and intended to gather at his tomb annually. This practice — gathering at martyr-tombs, which evolved into building churches over them — is the direct ancestor of the relic veneration practiced in all Oriental Orthodox churches. Cyril of Jerusalem Catechetical Lectures, Lecture 18 (c. AD 350) "…a virtue resides in the body of the saints, because of the righteous soul which has for so many years dwelt in it, and used it as its minister… for if handkerchiefs and aprons, which are from without, touching the bodies of the diseased, raised up the sick, how much more should the very body of the Prophet raise the dead?" VERBATIM Catechetical Lecture 18.16 (NPNF)

XIV. Icons in the Divine Liturgy Icons are not merely decorative elements in OO churches — they are liturgical participants. The Divine Liturgy is understood as a participation in the heavenly liturgy described in Revelation 4–5, where the saints, the angels, and all the redeemed surround the throne of the Lamb. The icons on the walls and sanctuary make this theology visible: the faithful at the earthly liturgy are surrounded by the saints in glory, joined to their unceasing worship. The Iconostasis In Eastern Orthodox and some OO traditions, the iconostasis — the icon screen — divides the nave from the sanctuary. It is covered with icons in a fixed arrangement: Christ Pantocrator, the Theotokos, the saint of the church, the Apostles. Far from being a wall that separates the people from God, the iconostasis is a declaration that the boundary between earth and heaven has been pierced by the Incarnation: the doors in the screen are passages through which the priest moves, carrying the gifts of bread and wine into the presence of the assembled saints.

The OO Coptic Tradition The Coptic church arranges its sanctuary with icons on every available surface. The sanctuary screen (haikal) in Coptic churches is itself typically carved with icons. Every celebration of the Divine Liturgy takes place surrounded by representations of the saints who have gone before — an embodied expression of the Communion of Saints spanning heaven and earth. Incense Before Icons The liturgical use of incense before icons expresses the same theology as Revelation 8:3–4 — the prayers of the saints rising as incense before the throne of God. When a deacon censes the icons at the beginning of the liturgy, he is greeting the saints present in the assembly, acknowledging their participation in the worship, and symbolically uniting the earthly and heavenly liturgies.

XV. OO Iconographic Traditions Each Oriental Orthodox church has developed its own distinctive iconographic tradition — sharing the same theology but expressing it through unique aesthetic and cultural forms. Coptic Iconography Egypt · Late Antiquity to Present Coptic icons are characterized by their flat, frontal figures, large expressive eyes (the windows of the soul), and rich earth tones — ochre, red, and deep blue — set against gold backgrounds. The distinctive large eyes are not artistic naivety but theological intentionality: the eyes of the saint look directly at the viewer, establishing a personal encounter. Major Coptic icon schools include the works of Isaac Fanous (1919–2007), who revived traditional Coptic iconography in the twentieth century, and his disciples who continue in his tradition. Ethiopian Iconography Ethiopia · 4th Century to Present Ethiopian icons are among the most distinctive in the Christian world. They typically feature frontal figures with large, almond-shaped eyes and bold, flat color fields.

The Theotokos is depicted in a uniquely Ethiopian style — holding the Christ child, surrounded by saints and angels in bright mineral-based pigments of red, yellow, blue, and green. Ethiopian icons often include borders divided into narrative panels depicting scenes from the life of the saint. The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela (traditionally late 12th to early 13th century) contain some of the most celebrated examples of Ethiopian sacred art. Armenian Iconography Armenia · 4th Century to Present Armenian sacred art blends Byzantine iconographic tradition with distinctive Armenian aesthetics — complex interlace patterns (derived from the ancient khachkar cross-stone tradition), illuminated manuscript illustration, and a characteristic use of gold and deep burgundy. The Armenian Gospel manuscripts (including the famous Gospels of Gladzor and the Gospels of Mughni) contain some of the finest illuminated icon-images in Christian art. The khachkar — a carved stone cross-icon — is Armenia's unique contribution to Christian sacred art, with thousands preserved from the medieval period.

Syriac Iconography Syria, Lebanon, Iraq, India · Late Antiquity to Present The Syriac Orthodox tradition preserves an ancient iconographic heritage deeply influenced by the Aramaic-speaking Christianity of the earliest centuries. Syriac manuscript illumination, from the Rabbula Gospels (AD 586, one of the oldest dated illuminated Gospel books) to the great 12th–13th century Gospel books, displays a distinctive style. The Malankara Orthodox Church in Kerala, India, has developed its own blend of Syriac iconography with South Indian artistic traditions.

secs.h: The Full Text of the Commandment
secs.x: XVI. The Second Commandment — "No Graven Images" The most common objection to icons — among Protestants, Muslims, and secular critics — is the Second Commandment: "You shall not make for yourself an image in the form of anything in heaven above or on the earth beneath" (Exodus 20:4; Deuteronomy 5:8). A careful examination of this commandment in its full context shows that it does not prohibit sacred images — it prohibits idolatry. The Full Text of the Commandment Exodus 20:4–5 "You shall not make for yourself an image in the form of anything in heaven above or on the earth beneath or in the waters below. You shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God…" The prohibition has two parts: do not make images AND do not worship them. The second clause explains the purpose of the first.

secs.h: The Full Text of the Commandment
secs.x: Protestant reading: All sacred images are forbidden — the making itself is the sin OO reading: The sin is worshipping images as gods (idolatry) — not making images for sacred use Why the "Making" Alone Cannot Be the Sin The argument that any sacred image is forbidden by Exodus 20:4 cannot be reconciled with Exodus 25:18–22 (God commands golden cherubim), Exodus 26:1 (cherubim woven into the Tabernacle curtains), Numbers 21:8–9 (bronze serpent commanded by God), or 1 Kings 6:23–35 (cherubim, palm trees, and flowers covering the Temple walls). If the making of any image were sinful, these passages — where God commands the making of images — would involve God commanding sin. This is impossible. The only coherent reading of the commandment is that it prohibits images made for the purpose of being worshipped as gods — the surrounding context (v.5: "you shall not bow down to them or worship them") makes this explicit.

secs.h: The Full Text of the Commandment
secs.x: The same reading is confirmed by Deuteronomy 4:15–19 (see Section V), where Moses explains the reason for the prohibition as rooted in Israel's not having seen God's form at Sinai — a reason that is definitively answered by the Incarnation. John of Damascus First Apology Against Those Who Attack the Divine Images "Is there only one God? You answer, 'Yes, there is only one Law-giver.' Why, then, does He command contrary things? The cherubim are not outside of creation; why, then, does He allow cherubim carved by the hand of man to overshadow the mercy-seat? Is it not evident that as it is impossible to make an image of God, who is uncircumscribed and impassible, or of one like to God, creation should not be worshipped as God." VERBATIM tr. M. H. Allies, 1898

XVII. Protestant Objections Addressed "Kissing an icon is bowing before an idol — it's worship." OO Response: The act of kissing does not constitute worship in itself. Abraham bowed before the Hittites (Genesis 23:7) — was that idolatry? The disciples fell on their faces before Jesus at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:6) — was that inappropriate? Honor is expressed through physical gesture in every culture. Kissing an icon is the same gesture as kissing a photograph of a loved one, or kissing the Gospel book, or kissing the cross on Good Friday — all of which are practiced in Protestant-adjacent traditions without accusation of idolatry. The intention and the object of the honor determine whether an act is worship or veneration. Kissing the icon of St. Mark is honoring St. Mark, not worshipping wood and paint. "Dulia vs. latria is a distinction without a difference — you invented Greek labels to rebrand worship.

Bowing, incense, and prayer just are worship." OO Response: The distinction is not a semantic trick invented to license a practice — it is a distinction Scripture itself operates, which the English word "worship" has simply flattened. In Hebrew and Greek the same outward word covers the gesture whether it is offered to God or to a man (Hebrew hishtachavah , Greek proskyneo ), and the biblical writers plainly distinguish the two by object and intent , without any hint of condemnation. Scripture repeatedly shows the identical act of bowing or prostration offered to creatures without sin: Abraham bows to the Hittites (Genesis 23:7); Jacob bows seven times to Esau (Genesis 33:3); Joseph's brothers bow before him (Genesis 42:6); Bathsheba and Nathan bow before King David (1 Kings 1:16, 23); Obadiah falls on his face before Elijah (1 Kings 18:7); "the sons of the prophets… bowed themselves to the ground before" Elisha (2 Kings 2:15). None of this is idolatry, because none of it is offered as to God .

The very same posture becomes idolatry only when it is latria — the adoration due to God alone — as when Israel bowed to the golden calf (Exodus 32). So the outward gesture does not, by itself, settle anything — which is exactly the Orthodox point. What separates veneration from worship is not the posture but the intention and the object. Latria is the total self-offering that confesses its recipient to be God, Creator and source of being; sacrifice , in the biblical sense, belongs to it alone. Dulia is the honor owed to what God has made holy. To collapse the two is to say that a soldier who salutes the flag "worships" cloth, or that a subject who kneels before a king "worships" the king — which no one actually believes. The New Testament itself runs the distinction. When John falls to venerate the angel, the angel refuses — "See thou do it not… worship God" (Revelation 19:10; 22:9) — precisely because that reverence, offered to the messenger, was slipping toward what belongs to God alone.

The test the Church applies is sharp and bright: to whom do we offer sacrifice? Israel could bow to kings and prophets, but sacrificed to God alone; the Orthodox venerate the saints and their icons, but the bloodless sacrifice of the Eucharist is offered to the Holy Trinity alone. Finally, the charge is self-refuting: the objector who stands for a judge, removes his hat at a graveside, or salutes a flag already practices honor-in-gesture toward creatures without confusing it with the worship of God. He simply denies the Orthodox the coherence he grants himself. "The early Church had no icons — they were introduced from paganism." OO Response: This is archaeologically false. The Dura-Europos house church (c. AD 232), the Roman catacombs (c. 200–AD 400), and Eusebius's references to portraits of Christ, Peter, and Paul (c. AD 313) all predate any plausible "pagan contamination" narrative. The catacombs were burial places rather than hideouts, but the Christians who buried their dead there decorated the chambers with images of Christ and biblical scenes.

There were also early voices of caution, such as canon 36 of the Synod of Elvira (c. 305) and a letter attributed to Eusebius refusing to send an image of Christ, and the Fathers of Nicaea II answered these. But an early Church without images is not what the evidence shows. "God is spirit — depicting him in any material form is wrong." OO Response: God is indeed spirit — in his divine nature. But the Son of God became flesh. The Incarnation is precisely the event in which the invisible took on visible form. To say that God may not be depicted in material form is to say that the Incarnation did not really happen — or that Christ's human nature was not really physical. The OO tradition affirms that icons do not depict Christ's divine nature (which is invisible and indepictable) but his human nature — the same human nature seen, touched, and handled by the Apostles (1 John 1:1–3). To refuse to depict this human nature is to subtly deny its reality.

"People obviously treat icons as magical objects — this proves the practice leads to idolatry." OO Response: The misuse of a practice does not condemn the practice. The Lord's Supper has been treated superstitiously (eating the bread for good luck, wearing a piece of it as an amulet) — this does not condemn the Eucharist. Money is worshipped as an idol (Matthew 6:24) — this does not make money sinful. Where popular piety has confused veneration with worship, or treated icons as magical objects rather than windows to the saints, the Church's response is correction and catechesis — not the abolition of an apostolic practice documented from the second century. The OO tradition is explicit in its teaching that the icon is a vehicle, not a source, of grace; a window, not a wall; a means of encountering the prototype, not an object of worship in itself. "We should relate to God through his Word, not through material images." OO Response: This dichotomy is foreign to biblical theology.

God relates to humanity through word AND matter throughout Scripture: through the burning bush, the pillar of cloud and fire, the Ark of the Covenant, the Temple, the serpent on the pole, the river Jordan, the clay Jesus used to heal the blind man, the water of Baptism, the bread and wine of the Eucharist. God chose to become matter in the Incarnation. The OO tradition does not privilege the immaterial over the material — it insists that matter, redeemed and sanctified by the Incarnation, can be a vehicle of divine grace. The icon is one expression of this sacramental theology of matter.

secs.h: The Root of the Islamic Position
secs.x: XVIII. The Islamic Objection to Icons The Islamic objection to Christian icons is categorical: God is absolutely transcendent and may not be depicted in any form. Making images of living beings — let alone of God — is forbidden in Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh) as a form of shirk (associating partners with God). The Islamic objection influenced Byzantine iconoclasm directly: Emperors Leo III and Constantine V were familiar with Muslim critiques of Christian image-veneration. The Root of the Islamic Position Islam's prohibition of images flows from its theology of God's absolute transcendence (tanzih) — God is wholly other, without form, without likeness, without any physical attributes. Any depiction of God is an arrogant attempt to bring the infinite within the finite, reducing God to human categories. This position is internally coherent within Islamic theology. The Christological Response The OO response is not a general defense of religious images — it is a specifically Christological response.

secs.h: The Root of the Islamic Position
secs.x: The Christian claim is not that God can be depicted in his divine nature (the OO tradition agrees he cannot). The Christian claim is that God the Son took on a human nature in the Incarnation — a nature that is visible, physical, and historical. The icon of Christ does not depict the divine nature; it depicts the human nature of the one who is both God and man. The Islamic objection assumes that Jesus is a mere prophet — a human being, not God incarnate. If that assumption is accepted, then Christian icon theology collapses: there is nothing special about depicting Jesus that makes it theologically significant. But if the Christian claim is true — that Jesus is the eternal Son of God made flesh — then the icon is not an act of arrogance but an act of confession: we are saying, with 1 John 1:1–3, "We have seen him. We have touched him. He was here." The Islamic critique of Christian icons ultimately reduces to the Islamic critique of the Incarnation. The Christian response to both is the same: The Word became flesh (John 1:14).

XIX. Frequently Asked Questions Is it sinful to have a bare church with no icons? The OO tradition does not teach that a church without icons is invalid or that the sacraments performed in it are ineffective. The question is whether the tradition of icon veneration is part of the Church's apostolic inheritance. The OO answer is yes — but the failure to observe a tradition does not constitute a moral sin in the same category as doctrinal heresy or moral wrongdoing. However, a church that actively prohibits and destroys icons — as the Byzantine iconoclast emperors did — is acting contrary to apostolic tradition and causing harm to the Body of Christ. Can icons be used for private devotion at home? Yes — and this has been the norm throughout Christian history. OO Christians typically maintain a "prayer corner" (or its equivalent) in the home, with icons of Christ, the Theotokos, and the family's patron saints. Morning and evening prayers are offered before these icons. The home is understood as a "domestic church," and the icon corner is the domestic sanctuary.

This practice is documented as far back as the Patristic period and is a central expression of the OO theology that the sacred is not confined to church buildings but pervades the whole of Christian life. Why do OO icons look so different from Western religious art? The difference is theological, not merely aesthetic. Western religious art (from the Renaissance onward) aimed at naturalistic representation — making the sacred figures look as real and three-dimensional as possible, placing them in recognizable earthly settings. OO iconography deliberately avoids this: the gold background places the figure outside ordinary time and space (in the Kingdom of God); the elongated proportions signal a body transfigured beyond physical limitations; the frontal posture and large eyes establish a meeting between the viewer and the saint, not the observation of a historical scene. Western art invites the viewer to look at the past; the icon invites the viewer to encounter the present. What should a Christian do if an icon is damaged or destroyed? A damaged icon should be treated with reverence.

In the OO tradition, worn or damaged icons are not thrown in the trash — they are respectfully buried, burned (with the ashes buried), or returned to the church for proper disposal. This reflects the same reverence given to the physical remains of something holy that has served its purpose. However, it is important to note that the destruction of an icon does not harm the saint depicted — the person is entirely beyond physical harm. The reverence for damaged icons is an expression of the theology that matter sanctified for holy purposes retains a dignity that should be honored in its disposal. Did the iconoclasts have any legitimate theological concerns? Yes — and honest OO apologists acknowledge this. The iconoclasts were genuinely concerned about the blurring of the line between veneration and worship in popular practice. They observed Christians who seemed to treat icons as magical objects and who appeared to offer them the same reverence as God. These were real problems then and remain real dangers today.

The iconodule response was not to abolish the practice but to articulate its theology more precisely — hence the careful formulations of John of Damascus and the Second Council of Nicaea. The Council's distinction between proskynesis timetike (veneration of honor) and latreia alethine (true worship) was a response to genuine pastoral and theological concern. The iconoclasts were wrong in their conclusion but right to identify popular confusion about the proper limits of icon veneration as a real problem.
