secs.h: Why We Steel Man — A Note on Method
secs.x: Why We Steel Man — A Note on Method A straw man argument misrepresents an opposing position in order to defeat it easily. It may win a debate, but it does not find truth — and truth is what the Christian is obligated to pursue. "And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free" (John 8:32) is not a promise to those who only engage comfortable versions of difficult questions. A steel man does the opposite: it presents the opposing argument in its strongest, most charitable form. If the case still holds after that, it holds on honest ground. This matters because millions of Christians in Muslim-majority countries are not served by propaganda — they need an honest account of what the texts say and what history shows, so they can engage their neighbors with both clarity and integrity. This site therefore begins with the best case for Islamic tolerance of Christians. It presents the genuine scholarly defenses of the contested passages. It acknowledges where historical reality is more complex than polemic allows.

secs.h: Why We Steel Man — A Note on Method
secs.x: Only after doing that does it examine what the primary sources — Qur’an, hadith, and 1,400 years of applied theology — actually demonstrate. The Standard Applied Here Every steel man argument is presented in its strongest form, sourced where possible to Muslim scholars. Every counter-argument is grounded in the primary texts (Qur’an, Sahih Bukhari, Sahih Muslim) or documented historical events. The reader is invited to weigh both. The conclusion of this site is that the evidence survives the steel man test — but the steel man is given first, in full.

secs.h: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance
secs.x: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance These are the strongest arguments made by Muslim scholars, historians, and apologists for a genuinely tolerant reading of Islam’s relationship with Christians. They are presented here at their best, not as a concession but as an obligation of honest inquiry. ▮ Steel Man Argument 1 1.8 billion Muslims are not persecuting Christians. If the texts mandated persecution, we would see it universally. The vast majority of the world’s Muslims live peacefully alongside Christians. Indonesia — the world’s largest Muslim-majority country — has a 30-million-strong Christian community that functions with relative freedom. Morocco, Jordan, Malaysia, and Senegal host Christian minorities without systematic violence. The Muslim man in Cairo who helps his Coptic neighbor, the Indonesian Muslim who attends a Christian friend’s wedding, and the millions of Muslim families who live alongside Christians in the West without incident are not aberrations — they are the majority.

secs.h: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance
secs.x: If the Qur’an commanded persecution, why don’t 1.8 billion people act on it? ▲ The Evidence’s Reply Individual Muslim behavior and Islamic doctrine are separate questions. What a person does and what their scripture teaches them to do are not the same thing, in any religion. Most people in any religious tradition do not fully apply all of its teachings. The question being examined here is not "do most Muslims persecute Christians?" — they do not. The question is "what do Islam’s foundational texts teach about Christians, and what happens when those texts are applied by people with political power?" The answer to the first question is "no"; the answer to the second is documented in 14 centuries of primary sources. The question this page tests is whether a theology that ranks unbelievers below believers tends, once it is given political form, to produce a law that ranks them below as well. The dhimmi system is the evidence that it did. ISIS cited Q.9:29 when it demanded jizyah from the Christians of Mosul in 2014.

secs.h: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance
secs.x: The Ottoman state administered a dhimmi system for more than five centuries, until the reforms of 1839 and 1856 abolished the jizyah and declared non-Muslims equal subjects. That most Muslims never become ISIS does not change what Q.9:29 says. ▮ Steel Man Argument 2 The hostile Qur’anic verses are context-specific, revealed during warfare — they are not permanent mandates against all Christians. Scholars such as Khaled Abou El Fadl, Tariq Ramadan, and Hamza Yusuf argue that Q.9:29 ("fight those … until they give jizyah") was revealed specifically in the context of the Tabuk campaign — a military confrontation with Byzantine forces in 630 AD. It was not a general mandate for all time against all Christians; it was a war-time instruction for a specific campaign. Similarly, classical commentators connect Q.5:51 ("do not take Jews and Christians as allies") with particular Medinan alliances, such as the Banu Qaynuqa affair or the aftermath of Uhud, rather than with friendship as such.

secs.h: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance
secs.x: The same surah permits Muslim men to marry Christian and Jewish women and to share their food (Q.5:5), which shows that 5:51 was never read as a ban on every personal bond. These verses, in this reading, are the equivalent of wartime operational orders, not permanent theological statements about all Christians everywhere. Many modern Muslim scholars support this contextual reading. ▲ The Evidence’s Reply The contextual argument is a real and honest position within Islamic scholarship, and it deserves acknowledgment. However, it is not the classical majority position. The four major Sunni schools of jurisprudence — Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i, and Hanbali — do not limit Q.9:29 to the Tabuk context. They apply it as a standing legal principle operative wherever the conditions are met (Islamic governance, non-Muslim presence, refusal to accept Islam). This was the basis for dhimmi law for 1,200 years across the entire breadth of the Islamic world. The contextual scholars are a minority in the tradition, not its mainstream.

secs.h: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance
secs.x: More importantly, the contextual argument does not address Q.98:6 ("worst of creatures"), which has no military context — it is purely theological. Nor does it address Sahih Muslim 2767 (Christians assigned to Hell for Muslims), which is also non-contextual. The contextual argument applies to some verses but not all the evidence. ▮ Steel Man Argument 3 The dhimmi system was more tolerant than what Christians did to Jews and heretics at the same time. When the Jews were expelled from Spain in 1492, they fled to the Ottoman Empire, not away from it. Islamic civilization produced the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, where Christian and Jewish scholars translated Greek, Syriac, and Persian texts into Arabic — preserving knowledge that might otherwise have been lost. The Umayyad caliphate in al-Andalus (Moorish Spain) allowed Jews and Christians to serve in the court, own property, and practice their faith in ways that were often more liberal than contemporary Christian Europe.

secs.h: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance
secs.x: Bernard Lewis, no apologist for Islam, judged that religious minorities under classical Islam generally fared better than minorities in most of Christian Europe. The dhimmi system, whatever its faults, provided legal existence and physical protection to minorities that many comparable medieval systems did not. ▲ The Evidence’s Reply This is the most historically defensible steel man, and it must be taken seriously. There were genuine periods of Islamic tolerance — the early Fatimid period in Egypt, Umayyad Spain, and parts of the Abbasid golden age were times of real, if qualified, coexistence. Bernard Lewis’s observation is honest. But the comparison has a crucial problem: it measures the dhimmi system against medieval Christian persecution of Jews and heretics, not against the standard of the communities it suppressed. The Oriental Orthodox churches — Coptic, Armenian, Syriac — existed before Islam. They were not a minority seeking refuge in a foreign empire; they were the indigenous populations of their own lands.

secs.h: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance
secs.x: Measuring the system that progressively reduced them from majorities to small minorities, and in some regions to nothing, against "better than the Inquisition" sets a very low bar. And the theological basis of the dhimmi system — Q.9:29’s requirement that they pay "while they are humbled" — is unambiguous regardless of how generously or harshly it was applied in any given period. ▮ Steel Man Argument 4 The Armenian Genocide was committed by secular nationalists, not by religious Muslims acting on Islamic doctrine. The Committee of Union and Progress (the "Young Turks") that ordered the Armenian deportations in 1915 was an overtly secular, nationalist, and in some respects anti-religious movement, influenced by Social Darwinism and pan-Turkic nationalism rather than Islamic theology. Several of its key architects — Talaat Pasha, Enver Pasha — were not devout Muslims. The target of the genocide was ethnic and political (Armenian nationalism, perceived disloyalty in wartime) as much as religious.

secs.h: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance
secs.x: Blaming Islam for the Armenian Genocide, in this reading, misattributes a primarily nationalist crime to a religious cause. ▲ The Evidence’s Reply The secular nationalist character of the Young Turk leadership is real, and most historians treat 1915 as a state-organised genocide driven chiefly by nationalist and wartime aims. But religion was part of how it was carried out. The Hamidiye, Kurdish irregular cavalry raised by Sultan Abdulhamid II in 1891, took a large part in the massacres of 1894 to 1896, which killed somewhere between 100,000 and 300,000 Armenians, alongside troops and town mobs. In November 1914 the Sheikh-ul-Islam proclaimed jihad. The proclamation was aimed at the Entente powers, not at Ottoman Christians, but it gave the war a religious frame that local killers turned against their Christian neighbours. Survivors repeatedly describe being offered their lives in exchange for conversion, and being called gavur (infidels). The leadership may have been secular; much of the mass participation was not.

secs.h: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance
secs.x: The Syriac genocide (Seyfo) is if anything harder to attribute purely to secular nationalism, as it was carried out in regions with no comparable nationalist political organization among the Syriac population. ▮ Steel Man Argument 5 Modern Islamic scholarship has evolved. Al-Azhar and mainstream Muslim leaders condemn terrorism and affirm religious freedom. Al-Azhar University in Cairo — the oldest and most prestigious institution of Islamic learning in the world — has issued statements condemning ISIS, condemning violence against Christians, and affirming that religious freedom is an Islamic value. In 2016, hundreds of Muslim scholars and leaders signed the Marrakesh Declaration, affirming the rights of religious minorities in Muslim-majority countries; in 2019, Al-Azhar’s Grand Imam Ahmed al-Tayeb co-signed the Document on Human Fraternity with Pope Francis in Abu Dhabi. Many Muslim-majority nations — Morocco, Tunisia, Jordan, the UAE — have enacted legal protections for religious minorities.

secs.h: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance
secs.x: Islam, like Christianity and Judaism, is a living tradition capable of reform and development. To judge Islam permanently by its worst historical applications ignores this capacity for growth. ▲ The Evidence’s Reply These developments are genuinely welcome and should be honestly acknowledged. The Marrakesh Declaration is a positive document. Al-Azhar’s condemnations of ISIS are real. However, several things remain true simultaneously. First, these reforms have not been accompanied by any revision of the Qur’anic text, which still contains Q.98:6, Q.9:29, and Q.9:30. Second, the reforms are contested within Islamic scholarship — Al-Azhar condemned the crimes of ISIS but in December 2014 formally declined to declare its members unbelievers, on the ground that no believer may be declared an apostate for his sins; and declarations such as Marrakesh bind no state and no law school. Third, blasphemy laws, restrictions on church construction, and prohibition of proselytism remain in force in many Muslim-majority states, including ostensibly moderate ones.

secs.h: The Steel Man — The Strongest Case for Islamic Tolerance
secs.x: In Egypt a church still needs state approval under the 2016 Church Construction Law, a procedure Coptic leaders have criticised as slow, although thousands of existing churches have since been licensed under it. Pakistan’s blasphemy law still carries the death penalty. The reforms exist; so do the laws derived from the texts. Both are real.

Why the Evidence Still Stands Having given Islam its best case, the following sections examine what the primary sources actually demonstrate. The steel man has been engaged honestly. The question now is whether, after that engagement, the evidence survives. The argument of this site is that it does — for three reasons. 1. The Texts Are Unambiguous Whatever the contextual or reformed readings of Q.9:29 or Q.5:51, the following texts admit no contextual escape: Qur’an 98:6 "Indeed, they who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell … Those are the worst of creatures." This verse has no military context. The classical commentators read it as a judgment on those of the People of the Scripture who rejected Muhammad; some modern Muslim scholars limit it to those who reject Islam knowingly (see below). Two things should be said fairly.

First, a verdict about the afterlife is not by itself a licence for persecution: the Gospel also says that "whoever does not believe is condemned already" (John 3:18), and Christians would not want that verse read as a political programme. Second, what the Gospel never does is attach to its verdict a law for ruling over unbelievers. The argument of this page therefore rests chiefly on Q.9:29 and the law built on it. Q.98:6 matters because it states the theological ranking that the law put into practice. Sahih Muslim 2767 "When it will be the Day of Resurrection Allah would deliver to every Muslim a Jew or a Christian and say: That is your rescue from Hell-Fire." This hadith, reported in several narrations in Sahih Muslim, all through Abu Burda from his father Abu Musa, is not a war-time instruction or a political statement. It is about the afterlife. Muslim commentators, notably al-Nawawi, deny that anyone is punished for another’s sin (see below), but the hadith still pictures Jews and Christians filling the places in Hell that Muslims are spared. 2.

The Historical Record Is a Test of the Theology The steel man correctly notes that many periods of Islamic governance were relatively tolerant. The better question is what Christians could rely on. Under the dhimma their security rested on the ruler’s will and the jurists’ reading, not on rights they could claim as equals. When rulers chose to enforce the classical conditions strictly, as al-Mutawakkil did in the 850s and several Mamluk sultans did in the fourteenth century, they could point to the law itself for their authority. Tolerance, when it came, was usually the law left unenforced; persecution was usually the law enforced. That asymmetry, rather than any claim that every Muslim ruler persecuted, is the point. 3.

The Demographic Record Cannot Be Explained Away Region Christian % Before Islam (7th c.) Christian % Today Egypt ~90% (est.) about 5 to 10% Syria Majority about 1 to 2% (2026), down from about 10% before 2011 North Africa Majority Near zero indigenous Anatolia (Turkey) ~20% (early 20th c.) <0.2% Iraq about 1 to 1.5 million (2003) <250,000 (post-ISIS) No single cause accounts for these numbers. Emigration, plague, economics, colonial disruption, and nationalist conflicts all played roles in specific cases. The steel man is right to resist monocausal explanation. But the consistent, directional trend across every region where Islam governed for multiple centuries — from Egypt to Iran to North Africa to Anatolia — cannot be coincidental. A system theologically designed to make Christian identity costly, to prohibit church construction, to restrict proselytism, and to reward conversion will, over centuries, produce exactly this demographic pattern. The patient logic of the dhimmi system required no massacre; it required only consistency.

The Conclusion of the Steel Man Test The steel man case for Islamic tolerance is not dishonest. It reflects real aspects of the tradition: peaceful Muslim majorities, reformist scholars, periods of genuine coexistence, and the distinction between individual practice and textual prescription. But it does not dissolve the primary sources. After giving Islam its best case, the Qur’an still ranks those of the People of the Scripture who reject Islam among the worst of creatures. The substitution hadith still assigns Christians to Hell for Muslims. The dhimmi system still derives from Q.9:29. The churches of North Africa, Anatolia, and much of Syria and Mesopotamia are still largely empty. The twenty Copts and their Ghanaian companion are still dead on a Libyan beach. These facts remain after the steel man is honestly given. That is the test. They pass it.

Phase 1 — The Meccan Outreach (AD 610–622) In the early years of his prophetic career in Mecca, Muhammad actively sought acceptance from Jews and Christians, presenting Islam as the original, uncorrupted form of their own faith. The Meccan Qur’an reflects this posture: affirming, respectful, and genuinely engaged with the older Abrahamic traditions. This period is not to be dismissed — it is historically real and represents Islam at its most receptive toward Christianity. Qur’an 3:3 — Confirmation of Earlier Scriptures "He has sent down upon you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it. And He revealed the Torah and the Gospel before, as guidance for the people." Qur’an 5:82 — Christians “Nearest in Affection” "You will find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, ‘We are Christians.’ That is because among them are priests and monks and because they are not arrogant." Qur’an 4:171 — Jesus as Word and Spirit of God "The Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah and His word which He directed to Mary and a soul [created at a

command] from Him." These affirmations were genuine overtures. The Hijra to Abyssinia (615 AD), where the Christian Negus sheltered Muslim refugees, represents a real moment of Muslim-Christian solidarity. When the Negus died, Muhammad announced his death and led a funeral prayer for him (Sahih al-Bukhari 1245). These are not fabrications, and they deserve honest recognition. One caution about dating: the three verses above come from Surahs 3, 4 and 5, which the tradition places in Medina, not Mecca. The Meccan surahs are also respectful (Surah 19, Maryam, honours Mary and Jesus, and 29:46 says "do not argue with the People of the Scripture except in a way that is best"), but the warmest and the harshest verses about Christians both come from the Medinan years. The shift described below is therefore less a clean break between two eras than a hardening within the Medinan period. AD 610–622 Meccan Period — Outreach and Affirmation Qur’an affirms Torah and Gospel. Jesus honored as Word of God born of virgin. Prayer directed toward Jerusalem, the city of the People of the Book.

AD 615 Hijra to Abyssinia — Christian King Shelters Muslims Muslim refugees protected by the Negus of Abyssinia. A genuine historical example of Christian-Muslim solidarity. Muhammad later mourned the Negus’s death. AD 622 The Hijra — Migration to Medina Muhammad’s migration to Medina changes his audience from Meccan polytheists to established Jewish tribes and Christian communities. The character of revelation begins to shift.

Phase 2 — The Medinan Reversal (AD 622–632) After the Hijra, Muhammad encountered established Jewish tribes in Medina — the Banu Qaynuqa, Banu Nadir, and Banu Qurayza — who declined to recognize him as a prophet foretold in their scriptures. The theological and political fallout of this rejection is recorded in the Medinan Qur’an with a directness that would define the legal treatment of Christians for the following 1,400 years. The Doctrine of Abrogation (Naskh) Classical Islamic jurisprudence holds that later Qur’anic revelations can supersede earlier ones where they conflict. This is the majority position of the four classical law schools. However, as the steel man correctly notes, this doctrine is genuinely contested. Modern reformist scholars argue that abrogation is limited in scope and that early affirming verses remain operative. This is an honest internal debate within Islam, and it should be acknowledged as such. What is not contested is that the hostile verses exist, that they are in the Qur’an, and that they were the basis of Islamic law for over a millennium.

Even if a Muslim scholar today argues that Q.9:29 is context-specific, the verse was applied as universal law by all four Sunni schools, and remains so in formal classical jurisprudence. The debate is real; so is the history that flowed from the majority reading. Qur’an 9:29 Late Medinan — Among the Final Revelations "Fight against those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day … from those who were given the Scripture — [fight] until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled." The phrase rendered "while they are humbled" (Arabic: ṣāghirūn ) means "in a state of humiliation." Many classical commentators read it as requiring that the payment visibly mark the payer’s subordination, though they differed on what that meant in practice (see “How the Jurists Read ‘Humbled’” below). Either way, the verse made subordination, not equality, the legal frame for Christians under Islamic rule.

Qur’an 9:30 — Divine Curse on Christians "The Christians say, ‘The Messiah is the son of Allah.’ … May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded?" Surah 9 is usually dated to the last two years of Muhammad’s life. Its curse on Christians for their confession of Christ is therefore among the final Qur’anic statements on the subject, which in the view of many classical scholars gives it governing weight over earlier affirming verses. Qur’an 5:51 — Prohibition on Christian Friendship "O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies (awliyā’). They are [in fact] allies of one another. And whoever is an ally to them among you — then indeed, he is [one] of them." Sahih Bukhari 3053 / Sahih Muslim 1767 Hadith "I will expel the Jews and Christians from the Arabian Peninsula and will not leave any but Muslim." — Attributed to Muhammad; carried out by Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (r. 634–644).

AD 624–627 Expulsion and Execution of Medinan Jewish Tribes Banu Qaynuqa expelled (624), Banu Nadir expelled (625), Banu Qurayza besieged (627) — with the adult men killed and the women and children enslaved (Sahih al-Bukhari 3043). The qibla shifts from Jerusalem to Mecca: a visible theological severance from the Jewish-Christian inheritance. AD 630 Surah al-Tawbah (Surah 9) Revealed Contains Q.9:29 (fight People of the Book until jizyah) and Q.9:30 (curse on Christians). The only surah in the Qur’an without the opening Bismillah, which some classical scholars explained by its severity. Revealed after the conquest of Mecca, when Muhammad’s position was militarily secure. AD 634–644 Expulsion of Christians and Jews from Arabia Caliph Umar executes Muhammad’s deathbed command. Christians of Najran and Jews of Khaybar expelled. Saudi Arabia to this day permits no churches and no public non-Muslim worship.

secs.h: The Qur’an on Christians — The Full Picture
secs.x: The Qur’an on Christians — The Full Picture The Qur’an speaks about Christians in multiple registers. The honest approach is to present both, note the scholarly debates about how to reconcile them, and let the reader see what the texts say and what the legal tradition did with them. The Affirming Verses Qur’an 2:62 "Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews or Christians or Sabeans … who believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteousness — will have their reward with their Lord." Often cited in interfaith dialogue. Muslim scholarly interpretation: Ibn Kathir, the most widely used classical commentator, holds this refers to members of those faiths who believed before Muhammad’s coming. After Muhammad, the only valid faith is Islam. This reading is the classical majority position — but reformist scholars such as Fazlur Rahman disputed it. The verse’s scope is a genuine internal debate. Qur’an 5:82 "You will find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, ‘We are Christians.’" Genuine early warmth toward Christians — historically real.

secs.h: The Qur’an on Christians — The Full Picture
secs.x: Context note: This verse appears in the same surah as Q.5:51 (forbidding Christian friendship) and Q.5:17 (declaring those who say God is Christ are disbelievers). The two positions coexist in Surah 5, which also permits Muslim men to marry Christian and Jewish women and to eat their food (Q.5:5). How a given Muslim scholar reconciles them depends on their hermeneutic. The honest reader must hold both texts. The Condemning Verses Qur’an 5:17 "They have certainly disbelieved (kafara) who say that Allah is Christ, the son of Mary." The Arabic kafara carries, in Islamic law, the full weight of unbelief — with legal and eternal consequences. This verse makes the core Christian confession an act of kufr. Qur’an 5:72–73 "They have certainly disbelieved who say, ‘Allah is the Messiah.’ … They have certainly disbelieved who say, ‘Allah is the third of three.’ … There will surely afflict the disbelievers among them a painful punishment." The Trinity is declared kufr. No contextual reading removes this — it is a straightforward theological claim, not a war-time instruction.

secs.h: The Qur’an on Christians — The Full Picture
secs.x: Qur’an 4:48 "Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him (shirk) …" Many classical scholars held that the Christian doctrine of the Trinity amounts to shirk, the one sin this verse says God does not forgive if a person dies in it; others kept the People of the Book in a category distinct from the polytheists. On the stricter view, the Christian stands under the gravest theological condemnation for the confession of faith itself. Qur’an 9:30 "…the Christians say, ‘The Messiah is the son of Allāh.’ … May Allāh destroy them; how are they deluded?" A divine curse against Christians for their confession of Christ. Among the last revelations — which, in the classical abrogation framework, carry the greatest authority.

secs.h: The Qur’an on Christians — The Full Picture
secs.x: The Greeting Prohibition Sahih Muslim 2167 Hadith "Do not greet the Jews and the Christians before they greet you and when you meet any one of them on the roads force him to go to the narrowest part of it." Al-Nawawi’s commentary takes it as forbidding Muslims to greet them first, and it shaped dhimmi etiquette in many periods; some Muslim scholars confine it to wartime, and contemporary scholars debate its applicability. What it says is plain: subordination acted out in public space.

secs.h: “The Worst of Creatures” — Q.98:6 and Its Interpreters
secs.x: “The Worst of Creatures” — Q.98:6 and Its Interpreters Qur’an 98:6 is the most unambiguous Qur’anic statement about Christians and requires no contextual unpacking. It has no military setting. It is a straightforward eschatological and ontological judgment. Qur’an 98:6 — Surah al-Bayyina "Indeed, they who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell, abiding eternally therein. Those are the worst of creatures (sharr al-barīyya)." Qur’an 98:7 — The Deliberate Contrast "Indeed, they who have believed and done righteous deeds — those are the best of creatures (khayr al-barīyya)." These two verses form a binary: believers who do righteous deeds are the best of created beings; those of the People of the Scripture who disbelieve are the worst. Not merely wrong, not merely misguided — the worst of all creation. This is the primary source. It stands on its own. The Classical Commentators Ibn Kathir (d.

secs.h: “The Worst of Creatures” — Q.98:6 and Its Interpreters
secs.x: 1373) — Tafsir al-Qur’an al-Azim "(They are the worst of creatures.) meaning, they are the worst creation that Allah has fashioned and created." (English abridgement as published on Quran.com) One of the most widely read classical commentaries. Al-Tabari (d. 923) — Jami’ al-Bayan Summary: Al-Tabari likewise reads the verse as describing those of the People of the Book and the idolaters who disbelieved as the worst of all creatures. (No published English translation is available to quote.) The earliest of the great classical commentaries, which reads the verse in the same way. Note on Contemporary Muslim Responses Some contemporary Muslim scholars argue that Q.98:6’s designation refers specifically to those who knowingly reject Islam after evidence has been made clear to them — a narrower category than all Christians. This is a genuine interpretive position. It does not change what the verse says; it adjusts who it applies to. Under this reading, a Christian who has sincerely never encountered a compelling case for Islam would be in a different category.

secs.h: “The Worst of Creatures” — Q.98:6 and Its Interpreters
secs.x: However, the classical majority position, confirmed by both al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, applies it to all People of the Scripture who reject Muhammad. The reformist reading is a minority position in the tradition. The First Christian Theologian to Engage Islam St. John of Damascus (c. 675–749) — De Haeresibus "There is also a coercive religion of the Ishmaelites which prevails at this time and deceives the people, being the forerunner of the Anti-Christ… a false prophet, called Mamed, sprung up among them; who, after conversing with an Arian monk concerning the Old and New Testament, fabricated his own heresy… he spread rumors that a book had been sent down to him from heaven by God… He says there is one God, creator of all things, who has neither been begotten nor has begotten." (tr. Roger Pearse) John of Damascus wrote from inside the Umayyad caliphate. His father and grandfather served the caliphs as officials, and the traditional Life says John did too before he became a monk at Mar Saba near Jerusalem, where he wrote this work.

secs.h: “The Worst of Creatures” — Q.98:6 and Its Interpreters
secs.x: He was not a polemicist operating at a safe distance; he was a Christian living under Islamic governance with direct knowledge of Islamic doctrine and practice. His assessment was not hostility born of ignorance but analysis born of proximity. He classified Islam as a heresy because, from his theological vantage point, it was a distortion of Christian claims about Jesus — affirming his prophethood, denying his divinity, and re-narrating his story in a way that removed the Incarnation and the Cross.

The Hadith of Substitution The following hadith, reported in several narrations in Sahih Muslim, describes an eschatological arrangement in which Christians are assigned to Hell in place of Muslims. It is not a contextual war-time instruction. It is a doctrine about the afterlife. Sahih Muslim 2767a — Narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari "When it will be the Day of Resurrection Allah would deliver to every Muslim a Jew or a Christian and say: That is your rescue from Hell-Fire." Sahih Muslim 2767b "No Muslim would die but Allah would admit in his stead a Jew or a Christian in Hell-Fire." — ‘Umar b. Abd al-‘Aziz had the narrator swear three times that his father had narrated it from the Prophet.

Sahih Muslim 2767d "There would come people amongst the Muslims on the Day of Resurrection with as heavy sins as a mountain, and Allah would forgive them and He would place in their stead the Jews and the Christians." Note on Scholarly Debate Al-Nawawi, in his commentary on Sahih Muslim, offers a clarifying interpretation: the Christians and Jews assigned to Hell were already destined for it by their unbelief; the hadith simply reveals that their spots in Hell correspond to spots vacated by Muslims who ultimately enter Paradise. In this reading, the Christian is not "punished instead of" the Muslim in a direct substitutionary sense — rather, the Muslim’s Hell-place is filled by a Christian whose own unbelief destined them there. This reading fits the Qur’an’s own principle that "no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" (Q.6:164), and it should be taken as the mainstream Muslim understanding. It removes the idea that Christians pay for Muslim sins.

What it leaves is the picture itself: the places in Hell that Muslims are spared are filled, in the hadith’s imagery, by Jews and Christians. The Theological Inversion St. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373) — On the Incarnation "For He was made man that we might be made God…" (On the Incarnation 54, NPNF) The contrast is still instructive. In the Gospel the exchange runs from God toward us: the Son takes our nature and our death so that we might share His life, and the innocent dies for the guilty. In this hadith, on either reading, no one takes anyone’s place out of love; places are simply reassigned. And the Qur’an denies the one substitution Christians proclaim, the crucifixion of Christ (Q.4:157).

secs.h: The Dhimmi System — Q.9:29 Applied as Law
secs.x: The Dhimmi System — Q.9:29 Applied as Law The steel man correctly observes that the dhimmi system provided legal existence and physical protection, and that in some periods it was administered more leniently than its theory required. These observations are accurate. They do not change what the system was designed to do, what its legal basis was, or what its multigenerational effects produced. What the Steel Man Concedes and What It Doesn’t Conceded: the dhimmi system was not a program of genocide; it offered legal existence. In specific periods and places, Christian communities maintained significant cultural and economic life within it. Jews expelled from Christian Spain did seek refuge in the Ottoman Empire. These facts are real. Not conceded: that the system was benign, that its theological basis was anything other than Q.9:29’s command to subdue Christians, or that its multigenerational effects were anything other than the demographic extinction of ancient Christian communities across the entire Islamic world.

secs.h: The Dhimmi System — Q.9:29 Applied as Law
secs.x: No New Churches The conditions attributed to the Pact of Umar forbid new churches and the repair of ruined ones; jurists differed on repairs, and rulers often granted exceptions. Where it was enforced across centuries, this provision alone reduced Christian institutional presence through attrition, with no violence required. Distinctive Dress Caliph al-Mutawakkil’s decree of 850 required Christians and Jews to wear honey-coloured hoods and belts and to fix wooden images of devils to their doors. Rules of distinctive dress, traced to the Pact of Umar, recur across Islamic history. Latin Christendom imposed distinctive dress on Jews from 1215, so the practice is not uniquely Islamic, but here it was justified as part of the humility the dhimmi owed. The Jizyah Many classical commentators and jurists read Q.9:29 as requiring that the jizyah be paid in a way that marks the payer's subordination, and some described a deliberately humiliating ceremony of collection; others disagreed.

secs.h: The Dhimmi System — Q.9:29 Applied as Law
secs.x: Where it was practised, the humiliation was meant as the legal expression of Q.9:29’s ṣāghirūn ("while they are humbled"). No Public Worship The same conditions forbid ringing bells loudly, showing crosses in public, and holding public processions. Invisible religion becomes a dying religion across multiple generations. No Legal Equality In most schools a Christian’s testimony was not accepted against a Muslim. The Maliki and Hanbali schools set a Christian’s blood-money at half a Muslim’s and the Shafi’i at one third; the Hanafi school, which the Ottomans followed, held it equal. Outside the Hanafi school, a Muslim who killed a dhimmi was generally not liable to retaliation. Death for Proselytism A dhimmi who tried to convert a Muslim was held by many jurists to have broken the pact, which could carry the death penalty. A Muslim who became a Christian was an apostate, for whom the classical schools prescribed death. The dhimma was a one-way door: you could enter Islam; you could not leave it, and no one could be invited in.

secs.h: The Dhimmi System — Q.9:29 Applied as Law
secs.x: How the Jurists Read “Humbled” Summary of the classical discussion Summary: Classical jurists disagreed about where the humbling of Q.9:29 lies. Al-Shafi'i read the verse as protecting the life and property of People of the Book who pay the jizyah while acknowledging their subordinate status. Jurists differed on whether the belittlement consists in paying the tax at all or in the manner of its collection, and some commentators and manuals went on to describe a deliberately humiliating ceremony of collection. Others, including many modern Muslim scholars, deny that the verse calls for any humiliation at all. The honest conclusion is not that every jurist demanded humiliation, but that the verse's own word, ṣāghirūn, was widely read in the classical tradition as a mark of subordination, and the dhimmi rules described above were built on that reading.

secs.h: The Historical Record — Theology Applied Over Fourteen Centuries
secs.x: The Historical Record — Theology Applied Over Fourteen Centuries The following is not a catalogue of every anti-Christian act in Islamic history, nor does it ignore the periods of relative tolerance. It is a representative survey of what happened when the Qur’anic and hadith theology documented above was applied by states and movements with the power to do so. These events are documented in Islamic chronicles, Byzantine records, Coptic synaxaria, Syriac histories, and Armenian historiography — not only in Western or Christian sources. 634–642 Arab Conquest of the Christian Heartlands Within a decade of Muhammad’s death, the Rashidun Caliphate conquered Egypt, Syria, and Mesopotamia — the founding territories of the Oriental Orthodox churches. Christian populations became tributaries paying jizyah; the fuller code of dhimmi restrictions took shape over the following two centuries. The conquest itself was often not especially violent compared to ancient warfare norms.

secs.h: The Historical Record — Theology Applied Over Fourteen Centuries
secs.x: The subsequent demographic transformation required no further armies — only the patient application of dhimmi law over generations. 847–861 Caliph al-Mutawakkil: Distinctive Dress and Church Demolitions The Abbasid Caliph al-Mutawakkil issued sweeping decrees against Christians and Jews: honey-coloured garments, wooden images of devils on their houses, demolition of newly built churches, dismissal from government posts. This was state policy, not a popular pogrom, and it was enforced in the name of the classical conditions. It was also only partly and temporarily carried out, which itself shows how much Christian life depended on whether the law was enforced. 1009 Caliph al-Hakim — Destruction of the Holy Sepulchre The Fatimid Caliph al-Hakim ordered the destruction of many churches across Egypt and the Levant (by some medieval reports, thousands), including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, and made Christians wear heavy wooden crosses.

secs.h: The Historical Record — Theology Applied Over Fourteen Centuries
secs.x: Al-Hakim was erratic: he also persecuted Sunni Muslims and Jews, and late in his reign he allowed churches to be rebuilt and forced converts to return to Christianity. His case shows less a theology applied than the volatility of a system in which Christian existence depended on the disposition of the ruler rather than on enforceable rights. 1301–1517 Mamluk Egypt: Waves of Anti-Coptic Measures Repeated waves of Mamluk anti-Coptic legislation across two centuries: dismissal of Christian officials, destruction of churches, forced conversions during popular violence. Many historians, notably Tamer el-Leithy, place the decisive wave of Coptic conversion, the point at which Egypt most likely became majority Muslim, in the fourteenth century under the Mamluks, though the timing is debated and reliable figures do not exist. No single massacre accomplished this — the dhimmi system did it by consistently making Christian identity socially, economically, and physically costly.

secs.h: The Historical Record — Theology Applied Over Fourteen Centuries
secs.x: 1529–1543 Ahmad Gran’s Jihad Against Ethiopia The Muslim ruler Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi (Ahmad Gran) launched a declared jihad against Christian Ethiopia, burning churches and monasteries across the highlands, among them Debre Libanos in 1531, together with much of their manuscript heritage, and forcing many Christians to convert. The Christian kingdom came close to collapse. The Portuguese force that arrived in 1541 and fought beside Emperor Galawdewos until Ahmad’s death at Wayna Daga in 1543 is one of history’s more remarkable acts of Christian solidarity. 1894–1923 The Genocides of Armenian, Syriac, and Assyrian Christians Between 1894 and 1923, the Christian minorities of the Ottoman Empire — Armenians, Syriacs (Seyfo), Assyrians, and Greeks — were subjected to massacres, deportations, and organized killing.

secs.h: The Historical Record — Theology Applied Over Fourteen Centuries
secs.x: Historians estimate the death toll at between 1 and 1.5 million Armenians alone (Kévorkian, The Armenian Genocide , 2011; International Association of Genocide Scholars), with additional hundreds of thousands of Syriac and Assyrian victims (Hannibal Travis, David Gaunt); the combined toll across all communities is estimated by scholars at 1.5–2.5 million. As the steel man correctly notes, the Young Turk leadership was secular-nationalist rather than primarily religious. However, the mechanism of mass participation was religious mobilization — the Sheikh-ul-Islam’s 1914 jihad proclamation (aimed at the Entente powers, but turned locally against Christians), Kurdish Hamidiye religious irregulars, and the consistent identification of victims as Christian gavur (infidels). The Hamidian massacres of 1894–1896, which killed perhaps 100,000 to 300,000 Armenians, took place under Sultan Abdulhamid II, who styled himself caliph; historians debate how far he directed them, but mobs and Hamidiye irregulars often carried them out in religious terms.

secs.h: The Historical Record — Theology Applied Over Fourteen Centuries
secs.x: The full picture is neither purely nationalist nor purely religious — it was both, with religion providing the mass participation that nationalism alone could not. 2014–2019 ISIS and the Nineveh Plain — Q.9:29 Cited by Name In Mosul in July 2014 the Islamic State summoned the Christian leaders and then issued an ultimatum: become Muslims, pay jizyah as dhimmis, or leave, with the sword as the alternative. Almost all the city’s remaining Christians fled by 19 July. On 6 and 7 August ISIS overran the Nineveh Plain, and the Christian towns of Qaraqosh, Bartella and Karamlesh emptied almost overnight; those who stayed were detained, pressed to convert, or abused, and some women suffered sexual violence (UN investigative team report, 2024). The enslavement of thousands of Yazidi women in the same weeks was worse still. ISIS did not invent the dhimma; it revived the classical framework with an explicitness that made the derivation plain.

Popes, Patriarchs & Scholars Respond These responses span 1,400 years, from the first Christian theologian who engaged Islam from within the Islamic world to modern popes addressing living persecution. They share a common thread: theological clarity that does not require hatred of Muslim people. St. John of Damascus (c. 675–749) First Systematic Theologian of Islam — Served under the Umayyad Caliphate "…after conversing with an Arian monk concerning the Old and New Testament, fabricated his own heresy… He also says that Christ was the Word of God and his Spirit, but only a creature and a servant…" (tr. Roger Pearse) Written from inside the Islamic world with direct, firsthand knowledge. John grew up in a family of Christian officials at the Umayyad court and knew Islamic teaching closely. He placed Islam in his catalogue of heresies because, theologically, it was a revision of Christian claims about Jesus. His engagement was confrontational in content but argued, not abusive.

Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos (1350–1425) Byzantine Emperor — Wrote During the Siege of Constantinople "Show me just what Mohammed brought that was new, and there you will find things only evil and inhuman, such as his command to spread by the sword the faith he preached." From the Dialogues with a Persian, which record conversations held in the winter of 1391 at Ankara, where Manuel was obliged to serve as a vassal in the Ottoman sultan’s camp; Constantinople itself would be besieged from 1394. When Pope Benedict XVI quoted the line in 2006 he said the emperor spoke with "a startling brusqueness, a brusqueness that we find unacceptable," and he later regretted that it had been taken as his own view. The lecture provoked angry protests, and an Italian nun, Sister Leonella Sgorbati, was murdered in Somalia days later in what many linked to the furore. It also prompted 138 Muslim scholars to write the open letter A Common Word (2007), which opened one of the more serious Muslim and Christian dialogues of recent decades. Patriarch Timothy I of the Church of the East (d.

823) Catholicos — Debated Caliph al-Mahdi in the Abbasid Court "Muhammad is worthy of all praise, by all reasonable people, O my Sovereign. He walked in the path of the prophets, and trod in the track of the lovers of God." (tr. Mingana) In the same dialogue Timothy declined to accept that the Paraclete promised in the Gospel is Muhammad, holding that it is the Holy Spirit. Timothy I engaged Caliph al-Mahdi in a famous two-day theological dialogue recorded in his Apology. His method is a model for engagement from within Islamic power: respectful, intellectually rigorous, diplomatically aware, and theologically uncompromising. He navigated the Abbasid court without surrendering the Trinity or the divinity of Christ. He lived under Islamic governance without becoming an apologist for it. Pope Benedict XVI (r. 2005–2013) Regensburg Address, September 12, 2006 "The emperor, after having expressed himself so forcefully, goes on to explain in detail the reasons why spreading the faith through violence is something unreasonable.

Violence is incompatible with the nature of God and the nature of the soul." Benedict’s argument was philosophical, not polemical: a God conceived as pure will, unbound even by his own word, could in principle command anything, including violence. He cited the eleventh-century Muslim writer Ibn Hazm for that view, and in fairness traced a parallel voluntarism in late medieval Christian theology after Duns Scotus. The Christian God, he argued, is Logos, and acting against reason is contrary to His nature. Pope Tawadros II of Alexandria (b. 1952) 118th Coptic Pope — On the 21 Libyan Martyrs, February 2015 Summary: Pope Tawadros received the twenty-one as martyrs of the Church, and within a week he announced that their names would be entered in the Synaxarium; they are commemorated each year on 15 February. (No verified English text of his words is quoted here.) Twenty Coptic migrant workers and a Ghanaian companion, Matthew Ayariga, were beheaded on a Libyan beach by ISIS.

The ISIS video was titled "A Message Signed with Blood to the Nation of the Cross." As the men were killed, witnesses reported they called on the name of Jesus. All twenty-one are now canonized martyrs of the Coptic Orthodox Church. The Church's response exemplifies what 1,700 years of Oriental Orthodox martyrology has produced: not hatred of the killers but clarity about why the dying was not in vain. Patriarch Ignatius Aphrem II (Syriac Orthodox, b. 1965) Appeals on behalf of the Christians of Syria and Iraq, 2014 onward Summary: Since his election in 2014 Patriarch Aphrem has repeatedly asked governments and international bodies to recognise and stop the destruction of Christian communities in Syria and Iraq, and to help those displaced to return. (No verified English text of a specific address is quoted here.) Patriarch Aphrem leads the Syriac Orthodox Church, whose liturgy is in Syriac, a dialect of Aramaic. His community has lived under Islamic governance since 637 AD and carries in its bones the memory of the Seyfo genocide.
He has named what was happening without diplomatic euphemism. His appeals have asked for protection and for the right of the displaced to return, not for retaliation.

Modern Persecution — The Living Reality The data below is from Open Doors World Watch List, Aid to the Church in Need, and United Nations documentation. Open Doors is a Christian advocacy organization whose methodology should be acknowledged; the UN and governmental sources corroborate its broad findings. Open Doors World Watch List 2026 More than 388 million Christians face high levels of persecution or discrimination. The top ten countries are North Korea, Somalia, Yemen, Sudan, Eritrea, Syria, Nigeria, Pakistan, Libya and Iran. Seven of these are Muslim-majority. North Korea is a communist state, Eritrea is roughly half Christian, and in Nigeria, which records the most killings, the violence mixes jihadist attacks with farmer and herder land conflict. Communist and nationalist states (North Korea, China, India, Myanmar) also rank among the worst, so Islamic oppression is the largest single driver but not the only one.

February 15, 2015 The 21 Coptic Martyrs — Libya Twenty Coptic migrant workers and a Ghanaian companion beheaded by ISIS on a Libyan beach; many were seen calling on Jesus as they died. All twenty-one were entered in the Coptic Synaxarium and are commemorated on 15 February, and in 2023 Pope Francis added them to the Roman Martyrology. August 2014 Nineveh Plain — Iraq Well over 100,000 Syriac, Chaldean and Assyrian Christians fled the Nineveh Plain within a night as ISIS advanced. Ancient churches and monasteries were looted, burned or blown up, among them the shrine of Mar Behnam in 2015. Some families returned after liberation in 2016 and 2017, but many communities have never recovered their former size. April 9, 2017 Palm Sunday Bombings — Egypt ISIS attacked St. George’s Church in Tanta and St. Mark’s Cathedral in Alexandria on Palm Sunday, killing some 45 people, most of them Copts, along with police officers guarding the Alexandria cathedral where Pope Tawadros had just celebrated. Targeting Holy Week was deliberate.

Ongoing Pakistan — Blasphemy Laws and Asia Bibi Section 295-C of Pakistan’s Penal Code makes insulting Muhammad punishable by death. Accusations fall on Muslims too, but Christians and Ahmadis are accused far out of proportion to their numbers, and mob violence often follows an accusation. Asia Bibi spent eight years on death row after a dispute over drinking water before the Supreme Court acquitted her in 2018. Punjab’s governor, Salman Taseer, was murdered in 2011 for defending her, and his killer is honoured as a hero by many. The law is defended by many mainstream clerics, not only by militants.

Frequently Asked Questions Does Islam respect Jesus? + Islam honors a figure named Jesus (Isa) as a prophet, born of a virgin, who performed miracles. This is genuine. However, it simultaneously denies everything Christianity holds to be essential about him: his divinity, the atoning significance of his crucifixion (Q.4:157 denies he was crucified), his resurrection as the basis of salvation, and his identity as the second Person of the Trinity. The Qur’anic Jesus and the biblical Christ share a name and some biographical data. They are theologically different persons. To honor the Qur’anic Isa while denying the Incarnation is not, from an Orthodox perspective, to respect Jesus — it is to replace him with a corrected version. Are the hostile verses really what classical Islam teaches, or is that extremism? + This is the most important question to answer honestly. The hostile verses — Q.9:29, Q.9:30, Q.5:51, Q.98:6 — and the dhimmi system derived from them are not extremist innovations.

They are the classical mainstream of Sunni jurisprudence, confirmed by all four law schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i, Hanbali) and by the most authoritative commentators (al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir). ISIS applied them more visibly and violently than most Islamic states do, but the framework it invoked is classical. In fairness, the same classical law bound the state to protect the lives, property and worship of dhimmis, and a well-known hadith warns that "whoever kills a Mu'ahid will not smell the fragrance of Paradise" (Sahih al-Bukhari 3166). By killing and enslaving people who had not taken up arms, ISIS broke that law even as it invoked it. What many contemporary Muslim scholars and institutions are attempting — the contextual and reformist readings discussed in the steel man section — is a genuine reform effort within Islam. It has not yet produced a settled alternative jurisprudence accepted by a majority of Islamic scholars worldwide.

The distinction between "ISIS-style extremism" and "mainstream classical Islam" on this specific question is less clear than interfaith diplomacy suggests. Doesn’t the Christian record of violence disqualify this critique? + Christian history contains genuine atrocities: the Crusader sack of Constantinople (1204) — an attack on fellow Christians; the Inquisition; religious wars; anti-Semitism. These are not defended here. The Oriental Orthodox churches were themselves victims of Byzantine Christian persecution for their Christology before Islam ever arrived. Still, two things should be said. First, the Christian atrocities were committed against the explicit teaching of Christ ("love your enemies," "blessed are the peacemakers"), and the New Testament contains no law for ruling over, taxing or subordinating unbelievers; Christian persecutors had to argue past their scripture. The dhimmi system, by contrast, was built by the jurists as an application of Q.9:29. Second, the honest historical comparison does not favour either side as neatly as polemicists claim.

Latin Christendom expelled its Jews from England, France and Spain, and expelled or forcibly converted the Muslims of Sicily and Spain, while large Christian communities survived for fourteen centuries in Egypt, Iraq, Syria and Lebanon. The dhimma rarely aimed at extermination; its effect was slower. The moral failures of Christians do not erase what Islamic law prescribed, and the failures of Muslim rulers do not excuse Christian ones. What is the Oriental Orthodox approach to Muslim neighbors? + The Oriental Orthodox tradition has practiced coexistence with Muslim neighbors for 1,400 years — by necessity and, often, genuinely. The Coptic church maintained channels with Islamic authorities through every dynasty from the Rashidun to the present. The Armenian Apostolic church navigated the Ottoman empire for five centuries. The Syriac church engaged Abbasid caliphs in theological dialogue. This is not capitulation; it is the long practice of a minority church living inside a majority-Muslim world.

The approach is: be clear about what you believe, do not compromise the faith, engage neighbors with charity, and do not mistake coexistence for theological equivalence. The church that buries its twenty-one martyrs while praying for those who killed them is practicing something harder and more honest than either hatred or naïve interfaith optimism. Is this site anti-Muslim? + No — and the distinction matters. Anti-Muslim sentiment is directed at Muslim people as people. This site is directed at specific texts and at the history of their application. The Muslim family living peacefully beside a Coptic family in Cairo, the Indonesian Muslim who attends his Christian friend’s wedding, the Pakistani lawyer who defended Asia Bibi at personal risk — these are not enemies. A verse that ranks unbelievers among the worst of creatures is a statement in a text, and these neighbours are people. Examining that text honestly is not hostility toward the people who read it; it is a service to truth. The Christian obligation is to love Muslim neighbors and to tell the truth about Muslim texts.
Both are required. Neither cancels the other.

Glossary Steel Man Presenting an opposing argument in its strongest, most charitable form before engaging it. The opposite of a straw man. The method used throughout this site. Ahl al-Kitab "People of the Book." Qur’anic term for Christians and Jews. A status granting both qualified protection (dhimmi) and explicit condemnation (Q.98:6). Dhimmi Non-Muslim subjects under Islamic governance. Protected legal existence in exchange for jizyah payment and codified subordination. Basis: Q.9:29. Jizyah Poll tax on dhimmis. Many classical jurists read Q.9:29 as requiring that it be paid in a way that marked subordination; some described a humiliating ceremony and others rejected one. Abolished in the Ottoman Empire in 1856. Naskh (Abrogation) Later Qur’anic verses supersede earlier conflicting ones. Q.2:106. The majority classical position; contested by modern reformists. Governs how hostile Medinan verses relate to affirming Meccan ones. Kafir / Kufr "Unbeliever / unbelief." Q.5:17 applies this to those who say God is Christ.

In Islamic law, kufr carries serious legal and social consequences. Shirk "Associating partners with God." The sin Q.4:48 says God does not forgive if a person dies in it. Many classical theologians classed the Trinity as shirk; others distinguished the People of the Book from polytheists. Sharr al-Barīyya "The worst of creatures." Q.98:6’s designation for those who disbelieve among the People of the Scripture. Applied by the classical commentators to those of the People of the Scripture who reject Islam. Tafsir Qur’anic commentary. Al-Tabari (9th c.), Ibn Kathir (14th c.), and al-Qurtubi (13th c.) represent the classical mainstream. Their readings are the basis for the interpretations cited in this site. Seyfo / Aghet "Sword" (Syriac) / "Catastrophe" (Armenian). Refer to the genocides of Syriac and Armenian Christians in the Ottoman Empire, 1914–1923. Najas "Impure." Q.9:28 says this of the polytheists. Most Sunni scholars read it as a spiritual impurity, not a physical one.

Twelver Shi’i law traditionally treated non-Muslims as physically impure, with rules on contact and shared use. Awliyā’ Allies / friends / protectors. Q.5:51 forbids Muslims from taking Christians as awliyā’. Interpreters differ on how broadly to read it; the same surah permits marriage to Christian women (Q.5:5).

pages.t: THE ISLAMIC DILEMMA — Scripture and the Qur'an

secs.x: I. Introduction This site examines one of the most significant challenges in Muslim-Christian dialogue: the Islamic Dilemma regarding the previous scriptures. This is not a polemical attack on Islam or Muslims, but a sincere examination of a logical tension within Islamic teaching that demands honest engagement. The Qur'an repeatedly and emphatically affirms that the Torah (Tawrat), Psalms (Zabur), and Gospel (Injil) given to Moses, David, and Jesus respectively are divine revelation from God. The Qur'an instructs Christians and Jews to judge by their scriptures and affirms that its own message confirms these earlier revelations. Yet the Qur'an also contradicts the Bible on major theological and historical points — the nature of Christ (denying his divinity and crucifixion), the Trinity, and the character of key biblical figures. If the Bible is genuinely from God, as the Qur'an affirms, then the Qur'an's contradictions of it are a serious problem. If the Bible has been corrupted and is no longer reliable, then the Qur'an's affirmations of it are empty. This is the Islamic Dilemma.

Note: This site presents the Christian perspective on a contested theological question. It is intended for thoughtful readers engaged in apologetics and interfaith dialogue. All Qur'anic citations are from Sahih International unless otherwise noted.

II. The Dilemma Defined The Islamic Dilemma can be stated precisely as a logical dilemma with two horns: Horn 1 — If the Bible is authentic: The Qur'an repeatedly commands people to believe the Torah and Gospel and to judge by them. If these scriptures are genuine and reliable, then Christians and Jews should follow them — and they teach the divinity of Christ, the Trinity (broadly understood), the atoning death of Jesus, and the resurrection. These teachings directly contradict Islamic doctrine. Therefore, if the Bible is authentic, Islam's core theological claims are refuted by the very scriptures the Qur'an endorses. Horn 2 — If the Bible has been corrupted: If Christians and Jews corrupted their scriptures, then the Qur'an's repeated commands to "judge by the Torah" and "judge by the Gospel" are commands to follow corrupted documents. Furthermore, Muhammad himself is told that if he is in doubt about what has been revealed to him, he should ask "those who have been reading the Scripture before you" (Q.

10:94) — but if those scriptures are corrupted, this instruction is worthless. Therefore, if the Bible is corrupted, the Qur'an's commands regarding it become absurd. Both horns of the dilemma are problematic for Islamic theology. This site examines the Qur'anic evidence for the Bible's authenticity, the historical evidence against the corruption theory, and the theological implications.

secs.h: III. The Qur'an Affirms the Previous Scriptures
secs.x: III. The Qur'an Affirms the Previous Scriptures The Qur'an's affirmations of the Torah, Psalms, and Gospel are not peripheral — they are central to its self-presentation as the final confirmation of the Abrahamic revelation. Qur'an 3:3–4 "He has sent down upon you, [O Muhammad], the Book in truth, confirming what was before it. And He revealed the Torah and the Gospel. Before, as guidance for the people. And He revealed the Criterion [i.e., the Qur’ān]." The Qur'an describes itself as "confirming what was before it" — the Torah and Gospel. The Arabic word musaddiqan means "affirming the truth of," "confirming as true." The Qur'an does not merely acknowledge the existence of previous scriptures; it declares them to be true divine revelation that it confirms. Qur'an 5:47 "And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed — then it is those who are the defiantly disobedient." This verse commands Christians to judge by the Gospel "which Allah has revealed therein" — a present command.

secs.h: III. The Qur'an Affirms the Previous Scriptures
secs.x: It is addressed to Christians of Muhammad's era (7th century AD), whose Gospel texts survive today in manuscripts copied centuries before him. If the Gospel in their hands were corrupted, this would be a command to judge by corruption. Qur'an 5:43–44 "But how is it that they come to you for judgement while they have the Torah, in which is the judgement of Allah?… Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light." The Qur'an refers to the Torah which Jews of Muhammad's day "have" — present tense. It calls this Torah a vehicle of God's judgment and guidance, with divine light in it. This is the Torah as it existed in the 7th century — substantially the same Torah we have today. Qur'an 10:94 "So if you are in doubt, [O Muhammad], about that which We have revealed to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you." Remarkably, the Qur'an instructs Muhammad himself — if he doubts — to consult the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) and their scriptures.

secs.h: III. The Qur'an Affirms the Previous Scriptures
secs.x: This implies that the scriptures in the hands of Jews and Christians in the 7th century were reliable enough to verify prophetic revelation. A corrupted text could not serve this verification function. Qur'an 6:34 "And none can alter the words [i.e., decrees] of Allāh." Christian writers often cite this verse (and 6:115) as proof that God's earlier books could not be corrupted. That argument should be used with care. The bracketed gloss in Sahih International reflects how commentators have usually read it: the context is God's promise of victory to His messengers, and "words" here means His decrees and promises, not the text of a book. The stronger case rests on the verses above, which tell the people of the Torah and the Gospel to judge by what they have.

secs.h: III. The Qur'an Affirms the Previous Scriptures
secs.x: Qur'an 2:75, 2:79 · the strongest counter-verses "…a party of them used to hear the words of Allāh and then distort it [i.e., the Torah] after they had understood it while they were knowing?" (2:75) · "So woe to those who write the 'scripture' with their own hands, then say, 'This is from Allāh,' in order to exchange it for a small price." (2:79) These are the verses Muslims most often cite, and they do accuse some people of distorting and even writing falsely. Read fairly, they describe a party of Jews in Medina twisting what they heard and passing off their own writing as scripture. They do not say that the Torah and Gospel in circulation were lost or replaced; the same book, in 5:43, still says the Jews "have the Torah, in which is the judgement of Allāh". So the question becomes historical: if particular passages were altered, which ones, and when? The manuscripts below make that testable.

secs.h: IV. What the Bible Actually Teaches
secs.x: IV. What the Bible Actually Teaches If the Qur'an affirms the Torah and Gospel as divine revelation that should be followed, what do those scriptures actually teach? They teach doctrines that Islam denies. John 1:1, 14 "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God… And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." The Gospel of John — which the Qur'an commands Christians to judge by — opens with the pre-existence, divinity, and incarnation of Jesus Christ. If the Gospel is from God, as the Qur'an affirms, then this teaching is from God. Yet Islam denies the divinity of Christ. Isaiah 53:3–5 "He was despised and rejected by men… he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities." The Torah (broadly: Old Testament prophets) predicts the suffering servant's death for the sins of others — the very atonement and crucifixion that Islam denies. If the Torah is from God, as the Qur'an affirms, this prophecy is divine revelation pointing to Christ's atoning death.

secs.h: IV. What the Bible Actually Teaches
secs.x: Matthew 28:19 "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." The Gospel — which the Qur'an commands Christians to follow — contains the Great Commission with an explicitly Trinitarian formula. If the Gospel is authentic, then the Trinity (at minimum, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as distinct divine persons) is authentic divine revelation. Islam denies the Trinity. 1 Corinthians 15:3–4 "That Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures." Paul's earliest summary of the Gospel — written c. AD 55, within 25 years of the crucifixion — explicitly states Christ's death, burial, and resurrection. This is the Gospel "in accordance with the Scriptures" — the Old Testament Torah. If these scriptures are from God, the death and resurrection of Christ are from God. Islam denies both.

secs.h: V. Early Christian Evidence — The Manuscripts
secs.x: V. Early Christian Evidence — The Manuscripts The Islamic corruption (tahrif) theory requires that the Bible was significantly altered before or during Muhammad's time, changing its teaching about Christ's divinity, crucifixion, and resurrection. The manuscript evidence decisively contradicts this theory. The Manuscript Record: We possess over 5,800 Greek New Testament manuscripts, the earliest being Papyrus 52 (John 18:31–33, 37–38), dated on handwriting to the second century; some papyrologists allow a date as late as the early third. These manuscripts, and the complete Bibles of the fourth century such as Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, preserve the texts we have today — including the divinity of Christ, the Trinity, and the crucifixion. There is no manuscript tradition showing an "uncorrupted" original Gospel different from what we have. The Dead Sea Scrolls: Discovered in 1947, the Dead Sea Scrolls include manuscripts of the Old Testament copied between the third century BC and AD 68, more than five centuries before Muhammad.

secs.h: V. Early Christian Evidence — The Manuscripts
secs.x: They are not all identical to the Masoretic Text: some books circulated in forms closer to the Greek Septuagint. But the Great Isaiah Scroll, a complete copy of Isaiah, agrees closely with the Isaiah read today, Isaiah 53 included, apart from spelling and small variants. The prophecies Christians read of Christ were in Jewish hands long before Jesus, and could not have been inserted later. The Geographic Distribution: By the end of the 2nd century the Gospels were read across the Roman world and into Mesopotamia, and by Muhammad's time they had been translated into Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, Georgian and Ge'ez, by churches that were often divided from one another and had no single authority over them. A coordinated rewriting of all these copies would have been impossible to organise and would have left two kinds of text behind. No such second text exists. The Patristic Citations: The Church Fathers (Clement, Ignatius, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen, Tertullian) cite the New Testament extensively from AD 96 onward.

secs.h: V. Early Christian Evidence — The Manuscripts
secs.x: Their citations match our current texts — including the passages affirming Christ's divinity, death, and resurrection. There is no patristic record of a different, uncorrupted version of the Gospels.

VI. Muslim Responses Muslim Response: The Bible has been corrupted (tahrif) The mainstream Islamic response is the tahrif (corruption) theory: the original Torah and Gospel were genuine divine revelations, but they were corrupted by Jewish and Christian scribes who changed the texts to remove prophecies of Muhammad, alter the teaching about Jesus, and introduce false doctrines. What we have today is not the original scripture but a corrupted version. Therefore the Qur'an's affirmations apply to the originals, not the corrupted versions we have. Christian Response: Tahrif contradicts the Qur'an and the manuscript evidence The tahrif theory faces multiple fatal problems: (1) The Qur'an tells Jews and Christians that they have the Torah and the Gospel and must judge by them (Q. 5:43–47); it never tells them their books were lost. (2) The Qur'an commands 7th-century Christians and Jews to judge by the scriptures they currently have — this implies those scriptures are reliable. (3) The manuscript record shows no pre-7th-century version of the Bible different from what we have.

(4) The Dead Sea Scrolls confirm the Old Testament's integrity centuries before Muhammad. (5) The geographic distribution of manuscripts across multiple independent regions makes coordinated corruption impossible. The tahrif theory is a theological necessity for Islam but has no historical or textual support. Muslim Response: The "Gospel" in the Qur'an refers to a lost original Gospel, not the four canonical Gospels Some Muslim scholars argue that the Injil (Gospel) referred to in the Qur'an was a single, original Gospel given directly to Jesus — different from the four Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, which were written by his followers. This original Gospel has been lost or suppressed. The Gospel of Barnabas (a medieval document presenting Jesus as a prophet who predicted Muhammad) is sometimes cited as preserving elements of the original.

Christian Response: The "lost Gospel" theory is historically untenable The "lost original Gospel" theory has no historical support: (1) There is no early Christian, Jewish, or pagan reference to a single Gospel given directly to Jesus as a written book. Jesus taught orally; the written Gospels were composed by his apostles and their companions, drawing on eyewitnesses. (2) The Gospel of Barnabas is a late medieval work. It survives in two manuscripts of the late 16th century, one Italian and one Spanish; a "Gospel of Barnabas" title appears in a 6th-century Latin list, but nothing ties that title to this text. It has Jesus say the jubilee comes every hundred years, a rule Pope Boniface VIII introduced in 1300; it pictures wine kept in wooden casks; and it echoes phrases from Dante. It also has Jesus deny that he is the Messiah, which contradicts the Qur'an itself, where Jesus is called the Messiah (3:45). (3) Paul's summary in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4 (c. AD 55) — within the lifetimes of eyewitnesses — already contains the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ.

This is not a later addition. (4) The Qur'an's reference to "those who have the Scripture before you" in Muhammad's time clearly means the scriptures in people's hands in the 7th century — the same texts we have today.

VII. The Christian Response — Conclusion From a Christian perspective, the Islamic Dilemma is not merely an apologetic puzzle — it is an invitation to take the Qur'an's own affirmations seriously and follow them to their logical conclusion. The Qur'an affirms the Torah and Gospel as divine revelation. The manuscript evidence confirms that the Torah and Gospel we have today are essentially the same documents that existed in Muhammad's time. Those documents teach the divinity of Christ, the Trinity, the atoning death and resurrection of Jesus, and the supremacy of his covenant over all previous covenants. The Christian conclusion is: the Qur'an, by affirming the previous scriptures, inadvertently endorses the very documents that refute Islam's central theological claims. The dilemma cannot be escaped by the tahrif theory, which sits uneasily with the Qur'an's own commands and finds no support in the manuscripts — nor by the "lost Gospel" theory, which is equally unsupported.

The resolution the Christian tradition offers is straightforward: accept the testimony of the scriptures that both the Bible and the Qur'an regard as divine revelation — and follow them to Jesus Christ, the Son of God, crucified for our sins and raised for our justification.

VIII. FAQ Q: Is this site anti-Muslim? No. This site engages seriously with Islamic theology and the Qur'an's own claims. It does not attack Muslims as persons or deny the sincerity of Muslim faith. It examines a genuine logical tension within Islamic teaching that Muslim and Christian scholars have discussed for centuries. Honest engagement with theological differences is a mark of respect, not hostility. Q: Do all Muslims accept the tahrif theory? No. The tahrif theory exists in multiple forms: (1) corruption of meaning (tahrif ma'nawi) — the texts were not changed in wording, but Jews and Christians interpret them incorrectly or hide their true meaning; (2) corruption of text (tahrif lafzi) — the actual wording of the texts was changed. Many early writers held only the first, or spoke of corruption by translators and copyists; before the eleventh century, accusations of textual corruption were brief and scattered. The first systematic case for textual corruption was made by Ibn Hazm of Córdoba (d. 1064), whose arguments shaped much later Muslim polemic.

The diversity of Muslim opinion on this question reflects its genuine theological difficulty. Q: Does the Qur'an anywhere explicitly say the Bible was corrupted? The Qur'an accuses some Jews of "distorting words from their places" (Q. 4:46; 5:13, 41) Many commentators understood these verses as twisting meaning and speech: 4:46 goes on to describe wordplay in the way some spoke to Muhammad. The nearest the Qur'an comes to written forgery is 2:79, on those who write with their own hands and call it scripture (see above), and even that describes particular people, not the loss of the Torah. The Qur'an never explicitly says "the Torah or Gospel texts have been changed." The tahrif of written texts is an inference made by later Muslim scholars, not an explicit Qur'anic teaching. Q. 6:34 and 6:115, sometimes cited on both sides, are usually read by commentators as concerning God's decrees and promises rather than the text of any book.
