I. Introduction Jehovah's Witnesses are among the most dedicated door-to-door evangelists in the world, and the Orthodox Christian who answers the knock should do so with respect: these are people who take God, Scripture, and evangelism seriously. But the message they carry — that Jesus is not God but a created angelic being, that the Trinity is a pagan corruption, and that true Christianity vanished from the earth until the 1870s — strikes at the heart of the faith. This page tests the Watchtower's distinctive claims against Scripture, history, and the movement's own record. The conversation matters because the question at stake is the oldest one in Christian theology, settled at Nicaea in AD 325 against Arius: is the Son true God, or the first and greatest creature? The Watchtower has revived Arius's answer. The Church's response is the same as it was then. For the full positive case, see The Divinity of Christ and The Trinity ; this page focuses on the Watchtower's specific arguments.

secs.h: II. Who Are the Jehovah's Witnesses?
secs.x: II. Who Are the Jehovah's Witnesses? The movement began with Charles Taze Russell, a Pennsylvania businessman who founded the Watch Tower Society in the early 1880s after years in Adventist circles. His successor, Joseph Rutherford, reorganized the movement and gave it the name "Jehovah's Witnesses" in 1931. Doctrine is set centrally by the Governing Body in Warwick, New York, and published through the Watchtower and Awake! magazines; members are expected to accept its teaching as the channel of God's communication. What they teach In summary: there is one God, Jehovah; Jesus is God's first creation — identified with Michael the Archangel — through whom all else was made; the Holy Spirit is not a person but God's impersonal "active force"; Christ died on a stake, not a cross; his return occurred invisibly in 1914; only 144,000 go to heaven, while other faithful Witnesses hope to live forever on a restored earth; the soul is not naturally immortal and the wicked are annihilated; and blood transfusions are forbidden.

secs.h: II. Who Are the Jehovah's Witnesses?
secs.x: Birthdays, holidays, military service, and voting are refused, and former members are subject to organized shunning. Each of these stands or falls with the movement's central claim: that all churches apostatized after the apostles died, and that God restored the truth through the Watch Tower Society. That claim is historical — and testable.

III. The New World Translation The Witnesses use their own Bible, the New World Translation (NWT, complete edition 1961, revised 2013). Produced by an anonymous committee whose members the Society has never fully disclosed, it differs from the major mainstream translations — Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox alike — precisely at the verses that bear on Christ's deity. John 1:1 NKJV: "and the Word was God." NWT: "and the Word was a god." Paraphrase The NWT inserts an indefinite article that is defensible in no mainstream translation. See Section IV for the Greek. Colossians 1:16–17 NKJV: "by Him all things were created." NWT: "by means of him all other things were created." Paraphrase The word "other" appears four times in the NWT of this passage; it is absent from the Greek every time. It is inserted to make the Creator of all things into a creature who made the rest. Hebrews 1:8 NKJV: "But to the Son He says: 'Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.'" NWT: "God is your throne forever." Paraphrase The verse quotes Psalm 45:6, where the Father addresses the Son as God.

The NWT's rendering turns God into a piece of furniture. "Jehovah" in the New Testament The NWT prints "Jehovah" 237 times in the New Testament. Paraphrase Not one of the thousands of Greek New Testament manuscripts contains the divine name there — they read "Lord" (Kyrios). The insertions conveniently break the New Testament's habit of applying "Lord" texts about YHWH directly to Jesus (e.g., Romans 10:9–13 quoting Joel 2:32). The pattern is consistent: wherever the Greek text identifies Jesus with God, the NWT adjusts the English. A translation that must rewrite the evidence is itself evidence.

IV. Is Jesus "a god"? — John 1:1 The grammatical argument The Watchtower argues that because the Greek of John 1:1c lacks the definite article before "God" (theos), it should read "a god." But Greek grammar does not work that way: a definite predicate noun placed before the verb regularly drops the article (the pattern described in Colwell's rule), and the very same anarthrous "theos" appears in John 1:6, 12, 13, and 18 — where the NWT itself translates "God," not "a god." The construction in John 1:1c is qualitative: the Word was God in nature — everything that God is. John's prologue then closes the loop: "No one has seen God at any time. The only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him" (John 1:18 NKJV). The theological problem is worse than the grammatical one Suppose the NWT rendering were granted: "the Word was a god ." Witnesses are then committed to two gods — one almighty, one mighty — which is precisely the polytheism they accuse Trinitarians of.

Isaiah leaves no room: "Before Me there was no God formed, nor shall there be after Me" Direct Quote (Isaiah 43:10). If no god was formed after Jehovah, then the Word is either Jehovah or no god at all; "a god" created in between is exactly what the verse excludes. Thomas's confession The risen Christ accepts the most direct confession in the Gospels without correction: "And Thomas answered and said to Him, 'My Lord and my God!'" Direct Quote (John 20:28). A faithful creature's first duty would be to refuse the title — as the angel does in Revelation 22:8–9, and as Paul and Barnabas do at Lystra (Acts 14:14–15). Jesus instead blesses those who will believe the same (John 20:29). The earliest Christians called Jesus God The confession did not begin at Nicaea. St. Ignatius of Antioch, a disciple of the apostles writing on his way to martyrdom around AD 107, calls Christ God without hesitation: "For our God, Jesus Christ, was, according to the appointment of God, conceived in the womb by Mary, of the seed of David, but by the Holy Ghost." Direct Quote (Letter to the Ephesians 18).

Two generations later St. Melito of Sardis preaches of the crucified Lord in the same breath: "God has been murdered; the King of Israel has been destroyed by an Israelite right hand." Direct Quote (On the Pascha 96, c. AD 170). These are not the words of men who thought Jesus was merely "a god" — they are the ordinary speech of the Church a lifetime before any council. And Paul had already taught the churches to await "our great God and Savior Jesus Christ" Direct Quote (Titus 2:13). For the full scriptural case — the worship of Christ, the divine names, "I AM" (John 8:58), Philippians 2, and the witness of the earliest fathers — see The Divinity of Christ .

V. The Failed Predictions The Watch Tower Society has repeatedly attached God's authority to specific dates. The record is documented in the Society's own publications: 1914 Russell's movement long taught that 1914 would mark the end of the present order; when the visible end did not come, the date was reinterpreted as Christ's invisible enthronement in heaven. Paraphrase 1925 Rutherford's booklet "Millions Now Living Will Never Die" pointed to 1925 for the resurrection of the patriarchs; a San Diego mansion ("Beth Sarim") was deeded for their use. The patriarchs did not arrive, and the house was quietly sold. Paraphrase 1975 Watchtower publications of the late 1960s pointed to 1975 as the likely end of six thousand years of human history, with strong hints of Armageddon; many Witnesses sold homes and postponed careers. The Society later acknowledged that expectations had been encouraged.

Paraphrase "This generation" For decades the Society taught that the generation alive in 1914 would not pass away before the end; as that generation died out, the doctrine was redefined repeatedly, most recently as "overlapping generations." Paraphrase Scripture supplies the test: "when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the thing does not happen or come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously" Direct Quote (Deuteronomy 18:22). An organization claiming to be God's sole channel must answer for dates announced in God's name that did not come to pass.

VI. Common Watchtower Arguments Examined "The Trinity is pagan — borrowed from Babylon and Plato" The Claim Three-in-one gods abound in paganism; the church absorbed the idea centuries after Christ. Response Pagan triads are three separate gods in a committee — the opposite of the Christian confession of one God in three persons. The Trinitarian pattern is in the New Testament itself: "baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19 NKJV) — one name, three persons. Christians were worshiping Christ "as to a god" while the apostles' students still lived (Pliny's letter to Trajan, c. AD 112). The fathers who articulated the doctrine were the fiercest opponents of paganism in the ancient world. See The Trinity . "Jesus is the 'firstborn of creation,' so he was created" The Claim Colossians 1:15 calls Christ "the firstborn over all creation" — the first thing Jehovah made.

Response "Firstborn" (prototokos) is a title of rank, not a birth certificate: David, the youngest of eight, is made "firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth" (Psalm 89:27), and Israel is God's "firstborn" among nations. Paul's very next sentence destroys the Watchtower reading: "For by Him all things were created... All things were created through Him and for Him" (Colossians 1:16 NKJV). If all created things were created through him, he is not one of the created things — unless one inserts "other," which is exactly what the NWT does, without Greek warrant. "The Father is greater than I" (John 14:28) The Claim Jesus himself says the Father is greater — so he cannot be God. Response "Greater" speaks of position, not nature — a king is greater than his son without being more human. The Son, "being in the form of God... made Himself of no reputation, taking the form of a bondservant" (Philippians 2:6–7 NKJV); in his voluntary humiliation the Father is greater, as the sender is greater than the one sent (John 13:16).

The same Gospel says "I and My Father are one" (John 10:30) and records the Jews' verdict on his meaning: "You, being a Man, make Yourself God" (John 10:33). The Orthodox fathers read John 14:28 of the incarnate economy — and some, of the Father as the eternal source (the Son is begotten of the Father), which implies no inequality of nature. "True worshipers must use the name Jehovah" The Claim God's name is Jehovah; churches that don't use it are not God's people. Response "Jehovah" is a medieval hybrid, popularised in the 16th century — the consonants YHWH fitted with the vowels of "Adonai"; it is not how Moses, Isaiah, or Jesus pronounced the name. More telling: the New Testament, written by Spirit-guided apostles, never once uses it — it calls God "Father" and "Lord," and applies "Lord" without embarrassment to Jesus. "Whoever calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved" (Joel 2:32) is quoted by Paul of calling on Jesus (Romans 10:9–13). The name above every name given to the risen Christ is the point of Philippians 2:9–11.

VII. The 144,000 and the "Other Sheep" Watchtower doctrine divides believers into two classes: an "anointed" 144,000 who go to heaven and partake of communion, and the "great crowd" of other Witnesses who hope for paradise on earth and must abstain from the bread and the cup. The 144,000 figure comes from Revelation 7 and 14 — read with selective literalism. The number is taken literally, but everything around it is not: the 144,000 are described as 12,000 from each of twelve named tribes of Israel, male, virgins, "not defiled with women" (Revelation 14:4). No Witness reads those details literally; only the bare number survives. In Revelation's own visions the sealed of Israel stand alongside "a great multitude which no one could number" standing before the throne in heaven (Revelation 7:9) — the great crowd is in heaven, not outside it. The two-class system collides with the words of Christ: "Most assuredly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you have no life in you" Direct Quote (John 6:53).

A doctrine that requires the vast majority of believers to pass the bread and the cup along untouched, refusing communion altogether, has no precedent in Scripture or in any century of Christian history. The Orthodox Church knows one flock and one cup: "there will be one flock and one shepherd" (John 10:16) — the verse the Watchtower cites for the two classes in fact announces their union.

VIII. FAQ Q: How should I talk with Witnesses at my door? With kindness and without fear. Don't try to win on twenty fronts; ask one good question and let it work — for example: "If the NWT translators were right about John 1:1, why do the translations made by Greek scholars outside the Society disagree?" or "If the Society announced 1925 and 1975 in God's name, what does Deuteronomy 18:22 ask me to conclude?" Remember that the person at the door is often sincere, lonely, and under real social pressure; harshness confirms what they've been told about "opposers." Hospitality and patience open more doors than debate. Q: Are Jehovah's Witnesses Christians? They sincerely intend to follow Christ, and Orthodox Christians should say so with respect. But by the historic standard — the faith of Nicaea confessed by all Christians East and West — a body that denies the deity of Christ and the personhood of the Holy Spirit, and whose baptism is not in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as the Church has always understood it, stands outside historic Christianity.

That is a statement about doctrine, not about the sincerity or moral character of individual Witnesses. Q: What about the blood transfusion ban? The ban rests on reading dietary commands about eating animal blood (Genesis 9:4; Acts 15:29) as if they covered medical transfusion — a use of blood unknown to the biblical writers, which involves no eating and no taking of life. The Old Testament itself subordinates ritual law to life: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice" (Hosea 6:6), a verse Jesus twice quotes against rule-keeping that costs lives (Matthew 12:7). No historic church before the Watchtower is known to have read these texts as forbidding the saving of life with blood, and mainstream Judaism holds that saving a life overrides nearly every command. Q: Don't Witnesses and Orthodox agree on annihilation of the wicked? No — the Orthodox Church teaches the resurrection of all and the eternal existence of every soul, with judgment to follow (John 5:28–29).

The question of how Scripture describes final punishment is treated on the Annihilationism page ; the Watchtower's denial of the soul's continued existence and of conscious communion with Christ after death ("today you will be with Me in Paradise," Luke 23:43 — which the NWT repunctuates to "I say to you today,") is rejected by the whole tradition East and West.

IX. Sources Scripture (NKJV) John 1:1–18; 6:53; 8:58; 10:16, 30–33; 14:28; 20:28–29; Isaiah 43:10; Deuteronomy 18:22; Colossians 1:15–17; Hebrews 1:8; Philippians 2:6–11; Romans 10:9–13; Revelation 7; 14:1–4; Luke 23:43; Matthew 28:19. Watchtower history Watch Tower Society publications on 1914, 1925 ("Millions Now Living Will Never Die"), Beth Sarim, 1975, and the "generation" teaching; Raymond Franz (former Governing Body member), Crisis of Conscience. Greek & translation Standard Greek grammars on anarthrous predicate nouns (Colwell's rule and qualitative theos); the absence of the Tetragrammaton from all Greek NT manuscripts; mainstream translations (KJV, NKJV, RSV, ESV, NIV, NABRE) at the disputed verses. Patristic & historical Pliny the Younger, Letters 10.96 (c. AD 112); Council of Nicaea (AD 325) against Arius; Ignatius of Antioch and the early confession of Christ's deity — see The Divinity of Christ page. Quotations marked "Paraphrase" faithfully summarize the cited source but are not verbatim; readers are encouraged to consult the originals. Information on websites can have errors — verify personally with an Abouna.

I. Introduction — Charity and Clarity Christianity owes an immeasurable debt to the Jewish people. The Scriptures of Israel are our Scriptures; the patriarchs, the prophets, the psalms, and the Law are our inheritance. Our Lord was born a Jew, of the tribe of Judah and the house of David; His mother, His apostles, and the first thousands of His followers were Jews. Any contempt for the Jewish people is a sin against the very root from which the Church grew (Romans 11:18), and the long history of "Christian" antisemitism is a betrayal of Christ, not an expression of Him. This page is written in friendship and respect. The question between Judaism and Christianity is not whether God chose Israel — He did — but a single, specific question: has the Messiah promised to Israel already come, in Jesus of Nazareth? Faithful Jews say not yet; Christians say He has come, and will come again in glory. This page sets out, from the Hebrew Scriptures themselves, why the Church believes Jesus is the Messiah of whom Moses and the prophets wrote.

Throughout, we state the traditional Jewish reading fairly before responding, and we argue from the Scriptures both faiths hold in common — not by importing the New Testament as proof, but by asking what the prophets foretold.

secs.h: II. What "Messiah" Means — The Hope of Israel
secs.x: II. What "Messiah" Means — The Hope of Israel "Messiah" (Hebrew Mashiach , Greek Christos ) means "anointed one." In Israel, kings, priests, and prophets were anointed with oil to mark them as set apart for God's service. Over time, the prophets spoke of a coming Anointed One above all others — a descendant of King David who would reign forever, bring God's justice to the nations, and usher in an age of peace and the knowledge of God. The Core Expectations From the Hebrew Scriptures, the traditional hope gathered several threads: the Messiah would be a son of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16), born in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2); He would be a king and deliverer , would gather Israel , draw the nations to the God of Israel (Isaiah 2:2–4; 49:6), and establish everlasting peace and righteousness (Isaiah 9:6–7; 11:1–10). The Tension Within the Prophets Yet the same Scriptures also describe an Anointed One who is despised, rejected, and made to suffer for the sins of others (Isaiah 53), who is "cut off" (Daniel 9:26), and who is "pierced" (Zechariah 12:10; Psalm 22).

secs.h: II. What "Messiah" Means — The Hope of Israel
secs.x: How can the Messiah be both a triumphant king and a rejected sufferer? The Christian answer — that He comes twice , first in humility to atone, then in glory to reign — resolves this tension. As we will see, even some of the rabbis sensed two messianic profiles in the text.

III. The Suffering Servant — Isaiah 53 The fourth "Servant Song" (Isaiah 52:13–53:12) is the single most striking messianic passage in the Hebrew Bible. Written centuries before Christ — and preserved in the Dead Sea Scrolls' great Isaiah scroll (c. 125 BC), so it cannot be a later Christian insertion — it describes a righteous servant who suffers and dies for the sins of others, and is then exalted. Isaiah 53:3–6 OO "He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief… But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed… and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all." A righteous, innocent sufferer bears the sins of others and brings them healing and peace. This is precisely the Christian understanding of the Cross — the Messiah suffering not for His own sin but for ours.

Isaiah 53:8–9 OO "By oppression and judgment he was taken away… stricken for the transgression of my people? And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth." The Servant dies ("cut off out of the land of the living," v.8), is buried, and is sinless. The detail of being with "the wicked" yet "a rich man in his death" matches the crucifixion between criminals and burial in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea. The Traditional Jewish Reading Following Rashi (11th c.), many later rabbis read the Servant as a personification of the nation of Israel , suffering among the gentiles. On this view Isaiah 53 is not about an individual Messiah at all. The Older & Christian Reading The Servant is an innocent individual who suffers for the people — "for the transgression of my people " (v.8). Israel cannot atone for Israel. Notably, several ancient Jewish sources (e.g.

the Targum, and the Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 98b) read the passage messianically, before the medieval national reading became standard. The honest point is this: the national reading is a relatively late development, adopted partly in response to Christian use of the chapter. The passage's own words — an individual, sinless, suffering "for the transgression of my people," then "see his offspring" and be exalted — fit a personal, atoning, then vindicated Messiah far better than a collective nation.

secs.h: IV. Bethlehem & the Throne of David
secs.x: IV. Bethlehem & the Throne of David The Messiah was to be a son of David, born in David's town. Both are foretold plainly, and both were fulfilled in Jesus — a Galilean whose family nonetheless traces to David and whose birth was in Bethlehem. Micah 5:2 OO "But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days." The ruler of Israel comes from the small town of Bethlehem — and his "coming forth is from of old, from ancient days," language hinting at an origin beyond mere human birth. Jewish tradition itself names Bethlehem as the Messiah's birthplace. 2 Samuel 7:12–13, 16 OO "I will raise up your offspring after you… and I will establish his kingdom… And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever." God's covenant with David promises an everlasting throne through David's line.

secs.h: IV. Bethlehem & the Throne of David
secs.x: The Messiah must therefore be a verifiable son of David — a point that becomes decisive once the genealogical records are considered (Section VIII). This is more than a coincidence of birthplace. The prophet ties the ruler's origin both to a definite town and to "ancient days," and Scripture binds the Messiah to an unbroken Davidic line. Jesus meets both: born in Bethlehem, of the house and lineage of David.

secs.h: V. Daniel's Seventy Weeks — The Timing of Messiah
secs.x: V. Daniel's Seventy Weeks — The Timing of Messiah Daniel 9 gives the most precise prophecy of when the Messiah would come — and, strikingly, that He would be "cut off" before the destruction of the city and Temple. That destruction happened in AD 70. The Messiah, therefore, had to come — and be killed — before then. Daniel 9:25–26 OO "From the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem to the coming of an anointed one, a prince, there shall be seven weeks. And for sixty-two weeks it shall be built again… And after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing. And the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary." An "anointed one" (Messiah) appears after a measured period from the decree to rebuild Jerusalem (5th c. BC), and is then "cut off" — killed — before the city and sanctuary are destroyed. The Temple fell in AD 70. So the prophecy locates the Messiah's coming and death in the late Second Temple era — exactly the time of Jesus.

secs.h: V. Daniel's Seventy Weeks — The Timing of Messiah
secs.x: The exact arithmetic of the "weeks" (taken as weeks of years) is debated, but the structural point is firm and was felt acutely in antiquity: the Messiah's death is placed before the destruction of the Second Temple. After AD 70, that window closed. This is part of why the talmudic sages themselves recorded a sense that the time for Messiah had already passed (e.g. the discussions in Sanhedrin 97–98), and why some lamented that the appointed times had come and gone.

secs.h: VI. The Pierced One — Psalm 22 & Zechariah 12
secs.x: VI. The Pierced One — Psalm 22 & Zechariah 12 Two further passages describe a figure who is pierced , in language that the Gospels apply to the crucifixion. Psalm 22:16–18 OO "A company of evildoers encircles me; they have pierced my hands and feet — I can count all my bones… they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." A psalm of David describes pierced hands and feet, exposed bones, and garments divided by lot — a vivid picture of crucifixion, a form of execution not practised in David's day. (See the note on the text below.) Zechariah 12:10 OO "And I will pour out on the house of David… a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, so that, when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child." God speaks: the people will look on "me" — and yet mourn for "him whom they have pierced," as for an only son. The pierced one is somehow identified with the LORD Himself, and is mourned in repentance. Christians see here both the Cross and the future turning of Israel to her Messiah.

secs.h: VI. The Pierced One — Psalm 22 & Zechariah 12
secs.x: A Note on the Text of Psalm 22:16 This is worth stating honestly. The standard Masoretic Hebrew here reads ka'ari ("like a lion"), while the Septuagint (Greek, 3rd–2nd c. BC) and other ancient versions read a verb meaning "they pierced/dug." A Dead Sea Scroll fragment from Nahal Hever supports a reading closer to "pierced." Both traditions are ancient; we do not hide the variant. But the older Greek translation made by Jewish scholars before Christ already read a verb ( ōryxan , "they dug" or "bored through") rather than "like a lion," which weighs against the idea that the Christian reading is a late invention.

secs.h: VII. Two Comings — Suffering, Then Glory
secs.x: VII. Two Comings — Suffering, Then Glory The most common Jewish objection is straightforward: the Messiah was to bring world peace, gather the exiles, and rebuild the Temple — and the world is plainly not at peace. So Jesus cannot be the Messiah. This deserves a serious answer. The Christian reply is that the Scriptures describe two distinct profiles of the Anointed One that cannot both be fulfilled at once: one suffering, rejected, and "cut off" (Isaiah 53; Daniel 9; Psalm 22), and one reigning in everlasting glory and peace (Isaiah 9; 11; Daniel 7:13–14). The simplest way to honour both sets of texts is that the Messiah comes twice : first in lowliness to atone for sin and open the way to God, and again in glory to judge the world and complete the kingdom. The peace of the messianic age belongs to the second coming, which Christians still await.

secs.h: VII. Two Comings — Suffering, Then Glory
secs.x: Remarkably, the rabbinic tradition itself wrestled with the same tension and produced a "two-Messiah" framework — Mashiach ben Joseph , a suffering and dying Messiah, and Mashiach ben David , the reigning one (see the discussion in Sukkah 52a). The rabbis split the offices between two figures; the Church confesses them united in one Person who comes in two advents. Either way, the suffering-then-glory pattern is not a Christian imposition but is read out of the Hebrew text. Daniel 7:13–14 OO "Behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man… And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom… an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away." Alongside the suffering Servant stands this glorious "son of man" who receives an everlasting kingdom. Both belong to the Messiah — and Jesus took "Son of Man" as His own title, pointing to this very text.

secs.h: VIII. The Sign of the Temple's Fall
secs.x: VIII. The Sign of the Temple's Fall Several prophecies require the Messiah to come while the Second Temple still stood and while Davidic descent could still be traced. The destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple in AD 70 — with the loss of the genealogical and priestly records — closed both windows. This is among the strongest reasons to look to the late Second Temple era for the Messiah. Genesis 49:10 OO "The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples." Authority would remain with Judah "until" the one comes to whom it belongs — and to whom even the nations will be obedient. With the loss of Jewish self-rule and records after AD 70, the tribal identity of a future claimant became unverifiable. The "until" points to a coming already in the Second Temple period. Malachi 3:1 OO "Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me.

secs.h: VIII. The Sign of the Temple's Fall
secs.x: And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple… behold, he is coming, says the LORD of hosts." "The Lord" comes to "his temple" — which requires the Temple to be standing at His coming. After its destruction in AD 70, this could no longer be fulfilled in the way the prophet describes. So the Lord's coming to the Temple must have occurred before then. Put together with Daniel's seventy weeks, the picture is consistent: the Messiah's first coming and "cutting off" were to fall in the era of the Second Temple, and the records needed to prove Davidic descent perished with it. A Messiah who arrives only after AD 70 cannot, in principle, demonstrate the lineage and Temple-presence that the prophets require — but Jesus, who came before, can.

IX. The Fathers Speak From the earliest centuries, Christians argued for Jesus as Israel's Messiah precisely from the Hebrew Scriptures, often in direct dialogue with Jewish teachers. Two witnesses stand out — one Greek, one Syriac (and so especially dear to the Oriental Orthodox tradition). St. Justin Martyr (c. 100–165) Dialogue with Trypho the Jew — c. AD 160 · ANF vol. 1 Paraphrase The prophets foretold two advents of the Christ: one in which He comes in dishonour and suffering, despised and pierced; and a second in which He comes in glory from the clouds of heaven, as Daniel foretold of the Son of Man. Significance: In the earliest surviving Christian–Jewish dialogue, Justin already answers Trypho's objection by distinguishing the two comings of the Messiah from the Hebrew prophets themselves. The "suffering then glory" solution is second-century, argued from Scripture, not a modern device. (Paraphrase of Justin's argument across Dialogue chs. 32, 49, and 110.) Aphrahat the Persian Sage (c. 280–345) Demonstrations 17, "On Christ the Son of God" · Syriac, NPNF Series 2, vol.

13 Paraphrase From the Law and the Prophets it is shown that the Messiah was to come of the seed of David, to be born in Bethlehem, to suffer and be rejected, and yet to be honoured as Lord — and that in Him the nations would come to worship the God of Israel. Significance: Aphrahat, a Syriac-speaking father writing in the Persian Empire, frames the whole case from the Hebrew Scriptures in conversation with Jewish neighbours — a model close to the Oriental Orthodox heritage. He shows the messianic argument was being made in the Semitic East as well as the Greek West. (Paraphrase of the themes of Demonstration 17.) St. Athanasius the Great (c. 296–373) On the Incarnation, §40 — NPNF Series 2, vol. 4 Paraphrase When did prophet and king cease in Israel, and Jerusalem and the Temple stand desolate, except from the time that Christ came? For the prophecy held only until His coming.

Significance: Athanasius makes the same historical argument as Section VIII — that the ceasing of the Jewish polity, prophecy, and Temple after the first century is itself a sign that the Messiah of the prophets had already appeared. (Paraphrase of On the Incarnation §§37–40.)

X. Objections & Responses "The Messiah was to bring world peace and gather the exiles. The world is not at peace, so Jesus is not the Messiah." Response This is the most serious objection, and it assumes the Messiah comes only once. But the Hebrew Scriptures describe two incompatible profiles — a suffering, "cut off" Servant (Isaiah 53; Daniel 9) and a glorious everlasting King (Isaiah 9; Daniel 7). They cannot both be true of a single coming. Christians hold that the Messiah comes twice: first to atone (already accomplished), then to reign in the peace of the messianic age (still awaited). Strikingly, the rabbis felt the same tension and proposed two Messiahs — ben Joseph (suffering) and ben David (reigning). The unfulfilled peace is not evidence against Jesus; it is the still-future part of His own work. See Section VII. "Isaiah 53 is about the nation of Israel suffering among the gentiles, not about a personal Messiah." Response The text resists this.

The Servant suffers "for the transgression of my people " (53:8) — distinguishing the Servant from the people he suffers for; Israel cannot atone for Israel. The Servant is sinless ("no deceit in his mouth," 53:9), which is not said of the nation. And the national reading, though ancient, became the standard Jewish reading only with Rashi in the 11th century, partly in response to Christian usage; older Jewish sources (the Targum; Sanhedrin 98b) read it of the Messiah. In fairness, the national reading is older than Rashi: Origen reports Jewish scholars in the 3rd century applying the passage to the whole people as one individual (Against Celsus 1.55). Jewish interpreters also answer the "my people" point by taking the speakers of chapter 53 to be the astonished kings of the nations (52:15), so that Israel suffers for the nations, not for itself. The Christian reply is that the Servant is innocent and suffers willingly to the point of death, which the prophets never say of the nation, whose sufferings they attribute to its own sins (Isaiah 40:2; 42:24).

The plain sense — an innocent individual suffering and dying for others, then exalted — fits a person, not a personified nation. "Isaiah 7:14 says 'young woman' (almah), not 'virgin' — so the virgin birth rests on a mistranslation." Response The Hebrew almah denotes a young woman of marriageable age, and in its biblical uses she is unmarried — hence the assumption of virginity. Jewish scholars themselves, in the Septuagint (c. 2nd century BC, long before Christ), translated almah here with the Greek parthenos , "virgin." So the "virgin" reading is pre-Christian and Jewish in origin, not a later Christian twist. In fairness, parthenos could be used loosely (the Septuagint calls Dinah a parthenos after she was violated, Genesis 34:3), so the translation alone does not settle the meaning; but it shows that Jewish readers before Christ could hear a virgin in this verse. And the verse calls the child Immanuel , "God with us" — a name pointing beyond an ordinary birth. Christians read this within the larger pattern of messianic prophecy, not as a lone proof-text.

"Christianity worships three gods (or a man as God), which violates the Shema — 'the LORD is one.'" Response Christians wholeheartedly confess the Shema: there is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). The doctrine of the Trinity is not three gods but one God in three Persons — one indivisible divine essence. The Hebrew Scriptures themselves contain hints of plurality-in-unity within the one God: the plural "let us make man" (Genesis 1:26), the Angel of the LORD who is both distinct from and identified with God, the Word and Spirit of God as agents of His action, and Zechariah 12:10, where the LORD says they will look on "me" yet mourn "him whom they pierced." On Jesus' divinity, that the Messiah is more than merely human is suggested by Micah 5:2 ("from ancient days"), Isaiah 9:6 ("Mighty God"), and Daniel 7's heavenly Son of Man. (See this site's page on the Trinity.) "Jesus didn't keep or fulfil the Torah, and Christianity abandoned the Law — so He broke the covenant." Response Jesus lived as an observant Jew and said He came "not… to abolish the Law… but to fulfill" it (Matthew 5:17).

The prophets themselves foretold a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34) and a day when the nations would worship the God of Israel (Isaiah 49:6; 56:6–7; Zechariah 8:23) — which is exactly what has happened through the Jewish Messiah. The Church holds that the ceremonial and sacrificial Law pointed forward to the Messiah and finds its goal in Him, while the moral law abides. Far from breaking the covenant, the Messiah extends the knowledge of the God of Israel to the whole world, as the prophets said He would.

XI. Frequently Asked Questions Q: Is it antisemitic to say Jesus is the Messiah? No. Believing that the Jewish Messiah has come is not hatred of Jews — it is, in fact, a deeply Jewish hope brought to fulfilment. What is sinful is contempt, persecution, or collective blame, which the Church condemns. We honour the Jewish people as the root onto which we gentiles were grafted (Romans 11), and we hold this conviction in love, not enmity. Q: Don't Christians just quote the Old Testament out of context? It is a fair caution, and some popular apologetics do overreach. That is why this page leans on passages whose messianic force is recognised even within Jewish tradition (Isaiah 53 in the Targum and Talmud; Bethlehem as the Messiah's birthplace; the two-Messiah idea), and is honest about textual variants (Psalm 22:16). The cumulative case — birthplace, lineage, timing, suffering, vindication — is stronger than any single verse.

Q: Why do most Jews not accept Jesus, if the case is so clear? The reasons are historical and human as much as exegetical: the expectation of a one-time, triumphant deliverer; the trauma of centuries of persecution carried out in Jesus' name, which understandably hardened hearts against Him; and the development of rabbinic Judaism as a distinct tradition after AD 70. None of this settles the question of truth, but it explains why sincere, faithful people read the same Scriptures differently — and why Christians should approach the conversation with humility and repentance for past wrongs. Q: What is the single strongest line of argument? The convergence of timing and suffering . Daniel 9 and the AD 70 destruction place the Messiah's "cutting off" in the Second Temple era; Genesis 49:10 and Malachi 3:1 require Him to come while Judah's identity and the Temple still stood; and Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, and Zechariah 12 describe Him as pierced and dying for others. A suffering, atoning Messiah who comes before AD 70 fits Jesus precisely — and no later claimant can meet those conditions.

XII. Sources Scripture The Holy Bible (ESV) — Crossway, 2001. Hebrew Scripture citations follow the Masoretic Text, with the Septuagint and Dead Sea Scrolls noted where relevant. Jewish Tradition Referenced Babylonian Talmud — Sanhedrin 97–98 (the times of Messiah); 98b (Isaiah 53 messianically); Sukkah 52a (Messiah ben Joseph & ben David). Targum Jonathan on Isaiah 52–53 (messianic reading). Rashi — the medieval national reading of Isaiah 53. Church Fathers Justin Martyr — Dialogue with Trypho — ANF vol. 1. Aphrahat — Demonstrations 17 — NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. Athanasius — On the Incarnation §§37–40 — NPNF Series 2, vol. 4. Reference The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaa) — Dead Sea Scrolls, c. 125 BC: confirms Isaiah 53 predates Christ. Nahal Hever Psalms fragment — supports "pierced" in Psalm 22:16. This page argues from the Scriptures shared by Jews and Christians, presents the traditional Jewish readings fairly, and is offered in friendship and respect toward the Jewish people — the root onto which the Church was grafted.

pages.t: Timeline of the Kings — Saul, David & Solomon

secs.x: c. 1105 BC: Birth of Samuel. Hannah, barren and grieved, pours out her soul before the LORD at Shiloh, vowing that if given a son she will give him back to God all the days of his life. Eli the high priest blesses her, and she bears Samuel — “asked of the LORD.” He will be the last judge, the first of the line of prophets after Moses, and the king-maker of Israel. (1 Samuel 1) c. 1102 BC: Samuel given to the Lord at Shiloh. When the child is weaned, Hannah brings him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh and leaves him to minister before Eli, clothed in a little linen ephod. Her song of thanksgiving — “my heart rejoiceth in the LORD... he raiseth up the poor out of the dust” — is the seed of the Theotokos’ Magnificat. Meanwhile the sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, profane the sacrifices. (1 Samuel 1:24–2:36)

c. 1090 BC: The call of Samuel — “Speak, LORD”. In days when “the word of the LORD was precious” and vision rare, God calls the boy Samuel three times by night in the temple; Eli teaches him to answer, “Speak, LORD, for thy servant heareth.” The first word given him is judgment on Eli’s house for his sons’ blasphemy. Samuel grows, and all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knows he is established as a prophet of the LORD. (1 Samuel 3) c. 1070 BC: Battle of Aphek — the Ark captured. Israel, defeated by the Philistines, carries the Ark of the Covenant into battle as a talisman — and loses 30,000 men. The Ark is captured, Hophni and Phinehas are slain, and old Eli falls dead at the news after judging Israel forty years. Phinehas’ dying wife names her son Ichabod: “the glory is departed from Israel.” (1 Samuel 4)

c. 1069 BC: The Ark humbles Dagon and returns. In Ashdod the idol Dagon falls twice on its face before the Ark, its head and hands broken off on the threshold; plagues strike every Philistine city that hosts it. After seven months the Philistines send it back on a new cart with golden trespass offerings. It comes to rest at Kiriath-jearim in the house of Abinadab, where it remains some twenty years. (1 Samuel 5–7:2) c. 1052 BC: Victory at Mizpah — the Ebenezer stone. Samuel gathers Israel to Mizpah in fasting and repentance: “put away the strange gods... and serve him only.” As he offers a suckling lamb, the LORD thunders upon the attacking Philistines and they are routed. Samuel sets up a stone named Ebenezer — “hitherto hath the LORD helped us” — and the Philistines are subdued all his days as judge. (1 Samuel 7:3–17)

c. 1050 BC: Israel demands a king. Samuel is old and his sons take bribes, so the elders come to Ramah: “make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” The LORD tells the grieved prophet, “they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.” Samuel solemnly warns them of “the manner of the king” — conscription, taxation, servitude — but the people refuse to listen. (1 Samuel 8) c. 1050 BC: Saul anointed privately at Ramah. Saul, a Benjamite “from his shoulders and upward higher than any of the people,” comes to Samuel seeking his father’s lost donkeys. The LORD has already told Samuel, “to morrow I will send thee a man.” Samuel pours a flask of oil on his head, kisses him, and the Spirit of God comes upon Saul so that he prophesies and is “turned into another man.” (1 Samuel 9–10:16)

c. 1050 BC: Saul proclaimed king at Mizpah. Chosen by lot before all the tribes, Saul is found hiding among the baggage. Standing head and shoulders above the people, he is acclaimed — “God save the king” — the first king of Israel. Samuel writes the manner of the kingdom in a book, though certain sons of Belial despise the new king. (1 Samuel 10:17–27) c. 1049 BC: Deliverance of Jabesh-gilead. Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and offers terms of shame: every right eye put out. The Spirit of God comes upon Saul; he hews his oxen in pieces and summons all Israel, mustering a great host that shatters the Ammonites by morning. The kingdom is renewed with sacrifices and rejoicing at Gilgal. (1 Samuel 11)

c. 1049 BC: Samuel's farewell address. Samuel calls Israel to witness his integrity — “whose ox have I taken?” — rehearses the LORD’s righteous acts, and calls down thunder and rain in wheat harvest as a sign of their sin in asking a king. Yet he comforts them: “God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you.” He remains prophet and intercessor beside the throne. (1 Samuel 12) c. 1048 BC: War with Philistia — Geba struck. Jonathan smites the Philistine garrison at Geba, and the Philistines gather an enormous host at Michmash — “as the sand on the sea shore.” Israel hides in caves, thickets, rocks and pits; there is no smith in all the land, so that only Saul and Jonathan carry sword and spear. (1 Samuel 13:1–7, 19–23)

c. 1048 BC: Saul's unlawful sacrifice — first rejection. Commanded to wait seven days at Gilgal for Samuel, Saul watches his army melt away and offers the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrives as he finishes: “Thou hast done foolishly... now thy kingdom shall not continue.” The LORD has sought “a man after his own heart” to be captain over His people — the first crack in Saul’s throne. (1 Samuel 13:8–14) c. 1047 BC: Battle of Michmash — Jonathan's exploit. Jonathan and his armour-bearer climb the pass between Bozez and Seneh alone — “there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few” — slay twenty men, and God sends an earthquake of panic through the Philistine camp. Israel routs the enemy, but Saul’s rash oath of fasting nearly costs Jonathan his life over a taste of honey; the people ransom him. (1 Samuel 14:1–46)

c. 1045 BC: Saul's wars round about. Saul fights valiantly on every side — against Moab, Ammon, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines — and “whithersoever he turned himself, he vexed them.” He smites Amalek and delivers Israel from those who spoiled them. Abner son of Ner is captain of his host. (1 Samuel 14:47–52) c. 1040 BC: Birth of David at Bethlehem. David is born in Bethlehem of Judah, youngest of the eight sons of Jesse, grandson of Obed the son of Boaz and Ruth. A shepherd, harpist, and poet, he will be thirty years old when he comes to the throne. From his line, according to the flesh, comes Christ the Son of David, born in this same city. (Ruth 4:17–22; 2 Samuel 5:4; Matthew 1:1–6)

c. 1028 BC: Amalek spared — final rejection of Saul. Sent to utterly destroy Amalek for its ancient ambush of Israel, Saul spares king Agag and the best of the flocks “to sacrifice unto the LORD.” Samuel answers: “Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice... rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft.” The kingdom is rent from Saul; Samuel himself hews Agag in pieces and sees Saul no more until his death, though he mourns for him. (1 Samuel 15) c. 1025 BC: David anointed at Bethlehem. Sent to Jesse’s house with a horn of oil, Samuel passes over seven imposing sons — “man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” — until the youngest is fetched from the sheep. Samuel anoints David in the midst of his brethren, and the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him from that day forward, while it departs from Saul. (1 Samuel 16:1–13)

c. 1024 BC: David the harpist at Saul's court. An evil spirit troubles the rejected king, and his servants seek out David of Bethlehem, “cunning in playing, and a mighty valiant man... and the LORD is with him.” When David plays, Saul is refreshed and the spirit departs. Saul loves him greatly and makes him his armour-bearer — not knowing he shelters his own successor. (1 Samuel 16:14–23) c. 1023 BC: David and Goliath in the Valley of Elah. For forty days the giant of Gath, six cubits and a span, defies the armies of the living God. The shepherd boy refuses Saul’s armour and takes five smooth stones: “the battle is the LORD’s.” One stone sinks into the giant’s forehead; David beheads him with his own sword, and the Philistines flee. The Fathers read here a type of Christ felling Satan. (1 Samuel 17)

c. 1022 BC: Covenant of Jonathan and David. The soul of Jonathan is “knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.” The crown prince strips off his robe, armour, sword, bow and girdle and gives them to David — a wordless surrender of his own succession to the LORD’s anointed. Their covenant will hold beyond death. (1 Samuel 18:1–4) c. 1022 BC: “David his ten thousands” — Saul's jealousy. The women sing, “Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands,” and Saul eyes David from that day. Twice he hurls his javelin at the harpist; then he offers Michal his daughter for a bride-price of a hundred Philistine foreskins, hoping David will fall — David brings two hundred. Michal loves David, and Saul fears him the more. (1 Samuel 18:5–30)

c. 1021 BC: David flees — Michal's ruse, Naioth. Jonathan pleads for David and Saul swears not to kill him — then hurls the spear again. Michal lets David down through a window and lays an idol with goats’ hair in his bed. David flees to Samuel at Naioth in Ramah, where the Spirit of God overwhelms three companies of Saul’s messengers, and Saul himself, so that he prophesies stripped all that day: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (1 Samuel 19) c. 1020 BC: The arrow signal — parting from Jonathan. At the new moon feast Saul’s murderous intent is proven; he casts his javelin even at Jonathan. By the arranged sign of arrows in the field Jonathan warns David. The friends weep and kiss one another farewell: “The LORD be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever.” David goes out a fugitive. (1 Samuel 20)

c. 1020 BC: Nob — the showbread and Goliath's sword. At the sanctuary of Nob, Ahimelech the priest gives David and his men the hallowed showbread and the sword of Goliath — “there is none like that.” Doeg the Edomite, Saul’s herdsman, watches. The Lord Christ Himself appeals to this event to teach that mercy outweighs ritual prescription. (1 Samuel 21:1–9; Mark 2:25–26) c. 1020 BC: David feigns madness at Gath. Fleeing to Achish king of Gath with Goliath’s sword at his side, David is recognized — “is not this David, the king of the land?” — and in terror scrabbles on the gate doors and lets spittle run down his beard until Achish drives him out. From this deliverance come Psalms 34 and 56: “I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.” (1 Samuel 21:10–15; Psalms 34, 56)

c. 1019 BC: The cave of Adullam. David escapes to the cave of Adullam, and his brethren and “every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented” gather to him — about four hundred men, the seed of his mighty army. He lodges his parents with the king of Moab, land of his great-grandmother Ruth, and at the word of the prophet Gad returns to Judah. (1 Samuel 22:1–5) c. 1019 BC: Massacre of the priests of Nob. Betrayed by Doeg, Ahimelech answers Saul with dignity — and Saul orders the slaughter of the priests. When his footmen refuse, Doeg the Edomite kills eighty-five priests of the LORD and puts Nob to the sword, man, woman and child. Abiathar alone escapes to David with the ephod, fulfilling the doom pronounced on Eli’s house. Psalm 52 answers Doeg. (1 Samuel 22:6–23; Psalm 52)

c. 1018 BC: Rescue of Keilah. Though a hunted man, David inquires of the LORD and saves the town of Keilah from Philistine raiders robbing the threshing-floors. When the LORD reveals by the ephod that the men of Keilah would deliver him to Saul, David and his six hundred slip away into the wilderness. (1 Samuel 23:1–13) c. 1018 BC: Ziph — Jonathan strengthens David's hand. In the wilderness of Ziph, Saul seeks David every day, “but God delivered him not into his hand.” Jonathan comes to him in the wood and “strengthened his hand in God”: “thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee.” The Ziphites betray David; at the Rock of Divisions only a Philistine invasion pulls Saul off the chase. (1 Samuel 23:14–29)

c. 1017 BC: Saul spared at En-gedi. Saul enters the very cave where David and his men hide. Urged to strike, David only cuts off the corner of Saul’s robe — and his heart smites him even for that: “The LORD forbid... seeing he is the anointed of the LORD.” Confronted with the evidence, Saul weeps: “thou art more righteous than I,” and confesses David will surely be king. (1 Samuel 24) c. 1016 BC: Death of the prophet Samuel. Samuel dies and all Israel gathers to lament him; he is buried at his house in Ramah. Judge, prophet, priest by service, intercessor and anointer of the first two kings, he stands with Moses and Aaron among those who “called upon his name” (Psalm 99:6). The Church honors him as a righteous forefather. (1 Samuel 25:1)

c. 1016 BC: Nabal and Abigail. Churlish Nabal repays David’s protection of his flocks with insult, and David straps on his sword to destroy his house. Abigail, wise and beautiful, rides to meet him with provisions and words that turn his wrath: “the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the LORD.” David blesses her for keeping him from bloodguilt; Nabal’s heart dies within him, and Abigail becomes David’s wife. (1 Samuel 25) c. 1015 BC: Saul spared a second time — Hachilah. Guided again by Ziphite informers, Saul camps on the hill of Hachilah. By night David and Abishai walk into the sleeping camp — “a deep sleep from the LORD was fallen upon them” — and take Saul’s spear and water jug from beside his head, but David restrains Abishai: “who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD’s anointed, and be guiltless?” Saul confesses, “I have sinned... I have played the fool.” (1 Samuel 26)

c. 1012 BC: David at Ziklag under Achish. Despairing of safety in Israel, David crosses to Achish of Gath, who gives him the border town of Ziklag; he dwells in Philistine country a year and four months. From there he raids the Geshurites and Amalekites — enemies of Judah — while letting Achish believe he raids his own people. Mighty men of Benjamin, Gad and Manasseh stream to him there. (1 Samuel 27; 1 Chronicles 12:1–22) c. 1010 BC: Saul and the medium of En-dor. With the Philistines massed at Shunem, the LORD answers Saul “neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets.” The king who once expelled the mediums now seeks one by night in disguise. The figure of Samuel pronounces the end: “to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me: the LORD also shall deliver the host of Israel into the hand of the Philistines.” (1 Samuel 28)

c. 1010 BC: Ziklag burned — David recovers all. The Philistine lords refuse to let David march with them against Israel, and he returns to find Ziklag burned and every wife and child carried off by Amalekites; his own men speak of stoning him. “But David encouraged himself in the LORD his God.” Guided by the ephod, he overtakes the raiders and recovers all, and decrees that they who guard the baggage share alike with those who fight. (1 Samuel 29–30) 1010 BC: Battle of Mount Gilboa — death of Saul and Jonathan. The Philistines break Israel on Gilboa. Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua fall; Saul, wounded by the archers, falls on his own sword rather than be abused. The Philistines fasten the bodies to the wall of Beth-shan, but the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead — the city Saul once saved — march all night to recover them and fast seven days. Saul reigned some forty years. (1 Samuel 31; Acts 13:21)

1010 BC: The Song of the Bow — David's lament. An Amalekite brings Saul’s crown and claims the killing, expecting reward; David has him executed for destroying the LORD’s anointed. Then he teaches Judah his lament: “The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen!... Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives... thy love to me was wonderful.” (2 Samuel 1) 1010 BC: David anointed king of Judah at Hebron. At the LORD’s word David goes up to Hebron, and the men of Judah anoint him king over the house of Judah. He reigns there seven years and six months, and sends a blessing to the men of Jabesh-gilead for their kindness to Saul’s body. (2 Samuel 2:1–7) c. 1008 BC: Ish-bosheth set up as rival king. Abner, Saul’s general, takes Ish-bosheth, Saul’s surviving son, to Mahanaim beyond Jordan and makes him king over Israel. The house of Saul and the house of David enter a long civil war: “David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker.” (2 Samuel 2:8–11; 3:1)

c. 1008 BC: Battle of Gibeon — Asahel slain. Twelve champions of each side grapple and fall together at the pool of Gibeon, and a fierce battle follows in which Abner is beaten. Swift-footed Asahel, Joab’s brother, refuses to turn aside from pursuing Abner and dies on the butt of his spear — a death that will demand blood. (2 Samuel 2:12–32) c. 1006 BC: Abner's defection and murder. Accused by Ish-bosheth over Saul’s concubine Rizpah, Abner swears to translate the kingdom to David and negotiates with the elders of Israel; Michal is restored to David. But Joab, avenging Asahel and fearing a rival, takes Abner aside in the gate of Hebron and kills him. David publicly mourns — “know ye not that there is a prince and a great man fallen this day in Israel?” — and disowns the deed. (2 Samuel 3)

c. 1005 BC: Assassination of Ish-bosheth. Two of his own captains, Rechab and Baanah, murder Ish-bosheth on his bed and carry his head to David expecting favor. David, who executed Saul’s claimed slayer, has them killed and hangs their bodies over the pool in Hebron; Ish-bosheth’s head is buried honorably in Abner’s tomb. The path to the throne remains unstained by David’s own hand. (2 Samuel 4) 1003 BC: David king over all Israel. All the tribes come to Hebron — “we are thy bone and thy flesh” — and the elders anoint David king over all Israel, his third anointing. He is thirty when he begins to reign and reigns forty years. The Chronicler pictures the vast joyful muster: “there was joy in Israel.” (2 Samuel 5:1–5; 1 Chronicles 11–12)

1003 BC: Capture of Jerusalem — the City of David. David takes the Jebusite stronghold of Zion, thought impregnable — “the blind and the lame” could hold it, its defenders taunt — Joab going up first, by the water shaft. David dwells in the fort and calls it the City of David, building round about from the Millo. The city of Melchizedek becomes the royal city, and in God’s design, the city of the Temple and of the Cross. (2 Samuel 5:6–10; 1 Chronicles 11:4–9) c. 1002 BC: Hiram of Tyre builds David a house. Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar trees, carpenters and masons, and they build David a palace. “And David perceived that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for his people Israel’s sake.” (2 Samuel 5:11–12)

c. 1002 BC: Philistines crushed at Baal-perazim. Hearing David is king, the Philistines spread through the valley of Rephaim. David inquires of the LORD and breaks them at Baal-perazim — “the LORD hath broken forth upon mine enemies... as the breach of waters” — and burns their abandoned idols. In a second battle he waits for the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, the sign that God goes out before him, and smites them from Geba to Gazer. (2 Samuel 5:17–25) c. 1001 BC: Uzzah and the Ark — Perez-uzzah. David brings the Ark from Kiriath-jearim on a new cart — the Philistine way, not the Levites’ shoulders as the Law commands. When the oxen stumble Uzzah takes hold of the Ark and God strikes him dead. Afraid, David leaves the Ark three months in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, and the LORD blesses all his household — a standing lesson that holy things are approached as God commands, not as man finds convenient. (2 Samuel 6:1–11; 1 Chronicles 13)

c. 1000 BC: The Ark enters Zion — David dances. This time the Levites bear the Ark on their shoulders “as Moses commanded,” with sacrifices at every six paces. David, girded in a linen ephod, dances before the LORD with all his might amid shouting and the trumpet; Michal despises him in her heart and remains childless. The Ark is set in the tent David pitched, with Asaph appointed to minister in psalms of thanksgiving. The Fathers see in the Ark a type of the Theotokos, who carried the Word in her womb. (2 Samuel 6:12–23; 1 Chronicles 15–16) c. 998 BC: The Davidic covenant — a house for ever. David, at rest in his cedar house, longs to build a house for the Ark. Through Nathan the LORD answers: it is I who will make thee a house. “I will set up thy seed after thee... and I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever... I will be his father, and he shall be my son.” Solomon builds the Temple in the near term, but the everlasting throne belongs to Christ, the Son of David, as Gabriel announces to the Virgin. (2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17; Luke 1:32–33)

c. 996 BC: David's conquests — the empire established. David subdues the Philistines and Moab; smites Hadadezer of Zobah and the Syrians of Damascus, garrisoning Damascus; takes shields of gold and much brass (later used for the Temple); Edom falls in the Valley of Salt and receives garrisons. Toi of Hamath sends tribute; David dedicates all the spoil to the LORD. His rule reaches from the Euphrates toward the border of Egypt, “and the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went; and David executed judgment and justice unto all his people.” (2 Samuel 8; 1 Chronicles 18) c. 995 BC: Kindness to Mephibosheth. “Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?” Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, lame in both feet since the flight after Gilboa, is brought from Lo-debar; David restores Saul’s lands to him and seats him at the king’s table continually — covenant-love (hesed) kept beyond death. (2 Samuel 9)

c. 994 BC: The Ammonite war — Joab at Rabbah. Hanun of Ammon shames David’s condolence envoys — half their beards shaved, garments cut off — and hires Aramean armies. Caught between two fronts, Joab and Abishai divide the host: “Be of good courage... and the LORD do that which seemeth him good.” The Arameans are broken, Shobach their commander falls at Helam, and the vassal kings make peace with Israel. (2 Samuel 10; 1 Chronicles 19) c. 993 BC: David and Bathsheba — the murder of Uriah. “At the time when kings go forth to battle,” David tarries in Jerusalem, sees Bathsheba washing from his rooftop, and takes her; she conceives. Her husband Uriah the Hittite, recalled from the siege, refuses the comforts of home while the Ark and Israel camp in the open field. David sends him back carrying his own death warrant: “set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle.” Uriah falls before Rabbah, David marries the widow — “but the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.” (2 Samuel 11)

c. 992 BC: “Thou art the man” — Nathan and Psalm 51. Nathan tells the king of a rich man who stole the poor man’s one ewe lamb; when David flares in judgment, the prophet answers: “Thou art the man.” The sword shall never depart from his house. David’s repentance is immediate and total — “I have sinned against the LORD” — and Psalm 51, the Miserere prayed at every Orthodox midnight office, pours out of it: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.” The child of the adultery dies despite David’s fasting. (2 Samuel 12:1–23; Psalm 51) c. 991 BC: Birth of Solomon — Jedidiah. David comforts Bathsheba, and she bears Solomon — “and the LORD loved him,” sending word by Nathan to name him Jedidiah, “beloved of the LORD.” Out of the ashes of the great sin, God in His mercy raises the heir of the promise and ancestor of Christ. (2 Samuel 12:24–25; Matthew 1:6)

c. 991 BC: Fall of Rabbah of Ammon. Joab reduces the royal city and summons David to take it, “lest I take the city, and it be called after my name.” David takes the crown of their king — a talent of gold with precious stones — and puts the Ammonites to forced labor. The long Ammonite war ends. (2 Samuel 12:26–31) c. 988 BC: Amnon and Tamar. Amnon, David’s firstborn, feigning sickness by the counsel of subtle Jonadab, violates his half-sister Tamar and then hates her with a hatred greater than his former love, casting her out desolate. David is very wroth — but does nothing. Absalom, Tamar’s full brother, says nothing to Amnon “either good or bad,” and waits. Nathan’s sword has entered the house. (2 Samuel 13:1–22) c. 986 BC: Absalom's revenge — Amnon slain. Two full years later, at sheep-shearing at Baal-hazor, Absalom’s servants strike Amnon down at his command when his heart is merry with wine. The king’s sons flee on their mules; Absalom escapes to his grandfather Talmai, king of Geshur, and remains three years while David mourns. (2 Samuel 13:23–39)

c. 983 BC: Absalom's return to Jerusalem. Joab, by the parable of the wise woman of Tekoa, moves the king to bring Absalom home — yet David will not see his face. After two more years Absalom sets Joab’s barley field on fire to force an audience, and at last the king kisses his son. In all Israel none is so praised for beauty: “from the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.” (2 Samuel 14) c. 979 BC: Absalom steals the hearts of Israel. Absalom gets him chariots and horses and fifty men to run before him, and rises early to stand beside the way of the gate, telling every man with a suit, “Oh that I were made judge in the land!” — kissing all who bow to him. “So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel,” preparing his conspiracy over four years. (2 Samuel 15:1–6)

c. 976 BC: Absalom's rebellion — David flees Jerusalem. The trumpet sounds in Hebron: “Absalom reigneth.” David abandons Jerusalem to spare it, crossing the Kidron and weeping barefoot up the Mount of Olives — where a greater Son of David would one day weep. He sends the Ark back — “if I shall find favour... he will bring me again” — plants Hushai as counter-counselor, and receives the loyalty of Ittai the Gittite: “whither my lord the king shall be... even there also will thy servant be.” Psalm 3 is his morning prayer of these days. (2 Samuel 15; Psalm 3)

c. 976 BC: Shimei's curses; Ahithophel against Hushai. Shimei of Saul’s house stones and curses the fleeing king — “let him curse; for the LORD hath bidden him,” David answers. In Jerusalem Absalom goes in to his father’s concubines on the roof, fulfilling Nathan’s word before all Israel. Ahithophel’s deadly counsel of immediate pursuit — counsel “as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God” — is defeated by Hushai’s delay, “for the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel.” Ahithophel sets his house in order and hangs himself. (2 Samuel 16–17) c. 976 BC: Forest of Ephraim — “O Absalom, my son”. David’s veterans break the rebel host in the forest of Ephraim; twenty thousand fall, “and the wood devoured more people that day than the sword.” Absalom, caught by his head in the boughs of a great oak, hangs between heaven and earth; Joab, defying the king’s charge to “deal gently,” thrusts three darts through his heart. David’s grief shakes the ages: “O my son Absalom... would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!” (2 Samuel 18)

c. 975 BC: The king's return; Sheba's revolt. Joab bluntly rouses David from grief to receive his people. Judah and Israel quarrel over bringing the king back, and Sheba son of Bichri blows the trumpet: “we have no part in David.” Amasa, appointed over the host, is treacherously slain by Joab, who then besieges Sheba in Abel of Beth-maachah until a wise woman has the rebel’s head thrown over the wall. Shimei is spared; Mephibosheth’s tale is heard; aged Barzillai is blessed. (2 Samuel 19–20) c. 974 BC: Famine, the Gibeonites, and Rizpah's vigil. Three years of famine expose Saul’s blood-guilt against the Gibeonites, whom Israel had sworn by covenant to spare. Seven of Saul’s descendants are given up and hanged; Mephibosheth is spared for Jonathan’s oath. Rizpah keeps vigil over the bodies from harvest until the rains, driving off bird and beast — and moved by her devotion, David gathers the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead and buries them in the sepulchre of Kish. (2 Samuel 21:1–14)

c. 973 BC: The giant wars — “the lamp of Israel”. In the later Philistine wars David faints in battle, and Ishbi-benob of the giants’ brood nearly slays him; Abishai rescues him, and his men swear: “Thou shalt go no more out with us to battle, that thou quench not the lamp of Israel.” Four more of the giants of Gath — including a brother of Goliath and a six-fingered champion — fall by the hands of David’s servants. (2 Samuel 21:15–22; 1 Chronicles 20:4–8) c. 972 BC: David's song, last words, and mighty men. David’s great song of deliverance — “The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer” — is preserved twice in Scripture (2 Samuel 22 = Psalm 18). His last words confess the Spirit’s inspiration: “The Spirit of the LORD spake by me, and his word was in my tongue.” The roll of the mighty men is honored — the three who broke through the Philistine host to draw well-water of Bethlehem, which David would not drink but poured out to the LORD, for it was “the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives.” (2 Samuel 22–23; Psalm 18)

c. 972 BC: The census, the plague, and Araunah's floor. David numbers Israel in pride against Joab’s protest, and his heart smites him. Offered three judgments, he chooses to fall into the hand of the LORD, “for his mercies are great”: seventy thousand die of pestilence, and the destroying angel stays his hand at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. David buys the floor and oxen for a price — “neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing” — builds an altar, and the plague is stayed. This floor on Mount Moriah becomes the site of the Temple. (2 Samuel 24; 1 Chronicles 21; 2 Chronicles 3:1)

c. 971 BC: David prepares for the Temple. Forbidden to build because he is a man of war who has shed blood, David prepares abundantly for his son “yet young and tender”: a hundred thousand talents of gold, a million of silver, brass and iron without weight, cedar, stone and skilled workmen. He organizes the twenty-four courses of priests, the Levites, the singers of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, the gatekeepers and treasurers — and delivers to Solomon the pattern of the house, “all this... the LORD made me understand in writing by his hand upon me.” (1 Chronicles 22–29) 971 BC: Adonijah's usurpation; Solomon anointed at Gihon. Adonijah, David’s eldest surviving son, exalts himself — “I will be king” — feasting his party at En-rogel with Joab and Abiathar. Nathan and Bathsheba rouse the aged David, who keeps his oath: Solomon rides the king’s own mule to Gihon, where Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him, and the earth rends with the shout, “God save king Solomon!” Adonijah’s guests scatter; he clings to the horns of the altar and is spared on condition. (1 Kings 1)

970 BC: David's charge and death. David charges Solomon: “Be thou strong... and keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways... that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest.” Having reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem, he sleeps with his fathers and is buried in the City of David. Prophet and psalmist, ancestor of Christ, the Church numbers him among the holy forefathers; his psalter is her daily prayer book. (1 Kings 2:1–11; Acts 2:29–30; 13:22–36) c. 970 BC: The throne established — judgments of Solomon. Adonijah asks for Abishag the Shunammite — a veiled claim on the throne — and dies for it. Abiathar is deposed from the priesthood, fulfilling the word spoken against the house of Eli at Shiloh; Zadok stands in his place. Joab, guilty of the blood of Abner and Amasa, is slain even at the altar by Benaiah; Shimei breaks his parole and follows. “And the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.” (1 Kings 2:12–46)

c. 969 BC: Marriage to Pharaoh's daughter. Solomon makes affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt and brings his daughter into the City of David until his own house and the Temple are built — a mark of Israel’s new standing among the nations, and the first thread of the foreign entanglements that will later snare his heart. (1 Kings 3:1) c. 969 BC: The dream at Gibeon — wisdom granted. At the great high place of Gibeon the LORD appears to Solomon in a dream by night: “Ask what I shall give thee.” The young king asks not long life, riches, nor the life of his enemies, but “an understanding heart to judge thy people.” The speech pleases the Lord, who grants wisdom beyond all before or after him — and adds riches and honor besides. (1 Kings 3:5–15; 2 Chronicles 1)

c. 968 BC: Judgment of the two mothers. Two harlots claim one living child. Solomon calls for a sword: “Divide the living child in two.” The true mother’s bowels yearn — “give her the living child, and in no wise slay it” — and the king restores her son. “And all Israel... feared the king: for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him, to do judgment.” (1 Kings 3:16–28) c. 967 BC: The kingdom in its glory — peace and plenty. Twelve officers provision the court month by month; Solomon reigns over all kingdoms from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt, receiving tribute. “Judah and Israel were many, as the sand which is by the sea in multitude, eating and drinking, and making merry... and Judah and Israel dwelt safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree... all the days of Solomon” — the Old Testament’s image of messianic peace. (1 Kings 4:1–28; Micah 4:4)

c. 967 BC: Solomon's wisdom renowned among the nations. God gives Solomon “wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart, even as the sand that is on the sea shore” — wiser than Ethan, Heman, Chalcol and Darda. He speaks three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs, discoursing of trees from the cedar to the hyssop, of beasts, fowl, creeping things and fishes; and men come from all peoples and kings of the earth to hear him. (1 Kings 4:29–34) c. 966 BC: Treaty with Hiram — cedars of Lebanon. Hiram of Tyre, who loved David, covenants with Solomon: cedar and fir floated in rafts by sea in exchange for wheat and pure oil year by year. Solomon raises a levy of thirty thousand men to Lebanon by courses, with eighty thousand hewers in the mountains and seventy thousand bearers of burdens, and great costly stones are cut for the foundation of the house. (1 Kings 5)

966 BC: The Temple begun on Mount Moriah. In the four hundred and eightieth year after the Exodus, in the fourth year of Solomon, in the month Zif, the house of the LORD is begun on Mount Moriah — where Abraham bound Isaac and where the angel stayed the plague at Araunah’s floor. The stone is made ready before it is brought, “so that there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building” — a silence the Fathers love as a figure of the Church built without clamor. (1 Kings 6:1–7; 2 Chronicles 3:1) 959 BC: The Temple completed. After seven years the house stands finished in all its parts: the oracle overlaid with pure gold, two cherubim of olive wood ten cubits high overshadowing the place of the Ark, walls carved with cherubim, palms and open flowers. Hiram of Tyre casts the two bronze pillars Jachin (“He shall establish”) and Boaz (“in it is strength”), the molten sea on twelve oxen, and all the vessels. To Solomon comes the word: obedience, not architecture, is the condition of God’s dwelling. (1 Kings 6:8–38; 7:13–51)

959 BC: Dedication — the glory fills the house. At the feast of the seventh month the priests bring up the Ark into the oracle, and the cloud of glory fills the house so that the priests cannot stand to minister. Solomon’s great prayer confesses that “the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house,” and pleads that God hear from heaven toward this place — the stranger included. Fire descends on the sacrifices (2 Chronicles 7:1); twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep are offered, and Israel keeps the feast fourteen days. (1 Kings 8; 2 Chronicles 5–7) c. 958 BC: Second appearance of the LORD. The LORD appears to Solomon a second time, as at Gibeon: “I have hallowed this house... mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually.” But the warning is equally solemn: if you or your children turn from Me to serve other gods, Israel will be cut off from the land, and this exalted house will become “a proverb and a byword among all people” — a word fulfilled in 586 BC. (1 Kings 9:1–9)

c. 953 BC: The palace complex; Cabul. Thirteen years build Solomon’s own house: the House of the Forest of Lebanon with its rows of cedar pillars, the porch of pillars, the porch of the throne where he judges, and a house for Pharaoh’s daughter — twenty years of building in all. To Hiram, who supplied gold and timber, Solomon gives twenty cities in Galilee; Hiram is displeased and names them Cabul, “good-for-nothing.” (1 Kings 7:1–12; 9:10–14) c. 950 BC: Fortresses and store cities. With the levy Solomon builds the Millo and the wall of Jerusalem, and fortifies Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer — Gezer being Pharaoh’s burnt-and-given dowry to his daughter — with Beth-horon, Baalath, Tadmor, and cities for chariots and horsemen. The remnant of the Canaanite peoples he puts to bond-service, but of Israel he makes soldiers and officers, not slaves. (1 Kings 9:15–25)

c. 948 BC: The fleet at Ezion-geber — gold of Ophir. Solomon builds a navy at Ezion-geber beside Eloth on the Red Sea, manned by Hiram’s seasoned sailors together with his own servants. From Ophir they bring four hundred and twenty talents of gold; the navy of Tarshish comes once in three years bearing gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks — Israel’s brief age as a maritime trading power. (1 Kings 9:26–28; 10:11, 22) c. 946 BC: Visit of the Queen of Sheba. The queen of Sheba comes from the ends of the earth with hard questions, and Solomon answers them all. Seeing his wisdom, the house, the table, and the ascent to the house of the LORD, “there was no more spirit in her”: “the half was not told me... Blessed be the LORD thy God, which delighted in thee.” She gives a hundred and twenty talents of gold and unmatched spices. Christ points to her as witness against an unbelieving generation: “behold, a greater than Solomon is here.” (1 Kings 10:1–13; Matthew 12:42)

c. 945 BC: The golden age — silver as stones. Six hundred threescore and six talents of gold come to Solomon yearly, beside merchandise and the tribute of Arabia. He makes a great ivory throne overlaid with gold, six steps flanked by twelve lions; all his drinking vessels are gold, “none were of silver: it was nothing accounted of.” The king “made silver to be in Jerusalem as stones,” and horses and chariots are brought out of Egypt and Kue — though the Law had warned the king against multiplying horses, wives and gold. (1 Kings 10:14–29; Deuteronomy 17:16–17)

c. 945 BC: The wisdom books. To Solomon the tradition ascribes the Song of Songs, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes — read by the Fathers as a ladder: the Song’s pure love, the Proverbs’ discipline for the young, and Ecclesiastes’ verdict on all things under the sun, “vanity of vanities.” Psalms 72 (“Give the king thy judgments, O God”) and 127 (“Except the LORD build the house”) bear his name, and the Church of the first centuries also received the Wisdom of Solomon among her Scriptures.
