AD 743) "The ever-virgin One thus remains even after the birth still virgin, having never at any time up till death consorted with a man." Byzantine Writer VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION What the Witnesses Show These writers lived in Alexandria, Cyprus, Cappadocia, Gaul, Antioch, Constantinople, Bethlehem, Pettau, North Africa and Palestine. They wrote in Greek and Latin, from the third century to the eighth. They disagree about who exactly the brothers were, which shows they were not copying one formula. Yet not one of them says that Mary had other children, and they say plainly and repeatedly that she did not.

Chrysostom and Augustine treat the idea as unthinkable; Jerome refuses it because Scripture never says it; Origen calls the honour of her virginity the view of those "with sound mind." The only early writers who taught otherwise are named in Section XVII, and none of them is venerated as a saint.

secs.h: The Body That Served the Word
secs.x: X. Why the God-Bearer Remained a Virgin Does the title Theotokos by itself require that Mary had no other children? Strictly, no. Ephesus defined the title to say who Christ is, and no council or Father defines it as including her lasting virginity. The homily attributed to St. Basil says openly that Mary's virginity was necessary up to the birth, and that what came afterwards would not have touched the teaching of the mystery (Section IX). Honesty requires saying so, and the case does not need more. What the Fathers do is argue from her divine motherhood to her lasting virginity, as a matter of what is fitting and holy. The connection is not a syllogism but it is not an afterthought either. Here it is in their own words. The Body That Served the Word Origen, in the passage quoted in Section IX, gives the reason those who hold the Ever-Virgin do so: "that that body of hers which was appointed to minister to the Word... might not know intercourse with a man after that the Holy Ghost came into her." The body that bore the Word is not returned to common use.

secs.h: The Body That Served the Word
secs.x: Such a Mother Chrysostom reasons the same way: "she having so become a mother, and having been counted worthy of a new sort of travail, and a child-bearing so strange," Joseph could never "have endured to know her." It is precisely because of whom she bore that he will not hear of it. St. John of Damascus Exposition of the Orthodox Faith IV.14 (c. AD 743) "For could it be possible that she, who had borne God and from experience of the subsequent events had come to know the miracle, should receive the embrace of a man. God forbid! It is not the part of a chaste mind to think such thoughts, far less to commit such acts." Byzantine Writer VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION This is the clearest statement of the link. The reason given is not a general rule about mothers.

secs.h: The Body That Served the Word
secs.x: It is that she "had borne God." The Gate the Lord Entered Ezekiel 44:2 "And the Lord said to me, 'This gate shall be shut; it shall not be opened, and no man shall enter by it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered by it; therefore it shall be shut." Orthodox reading: The gate is shut, and the prophet gives the reason: "because the Lord God of Israel has entered by it." The Fathers saw in this the Virgin through whom God came into the world. Her closing is the result of His entering. Protestant reading: The verse is about the east gate of the temple in Ezekiel's vision, not about Mary. Its application to her is typology. St. Jerome Letter 48, to Pammachius, 21 (c. AD 393) "Christ Himself is a virgin; and His mother is also a virgin; yea, though she is His mother, she is a virgin still. ...

secs.h: The Body That Served the Word
secs.x: She is the east gate, spoken of by the prophet Ezekiel, always shut and always shining, and either concealing or revealing the Holy of Holies; and through her the Sun of Righteousness, our high priest after the order of Melchizedek, goes in and out." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The Coptic Orthodox Church The Wednesday Theotokia, Midnight Praises The Coptic praises of the Theotokos recall Ezekiel's vision of the gate in the east that was sealed, which the Lord alone entered and left. They name the Virgin as that gate, and confess that she remained a virgin after giving birth, as the gate stayed shut after the Lord passed through. Coptic Liturgy PARAPHRASE The Love of the Faithful The Basil homily rests its case on the faithful: those who love Christ will not bear to hear that the Theotokos ever ceased to be a virgin. That is not a weak argument. It is the instinct of the whole Church, which saw in the God-bearer a vessel wholly given to God.

secs.h: The Body That Served the Word
secs.x: Where That Leaves the Question Put plainly: a person can, in logic, call Mary the Mother of God and still say she had other children. But that is not what any Father of the Church said. The Church that fought for the title Theotokos confessed her the Ever-Virgin in the same breath, and its Fathers explained her lasting virginity by appeal to the God she bore. The Theotokos and the Ever-Virgin are not two separate doctrines that happen to sit side by side. In the mind of the Fathers, the second is the fitting fruit of the first.

XI. "Till She Had Brought Forth" The text most often cited against Mary's lasting virginity is Matthew 1:25. If Joseph did not know her "till" she gave birth, surely he did afterwards? Matthew 1:25 "and did not know her till she had brought forth her firstborn Son. And he called His name Jesus." Orthodox reading: Matthew is guarding the virgin conception: Joseph had no part in it. "Till" tells us what was true up to the birth and says nothing about afterwards. Protestant reading: "Till" naturally implies that things changed after the birth. How Scripture Uses "Till" Matthew 28:20 "teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you; and lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.' Amen." Orthodox reading: The Greek is heos , the same word as in Matthew 1:25. Christ does not leave us when the age ends. 1 Corinthians 15:25 "For He must reign till He has put all enemies under His feet." Orthodox reading: Paul uses achri , another Greek word for "until." Christ's reign does not end when His enemies are under His feet.

"Till" marks a point without implying a change after it. 2 Samuel 6:23 "Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no children to the day of her death." Orthodox reading: The Greek Old Testament reads heos , "until" the day of her death. No one supposes Michal had children afterwards. Genesis 8:7 "Then he sent out a raven, which kept going to and fro until the waters had dried up from the earth." Orthodox reading: Chrysostom points out that the Greek says the raven did not return "till" the waters were dried up; and it never returned at all. St. John Chrysostom Homily 5 on Matthew, 5 (c. AD 390) "He has here used the word till, not that you should suspect that afterwards he did know her, but to inform you that before the birth the Virgin was wholly untouched by man. But why then, it may be said, has he used the word, till? Because it is usual in Scripture often to do this, and to use this expression without reference to limited times." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St. John of Damascus Exposition of the Orthodox Faith IV.14 (c.

AD 743) "And the word till signifies the limit of the appointed time but does not exclude the time thereafter. For the Lord says, And lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world, not meaning thereby that He will be separated from us after the completion of the age." Byzantine Writer VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION John Calvin Harmony of the Gospels, on Matthew 1:25 (1555) "Let us rest satisfied with this, that no just and well-grounded inference can be drawn from these words of the Evangelist, as to what took place after the birth of Christ. He is called first-born; but it is for the sole purpose of informing us that he was born of a virgin." Reformer VERBATIM · CALVIN TRANSLATION SOCIETY (1845) Even Calvin, no friend of Marian devotion, refused to draw the Helvidian conclusion from this verse.

XII. "Her Firstborn Son" Luke calls Jesus Mary's "firstborn." Does that imply a second-born? Luke 2:7 "And she brought forth her firstborn Son, and wrapped Him in swaddling cloths, and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn." Orthodox reading: "Firstborn" is the legal status of the child who opens the womb. Luke uses it because Jesus must be presented in the Temple as the firstborn (Luke 2:22-23), not to count Mary's children. Protestant reading: "Firstborn" suggests later children. Exodus 13:2 "'Consecrate to Me all the firstborn, whatever opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of man and beast; it is Mine.'" Orthodox reading: The firstborn had to be consecrated as soon as he opened the womb. Parents could not wait to see whether other children followed. An only child was a firstborn child. St. Jerome Against Helvidius 12 (c. AD 383) "Our position is this: Every only begotten son is a first-born son, but not every first-born is an only begotten.

By first-born we understand not only one who is succeeded by others, but one who has had no predecessor." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION An ancient Jewish grave inscription makes the same point. Found at Tell el-Yehudiyeh in Egypt and dated to about 5 BC, it remembers a woman named Arsinoe who died giving birth to her "firstborn" child. She had no second child. "Firstborn" was simply the name for the first child to open the womb.

XIII. Who Were the Brothers? Mark 6:3 "Is this not the carpenter, the Son of Mary, and brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? And are not His sisters here with us?' So they were offended at Him." Orthodox reading: Jesus alone is called "the Son of Mary." The four men are called His brothers, but never her sons. Protestant reading: The plain reading is that these are Mary's other children. Three explanations have been given in the history of the Church. Joseph's Sons by an Earlier Marriage Joseph was a widower with children when he was entrusted with Mary. The brothers are Jesus' brothers through Joseph, not Mary's sons. Found in the Protoevangelium of James and held by Origen, Eusebius, Hilary and Epiphanius. The view of the Oriental Orthodox Churches. Cousins The brothers were sons of Mary's kinswoman, "Mary the wife of Clopas," and so cousins of Jesus. Argued by Jerome, who held that Joseph too remained a virgin. The usual view in the West. Mary's Later Sons The brothers were children of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus. Argued by Helvidius around 383 and refuted by Jerome.

Rejected by the ancient Church; common among Protestants today. The Protoevangelium of James Chapter 9 (c. AD 150–200) "And the priest said to Joseph, You have been chosen by lot to take into your keeping the virgin of the Lord. But Joseph refused, saying: I have children, and I am an old man, and she is a young girl." Early Christian Writing VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION The Protoevangelium is not Scripture, and the Church does not read it as Scripture. But it shows that within a century or so of the apostles, Christians already explained the brothers of the Lord as Joseph's children and already believed Mary remained a virgin. Origen names it as a source for this view (Section IX). Both ancient views agree on the essential point: the brothers were not Mary's sons. Jerome sharply rejected the earlier-marriage view, and still he and the Fathers who held it stood together against Helvidius.

XIV. "Brother" in Scripture Hebrew and Aramaic have no separate word for cousin. The Hebrew ach , brother, covers half-brothers, nephews and other kinsmen, and the Greek Old Testament translates it with adelphos . The Gospel writers, steeped in that Greek Bible, use the word the same way. Genesis 14:14 "Now when Abram heard that his brother was taken captive, he armed his three hundred and eighteen trained servants who were born in his own house, and went in pursuit as far as Dan." Orthodox reading: Lot was Abram's nephew, the son of his brother Haran (Genesis 11:27), yet Scripture calls him Abram's brother. Genesis 13:8 "So Abram said to Lot, 'Please let there be no strife between you and me, and between my herdsmen and your herdsmen; for we are brethren." Orthodox reading: Uncle and nephew call each other brethren.

1 Chronicles 23:22 "And Eleazar died, and had no sons, but only daughters; and their brethren, the sons of Kish, took them as wives." Orthodox reading: The sons of Kish were cousins of Eleazar's daughters (verse 21), yet they are called "their brethren." Colossians 4:10 "Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, with Mark the cousin of Barnabas (about whom you received instructions: if he comes to you, welcome him)," Orthodox reading: Greek does have a word for cousin, anepsios , and Paul uses it here. Protestant reading: If the evangelists meant cousins, why not use anepsios ? The Protestant question is fair, and the answer is that the evangelists are following the Greek Bible's way of naming kin, and the early Church's way of naming the Lord's family. The word "brother" alone cannot settle the question. What settles it is who the brothers' mother was, which the cross scene answers (Section XVI), and the unbroken witness of the Fathers (Section IX).

XV. James, the Lord's Brother Galatians 1:19 "But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord's brother." Orthodox reading: "The Lord's brother" was James' title in the early Church, to set him apart from James the son of Zebedee. It does not say whose son he was. Protestant reading: Paul means a real brother, a son of Mary. Hegesippus, in Eusebius Church History II.23 (c. AD 170, quoted c. AD 325) "James, the brother of the Lord, succeeded to the government of the Church in conjunction with the apostles. He has been called the Just by all from the time of our Saviour to the present day; for there were many that bore the name of James. He was holy from his mother's womb; and he drank no wine nor strong drink, nor did he eat flesh." Church Historian VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Eusebius of Caesarea Church History II.1 (c.

AD 325) "This James was called the brother of the Lord because he was known as a son of Joseph, and Joseph was supposed to be the father of Christ, because the Virgin, being betrothed to him, was found with child by the Holy Ghost before they came together" Church Historian VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Eusebius, the first great historian of the Church, gives the reason for the title outright: James was known as Joseph's son. That is the view the Coptic Church holds. Jerome, by contrast, identified this James with "James the son of Alphaeus" among the Twelve (Matthew 10:3) and took him to be a cousin. On either view he was not Mary's son. To be fair to the other side, Hegesippus also speaks of Jude as "the Lord's brother according to the flesh" (Eusebius, Church History III.20). Protestants cite this phrase. But "according to the flesh" distinguishes earthly kinship from spiritual brotherhood; it does not say whose son Jude was.

The same Hegesippus says that Symeon, the next bishop of Jerusalem, was the son of Clopas, the Lord's uncle (below), and Eusebius speaks of Jude as one of "the so-called brothers of the Saviour" (III.32). Eusebius of Caesarea, citing Hegesippus Church History III.11 (c. AD 325) "They all with one consent pronounced Symeon, the son of Clopas, of whom the Gospel also makes mention; to be worthy of the episcopal throne of that parish. He was a cousin, as they say, of the Saviour. For Hegesippus records that Clopas was a brother of Joseph." Church Historian VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION John 7:5 "For even His brothers did not believe in Him." Orthodox reading: During the ministry the brothers did not believe. After the resurrection the Lord appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and the brothers are found praying with the apostles (Acts 1:14).

secs.h: Step One: Christ Gives His Mother to John
secs.x: XVI. The Cross: "Behold Your Mother" The scene at the cross is the strongest single piece of evidence in the Gospels that Mary had no other sons. It works in two steps. Step One: Christ Gives His Mother to John John 19:25-27 "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus His mother, and His mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus therefore saw His mother, and the disciple whom He loved standing by, He said to His mother, 'Woman, behold your son!' Then He said to the disciple, 'Behold your mother!' And from that hour that disciple took her to his own home." Orthodox reading: The care of a widowed mother fell to her sons. If James, Joses, Judas and Simon were her own sons, passing them over for a disciple from another family would make little sense and would shame them in public. Christ gives her to John because she had no other son to receive her. Protestant reading: The brothers did not yet believe (John 7:5), so Christ entrusted her to a believer. The Protestant answer does not hold.

secs.h: Step One: Christ Gives His Mother to John
secs.x: Within weeks the brothers are with the apostles in the upper room, praying "with Mary the mother of Jesus" (Acts 1:14), and James soon leads the Church in Jerusalem. If they were her sons, the Lord who knew all things would hardly have passed over them for a few weeks of unbelief. The Fathers saw the point at once. Origen of Alexandria Commentary on John I.6 (c. AD 230) "For if Mary, as those declare who with sound mind extol her, had no other son but Jesus, and yet Jesus says to His mother, Woman, behold your son, and not Behold you have this son also..." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION St. John Chrysostom Homily 5 on Matthew, 5 (c. AD 390) "For if he had known her, and had kept her in the place of a wife, how is it that our Lord commits her, as unprotected, and having no one, to His disciple, and commands him to take her to his own home?" Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Step Two: The Other Mary at the Cross Matthew 27:55-56 "And many women who followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to Him, were there looking on from afar, among whom were Mary Magdalene, Mary

secs.h: Step One: Christ Gives His Mother to John
secs.x: the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee's sons." Orthodox reading: Two of the Lord's brothers are named James and Joses (Mark 6:3). Here a woman at the cross is "the mother of James and Joses," and she is plainly not the Virgin, whom the evangelists would call "His mother." Mark 15:40 "There were also women looking on from afar, among whom were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the Less and of Joses, and Salome," Orthodox reading: Mark calls her the mother of "James the Less and of Joses." The brothers named in Mark 6:3 have a mother at the cross who is not the Virgin Mary. John's list at the cross includes "Mary the wife of Clopas" (John 19:25), and Hegesippus says Clopas was Joseph's brother (Section XV). Many, from Jerome onward, identify her with "the mother of James and Joses." Others count her separately. Either way, the James and Joses who are called the Lord's brothers had a mother who was not the Virgin Mary. The Gospels themselves, read side by side, rule out the claim that they were her sons.

XVII. The History of the Doctrine It is often said that Mary's perpetual virginity is a medieval invention. The record shows the opposite: the belief is attested in the second century, it was held by the Fathers generally (Tertullian is the notable early exception), the few writers who denied it were answered and censured, and even the leading Reformers kept it. Its abandonment is the late development. c. AD 150–200 The Protoevangelium of James presents Joseph as an elderly widower with children, and Mary as a consecrated virgin. c. AD 200 Tertullian in Carthage argues that Mary bore other children after Jesus. He later joins the Montanist sect, and the Church never receives him as a Father. c. AD 230–246 Origen in Alexandria and Caesarea teaches that Mary "had no other son but Jesus," and calls this the view of those who honour her "with sound mind." c. AD 300 Victorinus of Pettau, bishop and martyr, speaks of the Lord's brothers as kinsmen, not sons of Mary (as reported by Jerome). c. AD 340 St.

Athanasius calls Mary "Ever-Virgin" and "Bearer of God" in his Discourses Against the Arians. c. AD 377 St. Epiphanius writes against the "Antidicomarianites" in Arabia, who said Mary lived with Joseph as his wife after the birth of Christ. c. AD 383 Helvidius in Rome argues that Mary had other children. St. Jerome answers him in Against Helvidius. c. AD 390–393 Jovinian, who denied that Mary remained a virgin in giving birth, is condemned by synods at Rome under Pope Siricius and at Milan under St. Ambrose. c. AD 391–392 Bonosus, a bishop in Illyricum, teaches that Mary had other children. His case is referred by the Council of Capua to the bishops of Macedonia, and he is condemned. AD 431 The Council of Ephesus upholds the title Theotokos against Nestorius. AD 553 The Second Council of Constantinople, received by the Chalcedonian churches, names Mary "ever-virgin" in its anathemas.

16th century Luther and Zwingli affirm Mary's lasting virginity, Calvin rejects Helvidius' arguments from the word "brothers" without pressing the doctrine, and the Reformed Second Helvetic Confession (1566) speaks of "the ever virgin Mary" (Chapter XI). 18th–19th centuries Belief in Mary's perpetual virginity fades among Protestants, and by the nineteenth century the Helvidian view is common. Those Who Denied It The early writers known to have taught that Mary had other children are Tertullian, the Antidicomarianites, Helvidius and Bonosus. Each was opposed by the Church of his own day. St. Jerome Against Helvidius 19 (c. AD 383) "Of Tertullian I say no more than that he did not belong to the Church." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Jerome's verdict on Tertullian is blunt. Tertullian was a brilliant early writer, but he left the communion of the Church for the Montanists, and the Church never counted him among her Fathers. His opinion on this question is the opinion of one man, and the Church rejected it.

Nestorius, sometimes named in these debates, is not known to have denied Mary's lasting virginity. His quarrel was over the title Theotokos, not her virginity. The Reformers John Calvin Harmony of the Gospels, on Matthew 13:55 (1555) Calvin notes that in Hebrew idiom "brothers" can mean any relatives, and concludes: "Helvidius displayed excessive ignorance in concluding that Mary must have had many sons, because Christ's brothers are sometimes mentioned." Reformer VERBATIM · CALVIN TRANSLATION SOCIETY (1845) Martin Luther and Ulrich Zwingli Luther, Sermons on John 1–4 (1537–40); Zwingli, Sermon on Mary, the Pure Mother of God (1522) Luther preached that Mary remained a virgin after the birth of Christ and bore no other children. Zwingli taught that she remained a pure virgin before, in and after the birth of the Son of God.

Reformer PARAPHRASE The Reformed Churches Second Helvetic Confession, Chapter XI (1566) "...natum ex Maria semper virgine..." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · LATIN TEXT IN SCHAFF The Second Helvetic Confession, written by Heinrich Bullinger, Zwingli's successor at Zurich, became one of the most widely received Reformed confessions. In its chapter on Christ it confesses Him "born of Mary ever virgin." Calvin is more cautious than Luther and Zwingli. He calls the question one that should not be pressed out of curiosity, and he does not argue for the doctrine at length. But he rejects Helvidius' argument outright. None of the three Reformers taught that Mary had other children.

XVIII. Objections Answered The objections below are stated as a thoughtful Protestant would state them. "The plain meaning of 'brother' is a son of the same mother." OO Response: Plain meaning depends on the language and the people using it. In the Greek Bible the Gospel writers used, Lot is Abram's "brother" though he was his nephew (Genesis 14:14), and cousins are "brethren" (1 Chronicles 23:22). Augustine explains that "it was of the usage of Scripture to call blood relations and all other near kindred by the term brethren" (Section IX). More decisive, the Gospels name the mother of James and Joses, and she is not the Virgin (Section XVI). Scripture never once calls these men sons of Mary; it calls Jesus alone "the Son of Mary" (Mark 6:3). "'Till she had brought forth' means Joseph knew her afterwards." OO Response: In biblical Greek heos marks what was true up to a point and leaves the rest unsaid, as in Matthew 28:20 and 1 Corinthians 15:25.

Chrysostom, a native Greek speaker, says Matthew "used the word till, not that you should suspect that afterwards he did know her." Even Calvin says "no just and well-grounded inference can be drawn" from the verse about what came after (Section XI). "'Firstborn' implies later children." OO Response: The firstborn had to be consecrated when he opened the womb (Exodus 13:2), before anyone could know whether more children would follow. An only son was a firstborn son, as Jerome says, and as the Jewish epitaph of Arsinoe shows (Section XII). "Calling Mary the Mother of God does not mean she had no other children. Many Protestants call her Theotokos and still say she had other sons." OO Response: That is true as a matter of logic, and this page does not claim otherwise (Section X).

But the same Church that gave us the title Theotokos also confessed her Ever-Virgin, and its teachers reasoned from the one to the other: Origen speaks of the body "appointed to minister to the Word," Chrysostom of "a child-bearing so strange," and John of Damascus asks whether she "who had borne God" could "receive the embrace of a man." To separate the two titles is to keep the Fathers' word while setting aside their understanding of it. The Reformers themselves kept both: Luther taught her lasting virginity, and the Reformed Second Helvetic Confession of 1566 speaks of "the ever virgin Mary" (Chapter XI). "The perpetual virginity treats marriage as unclean." OO Response: The Church calls marriage a holy mystery, and Scripture says "Marriage is honorable among all, and the bed undefiled" (Hebrews 13:4). Jerome himself wrote that "virginity itself is the fruit of marriage." Mary's virginity is not a judgement on marriage. It is about her unique calling: the one who bore God was wholly given to Him.

"The brothers appear with Mary again and again (Matthew 12:46; John 2:12; Acts 1:14). They must be her sons." OO Response: Appearing with Mary shows a household, not a birth mother. On the Coptic view Joseph's sons grew up in the same home and would naturally travel with Mary, especially after Joseph's death. Cousins in an extended family would do the same. What Scripture never does is call any of them her son. "Psalm 69:8 prophesies that Christ would be 'an alien to my mother's children.'" OO Response: The verse is Hebrew poetry, and "my mother's children" stands in parallel with "my brothers." The same psalm says the Messiah is given vinegar to drink (Psalm 69:21), and it is applied to Christ because His own people rejected Him (John 1:11), not to count Mary's children. A doctrine about Mary's family cannot be built on one line of poetry against the plain evidence of the cross.

"The perpetual virginity is not taught in Scripture, so it cannot be required." OO Response: Scripture gives real support: Mary's question in Luke 1:34, the shut gate of Ezekiel 44:2, the cross scene of John 19:26-27, and the mother of James and Joses in Mark 15:40. Scripture never says she had other children, as Jerome points out: "That Mary was married after she brought forth, we do not believe, because we do not read it." And the Church that recognised the books of Scripture is the same Church that confessed her Ever-Virgin. See Sola Scriptura .

XIX. Frequently Asked Questions Is there a Father of the Church who taught that James was Mary's son? No. Every Father who speaks of the question denies it, whether he explains the brothers as Joseph's sons or as cousins. The few early writers who taught that Mary had other children, Tertullian, Helvidius and Bonosus, are not Fathers of the Church, and each was answered by the Church of his day. Note that the Fathers do call James "the brother of the Lord." It is Scripture's own title for him (Galatians 1:19). The question is what it means, and the Fathers answer that it does not mean a son of Mary. Does the title Theotokos prove the perpetual virginity on its own? Not by strict definition. Ephesus defined the title to protect the truth about Christ. But the Fathers who fought for the title confessed her the Ever-Virgin, and they argued from her bearing God to her lasting virginity (Section X). Did Nestorius deny that Mary remained a virgin? Not as far as the surviving evidence shows. Nestorius objected to the title Theotokos because of his teaching about Christ.

His case is about the title, not about Mary's other children. What is the Coptic view of the brothers of the Lord? The Coptic Church, with the other Oriental Orthodox Churches, holds that they were Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage. Joseph was an older widower who became the guardian of the Virgin. This is the view of the Protoevangelium, Origen, Eusebius, Hilary and Epiphanius. Why do some Fathers say cousins and others say step-brothers? Because Scripture does not say exactly how they were related. The Fathers proposed different answers to that open question. What they did not treat as open was whether the brothers were Mary's sons. On that point they agree. Did the Reformers believe Mary was ever-virgin? Luther and Zwingli taught it plainly. Calvin was more reserved, but he called Helvidius' argument "excessive ignorance" and said no inference about Mary's later life can be drawn from Matthew 1:25. The view that Mary had other children became common among Protestants only later. Do the Oriental Orthodox call Mary co-redeemer? No.

There is "one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5). The Church honours Mary as the Theotokos and asks for her prayers, but she is not a co-redeemer. Where should I start reading? Jerome's Against Helvidius is short and answers every argument still used today. Then Chrysostom's fifth homily on Matthew, and Augustine's tenth tractate on John. All are freely available online in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers.
