The Heart of the Matter Here is the whole argument in miniature. God created marriage and called it “very good”; the first miracle of Christ blessed a wedding at Cana; and the Church counts marriage among her holy mysteries. So the Church does not despise marriage — she anathematises anyone who does. At the same time, Christ Himself, His Mother, John the Baptist, and the Apostle Paul all lived in celibacy, and Christ spoke openly of those who become “eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake” (Matthew 19:12). Paul taught that the unmarried person can serve the Lord “without distraction” (1 Corinthians 7:35). Celibacy embraced for God is therefore not a rejection of a good thing but the free gift of a good thing back to its Giver — and a living sign that this world is passing and the kingdom is coming. The one-line answer: marriage is holy and celibacy is holy. One fills the earth with the image of God; the other anticipates the age when we shall be “like angels of God in heaven” (Matthew 22:30).
To exalt celibacy is not to insult marriage — any more than praising the marathon insults the walk.

Two Vocations, One Holiness The single most important thing to grasp is that the Church refuses to set marriage and celibacy against each other. Both are gifts; both are callings; both can lead a soul to God. St. Paul says exactly this when he writes that each person has “his own gift from God, one in this manner and another in that” (1 Corinthians 7:7). Marriage and celibacy are different charisms , not a good option and a bad one. This is why the early Church moved so sharply against sects that despised marriage. When a fourth-century group under Eustathius of Sebaste taught that married Christians could not be saved and that true holiness required abandoning one's spouse, the Council of Gangra (c. 340) condemned them outright.

Its canons are still binding in the Orthodox Church: “If any one shall condemn marriage, or abominate and condemn a woman who is a believer and devout, and sleeps with her own husband, as though she could not enter the Kingdom [of heaven] let him be anathema.” Council of Gangra, Canon I The same council was equally careful to protect the honour of celibacy — but for the right reason. Virginity is holy because of the beauty of virginity itself, not because marriage is shameful: “If any one shall remain virgin, or observe continence, abstaining from marriage because he abhors it, and not on account of the beauty and holiness of virginity itself, let him be anathema.” Council of Gangra, Canon IX St. John Chrysostom drew the two together in one memorable sentence. Far from lowering marriage to lift up virginity, he insisted that only a high view of marriage makes virginity shine: “Whoever denigrates marriage also diminishes the glory of virginity. Whoever praises it makes virginity more admirable and resplendent.” St.

John Chrysostom, On Virginity 10.1 (as quoted in the Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1620) So the Orthodox position is not “celibacy good, marriage tolerated.” It is “both are of God.” The rest of this page defends the higher counsel of celibacy precisely because it is so often attacked — but never at the expense of the marriage bed, which the Scripture calls “honorable among all” (Hebrews 13:4).

Marriage as a Holy Mystery For the Orthodox, marriage is not merely a contract or a licence for companionship. It is a sacrament — a holy mystery in which a man and a woman are joined by God into one flesh, and their love is made an icon of the love between Christ and His Church. Its dignity is written into the first pages of Scripture and confirmed by the Lord Himself. Woven Into Creation Marriage is older than sin, older than the Law, older than Israel. God made humanity male and female and gave the first command of union in the garden: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.” Genesis 2:24 (NKJV) When the Pharisees tried to trap Jesus on divorce, He reached back past Moses to this creation ordinance and sealed it with His own authority: “Have you not read that He who made them at the beginning ‘made them male and female,’ and said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’? So then, they are no longer two but one flesh.

Therefore what God has joined together, let not man separate.” Matthew 19:4–6 (NKJV) An Icon of Christ and the Church St. Paul lifts marriage to its highest meaning. The union of husband and wife is a living image of the union of Christ with His body, the Church — which is why he can call it a “great mystery.” Husbands are commanded not to dominate but to love sacrificially, to the point of death, as Christ loved the Church (Ephesians 5:25–32). The Lord Himself honoured a wedding by working His first sign there, turning water into wine at Cana of Galilee (John 2:1–11). Why this matters for the argument: a Church that guards marriage this jealously cannot possibly be accused of hating it. When such a Church still says celibacy is a higher counsel for those who can receive it, that is not contempt for marriage — it is the considered judgment of the very community that treasures marriage most.

The Call to Celibacy If marriage is so good, why would anyone give it up? The answer is not that celibacy flees something evil, but that it reaches for something greater still: undivided union with God, begun now and completed in the resurrection. The New Testament speaks of this calling plainly and honours it highly. The Lord's Own Words Immediately after teaching on marriage, Jesus turned to celibacy embraced for God's sake — and made clear it is a gift given to some, not a burden laid on all: “For there are eunuchs who were born thus from their mother's womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake. He who is able to accept it, let him accept it.” Matthew 19:11–12 (NKJV) “Eunuchs for the kingdom” does not mean literal mutilation — the Church condemned that — but the free renunciation of marriage in order to belong wholly to God.

And notice the pattern of the Gospel itself: Christ lived celibate; His Mother, the ever-Virgin Mary, is the Church's highest human icon; John the Baptist and, by ancient tradition, the beloved disciple John lived unmarried. Celibacy is not a fringe eccentricity but stands at the very centre of the Gospel story. Paul's Counsel: Freedom to Serve the Lord St. Paul, himself unmarried, gives the fullest teaching. He is careful never to command celibacy — “I have no commandment from the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:25) — but he recommends it as a gift that frees a person from the anxieties of family life to serve God with a single heart: “He who is unmarried cares for the things of the Lord — how he may please the Lord. But he who is married cares about the things of the world — how he may please his wife.

… And this I say for your own profit, not that I may put a leash on you, but for what is proper, and that you may serve the Lord without distraction.” 1 Corinthians 7:32–35 (NKJV) This is the whole logic of celibacy in one sentence: not that marriage is impure, but that the single person is free from its cares and can give to God the time, energy and love that a spouse and children rightly claim. Paul's conclusion is that the one who marries “does well,” and the one who chooses celibacy for the Lord “does better” (1 Corinthians 7:38) — two goods, ranked, not a good and an evil. The First Monks: A Calling the Church Welcomed from the Start Consecrated celibacy did not stay a teaching confined to Paul's letters. Within a few generations it became a lived, organised movement — and the Church's own highest authorities embraced it immediately, rather than viewing it with suspicion. c. AD 250 St. Paul of Thebes, honoured by the Church as the first Christian hermit, withdraws into the Egyptian desert during the Decian persecution and remains there in prayer for the rest of his long life.

c. AD 270 St. Antony the Great, hearing Christ's call to “sell what you have and give to the poor” (Matthew 19:21), gives away his inheritance and takes up the ascetic life in earnest — earning him the title “Father of Monks.” c. AD 320 St. Pachomius founds the first fully communal monastery at Tabennisi in Egypt, organising hermits into a common rule and giving monasticism a structure that would soon spread across the Christian world. c. AD 360 St. Athanasius — Patriarch of Alexandria and the chief defender of the Nicene faith — writes the Life of Antony , personally commending monastic celibacy to the whole Church and setting the entire monastic movement in motion across the Christian world. This timeline is worth pausing on. Within roughly a single century of the apostles, celibate monasticism was not tolerated grudgingly at the margins of the Church — it was championed in writing by the very bishop who had fought hardest for the Nicene faith at Nicaea itself.

A calling embraced this quickly, this publicly, and at this level of the Church's leadership is not a later corruption of a simpler apostolic Christianity; it is the Church recognising, almost from the beginning, a gift her Lord had already given her (see The Coptic Monastic Witness below for the fuller story).

Solitude, Not Isolation No part of the celibate calling is more misunderstood than the monk's withdrawal into solitude. To modern ears, a man leaving the world for a cell in the desert sounds like isolation — a retreat from love itself. The Church has never seen it that way. What looks like absence is, in her understanding, the deepest possible presence: to God first, and through Him, to everyone. Christ Himself Withdrew The pattern begins with the Lord. Far from being a later monastic invention, deliberate withdrawal into solitude for prayer is something Jesus did repeatedly, at the height of His ministry: “Now in the morning, having risen a long while before daylight, He went out and departed to a solitary place; and there He prayed.” Mark 1:35 (NKJV) “So He Himself often withdrew into the wilderness and prayed.” Luke 5:16 (NKJV) Before His public ministry even began, the Spirit drove Him into the wilderness for forty days (Matthew 4:1–2).

This was not an isolated event but a pattern woven through the whole of Scripture: Moses met God on Sinai alone; Elijah, fleeing to Horeb, found the Lord not in the wind or the fire but in “a still small voice” heard only in solitude (1 Kings 19:11–13); John the Baptist was formed in the wilderness before he preached a word (Luke 1:80; Matthew 3:1–3). The desert, in Scripture, is not where God is absent — it is repeatedly where He is found. Separated From All, United to All The great danger the objection rightly senses is real: solitude can curdle into isolation, a wound rather than a gift. Genesis itself says “it is not good that man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18). But the Church has always distinguished the two. Adam's aloneness in Eden was a lack waiting to be filled — there was no one of his kind, no communion at all. The monk's solitude is the opposite: freely chosen, not imposed; sought for communion with God, not as an escape from all relationship; and lived within, not outside, the Body of Christ.

A hermit is still remembered by name in the Liturgy, still receives the Eucharist, still answers to a spiritual father or abbot, and still exists to intercede for the very world he has physically left. The Egyptian desert father Evagrius Ponticus put the paradox in one line that the whole tradition has treasured: a monk is one who is “separated from all, and united to all.” This is also why the Coptic tradition has never treated the solitary life as a starting point. St. Antony himself, before going deeper into the desert, first placed himself under the discipline of an older ascetic near his village, learning obedience and self-mastery in relationship before God called him further in. The pattern set by St. Pachomius makes this explicit: the common life, in community, under a rule and an abbot, normally comes first; the hermit's cell is reserved for those who have already been tested and matured in fellowship.

Solitude in the Orthodox tradition is a fruit of formation, not a substitute for it — the Church has always been wary of monks who sought the desert to flee people rather than to find God. The Desert Made a City St. Athanasius, introducing his Life of Antony , described the result of this movement in a phrase the Coptic Church still repeats with pride: “…the desert was colonised by monks, who came forth from their own people, and enrolled themselves for the citizenship in the heavens.” St. Athanasius, Life of Antony , Prologue (NPNF 2nd Series, vol. 4) Antony did not vanish from the world by going into the wilderness; he became one of the most sought-after men in it. Bishops, emperors, philosophers, and the sick and troubled of every rank travelled to find him, because a life poured wholly into prayer produced a depth of wisdom and love that ordinary busyness rarely does.

This is the constant testimony of the desert fathers: solitude with God does not shrink a person's capacity to love their neighbour — it deepens it, the way a reservoir must first be filled before it can overflow to water anything else.

Common Objections Consecrated celibacy and monastic life face several common objections. Each has a clear answer from Scripture itself. Tap any question to expand it. Objection 1 “There is no marriage in the age to come — so celibacy devalues it” Critics sometimes cite the Lord's words about the resurrection as if they cheapened marriage. In fact they do the opposite — they reveal why celibacy is prophetic: “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels of God in heaven.” Matthew 22:30 (NKJV) Marriage is a great good, but it belongs to this age; it serves the bringing of new life into a world under death. In the resurrection there is no more death, and so no more marrying. The celibate does not despise marriage; he lives now, ahead of time, the life everyone will live then. Far from insulting marriage, celibacy honours it as a holy thing whose earthly work will one day be complete — and points every married Christian toward the greater wedding, the marriage of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9), in which all the saved are the Bride.

Objection 2 “Monks withdraw to pray instead of evangelising” The charge is that a monk who leaves the world to seek God is selfish and neglects the Great Commission. But this misreads both prayer and mission. First, the “great and first commandment” is to love God with all one's heart (Matthew 22:37–38); a life given wholly to that love is not a lesser Christianity but the fountain of all the rest. Mary, who “sat at Jesus' feet,” was told she had chosen “that good part, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). Second, the claim is historically false. The monasteries were the great engines of evangelism. It was monks who converted the nations — Egypt's deserts sent missionaries across the Christian world; monastics carried the Gospel to Armenia, Ethiopia, Ireland, and the Slavic lands; the desert produced the theologians who defended the faith at the councils.

A monk interceding for the world, copying Scripture, feeding the poor at the monastery gate, and forming the bishops who would teach the Church is not opting out of the mission — he is holding up its arms, as Aaron and Hur held up the arms of Moses (Exodus 17:12). The Church needs both Martha and Mary; it has never been forced to choose. Objection 3 “God said ‘be fruitful and multiply’ — so celibacy disobeys a command” Genesis 1:28 is a blessing given to humanity as a whole at the dawn of creation, and it has been abundantly fulfilled — the earth is filled. It was never a command binding on every single individual; if it were, then Jesus, Paul, Jeremiah and John the Baptist all sinned by remaining unmarried, which is absurd. Scripture plainly commends those who forgo children for God's sake, and Isaiah foretold a day when the barren and the “eunuch” who keeps God's covenant would be given “a name better than that of sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:4–5).

Under the New Covenant, fruitfulness is no longer measured only in physical children but in spiritual ones — and a celibate father or mother in the faith may beget thousands. Objection 4 “Requiring celibacy is a ‘doctrine of demons’ (1 Timothy 4:1–3)” This is the sharpest charge, so it deserves the most careful answer. Paul does warn against those who forbid marriage: “… some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons … forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving.” 1 Timothy 4:1–3 (NKJV) But read what Paul actually condemns: teachers who forbid marriage and forbid foods because they believe these things are evil in themselves — the very Gnostic and Manichaean error that matter and the body are corrupt. That is exactly the teaching the Council of Gangra later anathematised. The Orthodox Church holds the opposite: marriage is holy and food is God's good gift. It does not forbid anyone to marry.

Monks and nuns are not forbidden marriage; they freely vow celibacy, the same free choice Paul recommends three chapters' worth in 1 Corinthians 7. A voluntary vow to God is the opposite of a demonic prohibition. Note too that the same Paul who wrote 1 Timothy 4 also wrote 1 Corinthians 7 praising celibacy — he cannot be contradicting himself. The heresy is calling marriage evil; the virtue is offering one's singleness to God. (The requirement that monastics and, in the Coptic tradition, bishops be celibate is a matter of church discipline, not a claim that marriage is unclean. Coptic Orthodox priests, by contrast, are usually married men. The Church requires celibacy of some servants for the sake of undivided devotion, exactly as Paul described — not because the marriage bed defiles.) Objection 5 “Celibacy is unnatural and represses a God-given drive” The modern form of the objection is that lifelong continence is impossible or unhealthy.

But the Church never claims celibacy is for everyone — Christ said plainly, “He who is able to accept it, let him accept it.” It is a gift and a calling, not a universal rule. For those to whom it is given, grace makes it not a grim repression but a genuine freedom — the witness of countless joyful monks and nuns across twenty centuries is evidence enough. And the deepest answer is theological: the human person is made ultimately not for another creature but for God. Celibacy testifies that the heart's final rest is in Him — “You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in You,” as Augustine prayed. What looks like a lack is in fact a fullness aimed higher. Objection 6 “God said ‘it is not good that man should be alone’ — so monastic isolation is unhealthy” This objection deserves a careful answer, because it points at something true: human beings are made for communion, and isolation as a wound is real. But Genesis 2:18 is describing Adam's condition before the gift of Eve — a total absence of any communion with another human person.

That is not what monastic solitude is. It is not imposed but freely chosen, undertaken for deeper communion with God rather than as flight from all relationship, and it is never lived outside the Church: a monk or hermit is still named in the Liturgy, still receives the sacraments, still lives under a spiritual father and, in the Coptic tradition, is normally formed for years in the common life before any solitary calling is tested (see Solitude, Not Isolation above). The Church has always been suspicious of a monk who fled to the desert merely to avoid people; genuine solitude bears fruit in a greater, not a smaller, capacity to love — which is exactly why the desert fathers became the most sought-after counsellors of their age, not the most forgotten men in it.

The Coptic Monastic Witness No tradition can speak about consecrated celibacy with more authority than the Coptic Orthodox Church, because Christian monasticism was born in Egypt . What began as a handful of hermits in the desert became a movement that reshaped the whole Christian world — and it is alive and flourishing among the Copts today. St. Antony the Great — Father of Monks Around the year 270, a young Egyptian named Antony (c. 251–356) heard the Gospel words “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor … and come, follow Me” (Matthew 19:21) read in church, and took them as spoken to him. He gave away his inheritance, placed his sister with a community of consecrated virgins, and withdrew into the Egyptian desert to seek God in prayer and ascetic struggle. His disciple St. Athanasius of Alexandria wrote his Life of Antony , and that little book set the whole monastic movement in motion across the Christian world. Antony is rightly called the Father of Monks. St. Pachomius — The Common Life A generation later, St. Pachomius (c.

292–348), also an Egyptian, gathered hermits into organised communities under a common rule — the birth of cenobitic (communal) monasticism. From these Egyptian roots, monastic life spread to Palestine, Syria, Asia Minor, and eventually the Latin West, where St. Benedict's rule would carry the same fire into Europe. Still Living Today This is not merely ancient history for the Copts. The great desert monasteries — St. Antony's, St. Paul's, the monasteries of the Wadi Natrun — are full of monks again after a twentieth-century revival. Coptic bishops are drawn from the monasteries, and the late Pope Shenouda III (1923–2012), one of the most beloved patriarchs in Coptic history, was himself a monk and even a desert hermit before his election. The living Coptic Church is the standing refutation of the claim that celibacy is a cold or lifeless thing: it is the seedbed of her holiness and her leadership. See also: Monasticism & the Desert Fathers for the fuller story of St. Antony, St. Pachomius, and the desert, and Fasting & the Coptic Year for the ascetic life the whole Church shares.

Voices of the Fathers The Fathers who most exalted virginity were the same men who most vigorously defended marriage. Their witness is unanimous: both are of God, and celibacy is a higher counsel for those given the gift. St. John Chrysostom c. 347–407 AD In his treatise On Virginity , Chrysostom insists that virginity can only be praised rightly by one who also honours marriage: “Whoever denigrates marriage also diminishes the glory of virginity.” He wrote whole homilies calling husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the Church — the great defender of virginity was also the great preacher of Christian marriage. St. John Chrysostom, On Virginity — direct quotation St. Gregory of Nyssa c. 335–395 AD In his own work On Virginity , Gregory praises the virgin life as the soul's freedom to contemplate God — yet is careful to add, in his own words, that “we are well aware that it is not a stranger to God's blessing” when he speaks of marriage. Virginity is exalted not by degrading marriage but by directing the whole person toward the source of all beauty. St.

Gregory of Nyssa, On Virginity — direct quotation embedded, surrounding summary paraphrased St. Athanasius of Alexandria c. 296–373 AD The great Coptic patriarch wrote the Life of Antony , the book that spread monasticism through the world, and elsewhere taught that the Church holds two honourable ways of life: marriage, which is lawful and blessed, and the way of virginity and continence for those who consecrate themselves wholly to Christ. St. Athanasius, Life of Antony and letters — summary paraphrase Council of Gangra c. 340 AD This local council, whose canons the Orthodox Church still receives, anathematised those who taught that married people cannot be saved — and equally those who took up virginity out of contempt for marriage rather than love for God. It is the Church's permanent guardrail: honour both, despise neither. Council of Gangra, Canons I, IX, X — direct quotation (Canons I & IX quoted above)

Frequently Asked Questions Does the Coptic Church require its priests to be celibate? No. Coptic Orthodox parish priests are normally married men, married before ordination. Celibacy is required of monks, nuns, and bishops (who are chosen from among the monks). So the Coptic Church visibly honours both callings at the very altar — married priests serving the liturgy, celibate monks and bishops shepherding the Church. Is celibacy “higher” than marriage? Doesn't that insult married people? The Church, following St. Paul, calls celibacy-for-the-Lord a higher counsel — but “higher” here means freer for undivided service, not holier in the sense of more loved by God. A married saint is greater than a lukewarm monk. Holiness is measured by love, and love is possible in either state. Marriage and celibacy are two roads up the same mountain. If everyone became celibate, wouldn't humanity die out? This objection assumes celibacy is being urged on everyone, which the Church never does — it is a gift for those “able to accept it.” Only a small minority are ever called to it.

The worry is like objecting that if everyone became a doctor there would be no farmers; callings are distributed, not universal. Weren't monasteries just a way to escape responsibility? The opposite is true. Monastic life is famously demanding — long hours of prayer, fasting, manual labour, obedience, and the inner warfare the desert fathers called the hardest work of all. And monasteries carried enormous responsibility for the wider world: schooling, copying the Scriptures, feeding the poor, healing the sick, and producing the Church's bishops and theologians. Does the Bible actually command celibacy for anyone? It commands it for no one and commends it for many. Christ says “he who is able to accept it, let him accept it”; Paul says the celibate “does better” but the married “does well.” Celibacy in the Church is always a free offering, never a forced law — which is exactly why 1 Timothy 4's condemnation of those who “forbid marriage” does not touch it.
Related reading: Monasticism & the Desert Fathers • Male & Female: Sex, Gender & the Body • Mary, the Ever-Virgin • Modern Ethical Topics .

pages.t: Our Method — How We Verify Every Quote

secs.x: Why This Page Exists Truth needs no exaggeration. A single fabricated quotation, once exposed, casts doubt on everything else a writer has said — and the Fathers have suffered more than their share of forgery, loose paraphrase, and words lifted out of context. We would rather present a smaller number of quotations that are genuinely defensible than a large number that impress at first glance and crumble under scrutiny. So we commit publicly to a standard. Every quotation on this site is checked against a printed critical edition or a recognised scholarly translation before it is published. Where a saying is famous but its source is doubtful, we say so plainly or leave it out. This page is our promise, and our invitation: verify us.

Direct Quote vs. Paraphrase Every patristic quotation on this site carries one of two small tags, so you always know exactly what you are reading: Example Father (d. 407) “The word-for-word rendering of a passage as it stands in a recognised translation.” Homily 1 Direct quote A Direct quote means the words are reproduced verbatim from a published translation, changed in nothing but the removal of an ellipsis or a bracketed word for clarity. You can open the cited edition and find those exact words. Example Father (d. 407) “A faithful restatement of the Father’s argument in condensed, modern English.” Homily 1 Paraphrase A Paraphrase means we have summarised or modernised the Father’s wording — because the original is long, archaic, or technical — while remaining faithful to his meaning. We never present a paraphrase as though it were his exact words, and the underlying passage is always real and cited. If you ever see a Father quoted here without one of these two tags, treat it as an oversight and tell us.

The Editions We Cite We do not quote the Fathers from memory, from social media, or from anthologies of uncertain provenance. Patristic quotations are checked against standard printed collections, chiefly: The Ante-Nicene Fathers (ANF) — the standard English collection of the writers before the First Council of Nicaea (325). The Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers (NPNF, First and Second Series) — the standard English collection for the great fourth- and fifth-century Fathers. The Fathers of the Church series and other recognised scholarly translations (e.g. Popular Patristics, ACW, ACT) for texts outside or improving upon the older collections. Critical editions and primary-language sources (PG/PL, CSCO for the Syriac and Coptic material) where a translation is disputed or a rendering needs to be confirmed.

As an Oriental Orthodox site, we give particular weight to the Eastern and Oriental Fathers — the Alexandrians, the Cappadocians, the Syriac and Coptic writers — and, where their works survive in Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, or Ge’ez rather than Greek, we rely on the scholarly editions that preserve them.

How We Verify a Quote Before a patristic quotation is allowed onto a page, it passes through the same steps: Locate the source. We identify the actual work, book, homily, or letter — not just “St So-and-so said.” A quotation with no traceable source is not used. Check it against a reputable edition. The wording is compared to ANF/NPNF, a recognised scholarly translation, or the primary text. Anything that does not match is corrected or dropped. Read the surrounding context. We confirm the Father is actually saying what the quotation implies, and is not being reversed by the sentences around it. Label it honestly. Verbatim wording is tagged Direct quote ; a faithful summary is tagged Paraphrase . Cite the reference. The specific work and, where possible, the section is named so you can look it up yourself. Re-audit after publishing. Pages are reviewed again after they go live, because errors are easiest to catch in the finished form. If a quotation cannot survive every one of these steps, it is removed — however rhetorically useful it might have been.

What We Refuse To Do What we do Trace every quotation to a real, named work Check wording against a printed critical edition or scholarly translation Distinguish verbatim quotes from paraphrases with a visible tag Read context so a Father is never made to say the opposite of his meaning Drop any quotation we cannot verify, however persuasive What we refuse to do Circulate “famous” quotations with no traceable source Pass off a paraphrase as the Father’s exact words Clip a sentence to reverse its plain meaning Invent, embellish, or “improve” a quotation for effect Use AI-generated imagery in place of authentic Christian art The last point matters to us: the icons and imagery on this site are drawn from the authentic tradition of the Church, never machine-generated. What we say about our words, we hold for our images too.

How We Cite Scripture Biblical quotations are given from standard English translations, with the translation named in the citation — for example: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Galatians 3:28 (ESV) Where a verse turns on a disputed word, we note the underlying Hebrew or Greek and, where it helps, compare renderings. Chapter-and-verse references are given in full so every citation can be checked in seconds. As an Orthodox site we recognise the wider canon received by the Church, and we name the book and version whenever we quote from the Deuterocanon.

Found an Error? We are not infallible, and we would genuinely rather be corrected than be wrong. If you find a quotation on this site that is misattributed, mistranslated, taken out of context, or that you cannot trace to its source, we want to know. A well-founded correction will be checked against the sources and, if it stands, the page will be fixed. Holding us to this standard is not hostility — it is exactly what this page invites. The faith has nothing to fear from careful checking; only careless apologetics does.

secs.h: What Miaphysitism Is — and Is Not
secs.x: What Miaphysitism Is — and Is Not Monophysitism (Eutyches) — condemned The humanity is absorbed into the divinity — ‘like a drop of honey in the sea’ Christ’s human nature ceases to be fully human after the union One simple nature (Greek monos = single, sole) Condemned by the Oriental Orthodox as firmly as by Chalcedon Miaphysitism (St. Cyril) — Oriental Orthodox Divinity and humanity are united , each remaining whole and complete Christ is fully God and fully man — the manhood is never diminished One composite nature (Greek mia = a united one, not monos ) Without confusion, without change — and without division or separation The whole misunderstanding rests on two Greek words. Monos means single, sole, alone . Mia is the ordinary feminine word for one — the same ‘one’ used of a married couple who become “one flesh,” two whole realities in one union. The Oriental Orthodox have always confessed mia physis , never mono physis .

secs.h: What Miaphysitism Is — and Is Not
secs.x: Eutyches, who taught that Christ’s humanity was swallowed up by his divinity, was rejected by them — his own condemned formula shows exactly what Miaphysites do not believe: Eutyches (condemned, d. c. 456) “I confess that our Lord was of two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one nature.” Eutyches at the Synod of Constantinople, 448 (under Patriarch Flavian; recorded in the Acts of Chalcedon, Session I) — his own words, for which he was condemned Direct quote

St. Cyril’s Formula The theological heart of Oriental Orthodoxy is the Christology of St. Cyril of Alexandria (d. 444), the great champion against Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus (431). Cyril’s celebrated phrase became the touchstone of the tradition: St. Cyril’s Formula Greek: mia physis tou Theou Logou sesarkomenē (μία φύσις τού Θεού Λόγου σεσαρκωμένη) “One incarnate nature of God the Word.” The key word is sesarkomenē — “ enfleshed .” The one nature is not divinity alone; it is the divine Word who has taken full humanity into his own single subsistence. The flesh is not deleted; it is what the “one nature” is incarnate in . Cyril believed the phrase came from St. Athanasius (in fact it descended from an Apollinarian source), but he used it in a strictly orthodox sense, insisting always on the completeness of Christ’s humanity — a rational soul and a real body. He was equally willing to speak of Christ “in two natures” in his reconciliation with the Antiochenes (the Formula of Reunion, 433).

For Cyril the concern was never to erase the humanity but to affirm that there is one Christ, one Son, one acting subject — not two persons loosely joined, as Nestorius seemed to teach. St. Cyril of Alexandria (d. 444) There is one Lord Jesus Christ — the Word of God united to flesh, not by a mingling or blending of natures, but so that the same one is at once truly God and truly man, the natures that were brought together in a true union being without division. Third Letter to Nestorius — the union without division or confusion Paraphrase

Chalcedon 451 — The Tragedy of Words In 451 the Council of Chalcedon defined that Christ is made known in two natures (Greek en dyo physesin ), united in one person and hypostasis. To guard against Nestorius it added four adverbs — the union is: The Chalcedonian Definition “…made known in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation ” ( asynchytōs, atreptōs, adiairetōs, achōristōs ). The Oriental Orthodox affirm every one of those four adverbs. Their objection was to the phrase in two natures . To Cyrilline ears, after the union one should speak of the one incarnate nature; to number “two natures” following the union sounded like the Nestorian division they had just condemned at Ephesus. It did not help that Chalcedon leaned on the Latin theology of Pope Leo’s Tome , which spoke of each nature “doing what belongs to it” — language that, read in isolation, seemed to make Christ two operating subjects: Pope St.

Leo the Great (Tome to Flavian, 449) “For each form does what is proper to it with the co-operation of the other; that is the Word performing what appertains to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what appertains to the flesh.” (NPNF) Leo’s Tome to Flavian — the phrase Cyrilline theologians found dangerously divisive Direct quote Chalcedon deposed St. Dioscorus of Alexandria , Cyril’s successor — the Oriental Orthodox hold, not for heresy, but for refusing to sign the new formula and for his handling of the earlier council. What followed was not, at root, two different faiths, but two vocabularies for one mystery — hardened by imperial politics, language barriers, and mutual anathema into a schism that has lasted to this day.

St. Severus of Antioch If Cyril is the fountainhead, St. Severus of Antioch (d. 538) is the great systematizer of miaphysite theology after Chalcedon. Against both Nestorius and Eutyches he insisted with precision: in Christ there is one nature out of two — a real composition in which the divinity and the humanity each remain complete, with all their natural properties intact, yet belong to a single incarnate subject. Severus taught that the difference between the natures is preserved in contemplation (the mind can distinguish godhead and manhood) even though they are never separated in reality. This is why the miaphysite tradition can affirm everything Chalcedon wanted to protect — that Christ is consubstantial with the Father in his divinity and consubstantial with us in his humanity, that he hungered and wept as man and raised the dead as God — while still confessing the one incarnate nature. The properties of both natures are fully present; they are simply not parceled out to two subjects.

secs.h: Physis, Hypostasis, Ousia — The Semantic Knot
secs.x: Physis, Hypostasis, Ousia — The Semantic Knot Much of the division comes down to the fact that the same Greek words carried different weights in Alexandria and Constantinople. Untangling them shows how much of the quarrel was linguistic: Ousia (οὐσία) Essence or being — what a thing is in common with others of its kind. Both sides agree Christ is one ousia with the Father (divinity) and one with us (humanity). Hypostasis (ὑπόστασις) The concrete individual subject — the “who.” Both families confess one hypostasis in Christ: one Son, one person. There is no disagreement here. Physis (φύσις) Nature. Here is the knot. For Cyril and Severus, physis often meant a concrete existing reality — close to hypostasis . For Chalcedon it meant the abstract “whatness.” So “one physis” (OO) and “two physes” (Chalcedon) could describe the same Christ.

secs.h: Physis, Hypostasis, Ousia — The Semantic Knot
secs.x: When an Oriental Orthodox says “one nature,” he means one concrete Christ, one acting subject — exactly what Chalcedon meant by “one hypostasis.” When a Chalcedonian says “two natures,” he means the abiding fullness of godhead and manhood — exactly what the Oriental Orthodox mean by confessing Christ “out of two” and consubstantial with both the Father and us. The modern dialogues concluded that the two families have been confessing one faith in two idioms.

Are We Really Divided? In the twentieth century, unofficial and then official theological dialogues between the Eastern Orthodox and the Oriental Orthodox worked patiently through the old vocabulary. Their conclusions were striking. The First Agreed Statement (Anba Bishoy Monastery, Egypt, 1989) declared that both families have always been faithful to the same apostolic Christology of St. Cyril, in different terminology. The Second Agreed Statement (Chambésy, Geneva, 1990) put it plainly: the two families agree in substance on the doctrine of the person of Christ, each confessing the one Lord Jesus Christ, perfect in his divinity and perfect in his humanity; the Orthodox commission recommended lifting the mutual anathemas and condemnations of the past. The Fruit of Dialogue Both commissions concluded that the Oriental Orthodox are not Monophysites (Eutychians) and never were, and that the historic condemnation was based on a misreading of terminology rather than a genuine difference in faith.

Full sacramental reunion still awaits reception, but the Christological barrier has, in the judgment of the theologians, fallen. This is the great hope of the age: that a fifteen-hundred-year wound, born as much of Greek and Coptic and Syriac speaking past one another as of any real heresy, may yet be healed — because the one incarnate Word was never actually confessed in two contradictory ways, but adored by one Church in many tongues. See also The Chalcedonian Schism → and Eastern & Oriental Orthodox Differences → .

The Scriptural Ground The one incarnate Word is not a philosophical construction but the plain confession of the New Testament: one Christ, in whom the fullness of God dwells bodily. “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.” John 1:14 — not the Word alongside flesh, but the Word become flesh: one subject “For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily.” Colossians 2:9 — the total godhead and a real body, in one Christ “Who, though he was in the form of God… emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men.” Philippians 2:6-7 — one ‘he’ who is both in the form of God and in the form of a servant

FAQ Are the Oriental Orthodox ‘Monophysites’? No — this is the central misunderstanding. Monophysitism is the teaching of Eutyches, that Christ’s humanity was absorbed into his divinity so that only one (divine) nature remained. The Oriental Orthodox condemned Eutyches. Their position is Miaphysite : one united nature (Greek mia ) in which both the full divinity and the full humanity are preserved without confusion. The modern EO–OO dialogues formally concluded they are not and never were Monophysites. Do Miaphysites deny that Christ is fully human? Not at all. St. Cyril and St. Severus insisted that Christ has a rational human soul and a real human body, consubstantial with us in everything except sin. He genuinely hungered, thirsted, wept, suffered, and died as man. The ‘one nature’ is the divine Word enfleshed — the humanity is exactly what he became incarnate in, never something deleted. Was the split more about words than substance? Largely, yes — that is the conclusion of both Orthodox families’ official commissions.

The Greek word physis meant different things in Alexandria and Constantinople. When the Oriental Orthodox said ‘one nature’ they meant one concrete Christ (what Chalcedon called ‘one hypostasis’); when Chalcedon said ‘two natures’ it meant the abiding fullness of godhead and manhood, which the Oriental Orthodox also confess. Imperial politics and mutual anathemas then hardened a terminological difference into schism. Do Eastern and Oriental Orthodox now agree on Christology? The joint theological commissions (Agreed Statements of 1989 and 1990) concluded that the two families confess one and the same faith in the person of Christ, and recommended lifting the historic mutual condemnations. Full sacramental communion has not yet been formally restored, and reception varies among the churches, but the Christological barrier itself is widely regarded by the theologians of both families as resolved.

Why does the difference still matter if the faith is the same? Because for fifteen centuries the Oriental Orthodox were slandered as heretics for a heresy they rejected, and cut off from communion over it. Recovering the true meaning of Miaphysite Christology vindicates the faith of Cyril, Dioscorus, Severus, and the martyrs, and opens the door — not yet walked all the way through — to the reunion of the ancient churches.

Glossary Miaphysite The Oriental Orthodox Christology: one united nature of the incarnate Word (Greek mia physis ), in which full divinity and full humanity are preserved without confusion or separation. Monophysite The heresy of Eutyches: one sole nature (Greek monos ), the humanity being absorbed into the divinity. Condemned by the Oriental Orthodox themselves. Dyophysite The Chalcedonian and Eastern Orthodox / Catholic formula: Christ known in two natures after the union, in one person and hypostasis. Hypostatic union The union of divinity and humanity in the one person (hypostasis) of the Word. Affirmed by all sides — there is one Son, one subject, one Christ. Theotokos ‘God-bearer,’ the title of the Virgin Mary defended by St. Cyril at Ephesus (431) — because the one born of her is the incarnate God the Word, not a mere man. Communicatio idiomatum The ‘communication of properties’: because there is one subject, what is said of the humanity and of the divinity is said of the one Christ — God was crucified in the flesh; the child in the manger upholds the universe.

I. Introduction Beneath most modern unbelief lies a single quiet premise: miracles do not happen. Grant that, and every argument on this site can be waved away in advance — the Resurrection must have a natural explanation, whatever the evidence, because resurrections are impossible. The premise rarely gets argued; it functions as the air educated people breathe. When it is argued, the argument is almost always David Hume's, from his 1748 essay "Of Miracles" — perhaps the most influential short essay ever written against the miraculous. This page takes Hume seriously: states his case at full strength, then shows where it fails — partly through criticisms philosophers, including non-Christians, have pressed for two centuries. The stakes are concrete: if miracles cannot be ruled out in advance, then the evidence for the central Christian claim must actually be weighed, on the page where it is laid out ( The Resurrection — Answering the Skeptics ).

II. Hume's Argument, Stated Fairly David Hume — Scottish philosopher Direct Quote An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X (1748) "A miracle is a violation of the laws of nature; and as a firm and unalterable experience has established these laws, the proof against a miracle, from the very nature of the fact, is as entire as any argument from experience can possibly be imagined." Hume adds the famous maxim: no testimony suffices to establish a miracle unless the testimony's falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact it reports — and, he judges, it never is. The argument's force is real, so state it honestly. Laws of nature are supported by the most massive, uniform experience humans possess — every funeral confirms that the dead stay dead. Any report of a miracle is supported by something far weaker: human testimony, which is known to err through deception, credulity, legend, and the love of wonder. So when testimony collides with uniform experience, rationality sides with experience — always.

Hume seasons this with observations about miracle reports flourishing among "ignorant and barbarous nations," and about rival religions canceling each other's miracles out. The conclusion: a wise man can never believe a miracle on testimony, no matter the witnesses.

secs.h: III. The Circle in the Argument
secs.x: III. The Circle in the Argument The central flaw was spotted early and has never been repaired: the argument assumes what it set out to prove. Hume's engine is "firm and unalterable experience" — but whether experience against miracles is truly unalterable is precisely the question. The experience of the apostles, of the five hundred witnesses Paul cites (1 Corinthians 15:6), of every reporter of every miracle, is part of the human record too. Hume counts only the non-miraculous experience as "experience," which is to say: he assumes all miracle reports are false in order to prove no miracle report can be believed. C. S. Lewis put the point crisply in Miracles : we can know experience against miracles to be uniform only if we already know all the reports are false, and we can know that only by assuming miracles never occur — a circle Paraphrase . Notice also what the argument would prove if sound — far too much.

secs.h: III. The Circle in the Argument
secs.x: Any sufficiently rare, unrepeated event becomes unbelievable on testimony: the method that dismisses the Resurrection in advance would, applied consistently, have dismissed reports of meteorites, of ball lightning, of every singular historical surprise, because the reporter's error was always antecedently "more probable." A rule of reasoning that forbids ever learning of the genuinely unprecedented is not rigor; it is a blindfold. Later philosophers — including the agnostic John Earman, whose book title Hume's Abject Failure states his verdict — have argued that Hume's maxim, made mathematically precise, either collapses or proves nothing against well-attested singular events Paraphrase .

secs.h: IV. What a Law of Nature Is
secs.x: IV. What a Law of Nature Is Hume's definition — a miracle "violates" the laws of nature — smuggles in a picture of laws as inviolable decrees that even God must obey. But laws of nature, as science actually uses them, are descriptions : compact statements of how the natural order runs when nothing outside the described system intervenes. They predict what matter does left to itself; they are silent about what happens if something beyond nature acts. If I catch a falling apple, I do not violate the law of gravity — I introduce a new factor the law's description did not include, and the law continues to hold perfectly. A miracle, on the Christian account, is exactly that, at the level of the whole system: the Author of nature acting directly within it. Nothing is "broken." Water still ordinarily stays water; the dead still ordinarily stay dead — indeed the miracle is only visible because the regularities hold. The disciples could recognize the Resurrection as God's act precisely because they knew, as well as any modern, that crucified men stay dead.

secs.h: IV. What a Law of Nature Is
secs.x: Miracles presuppose the laws; they do not compete with them. So the real question is not scientific but theological: does anything exist beyond the system? If God exists, miracles are possible — full stop; a Creator who fashioned nature from nothing is not locked out of it. If God does not exist, miracles are impossible. Hume's argument, dressed as a lesson about evidence, is in substance a conclusion about God — assumed, not established. For the case that God exists, see Explanations for God's Existence .

secs.h: V. Weighing Evidence for the Extraordinary
secs.x: V. Weighing Evidence for the Extraordinary "Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence," the modern slogan runs. Rightly understood, Christians agree: a resurrection claim needs far better support than a claim that it rained. The slogan goes wrong only when "extraordinary evidence" is defined as "evidence that could never exist" — at which point it is Hume's circle again, restated. What evidence can rationally support a miracle? The same kinds that support any past event, raised to strength: multiple independent witnesses; testimony against the witnesses' own interests, maintained under persecution to death; public claims checkable by enemies in the place and generation they were made; transformation of the witnesses themselves; and the absence of any natural explanation that fits the agreed facts.

secs.h: V. Weighing Evidence for the Extraordinary
secs.x: These are not hypothetical criteria — they are the actual shape of the case for the Resurrection, laid out in detail on its own page , where the skeptics' alternative explanations (hallucination, theft, legend, swoon) are weighed one by one and found to require more credulity than the miracle. Background beliefs do their work here, and honestly so: for the convinced atheist, any natural explanation, however strained, beats a miracle; for the theist, a miracle is possible and the evidence may simply win. That is why this page insists on the order of questions: first whether God exists, then whether He has acted. What is not rational is the shortcut — ruling out the miracle in advance and calling the refusal to weigh evidence a weighing of evidence.

VI. Common Objections Examined "Every religion claims miracles — they cancel out" The Claim Hume's own point: rival religions' miracles are equal and opposite testimony, mutually destroying. Response Claims do not cancel; evidence is weighed case by case — that two murder trials both feature witnesses does not acquit both defendants. Most religious miracle claims are private, late, or unfalsifiable, and Christianity is not obliged to defend them; some may even be true without threatening Christianity (the question is always what a given event evidences). The Christian wager is specific: one central public miracle, the Resurrection, attested early, by named witnesses, at known cost to themselves, in the city where it could be refuted. Put every religion's best-attested miracle on the table under the same criteria and compare — that is the opposite of special pleading. "Why are there no miracles today, under cameras?" The Claim Miracles flourish exactly where evidence is thin — distant past, remote places — which is what fraud and legend predict.

Response First, the premise is overstated: claimed healings and answered prayers are reported constantly, including in documented medical literature of unexplained recoveries; the modern world filters them as anecdote, which is its right — but "never investigated" is not "never occurs." Second, Christianity never promised miracles on demand; they cluster, in Scripture itself, around decisive revelatory moments, and Christ rebuked the demand for signs as a substitute for faith (Matthew 12:39). Third, the faith's evidential weight does not rest on contemporary wonders but on a historical event — a deliberate design, one might say, since a public past event can be examined by every generation equally, while a private experience cannot. The absence of miracles in your news feed is not evidence about a tomb in first-century Jerusalem. "Science has progressively explained miracles away" The Claim What looked miraculous — disease, lightning, eclipses — turned out natural; the trend line points to zero.

Response The trend concerns phenomena once attributed to direct divine action for lack of a mechanism — and Christians should cheerfully concede it; the "God of the gaps" was always bad theology (see Science & Christianity ). But the biblical miracles were never gap-filling explanations of recurring phenomena; they are singular acts in history, recognized as extraordinary by their own witnesses precisely against the known regularities. No advance in medicine explains an empty tomb; better embryology will never make a virgin conception ordinary. Science narrows ignorance of mechanisms; it has nothing to say about whether the Author of mechanisms once acted directly. The categories do not meet.

secs.h: VII. Miracles and the Orthodox Faith
secs.x: VII. Miracles and the Orthodox Faith Orthodoxy's relationship to the miraculous differs from both the skeptic's and the enthusiast's. The Church is unembarrassed by miracles — her calendar is full of them, her saints' lives report them, and the Coptic Church in particular remembers wonders in living memory around which her people's devotion gathered. Yet the faith does not rest on wonder-stories, and the Church has always tested claims soberly, knowing that credulity dishonors God as much as unbelief. "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God" (1 John 4:1). What the faith rests on is the miracle: "if Christ is not risen, then our preaching is empty and your faith is also empty" (1 Corinthians 15:14). Paul stakes everything on one public event — and invites verification, listing living witnesses (15:6). The sacramental life of the Church flows from that event: not a weekly suspension of nature, but the risen Christ giving Himself in the mysteries.

secs.h: VII. Miracles and the Orthodox Faith
secs.x: And the deepest answer to Hume is finally a Person, not a syllogism: a God who made the world is not a prisoner of it, and "with God nothing will be impossible" (Luke 1:37). The arguments clear the road; the empty tomb stands at the end of it — examine it .

VIII. FAQ Q: Isn't believing in miracles believing in magic? No — the categories are opposites. Magic, in the ancient and modern sense alike, is technique: manipulating hidden forces to compel outcomes. A miracle is personal: the free act of a personal God, never compelled, never a technology. That is why Scripture forbids sorcery while recording miracles — and why miracles carry meaning (they attest, reveal, redeem) rather than merely astonishing. The Resurrection is not a trick that needs a bigger stage; it is the vindication of the Son of God (Romans 1:4). Q: Should I believe every miracle story I hear in church? No — and Orthodoxy does not ask it. Test claims with the sobriety the Church herself uses (1 John 4:1); hold loosely what is unverified; let nothing peripheral bear the weight of faith. The hierarchy of confidence is deliberate: the Resurrection is attested as history and holds everything; particular wonders of particular saints edify but do not carry the structure. A faith that believed everything would be as defenseless as one that believed nothing.

Q: If miracles are possible, doesn't that make science pointless — anything could happen? The reverse. Science requires regularity; Christianity supplies a reason for it — a faithful Creator who sustains an ordered cosmos, "who covers the heavens with clouds" in pattern and season (cf. Psalm 147:8). Miracles, on the biblical record, are vanishingly rare, purposeful, and recognizable only against that order. A world of constant divine interruption would indeed make science impossible — and would equally make miracles invisible. The Christian picture — deep regularity, rare signs — is exactly the world science finds, with a signature in the margin. Q: Where should a skeptical friend start? With the order of questions. Ask whether they reject the Resurrection because the evidence is weak, or because miracles "can't happen" — most discover it is the second, and that they have never examined the first. Then offer the two pages in sequence: the case that God exists (which makes miracles possible), and the case that He raised Jesus (which makes Christianity true).
Hume's ghost loses its power the moment the question is allowed to be asked.
