secs.h: IV. How the Creed Came to Be
secs.x: IV. How the Creed Came to Be The Creed did not appear from nowhere in 325. It gives conciliar form to a rule of faith the churches had confessed at baptism since the apostles, and its later history explains why Christians who recite it today do not all recite the same text. c. AD 180 St. Irenaeus records the rule of faith the Church holds throughout the world: one God the Father, one Christ Jesus, and the Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets. AD 325 The Council of Nicaea condemns Arius and issues its Creed, confessing the Son "of one substance with the Father." St. Athanasius, then a deacon of Alexandria, attends with his bishop, St. Alexander. c. AD 350 St. Cyril of Jerusalem delivers his Catechetical Lectures, explaining the creed of his Church article by article to candidates for baptism. AD 381 The Council of Constantinople confirms the faith of Nicaea, expands the article on the Holy Spirit, and completes the Creed with the articles on the Church, baptism and the life to come.

secs.h: IV. How the Creed Came to Be
secs.x: AD 431 The Council of Ephesus upholds the title Theotokos and forbids anyone to compose "a different Faith as a rival" to that of Nicaea (canon 7). AD 451 The Creed of 381 is read at Chalcedon, the earliest surviving record of its text. The Oriental Orthodox reject Chalcedon's definition, but they have always kept the Creed itself. AD 589 In Spain, the Third Council of Toledo is commonly cited as the first council to use the Creed with "and the Son" (filioque) added. c. 1014 The Creed with the filioque is sung at the Mass in Rome. 1530 The Augsburg Confession, the founding Lutheran confession, opens by affirming "the decree of the Nicene Synod." 1561 The Belgic Confession of the Reformed churches receives "the three creeds" of the Apostles, of Nicaea and of Athanasius. 1571 The Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England, in their final English form, declare that the three Creeds are to be received and believed. 1580 The Lutheran Book of Concord is published, beginning with the three ecumenical creeds.

secs.h: IV. How the Creed Came to Be
secs.x: 1646 The Westminster Confession of Faith defines the catholic Church as invisible, "the whole number of the elect," alongside the visible Church.

secs.h: V. "We Believe in One God, the Father Almighty"
secs.x: V. "We Believe in One God, the Father Almighty" The Creed begins where the apostles began: "for us there is one God, the Father." It does not open with an abstract divine essence but with a Person, the Father, the source of the Son and the Spirit. Its three paragraphs follow the three Names in which every Christian is baptized, which is why the Fathers handed it on as the faith of baptism. 1 Corinthians 8:6 "yet for us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we for Him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and through whom we live." Shared reading: Paul's confession already has the Creed's shape: one God the Father, and one Lord Jesus Christ through whom all things were made. The Creed takes up both phrases. Matthew 28:19 "Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," Shared reading: The baptismal command gives the Creed its order. The candidate confesses the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and is baptized into the one Name of all three. St.

secs.h: V. "We Believe in One God, the Father Almighty"
secs.x: Irenaeus of Lyons Against Heresies I.10.1 (c. AD 180) "The Church, though dispersed throughout the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, has received from the apostles and their disciples this faith: [She believes] in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them; and in one Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who became incarnate for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit, who proclaimed through the prophets the dispensations of God, and the advents, and the birth from a virgin, and the passion, and the resurrection from the dead, and the ascension into heaven in the flesh of the beloved Christ Jesus, our Lord..." Church Father VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Irenaeus wrote about a century and a half before Nicaea, and the outline is already the Creed's. He also says where this faith is found: the Church "has received from the apostles and their disciples this faith." The Creed did not invent the apostolic faith. It gave the Church's long-held confession a fixed conciliar form. St. Cyril of Jerusalem Catechetical Lecture 5.12 (c.

secs.h: V. "We Believe in One God, the Father Almighty"
secs.x: AD 350) "...at the proper season expect the confirmation out of Holy Scripture of each part of the contents. For the articles of the Faith were not composed as seemed good to men; but the most important points collected out of all the Scripture make up one complete teaching of the Faith. ... Take heed then, brethren, and hold fast the traditions which you now receive, and write them on the table of your heart." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Cyril holds together two things that are often set against each other. The Creed is drawn "out of all the Scripture," and each article is to be confirmed from Scripture. Yet he hands it to his candidates as "the traditions which you now receive," to be learned by heart before they have been taught its proofs. Scripture and tradition do not compete here. The Church hands on, in a few words, what Scripture teaches at length.

secs.h: VI. "And in One Lord Jesus Christ"
secs.x: VI. "And in One Lord Jesus Christ" The heart of the Creed of 325 is its confession of the Son: "of the substance of the Father, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made," and "of one substance with the Father." Arius taught that the Son was the first and greatest of creatures. The council answered with a word that is not found in Scripture: homoousios , of one essence. St. Athanasius the Apostolic De Decretis (Defence of the Nicene Definition) 20 (AD 350s) "But the Bishops discerning in this too their dissimulation ... were again compelled on their part to collect the sense of the Scriptures, and to re-say and re-write what they had said before, more distinctly still, namely, that the Son is 'one in essence' with the Father" Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION This is the method of Nicaea in the words of the man who defended it for half a century. The bishops did not set out to add to Scripture. They gathered "the sense of the Scriptures" into a word the Arians could not twist.

secs.h: VI. "And in One Lord Jesus Christ"
secs.x: Here Orthodox and Protestant Christians stand on the same ground: both confess the homoousios , and both accept that a council could rightly use a word from outside Scripture to guard Scripture's meaning. The difference, which this page returns to in Sections XIII and XIV, is over what gives such a council its authority. John 1:1-3 "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made that was made." Shared reading: "By whom all things were made" is John's own phrase. The one through whom everything was made cannot Himself be among the things that were made, which is the whole case against Arius in a sentence. For the full scriptural and patristic case, see the pages on the Divinity of Christ and the Holy Trinity .

VII. Incarnate, Crucified, Risen "Who for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven and was incarnate by the Holy Ghost and the Virgin Mary, and was made man." The subject of every verb in this paragraph is the one Lord confessed in the paragraph before. The eternal Son is the one who came down, was incarnate, was crucified, suffered, was buried and rose. The Creed does not divide its story between God and a man. That single subject is the foundation of St. Cyril of Alexandria's Christology and of the Oriental Orthodox confession of one incarnate nature of God the Word; see Miaphysite Christology and the Will of Christ . Because the one born of the Virgin is the eternal Son, she is rightly called Theotokos, the one who gave birth to God. The Council of Ephesus defended that title in 431, and the Coptic introduction to the Creed confesses it each time the Creed is said: "We glorify you, O holy Virgin, Mother of God, for you have borne for us the Saviour of the whole world." See The Virgin Mary as Theotokos . "For us men and for our salvation" governs everything that follows.

The Creed confesses the incarnation, the cross and the resurrection as acts done for us. Its last paragraph then names the means by which that salvation reaches us: the Holy Spirit, the Church and baptism. The Creed's own order already suggests that these last articles are not optional extras. They answer the question the middle paragraph raises, which is how what Christ did for us becomes ours.

secs.h: VIII. "The Lord, the Giver of Life"
secs.x: VIII. "The Lord, the Giver of Life" The Creed of 325 ended its third paragraph with a single line: "And [we believe] in the Holy Ghost." By 381 a party had arisen that denied the Spirit's divinity, and the council answered by confessing Him "the Lord and Giver-of-Life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified." He is not called "God" in so many words, but He is given the worship that belongs to God alone. John 15:26 "But when the Helper comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, He will testify of Me." Orthodox reading: The Creed takes its words from Christ's: the Spirit "proceeds from the Father." The Son sends the Spirit into the world; the Spirit's eternal origin is the Father. Protestant reading: Most Protestant churches inherited the Western form of the Creed, which adds "and the Son," together with the Western teaching that the Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son.

secs.h: VIII. "The Lord, the Giver of Life"
secs.x: The Third Ecumenical Council Council of Ephesus, Canon 7 (AD 431) "...it is unlawful for any man to bring forward, or to write, or to compose a different (ἑτέραν) Faith as a rival to that established by the holy Fathers assembled with the Holy Ghost in Nicæa." Ecumenical Council VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The Oriental Orthodox receive three ecumenical councils: Nicaea, Constantinople and Ephesus. The Creed they confess is therefore the Creed of 381 as Ephesus guarded it, without later additions. The question of the filioque is treated in full on the Filioque page .

IX. "One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church" "And [we believe] in one, holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church." The Creed places the Church inside the confession of faith, directly after the Holy Spirit. For the Fathers, the Church is the work of the Spirit, confessed in the same breath as the Spirit Himself. Each of the four words has a history, and the Fathers explain each one. One Ephesians 4:4-6 "There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all." Orthodox reading: One body stands in the same list as one faith and one baptism. As the faith and the baptism are definite and recognisable, so is the body. Protestant reading: The unity of the body is spiritual, shared by all true believers across communions, and it is expressed wherever the Gospel is rightly preached and the sacraments rightly administered. St.

Cyprian of Carthage On the Unity of the Church 6 (AD 251) "He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother. If any one could escape who was outside the Ark of Noah, then he also may escape who shall be outside of the Church." Church Father VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Cyprian, bishop and martyr, wrote this during a schism in Carthage. His concern is division: no one can claim Christ while separating from His body. The image of the Church as mother has a long life, and it appears again, in Calvin, in Section XIII. Holy The Church is holy because her Head is holy and the Spirit sanctifies her, not because her members are without sin. Cyril of Jerusalem says that she "universally treats and heals the whole class of sins." Her holiness lies in what she gives, the life of the Spirit in the mysteries, rather than in the record of those who receive it. Catholic St. Ignatius of Antioch Letter to the Smyrnaeans 8 (c. AD 107) "Let no man do anything connected with the Church without the bishop.

Let that be deemed a proper Eucharist, which is [administered] either by the bishop, or by one to whom he has entrusted it. Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church. It is not lawful without the bishop either to baptize or to celebrate a love-feast" Church Father VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION This is the earliest surviving use of "catholic" for the Church, written by a bishop on his way to martyrdom in Rome. Notice where Ignatius places the word. The Catholic Church is where Jesus Christ is, and in the local church it is found gathered around the bishop, at a Eucharist the bishop has authorised, and at a baptism he has sanctioned. For Ignatius, catholicity is more than geography: it is the whole Christ present in each church gathered around its bishop. St. Cyril of Jerusalem Catechetical Lecture 18.23 (c.

AD 350) "It is called Catholic then because it extends over all the world, from one end of the earth to the other; and because it teaches universally and completely one and all the doctrines which ought to come to men's knowledge, concerning things both visible and invisible, heavenly and earthly; and because it brings into subjection to godliness the whole race of mankind, governors and governed, learned and unlearned; and because it universally treats and heals the whole class of sins, which are committed by soul or body, and possesses in itself every form of virtue which is named, both in deeds and words, and in every kind of spiritual gifts." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Cyril's first reason is geographical: the Church "extends over all the world." Protestant writers rightly point to this, and the Orthodox agree. But Cyril gives four more reasons, and they concern wholeness: the Church teaches the whole faith, gathers every kind of person, heals every kind of sin, and holds every grace. Catholic means universal in reach and complete in content. St.

Cyril of Jerusalem Catechetical Lecture 18.26 (c. AD 350) "...that you may avoid their wretched meetings, and ever abide with the Holy Church Catholic in which you were regenerated. And if ever you are sojourning in cities, inquire not simply where the Lord's House is (for the other sects of the profane also attempt to call their own dens houses of the Lord), nor merely where the Church is, but where is the Catholic Church. For this is the peculiar name of this Holy Church, the mother of us all, which is the spouse of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Only-begotten Son of God..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION This passage matters more than any other for what the Creed meant to those who first confessed it. Cyril's candidates were told that "Catholic" was a name they could ask for in a strange city and expect to find: a visible communion, distinct from the sects that also called their meetings churches. And it is the Church "in which you were regenerated," that is, in which they were baptized.

In Cyril's teaching, the Church of the Creed and the font of the Creed belong together. 1 Timothy 3:15 "...the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth." Orthodox reading: Cyril cites this verse for the Catholic Church. The truth is upheld by the Church, which is why the Church could confess it in council and hand it on in the Creed. Protestant reading: The Church upholds the truth by faithfully proclaiming Scripture. Her authority is ministerial, exercised under the Word rather than over it. Apostolic St. Clement of Rome First Letter to the Corinthians 42 (c. AD 96) "The apostles have preached the gospel to us from the Lord Jesus Christ; Jesus Christ [has done so] from God. Christ therefore was sent forth by God, and the apostles by Christ. ... And thus preaching through countries and cities, they appointed the first fruits [of their labours], having first proved them by the Spirit, to be bishops and deacons of those who should afterwards believe." Church Father VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION St.

Clement of Rome First Letter to the Corinthians 44 (c. AD 96) "Our apostles also knew, through our Lord Jesus Christ, that there would be strife on account of the office of the episcopate. For this reason, therefore, inasmuch as they had obtained a perfect fore-knowledge of this, they appointed those [ministers] already mentioned, and afterwards gave instructions, that when these should fall asleep, other approved men should succeed them in their ministry." Church Father VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Clement wrote at the end of the first century, within living memory of the apostles. He describes a chain: God sent Christ, Christ sent the apostles, the apostles appointed bishops and deacons, and they gave instructions that "other approved men should succeed them in their ministry." St. Irenaeus of Lyons Against Heresies III.3.1 (c.

AD 180) "It is within the power of all, therefore, in every Church, who may wish to see the truth, to contemplate clearly the tradition of the apostles manifested throughout the whole world; and we are in a position to reckon up those who were by the apostles instituted bishops in the Churches, and [to demonstrate] the succession of these men to our own times" Church Father VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Tertullian of Carthage The Prescription Against Heretics 32 (c. AD 200) "Let them produce the original records of their churches; let them unfold the roll of their bishops, running down in due succession from the beginning in such a manner that [that first] bishop shall be able to show for his ordainer and predecessor some one of the apostles or of apostolic men, a man, moreover, who continued steadfast with the apostles." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Irenaeus and Tertullian use the same test against the Gnostics, who claimed a secret tradition from the apostles.

Apostolic teaching, they answer, is public, and it can be traced through the bishops of the churches the apostles founded. Neither writer treats succession as a substitute for apostolic doctrine. Succession is how the churches show that their doctrine is the apostles' own. Tertullian later joined the Montanist movement, but on this point he speaks for the Church of his day. Ephesians 2:19-20 "...members of the household of God, having been built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the chief corner stone," Orthodox reading: The apostles are the Church's foundation: the faith they preached, the worship they handed on, and the ministry they appointed to keep both. Protestant reading: The foundation is the apostles' teaching, now held in the New Testament. A church is apostolic when it teaches what the apostles taught.

Acts 2:42 "And they continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers." Orthodox reading: The first church's life is described in four parts that cannot be separated: the apostles' doctrine, their fellowship or communion, the Eucharist, and the prayers. Protestant reading: These are the marks of a true church in any age: apostolic teaching, fellowship, the Lord's Supper and prayer. For the full treatment, see Order of the Church & Apostolic Succession and The Authority of the Church .

X. The Church in the Council's Canons A creed can be read in isolation, but it was not written in isolation. The bishops who issued the Creed of 325 issued twenty canons at the same council, and the bishops of 381 added canons of their own. If we want to know what these men meant by "the Catholic and Apostolic Church," the plainest evidence is how they governed it. First Council of Nicaea Canon 4 (AD 325) "It is by all means proper that a bishop should be appointed by all the bishops in the province; but should this be difficult, either on account of urgent necessity or because of distance, three at least should meet together, and the suffrages of the absent [bishops] also being given and communicated in writing, then the ordination should take place.

But in every province the ratification of what is done should be left to the Metropolitan." Ecumenical Council VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION First Council of Nicaea Canon 8 (AD 325) "Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, if they come over to the Catholic and Apostolic Church, the great and holy Synod decrees that they who are ordained shall continue as they are in the clergy. But it is before all things necessary that they should profess in writing that they will observe and follow the dogmas of the Catholic and Apostolic Church..." Ecumenical Council VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION First Council of Nicaea Canon 18 (AD 325) "It has come to the knowledge of the holy and great Synod that, in some districts and cities, the deacons administer the Eucharist to the presbyters, whereas neither canon nor custom permits that they who have no right to offer should give the Body of Christ to them that do offer." Ecumenical Council VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION First Council of Nicaea Canon 19 (AD 325) "Concerning the Paulianists who have flown for refuge to the Catholic Church, it has been

decreed that they must by all means be rebaptized..." Ecumenical Council VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION First Council of Constantinople Canon 2 (AD 381) "The bishops are not to go beyond their dioceses to churches lying outside of their bounds, nor bring confusion on the churches; but let the Bishop of Alexandria, according to the canons, alone administer the affairs of Egypt..." Ecumenical Council VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION What the Canons Show Read together, the canons describe the Church the Creed confesses. It has bishops, ordained by other bishops and confirmed by the metropolitan of the province. It has defined territories, so that the Bishop of Alexandria administers Egypt and bishops do not cross into one another's churches. It has presbyters who "offer," and a Eucharist the council calls "the Body of Christ." And it has boundaries: those outside it are received back on stated terms, some by written profession and some by baptism. None of this settles by itself which body today is the Church of the Creed. It does show what the words meant to the men who wrote them.

"The Catholic and Apostolic Church" of 325 and 381 was not an invisible fellowship known only to God. It was a communion of churches with bishops, sacraments and canons, which could receive a schismatic, depose a bishop and anathematise a heresy.

XI. "One Baptism for the Remission of Sins" "We acknowledge one Baptism for the remission of sins." The Greek verb is ὁμολογοῦμεν, "we confess." Baptism is the only sacrament named in the Creed, and it is named as an object of faith: the Church does not only practise baptism, she confesses what it does. The phrase "for the remission of sins" is taken from St. Peter's preaching at Pentecost. The Scriptural Ground Acts 2:38 "Then Peter said to them, 'Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.'" Orthodox reading: Peter joins repentance, baptism and forgiveness in a single command, and the Creed repeats his phrase. Forgiveness is given in baptism and received by repentance and faith. Protestant reading: Reformed interpreters read baptism here as the sign and seal of the forgiveness promised to faith. Some Baptist interpreters read "for" in the sense of "because of" a forgiveness already received. Lutherans read the verse much as the Orthodox do.

Acts 22:16 "And now why are you waiting? Arise and be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord." Orthodox reading: Paul had already met the risen Christ and spent three days in prayer and fasting, yet Ananias tells him to be baptized and "wash away your sins." The washing happens at the font. Protestant reading: Many read "calling on the name of the Lord" as the act of faith that saves, with baptism as its outward expression. John 3:5 "Jesus answered, 'Most assuredly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.'" Orthodox reading: The Fathers read "born of water and the Spirit" as baptism with near unanimity. Justin and Cyril of Jerusalem both cite this verse for it. Protestant reading: Lutherans and many Anglicans read it of baptism. Many Reformed and Baptist interpreters read the water as a figure for the Spirit's cleansing, or for natural birth.

Titus 3:5 "not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit," Orthodox reading: "The washing of regeneration" is baptism, set in the same sentence as "not by works." Baptism is God's mercy at work, not a human work that competes with grace. Protestant reading: The Lutheran reading agrees. Others read the washing as the inner cleansing of the Spirit, which outward baptism signifies. 1 Peter 3:21 "There is also an antitype which now saves us, baptism (not the removal of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God), through the resurrection of Jesus Christ," Orthodox reading: "Baptism... now saves us," and its power comes from the resurrection of Christ. The water does not save as water; Christ saves in the water.

Protestant reading: The weight falls on the parenthesis: what saves is not the outward washing but "the answer of a good conscience toward God." Romans 6:3-4 "Or do you not know that as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? Therefore we were buried with Him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." Orthodox reading: Baptism unites the believer to Christ's death and resurrection. It is the beginning of the new life, not only a picture of it. Protestant reading: All agree that the passage speaks of union with Christ. Traditions differ over whether baptism brings about that union or signifies and seals it. The Fathers on Baptism St. Justin Martyr First Apology 61 (c. AD 155) "Then they are brought by us where there is water, and are regenerated in the same manner in which we were ourselves regenerated.

For, in the name of God, the Father and Lord of the universe, and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, they then receive the washing with water. ... in order that we may not remain the children of necessity and of ignorance, but may become the children of choice and knowledge, and may obtain in the water the remission of sins formerly committed..." Church Father VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Justin is describing the practice of the Church at Rome to a pagan emperor, a century and a half before Nicaea. Baptism is regeneration; it is in the Name of the Trinity; and in the water the candidate obtains "the remission of sins formerly committed." The Creed's phrase was already the Church's plain description of what happens at the font. St. Cyril of Jerusalem Catechetical Lecture 3.3–4 (c. AD 350) "Regard not the Laver as simple water, but rather regard the spiritual grace that is given with the water. ...

When going down, therefore, into the water, think not of the bare element, but look for salvation by the power of the Holy Ghost: for without both you can not possibly be made perfect." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St. Cyril of Jerusalem Catechetical Lecture 3.10 (c. AD 350) "If any man receive not Baptism, he has not salvation; except only Martyrs, who even without the water receive the kingdom. For when the Saviour, in redeeming the world by His Cross, was pierced in the side, He shed forth blood and water; that men, living in times of peace, might be baptized in water, and, in times of persecution, in their own blood." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Cyril's exception is worth noticing. Martyrs who die for Christ before reaching the font are baptized in their own blood. The water is what God has given to His Church, and Cyril urges it without hesitation; yet he does not imagine God unable to save the martyr whom persecution kept from it. St. Basil the Great On the Holy Spirit 12.28 (c.

AD 375) "Faith and baptism are two kindred and inseparable ways of salvation: faith is perfected through baptism, baptism is established through faith, and both are completed by the same names. For as we believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost, so are we also baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost; first comes the confession, introducing us to salvation, and baptism follows, setting the seal upon our assent." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Basil states the relation that later debates pulled apart. Faith and baptism are not rivals. Faith is "perfected through baptism," and baptism is "established through faith." The confession comes first and the font seals it, which is the order of the Creed itself, learned and confessed by candidates before their baptism. St. Gregory the Theologian Oration 40, On Holy Baptism, 3 (AD 381) "Illumination is the splendour of souls, the conversion of the life, the question put to the Godward conscience.

It is the aid to our weakness, the renunciation of the flesh, the following of the Spirit, the fellowship of the Word, the improvement of the creature, the overwhelming of sin, the participation of light, the dissolution of darkness." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Why "One" Baptism "One" means unrepeatable. As there is "one Lord, one faith, one baptism," a person is born again only once. Nicaea's canons show how carefully the Church applied this. The Cathari, schismatics whose baptism was the Church's own, were received without being baptized again, and their clergy kept their rank (canon 8). The Paulianists, followers of Paul of Samosata, whose teaching on God and on Christ was heretical, "must by all means be rebaptized" (canon 19), because what they had received was not the one baptism at all. For how the Oriental Orthodox apply this today, see The Acceptance of External Baptism , and for the baptism of children, Infant vs Believers' Baptism .

secs.h: XII. "The Resurrection of the Dead and the Life of the Age to Come"
secs.x: XII. "The Resurrection of the Dead and the Life of the Age to Come" "We look for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come." The Creed ends in hope. The Coptic text reads "the life of the age to come," which is closer to the Greek αἰῶνος, "age." St. Cyril of Jerusalem Catechetical Lecture 18.28 (c. AD 350) "In this Holy Catholic Church receiving instruction and behaving ourselves virtuously, we shall attain the kingdom of heaven, and inherit eternal life; for which also we endure all toils, that we may be made partakers thereof from the Lord." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Cyril joins the last articles in a single sentence. It is in the Holy Catholic Church, instructed and living virtuously, that Christians reach the kingdom. The order of the Creed's last paragraph is the order of salvation: the Spirit gives life, the Church receives it, baptism begins it, and the resurrection completes it.

XIII. Do Protestants Hold the Nicene Creed? This question is often asked with heat. It deserves to be answered with documents. The magisterial Reformation (Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican) did not reject the Creed. It received it formally, and those churches confess it to this day. What follows sets out, in the Reformers' own words, what they affirmed and how they read the articles on the Church and baptism. What the Reformation Churches Affirm The Lutheran Churches Augsburg Confession, Article I (1530) "The churches, with common consent among us, do teach that the decree of the Nicene Synod concerning the unity of the divine essence and of the three persons is true, and without doubt to be believed: to wit, that there is one divine essence which is called and is God, eternal, without body, indivisible [without part], of infinite power, wisdom, goodness, the Creator and Preserver of all things, visible and invisible; and that yet there are three persons of the same essence and power, who also are co-eternal, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost." Lutheran Confession VERBATIM ·

SCHAFF, CREEDS OF CHRISTENDOM The Reformed Churches Belgic Confession, Article IX (1561) "Therefore, in this point, we do willingly receive the three creeds, namely, that of the Apostles, of Nice, and of Athanasius; likewise that which, conformable thereunto, is agreed upon by the ancient fathers." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · SCHAFF, CREEDS OF CHRISTENDOM The Church of England Thirty-Nine Articles, Article VIII (1571 text) "The three Credes, Nicene Crede, Athanasian Crede, and that whiche is commonlye called the Apostles' Crede, ought throughlye to be receaued and beleued: for they may be proued by moste certayne warrauntes of holye scripture." Anglican Articles VERBATIM · SCHAFF, CREEDS OF CHRISTENDOM The agreement here is real and should be said plainly. On the Trinity and the person of Christ, the confessions of Augsburg, the Netherlands and England stand with Nicaea against Arius, and they condemn the same ancient heresies the Fathers condemned.

Notice also the reason the English Articles give: the Creeds are to be believed "for they may be proued by moste certayne warrauntes of holye scripture." The Creed is received because, and in so far as, it agrees with Scripture. How They Read "One Holy Catholic and Apostolic Church" The Lutheran Churches Augsburg Confession, Article VII (1530) "Also they teach that one holy Church is to continue forever. But the Church is the congregation of saints [the assembly of all believers], in which the Gospel is rightly taught [purely preached] and the Sacraments rightly administered [according to the Gospel]. And unto the true unity of the Church, it is sufficient to agree concerning the doctrine of the Gospel and the administration of the Sacraments." Lutheran Confession VERBATIM · SCHAFF, CREEDS OF CHRISTENDOM The Reformed Churches Belgic Confession, Article XXVII (1561) "We believe and profess one catholic or universal Church, which is a holy congregation and assembly of true Christian believers, expecting all their salvation in Jesus Christ, being washed by his blood, sanctified and

sealed by the Holy Ghost." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · SCHAFF, CREEDS OF CHRISTENDOM The Reformed Churches Westminster Confession of Faith 25.1–2 (1646) "The catholic or universal Church, which is invisible, consists of the whole number of the elect, that have been, are, or shall be gathered into one, under Christ the head thereof; and is the spouse, the body, the fullness of him that filleth all in all. ... The visible Church, which is also catholic or universal under the gospel (not confined to one nation as before under the law) consists of all those, throughout the world, that profess the true religion, and of their children; and is the kingdom of the Lord Jesus Christ, the house and family of God, out of which there is no ordinary possibility of salvation." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · SCHAFF, CREEDS OF CHRISTENDOM The Church of England Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XIX "The visible Church of Christ is a congregation of faithful men, in the which the pure Word of God is preached, and the Sacraments be duly ministered according to Christ's ordinance, in all those things

that of necessity are requisite to the same." Anglican Articles VERBATIM · SCHAFF, CREEDS OF CHRISTENDOM John Calvin Institutes of the Christian Religion IV.1.4 (1559) "But as it is now our purpose to discourse of the visible Church, let us learn, from her single title of Mother, how useful, nay, how necessary the knowledge of her is, since there is no other means of entering into life unless she conceive us in the womb and give us birth, unless she nourish us at her breasts, and, in short, keep us under her charge and government, until, divested of mortal flesh, we become like the angels ... Moreover, beyond the pale of the Church no forgiveness of sins, no salvation, can be hoped for" Reformer VERBATIM · BEVERIDGE TRANSLATION (1845) The Reformers did not abandon the visible Church. Calvin calls her mother in words close to Cyprian's, and Westminster says that outside the visible Church "there is no ordinary possibility of salvation." What changed is how the Church is identified.

She is known by her marks, the Gospel rightly preached and the sacraments rightly administered, rather than by communion with bishops in succession from the apostles. Westminster also sets alongside the visible Church "the catholic or universal Church, which is invisible," made up of the elect. That distinction has roots in St. Augustine's teaching on the Church as a mixed body, but the Creed itself does not draw it. How They Read "One Baptism for the Remission of Sins" The Lutheran Churches Augsburg Confession, Article IX (1530) "Of Baptism they teach that it is necessary to salvation, and that by Baptism the grace of God is offered, and that children are to be baptized, who by Baptism, being offered to God, are received into God's favor." Lutheran Confession VERBATIM · SCHAFF, CREEDS OF CHRISTENDOM The Church of England Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXVII "Baptism is not only a sign of profession, and mark of difference, whereby Christian men are discerned from others that be not christened, but it is also a sign of Regeneration or New-Birth, whereby, as by an instrument, they

that receive Baptism rightly are grafted into the Church; the promises of the forgiveness of sin, and of our adoption to be the sons of God by the Holy Ghost, are visibly signed and sealed..." Anglican Articles VERBATIM · SCHAFF, CREEDS OF CHRISTENDOM The Reformed Churches Westminster Confession of Faith 28.5 (1646) "Although it be a great sin to contemn or neglect this ordinance, yet grace and salvation are not so inseparably annexed unto it, as that no person can be regenerated or saved without it, or that all that are baptized are undoubtedly regenerated." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · SCHAFF, CREEDS OF CHRISTENDOM On baptism the Reformation churches differ among themselves. The Augsburg Confession teaches that baptism "is necessary to salvation." The Thirty-Nine Articles call it an "instrument" by which those who receive it rightly "are grafted into the Church." The Westminster Confession makes it a sign and seal whose grace is "not so inseparably annexed unto it" that no one can be saved without it.

Baptist and many evangelical churches treat baptism as an ordinance of obedience for believers, signifying a salvation already received. Some free-church traditions, notably the Restoration movement with its slogan "no creed but the Bible," do not use creeds at all. The Traditions Side by Side Article Oriental Orthodox Lutheran Reformed Anglican Baptist & Evangelical One, holy, catholic Church One visible communion of apostolic churches holding the whole faith, as in Cyril of Jerusalem. The congregation of saints, where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered (Augsburg VII). The invisible Church of the elect, and the visible Church of all who profess the true religion (Westminster 25). The visible Church is a congregation of faithful men where the Word is preached and the sacraments duly ministered (Article XIX). Commonly, the universal body of all believers, gathered in local congregations. Apostolic The apostles' faith, worship and ministry, handed down through bishops in succession. Apostolic doctrine.

Some Lutheran churches kept bishops, but succession is not required for a true church. Apostolic doctrine, with government by presbyters (elders). Apostolic doctrine, with the historic episcopate retained. The teaching of the apostles in Scripture; congregational government is common. One baptism for the remission of sins Baptism truly washes away sins and gives new birth; it is never repeated. "Necessary to salvation"; God's grace is offered in it; infants are baptized (Augsburg IX). A sign and seal of the covenant; grace "not so inseparably annexed" to it (Westminster 28.5). A sign of regeneration, by which, "as by an instrument," the baptized are grafted into the Church (Article XXVII). Commonly an ordinance of obedience for believers, signifying a salvation already received by faith. Who proceeds from the Father From the Father, as in 381, with nothing added. "And the Son," in the Western text. "And the Son," in the Western text. "And the Son," in the Western text. Where the Creed is used, usually the Western text.

Authority of the Creed The faith of the Church, confessed by the councils in the Holy Spirit. A true exposition of Scripture, received under it (norma normata, "the ruled rule"). Received because it agrees with Scripture (Belgic IX). Received because it "may be proued by moste certayne warrauntes of holye scripture" (Article VIII). Varies: some churches confess it, others hold to "no creed but the Bible." Positions are summarised from each tradition's principal confessions. Individual churches and theologians vary, especially in the last column, which covers a wide family of churches. Same Words, Different Meanings? Both sides of this question can be put in their strongest form. The Protestant case. The Creed's words are Scripture's words, and Scripture should interpret them. "Catholic" means universal, as Cyril's first definition says, and Protestants confess the universal Church of all believers. The Creed nowhere mentions bishops or succession, and adding them reads later practice into the text.

The Reformers did not think they were leaving the ancient Church; they thought they were recovering it, which is why the Augsburg Confession appeals to the Fathers and Calvin borrows Cyprian's language. And on baptism, the Lutheran and Anglican confessions affirm much of what the Fathers taught. The Orthodox case. A creed means what its confessors meant, and the bishops of 325 and 381 have told us what they meant, in canons written at the same councils. Catechists such as Cyril taught that meaning to the people who first recited the Creed. In that teaching the "Catholic Church" is a visible communion one can find in a city and distinguish from the sects, the Church "in which you were regenerated." The Church that wrote the Creed was episcopal, eucharistic and bounded by canons. And "one baptism for the remission of sins" is Peter's preaching at Pentecost, and the Fathers quoted on this page teach that sins are forgiven in that washing.

To confess the words while identifying the Church by different marks, or while treating baptism as a sign of forgiveness already received, is to give the words a meaning their authors did not give them. Where that leaves the question. No one doubts that Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican Christians confess the Creed sincerely, and on the Trinity and the person of Christ they confess it in the same sense as the Fathers. The disagreement lies in the last paragraph. It is not about whether the words are said, but about whether "Church" and "baptism" are confessed in the sense the councils gave them. The documents above are set out so that readers can make that comparison for themselves.

XIV. Objections Answered The objections below are stated as a thoughtful Protestant would state them. "The Creed never mentions bishops. Reading apostolic succession into 'apostolic' adds to the text." OO Response: The word "apostolic" does not list a church order, and the Orthodox do not claim that it does. But a word in a creed takes its meaning from those who used it. The council that confessed "the Catholic and Apostolic Church" was an assembly of bishops, and its canons regulated their ordination (Section X). Irenaeus and Tertullian, more than a century earlier, had already identified the apostolic churches as those that could show their bishops' succession from the apostles. Succession is never offered as a replacement for apostolic doctrine. Irenaeus appeals to it precisely as the guarantee of doctrine against those who claimed secret teaching. The Orthodox hold the two together as he did: the apostolic faith, kept by churches whose ministry descends from the apostles. "'Catholic' simply means universal.

We confess the universal Church of all true believers." OO Response: Cyril of Jerusalem agrees that "Catholic" means universal, and gives that meaning first. But he goes on to say that it means complete in doctrine, and he tells his hearers to ask in any city "where is the Catholic Church," distinguishing it from other gatherings that also called themselves churches. A universal Church that cannot be found in a city is not the Church Cyril was describing. The Westminster Confession's "invisible" catholic Church may express something true about God's knowledge of His elect. But it is a different category from the Church of the Creed, which the councils treated as a visible body they could govern, define and defend. "'Baptism for the remission of sins' means baptism is a sign of the forgiveness received by faith." OO Response: The phrase comes from Acts 2:38, and Acts 22:16 tells a man who already believed to "be baptized, and wash away your sins." The Fathers quoted on this page, from Justin to Cyril of Jerusalem, teach plainly that forgiveness is given in baptism.

Faith is not set aside. Basil calls faith and baptism "two kindred and inseparable ways of salvation," and Titus 3:5 places the washing of regeneration under God's mercy, "not by works of righteousness which we have done." Baptism is not a human work that competes with grace; it is where grace is given. On this point the Lutheran Augsburg Confession, which calls baptism "necessary to salvation," stands closer to the Creed than many later Protestant readings. "We accept the Creed because it agrees with Scripture. Scripture, not the council, is the authority." OO Response: Cyril says much the same about the Creed's content: its articles were "collected out of all the Scripture," and his hearers should confirm each one from Scripture. Athanasius says the bishops gathered "the sense of the Scriptures." On that there is no quarrel. The difference is who reads Scripture rightly when readers disagree. Arius quoted Scripture too. Nicaea settled the question by a council of bishops speaking for the Church, and that is the authority the Creed itself rests on.

A Christian who accepts the homoousios because the council read Scripture correctly has already granted that the Church can read Scripture rightly in council. The question is why that authority should stop at the Trinity and not extend to the articles on the Church and baptism that the same councils confessed. "The Orthodox recite the Creed but add teachings it never mentions, such as icons and the intercession of the saints." OO Response: The Creed was never meant to list every teaching. It settled the questions disputed at the time, chiefly the divinity of the Son and of the Spirit. Some things the Orthodox confess follow directly from its words: the Virgin is Theotokos because the one "incarnate of the Holy Spirit and of the Virgin Mary" is the eternal Son. For the rest, St.

Basil, writing a few years before the Council of 381, distinguishes teaching "derived from written teaching" from what the Church has "received delivered to us in a mystery by the tradition of the apostles," and says that "both of these in relation to true religion have the same force." The Creed was received within that same Church, alongside her worship and her unwritten tradition, not as a fence around them. See Sola Scriptura and Icon Veneration .

XV. Frequently Asked Questions Why does the Coptic Creed say "we believe" when many Western churches say "I believe"? The councils wrote in the plural: Πιστεύομεν, "we believe." The Latin liturgical text later used Credo , "I believe," and many Western translations follow it. The plural expresses what the Creed is: the confession of the Church gathered together, said with one voice. Does "Catholic" in the Creed mean the Roman Catholic Church? No. The word was used of the Church from the early second century, centuries before the division of East and West. The Oriental Orthodox confess it at every liturgy, and some Coptic English translations add "(Universal)" after it to make the meaning clear. Why is there no "and the Son" in the Coptic Creed? Because it is not in the text of 381, and the Council of Ephesus forbade any rival form of the faith of Nicaea. The addition arose later in the West. See The Filioque . Do the Oriental Orthodox use the Apostles' Creed? The Apostles' Creed is a Western baptismal creed that grew from the ancient creed of the Church of Rome.

The Oriental Orthodox Churches use the Creed of Nicaea and Constantinople in their liturgy and prayers. When is the Creed said in Coptic worship? The people say it together in the Divine Liturgy, before the Prayer of Reconciliation, and it is prayed in the hours of the Agpeya, preceded by the Introduction to the Creed. Who wrote the Introduction to the Creed? Coptic tradition associates it with the Council of Ephesus in 431, which upheld the title Theotokos. Whatever its exact origin, it has long stood before the Creed in Coptic prayer, so that the Church honours the Mother of God before confessing the incarnation of her Son. Can a Protestant say the Creed in good conscience? Many do, sincerely, and on the Trinity and the person of Christ they confess what the councils confessed. This page offers a test any reader can apply: read Cyril of Jerusalem's lectures on the Church and on baptism, written for people about to say the Creed for the first time, and ask whether you believe what Cyril taught them the words mean.

Where should I start reading? Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lecture 18 on the last articles of the Creed, then Lecture 3 on baptism. Both are in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, volume 7, and freely available online.

One Communion, Six Churches The Oriental Orthodox are not a single centralized body but a communion of six autocephalous (self-governing) churches, each with its own patriarch or catholicos, its own liturgical language, and its own ancient culture — yet all confessing one faith, sharing one sacramental life, and recognizing one another’s mysteries fully. What unites them is the Christology of St. Cyril (see Miaphysite Christology → ) and the first three ecumenical councils. Coptic Orthodox See of Alexandria, founded by St. Mark. Egypt. Liturgy in Coptic & Arabic. The cradle of Christian monasticism. Syriac Orthodox See of Antioch, where believers were first called Christians. Aramaic/Syriac liturgy. Home of St. Ephrem. Armenian Apostolic Founded by Sts. Thaddeus & Bartholomew. Armenia was the first nation to adopt Christianity as its state religion. Ethiopian Tewahedo Ancient Christianity in the Horn of Africa. Ge'ez liturgy. The broadest biblical canon in Christendom (81 books). Eritrean Tewahedo Sister church to the Ethiopian, granted autocephaly in 1994.

Shares the Ge'ez liturgical tradition. Malankara (India) The St. Thomas Christians of Kerala, tracing their origin to the Apostle Thomas (A.D. 52). Syriac heritage. The word Tewahedo (Ge’ez for “made one, unified”) in the Ethiopian and Eritrean names is itself a confession of the miaphysite faith: the one united nature of the incarnate Word.

The Coptic Orthodox Church The Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria traces its foundation to St. Mark the Evangelist , who according to tradition preached in Egypt and was martyred in Alexandria around A.D. 68. Its head bears the title Pope and Patriarch of Alexandria — a title older than the Roman use of “Pope.” From the See of Alexandria came giants of the whole Church: St. Athanasius, defender of the Nicene faith, and St. Cyril, champion of the Theotokos at Ephesus. Egypt is the birthplace of Christian monasticism . St. Antony the Great went into the desert around A.D. 270; St. Pachomius founded communal monasticism; the deserts of Scetis and Nitria filled with the Desert Fathers whose sayings still guide Christians of every tradition. See Monasticism → . St. Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373) The Life of Antony — the account that carried the monastic ideal across the whole Christian world.

Life of Antony — the founding text of Christian monasticism Paraphrase The Coptic Church has survived under Islamic rule since the seventh century with remarkable endurance, keeping its own calendar (the Era of the Martyrs, dated from Diocletian’s persecution) as a permanent memorial of what it has cost to remain faithful.

The Armenian Apostolic Church Armenia holds a unique honour: it was the first nation in the world to adopt Christianity as its state religion , traditionally in A.D. 301, when St. Gregory the Illuminator baptized King Tiridates III. The church traces its apostolic roots to Sts. Thaddeus and Bartholomew, which is why it is called “Apostolic.” Its spiritual centre is Holy Etchmiadzin, and its head bears the title Catholicos of All Armenians. In the early fifth century St. Mesrop Mashtots invented the Armenian alphabet expressly so that Scripture and the liturgy could be given to the people in their own tongue — one of the great acts of Christian literacy in history. The Armenian Genocide (1915) During the First World War, the Ottoman Empire deported and killed an estimated one million to 1.5 million Armenian Christians . It was one of the first genocides of the modern age and remains central to Armenian identity. The Armenian Church has canonized the victims as martyrs of the faith. To be Armenian Orthodox is, in large part, to remember.

The Ethiopian & Eritrean Tewahedo Churches Christianity reached the Kingdom of Aksum (modern Ethiopia and Eritrea) in the fourth century, when St. Frumentius converted King Ezana — making Ethiopia one of the earliest Christian states on earth. But Ethiopian tradition reaches back further still, to the Ethiopian eunuch baptized by the Apostle Philip ( Acts 8:26-39 ) and to ancient ties with Israel. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church preserves the broadest biblical canon in all of Christendom — 81 books , including works treasured nowhere else as Scripture, such as 1 Enoch, Jubilees, and the books of Meqabyan. It keeps a strong sense of Old Testament continuity: a rich fasting discipline, distinctions once tied to Levitical practice, and in every church a tabot (a replica of the Ark of the Covenant) without which the building is not consecrated. The Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church , sharing the same Ge’ez liturgical heritage, was granted autocephaly in 1994 following Eritrea’s national independence. The two churches remain sisters in faith and tradition.

The Syriac & Malankara Churches The Syriac Orthodox Church is heir to the ancient See of Antioch — the very city where, as the Book of Acts records, “the disciples were first called Christians” ( Acts 11:26 ). Its liturgy is celebrated in Syriac, a dialect of Aramaic close to the language Christ himself spoke. From this tradition comes St. Ephrem the Syrian (d. 373), the “Harp of the Spirit,” whose hymns are among the treasures of the whole Church. St. Ephrem the Syrian (d. 373) The Nisibene Hymns — poetry that taught theology through song, sung to this day in the Syriac tradition. Nisibene Hymns — the great hymnographer of the Syriac Church Paraphrase Far to the east, the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church of Kerala, India, traces its origin to the Apostle St. Thomas , who according to firm local tradition landed on the Malabar coast in A.D. 52 and planted the faith among communities that endure to this day. Historically linked to the Syriac tradition of Antioch, the St. Thomas Christians are living proof that the Church of the East reached India long before it reached much of Europe.

A Church of the Martyrs More than any other Christian family, the Oriental Orthodox understand themselves through martyrdom. The Coptic calendar itself is dated from the Great Persecution under Diocletian. The Armenians remember 1915. And in our own time the witness has continued. The 21 Martyrs of Libya (2015) In February 2015, twenty-one Christian workers were beheaded on a Libyan beach by ISIS for refusing to deny Christ. Twenty were Coptic Egyptians; the twenty-first, a man from Ghana, watched their faith and reportedly declared, “Their God is my God” — and died with them. The Coptic Orthodox Church canonized all twenty-one and added them to its Synaxarium within weeks. Their images now stand in Coptic churches as icons of a faith worth dying for.

“Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Matthew 5:10 — the beatitude the Oriental Orthodox have lived out for centuries To love these churches is to love a faith that has been tested by fire and has not been consumed — the lamp still burning in Egypt, in Armenia, in Ethiopia, in Syria, and in India.

FAQ How many Oriental Orthodox churches are there? Six autocephalous (self-governing) churches in full communion with one another: the Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria, the Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch, the Armenian Apostolic Church, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and the Malankara (Indian) Orthodox Syrian Church. Together they number roughly 60 to 80 million faithful (estimates vary widely). Are the Oriental Orthodox the same as the Eastern Orthodox? No, though the names are similar and both are ancient, apostolic, and non-papal. The Eastern Orthodox (Greek, Russian, Serbian, etc.) accept the Council of Chalcedon (451); the Oriental Orthodox accept only the first three ecumenical councils. The two families are not currently in sacramental communion, though modern dialogue has found their Christological faith to be substantially the same. Why are they called Oriental Orthodox? Oriental simply means eastern, and the term distinguishes this family of pre-Chalcedonian churches from the Eastern (Byzantine) Orthodox.

They are also called the Non-Chalcedonian, Pre-Chalcedonian, or Miaphysite churches. Each church usually prefers its own name (Coptic, Armenian, and so on). What holds these different churches together? One shared faith. Despite worshipping in Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ge'ez, and Malayalam, and spanning Egypt, the Middle East, the Caucasus, the Horn of Africa, and India, all six confess the same Miaphysite Christology of St. Cyril, accept the same first three councils, share the same sacramental life, and recognise one another's orders and mysteries fully. Is it true these are churches of martyrs? Profoundly so, in both ancient and modern times. The Armenian Genocide of 1915 killed somewhere between about one million and 1.5 million; the Coptic Church has endured centuries of pressure and, in 2015, canonised 21 men beheaded in Libya. Persecution of Christians in Egypt, Syria, Ethiopia, and Armenia continues. The Oriental Orthodox often describe themselves as the Church of the martyrs.

secs.h: Apostolic Origins — How Each Church Was Founded
secs.x: Apostolic Origins — How Each Church Was Founded Each of the Oriental Orthodox churches traces its founding directly to an apostle or apostolic figure of the first century. Some of these foundations are well attested in early writers; others rest on ancient tradition that the churches have handed down. Coptic Church — Egypt Founded by St. Mark the Evangelist, c. AD 42–68. Mark arrived in Alexandria — then the second city of the Roman Empire and its intellectual capital — and healed a cobbler named Anianus, who became the first convert. Mark established what Coptic tradition holds to be the first Christian school in history: the Catechetical School of Alexandria, which would become the greatest intellectual institution of the ancient Church. According to tradition he was martyred in Alexandria in AD 68, dragged through the streets with a rope around his neck. Ethiopian Church Biblical roots: Acts 8:26–40. The Ethiopian eunuch, treasurer of Queen Candace, was baptized by Philip the Evangelist on his return from Jerusalem.

secs.h: Apostolic Origins — How Each Church Was Founded
secs.x: He is often counted among the first Gentile converts, though he may already have been a worshipper of the God of Israel. The Church formally established c. AD 330 when King Ezana of Aksum was converted by St. Frumentius (Abba Salama), who was consecrated bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria. Aksum became one of the first Christian kingdoms in history, alongside Armenia and Georgia. Armenian Church Founded by Sts. Thaddeus and Bartholomew, 1st century AD. The apostles Thaddeus (Jude) and Bartholomew preached in Armenia and were both martyred there. The Church was formally established as a state religion in AD 301 when King Tiridates III was baptized by St. Gregory the Illuminator , making Armenia the first nation in history to adopt Christianity as its official religion (301 is the traditional date; some historians prefer 314). Syriac Orthodox Church Apostolic see of Antioch, founded 1st century AD. The church of Antioch is described in Acts as the place where disciples were first called “Christians” (Acts 11:26). Its first bishop was St. Peter the Apostle , followed by St.

secs.h: Apostolic Origins — How Each Church Was Founded
secs.x: Evodius and then St. Ignatius. The Syriac Orthodox Church considers itself the direct continuation of the original Antiochene see, preserving the apostolic tradition of Syria and Mesopotamia in Syriac, a dialect of Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke. Malankara / Indian Church Founded by St. Thomas the Apostle, AD 52. Thomas traveled to Kerala (southwest India) and established seven churches — the Ezharappallikal (seven and a half churches). He was martyred near Madras (Chennai) around AD 72. The Thomas Christians of Kerala are one of the oldest continuous Christian communities on earth, maintaining their apostolic identity through 2,000 years of Indian history. Their tradition predates the arrival of Western Christianity in India by some 1,450 years. For most of their history they looked to the Church of the East (East Syriac) for bishops; after the Coonan Cross Oath of 1653, in which many rejected Portuguese Latinization, part of the community received bishops from the Syriac Orthodox Church (from 1665), which is how they entered the Oriental Orthodox family.

secs.h: Apostolic Origins — How Each Church Was Founded
secs.x: “…the eunuch said, ‘See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?’ And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.” — Acts 8:36 –38

secs.h: The Alexandrian School — Golden Age of Theology
secs.x: The Alexandrian School — Golden Age of Theology The Catechetical School of Alexandria, founded by St. Mark and developed through the 2nd–5th centuries, was the intellectual engine of the entire early Church. Its teachers produced the most profound theological writings of Christian antiquity and shaped every subsequent tradition — Catholic, Protestant, and Orthodox alike. c. AD 42 Tradition: St. Mark Founds the School Tradition credits Mark with founding the first Christian educational institution in Alexandria, the Roman Empire’s center of learning. The school’s mission: training catechumens in both scripture and philosophy, engaging the educated pagan world on its own terms. c. AD 160–180 Pantaenus — First Named Head Pantaenus, a former Stoic philosopher, becomes head of the school. According to Eusebius, he traveled as far as India to preach the Gospel and found a community using a Hebrew copy of Matthew’s Gospel, brought earlier by Bartholomew. c.

secs.h: The Alexandrian School — Golden Age of Theology
secs.x: AD 180–202 Clement of Alexandria Clement makes the first systematic attempt to bring Greek philosophy into dialogue with Christian theology. His trilogy — Protrepticus, Paedagogus, Stromata — argues that Greek philosophy was a preparation for the Gospel, as the Law was for the Jews. He quotes some 350 classical authors, demonstrating that Christianity need not fear intellectual engagement. c. AD 202–232 Origen — The Greatest Scholar Origen produces the Hexapla (six-column Bible comparing OT texts), writes the first systematic theology ( On First Principles ), produces commentaries on nearly every biblical book, and does more than anyone to establish the allegorical method of interpretation that shaped biblical exegesis for a thousand years. Some of his speculations, such as the pre-existence of souls, were later condemned. He traveled the known world, corresponded with emperors, and attracted students from across the Empire. His influence on Athanasius, the Cappadocians, and Jerome is incalculable.

secs.h: The Alexandrian School — Golden Age of Theology
secs.x: AD 328–373 Athanasius — Champion of Orthodoxy Athanasius becomes Patriarch of Alexandria at age 30 and spends his life defending the full divinity of Christ against Arianism. Exiled five times by four different emperors, he holds firm when much of the imperial church gives way to Arian formulas — later summed up in the phrase Athanasius contra mundum (Athanasius against the world). He also writes the Life of Anthony , which spreads the monastic ideal across the Christian world. AD 412–444 Cyril of Alexandria — Seal of the Fathers Cyril fights the Nestorian heresy (which divided Christ into two persons) and secures the title Theotokos (God-bearer) for the Virgin Mary at the Council of Ephesus in 431. His Christological writings — twelve anathemas against Nestorius — define the miaphysite understanding that the OO tradition carries to the present day. He is called the “Seal of the Fathers.” Origen of Alexandria c. 185–253 AD “According to strict truth, God is incomprehensible, and incapable of being measured.

secs.h: The Alexandrian School — Golden Age of Theology
secs.x: For whatever be the knowledge which we are able to obtain of God, either by perception or reflection, we must of necessity believe that He is by many degrees far better than what we perceive Him to be” ( On First Principles I.1.5). Origen’s vision of theology as endless ascent toward God shaped the Alexandrian school. In honesty, some of his speculations were condemned after his death, and the Coptic Church does not venerate him as a saint. St. Athanasius of Alexandria 296–373 AD Jerome described the moment after the Council of Ariminum (359): “The whole world groaned, and was astonished to find itself Arian” ( Dialogue against the Luciferians 19). Athanasius held to the Nicene faith through all of it. The famous phrase “Athanasius against the world” ( Athanasius contra mundum ) is a later summary of his stand, not his own words. Exiled five times by four emperors, he was restored each time and died in his own see in 373. St.

secs.h: The Alexandrian School — Golden Age of Theology
secs.x: Cyril of Alexandria 376–444 AD “Confessing the Word to be made one with the flesh according to substance, we adore one Son and Lord Jesus Christ: we do not divide the God from the man” ( Third Letter to Nestorius ). Cyril’s formula “one nature of God the Word incarnate” ( mia physis ) is the cornerstone of Oriental Orthodox Christology. Cyril received it as a saying of Athanasius; modern scholars have shown it came from a text circulated under Athanasius’ name. The Council of Ephesus upheld Cyril against Nestorius in 431.

secs.h: The Era of Martyrs — Diocletian's Persecution
secs.x: The Era of Martyrs — Diocletian's Persecution Few persecutions in Roman history equaled in ferocity what the Great Persecution, begun by Diocletian in AD 303, brought on the Christians of Egypt (the Coptic calendar counts from 284, the year Diocletian became emperor, for symbolic reasons). The numbers preserved in Coptic tradition are staggering: the Coptic Church remembers hundreds of thousands of martyrs from Diocletian’s reign — traditional counts reach 800,000 — while modern historians give far lower figures, though all agree the persecution in Egypt was exceptionally severe. The martyrs died — beheaded, burned, crucified, drowned, and tortured in every conceivable way across Egypt and North Africa. The Coptic Calendar (Anno Martyrum): The Coptic Church counts its years from AD 284 — the year Diocletian came to power. It is called the Era of the Martyrs (AM). The Coptic year that that began in September 2026 is 1743 AM. This is not merely a historical curiosity; it is a theological statement that the identity of the Coptic Church is inseparable from the blood of its martyrs.

secs.h: The Era of Martyrs — Diocletian's Persecution
secs.x: The Scale of the Persecution Diocletian’s Great Persecution (AD 303–311) demanded that all Christians hand over their scriptures for burning (giving rise to the word “traditor” — traitor — for those who complied, and to the later Donatist controversy). Churches were demolished. Clergy were imprisoned and tortured until they sacrificed to Roman gods. Eusebius, who was there, describes the Thebaid in Upper Egypt: "Sometimes more than ten, at other times above twenty were put to death. Again not less than thirty, then about sixty, and yet again a hundred men with young children and women, were slain in one day" (Church History 8.9.3). Coptic tradition remembers the martyrs of Esna, a whole town put to death. “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” — Revelation 2:10 The Holy Family in Egypt The Coptic Church also preserves the tradition of the Holy Family’s flight into Egypt (Matthew 2:13–15), tracing a detailed route through Egyptian towns where Jesus, Mary, and Joseph stayed.

secs.h: The Era of Martyrs — Diocletian's Persecution
secs.x: Every site along the route — from Sinai to Assiut — became a center of Christian community. The prophecy of Isaiah 19:19 (“In that day there will be an altar to the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt”) is read by Copts as fulfilled in this journey. Egypt was prepared to receive the Messiah — and later to die for him. St. Peter of Alexandria d. AD 311 The last Patriarch of Alexandria martyred under the Great Persecution. Called the “Seal of the Martyrs,” Peter was beheaded outside the city in 311. He had pastored a church living under threat of death, writing canons on how to receive those who had lapsed under torture, with precision and mercy. The Coptic Church commemorates him on 29 Hatour. St. Menas of Egypt d. c. AD 296 or 309 An Egyptian soldier in the Roman army who publicly declared his Christianity and was executed under the Great Persecution (traditionally c. 296 or 309). His shrine at Abu Mena, southwest of Alexandria, became one of the great pilgrimage sites of the ancient world, and later emperors enlarged its basilica.

secs.h: The Era of Martyrs — Diocletian's Persecution
secs.x: Thousands of small clay flasks stamped with his image, carried home by pilgrims, have been found all over the Mediterranean world and beyond.

secs.h: The Council of Chalcedon (451) — The Defining Schism
secs.x: The Council of Chalcedon (451) — The Defining Schism The Council of Chalcedon in AD 451 is the event that divided the Christian East and has defined the Oriental Orthodox identity ever since. Understanding what happened there — and what was actually at stake — is essential for understanding the OO tradition. The Background The Council of Ephesus (431) had vindicated Cyril of Alexandria’s Christology against Nestorius: Christ is one person, not two. But within decades, a monk named Eutyches went too far in the opposite direction, teaching that Christ’s humanity was absorbed into his divinity a view later pictured as a drop of vinegar dissolved in the sea. Patriarch Flavian of Constantinople condemned Eutyches. At a council in Ephesus in 449 the Alexandrian Patriarch Dioscorus, Cyril’s successor, accepted Eutyches’ profession of faith and restored him; OO tradition holds that Eutyches deceived the council, and the OO churches later condemned him.

secs.h: The Council of Chalcedon (451) — The Defining Schism
secs.x: Flavian was deposed and died soon after, having been roughly treated; Chalcedonian sources blame Dioscorus, while OO tradition denies that he ordered any violence. Pope Leo I called the council a “Robber Synod.” The Council and Its Formula Emperor Marcian called a new council at Chalcedon in 451. The council deposed Dioscorus and defined Christ as having two natures (divine and human) in one person, united “without confusion, without change, without division, without separation” (the four adverbs). The Oriental Orthodox churches rejected this formula — not because they believed in Eutyches’ error — but because they believed it contradicted the Cyrillian formula they had always confessed: one nature of the incarnate Word ( mia physis tou Theou Logou sesarkomene ). The Christological Position: The Oriental Orthodox are miaphysites — they confess one united nature in Christ, divine and human, without separation or confusion.

secs.h: The Council of Chalcedon (451) — The Defining Schism
secs.x: This is not Eutychianism (which collapsed the human into the divine) but a different philosophical framework for expressing the same mystery that Chalcedon was trying to define. As the 1990 Agreed Statement between OO and EO affirms: both families confess the same Christ — the separation was a tragedy of terminology, politics, and mutual misunderstanding. Dioscorus of Alexandria Dioscorus was deposed at Chalcedon and exiled to Gangra in Paphlagonia, where he died in AD 454. The Oriental Orthodox tradition venerates him as a confessor — one who suffered for the faith. Formally he was deposed for procedural reasons, such as refusing to appear when summoned, rather than for heresy; in Chalcedonian eyes his fault was shielding Eutyches. His defense, in OO eyes, was defending the Cyrillian theology he had received. The deposition of Dioscorus was the moment the Oriental Orthodox churches became a distinct family. St. Severus of Antioch c.

secs.h: The Council of Chalcedon (451) — The Defining Schism
secs.x: 465–538 AD Severus defended “one nature of God the Word incarnate” as the teaching of Cyril, not of Eutyches, and insisted that Christ’s divinity and humanity remain complete in their union. (Summary, not a quotation.) He became the greatest theological defender of the Oriental Orthodox position after Chalcedon. He wrote thousands of letters, of which some three hundred survive in Syriac, along with 125 cathedral homilies. Deposed under the Chalcedonian Emperor Justin I in 518, he died in exile in Egypt in 538, and his theology became the doctrinal foundation of the OO churches. Patriarch Dioscorus of Alexandria d. AD 454 Deposed at Chalcedon, Dioscorus spent his last three years in exile at Gangra in Paphlagonia, where he died in 454 without recanting. His steadfastness set the pattern of holy resistance that the OO churches would follow through every later persecution. (No sayings from his exile are quoted here, since those that circulate cannot be traced to early sources.)

secs.h: Byzantine Persecution — The Church Under Imperial Pressure
secs.x: Byzantine Persecution — The Church Under Imperial Pressure After Chalcedon, the Byzantine Empire launched a sustained effort to impose the Chalcedonian formula on the Oriental Orthodox populations of Egypt, Syria, and Palestine. What followed was more than a century of theological persecution — bishops deposed, replaced by imperial appointees, populations coerced — that left permanent wounds. The Henotikon and Its Failure (AD 482–519) Emperor Zeno attempted a compromise formula — the Henotikon — which affirmed Cyril and condemned both Nestorius and Eutyches without endorsing Chalcedon. It satisfied no one: Rome broke communion with Constantinople (the Acacian Schism, 484–519), and while many Oriental Orthodox, including Severus, accepted it as a basis for communion, the stricter party rejected it as insufficient. The attempt to paper over theological differences with vague imperial formulae failed completely.

secs.h: Byzantine Persecution — The Church Under Imperial Pressure
secs.x: The Dual Hierarchies The most damaging consequence of the post-Chalcedon period was the installation of parallel Chalcedonian patriarchs alongside the Oriental Orthodox patriarchs. In Alexandria, Egypt had simultaneously a Coptic patriarch and an imperial “Melkite” (king’s man) patriarch — two claimants to the same see. The same occurred in Antioch. This created centuries of conflict, property disputes, and occasional violence. The Coptic faithful remained stubbornly loyal to their own patriarch, resisting imperial pressure at great personal cost. Emperor Justinian's Persecutions (527–565) Justinian I — who also built the Hagia Sophia — was the most aggressive persecutor of the Oriental Orthodox churches. He deposed and exiled multiple Oriental Orthodox patriarchs, used force to install a Chalcedonian patriarch in Alexandria, and drove non-Chalcedonian monks from their monasteries, especially in Syria.

secs.h: Byzantine Persecution — The Church Under Imperial Pressure
secs.x: His wife, the Empress Theodora, openly favored the Oriental Orthodox — a fact that gave the OO churches some protection and enabled the eventual consecration of miaphysite bishops for Syria, creating what became the Syriac Orthodox Church’s episcopal succession under Jacob Baradaeus. Jacob Baradaeus (c. 500–578 AD): A monk who was secretly consecrated bishop and spent four decades traveling in disguise across Syria, Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Arabia — ordaining hundreds of priests and bishops for the Oriental Orthodox under Byzantine noses. He is single-handedly credited with saving the Syriac Orthodox Church from extinction under Justinian’s persecution. Outsiders long called the Syriac Orthodox Church “Jacobite” after him, a name the church itself rejects, since it was not founded by Jacob.

The Arab Conquest — Islam Arrives (AD 639–641) In AD 639, Arab armies under General Amr ibn al-As invaded Byzantine Egypt. By 641 the Byzantine garrison at Alexandria had agreed to surrender and Egypt — largely Christian for three centuries — passed into Arab hands. The conquest was swift, and its consequences for the Oriental Orthodox churches were permanent and transformative. Why Copts Initially Welcomed the Arabs: After a century and a half of Byzantine theological persecution — coercion, exiled patriarchs, murdered monks — many Egyptian Christians saw the Arab conquest as liberation from a Christian empire that had treated them as heretics. Patriarch Benjamin I of Alexandria, who had spent thirteen years hiding in the desert to escape the Byzantines, came out of hiding to cooperate with Amr ibn al-As.
