secs.x: read in the church and its confessions Critics point to division; Protestants answer that unity lies in the gospel, not in structures The OO see their model as a middle way between the Roman claim of one-man universal authority and the Protestant placing of all church authority under Scripture alone. The Church is visibly structured, episcopally governed, and conciliarly defined — but no single bishop stands as monarch over his peers.

secs.h: Vatican I (1870) and Pastor Aeternus — The Formal Definition
secs.x: Vatican I (1870) and Pastor Aeternus — The Formal Definition The First Vatican Council (1869–1870), convened by Pope Pius IX, formally defined two dogmas that the OO regard as innovations departing from Apostolic tradition: universal papal jurisdiction and papal infallibility. The defining document is Pastor Aeternus ("The Eternal Pastor"), promulgated July 18, 1870 — one day before the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War that ended the council prematurely. The Definition of Papal Infallibility — Pastor Aeternus, Chapter IV "We teach and define as a divinely revealed dogma that when the Roman Pontiff speaks EX CATHEDRA, that is, when, in the exercise of his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, he possesses, by the divine assistance promised to him in blessed Peter, that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his Church to enjoy in defining doctrine concerning faith or morals.

secs.h: Vatican I (1870) and Pastor Aeternus — The Formal Definition
secs.x: Therefore, such definitions of the Roman Pontiff are of themselves, and not by the consent of the Church, irreformable." Condition 1: Ex Cathedra Must speak "from the chair" — in his official capacity as universal teacher, not in personal theological opinion or ordinary teaching. Condition 2: Faith or Morals Must be defining a doctrine on faith (what to believe) or morals (how to act) — not on history, science, politics, or prudential matters. Condition 3: For Universal Church Must explicitly bind the entire universal Church — not merely a local church or a particular group. Condition 4: Irreformable "Not by the consent of the Church" — the definition is not subject to correction or revision by any council, synod, or gathering. It stands on its own. It is important to note what papal infallibility does not claim: it does not claim the Pope is personally sinless, personally impeccable, or incapable of error in ordinary teaching, political judgment, or private theological opinion. The conditions are narrow.

secs.h: Vatican I (1870) and Pastor Aeternus — The Formal Definition
secs.x: Most Roman Catholic theologians agree on only two clear cases of ex cathedra definition: the Immaculate Conception (1854, before Vatican I) and the Assumption of Mary (1950). OO response: Even granting the narrow conditions, the claim that any single bishop — however ancient his see — can define doctrine "not by the consent of the Church" and have it stand "irreformable" is irreconcilable with the conciliar model the OO find in Scripture (Acts 15), in the Fathers (Irenaeus, Cyprian, Basil), and in the pre-schismatic councils. The problem is not the conditions but the principle itself.

secs.h: What Infallibility Claims — and What It Implies
secs.x: What Infallibility Claims — and What It Implies The doctrine of papal infallibility is grounded in Luke 22:32 — Christ's prayer that Peter's "faith may not fail" — and in the general promise of the Spirit guiding the Church into all truth (John 16:13). Rome applies these promises to the Petrine office in a specific, formal way. The OO analysis examines whether this application is exegetically or historically warranted. Luke 22:32 — Rome's Primary Proof Text "But I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers." Roman Catholic reading: Christ's prayer guarantees that Peter's successors, when defining doctrine for the whole Church, will not err in matters of faith. OO reading: (1) The prayer is to Peter personally in an immediate crisis — his approaching denial. (2) "When you have turned again" implies Peter will fall first, then recover. (3) The prayer preserves Peter's ultimate faith, not his magisterial pronouncements.

secs.h: What Infallibility Claims — and What It Implies
secs.x: (4) There is nothing in the text about "successors" — the transfer of this prayer's guarantee to a Roman episcopal succession requires enormous exegetical weight placed on a text that cannot bear it. Roman Catholic Reading Oriental Orthodox Reading More fundamentally, the OO observe that the promise of John 16:13 — "He will guide you into all truth" — is made to the Apostles collectively, not to Peter alone. The Spirit's guidance is ecclesial and conciliar, not concentrated in one office. If Luke 22:32 grounds infallibility for Peter's successors, then John 16:13 grounds it for the whole college of bishops — which is precisely the conciliar model the OO embrace. The Oriental Orthodox accept the Church's indefectibility — she will not permanently and definitively err in defining the Apostolic faith. What we deny is that this indefectibility belongs to any one bishop as a personal charism of his office. The Spirit guards the Church; He does not attach Himself to a chair in Rome as a guarantee for whoever sits in it.

Historical Problems for Papal Infallibility The history of the papacy presents several cases that create severe difficulties for the doctrine of infallibility — even granting its narrow conditions. Roman Catholic apologists have responses to each, but those responses involve significant interpretive gymnastics that the OO find unconvincing. Pope Honorius I Pontificate: 625–638 AD Honorius corresponded with Sergius, Patriarch of Constantinople, in a way that supported Monothelitism — the heresy that Christ has only one will. He wrote that "we confess one will of our Lord Jesus Christ," and advised that the dispute over "one or two operations" be dropped as a question of words. The Third Council of Constantinople (681 AD) — the Sixth Ecumenical Council — formally condemned Honorius as a heretic. Subsequent popes (Leo II, Adrian II) confirmed this condemnation. His name was anathematized in the official council acts. Condemned as heretic by Ecumenical Council Pope Vigilius Pontificate: 537–555 AD Vigilius was notoriously inconsistent during the Three Chapters controversy.

He issued his Iudicatum in 548, condemning writings condemned by Emperor Justinian. He then withdrew it. He issued a Constitutum in 553 forbidding condemnation of the Three Chapters. He then reversed course entirely, accepting the condemnation at Constantinople II. His zigzag behavior shows a pope contradicting himself in areas touching doctrine and authority under imperial pressure. Severe doctrinal inconsistency under pressure Pope Liberius Pontificate: 352–366 AD Under pressure from the Emperor Constantius II, after two years of exile, Liberius signed a compromise creed and abandoned communion with Athanasius, the champion of Nicene orthodoxy. Athanasius and Jerome both record his lapse. Which formula he signed is debated, and he later returned to the Nicene faith; he is not commemorated as a saint in the Roman calendar, though the Eastern Orthodox do commemorate him.

Signed Arian formula under imperial pressure The Three-Pope Schism 1378–1417 AD — The Western Schism For nearly 40 years, the Catholic West had two — and at times three — simultaneous claimants to the papacy, each excommunicating the other. The Council of Constance (1414–1418) resolved the crisis by deposing two claimants (John XXIII and Benedict XIII), accepting the resignation of the third (Gregory XII), and electing Martin V. Catholics reply that Gregory XII was the true pope and formally convoked the council before resigning, so that Constance acted with papal authority. Even so, if the Pope is the supreme authority over councils, how did a council depose popes? And which of the three was the "infallible" voice during the schism? Council deposed competing popes — conciliarism over papalism Galileo Affair 1616 and 1633 AD In 1616 the theologians of the Holy Office declared heliocentrism "formally heretical," and in 1633 the Inquisition under Pope Urban VIII condemned Galileo as "vehemently suspected of heresy." Catholic apologists argue this was not an ex cathedra definition.

This is probably correct technically, but the condemnation shows the magisterium making confident pronouncements on matters it later reversed — which raises questions about the practical reliability of the teaching office regardless of technical infallibility categories. Not ex cathedra — but illustrates ordinary magisterium error Immaculate Conception (1854) Pius IX — Ineffabilis Deus The first papal definition often cited as ex cathedra. Defined that Mary was conceived without original sin. Bernard of Clairvaux, Thomas Aquinas, and Bonaventure — pillars of Western theology — all denied or doubted this doctrine. If it was always the faith of the Church, why did its greatest theologians reject it? The OO regard this as genuine doctrinal innovation, not recovery of ancient truth. Denied by Aquinas and Bernard — is it truly ancient tradition?

secs.h: Pope Honorius — Condemned as a Heretic by an Ecumenical Council
secs.x: Pope Honorius — Condemned as a Heretic by an Ecumenical Council The case of Pope Honorius I deserves extended treatment because it is, for the OO (and for Eastern Orthodoxy), the single most devastating historical challenge to papal infallibility. It is not a matter of Protestant polemic — it is the documented verdict of the Sixth Ecumenical Council, confirmed by successive popes. The Third Council of Constantinople (680–681 AD) — Condemnation of Honorius "And with these we define that there shall be expelled from the holy Church of God and anathematized Honorius who was some time Pope of Old Rome, because of what we found written by him to Sergius, that in all respects he followed his view and confirmed his impious doctrines." This is not a local council's opinion — it is the sixth ecumenical council's formal doctrinal verdict, accepted by East and West. Honorius was not condemned merely for imprudence or bad governance. He was anathematized — cast out — for doctrinal error on a matter of Christology (the number of Christ's wills).

secs.h: Pope Honorius — Condemned as a Heretic by an Ecumenical Council
secs.x: Ecumenical Council, 681 AD Christology — Monothelitism Pope Leo II (Confirming the Condemnation) 682 AD — Letter to Emperor Constantine IV Summary: Leo II anathematizes the authors of the new error, Theodore of Pharan, Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul and Peter, and with them Honorius, who, he says, did not keep the apostolic Church pure with the teaching of apostolic tradition but allowed it to be defiled. In his letter to the bishops of Spain he says Honorius failed, as befitted apostolic authority, to put out the flame of heresy at its beginning, and instead fed it by his negligence. Leo II — a Pope condemning his predecessor as one who "permitted" doctrinal pollution. Rome herself confirmed Honorius's condemnation. The Papal Oath (Until 11th Century) Pre-11th Century Summary: New popes, upon consecration, swore an oath that named Honorius among those condemned, as one who had encouraged the heretics' assertions. The condemnation of Honorius was built into the papal consecration oath for centuries.

secs.h: Pope Honorius — Condemned as a Heretic by an Ecumenical Council
secs.x: Liber Diurnus Romanorum Pontificum — the official Roman papal formula book The dilemma for Vatican I: If a pope can be condemned as a heretic by an ecumenical council (a council confirmed by subsequent popes), then either: (a) Honorius was not speaking ex cathedra when he wrote to Sergius — in which case, the conditions for infallibility are so narrow as to be nearly useless in practice; or (b) the doctrine of infallibility was simply unknown to the Church of the 7th century, whose greatest ecumenical council had no problem condemning a deceased pope for heresy. The OO find both options damaging to the Roman case. Roman Catholic apologists respond that Honorius was condemned for moral negligence rather than formal heresy, and that his letters to Sergius were private correspondence, not ex cathedra definitions. The OO note that the council's language ("in all respects he followed his view and confirmed his impious doctrines") reads as doctrinal condemnation, not mere negligence.

secs.h: Pope Honorius — Condemned as a Heretic by an Ecumenical Council
secs.x: And if the Church's "infallible" office cannot even communicate clearly enough for the Church to recognize when he is speaking infallibly versus negligently, the practical value of the doctrine is severely diminished.

secs.h: The OO Response to Papal Infallibility — A Systematic Critique
secs.x: The OO Response to Papal Infallibility — A Systematic Critique The Oriental Orthodox response to papal infallibility is not simply a refusal to submit — it is a principled theological position grounded in Scripture, history, and a different (and earlier) ecclesiology. Here we lay out the OO critique systematically. 1. It concentrates the Spirit's guidance in one office, contrary to the NT model John 16:13 promises the Spirit will guide "you" (plural) — the Apostles collectively — into all truth. Acts 15:28 says "it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" — the council, not a single bishop. 1 Timothy 3:15 says the Church (the whole body) is the pillar and bulwark of truth. The New Testament's pattern of Spirit-guided authority is consistently plural, corporate, and conciliar. Concentrating it in one man's solemn pronouncements is a departure from this pattern, not a fulfillment of it. 2.

secs.h: The OO Response to Papal Infallibility — A Systematic Critique
secs.x: It is historically novel — the early Church did not operate this way If papal infallibility were the known doctrine of the early Church, we would expect to see: (a) popes settling controversies by issuing infallible definitions; (b) councils ratifying these definitions or explicitly appealing to them; (c) Fathers referencing this papal charism in their writings. Instead we find: controversies settled by councils (Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus); popes whose definitions were debated or rejected by the East; Fathers who located infallibility in the Church as a body, not a single bishop. The doctrine's formal articulation at Vatican I in 1870 is historically its beginning, not its retrieval. 3. It makes genuine ecumenical councils redundant If the Pope can define doctrine infallibly alone — "not by the consent of the Church" — why call councils at all? And indeed, since Vatican I the Catholic Church has defined dogma once (the Assumption, 1950) by papal definition alone, and once shortly before it (the Immaculate Conception, 1854), without conciliar process.

secs.h: The OO Response to Papal Infallibility — A Systematic Critique
secs.x: For the OO, this represents the effective replacement of the Apostolic conciliar model with a papal monocracy. The conciliar model of Acts 15 — bishops gathered in the Spirit — is the biblical and historical norm; papal definition alone is not. 4. It creates a standard that cannot be reliably applied Roman Catholic theologians themselves disagree about which papal statements qualify as ex cathedra. Lists of possible ex cathedra statements range from two to a dozen or more, depending on the theologian. The Galileo condemnation, various medieval papal decrees, and even some statements about Scripture's inerrancy are debated. If the Church's supreme teaching authority cannot consistently identify when that authority is being exercised, the doctrine is practically unworkable as a criterion of certainty — which is its entire purpose. 5.

secs.h: The OO Response to Papal Infallibility — A Systematic Critique
secs.x: It introduces new doctrines — Immaculate Conception, Assumption — without Apostolic basis The two clearest exercises of papal infallibility since Vatican I — the Immaculate Conception (Pius IX, 1854) and the Assumption of Mary (Pius XII, 1950) — are doctrines without explicit scriptural basis and without clear universal patristic consensus. Thomas Aquinas denied the Immaculate Conception. No ecumenical council defined the Assumption. The OO honor Mary profoundly as Theotokos, as Ever-Virgin, as the preeminent saint — but these specific doctrines, defined by papal fiat as binding dogma, represent exactly the kind of development beyond the Apostolic deposit that the OO regard as impermissible.

secs.h: Indefectibility vs. Infallibility — What the OO Do Affirm
secs.x: Indefectibility vs. Infallibility — What the OO Do Affirm To be clear: the Oriental Orthodox are not skeptics about the Church's capacity to know and teach truth. We are not saying that all authority is relative, that no one can know anything, or that doctrine is perpetually up for revision. We affirm the indefectibility of the Church — that she will not permanently and irrecoverably err in defining the Apostolic faith. What we deny is that this indefectibility is attached to one human office as a personal charism. OO: Indefectibility of the Church The Church as a whole will not permanently err The Spirit guides the conciliar process Individual bishops and even councils can err Errors are corrected by subsequent councils Reception by the faithful confirms true definitions No single office holds the guarantee personally Grounded in Matthew 16:18 — the whole Church RC: Infallibility of the Papal Office The Pope personally holds the infallibility charism Ex cathedra definitions are irreformable Not subject to correction by councils or church The Spirit guarantees this one office

secs.h: Indefectibility vs. Infallibility — What the OO Do Affirm
secs.x: specifically Reception by faithful is not required for validity Grounded in Luke 22:32 applied to Petrine succession Formally defined 1870 — unknown to early Church The OO find the RC distinction between the "ordinary magisterium" (fallible) and "extraordinary magisterium" (infallible) theologically artificial. If the ordinary teaching of the Church's appointed teachers can err substantially, what confidence can the faithful have in the body of doctrine presented to them? The OO answer is that the confidence lies in the conciliar process, in the reception of the faithful, and in the witness of the Fathers — not in a technical doctrine of one man's solemn guarantee. St. Basil the Great c. 372–375 AD — Letter 90; On the Holy Spirit "The doctrines of the Fathers are despised; apostolic traditions are set at nought; the devices of innovators are in vogue in the Churches." In On the Holy Spirit he likens the strife of the churches to a naval battle fought in darkness and storm, where friend and foe can no longer be told apart.

secs.h: Indefectibility vs. Infallibility — What the OO Do Affirm
secs.x: Letter 90.2 (NPNF) and On the Holy Spirit 30.76 (summarised) — Basil's famous description of the Arian crisis. Letter 90 is in fact addressed to the bishops of the West: Basil appealed to Rome and the Westerners for help, as to brothers whose support he needed, and he complained when it was slow in coming. He stands with the conciliar faith of Nicaea, and nowhere treats papal authority as its guarantee. St. Athanasius of Alexandria Letter to his flock (attributed) Summary: The letter tells the faithful who had been driven from their churches that their opponents hold the buildings but have left the apostolic faith, while they themselves are outside the buildings but keep the faith within them. A short letter preserved among Athanasius's works (Patrologia Graeca 26); some scholars doubt that it is his. Popularly paraphrased as: they have the buildings, we have the Faith. Athanasius preserves orthodoxy against the world, including compromised bishops, by holding to the conciliar faith of Nicaea.

Catholic–Oriental Orthodox Dialogue Today Despite deep historical divisions, the Catholic and Oriental Orthodox churches have been engaged in formal ecumenical dialogue since the Second Vatican Council. The results have been encouraging at the Christological level — far less so at the ecclesiological level. Common Christological Declaration — Catholic-Coptic 1973 AD — Pope Paul VI and Pope Shenouda III "We confess that our Lord and God and Saviour and King of us all, Jesus Christ, is perfect God with respect to His Divinity, perfect Man with respect to His Humanity." A landmark declaration acknowledging that the centuries-long Chalcedonian divide may be largely a terminological rather than substantive theological disagreement. A genuine step toward mutual recognition.

Joint Commission of the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox Churches 1989–1993 AD Paraphrase: in its agreed statements (Anba Bishoy 1989, Chambésy 1990), the Commission declared that both families have loyally kept the same Orthodox Christological faith, and recommended that the anathemas of the past be lifted as a step toward full communion. This dialogue is between the two Orthodox families, not with Rome; papal authority is not an issue in it. The separate Catholic and Oriental Orthodox dialogue, including the earlier unofficial Pro Oriente consultations in Vienna (from 1971), reached similar Christological agreement, and there the remaining obstacles are ecclesiological, above all papal authority and infallibility. The Christological rapprochement is real and important. But full communion between Rome and the Oriental Orthodox remains impossible so long as Rome requires acceptance of Vatican I's definitions — universal papal jurisdiction and infallibility — as dogmatic conditions of communion.

These are precisely the points the OO cannot accept without abandoning their own ecclesiology and their understanding of the Apostolic tradition. The OO hope and pray for unity. We believe that unity, if it comes, must be on the basis of the faith of the first millennium — before the medieval developments that produced the papal monarchy as it is now defined. This is not hostility toward Rome; it is fidelity to what both East and West once shared. A note of charity: The Oriental Orthodox deeply honor the Bishop of Rome as heir to the great see of Peter and Paul, as a shepherd of a vast flock who has spoken prophetically on issues of human dignity, peace, and justice. The dispute is not about the Pope as a person or as a pastor, but about a specific constitutional claim — universal jurisdiction and personal infallibility — that we believe exceeds the Apostolic deposit and cannot be required as a condition of Christian communion.

Catholic Objections Answered "Without the Pope, the Church is a headless body — who settles disputes?" Disputes are settled the way the New Testament shows them being settled: by councils of bishops (Acts 15), by appeal to the Apostolic rule of faith, by reception of the faithful, and by the testimony of the whole Patristic tradition. The OO and Eastern Orthodox have settled doctrinal questions this way for two millennia — including the three great Christological controversies — without a monarchical papacy. The assumption that unity requires a supreme monarch is a medieval Western assumption, not an Apostolic one. Furthermore, the existence of a "supreme head" has not prevented division in the Catholic Church itself. Schisms, antipopes, conciliarist movements, and the Western Schism demonstrate that a monarchical papacy does not guarantee unity — it relocates the question of unity to who is the legitimate pope, which can be just as contested as any conciliar dispute.

"The Fathers consistently speak of Rome's primacy — this proves the papal claim." The Fathers speak of Rome's honor (τιμή) and its role as a doctrinal reference point — which the OO fully acknowledge. They do not consistently speak of Rome's universal jurisdiction or of a personal charism of infallibility attached to the Roman bishop. When Patristic texts are cited for papal primacy, they are almost always citing exactly what the OO already affirm: that Rome holds first place of honor, that Rome's faith has historically been orthodox, and that appeal to Rome was natural given its apostolicity and prestige. None of this requires the full Vatican I doctrine. The clearest test is this: did the Fathers appeal to Rome to settle Nicaea? No — they called a council. Did the Fathers say Rome's judgment is irreformable? No — Nicaea's canons did not include that. Did the Fathers condemn Honorius? Yes — they did. The patristic evidence, read honestly, supports the OO conciliar model far better than the Roman monarchical one.

"Doctrinal development is legitimate — Vatican I is a development of what was implicit in Apostolic faith." The OO accept that genuine doctrinal development exists — the formulation of Trinitarian and Christological doctrine is itself a development of what was implicit in Scripture. But not all development is legitimate. Newman's criterion for authentic development requires, among other things, that it preserve type — that the developed doctrine be the same organism, not a different plant. A development that makes one bishop the irreformable definer of faith for the entire Church — when the early Church operated conciliarly — is not a development of the same organism. It is a mutation. Furthermore, the OO criterion of authentic tradition is antiquity, universality, and consent — the Vincentian canon.

Papal infallibility fails this test: it was not believed everywhere (the East consistently rejected it), always (it is post-medieval in its full form), or by all (even among Western bishops at Vatican I, a significant minority initially opposed it, with some leaving before the final vote). "Vatican II softened Vatican I — the Pope now governs in collegiality with the bishops." Vatican II (1962–1965) did introduce the language of episcopal collegiality more prominently. Lumen Gentium teaches that the bishops as a college, together with the Pope, exercise supreme authority over the Church. This is a genuine development toward the OO position. However, Vatican II explicitly did not revoke or qualify Vatican I's definitions — universal jurisdiction and infallibility remain dogma. And the collegiality of Vatican II is exercised under and with the Pope, never against him or independently of him. The Pope retains the right to act alone, without collegial process, with full binding authority. This is still a monarchical system — the college advises and collaborates, but the monarchy stands.

"The OO themselves have a Pope (the Coptic Pope) — isn't that the same thing?" This is a common confusion worth clearing up. The title "Pope" (from Greek "Pappas" — father) is an ancient title used for bishops in Alexandria and Rome alike. The Coptic Pope of Alexandria does not claim universal jurisdiction over other patriarchs or over Christians beyond the Coptic church. He does not claim personal infallibility. He governs through the Holy Synod — a body of bishops with genuine authority. His "primacy" among the OO churches is a primacy of honor, not jurisdiction. The title is shared; the doctrine is entirely different.

Frequently Asked Questions Does the OO Church recognize the Pope as a legitimate bishop? Yes. The Oriental Orthodox regard the Bishop of Rome as a legitimate bishop with a validly ordained episcopate in Apostolic succession, presiding over an ancient and honorable see. We do not regard Roman Catholics as unchristian or their sacraments as void. What we deny is the specific constitutional claim of universal jurisdiction and personal infallibility. We regard Roman Catholics as separated brethren, not strangers, and we pray for the unity of all Christians. Was Peter ever in Rome? The historical evidence is strong that Peter was in Rome and was martyred there. 1 Clement (c. 96 AD) associates Peter with Rome; Ignatius of Antioch implies it; Irenaeus confirms it; early Roman monuments and traditions support it. The OO do not dispute Peter's presence and martyrdom in Rome. What we dispute is that Peter's presence in Rome automatically grants his successors there a universal jurisdictional supremacy — a conclusion that does not follow from the historical fact of his martyrdom.

How does the OO Church handle the "Tu es Petrus" — you are Peter? The OO acknowledge that Peter received a real commission and real authority in Matthew 16. The question is whether this commission transfers in full to Roman bishops as his "successors" in a way that gives them universal jurisdiction. The OO note: (1) Peter himself founded and taught at Antioch before Rome; (2) Paul, co-founder of the Roman church, has equal apostolic standing; (3) the keys given to Peter are also given to the whole Apostolic college (Matt 18:18); (4) no canon of an Ecumenical Council grounds Roman jurisdiction in Matthew 16; the one canon that explains Rome's rank (Chalcedon 28) cites its imperial status instead. The commission to Peter is real; the Roman interpretation of its transfer is contested.

What would it take for Rome and the OO to achieve full communion? From the OO perspective: (1) Resolution of the Christological question — largely accomplished already through the 1973 and subsequent dialogues; (2) Rome's willingness to revisit its understanding of papal authority — not necessarily abandoning Petrine primacy of honor, but moving from universal jurisdiction and personal infallibility toward a genuinely conciliar model; (3) Resolution of the Filioque (shared with Eastern Orthodoxy); (4) Mutual recognition without requiring one side to adopt the other's specific historical formulations. This is a significant agenda. The OO are not optimistic about quick resolution — but we are committed to honest dialogue in the Spirit of Christ's prayer "that they may all be one." Does the OO rejection of papal infallibility mean the Church can teach error? No. The OO affirm the Church's indefectibility — Christ promised the gates of hell would not prevail, and the Spirit guides the Church into all truth.

What the OO deny is that this protection is guaranteed through the mechanism of one man's solemn pronouncements. The guarantee operates through the conciliar process, confirmed by the reception of the faithful and the witness of the whole Patristic tradition. Local councils can err; individual bishops can err; but the Spirit working through the whole body of bishops in genuine ecumenical council, received by the faithful, has preserved and will preserve the Apostolic faith inviolate.

Glossary of Key Terms Papal Infallibility Ex cathedra — from the chair Vatican I (1870) dogma: when the Pope speaks ex cathedra on faith or morals for the universal Church, his definitions are irreformable by divine assistance. Rejected by OO as historically novel and theologically unfounded. Universal Jurisdiction Plena potestas — full power Vatican I dogma: the Pope holds full, immediate, and supreme power of jurisdiction over the entire Church and every bishop and faithful in it. The OO regard this as exceeding the early Church's conciliar model. Primacy of Honor Πρωτεῖον τιμῆς — proteion times The OO acknowledge Rome's (and Alexandria's, within the OO) first place of honor among the patriarchates. This is an honorific, not a jurisdictional, primacy — "first among equals." Pentarchy Πενταρχία — rule of five The ancient model of five patriarchates (Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem) governing the Church collegially, each in its own sphere, with Rome as first in honor. Rejected by Rome's development toward universal jurisdiction.

Indefectibility From Latin: indefectibilis The guarantee that the Church as a whole will not permanently and irrecoverably err in defining the Apostolic faith. The OO affirm indefectibility of the Church; they deny infallibility of one office within it. Monothelitism Μονοθελητισμός — one-will-ism In Chalcedonian terms, the teaching that Christ has only one will rather than two. Condemned at Constantinople III (680–681), which also condemned Honorius I. The OO were not party to this council: they confess one composite, theandric will of the incarnate Word in which His divine and full human will are united without confusion. See The Will of Christ . Protos Πρῶτος — first The "first" bishop in a collegial assembly — a role of honor, presidence, and initiative, not monarchical rule. Peter was protos among the Apostles; the bishop of Rome protos among the patriarchs. "Protos" is not "monarch." Conciliarism From Latin: concilium The theological position that ecumenical councils of bishops, not the Pope alone, hold supreme authority in the Church.

The OO hold a form of conciliarism; Rome condemned conciliarism at Vatican I. Vincentian Canon Quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus That faith "which has been believed everywhere, always, by all" (NPNF). St. Vincent of Lérins' (c. 434) standard for authentic Catholic tradition. The OO apply it to evaluate papal claims: universal jurisdiction and infallibility fail this test. Pastor Aeternus Latin: The Eternal Pastor The Vatican I dogmatic constitution (July 18, 1870) defining universal papal jurisdiction (Chapter III) and papal infallibility (Chapter IV). The OO regard both definitions as innovations beyond the Apostolic deposit.

The Core Difference Oriental Orthodox Married men may be ordained deacon and priest Marriage must occur before ordination to the diaconate Ordained men may not marry after ordination Bishops are always celibate — drawn from monks Celibacy is honored as a charism, not imposed as a rule Roman Catholic (Latin Rite) Celibacy mandatory for all Latin Rite priests Married men may not be ordained (with narrow exceptions) Celibacy treated as integral to the priestly vocation Eastern Catholic churches in communion with Rome retain married priesthood Mandatory celibacy codified at Second Lateran Council (1139) The important distinction in the Oriental Orthodox practice: it is not that priests may marry, but that married men may become priests. The sequence matters — marriage comes first. A widowed priest does not remarry, and a man ordained as a celibate cannot later marry. Celibacy chosen freely is deeply honored; it is compelled celibacy the Tradition does not know.

The Scriptural Witness The New Testament is explicit: the Apostles and early leaders of the Church included married men. The requirement that a bishop be "the husband of one wife" assumes marriage as the normal state. "Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach…" 1 Timothy 3:2 "…if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination." Titus 1:6 "Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?" 1 Corinthians 9:5 — Paul confirming Peter and the apostles had wives The Gospels confirm Peter's marriage directly: Jesus healed his mother-in-law (Matthew 8:14). Paul himself was celibate and commends celibacy as a gift (1 Cor 7:7) — but explicitly as a charism, not a requirement. "Each has his own gift from God" (1 Cor 7:7) — celibacy and marriage are both callings, neither is obligatory for ministry.

The prohibition of marriage after ordination in the East follows from "husband of one wife" — once ordained, a man is wedded to his flock. But this is different from requiring celibacy before ordination.

How the Latin Rule Developed The shift to mandatory celibacy in the Western Church was gradual and driven by reform movements, not apostolic tradition. Early Church Married clergy normal East and West. No universal celibacy rule. Bishops, priests, and deacons commonly married. Council of Nicaea (325) Bishop Paphnutius of Egypt reportedly opposed imposing celibacy, arguing it was too heavy a burden and contrary to ancient tradition. The Council declined to mandate it. Council of Trullo (692) The Quinisext Council codified Eastern practice: married men may be ordained deacon and priest; bishops must be celibate; clergy may not marry after ordination. Rome refused to ratify this council — a sign of the already diverging practices. Gregorian Reform (11th c.) Pope Gregory VII's reform movement targeted simony, nepotism, and married clergy (whose sons often inherited parishes). Celibacy was enforced as part of cleansing the Western church from feudal entanglements, not as a theological principle per se.

Second Lateran Council (1139) Declared priestly marriages not merely forbidden but invalid. Mandatory celibacy became law for the entire Latin Rite — a discipline unknown to the Apostolic Church as a universal rule. St. Paphnutius of Egypt (d. c. 360) "…Paphnutius having arisen in the midst of the assembly of bishops, earnestly entreated them not to impose so heavy a yoke on the ministers of religion: asserting that 'marriage itself is honorable, and the bed undefiled'… It would be sufficient, he thought, that such as had previously entered on their sacred calling should abjure matrimony, according to the ancient tradition of the Church: but that none should be separated from her to whom, while yet unordained, he had been united." Socrates Scholasticus, Church History I.11 (NPNF), writing about a century later; some historians doubt the episode.

Note the "ancient tradition" he cites is that men already ordained do not marry afterward Council of Trullo, Canon 13 (692) "Since we know it to be handed down as a rule of the Roman Church that those who are deemed worthy to be advanced to the diaconate or presbyterate should promise no longer to cohabit with their wives, we, preserving the ancient rule and apostolic perfection and order, will that the lawful marriages of men who are in holy orders be from this time forward firm…" (NPNF) Quinisext Council, Canon 13 — explicitly upholding the Eastern Apostolic norm against Roman practice The Apostolic Canons, Canon 5 "Let not a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, put away his wife under pretence of religion; but if he put her away, let him be excommunicated; and if he persists, let him be deposed." (NPNF) Ancient canonical collection received across the East — it penalizes clergy who separate from their wives, rather than requiring it St. Clement of Alexandria (c.

150–215) "For Peter and Philip begot children; and Philip also gave his daughters in marriage." Stromata 3.6 , as quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.30 (NPNF) — the Alexandrian master defending the married apostles against a sect that scorned marriage

Oriental Orthodox Practice Today Across all six Oriental Orthodox churches the practice is essentially the same, rooted in the Apostolic norm confirmed at Trullo: Coptic Orthodox: The majority of parish priests are married. A man discerning priesthood must marry before his ordination as a deacon. Celibate priests (monks) also serve parishes and are eligible for episcopacy. Ethiopian & Eritrean Orthodox: Married priesthood is the norm for parish clergy. The Tewahedo tradition has a very large monastic community from which bishops are drawn. Armenian Apostolic: Two orders of clergy — married parish priests (kahanas) and celibate vardapets (archimandrites). Only vardapets may become bishops. Syriac Orthodox & Malankara: Married men ordained to the priesthood. Episcopal candidates drawn from monks or widowed priests who take monastic vows. In none of these traditions is marriage seen as a compromise of priestly holiness.
The married priest who serves his parish, raises children in the faith, and shepherds his flock is not a lesser priest — he is a different icon of Christ than the monk-bishop, and both are needed.

Why Bishops Must Be Celibate The Oriental Orthodox do require celibacy of their bishops — this is ancient and universal in both Eastern and Oriental Orthodoxy. The reasons are theological and practical, not a concession to the Latin argument for celibacy. Theologically, the bishop is the spouse of his diocese (a concept in both East and West). Just as Christ is the one Bridegroom of the one Church, the bishop is wholly given to his flock — undivided. A bishop with a wife and children would face the impossible tension between his family and his diocese scattered across a region. The monastic vow resolves this by a prior, total self-offering. Practically, bishops in the apostolic East are normally drawn from the monastic order — men who have already embraced a life of prayer, ascetic discipline, and communal obedience. This ensures that the episcopate is drawn from proven men of prayer, not merely from the most administratively capable. The monk-bishop is a shepherd who has first learned to shepherd his own soul. "If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.

Therefore an overseer must be above reproach…" 1 Timothy 3:1-2 — the standard of total self-giving The key distinction from Rome: the Oriental Orthodox impose celibacy on bishops as a function of the episcopal charism and its demands, not on all clergy as a discipline of purity. The married priest is not thereby less pure or less holy — he is living a different calling.

FAQ Doesn't Paul say celibacy is better (1 Cor 7)? Yes — and the Oriental Orthodox fully honor celibacy as a higher charism when it is freely given. Paul says "each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another" (1 Cor 7:7). He recommends celibacy for those who can receive it. He never says married men are unfit for ministry — in the same letter he confirms the apostles have wives (1 Cor 9:5). The OO position is not that celibacy is inferior; it is that it cannot be imposed as a requirement for valid ministry. Can a widowed priest in the OO remarry? No. Once ordained, a priest may not remarry even if widowed. This follows from the canon that a bishop, priest, or deacon be "husband of one wife" — not sequentially, but faithfully. A widowed priest who wishes to remain in ministry continues as a celibate priest; if he wishes to remarry, he must leave the active priesthood. Many widowed priests take monastic vows and can then be elevated to the episcopate. What about Eastern Catholic churches — do they also have married priests? Yes.

Eastern Catholic churches in full communion with Rome (Coptic Catholic, Melkite, Maronite, etc.) retain the Eastern discipline of married priesthood, because Rome has historically recognized this as an authentic apostolic tradition. This itself undercuts the claim that celibacy is theologically necessary for priesthood — Rome's own Eastern rites demonstrate it is not. The mandatory celibacy rule is a Latin Rite discipline, not a universal doctrine of the Church. Is the RC church considering changing the celibacy requirement? The question has been raised in synods, particularly with the 2019 Synod for the Amazon where the shortage of priests led to proposals for ordaining married men (viri probati — proven married men). Pope Francis received the synod's recommendations but did not change the discipline in his follow-up document. The debate continues within the RC church itself. The Oriental Orthodox simply note that the ancient Apostolic practice they have maintained all along is exactly what is being discussed as a possible reform.

Glossary Celibacy The state of remaining unmarried and abstaining from sexual relations, offered as a complete self-giving to God. Valued as charism in OO; mandatory in the Latin Rite. Council of Trullo (692) The Quinisext Council, which codified Eastern canonical practice including married priesthood. Rome refused to ratify it, foreshadowing the divergence. Husband of One Wife The scriptural criterion (1 Tim 3:2, Tit 1:6) for clergy — read by the Eastern tradition as requiring fidelity in one marriage, not celibacy. Monk-Bishop The Eastern/OO pattern: bishops are drawn from the monastic order, who have already made a vow of celibacy. The episcopal charism thus builds on the monastic. Charism A gift of grace given by the Holy Spirit for the building up of the Body. Celibacy is a charism — given to some, not imposed on all. Viri Probati Latin: "proven men." The proposed RC category of mature, married men of faith who might be ordained in areas of extreme priest shortage.

secs.h: The Objection Stated — At Its Strongest
secs.x: The Objection Stated — At Its Strongest Honesty requires stating the objection at full strength. The classical form is the trilemma attributed to Epicurus, transmitted by the Christian writer Lactantius: The Epicurean Trilemma — as transmitted by Lactantius, On the Anger of God 13 (c. AD 313) "God … either wishes to take away evils, and is unable; or He is able, and is unwilling; or He is neither willing nor able, or He is both willing and able. If He is willing and is unable, He is feeble, which is not in accordance with the character of God; if He is able and unwilling, He is envious, which is equally at variance with God; if He is neither willing nor able, He is both envious and feeble, and therefore not God; if He is both willing and able, which alone is suitable to God, from what source then are evils? Or why does He not remove them?" Lactantius records the argument precisely in order to answer it — the Church has been engaging this objection since before Nicaea.

secs.h: The Objection Stated — At Its Strongest
secs.x: Modern philosophy sharpened it into three distinct forms, and each needs a different answer: The Three Modern Formulations The logical problem (J. L. Mackie, "Evil and Omnipotence," 1955): the mere existence of any evil logically contradicts an all-good, all-powerful God. The evidential problem (William Rowe, 1979): perhaps not a strict contradiction, but apparently pointless suffering — a fawn burning slowly in a forest fire no one sees — makes God improbable. The emotional problem (Ivan Karamazov in Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov , 1880): even if heaven justifies everything, the torture of one innocent child is a price no decent person should accept. Ivan does not disprove God — he "returns his ticket." The Shape of the Orthodox Response Evil is not a thing God made — it is the privation and parasite of good (Athanasius, Basil). A world with genuine creaturely freedom — the precondition of love — is a world where evil is possible (Irenaeus, Justin, Gregory of Nyssa). Death and natural corruption entered through the Fall; creation itself is wounded (Romans 5, Romans 8).

secs.h: The Objection Stated — At Its Strongest
secs.x: God's answer is not an explanation delivered from a safe distance but His own entry into suffering: the Word of God suffered in the flesh (Cyril of Alexandria). Evil will not merely be outweighed but undone : "death shall be no more" (Revelation 21:4).

secs.h: What Evil Is — The Privation of Good
secs.x: What Evil Is — The Privation of Good The trilemma asks "from what source are evils?" as though evil were a substance that must have been manufactured by someone. The Fathers reject the premise. Scripture is explicit that everything God made is good, and that death is an intruder: "And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good." Genesis 1:31 "…God did not make death, and he does not delight in the death of the living. For he created all things that they might exist, and the generative forces of the world are wholesome, and there is no destructive poison in them." Wisdom of Solomon 1:13–14 (RSV), in the Oriental Orthodox canon "God created us for incorruption, and made us in the image of his own eternity, but through the devil's envy death entered the world." Wisdom of Solomon 2:23–24 (NRSV) Evil, then, is not a created thing but a corruption, absence, or twisting of created good — as blindness is not a thing added to the eye but the loss of sight, and rust is nothing without the iron it eats. Evil is parasitic: it can only exist in and against something good.

secs.h: What Evil Is — The Privation of Good
secs.x: This is why the question "why did God create evil?" is malformed — He didn't, and it isn't a creature. St. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373) "Evil has not from the beginning been with God or in God, nor has any substantive existence; but … men, in default of the vision of good, began to devise and imagine for themselves what was not, after their own pleasure." Against the Heathen (Contra Gentes) 7.3 — evil as a privation devised by the misuse of freedom, not a creation of God St. Basil the Great (c. 330–379) "Evil is not a living animated essence; it is the condition of the soul opposed to virtue, developed in the careless on account of their falling away from good. Do not then go beyond yourself to seek for evil, and imagine that there is an original nature of wickedness." Hexaemeron, Homily 2.4–5 — and at length in his homily "That God Is Not the Author of Evil" This first move already dissolves half the trilemma: God is not the "source" of evils, because evils have no source in the sense the objection assumes.

secs.h: What Evil Is — The Privation of Good
secs.x: They are the shadow cast when free creatures turn away from the Good — and a shadow is not manufactured by the sun.

"I Create Evil"? — The Isaiah 45:7 Objection Atheist polemics often quote the King James rendering of Isaiah 45:7 — "I make peace, and create evil" — as a divine confession. The objection rests on an English ambiguity, not on the Hebrew. Isaiah 45:7 — What the Hebrew Says Hebrew עֹשֶׂה שָׁלוֹם וּבוֹרֵא רָע — oseh shalom u-vore ra The word raʻ Has a wide range: "disaster, calamity, adversity" as well as "moral evil." The poetic parallel in the verse fixes the meaning: light/darkness, shalom (peace, well-being) / ra (calamity, woe). Modern translations "I make well-being and create calamity" (ESV); "I bring prosperity and create disaster" (NIV). The context is God telling Cyrus of Persia that history — the rise and fall of empires, victory and catastrophe — is in His sovereign hand, against Persian dualism which assigned light and darkness to two rival gods. It is a claim about providence over calamity, not a confession of authoring wickedness. The same idiom appears in Amos 3:6.

Scripture elsewhere flatly excludes God as author of moral evil: "God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one" (James 1:13); "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" (1 John 1:5).

secs.h: Freedom: Why Evil Is Possible at All
secs.x: Freedom: Why Evil Is Possible at All If evil has no substance, why does God permit free creatures to introduce it? Because the purpose of creation is love — communion between God and rational creatures — and love that is coerced is not love. A being incapable of refusing God is also incapable of freely loving Him. Scripture places the choice squarely in human hands: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life." Deuteronomy 30:19 "Do not say, 'It was the Lord's doing that I fell away' … It was he who created humankind in the beginning, and he left them in the power of their own free choice. If you choose, you can keep the commandments … Before each person are life and death, and whichever one chooses will be given." Sirach 15:11–17 — in the Oriental Orthodox canon St. Irenaeus of Lyons (c.

secs.h: Freedom: Why Evil Is Possible at All
secs.x: 130–202) "Man is possessed of free will from the beginning, and God is possessed of free will, in whose likeness man was created … And in man, as well as in angels, He has placed the power of choice (for angels are rational beings), so that those who had yielded obedience might justly possess what is good, given indeed by God, but preserved by themselves." Against Heresies 4.37 — the same chapter insists "there is no coercion with God" St. Justin Martyr (c. 100–165) "Unless the human race have the power of avoiding evil and choosing good by free choice, they are not accountable for their actions, of whatever kind they be." First Apology 43 — the earliest sustained Christian rejection of fatalism St. Gregory of Nyssa (c.

secs.h: Freedom: Why Evil Is Possible at All
secs.x: 335–395) "He who made man for the participation of His own peculiar good, and incorporated in him the instincts for all that was excellent, in order that his desire might be carried forward by a corresponding movement in each case to its like, would never have deprived him of that most excellent and precious of all goods; I mean the gift implied in being his own master, and having a free will. For if necessity in any way was the master of the life of man, the image would have been falsified in that particular part." The Great Catechism 5 — freedom as constitutive of the image of God Note what this argument does and does not claim. It does not say every particular evil produces a greater good. It says that a world containing free creatures — the only kind of world in which love, virtue, courage, repentance, and sanctity are possible — is a world in which evil can occur, and that God judged such a world worth creating and worth redeeming at the cost of His own Son. Angels and men fell by the same gift by which the saints stand.

secs.h: The Fall: How Death and Natural Evil Entered
secs.x: The Fall: How Death and Natural Evil Entered Free creatures did, in fact, turn away — and the consequences were not confined to the morally guilty. The Oriental Orthodox understanding of ancestral sin holds that what we inherit from Adam is not his guilt but his condition: mortality, corruption, and a world knocked off its axis. "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men…" Romans 5:12 "For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it … the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now." Romans 8:20–22 — the biblical root of "natural evil": a wounded cosmos, not a divine design specification This is the Orthodox frame for earthquakes, disease, and death itself: they belong to a creation in bondage to corruption, awaiting liberation — not to God's original intent, and not to His final word. St. Athanasius describes the catastrophe and its remedy in one sweep: St. Athanasius — On the Incarnation 4–5 (c.

secs.h: The Fall: How Death and Natural Evil Entered
secs.x: AD 318) Transgression set in motion a return to non-existence: "For transgression of the commandment was turning them back to their natural state, so that just as they have had their being out of nothing, so also, as might be expected, they might look for corruption into nothing in the course of time." Death as disintegration intruding on creation — the disease the Incarnation came to cure The Epistle to the Hebrews "That through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery." Hebrews 2:14–15 — evil and death treated as an enemy occupation to be broken, not a divine arrangement to be excused Notice the consistent biblical grammar: God is never the ally of death. Death is "the last enemy" (1 Corinthians 15:26). Any theodicy that makes God comfortable with evil has parted company with Scripture, which portrays Him at war with it.

secs.h: Scripture Does Not Flinch — The Bible Raises the Problem Itself
secs.x: Scripture Does Not Flinch — The Bible Raises the Problem Itself The problem of evil is not an outside attack the Bible never anticipated. It is raised, at full volume, inside the canon — which means the faith was never built on ignorance of it. "O Lord, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? … Why do you make me see iniquity, and why do you idly look at wrong?" Habakkuk 1:2–3 — a prophet interrogating God; the answer he receives is "the righteous shall live by his faith" (2:4) "But when I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end." Psalm 73:16–17 — the prosperity of the wicked, resolved not by argument but in worship and eschatology The Book of Job is the longest sustained treatment. Job's comforters defend a tidy theology — suffering is always punishment — and God condemns them for it (Job 42:7).

secs.h: Scripture Does Not Flinch — The Bible Raises the Problem Itself
secs.x: God's own answer comes not as a theory but as a whirlwind of questions ("Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" — Job 38:4) and, decisively, as presence: "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you." Job 42:5 — the sufferer is satisfied by encounter, not by explanation; and note Job 1–2: the reader is shown a cosmic context the sufferer never sees Jesus Himself explicitly severs the automatic link between suffering and personal guilt — twice: "Those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? No, I tell you…" Luke 13:4–5 "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?" Jesus answered, "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him." John 9:2–3 And at the tomb of Lazarus — knowing He was about to raise him — "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). The Word of God stood before death, the thing He would shortly destroy, and His response was tears and anger (John 11:33,38).

secs.h: Scripture Does Not Flinch — The Bible Raises the Problem Itself
secs.x: That is God's emotional posture toward evil.

secs.h: The Cross: God's Answer in Person
secs.x: The Cross: God's Answer in Person Here the Oriental Orthodox tradition speaks with particular force. Every other worldview answers suffering from outside it. In the Gospel, God answers from inside: the Word became flesh and went to the place of maximum injustice, betrayal, torture, and godforsakenness — and made it the instrument of salvation. The Oriental Orthodox Churches confess this with unmatched directness: it is why our Trisagion is addressed to Christ — "Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, who was crucified for us , have mercy on us." St. Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444) "Whosoever shall not recognize that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, that he was crucified in the flesh, and that likewise in that same flesh he tasted death and that he has become the first-begotten of the dead … let him be anathema." Twelfth Anathema, Third Letter to Nestorius (AD 430) — received by the Council of Ephesus (431).

secs.h: The Cross: God's Answer in Person
secs.x: Cyril adds elsewhere that the impassible Word "suffered impassibly": the divine nature is not diminished, yet the suffering is truly His own, because the One who suffers is God the Word incarnate. St. Athanasius — On the Incarnation 27 "But now that the Saviour has raised His body, death is no longer terrible; for all who believe in Christ tread him under as nought, and choose rather to die than to deny their faith in Christ. For they verily know that when they die they are not destroyed, but actually [begin to] live." Written within living memory of the Diocletian persecution — this was an empirical claim about the martyrs of Egypt "Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows … he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed." Isaiah 53:4–5 The pattern was laid down in Genesis: Joseph, betrayed and sold by his brothers, tells them, "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20).

secs.h: The Cross: God's Answer in Person
secs.x: The Cross is that verse written across the cosmos: the worst act in history — the murder of the incarnate God — became the salvation of the world. This does not make the evil good; Judas remains Judas. It reveals a God whose providence is so deep that even evil freely committed cannot escape being woven into redemption. And the answer is unfinished by design. Christian hope is not that evil will be philosophically balanced, but that it will be abolished : "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away." Revelation 21:4 "In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world." John 16:33

The Three Formulations Answered 1. The logical problem: "Any evil at all contradicts an omnipotent, all-good God." The argument requires a hidden premise: a good God would prevent every evil He is able to prevent. That premise is false if God can have morally sufficient reasons to permit an evil — and creaturely freedom is exactly such a reason: not even omnipotence can force a free act of love, any more than it can make a square circle, for "forced free love" is not a thing power could produce but a contradiction in terms. This is the substance of Alvin Plantinga's free-will defense ( God, Freedom, and Evil , 1974), and it is now widely conceded. J. L. Mackie himself, the author of the modern logical argument, wrote in his final book: "We can concede that the problem of evil does not, after all, show that the central doctrines of theism are logically inconsistent with one another" ( The Miracle of Theism , 1982), though he still held that evil made theism less reasonable. The strict logical argument is, by the admission of its own champion, dead.

The Fathers had said it sixteen centuries earlier: "there is no coercion with God" (Irenaeus). 2. The evidential problem: "So much suffering looks pointless — a God is improbable." The argument moves from "I can see no justifying reason for this evil" to "there is no justifying reason." But that inference is only as strong as the assumption that a finite observer would see God's reasons if they existed — precisely what Job 38–41 denies in four chapters of divine questions. We routinely accept this logic elsewhere: a child cannot see the reason for the surgeon's knife, yet the reason exists. The Book of Job is structured to make the point formally: the reader sees the heavenly context of chapters 1–2; Job never does. St. Anthony of Egypt received the same answer in the desert — asked why the wicked prosper and the innocent die young, he heard: "Antony, keep your attention on yourself; these things are according to the judgement of God, and it is not to your advantage to know anything about them" (Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Anthony 2, tr. Ward).

This is not evasion; it is the honest epistemology of finitude. The evidential argument cannot get off the ground without claiming a God's-eye view — the very thing the objector denies anyone has. 3. The emotional problem: Ivan Karamazov — "Even if it all works out, I return my ticket." Ivan's protest deserves reverence, not refutation — and Dostoevsky, a Christian, gives the answer in the novel itself: not an argument, but Alyosha's silent kiss, and the figure of Christ who kisses the Grand Inquisitor. The Church's answer to the emotional problem has never been a syllogism. It is the crucified Christ, the tears at Lazarus' tomb, and the practical presence of the Church beside the suffering: the "God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction" (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). Note also what Ivan's outrage presupposes: that the child's suffering objectively matters — that it is not merely chemistry he happens to dislike. That intuition is correct, and it is borrowed capital from theism (see next section).

The Orthodox do not ask the grieving to admire a theodicy. We ask them to look at the wounds in the risen Christ's hands — evil neither denied, nor explained away, but borne by God Himself and turned to glory.

secs.h: The Objection Turned Around: Evil Presupposes Good
secs.x: The Objection Turned Around: Evil Presupposes Good The argument from evil is the atheist's strongest weapon — and it is borrowed. To call the torture of a child evil — not "unpleasant to me," not "disadvantageous to the species," but objectively, absolutely wrong — is to invoke a standard of goodness that transcends opinion, culture, and evolutionary utility. Materialism has no shelf to keep such a standard on. If humans are accidental arrangements of matter, the torture of a child is an event like erosion: regrettable to some observers, but not wrong in any sense the universe underwrites. C. S. Lewis (1898–1963) "My argument against God was that the universe seemed so cruel and unjust. But how had I got this idea of just and unjust? A man does not call a line crooked unless he has some idea of a straight line.

secs.h: The Objection Turned Around: Evil Presupposes Good
secs.x: What was I comparing this universe with when I called it unjust?" Mere Christianity, Book II.1 — Lewis describing the collapse of his own atheism The Apostle Paul "They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness…" Romans 2:15 — the moral outrage of the unbeliever is itself evidence of the Lawgiver So the objection boomerangs: the louder the protest against evil, the more it testifies to an objective Good — and an objective Good is precisely what atheism cannot supply. The atheist also inherits a mirror-image problem rarely acknowledged: the problem of good . If the universe is blind and indifferent, why is it saturated with beauty, self-sacrifice, forgiveness, and saints? Evil is a problem for the Christian; good and evil are both problems for the atheist — and he has only one of the two even in principle. One more asymmetry deserves notice: the argument from evil, even if it worked, would prove at most that God is not good — a conclusion in tension with the atheist's other arguments, which deny He exists at all.

secs.h: The Objection Turned Around: Evil Presupposes Good
secs.x: It is a protest addressed to Someone. As the Psalms show, protest addressed to God is not atheism; it is prayer's rawest form.

secs.h: The Church of the Martyrs — Theodicy Lived, Not Theorized
secs.x: The Church of the Martyrs — Theodicy Lived, Not Theorized The Oriental Orthodox Churches did not learn about suffering from a philosophy seminar. The Coptic Church dates her calendar from AD 284 — the accession of Diocletian, her fiercest persecutor: the Anno Martyrum , the Era of the Martyrs. The Armenian Church passed through the genocide of 1915. The Syriac Church through Sayfo. The Ethiopian Church through invasion and revolution. And in February 2015, twenty Coptic laborers and one Ghanaian companion were beheaded on a Libyan beach with the name of Jesus on their lips — canonized by the Coptic Church as the 21 Martyrs of Libya. "These martyrs were baptized not only with water and the Spirit, but also in blood, in a blood that is the seed of unity for all followers of Christ." Pope Francis, receiving Pope Tawadros II on 11 May 2023, when he added the 21 to the Roman Martyrology (the Coptic Church had proclaimed them martyrs in 2015). It echoes Tertullian: "the blood of Christians is seed" (Apology 50).

secs.h: The Church of the Martyrs — Theodicy Lived, Not Theorized
secs.x: A Church that responds to seventeen centuries of persecution with hymns rather than apostasy is itself a datum in this debate. The martyrs are what the doctrine looks like when it is believed: evil is real, evil is temporary, and evil loses. St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) "The waters have risen and severe storms are upon us, but we do not fear drowning, for we stand firmly upon a rock. Let the sea rage, it cannot break the rock. Let the waves rise, they cannot sink the boat of Jesus." From the homily traditionally attributed to him before his first exile (AD 403), read in the Church's office on his feast. Deposed and exiled unjustly, he died on the forced march in 407; his reported last words were "Glory be to God for all things" (Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom) St. Severus of Antioch (c.

secs.h: The Church of the Martyrs — Theodicy Lived, Not Theorized
secs.x: 465–538) Deposed from his see in 518 for refusing Chalcedon, Severus — the great theological voice of Oriental Orthodoxy — spent his final twenty years a hunted exile in the monasteries of Egypt, governing his suffering church by letter, and never once treating his persecution as evidence against the goodness of God. The patriarch-in-exile as a living commentary on Romans 8:18 "For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us." Romans 8:18 — and 8:28: "for those who love God all things work together for good" "Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings…" 1 Peter 4:12–13

FAQ — Honest Questions, Honest Answers Why doesn't God just stop each atrocity as it begins? Follow the request to its end: a world where God overrides every evil choice is a world with no effective choices at all — a puppet theater. The intuition "God should stop the big ones" also has no stable stopping point: once murder is prevented, assault becomes the worst evil and the argument repeats, all the way down to a world where no one can so much as wound another's feelings — which is to say, a world without persons. God's actual policy is stranger and costlier: He permits, He enters, He suffers, He redeems, and He will judge. "He has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness" (Acts 17:31). Evil has a deadline. Free will may explain murder — but earthquakes? Cancer? Animal suffering? Scripture's category for this is the wounded cosmos: creation "subjected to futility… its bondage to corruption" (Romans 8:20–21), groaning for liberation. The Fall was not a private moral event; humanity was creation's priest, and the rupture ran through everything he was head of.

The Fathers add that a stable, law-governed world — the only kind in which free agents can act meaningfully — is also a world whose fixed laws (tectonics, biology) can wound. What Orthodoxy refuses to say is that cancer is God's design or an earthquake His preference: death is "the last enemy" (1 Corinthians 15:26), and Christ's miracles — healing the sick, calming the storm, raising the dead — are previews of nature restored, not violations of it. Did God create the devil evil? No. Satan was created a good angel and fell by the same free will by which angels stand — "through the devil's envy death entered the world" (Wisdom 2:24); "he was a murderer from the beginning" describes his choice, not his manufacture (John 8:44). The Fathers are unanimous: nothing God made is evil by nature; evil is always a use, never a substance. Is my suffering a punishment for my sin? Christ explicitly forbids that arithmetic (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:1–3), and God rebukes Job's friends for practicing it (Job 42:7). Suffering may discipline, refine, or simply befall; only God sees which.

The pastoral rule of the Fathers: examine yourself in your own suffering if it bears fruit, but never construct guilt for another from theirs. "Antony, keep your attention on yourself." Couldn't God have created free beings who always freely choose good? If "free" means genuinely able to do otherwise, then "guaranteed always to choose good" contradicts it — what is guaranteed is not chosen. This is Plantinga's point against Mackie, and the Fathers' before him. Heaven, note, is not such a world retroactively: the saints confirmed in glory passed through real choice to get there. God's plan produces creatures who freely and finally love Him — but produced is the wrong word; they are persons, and persons must arrive. Doesn't hell make the problem infinitely worse? Hell is the problem of evil's solution misread as its aggravation: it is the quarantine of evil, not its eternalization in God's good world.

The Orthodox tradition understands damnation primarily as the self-chosen state of a creature that refuses the only Source of joy — "the doors of hell are locked on the inside," as Lewis put it. God "desires all people to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:4) and "is patient … not wishing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9). What He will not do is the one thing the objector keeps demanding elsewhere in this debate: override freedom. If God has reasons, why does He hide them — and Himself? He has not hidden Himself; He has hidden the ledger. The difference matters. "he did not leave himself without witness" (Acts 14:17) — creation, conscience, Scripture, the Church, and above all the Incarnation are public. But the particular accounting of each evil is withheld, as it was from Job, because the creature who demanded it could not audit infinity anyway. What is offered instead is a Person whose scars certify that He is not aloof from the cost. Faith is trusting the surgeon you know in the operation you don't understand.

Glossary Theodicy vs. Defense A theodicy claims to give God's actual reasons for permitting evil; a defense shows only that good reasons are possible, defeating the charge of contradiction. The Fathers offer elements of both, but Orthodoxy's final word is neither — it is the Cross. Privatio Boni "Privation of good" — the patristic teaching (Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa) that evil has no substance or independent existence; it is the corruption, absence, or misuse of created good, as blindness is to sight. Ancestral Sin The Eastern and Oriental understanding of the Fall: we inherit Adam's mortality and a corrupted condition, not his personal guilt. See the dedicated page on this site. Logical / Evidential / Emotional Problem The three modern forms of the objection: strict contradiction (Mackie, 1955 — now conceded to fail), improbability from apparently pointless suffering (Rowe, 1979), and existential protest (Dostoevsky's Ivan Karamazov). Raʻ (רָע) Hebrew word in Isaiah 45:7 covering both moral evil and calamity/disaster; context determines sense.

In Isaiah 45 it means calamity, paralleling "darkness" against "peace." "Who was crucified for us" The clause the Oriental Orthodox add to the Trisagion hymn, addressing it to Christ — the liturgical confession that the Crucified One is true God, the heart of the OO answer to suffering. Era of the Martyrs (Anno Martyrum) The Coptic calendar, counted from AD 284, the accession of Diocletian. The Coptic Church literally tells time from her greatest persecution. "Suffered impassibly" St. Cyril of Alexandria's formula: the divine nature is beyond suffering, yet the sufferings of the flesh are truly the Word's own, because the one subject who suffers is God the Word incarnate.
