One Root, Two Paths Until the middle of the fifth century the Churches of Alexandria, Antioch, Rome, Constantinople, and Jerusalem shared a single communion and faith. The Great Schism of 1054 between Rome and Constantinople deepened the divide, and in the centuries that followed, the Western Church developed a series of theological positions that the Eastern and Oriental Orthodox traditions could not receive as belonging to the original deposit of faith. Oriental Orthodox churches — Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Armenian, Syriac, and Malankara — accept the first three Ecumenical Councils (Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381, Ephesus 431) as binding expressions of the universal faith. Doctrines defined after the schism, or that contradict the earlier Tradition, are received not as binding dogma but as later Latin theological developments.

Accepted by Oriental Orthodox Nicene Creed (without Filioque) Theotokos (God-bearer) of Mary Miaphysite Christology Apostolic succession & valid sacraments Real Presence in the Eucharist Prayer for the dead Veneration of saints & icons Not Received by Oriental Orthodox Filioque addition to the Creed Purgatory as defined doctrine Immaculate Conception of Mary Papal Infallibility & universal jurisdiction Treasury of Merit & indulgences Created grace (vs. uncreated energies) Satisfaction theory of atonement The Oriental Orthodox position is not rejection of Rome for its own sake. It is fidelity to the Vincentian Canon: quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus — that faith "which has been believed everywhere, always, by all."

Post-Schism Dogmatic Definitions The Roman Catholic Church has defined a number of dogmas since the Great Schism of 1054 — doctrines binding on all Catholics under pain of heresy. Many of these are defined by papal decree alone, a method the Oriental Orthodox cannot accept. Below is a summary of the major post-schism doctrinal definitions. 1439 Council of Florence — Purgatory, Papal Primacy Defined purgatorial cleansing after death (by "cleansing pains", leaving the question of fire open after Greek objections); affirmed papal primacy over the whole Church. 1545–63 Council of Trent — Justification, Indulgences, Purgatory Formalized the doctrine of merit, indulgences, and the purgatorial system against Protestant objections. 1854 Ineffabilis Deus — Immaculate Conception Pius IX defined ex cathedra that Mary was conceived without original sin. Later regarded as an exercise of papal infallibility, sixteen years before Vatican I defined it.

1870 Vatican I — Papal Infallibility & Universal Jurisdiction Defined that the pope, speaking ex cathedra on faith and morals, is infallible; that he holds immediate jurisdiction over every diocese. 1950 Munificentissimus Deus — Bodily Assumption Pius XII defined Mary's bodily assumption into heaven as dogma. (Note: The Dormition is celebrated by OO; the definition method is the issue.) Each of these definitions was either issued by papal decree without an Ecumenical Council, or at councils the Oriental Orthodox do not recognize as ecumenical. The objection is therefore as much about how dogma is defined as about the content itself.

Purgatory The doctrine of purgatory holds that souls who die in grace but with unforgiven venial sins or unpaid temporal punishment undergo a process of purification before entering heaven. This purification involves suffering — often described as fire. Roman Catholic Definition — Council of Florence (1439) "…if truly penitent people die in the love of God before they have made satisfaction for acts and omissions by worthy fruits of repentance, their souls are cleansed after death by cleansing pains." Council of Florence, Laetentur Caeli (1439); confirmed at Council of Trent (1563) Oriental Orthodox Position The Oriental Orthodox affirm prayer for the dead — it is ancient practice, present in our liturgies from the beginning. What we do not accept is the specific Latin framework: a third place between heaven and hell, temporal punishment satisfying divine justice, and (especially) indulgences reducing that punishment. The state of the departed is known to God alone. We pray for them in hope, not according to a doctrine of juridical debt.

The scriptural basis most often cited — 1 Corinthians 3:15 ("saved, yet as through fire") and 2 Maccabees 12:45 ("he made atonement for the dead," RSV; 12:46 in the Vulgate) — is accepted by Oriental Orthodox as supporting prayer for the dead. But neither passage specifies a place of punitive purification. The concept of purgatory as a formal doctrine is a medieval Western development, crystallized by scholastic theology (Aquinas, Bonaventure) before being dogmatically defined at Florence and Trent. St. John Chrysostom (d. 407) "Let us then give them aid and perform commemoration for them. For if the children of Job were purged by the sacrifice of their father, why do you doubt that when we too offer for the departed, some consolation arises to them?" Homilies on 1 Corinthians 41 (NPNF). Prayer for the dead affirmed, purgatorial system absent St. Cyril of Jerusalem (d.

386) "Then on behalf also of the Holy Fathers and Bishops who have fallen asleep before us, and in a word of all who in past years have fallen asleep among us, believing that it will be a very great benefit to the souls, for whom the supplication is put up, while that holy and most awful sacrifice is set forth." Catechetical Lecture 23.9 (NPNF). Prayer for the departed at the Liturgy, with no indulgences or satisfaction payments The Oriental Orthodox Liturgy of St. Basil and the Anaphora of St. Mark both include commemorations of the departed. But the theology is one of commending souls to God's mercy — not of administering punishments owed to divine justice.

The Immaculate Conception of Mary On December 8, 1854, Pope Pius IX issued Ineffabilis Deus , defining as dogma that "the most Blessed Virgin Mary, in the first instance of her conception, by a singular grace and privilege granted by Almighty God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, was preserved free from all stain of original sin." Roman Catholic Dogma — Ineffabilis Deus (1854) "We declare, pronounce, and define that the doctrine which holds that the most Blessed Virgin Mary, in the first instance of her conception… was preserved free from all stain of original sin, is a doctrine revealed by God and therefore to be believed firmly and constantly by all the faithful." Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus, 8 December 1854 Oriental Orthodox Position The Oriental Orthodox hold Mary in the highest veneration as Theotokos (God-bearer) and Panagia (All-Holy). But the Immaculate Conception rests on a distinctly Western (Augustinian) understanding of original sin as inherited guilt transmitted at conception.

The Eastern and Oriental traditions understand ancestral sin differently: all humans inherit the consequences of Adam's fall — mortality, passions, the tendency toward sin — but not the guilt of Adam's act. On this anthropology, the Immaculate Conception is not needed: Mary did not need to be exempted from guilt she would not have borne anyway. She was wholly sanctified and prepared as the vessel of the Incarnation — above all, at the Annunciation when the Holy Spirit came upon her (Luke 1:35). This is not a rejection of Mary's holiness — it is a different theological grammar about sin and grace. St. Athanasius, St. Cyril of Alexandria, and St. Ephrem all celebrate Mary as utterly holy. None of them employ the Latin framework of original guilt as the starting point. St. Cyril of Alexandria (d. 444) "Mary, Mother of God, we salute you.

Precious vessel, worthy of the whole world's reverence, you are an ever-shining light, the crown of virginity, the symbol of orthodoxy, an indestructible temple, the place that held him whom no place can contain, mother and virgin." Homily 4 at Ephesus, 431 (as published by Crossroads Initiative). Highest praise, but no exemption from ancestral nature St. Gregory of Nazianzus (d. 390) "Conceived by the Virgin, who first in body and soul was purified by the Holy Ghost (for it was needful both that Childbearing should be honoured, and that Virginity should receive a higher honour), He came forth then as God with that which He had assumed." Oration 38.13 (NPNF). Purification at the Annunciation, not at conception Furthermore, the definition itself was problematic by ecclesiological standards: it was issued by a single pope without an Ecumenical Council. Thomas Aquinas himself had argued against the Immaculate Conception. It was disputed within Western scholasticism for centuries before being defined as dogma by papal decree.

Papal Infallibility & Universal Jurisdiction The First Vatican Council (1870) defined two interlinked dogmas that the Oriental Orthodox regard as the most significant departure from ancient ecclesiology. Vatican I — Pastor Aeternus (1870) "We teach and define as a divinely revealed dogma that when the Roman pontiff speaks ex cathedra… he possesses, by the divine assistance promised to him in blessed Peter, that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his church to enjoy in defining doctrine concerning faith or morals." Vatican I, Pastor Aeternus, Ch. 4 (1870) Oriental Orthodox Position Infallibility belongs to the Church as a whole, expressed through Ecumenical Councils received by the whole Body. No single bishop — not even the Bishop of Rome — holds infallibility in his own person. In the Orthodox reading, the ancient Church knew a primacy of honor for Rome (Canon 3 of Constantinople 381 was given to New Rome for the same reason — imperial prestige, not Petrine succession).

Immediate universal jurisdiction over every diocese contradicts the canonical independence of each patriarchate and was unknown in the pre-schism Church. For a thorough examination of the Petrine texts, the historical rise of Roman claims, the problem cases (Honorius I, Vigilius, Liberius), and the OO patristic counter-reading, see the dedicated site: Papal Authority & Infallibility →

The Filioque The Filioque ( and the Son ) is the addition to the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed that the Western Church inserted unilaterally, so that the clause reads: "…the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son ." The original Creed, ratified by the Ecumenical Councils and never altered by conciliar authority, reads: "…who proceeds from the Father." The Filioque in the Latin Creed "I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son …" Latin Rite Creed — insertion first used in Spain (6th c.), imposed universally by Rome c. 1014 Oriental Orthodox Position The OO objects on two grounds. Theologically: the Filioque compromises the monarchy of the Father as the sole source and principle within the Trinity. The Spirit proceeds from the Father alone (John 15:26). Canonically: no single church has authority to alter a creed ratified by an Ecumenical Council. The Third Ecumenical Council (Ephesus 431) explicitly forbade composing any other creed.

Adding to it is therefore an act of unilateral authority the ancient Church did not grant to any see. For a full treatment including the patristic evidence, Augustine's theology of the Spirit, and the modern ecumenical dialogue, see the dedicated site: The Filioque →

Indulgences & the Treasury of Merit The Roman Catholic doctrine of indulgences rests on several interconnected premises: (1) sin incurs both guilt and temporal punishment; (2) guilt is forgiven in confession but temporal punishment remains; (3) the Church holds a "treasury of merit" accumulated by Christ and the saints; (4) the Pope has authority to apply this treasury to reduce punishment in purgatory. Council of Trent — Decree on Indulgences (1563) "Whereas the power of conferring Indulgences was granted by Christ to the Church; and she has, even in the most ancient times, used the said power, delivered unto her of God; the sacred holy Synod teaches, and enjoins, that the use of Indulgences, for the Christian people most salutary… is to be retained in the Church." (tr. Waterworth) Council of Trent, Session 25, Decree on Indulgences (1563) Oriental Orthodox Position This entire system presupposes the Latin juridical framework of atonement: sin as debt, punishment as satisfying divine justice, a treasury that can be administered.

The Oriental Orthodox understand salvation not as the satisfaction of a legal debt but as theosis — participation in the divine life. There is no treasury of merit in the ancient Tradition. God forgives because he is Love, not because a sufficient quantity of merit has been deposited and transferred. The system of indulgences was unknown to the early Church and was, historically, the immediate cause of the Protestant Reformation — a judgment that speaks to its departure from the Tradition. "If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared." Psalm 130:3-4 The Church's authority to "loose" (Matthew 18:18) refers to the forgiveness of sins and the restoration of the sinner to communion — not the administration of a celestial accounting ledger. The Fathers who wrote on forgiveness (Chrysostom, Cyril, Ephrem) uniformly speak of God's mercy and the sinner's repentance, not of merit transferred between accounts.

Created Grace vs. Uncreated Energies This is perhaps the most philosophically profound divide between Eastern/Oriental Orthodox theology and Latin scholasticism. The question: when God saves and sanctifies us, what is it that we receive? Latin Scholastic (Aquinas) Grace is a created quality infused into the soul It is a habit (habitus) — a disposition God creates within us We participate in divine life through a created intermediary God himself remains inaccessible in his essence; we receive created gifts Eastern/Oriental Orthodox (Palamas) Grace is the uncreated divine energies — God himself, acting ad extra God is truly and fully present in his energies, though his essence remains transcendent Theosis is real participation in God, not in a created substitute Peter's "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Pet 1:4) is taken literally The Palamite distinction between God's unknowable essence and his knowable-yet-truly-divine energies was affirmed by a series of councils in Constantinople (1341, 1347, 1351) and is considered a permanent doctrinal achievement of Orthodox theology.

The Latin view, by contrast, would mean we are never truly united to God himself — only to a created reality God produces. "He has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature." 2 Peter 1:4 St. Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373) "For He was made man that we might be made God." (θεοποιηθῶμεν) On the Incarnation 54 (NPNF). Theosis as real union, not mediated through a created quality St. Gregory Palamas (d. 1359) "Only those beings united to It are deified «by the total presence of the Anointer»; they have received an energy identical to that of the deifying essence, and possessing it in absolute entirety, reveal it through themselves." Triads III.1 (tr. Gendle). The deifying energy is truly God, not a creature The Oriental Orthodox share the Eastern framework of theosis.

While the Palamite councils are Eastern Orthodox patrimony specifically, the underlying conviction — that we are genuinely united to God himself, not to a created substitute — is native to the entire patristic East and is expressed in every OO anaphora.

Satisfaction Theory of Atonement Anselm of Canterbury (d. 1109) developed the satisfaction theory in Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man). The logic: sin offends the infinite honor of God; only an infinite satisfaction can repair it; only God can offer infinite satisfaction; therefore God became man to offer it. The Incarnation and Cross are understood primarily as the payment of a debt owed to divine justice. Anselm's Framework (Cur Deus Homo, 1098) "…satisfaction or punishment must needs follow every sin." (I.15) "Therefore none but God can make this satisfaction… But none but a man ought to do this, otherwise man does not make the satisfaction." (II.6) Anselm, Cur Deus Homo I.15 and II.6 (1098; tr. Deane) Oriental Orthodox Position The Oriental Orthodox understand the Incarnation, Cross, and Resurrection as the healing and deification of human nature — not the payment of a legal fine. God became flesh to unite humanity to divinity, to sanctify human nature from within, to destroy death by death (the Paschal mystery), and to restore the image of God in us.

The Cross is not primarily a transaction with divine justice but the total self-offering of God in love, which defeats the power of sin, death, and the devil. This "Christus Victor" and "healing" framework is native to Athanasius, Cyril, Ephrem, and the entire patristic East. St. Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373) "And thus taking from our bodies one of like nature, because all were under penalty of the corruption of death He gave it over to death in the stead of all, and offered it to the Father — doing this, moreover, of His loving-kindness, to the end that, firstly, all being held to have died in Him, the law involving the ruin of men might be undone." On the Incarnation 8 (NPNF). Death undone, not a debt paid to an offended judge St. Irenaeus of Lyon (d. c. 202) "…the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself." Against Heresies V, Preface (ANF).

Recapitulation, not satisfaction The satisfaction theory is not explicitly condemned by the Oriental Orthodox — it captures something real about sin as offense and Christ's atoning work. But when elevated to the primary or only framework for understanding the Cross, it distorts the full scope of salvation, fits closely with the purgatorial-indulgence system (though that system's roots in the penitential practice of the early medieval West are older than Anselm), and ultimately portrays the Father as an offended feudal lord requiring payment rather than the loving God who "so loved the world" that he entered it. In fairness, Catholic theologians answer that Anselm was never meant to be the whole account, and that Catholic teaching also confesses deification: the Catechism of the Catholic Church (§460) quotes Athanasius, "For the Son of God became man so that we might become God." The Orthodox concern is less that Rome denies theosis than that, in Western practice and preaching, the language of debt and satisfaction came to dominate it.

secs.h: The Method Problem: How Are Dogmas Defined?
secs.x: The Method Problem: How Are Dogmas Defined? Beyond disagreeing with the content of several post-schism dogmas, the Oriental Orthodox have a fundamental objection to the method by which they were defined. This is not a secondary issue — it goes to the heart of what the Church is. The Ancient Method Doctrine was defined by Ecumenical Councils — gatherings of bishops from the entire Church, whose definitions were subsequently received by the whole Body. The council's authority was validated not by the presiding bishop's office alone but by the reception of the universal Church over time. This is conciliarism: truth is discerned collegially and confirmed by reception. The Post-Vatican I Method The Immaculate Conception (1854) and Bodily Assumption (1950) were defined by single popes, without Ecumenical Councils, as dogmas binding under pain of heresy. The authority invoked was the infallibility of the papal office itself — an office defined as infallible by Vatican I (1870), which was itself convened and presided over by the papacy.

secs.h: The Method Problem: How Are Dogmas Defined?
secs.x: The Oriental Orthodox see here a circular validation of unprecedented authority. The question is not merely political. If any single bishop can bind the universal Church to new dogmas by his personal declaration, then the Church's authority is concentrated in one office in a way the ancient canons never envisioned and the Fathers never described. The Council of Nicaea was not convened because Constantine or Sylvester of Rome declared the answer — it was convened to seek the answer through collegial discernment. "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us…" Acts 15:28 — the apostolic model: conciliar discernment, not singular declaration The 1973 Common Declaration between Pope Paul VI and Coptic Pope Shenouda III, and the 1984 Common Declaration between Pope John Paul II and Syriac Patriarch Ignatius Zakka I, demonstrate that genuine dialogue is possible. But full communion remains impossible while Rome holds that the post-schism papal dogmas are irreformable and binding on all Christians everywhere.

Catholic Objections RC "Doesn't development of doctrine mean the Church can define new dogmas over time?" Yes — the Oriental Orthodox affirm that doctrine develops. The Council of Nicaea (325) produced the word homoousios , not found in Scripture. The Council of Ephesus (431) defined Theotokos. Development is real. But there is a crucial distinction between organic development — explicating what was always implicitly believed, through conciliar reception — and innovation that introduces new content previously unknown to the Tradition. The Immaculate Conception was disputed for centuries even within Western theology (Aquinas denied it). Purgatory as a punitive holding-place has no clear patristic consensus. Defining disputed novelties as binding dogma by papal decree is a different kind of act than the Councils explicating the Apostolic faith. RC "The Oriental Orthodox also accept things not explicitly in Scripture — icons, Theotokos, canon lists.

Why draw the line here?" Every example cited by OO — the veneration of icons, the Theotokos, the canon of Scripture — was either affirmed by an Ecumenical Council received by the universal Church, or expresses the universal and unbroken liturgical practice of the whole Tradition from the earliest centuries. The criterion is not "is this in the Bible alone?" — it is "does this belong to the Apostolic Tradition as believed everywhere, always, by all?" The post-schism RC dogmas fail that test: they were either unknown to the pre-schism Church, or were disputed questions within it, or were defined by a method (sole papal decree) the pre-schism Church did not recognize. RC "Mary's holiness surely required that she be preserved from all sin, including original sin." This argument presupposes the Western Augustinian understanding of original sin as inherited guilt. The Oriental Orthodox — along with the Eastern Orthodox — understand ancestral sin differently. We inherit the consequences (mortality, the tendency to sin, the passions) but not the guilt of Adam's act.

On this anthropology, no one is born guilty; they become guilty through their own personal sins. There is therefore no inherited guilt for Mary to be exempt from. Her utter holiness is affirmed — she is Panagia, All-Holy — but it is achieved through God's grace working in and with her nature, not by a retroactive exemption from something she never bore in the Eastern framework. RC "Purgatory just means souls are purified before heaven — surely you believe that too?" The Oriental Orthodox absolutely believe in God's mercy toward the dead and in the value of prayer for the departed. What OO does not accept is the specific Latin juridical apparatus: (a) a third distinct place/state called purgatory, (b) the theory that temporal punishment must be satisfied even after forgiveness, (c) the Treasury of Merit by which the Church administers stored merit to reduce that punishment, and (d) indulgences as official church instruments for doing so. Prayer for the dead — yes, ancient and necessary.

A divinely-managed punishment-satisfaction system with an ecclesiastical treasury — no, this is a medieval Latin development with no equivalent in the patristic East. RC "The Oriental Orthodox have their own councils and theological developments — aren't you doing the same thing?" The Oriental Orthodox have no post-schism dogmatic definitions equivalent to those cited above. The doctrines they hold — Miaphysite Christology, the veneration of Theotokos, the seven sacraments, the Apostolic succession — all have roots in the pre-schism universal Tradition and were either defined by the first three Ecumenical Councils or represent continuous and universal practice. No OO patriarch has issued a bull defining new binding dogma by his own authority. The objection is therefore not that development is wrong, but that the Roman Catholic post-schism method of papal-decree dogma-definition exceeds any authority the pre-schism Church recognized.

Frequently Asked Questions Does the Oriental Orthodox Church consider the Catholic Church heretical? Not in the same way that, say, a denial of the Trinity would be called heretical. The RC Church preserves Apostolic succession, valid sacraments, and the ancient Christological faith. The OO objections are to specific post-schism doctrinal developments and to the ecclesiological claims of Vatican I. Many OO theologians speak of the RC as a sister church that has departed in certain areas, rather than as a heretical sect. The 1973 Common Declaration between Pope Paul VI and Pope Shenouda III explicitly affirmed shared faith in Christ. Would OO and RC union require Catholics to abandon these dogmas? Practically, yes — this is the central obstacle. Vatican I defines the Immaculate Conception, Papal Infallibility, and Purgatory as dogmas binding on all Christians. The OO cannot accept these as binding. Full communion would require either Rome to revise how these dogmas are held (as binding on all vs.

as Western theological expressions), or a recognition that different theological schools within one Church can differ on these points — similar to how the RC currently tolerates diverse schools on grace and free will. This is a genuine impasse, though dialogue continues. Do the Oriental Orthodox pray for the dead? Yes, extensively. The Liturgy of St. Basil, the Anaphora of St. Mark, and all OO liturgical traditions include commemoration of the departed. The Saturday of the Dead (Sbt el-Amwat in the Coptic tradition) is a regular liturgical observance. The OO affirm that prayer for the dead is ancient, apostolic, and salutary. What they reject is the specific purgatorial framework — a third place, temporal punishment debt, and the treasury/indulgence system — not the practice of praying for those who have died. What about the Bodily Assumption of Mary — do OO believe in that? Yes. The Feast of the Dormition (Falling Asleep) of the Theotokos is celebrated by all Oriental Orthodox churches. The OO believe Mary was taken body and soul into heaven.

The objection is not to the content of the 1950 definition but to the method: Pius XII defined it ex cathedra as dogma binding on all Christians without an Ecumenical Council. The OO cannot accept a pope's personal decree as sufficient authority to bind the universal Church. The Dormition is held as a pious and certain belief; its elevation to infallibly-defined dogma by papal decree is the problem. Is there any hope for Catholic-Oriental Orthodox union? There is genuine hope rooted in genuine agreement. The 1973 Common Declaration, the Pro Oriente consultations, and recent papal meetings with Oriental Orthodox patriarchs all demonstrate goodwill. The shared Christological agreements of 1973 and 1984 (OO and RC agree on one Christ, fully human and fully divine, despite different technical vocabulary) removed a major doctrinal barrier. What remains are the issues addressed in this site. Progress is slow because the issues are real — but the Spirit is not bound, and the prayer "that they may all be one" (John 17:21) drives the dialogue forward.

Glossary Purgatory RC doctrine: a state of purifying suffering after death for those who die in grace but with remaining temporal punishment for sin. Defined at Florence (1439) and Trent (1563). Immaculate Conception RC dogma (1854): that Mary was preserved from original sin from the moment of her conception, by anticipatory application of Christ's merits. Ex Cathedra Latin: "from the chair." A formal papal definition of doctrine, claimed to be infallible under Vatican I's definition. By common Catholic reckoning invoked only twice: Immaculate Conception (1854) and Bodily Assumption (1950). Treasury of Merit RC doctrine: the inexhaustible store of merit accumulated by Christ and the saints, administered by the Church through indulgences to reduce temporal punishment. Indulgence The remission of temporal punishment due to sin, granted by Church authority from the Treasury of Merit, applicable to the living or (by suffrage) to souls in purgatory. Created Grace Scholastic theology: grace as a created habit (quality) infused into the soul by God, as distinct from God's own being.

Contrasted with the Orthodox doctrine of uncreated energies. Uncreated Energies Orthodox theology: grace is the uncreated divine energies — God himself acting and communicating himself — truly God, yet distinct from the unknowable divine essence. Defined at the Palamite Councils (1341–1351). Theosis Deification; the process by which the human person participates in the divine nature (2 Pet 1:4). The goal of Christian life in Eastern/Oriental theology: union with God, not merely forgiveness of legal debt. Satisfaction Theory Anselm's atonement model: Christ's death satisfies the infinite honor of God offended by human sin. Basis for the RC purgatorial and indulgence system. Contrasted with the patristic models of theosis and Christus Victor. Vincentian Canon The criterion of St. Vincent of Lérins (d. 445): true Christian doctrine is that faith "which has been believed everywhere, always, by all" (quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus). The standard by which OO evaluates doctrinal claims.

Conciliarism The ecclesiological principle that doctrinal authority resides in Ecumenical Councils of the whole Church, not in any single bishop or see. The ancient and OO position, contrasted with Vatican I's papal supremacy. Filioque Latin: "and the Son." The phrase added by the Western Church to the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, asserting that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son. Rejected by Eastern and Oriental Orthodox as theological error and canonical violation.

I. Introduction: The Rest of the Argument Romans 9 is often read as if it stood alone. It does not. Paul's answer to the question "Has God's word to Israel failed?" runs through chapters 10 and 11, and it is only at the end of chapter 11 that he bursts into praise: "Oh, the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" Chapter 10 turns from God's freedom to Israel's responsibility. Israel had zeal but not knowledge, and sought righteousness by the law instead of by faith in Christ, who is the end of the law. The gospel is near: "if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you will be saved." But how will people believe unless someone is sent to preach? Chapter 11 answers whether God has cast away His people. He has not. There is a remnant chosen by grace.

Some branches were broken off the olive tree for unbelief, and Gentiles were grafted in by faith, but the broken branches can be grafted in again, and "all Israel will be saved." This page reads these chapters with St John Chrysostom, St Justin, St Augustine and Calvin, and shows how they complete the argument of Romans 9. "For it was not God that cut them off, but they have broken themselves off and fallen... You see what a great thing a man's free choice is." St John Chrysostom, Homily 19 on Romans This page is part of Romans with the Fathers , a series of nine pages that read St Paul's letter to the Romans section by section with the Church Fathers, setting their reading beside the main Protestant readings. Use the bar at the top of the page to move between the sections of the letter.

A Note on Quotations Every quotation marked VERBATIM has been checked word for word against a public domain translation: St John Chrysostom's thirty-two Homilies on Romans and the other Fathers in the Ante-Nicene and Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series, John Calvin's Commentary on Romans in John Owen's translation (1849), and the Reformation confessions in Philip Schaff's Creeds of Christendom . Chrysostom's homilies follow J. B. Morris's translation as revised by W. H. Simcox, in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, volume 11. Where a work has no public domain English translation, its teaching is summarised and marked PARAPHRASE . Scripture follows the NKJV.

II. Glossary of Terms End, goal τέλος · telos "Christ is the end of the law" (10:4): its goal and fulfilment, and also its conclusion as a way to righteousness. Confess ὁμολογέω · homologeō To say the same thing, to declare publicly. "Jesus is Lord" was the confession of faith at baptism (10:9). Hearing ἀκοή · akoē What is heard, the message preached (10:17). Sent ἀποστέλλω · apostellō To send with authority, the root of "apostle" (10:15). Remnant λεῖμμα · leimma What is left over, the faithful few (11:5). Hardening, blindness πώρωσις · pōrōsis A callus, dullness of heart (11:25). Stupor, slumber κατάνυξις · katanyxis A numbness of spirit (11:8, quoting Isaiah 29:10). Broken off ἐκκλάω · ekklaō Broken off like a branch (11:17–20). Graft in ἐγκεντρίζω · enkentrizō To graft a branch into a tree (11:17–24). Mystery μυστήριον · mystērion A purpose of God once hidden and now revealed (11:25). Fullness πλήρωμα · plērōma The full number or completion (11:12, 25). Irrevocable ἀμεταμέλητα · ametamelēta Without regret. God's gifts and calling are not taken back (11:29).

secs.h: III. Zeal Without Knowledge: Christ the End of the Law (10:1–8)
secs.x: III. Zeal Without Knowledge: Christ the End of the Law (10:1–8) Romans 10:1-4 "Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted to the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes." Orthodox reading: Israel's problem was not lack of zeal but seeking their own righteousness instead of submitting to God's. Christ is the goal of the law for all who believe. St John Chrysostom Homily 17 on Romans (on 10:4) "For if Christ be the end of the Law, he that has not Christ, even if he seem to have that righteousness, has it not. But he that has Christ, even though he have not fulfilled the Law aright, has received the whole.

secs.h: III. Zeal Without Knowledge: Christ the End of the Law (10:1–8)
secs.x: For the end of the physician's art is health." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 17 on Romans (on 10:4) "For what was the object of the Law? To make man righteous. But it had not the power, for no one fulfilled it. This then was the end of the Law and to this it looked throughout..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Notice what Paul says the cause of Israel's failure was: "they, being ignorant of God's righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted to the righteousness of God" (10:3). This is the same reason he gave at the end of chapter 9 (9:32). The stumbling was not because God refused them, but because they refused the way He offered. Romans 9 must be read in the light of this.

IV. Confess with Your Mouth (10:9–13) Romans 10:9-10 "that if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Orthodox reading: Faith in the heart and confession with the mouth belong together. The confession is that Jesus is Lord and that God raised Him from the dead. Romans 10:11-13 "For the Scripture says, 'Whoever believes on Him will not be put to shame.' For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord over all is rich to all who call upon Him. For 'whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.'" Orthodox reading: No distinction between Jew and Greek: whoever calls on the Lord's name will be saved.

St John Chrysostom Homily 17 on Romans (on 10:9) "For that requires the fulfilment of all things (for when you do all, then you shall live); but the righteousness which is of faith does not say this, but what? If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you shall be saved. Then again that we may not seem to be making it contemptible by showing it to be easy and cheap, observe how he expands his account of it." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 17 on Romans (on 10:6–8) "...thus, when one is required to believe, there are reasonings which confuse and make havoc of the minds of most men, and it wants a soul of some vigor to shake them thoroughly off." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION In many evangelical churches Romans 10:9 is used as the basis of the "sinner's prayer": a person prays to receive Christ and is assured of salvation. The Orthodox share the conviction behind it, that salvation is near and offered to everyone who believes and calls on the Lord.

But in the early Church "Jesus is Lord" was the confession made at baptism, and the Orthodox still have catechumens confess the faith before they are baptised. Confession is not a one-time formula but the beginning of a life, as Christ said: "Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father" (Matthew 7:21).

secs.h: V. How Shall They Preach Unless Sent? (10:14–21)
secs.x: V. How Shall They Preach Unless Sent? (10:14–21) Romans 10:14-15 "How then shall they call on Him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel of peace, Who bring glad tidings of good things!'" Orthodox reading: Calling depends on believing, believing on hearing, hearing on a preacher, and preaching on being sent. Romans 10:17 "So then faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God." Orthodox reading: Faith comes by hearing the word of God. St John Chrysostom Homily 18 on Romans (on 10:14–15) "Yet hear they did, he implies. Then another objection again. And how could they hear without a preacher? Then an answer again.

secs.h: V. How Shall They Preach Unless Sent? (10:14–21)
secs.x: Yet preach they did, and there were many sent forth for this very purpose." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Paul's chain ends with "unless they are sent." The Orthodox see here one of the roots of apostolic order: the gospel is preached by those whom Christ sends through His Church, as the apostles sent others and laid hands on them. Protestants rightly answer that every Christian is called to bear witness. Both are true; the question of who is sent to preach and lead the Church is treated on Apostolic Succession . "Faith comes by hearing" also explains why the Orthodox Liturgy is so full of Scripture read and sung aloud. For most of Christian history most believers could not read. They heard the word in church, and it formed their faith.

secs.h: V. How Shall They Preach Unless Sent? (10:14–21)
secs.x: Romans 10:20-21 "But Isaiah is very bold and says: 'I was found by those who did not seek Me; I was made manifest to those who did not ask for Me.' But to Israel he says: 'All day long I have stretched out My hands To a disobedient and contrary people.'" Orthodox reading: God was found by Gentiles who did not seek Him, and all day long He stretched out His hands to a disobedient Israel. That last verse is a picture of the potter of Jeremiah 18: God's hands are not closed against Israel but stretched out all day long. The refusal is theirs.

secs.h: VI. A Remnant by the Election of Grace (11:1–10)
secs.x: VI. A Remnant by the Election of Grace (11:1–10) Romans 11:1-2 "I say then, has God cast away His people? Certainly not! For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not cast away His people whom He foreknew. Or do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel, saying," Orthodox reading: God has not cast away His people. Paul himself is the proof. Romans 11:5-6 "Even so then, at this present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace. And if by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if it is of works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work." Orthodox reading: As in Elijah's day, there is a faithful remnant, chosen by grace and not by works. St John Chrysostom Homily 18 on Romans (on 11:5) "Observe that each word maintains its own rank, showing at once God's grace, and the obedient temper of them that receive salvation.

secs.h: VI. A Remnant by the Election of Grace (11:1–10)
secs.x: For by saying election, he showed the approval of them, but by saying grace, he showed the gift of God." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 18 on Romans (on 11:4–5) "...since in Elijah's time the part to be saved had come down to seven thousand: and now also there are probably many that believe. But if you do not know who they are, this is no wonder, for that prophet, who was so great and good a man, did not know." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Romans 11:7-8 "What then? Israel has not obtained what it seeks; but the elect have obtained it, and the rest were blinded. Just as it is written: 'God has given them a spirit of stupor, Eyes that they should not see And ears that they should not hear, To this very day.'" Orthodox reading: The rest were hardened, and God gave them "a spirit of stupor." St John Chrysostom Homily 19 on Romans (on 11:8) "Now whence came this blinding? He had indeed mentioned the causes of it before, and turned it all upon their own heads, to show that it was from their unseasonable obstinacy that they had to bear

secs.h: VI. A Remnant by the Election of Grace (11:1–10)
secs.x: this... And the He gave, do not imagine to mean here an agency, but a permission only." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION This is the same rule St John of Damascus gave for Romans 1 and Romans 9: Scripture often speaks of what God permits as if He did it. The hardening of Israel in 11:7–10 is God's judgement on a refusal, not the cause of it. And, as the next verses show, it is not final.

VII. The Olive Tree (11:11–24) Romans 11:11-12 "I say then, have they stumbled that they should fall? Certainly not! But through their fall, to provoke them to jealousy, salvation has come to the Gentiles. Now if their fall is riches for the world, and their failure riches for the Gentiles, how much more their fullness!" Orthodox reading: Israel's stumbling is not a fall beyond recovery. It opened the door to the Gentiles, and Israel's fullness will mean even greater riches. Romans 11:17-18 "And if some of the branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive tree, were grafted in among them, and with them became a partaker of the root and fatness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you do boast, remember that you do not support the root, but the root supports you." Orthodox reading: Gentile believers are wild branches grafted into Israel's olive tree. They must not boast against the natural branches. Romans 11:19-21 "You will say then, 'Branches were broken off that I might be grafted in.' Well said.

Because of unbelief they were broken off, and you stand by faith. Do not be haughty, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, He may not spare you either." Orthodox reading: The branches were broken off because of unbelief, and you stand by faith. Do not be haughty, but fear. Romans 11:22-23 "Therefore consider the goodness and severity of God: on those who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness, if you continue in His goodness. Otherwise you also will be cut off. And they also, if they do not continue in unbelief, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again." Orthodox reading: God's goodness to those who continue in it, His severity to those who fell, and the promise that the broken branches can be grafted in again if they do not continue in unbelief. St John Chrysostom Homily 19 on Romans (on 11:23) "For it was not God that cut them off, but they have broken themselves off and fallen, and he did well to say have broken themselves off. For He has never yet so... cast them off, though they have sinned so much and so often.

You see what a great thing a man's free choice is, how great the efficacy of the mind is. For none of these things is immutable, neither your good nor his evil." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 19 on Romans (on 11:22–23) "The reason why He cut you off in severity was, that you might long to come back. The reason why He showed goodness to you was, that you might continue in (he does not say the faith, but) His goodness, that is, if you do things worthy of God's love toward man." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Here, in Paul's own words, is the potter's house of Jeremiah 18. The branches broken off can be grafted back; the branches grafted in can be cut off. God's severity aims at return; His goodness asks for perseverance. "None of these things is immutable." This is the end of the argument that began in Romans 9, and it confirms that the potter of 9:21 is the potter who remakes the spoiled vessel.

Calvin, who read Romans 9 as a decree concerning individuals, reads the condition in 11:22 as applying to peoples, not to the elect individually: John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 11:22) "But as he speaks not of the elect individually, but of the whole body, a condition is added, If they continued in his kindness... but it would be improper to say of any one of the godly particularly, that God had mercy on him, when he chose him, provided he would continue in his mercy; for the perseverance of faith, which completes in us the effect of God's grace, flows from election itself." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) This is worth noticing. When the text is conditional, Calvin says it speaks of peoples, not individuals; when the text speaks of peoples in Romans 9 (Jacob and Esau, "two nations"), he reads it as a decree about individuals. The Orthodox read both chapters the same way: God deals with peoples and with persons, and in both cases He responds to faith and unbelief. Calvin is right, though, about one thing: these warnings are meant to humble, not to terrify.
Even Calvin says here that those who "begin to loathe the kingdom of heaven" deserve to be blinded again.

secs.h: 1. The Jewish people, turning to Christ at the end
secs.x: VIII. "All Israel Will Be Saved" (11:25–27) Romans 11:25-27 "For I do not desire, brethren, that you should be ignorant of this mystery, lest you should be wise in your own opinion, that blindness in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And so all Israel will be saved, as it is written: 'The Deliverer will come out of Zion, And He will turn away ungodliness from Jacob; For this is My covenant with them, When I take away their sins.'" Orthodox reading: Israel's hardening is partial and temporary, until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved. Who is "all Israel"? There have been three main answers. 1. The Jewish people, turning to Christ at the end St John Chrysostom Homily 19 on Romans (on 11:26–27) "Not when they are circumcised, not when they sacrifice, not when they do the other deeds of the Law, but when they attain to the forgiveness of sins.

secs.h: 1. The Jewish people, turning to Christ at the end
secs.x: If then this has been promised, but has never yet happened in their case, nor have they ever enjoyed the remission of sins by baptism, certainly it will come to pass." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 19 on Romans (on 11:28) "Nevertheless God has not even now cut short the calling of you, but He waits for all the Gentiles that are to believe to come in, and then they also shall come." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Augustine of Hippo City of God XX.29 "It is a familiar theme in the conversation and heart of the faithful, that in the last days before the judgment the Jews shall believe in the true Christ, that is, our Christ, by means of this great and admirable prophet Elias who shall expound the law to them." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Malachi 4:5-6 "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet Before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord.

secs.h: 1. The Jewish people, turning to Christ at the end
secs.x: And he will turn The hearts of the fathers to the children, And the hearts of the children to their fathers, Lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.'" Orthodox reading: The promise of Elijah before the great day of the Lord, which many Fathers connected with Israel's turning to Christ. 2. The whole people of God, Jews and Gentiles together John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 11:26) "Many understand this of the Jewish people, as though Paul had said, that religion would again be restored among them as before: but I extend the word Israel to all the people of God... The Israel of God is what he calls the Church, gathered alike from Jews and Gentiles..." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Galatians 6:16 "And as many as walk according to this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God." Orthodox reading: Paul's phrase "the Israel of God," which Calvin and many others take to mean the Church. St Justin Martyr Dialogue with Trypho 11 "For the true spiritual Israel, and descendants of Judah, Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham...

secs.h: 1. The Jewish people, turning to Christ at the end
secs.x: are we who have been led to God through this crucified Christ..." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION 3. Israel on a separate track In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries many evangelical Protestants adopted dispensationalism, which teaches that God has two distinct peoples with distinct destinies, Israel and the Church, and that Romans 11 refers to a future national restoration connected with the rapture and a millennium. This view is unknown in the Fathers and is discussed on The Rapture & End Times . A few modern writers go further and suggest that Jews may be saved by the old covenant apart from faith in Christ. Paul's own words rule this out: they will be grafted in again "if they do not continue in unbelief" (11:23). The Orthodox hold together what the Fathers held: the Church, made of Jews and Gentiles in Christ, is the Israel of God; and the Jewish people remain "beloved for the sake of the fathers" (11:28), and the Church prays and hopes for their turning to Christ, which many Fathers expected before the end.

secs.h: 1. The Jewish people, turning to Christ at the end
secs.x: A Hard Fact Romans 11 forbids Gentile Christians to "boast against the branches." It must be said honestly that Christians have often done exactly that. St John Chrysostom himself, whose reading of Romans 11 is so generous, preached eight sermons Against the Jews in Antioch in 386 and 387. They were aimed at Christians who were attending synagogue festivals, but their language about the Jewish people is harsh, and in later centuries it was used to justify hatred. The Orthodox honour Chrysostom as a saint and teacher; that does not mean every sentence he spoke in the heat of controversy is the mind of the Church. Paul's command stands over all of us: "Do not be haughty, but fear."

IX. Mercy on All (11:28–32) Romans 11:28-29 "Concerning the gospel they are enemies for your sake, but concerning the election they are beloved for the sake of the fathers. For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable." Orthodox reading: Israel remains beloved because of the patriarchs. God's gifts and calling are irrevocable. Romans 11:30-32 "For as you were once disobedient to God, yet have now obtained mercy through their disobedience, even so these also have now been disobedient, that through the mercy shown you they also may obtain mercy. For God has committed them all to disobedience, that He might have mercy on all." Orthodox reading: God has shut up all in disobedience so that He may have mercy on all. St John Chrysostom Homily 19 on Romans (on 11:32) "However, they will not perish forever.

For God has concluded them all in unbelief, that is, has convinced them, has shown them disobedient; not that they may remain in disobedience, but that He may save the one by the captiousness of the other, these by those and those by these." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Here the long argument of Romans 9 to 11 reaches its goal. It does not end with some vessels fixed for honour and others for wrath, but with God's purpose to have mercy on all, Jew and Gentile, each brought in by way of the other. That is the context in which Romans 9 must be read. Does "mercy on all" mean everyone will finally be saved? Origen speculated that in the end all rational beings, perhaps even demons, would be restored. That speculation was rejected, and Pope Theophilus of Alexandria condemned Origen's errors. Paul is speaking of Jews and Gentiles as peoples, and the same chapter says that branches which do not continue in God's goodness will be cut off (11:22). God's will is that all be saved; whether each person accepts that mercy is the freedom He has given.
The Church hopes and prays for all, and does not presume to declare that no one will be lost.

X. O the Depth! (11:33–36) Romans 11:33-36 "Oh, the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments and His ways past finding out! 'For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has become His counselor?' 'Or who has first given to Him And it shall be repaid to him?' For of Him and through Him and to Him are all things, to whom be glory forever. Amen." Orthodox reading: Paul's argument ends not in a system but in worship. God's judgements are unsearchable, and all things are from Him, through Him and to Him. St John Chrysostom Homily 19 on Romans (on 11:33) "That it is a depth then, he knows: but how great, he knows not. For the language is that of a person wondering, not of one that knew the whole.

But admiring and being awe-struck at the goodliness, so far forth as in him lay, he heralds it forth by two intensitive words, riches and depth, and then is awestruck at His having had both the will and the power to do all this, and by opposites effecting opposites." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION This is a good place for every reader of Romans 9 to 11 to end, whatever his tradition. Paul does not finish with a diagram of the decrees. He finishes on his knees. The Orthodox reading of these chapters does not claim to explain everything about God's ways. It claims only what Paul himself says: that God's wisdom brings mercy out of disobedience, that no one is beyond the reach of His outstretched hands, and that "of Him and through Him and to Him are all things, to whom be glory forever. Amen."

XI. Objections Answered ""The election of grace" (11:5) proves that God chose the remnant regardless of their response." OO Response: Paul's point is that the remnant was not chosen because of works of the law; it was God's gift. Chrysostom notes that Paul's two words keep "their own rank": "election" shows the approval of those who received salvation, and "grace" shows the gift of God. And in the same chapter Paul explains why others were not in the remnant: "because of unbelief they were broken off" (11:20). ""God has given them a spirit of stupor" shows that God causes unbelief." OO Response: Paul is quoting Isaiah 29:10 about people who had already refused God's word. Chrysostom: "do not imagine to mean here an agency, but a permission only," and "He had indeed mentioned the causes of it before, and turned it all upon their own heads." And the hardening is "in part" and "until" (11:25). God's purpose in it is mercy, not destruction.

"The Church has replaced Israel, so Romans 11 has nothing more to say about the Jewish people." OO Response: The Church is the Israel of God, but Paul is clear that God has not cast away His people (11:1), that they are still "beloved for the sake of the fathers" (11:28), and that His gifts and calling are irrevocable (11:29). The Fathers expected Israel's turning to Christ, not its disappearance. What Paul rules out is a salvation apart from Christ. The natural branches are grafted back into the same tree, the one people of God in Christ. "Confessing "Jesus is Lord" is all that is needed for salvation, so baptism and the Church are optional." OO Response: Paul is not describing a formula separate from baptism; he is describing the faith that is confessed at baptism and lived afterwards. In Romans 6 he has already said that "as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death." Christ Himself warned that saying "Lord, Lord" is not enough without doing the Father's will (Matthew 7:21).
Confession with the mouth is real and necessary, and it is the beginning of the Christian life, not the whole of it.

XII. FAQ What is the Orthodox view of the modern state of Israel? The Church has no doctrine that ties Romans 11 to any modern state. The promises of Romans 11 concern Israel's turning to Christ, not a political event. Orthodox Christians, including many Palestinian and Arab Orthodox in the Holy Land, hold a range of views on the politics of the region, and the Church calls all to justice and peace. Should Christians evangelise Jewish people? Paul did, at the cost of his life, and said his heart's desire was for their salvation (10:1). The gospel is "for the Jew first" (1:16). Christians are called to share it with love, humility and respect, never with contempt, remembering that they themselves are grafted into Israel's tree. Does Romans 11 teach that a Christian can lose his salvation? Paul warns Gentile believers that they too can be cut off "if you do not continue in His goodness" (11:22), and Chrysostom says "none of these things is immutable." Calvin reads the warning as addressed to the Gentiles as a body.

The Orthodox take it as a real warning to every believer, given so that we will continue, not so that we will live in fear. See Assurance of Salvation . What comes next? "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God..." Having shown God's mercy, Paul turns to the life that answers it: the living sacrifice, the body of Christ, love, the authorities, the weak and the strong, and his greetings to the saints in Rome. That is Romans 12–16 .
