I. Introduction: The Life That Answers Mercy Romans 12 begins with "therefore." After eleven chapters on what God has done, Paul turns to how we should live: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice." The last five chapters of Romans are not an appendix. They are what the first eleven were for. These chapters touch many questions that still matter between Christians: what worship is, how the gifts of the Spirit work in one body, the Christian and the state, fasting and feast days, the ministry of women, and the place of Rome. They end with a long list of names, men and women Paul loved, and with a hymn of glory. St John Chrysostom ends his thirty-two homilies standing, as it were, at Paul's tomb in Rome. This last page of the series reads these chapters with Chrysostom, St Augustine, St Irenaeus and the Didache, beside Calvin and the Westminster Confession, and gathers up what the whole letter has been saying.

"Let the eye look upon no evil thing, and it has become a sacrifice; let your tongue speak nothing filthy, and it has become an offering; let your hand do no lawless deed, and it has become a whole burnt offering." St John Chrysostom, Homily 20 on Romans This page is part of Romans with the Fathers , a series of nine pages that read St Paul's letter to the Romans section by section with the Church Fathers, setting their reading beside the main Protestant readings. Use the bar at the top of the page to move between the sections of the letter. A Note on Quotations Every quotation marked VERBATIM has been checked word for word against a public domain translation: St John Chrysostom's thirty-two Homilies on Romans and the other Fathers in the Ante-Nicene and Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series, John Calvin's Commentary on Romans in John Owen's translation (1849), and the Reformation confessions in Philip Schaff's Creeds of Christendom . Chrysostom's homilies follow J. B. Morris's translation as revised by W. H. Simcox, in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, volume 11.
Where a work has no public domain English translation, its teaching is summarised and marked PARAPHRASE . Scripture follows the NKJV.

II. Glossary of Terms Reasonable service λογικὴ λατρεία · logikē latreia "Reasonable" or "spiritual" worship (12:1): worship offered by the whole rational person, not only by animal sacrifice. Be transformed μεταμορφόω · metamorphoō The same verb as the Transfiguration of Christ (Matthew 17:2). "Be transformed by the renewing of your mind" (12:2). Gift χάρισμα · charisma A gift of grace given for the good of the body (12:6). Without hypocrisy ἀνυπόκριτος · anypokritos Unfeigned, without play-acting. "Let love be without hypocrisy" (12:9). Authority ἐξουσία · exousia Power or authority, here civil government (13:1). Weak ἀσθενής · asthenēs Weak in faith, scrupulous about food or days (14:1). Ministering as a priest ἱερουργέω · hierourgeō To perform sacred, priestly service. Paul's word for his preaching to the Gentiles (15:16). Deacon, servant διάκονος · diakonos Servant or deacon. Phoebe is "diakonos of the church in Cenchrea" (16:1). Patron, helper προστάτις · prostatis A patron or benefactor. Phoebe "has been a helper of many and of myself also" (16:2).
Of note ἐπίσημος · episēmos Distinguished, outstanding. Andronicus and Junia were "of note among the apostles" (16:7).

III. A Living Sacrifice (12:1–2) Romans 12:1-2 "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service. And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, that you may prove what is that good and acceptable and perfect will of God." Orthodox reading: The response to God's mercy is the offering of the whole self, body included, and the transformation of the mind. St John Chrysostom Homily 20 on Romans (on 12:1) "And how is the body, it may be said, to become a sacrifice? Let the eye look upon no evil thing, and it has become a sacrifice; let your tongue speak nothing filthy, and it has become an offering; let your hand do no lawless deed, and it has become a whole burnt offering.

Or rather this is not enough, but we must have good works also: let the hand do alms, the mouth bless them that cross one, and the hearing find leisure evermore for lections of Scripture." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 20 on Romans (on 12:1) "That presented the thing sacrificed dead: this makes the thing sacrificed to be living. For when we have mortified our members, then we shall be able to live. For the law of this sacrifice is new, and so the sort of fire is a marvellous one." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Paul's phrase "reasonable service" ( logikē latreia ) found its way into the ancient liturgies of the East, which speak of the Eucharist as a "reasonable" or "rational" and bloodless sacrifice. For the Orthodox, the living sacrifice of 12:1 and the Eucharistic sacrifice are not rivals. Christians offer themselves to God by uniting their lives to Christ's one offering, made present at the altar. See The Eucharist as Sacrifice . "Be transformed" uses the word of the Transfiguration.
The Christian life is meant to be a slow transfiguration, the renewal of the mind until it shares the mind of Christ. That is theosis again, the theme that has run through the whole letter.

IV. One Body, Many Gifts (12:3–8) Romans 12:4-5 "For as we have many members in one body, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, being many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another." Orthodox reading: The Church is one body in Christ, with many members and many functions. Paul lists prophecy, ministry, teaching, exhortation, giving, leading and mercy. Every member has a gift, and none is to think of himself more highly than he ought. The Orthodox see the Church as exactly this body, ordered and many-gifted: clergy and laity, monastics and married, each with a place. Protestants rightly stress that every believer has a ministry. The Orthodox would add that the body has a shape given by Christ, which includes the ordained ministry, and that gifts are exercised within the communion of the Church, not apart from it.

V. Love Without Hypocrisy (12:9–21) Romans 12:9-13 "Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor what is evil. Cling to what is good. Be kindly affectionate to one another with brotherly love, in honor giving preference to one another; not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord; rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, continuing steadfastly in prayer; distributing to the needs of the saints, given to hospitality." Orthodox reading: Genuine love: hating evil, holding to good, honouring others, fervent in spirit, patient in trouble, generous and hospitable. Romans 12:14-18 "Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. Be of the same mind toward one another. Do not set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Do not be wise in your own opinion. Repay no one evil for evil. Have regard for good things in the sight of all men.

If it is possible, as much as depends on you, live peaceably with all men." Orthodox reading: Bless persecutors, weep with those who weep, live at peace with all as far as it depends on you. Romans 12:19-21 "Beloved, do not avenge yourselves, but rather give place to wrath; for it is written, 'Vengeance is Mine, I will repay,' says the Lord. Therefore 'If your enemy is hungry, feed him; If he is thirsty, give him a drink; For in so doing you will heap coals of fire on his head.' Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." Orthodox reading: Leave vengeance to God. Feed your enemy. Overcome evil with good. St John Chrysostom Homily 22 on Romans (on 12:20) "Why, he means, am I telling you that you must keep peace? For I even insist upon your doing kindness. For he says, give him to eat, and give him to drink." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION These verses are among the most quoted in the history of the Church, and on them every Christian tradition agrees.

The Coptic Church, which has lived for centuries as a minority and has many modern martyrs, has given the world striking examples of Romans 12:14 and 12:21: families of martyrs publicly forgiving those who killed their loved ones. That is Romans 12 lived.

VI. The Governing Authorities (13:1–7) Romans 13:1-2 "Let every soul be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and the authorities that exist are appointed by God. Therefore whoever resists the authority resists the ordinance of God, and those who resist will bring judgment on themselves." Orthodox reading: Civil authority as such is part of God's ordering of the world. Christians are to be subject to it. Romans 13:3-4 "For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to evil. Do you want to be unafraid of the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from the same. For he is God's minister to you for good. But if you do evil, be afraid; for he does not bear the sword in vain; for he is God's minister, an avenger to execute wrath on him who practices evil." Orthodox reading: Government exists to restrain evil and reward good; it is God's servant for that purpose.

Does this mean every ruler is chosen by God and must be obeyed in everything? Chrysostom and Calvin give almost the same answer: St John Chrysostom Homily 23 on Romans (on 13:1) "What say you? It may be said; is every ruler then elected by God? This I do not say, he answers. Nor am I now speaking about individual rulers, but about the thing in itself. For that there should be rulers, and some rule and others be ruled, and that all things should not just be carried on in one confusion, the people swaying like waves in this direction and that; this, I say, is the work of God's wisdom." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 13:1) "For though tyrannies and unjust exercise of power, as they are full of disorder, (ataxias) are not an ordained government; yet the right of government is ordained by God for the wellbeing of mankind." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Acts 5:29 "But Peter and the other apostles answered and said: 'We ought to obey God rather than men." Orthodox reading: When rulers command what God forbids, the apostles'

answer stands: obey God rather than men. This is the balance the martyrs kept. They paid taxes, prayed for emperors and honoured rulers, and they died rather than offer incense to idols or deny Christ. The Coptic Church remembers its martyrs in its very calendar, the Era of the Martyrs, which begins in AD 284 with the reign of the emperor Diocletian. Romans 13 teaches respect for the order God has given; it does not teach that Caesar may claim what belongs to God.

secs.h: VII. Love Fulfils the Law; Put On the Lord Jesus Christ (13:8–14)
secs.x: VII. Love Fulfils the Law; Put On the Lord Jesus Christ (13:8–14) Romans 13:8-10 "Owe no one anything except to love one another, for he who loves another has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, 'You shall not commit adultery,' 'You shall not murder,' 'You shall not steal,' 'You shall not bear false witness,' 'You shall not covet,' and if there is any other commandment, are all summed up in this saying, namely, 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' Love does no harm to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law." Orthodox reading: Love fulfils the law. Every commandment is summed up in "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." Romans 13:11-14 "And do this, knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep; for now our salvation is nearer than when we first believed. The night is far spent, the day is at hand. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armor of light. Let us walk properly, as in the day, not in revelry and drunkenness, not in lewdness and lust, not in strife and envy.

secs.h: VII. Love Fulfils the Law; Put On the Lord Jesus Christ (13:8–14)
secs.x: But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to fulfill its lusts." Orthodox reading: The night is far spent. Cast off the works of darkness and put on the Lord Jesus Christ. These are the verses that converted St Augustine. In the garden at Milan in 386, torn between his desire for God and his bondage to his passions, he heard a child's voice chanting "Take up and read": St Augustine of Hippo Confessions VIII.12.29 "I grasped, opened, and in silence read that paragraph on which my eyes first fell... Not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof. No further would I read, nor did I need; for instantly, as the sentence ended... all the gloom of doubt vanished away." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION "Put on Christ" is also the language of baptism (Galatians 3:27).

secs.h: VII. Love Fulfils the Law; Put On the Lord Jesus Christ (13:8–14)
secs.x: In the Byzantine baptismal service the Church sings, "As many as have been baptised into Christ have put on Christ," and in the Coptic rite too the newly baptised are clothed in white. What Augustine experienced in the garden, he received sacramentally at his baptism the following Easter, from the hands of St Ambrose.

secs.h: VIII. The Weak and the Strong: Food and Days (14:1–15:13)
secs.x: VIII. The Weak and the Strong: Food and Days (14:1–15:13) Romans 14:1-3 "Receive one who is weak in the faith, but not to disputes over doubtful things. For one believes he may eat all things, but he who is weak eats only vegetables. Let not him who eats despise him who does not eat, and let not him who does not eat judge him who eats; for God has received him." Orthodox reading: Some ate everything; others ate only vegetables. Neither was to despise or judge the other. Romans 14:5-6 "One person esteems one day above another; another esteems every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind. He who observes the day, observes it to the Lord; and he who does not observe the day, to the Lord he does not observe it. He who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives God thanks; and he who does not eat, to the Lord he does not eat, and gives God thanks." Orthodox reading: Some honoured certain days; others regarded every day alike. Each was to be fully convinced and to act for the Lord.

secs.h: VIII. The Weak and the Strong: Food and Days (14:1–15:13)
secs.x: Romans 14:17 "for the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." Orthodox reading: The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Some Protestants use Romans 14 to object to Orthodox fasting and feast days: surely Paul says such things do not matter? The Fathers read the chapter more carefully. Chrysostom thought the dispute in Rome involved new converts still attached to Jewish food laws and observances, and some quarrelling over fasting, and that Paul's concern was to stop the judging: St John Chrysostom Homily 25 on Romans (on 14:5) "Here he seems to me to be giving a gentle hint about fasting. For it is not unlikely that some who fasted were always judging those who did not, or among the observances it is likely that there were some that on fixed days abstained, and on fixed days did not." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Romans 14 does not forbid fasting.

secs.h: VIII. The Weak and the Strong: Food and Days (14:1–15:13)
secs.x: Christ Himself said His disciples would fast once the Bridegroom was taken away (Matthew 9:15), and from the first century the Church fasted together on fixed days: The Didache Didache 8 "But let not your fasts be with the hypocrites; for they fast on the second and fifth day of the week; but fast on the fourth day and the Preparation (Friday)." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION The Orthodox still fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, as the Didache says, and in the great fasts of the year. What Romans 14 forbids is turning these things into grounds for contempt or condemnation: "Who are you to judge another's servant?" (14:4). An Orthodox Christian who looks down on a Protestant for not fasting breaks Romans 14 just as much as a Protestant who mocks the Orthodox for fasting. The Church's fasts are a shared discipline of love, not a law that earns salvation, and they are always kept with mercy for the sick, the young and the weak. See Fasting and Sabbath & the Lord's Day .

secs.h: VIII. The Weak and the Strong: Food and Days (14:1–15:13)
secs.x: Romans 15:5-7 "Now may the God of patience and comfort grant you to be like-minded toward one another, according to Christ Jesus, that you may with one mind and one mouth glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore receive one another, just as Christ also received us, to the glory of God." Orthodox reading: The goal is one mind and one voice glorifying God, receiving one another as Christ received us. It is worth noticing that Romans 14 is about matters of conscience within one church that shared the same faith and the same table. It is not a charter for treating every disagreement about doctrine as a matter of indifference. Paul ends the letter by warning against those who cause divisions "contrary to the doctrine which you learned" (16:17).

IX. Paul's Priestly Service (15:14–33) Romans 15:15-16 "Nevertheless, brethren, I have written more boldly to you on some points, as reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God, that I might be a minister of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles, ministering the gospel of God, that the offering of the Gentiles might be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit." Orthodox reading: Paul describes his preaching in priestly language: he ministers the gospel so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. St John Chrysostom Homily 29 on Romans (on 15:16) "For after his abundant proof of his statements, he draws his discourse to a more lofty tone, not speaking of mere service, as in the beginning, but of service and priestly ministering. For to me this is a priesthood, this preaching and declaring. This is the sacrifice I bring." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 29 on Romans (on 15:16) "For my knife, he says, is the Gospel, the word of the preaching.

And the cause is not that I may be glorified, not that I may appear conspicuous, but that the offering up of the Gentiles may be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION This verse matters for a debate between Orthodox and Protestants. Many Protestants hold that the New Testament knows no priesthood except Christ's and that of all believers. Paul here uses priestly language for an apostolic ministry, and the early Church soon used it for bishops and presbyters who offer the Eucharist. Chrysostom, a priest himself, sees the preaching of the gospel as priestly work. The Orthodox affirm both: the royal priesthood of all the baptised (1 Peter 2:9) and the ministerial priesthood that serves it. See Apostolic Grace . Romans 15:23-24 "But now no longer having a place in these parts, and having a great desire these many years to come to you, whenever I journey to Spain, I shall come to you.

For I hope to see you on my journey, and to be helped on my way there by you, if first I may enjoy your company for a while." Orthodox reading: Paul planned to visit Rome on his way to Spain. Early tradition says he was released after his first Roman imprisonment and preached in the west before his martyrdom. St Clement of Rome, writing around AD 96, says Paul reached "the extreme limit of the west" before he was martyred, which many have taken as Spain. Paul's plan in Romans 15 is one reason that tradition is taken seriously.

secs.h: X. Phoebe, Junia and the Women of Romans 16
secs.x: X. Phoebe, Junia and the Women of Romans 16 Romans 16:1-2 "I commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is a servant of the church in Cenchrea, that you may receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her in whatever business she has need of you; for indeed she has been a helper of many and of myself also." Orthodox reading: Phoebe, a deacon of the church at Cenchrea, carried the letter to Rome. Paul asks the Romans to receive her and help her. St John Chrysostom Homily 30 on Romans (on 16:1) "See how many ways he takes to give her dignity. For he has both mentioned her before all the rest, and called her sister. And it is no slight thing to be called the sister of Paul. Moreover he has added her rank, by mentioning her being deaconess." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Romans 16:7 "Greet Andronicus and Junia, my countrymen and my fellow prisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me." Orthodox reading: Andronicus and Junia, Paul's kinsmen and fellow prisoners, were "of note among the apostles" and in Christ before him.

secs.h: X. Phoebe, Junia and the Women of Romans 16
secs.x: St John Chrysostom Homily 31 on Romans (on 16:7) "Who are of note among the Apostles. And indeed to be apostles at all is a great thing. But to be even among these of note, just consider what a great encomium this is! But they were of note owing to their works, to their achievements. Oh! How great is the devotion of this woman, that she should be even counted worthy of the appellation of apostle!" Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 16:7) "In the third place, he calls them Apostles: he uses not this word in its proper and common meaning, but extends it wider, even to all those who not only teach in one Church, but also spend their labor in promulgating the gospel everywhere." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Both Chrysostom and Calvin read 16:7 as calling Andronicus and Junia apostles, and Chrysostom says plainly that Junia was a woman. In the Middle Ages some copyists and translators turned her into a man, "Junias," a name not found in ancient sources.

secs.h: X. Phoebe, Junia and the Women of Romans 16
secs.x: Some modern translations, such as the ESV, render the phrase "well known to the apostles," following an argument made in 2001 by Michael Burer and Daniel Wallace; most Greek scholars, and the Fathers, read it as "outstanding among the apostles." What does this mean for the Church today? The Orthodox honour Junia as a saint, and many Orthodox calendars commemorate Andronicus and Junia together. "Apostle" here, as Calvin says, is used in the wider sense of a missionary sent to spread the gospel, not one of the Twelve, and the Fathers who praised Junia did not conclude that women should be ordained bishops or priests. Women deacons, however, are well attested in the early Church, beginning with Phoebe. In the Oriental Orthodox Churches the Armenian Church has ordained women deacons in modern times, and the Coptic Church has consecrated women to serve the Church. The fuller discussion is on Women in the Church .

secs.h: X. Phoebe, Junia and the Women of Romans 16
secs.x: Romans 16:3-5 "Greet Priscilla and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their own necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles. Likewise greet the church that is in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia to Christ." Orthodox reading: Priscilla, named before her husband Aquila, risked her life for Paul. A church met in their house. Of the people Paul commends or greets in 16:1–15, ten are women. Whatever one's view of ordination, no one can read this chapter and think the women of the early Church were on the edge of its life. They were at its heart.

secs.h: Why Does Paul Not Greet Peter?
secs.x: XI. Greetings, Warnings, and Peter in Rome (16:3–27) Romans 16:17-18 "Now I urge you, brethren, note those who cause divisions and offenses, contrary to the doctrine which you learned, and avoid them. For those who are such do not serve our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly, and by smooth words and flattering speech deceive the hearts of the simple." Orthodox reading: Avoid those who cause divisions contrary to the teaching you received. Romans 16:20 "And the God of peace will crush Satan under your feet shortly. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen." Orthodox reading: The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet, an echo of the first promise of the gospel in Genesis 3:15. Why Does Paul Not Greet Peter? Protestant writers often point out that Romans 16 greets many people in Rome but not Peter, and argue that Peter cannot have been the bishop of Rome at the time. That is a fair observation. Paul wrote around AD 57; Peter most likely came to Rome later, and was martyred there in the 60s. The Orthodox have no difficulty with this.

secs.h: Why Does Paul Not Greet Peter?
secs.x: The ancient tradition is not that Peter founded the Roman church alone, but that Peter and Paul together established it and were both martyred there: St Irenaeus of Lyons Against Heresies III.3.2 "...the very great, the very ancient, and universally known Church founded and organized at Rome by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul..." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION The Orthodox honour the Church of Rome as the church of two apostles and martyrs. What they do not accept is that this gives its bishop universal jurisdiction over the whole Church. See Papal Authority . Chrysostom at Paul's Tomb Chrysostom ends his thirty-two homilies not with an argument but with love for Paul, and for the city where Paul's body lies: St John Chrysostom Homily 32 on Romans "And as a body great and strong, it has as two glistening eyes the bodies of these Saints. Not so bright is the heaven, when the sun sends forth his rays, as is the city of Rome, sending out these two lights into all parts of the world.

secs.h: Why Does Paul Not Greet Peter?
secs.x: From thence will Paul be caught up, from thence Peter." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 32 on Romans "Therefore I admire the city, not for the much gold, not for the columns, not for the other display there, but for these pillars of the Church." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Here, at the end of his greatest work on the letter of grace, Chrysostom speaks as every Orthodox Christian still does about the saints: with love for their relics, confidence in their resurrection, and longing to be near them. The theology of Romans and the veneration of the saints were never at odds for him. See The Intercession of the Saints . Romans 16:25-27 "Now to Him who is able to establish you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept secret since the world began but now made manifest, and by the prophetic Scriptures made known to all nations, according to the commandment of the everlasting God, for obedience to the faith— to God, alone wise, be glory through Jesus Christ forever.

secs.h: Why Does Paul Not Greet Peter?
secs.x: Amen." Orthodox reading: The letter ends as it began, with the gospel of Jesus Christ made known to all nations "for obedience to the faith," and with glory to the only wise God. The Whole Letter Romans begins and ends with "the obedience of faith" (1:5; 16:26). In between, Paul has shown that all have sinned; that God's righteousness is given freely through faith in Christ; that Adam's death is overcome by Christ's life; that in baptism we die and rise with Him; that the law could not do what the Spirit does; that nothing outside us can separate us from God's love; that the potter remakes the clay that turns to Him; that God's purpose is mercy on all; and that the answer to such mercy is a life offered as a living sacrifice. That is the gospel the Fathers preached, and it is the gospel the Orthodox Church still proclaims.

XII. Objections Answered "Romans 14 shows that fasting rules and holy days are matters of indifference, so the Orthodox are legalistic." OO Response: Romans 14 forbids judging one another over food and days; it does not forbid fasting. Christ said His disciples would fast (Matthew 9:15), and the Didache shows the first-century Church fasting together on Wednesdays and Fridays. The Orthodox fast as a family discipline of love and prayer, not as a way of earning salvation, and Romans 14 binds them not to despise those who do not. Mocking those who fast is just as contrary to Romans 14. "Romans 13 means Christians must obey any government." OO Response: Chrysostom and Calvin both say that Paul is speaking of the institution of government, not approving every ruler or every command. The apostles themselves disobeyed when ordered to stop preaching (Acts 5:29), and the martyrs refused to worship the emperor.

"If Junia was an apostle, women should be ordained priests and bishops." OO Response: Paul uses "apostle" in more than one sense, including missionaries sent by the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23). Calvin and Chrysostom both understand Junia's apostleship in this wider sense. The early Church honoured her and had women deacons, but did not ordain women as presbyters or bishops. The Orthodox take Junia seriously as a woman apostle in that sense and a saint. The question of ordination rests on the whole tradition of the Church, discussed on Women in the Church . "Paul's silence about Peter in Romans 16 disproves that Peter was ever in Rome." OO Response: It shows only that Peter was probably not in Rome in AD 57. Early sources, including 1 Clement, Ignatius and Irenaeus, place both Peter and Paul in Rome and connect their martyrdoms with the city. The Orthodox accept that tradition while rejecting later claims of papal supremacy built on it.

XIII. FAQ What does "heap coals of fire on his head" mean? It is a quotation from Proverbs 25:21–22. Interpreters differ: some take it as the burning shame that leads an enemy to repentance, others as God's judgement left in His hands. Chrysostom took it partly as a concession to the wronged person's feelings, leading on to the higher command: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." Was Phoebe really a deacon? The word is diakonos , used of deacons in Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3:8. Chrysostom calls her a deaconess and says Paul mentions "her rank." The early Church had women deacons, especially for the baptism of women and pastoral care of women. Why is Romans read so much in the Orthodox Church? In the Coptic Church a reading from Paul, the Pauline, is read at every Divine Liturgy, and the other Orthodox Churches read the Epistles throughout the year. Romans 6:3–11 is the Epistle read at baptism in the Byzantine rite.

Where should I start if I want to read Romans with the Fathers? Begin with St John Chrysostom's homilies, freely available online, reading one homily alongside each section of the letter. Then return to the pages in this series, starting with Romans 1–2 .
