I. Introduction: The Letter that Shaped the West No book of the New Testament has been argued over more than St Paul's letter to the Romans. Augustine was converted reading a verse from it (Romans 13:13–14). Martin Luther said that Romans 1:17 opened the gates of paradise to him, and the Reformation was fought largely over its third and fourth chapters. John Calvin's doctrine of predestination leans heavily on its ninth chapter. For many Protestants, Romans is the clearest statement of the gospel in Scripture. The Orthodox Church reads Romans too, and has read it for far longer. The Fathers preached on it, wrote commentaries on it, and quoted it constantly. The fullest of these commentaries to survive in its original Greek is the series of thirty-two homilies preached by St John Chrysostom at Antioch. St Paul is read at every Divine Liturgy of the Coptic Church, in the reading called the Pauline, before the Catholic Epistle, the Acts and the Gospel.

The aim of these pages is simple: to let the Fathers explain Romans in their own words, to set beside them the main Protestant readings fairly and in their own words, and to show where the two really differ and where they are closer than people assume. This first page covers chapters 1 and 2. Paul introduces the gospel, then shows that the whole world stands in need of it: the Gentiles who knew God from creation and turned to idols, and the Jews who had the law and did not keep it. Along the way it raises questions that still divide Christians. What can people know of God without the Bible? Does God cause people to sin when He "gives them up"? And if we are saved by faith, why does Paul say that God "will render to each one according to his deeds"? "...the well-ordered harmony of all things spoke out more clearly than a trumpet." St John Chrysostom, Homily 3 on Romans A Note on Quotations Every quotation marked VERBATIM has been checked word for word against a public domain translation: St John Chrysostom's thirty-two Homilies on Romans and the other Fathers in the Ante-Nicene and

Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series, John Calvin's Commentary on Romans in John Owen's translation (1849), and the Reformation confessions in Philip Schaff's Creeds of Christendom . Chrysostom's homilies follow J. B. Morris's translation as revised by W. H. Simcox, in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, volume 11. Where a work has no public domain English translation, its teaching is summarised and marked PARAPHRASE . Scripture follows the NKJV.

II. Glossary of Terms Gospel εὐαγγέλιον · euangelion "Good news." For Paul, the announcement of what God has done in Jesus Christ, His Son, "the power of God to salvation for everyone who believes" (1:16). Righteousness of God δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ · dikaiosynē theou The phrase at the heart of Romans (1:17). Read as God's own faithfulness and justice, as the righteousness He gives to us, or both. How it is given is where Orthodox and Protestants part. Faith πίστις · pistis Trust, belief and faithfulness. Paul speaks of "the obedience of faith" (1:5), faith that obeys. Wrath ὀργή · orgē God's just opposition to sin. The Fathers insist it is not a passion or a fit of temper in God, but His righteous judgement (2:5). Without excuse ἀναπολόγητος · anapologētos Having no defence. Paul uses it of those who knew God from creation (1:20) and of those who judge others while doing the same things (2:1). Gave them up παρέδωκεν · paredōken "Handed over" (1:24, 26, 28). The Fathers read it as God withdrawing His help from those who refused Him, not as God pushing them into sin.

Conscience συνείδησις · syneidēsis The inner witness that accuses or excuses (2:15). It can be trained or darkened, but it is never wholly lost. Nature φύσις · physis What something is made to be. Paul uses it of what is "natural" and "against nature" (1:26–27) and of Gentiles who "by nature" do what the law requires (2:14). Repentance μετάνοια · metanoia A change of mind and life. God's kindness is meant to lead us to it (2:4). Circumcision of the heart περιτομὴ καρδίας · peritomē kardias The inward cutting away of sin promised in Deuteronomy 30:6. Paul says it is the true circumcision (2:29). Colossians 2:11–12 links it with baptism.

III. Reading Romans with the Fathers Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, most likely around AD 56 to 58, as he was about to take the collection from the Greek churches to Jerusalem (15:25–26). He had never visited Rome. The church there was a mix of Jewish and Gentile believers, and much of the letter is about how the two belong together in one people of God. Many scholars connect this with the expulsion of Jews from Rome under the emperor Claudius around AD 49 (Acts 18:2) and their return a few years later, which would have left Gentile believers leading a church into which Jewish believers were coming back. That reconstruction is likely but not certain. St John Chrysostom worked out the date the same way, from the collection for Jerusalem, and placed Romans after the letters to the Corinthians.

He began his homilies by telling his people why he loved Paul so much: St John Chrysostom Argument to the Homilies on Romans "As I keep hearing the Epistles of the blessed Paul read, and that twice every week, and often three or four times, whenever we are celebrating the memorials of the holy martyrs, gladly do I enjoy the spiritual trumpet, and get roused and warmed with desire at recognizing the voice so dear to me, and seem to fancy him all but present to my sight, and behold him conversing with me." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Argument to the Homilies on Romans "For from this it is that our countless evils have arisen, from ignorance of the Scriptures; from this it is that the plague of heresies has broken out; from this that there are negligent lives; from this labors without advantage." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Three Keys the Fathers Bring First, Jew and Gentile. Chrysostom reads Romans as a letter about two peoples being made one.

Early in his homilies he says Paul is "breaking through the partition between the circumcision and the uncircumcision." Many Protestants since the Reformation have read Romans mainly as an answer to the question "How can I, a sinner, be right with God?" Both questions are really in the letter. The Fathers simply never forget the first. Second, faith and life together. The Fathers speak of salvation as a gift received by faith, and in the same breath of a life that must be lived, judged and rewarded. They do not feel the tension between Romans 1:17 and Romans 2:6 that later debates created, because for them faith is the beginning of a life of union with God, not a single moment set over against the rest. Third, the free will of man. The Fathers before Augustine, and the Greek and Oriental Fathers after him, read Romans with the conviction that God made man free and never forces him. Chrysostom says of 2:8 that Paul chose his words "that one may learn that the fall is one of free choice." This conviction matters most on Romans 9, which has its own page in this series.

The Nine Pages of This Series Romans 1–2 Creation & Judgement (this page): The gospel, what every person can know of God, God giving people up to their desires, and judgement according to works. Romans 3–4 Justification & Faith : All have sinned, justification by faith apart from works of the law, and Abraham the father of all who believe. Romans 5 Adam & Ancestral Sin : Peace with God, and Adam and Christ: what we inherit from Adam, and how the Fathers differ from Augustine on Romans 5:12. Romans 6 Baptism : Buried with Christ in baptism and raised to walk in newness of life. Romans 7 The Law & the Divided Self : The law, sin and the divided self: who is the "wretched man" of Romans 7? Romans 8 Life in the Spirit : Life in the Spirit, adoption, the groaning creation, and "all things work together for good." Romans 9 Election & the Potter : Jacob and Esau, Pharaoh, and the potter and the clay: election read with Jeremiah 18 and the Fathers. Romans 10–11 Israel & the Nations : Faith comes by hearing, the remnant, and the olive tree: Israel and the nations.
Romans 12–16 The Christian Life : The living sacrifice, the body of Christ, the governing authorities, the weak and the strong, and Phoebe and the saints at Rome.

secs.h: Where They Agree and Where They Part
secs.x: IV. The Gospel & "The Just Shall Live by Faith" (1:1–17) Paul opens by calling himself a slave of Christ, set apart for the gospel, and says that through Christ he has received "grace and apostleship for obedience to the faith among all nations." Chrysostom notices that Paul claims nothing for himself: Romans 1:5 "Through Him we have received grace and apostleship for obedience to the faith among all nations for His name," Orthodox reading: Faith is something you obey. It is trust that hands itself over to Christ, not merely an opinion held in the mind. St John Chrysostom Homily 1 on Romans (on 1:5) "So it was not the Apostles that achieved it, but grace that paved the way before them.

secs.h: Where They Agree and Where They Part
secs.x: For it was their part to go about and preach, but to persuade was of God, Who wrought in them." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Then come the two verses that the whole letter unfolds: Romans 1:16 "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God to salvation for everyone who believes, for the Jew first and also for the Greek." Orthodox reading: The gospel is not only a message about power. It is itself God's power at work, and it is offered to Jew and Greek alike. Romans 1:17 "For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith; as it is written, 'The just shall live by faith.'" Orthodox reading: God's righteousness is revealed and given in the gospel, and it is received by faith from beginning to end. Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4. Protestant reading: This is the verse of the Reformation. Luther came to see "the righteousness of God" not as the standard by which God condemns sinners but as the gift by which He justifies them through faith.

secs.h: Where They Agree and Where They Part
secs.x: It surprises many Protestants to find how close Chrysostom's comment on 1:17 sounds to their own reading: St John Chrysostom Homily 2 on Romans (on 1:17) "...and righteousness, not your own, but that of God; hinting also the abundance of it and the facility. For you do not achieve it by toilings and labors, but you receive it by a gift from above, contributing one thing only from your own store, believing." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 2 on Romans (on 1:17) "...that it is not in the nature of things for him who is to live, to live otherwise save by faith; for the just, he says, shall live by faith, speaking about the life to come.

secs.h: Where They Agree and Where They Part
secs.x: For since what God gives transcends reasoning entirely, it is but reason that we need faith." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Calvin, commenting on the same verse, takes "the righteousness of God" to be the righteousness that stands before God's judgement seat, and he deliberately separates it from the renewal of our lives: John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 1:17) "I take the righteousness of God to mean, that which is approved before his tribunal..." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 1:17) "Of greater moment is what some think, that this righteousness does not only consist in the free remission of sins, but also, in part, includes the grace of regeneration. But I consider, that we are restored to life because God freely reconciles us to himself, as we shall hereafter show in its proper place." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Where They Agree and Where They Part Both say that righteousness is God's gift, that we cannot earn it by our labours, and that it is received by faith.

secs.h: Where They Agree and Where They Part
secs.x: That is real common ground, and it should be said plainly. The difference is what the gift is. For Calvin and the Reformed tradition, justification is God's verdict: He forgives the sinner and counts him righteous for Christ's sake. Regeneration and holiness always follow and are never absent, but they are a distinct gift and form no part of the ground on which we are accepted. For the Fathers, the righteousness God gives is not only a verdict but a healing. Chrysostom says in the same homily that the sinner is "not only to be suddenly freed from punishment but to become just." To be justified is to be forgiven and made righteous by sharing in Christ, which the Orthodox call theosis . That is why the Fathers can speak of faith alone at the start of the Christian life and of works at the judgement without any sense of contradiction, as the next sections show. The fuller argument over justification belongs to Romans 3 and 4 .

V. God Known Through Creation (1:18–23) Paul now turns to why the world needs the gospel. He begins with the Gentiles, and with a claim that every Father took seriously: that God can be known, truly if not fully, from the world He made. Romans 1:19 "because what may be known of God is manifest in them, for God has shown it to them." Orthodox reading: The knowledge of God is not something people must climb to by cleverness. God Himself has shown it to them. Romans 1:20 "For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead, so that they are without excuse," Orthodox reading: Creation is a real revelation of God's power and divinity, plain enough that those who refuse it have no defence. Romans 1:21 "because, although they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God, nor were thankful, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish hearts were darkened." Orthodox reading: The fault was not ignorance but ingratitude.

They knew God and would not glorify Him or give thanks, and their hearts grew dark as a result. St John Chrysostom Homily 3 on Romans (on 1:19–20) "...by putting before them the Creation, so that both wise, and unlearned, and Scythian, and barbarian, having through sight learned the beauty of the things which were seen, might mount up to God." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 3 on Romans (on 1:20) "Did ye then not hear the heaven sending forth a voice by the sight, while the well-ordered harmony of all things spoke out more clearly than a trumpet? Did ye not see the hours of night and day abiding unmoved continually, the goodly order of winter, spring, and the other seasons remaining both sure and unmoved...?" Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 3 on Romans (on 1:20–21) "And yet it is not for this God has made these things, even if this came of it.

For it was not to bereave them of all excuse, that He set before them so great a system of teaching, but that they might come to know Him." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Athanasius, writing as a young man before the Arian crisis, makes the same argument and cites the same verse: St Athanasius of Alexandria Against the Heathen 34–35 "...it is further possible to attain to the knowledge of God from the things which are seen, since Creation, as though in written characters, declares in a loud voice, by its order and harmony, its own Lord and Creator." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Athanasius of Alexandria Against the Heathen 35 "For often the artist even when not seen is known by his works.

And as they tell of Phidias the Sculptor that his works of art by their symmetry and by the proportion of their parts betray Phidias to those who see them although he is not there, so by the order of the Universe one ought to perceive God its maker and artificer, even though He be not seen with the bodily eyes." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Over a century earlier, St Theophilus of Antioch (around AD 180) had put it the same way, and added what Paul says in verse 21: that sin darkens the eye that should see. St Theophilus of Antioch To Autolycus I.5 "For as the soul in man is not seen, being invisible to men, but is perceived through the motion of the body, so God cannot indeed be seen by human eyes, but is beheld and perceived through His providence and works.

For, in like manner, as any person, when he sees a ship on the sea rigged and in sail, and making for the harbour, will no doubt infer that there is a pilot in her who is steering her; so we must perceive that God is the governor of the whole universe..." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION St Theophilus of Antioch To Autolycus I.2 "For God is seen by those who are enabled to see Him when they have the eyes of their soul opened: for all have eyes; but in some they are overspread, and do not see the light of the sun... So also you, O man, have the eyes of your soul overspread by your sins and evil deeds." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION The Reformed Reading The Reformed tradition affirms that creation reveals God, but stresses how little fallen people can do with that knowledge: John Calvin Institutes of the Christian Religion I.5.14 "In vain for us, therefore, does Creation exhibit so many bright lamps lighted up to show forth the glory of its Author.

Though they beam upon us from every quarter, they are altogether insufficient of themselves to lead us into the right path... When Paul says that that which may be known of God is manifested by the creation of the world, he does not mean such a manifestation as may be comprehended by the wit of man (Rom. 1:19); on the contrary, he shows that it has no further effect than to render us inexcusable." Reformer VERBATIM · BEVERIDGE TRANSLATION (1845) Westminster Confession (1646) Westminster Confession of Faith I.1 "Although the light of nature, and the works of creation and providence, do so far manifest the goodness, wisdom, and power of God, as to leave men inexcusable; yet are they not sufficient to give that knowledge of God, and of his will, which is necessary unto salvation..." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · WESTMINSTER CONFESSION, SCHAFF The Fathers Creation is a real and open book about God, given so that people might know Him and rise to Him. Sin darkens the eye of the soul, but it does not put the light out.

Reformed Creation reveals God truly, but fallen man cannot rightly receive it. In practice it serves to leave him without excuse until God opens his eyes by faith and Scripture. The two are closer than they first look. Both agree that no one is saved by nature alone and that all are without excuse. Calvin himself grants that creation gives off "some sparks." The difference is one of emphasis, and it matters: Chrysostom insists that God's purpose in creation was not to condemn but to draw people to Himself, and that condemnation came only from their refusal. That fits the Orthodox conviction that God desires all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4). It is also why the Orthodox can use the arguments from creation found on Evidence for God with a clear conscience: Paul and the Fathers did the same.

VI. "God Gave Them Up" (1:24–32) Three times Paul says that God "gave them up": to uncleanness (1:24), to vile passions (1:26) and to a debased mind (1:28). Does that mean God drove them into sin? Romans 1:24 "Therefore God also gave them up to uncleanness, in the lusts of their hearts, to dishonor their bodies among themselves," Orthodox reading: God's "giving up" is His judgement on a refusal that came first. They exchanged the truth for a lie, and He let them have what they chose. Romans 1:28 "And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a debased mind, to do those things which are not fitting;" Orthodox reading: The pattern is exact: they did not want God in their knowledge, so God let their minds go where they wished. St John Chrysostom Homily 3 on Romans (on 1:24) "...he shows, that even of the perversion of the laws it was ungodliness which was the cause...

For as he that has the command in an army, if upon the battle lying heavy upon him he retreat and go away, gives up his soldiers to the enemies not by thrusting them himself, but by stripping them of his own assistance; thus too did God leave those that were not minded to receive what comes from Him..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John of Damascus, summing up the teaching of the Greek Fathers in the eighth century, lays down a rule for reading all such verses: St John of Damascus Exposition of the Orthodox Faith IV.19 "It is to be observed that it is the custom in the Holy Scripture to speak of God's permission as His energy..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John of Damascus Exposition of the Orthodox Faith IV.19 "...all these must be understood not as though God Himself were energising, but as though God were permitting, both because of free-will and because goodness knows no compulsion." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Calvin agrees that God is not the cause of sin, but he will not reduce "gave them up" to permission.

He sees in it God's active judgement: John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 1:24) "It is indeed certain, that he not only permits men to fall into sin, by allowing them to do so, and by conniving at them; but that he also, by his equitable judgment, so arranges things, that they are led and carried into such madness by their own lusts, as well as by the devil." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 1:24) "God, however, is not on this account cruel, nor are we innocent, inasmuch as Paul plainly shows, that we are not delivered up into his power, except when we deserve such a punishment. Only we must make this exception, that the cause of sin is not from God, the roots of which ever abide in the sinner himself..." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) To be fair to Calvin, both readings agree on three things: the people in Romans 1 deserved judgement, God's handing over is a just punishment, and the root of sin is in the sinner.

The difference is whether God's role is to withdraw (the Fathers) or to withdraw and also actively arrange (Calvin). The Orthodox concern is that the second, pushed far enough, makes God the author of the very sins He punishes. That question, and how God can govern a world full of sin without causing it, is treated on The Problem of Evil , and it returns in force on Romans 9 . Romans 1:26–27 Romans 1:26-27 "For this reason God gave them up to vile passions. For even their women exchanged the natural use for what is against nature. Likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust for one another, men with men committing what is shameful, and receiving in themselves the penalty of their error which was due." Orthodox reading: Paul gives same-sex relations as an example of the "exchange" he has been describing: turning from the pattern of the Creator to what is against it. The Church has always read these verses as moral teaching.

Chrysostom notes that Paul uses the word "nature" both to make the charge and to keep his language modest: St John Chrysostom Homily 4 on Romans (on 1:26–27) "But when God has left one, then all things are turned upside down." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 4 on Romans (on 1:26–27) "...by naming nature has at once given additional force to his accusation, and also used this as a sort of veil, to keep the chasteness of his description." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The Fathers, the Orthodox and Catholic Churches, and most Protestant churches read these verses in the same way. Since the late twentieth century some Protestant scholars and denominations have argued that Paul had in mind only exploitative practices of his day, or acts done out of excess by people who were not so inclined. Their case, and the Church's answer, are set out on Sex & Gender . Two things from Romans itself belong here. First, Paul's list goes straight on to envy, deceit, gossip, pride and disobedience to parents (1:29–31), so no reader escapes it.
Second, the very next verse turns on anyone who reads the list with satisfaction.

VII. The Judge Judged (2:1–5) Paul has led his reader through the sins of the pagan world, and a reader who kept the law would have agreed with every word. Then the trap closes: Romans 2:1 "Therefore you are inexcusable, O man, whoever you are who judge, for in whatever you judge another you condemn yourself; for you who judge practice the same things." Orthodox reading: The person who condemns others for what he does himself has signed his own sentence. This is not a ban on calling sin sin. Paul has just done that. It is a warning against hypocrisy. St John Chrysostom Homily 5 on Romans (on 2:1) "You are depriving yourself of defense, whoever you may be; for when you condemn an adulterer, and yourself commit adultery, although no man condemns you, in your judgment upon the guilty person you have also passed sentence against yourself." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Romans 2:4 "Or do you despise the riches of His goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?" Orthodox reading: God's patience is not weakness or

indifference. It is kindness meant to bring us to repentance. St John Chrysostom Homily 5 on Romans (on 2:4) "For God shows His goodness that you may get free from your sins, not that you may add to them. If then thou make not this use thereof, the judgment will be more fearful." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Romans 2:5 "But in accordance with your hardness and your impenitent heart you are treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God," Orthodox reading: The hard heart stores up wrath for itself. The sinner, not God, is the author of his own condemnation. St John Chrysostom Homily 5 on Romans (on 2:5) "...you store up for yourself, not God for you.

For He did all, whatsoever things were fitting, and created you with a power to discern between good and what was not so, and showed long-suffering over you, and called you to repentance, and threatened a fearful day, so by every means drawing you to repentance." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 5 on Romans (on 2:5) "For lest on hearing of wrath you should think of any passion, he adds, the righteous judgment of God." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Irenaeus, writing around AD 180, quotes these very verses to prove that man is free and that God's judgement is just: St Irenaeus of Lyons Against Heresies IV.37.1 "God therefore has given that which is good, as the apostle tells us in this Epistle, and they who work it shall receive glory and honour, because they have done that which is good when they had it in their power not to do it; but those who do it not shall receive the just judgment of God, because they did not work good when they had it in their power so to do." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION This is the seed of what

the Fathers will say about Romans 9. If God's patience leads to repentance and the hard heart stores up its own wrath, then God's dealings with us are not fixed in advance without regard to how we respond. The same patience appears in 9:22, where God "endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath."

VIII. Judgement According to Works (2:6–13) Here is the passage that every reading of Romans has to explain. Paul, who will soon say that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law (3:28), says this: Romans 2:6-7 "who 'will render to each one according to his deeds': eternal life to those who by patient continuance in doing good seek for glory, honor, and immortality;" Orthodox reading: There will be a real judgement of real lives. Those who keep on doing good, seeking what God gives, will receive eternal life. Protestant reading: Most Protestants agree that the judgement looks at works, but as the evidence and fruit of a faith that alone justifies. Many Reformed readers also see 2:7 as stating the law's standard, which no one in fact meets apart from Christ. Romans 2:13 "for not the hearers of the law are just in the sight of God, but the doers of the law will be justified;" Orthodox reading: Hearing the law is not enough. God justifies those who do it.

John 5:28-29 "Do not marvel at this; for the hour is coming in which all who are in the graves will hear His voice and come forth— those who have done good, to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of condemnation." Orthodox reading: Christ Himself describes the last judgement in the same terms. The Fathers St John Chrysostom Homily 5 on Romans (on 2:7) "Here also he awakens those who had drawn back during the trials, and shows that it is not right to trust in faith only. For it is deeds also into which that tribunal will enquire." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 5 on Romans (on 2:8) "And he does not say, who are compelled by, lorded over by, but who obey unrighteousness, that one may learn that the fall is one of free choice..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The same Chrysostom who said on 1:17 that righteousness is received "by a gift from above" here warns against trusting "in faith only." He does not think he is contradicting himself.

The earliest Father outside the New Testament holds the two together in exactly the same way: St Clement of Rome First Epistle of Clement 32–33 "And we, too, being called by His will in Christ Jesus, are not justified by ourselves, nor by our own wisdom, or understanding, or godliness, or works which we have wrought in holiness of heart; but by that faith through which, from the beginning, Almighty God has justified all men... What shall we do, then, brethren? Shall we become slothful in well-doing, and cease from the practice of love? God forbid that any such course should be followed by us!" Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION St Augustine, the Father most quoted by the Reformers, answers the question of merit in a way both sides claim.

Good works are truly rewarded, because they are God's own gifts working in us: St Augustine of Hippo On Grace and Free Will 15 "If, then, your good merits are God's gifts, God does not crown your merits as your merits, but as His own gifts." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Augustine of Hippo On the Spirit and the Letter 45 (on 2:13) "...the statement that the doers of the law shall be justified must be so understood, as that we may know that they are not otherwise doers of the law, unless they be justified, so that justification does not subsequently accrue to them as doers of the law, but justification precedes them as doers of the law.

For what else does the phrase being justified signify than being made righteous..." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Calvin John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 2:6) "...as he sanctifies those whom he has previously resolved to glorify, he will also crown their good works, but not on account of any merit: nor can this be proved from this verse; for though it declares what reward good works are to have, it does yet by no means show what they are worth, or what price is due to them. And it is an absurd inference, to deduce merit from reward." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 2:7) "The meaning then is, that the Lord will give eternal life to those who, by attention to good works, strive to attain immortality." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 2:13) "They who pervert this passage for the purpose of building up justification by works, deserve most fully to be laughed at even by children...

Still more, we can prove from this passage that no one is justified by works; for if they alone are justified by the law who fulfill the law, it follows that no one is justified; for no one can be found who can boast of having fulfilled the law." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) The Fathers We are justified by grace through faith, not by works we produce on our own. But faith is the start of a new life, and at the judgement God will look at that life. Good works done in Christ are His gifts in us, and they truly count, because He crowns them. Calvin and the Reformed God will reward good works, and only those who persevere in them will be saved. But the works are not the ground of acceptance or a merit before God. On 2:13 Paul is stating the law's demand, which no sinner can meet, so another righteousness must be sought. Notice how much is shared. Calvin agrees that God "will give eternal life to those who, by attention to good works, strive to attain immortality," and Augustine agrees that no good work is ours apart from God's gift.

Nobody here teaches that a person can earn heaven on his own; that was the teaching of Pelagius, which the Fathers condemned and the Council of Ephesus in 431 confirmed. The real question is whether works done in God's grace are part of the way we are finally saved (the Fathers) or only its fruit and evidence (the Reformers). The Orthodox call this synergy : God gives everything, and we freely work with what He gives. The case against faith alone is made in full on Sola Fide .

secs.h: 1. Righteous Gentiles before Christ: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: IX. The Law Written on the Heart (2:14–16) Romans 2:14-15 "for when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do the things in the law, these, although not having the law, are a law to themselves, who show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and between themselves their thoughts accusing or else excusing them." Orthodox reading: There is a moral law written into human nature. Even those without the law of Moses know right from wrong, and their conscience bears witness. Romans 2:16 "in the day when God will judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ, according to my gospel." Orthodox reading: Every conscience will be laid open on the day when God judges through Christ. Who are these Gentiles who "by nature do the things in the law"? The question sounds technical, but the answer shows how each tradition reads the whole chapter. There are three main readings. 1.

secs.h: 1. Righteous Gentiles before Christ: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: Righteous Gentiles before Christ: St John Chrysostom On 2:10, where Paul promises "glory, honor, and peace to everyone who works what is good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek," Chrysostom says Paul is speaking of the times before Christ: St John Chrysostom Homily 5 on Romans (on 2:10) "But by Greeks he here means not them that worshipped idols, but them that adored God, that obeyed the law of nature, that strictly kept all things, save the Jewish observances, which contribute to piety, such as were Melchizedek and his [company], such as was Job, such as were the Ninevites, such as was Cornelius." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 5 on Romans (on 2:14–15) "But whenever he says by nature, he means by the reasonings of nature...

secs.h: 1. Righteous Gentiles before Christ: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: For on this ground he means they are to be admired, because they required not a law, and yet exhibited all the doings of the Law, having the works, not the letters, graven upon their minds." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Acts 10:34-35 "Then Peter opened his mouth and said: 'In truth I perceive that God shows no partiality. But in every nation whoever fears Him and works righteousness is accepted by Him." Orthodox reading: Cornelius, a Gentile who feared God, prayed and gave alms, was "accepted" by God and was then brought to Christ and baptised. This is the kind of person Chrysostom has in mind. 2. Gentile Christians: St Augustine Augustine argues that the Gentiles of 2:14–15 are believers in whom the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33 has come true, God writing His law on their hearts: St Augustine of Hippo On the Spirit and the Letter 46 "...belonging to the new testament means having the law of God not written on tables, but on the heart...

secs.h: 1. Righteous Gentiles before Christ: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: embracing the righteousness of the law with innermost affection, where faith works by love." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION He also allows a second reading: that even in unbelievers "what was impressed on their hearts when they were created in the image of God has not been wholly blotted out" (chapter 48). 3. Knowledge of the law, not keeping it: Calvin John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 2:15) "Without reason then is the power of the will deduced from this passage, as though Paul had said, that the keeping of the law is within our power; for he speaks not of the power to fulfill the law, but of the knowledge of it." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Westminster Confession (1646) Westminster Confession of Faith XVI.7 "Works done by unregenerate men, although for the matter of them they may be things which God commands, and of good use both to themselves and others...

secs.h: 1. Righteous Gentiles before Christ: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: yet because they proceed not from a heart purified by faith, nor are done in a right manner, according to the Word, nor to a right end, the glory of God; they are therefore sinful, and can not please God, or make a man meet to receive grace from God. And yet their neglect of them is more sinful and displeasing unto God." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · WESTMINSTER CONFESSION, SCHAFF Chrysostom Real Gentiles before Christ, like Job and Cornelius, who honoured God and lived by the law of nature. God's judgement had no favourites even then. Augustine Gentile Christians, in whom God has written His law on the heart by grace. Or, in a weaker sense, unbelievers in whom God's image is not wholly erased. Calvin and Westminster All people know the law's demands, but no unregenerate person truly keeps it. Their good deeds are useful but cannot please God. The Orthodox Church follows Chrysostom's instinct without claiming more than Scripture says. Every human being bears the image of God, and that image, though damaged by sin, is not destroyed (Genesis 9:6; James 3:9).

secs.h: 1. Righteous Gentiles before Christ: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: God is at work everywhere, drawing people toward Him, as He drew Cornelius. But no one is saved apart from Christ, and Cornelius, once he had heard, was baptised. Notably, a number of modern Protestant scholars, among them C. E. B. Cranfield and N. T. Wright, now take Augustine's view of these verses, reading them as real Christian Gentiles rather than a hypothetical case.

X. Circumcision of the Heart (2:17–29) Paul now addresses the Jew directly: you who rest in the law, boast in God, teach others, do you teach yourself? Circumcision profits if you keep the law, but if you break it, it becomes uncircumcision. Then he says what true circumcision is: Romans 2:28-29 "For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the Spirit, not in the letter; whose praise is not from men but from God." Orthodox reading: What counts before God is the inward reality. The heart is circumcised by the Spirit, and the praise comes from God, not men. Deuteronomy 30:6 "And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your descendants, to love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live." Orthodox reading: This was always the promise: God Himself would circumcise the heart. St John Chrysostom Homily 6 on Romans (on 2:29) "By saying this he sets aside all things bodily.

For the circumcision is outwardly, and the sabbaths and the sacrifices and purifications: all of which he hints in a single word..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 6 on Romans (on 2:29) "But when he has said in the spirit he thereafter paves the way for the conversation of the Church, and introduces the faith. For it too is in the heart and spirit and has its praise of God." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Where does this circumcision of the heart happen? Paul answers in Colossians, and St Justin Martyr, writing around AD 155, answers the same way: Colossians 2:11-12 "In Him you were also circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the sins of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, buried with Him in baptism, in which you also were raised with Him through faith in the working of God, who raised Him from the dead." Orthodox reading: The circumcision made without hands takes place when we are buried and raised with Christ in baptism, through faith in the working of God.

St Justin Martyr Dialogue with Trypho 43 "And we, who have approached God through Him, have received not carnal, but spiritual circumcision, which Enoch and those like him observed. And we have received it through baptism, since we were sinners, by God's mercy; and all men may equally obtain it." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Protestants agree that true circumcision is inward and the work of the Spirit. The Reformed also see a link between circumcision and baptism, and use it to argue for infant baptism . Baptists and many evangelicals see baptism as an outward sign of an inward change that has already happened. For the Fathers, baptism is where God does the inward work, which is why Paul can say we were circumcised "buried with Him in baptism." This is the theme of Romans 6 . With this, Paul has shown that Gentile and Jew alike stand in need of God's mercy. In chapter 3 he will say it outright: "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (3:23), and then announce the righteousness of God revealed apart from the law.

XI. Objections Answered "Romans 1:17 proves justification by faith alone. The Fathers who talk about works have misread Paul." OO Response: Chrysostom read 1:17 and said righteousness comes "by a gift from above, contributing one thing only from your own store, believing." The Fathers had no trouble with grace received by faith. What they did not do was pull 1:17 away from 2:6–7, where the same Paul says God will give eternal life "to those who by patient continuance in doing good seek for glory, honor, and immortality." Any reading of Romans must hold both verses. The Fathers hold them by seeing faith as the entrance into a life of union with Christ that bears fruit and will be judged. Calvin holds them by saying the works are rewarded but are not the ground of salvation. Both are serious attempts. The Fathers' reading has the advantage of being the one the Church held from the beginning, as St Clement's letter from the first century shows. "Romans 2:13 is only hypothetical.

Nobody actually keeps the law, so nobody is justified that way." OO Response: This is Calvin's reading, and it fits Paul's conclusion in 3:20. But Paul in this chapter keeps describing real people: those who "by patient continuance in doing good" seek glory (2:7), Gentiles who "by nature do the things in the law" (2:14), the uncircumcised man who "keeps the righteous requirements of the law" (2:26) and the Jew "who is one inwardly" (2:29). Chrysostom and Augustine disagreed about who these people were, but neither thought they were imaginary. Augustine read 2:13 to mean that God makes people righteous so that they become doers of the law. Several modern Protestant commentators now agree that Paul has real people in view. "If God "gave them up," then God caused their sin." OO Response: Paul says God gave them up because they had already exchanged the truth for a lie (1:25) and did not want to keep God in their knowledge (1:28). The handing over is a judgement on a choice they had made.

Chrysostom compares it to a general who withdraws, leaving the soldiers to the enemy "not by thrusting them himself, but by stripping them of his own assistance." St John of Damascus says Scripture often speaks of what God permits as if He did it. Even Calvin, who gives the verse a stronger sense, insists that "the cause of sin is not from God." "Natural revelation cannot save, so Romans 1 means that everyone who never heard the gospel is lost." OO Response: Paul's point in Romans 1 is that everyone is without excuse and needs the gospel. He is not drawing up a list of who will be saved. The Church proclaims that salvation is in Christ alone and calls every person to faith and baptism. At the same time, the Fathers did not presume to judge those God has not shown us. Chrysostom names Job, Melchizedek, the Ninevites and Cornelius as Gentiles who honoured God. The Church knows where grace is given, in Christ and His Church; she does not claim to know the limits of God's mercy towards those who never heard. That is left to Him, and it is a reason for mission, not complacency.

"Teaching that God judges by works is Pelagianism." OO Response: Pelagius taught that man can keep God's commands by his own natural powers. The Fathers condemned this, and the Council of Ephesus in 431 confirmed the condemnation of his follower Celestius. Saying that God judges works is not Pelagian. It is what Paul says in 2:6 and Christ says in John 5:29. The question is where good works come from. The Orthodox answer with Augustine: from God's grace working in us, so that when God crowns them, He crowns His own gifts. Without grace we can do nothing (John 15:5); with grace we freely work. "Romans 2:1 means Christians should not say anything is a sin." OO Response: Paul has just named a long list of sins and called them deserving of death (1:32). He does not take any of it back. What he condemns in 2:1 is condemning others for what you do yourself. Chrysostom applies it to the judge who punishes an adulterer while committing adultery. The answer to hypocrisy is not silence about sin but repentance, beginning with one's own, which is what God's kindness is meant to lead to (2:4).

XII. FAQ Why read Romans with Chrysostom in particular? His thirty-two homilies are the fullest commentary on Romans from the early Church that survives in its original language. Origen wrote an earlier commentary, but it survives mostly in a shortened Latin version made by Rufinus. Chrysostom was a skilled reader of Greek, a pastor preaching to ordinary people, and a lifelong lover of Paul. The Greek and Oriental Fathers who came after him drew on him constantly. Is Romans mainly about how an individual is saved? It is about that, but not only that. Paul's argument runs from the need of all people (chapters 1 to 3), to God's gift in Christ (3 to 8), to God's faithfulness to Israel (9 to 11), to life together in one Church of Jews and Gentiles (12 to 16). Reading the first eight chapters on their own makes it easy to miss how much the letter is about God gathering one people from both. What does "the wrath of God" mean if God has no passions? The Fathers taught that God is not moved by changing emotions as we are.

Chrysostom says Paul adds "the righteous judgment of God" to "wrath" in 2:5 precisely "lest on hearing of wrath you should think of any passion." Wrath is God's just judgement on sin, and in Romans 1 it is shown first in God letting people have the darkness they chose. Can people really know God without the Bible? They can know that He exists and something of His power and divinity, as Paul says in 1:20 and Athanasius and Theophilus explain. They cannot know from nature alone the Trinity, the Incarnation or the way of salvation. That needs God's own revelation in Christ. The Westminster Confession says the same, and here Orthodox and Reformed largely agree. Is conscience always right? No. Paul says the conscience can accuse or excuse (2:15), and elsewhere speaks of consciences that are weak (1 Corinthians 8:7) or seared (1 Timothy 4:2). Conscience is a real witness that God placed in us, but it must be formed by God's word and by the life of the Church.

What comes next? Chapter 3 draws the conclusion that all, Jew and Gentile, are under sin, and then announces the righteousness of God revealed through faith in Jesus Christ apart from the law. That is where the debate over faith and works is fought most fiercely, and it is the subject of the next page, Romans 3 and 4: Justification and Faith .

I. Introduction: The Battlefield of the Reformation If Romans is the letter of the Reformation, chapters 3 and 4 are its battlefield. Here Paul says that "by the deeds of the law no flesh will be justified" (3:20), that "a man is justified by faith apart from the deeds of the law" (3:28), and that "Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness" (4:3). When Martin Luther translated the New Testament into German in 1522, he rendered 3:28 as "justified by faith alone ," adding a word that is not in the Greek, and defended it in his Open Letter on Translating of 1530. "Faith alone," sola fide , became the banner of the Reformation. The Orthodox Church does not confess sola fide as the Reformers defined it. But it would be dishonest to pretend that the Fathers never spoke of being justified by faith without works. They did, and this page shows where. It also shows what they meant by it, and why their meaning is not the same as the Reformers'. The real disagreement is narrower than the slogans suggest, and also deeper: it is about what justification is.

The questions are these. Who is under sin? What are "the works of the law"? What did the Fathers mean when they said "faith only"? Is the believer counted righteous, or made righteous, or both? And how does Paul's Abraham, justified by faith, fit with James's Abraham, "justified by works"? "For for this cause He both died and rose again, that He might make us righteous." St John Chrysostom, Homily 9 on Romans This page is part of Romans with the Fathers , a series of nine pages that read St Paul's letter to the Romans section by section with the Church Fathers, setting their reading beside the main Protestant readings. Use the bar at the top of the page to move between the sections of the letter.

II. Glossary of Terms Justify δικαιόω · dikaioō To declare or make righteous. Whether Paul's word means only a verdict, or a verdict that also heals and renews, is the heart of the debate. Account, reckon, impute λογίζομαι · logizomai To count, credit or reckon. Used eleven times in Romans 4. "Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness." Works of the law ἔργα νόμου · erga nomou The deeds commanded by the law of Moses (3:20, 28). Whether Paul means the whole law or chiefly the marks that set Israel apart is disputed. Grace χάρις · charis God's free gift and favour, and in the Fathers also His active presence and power in us. Freely δωρεάν · dōrean As a gift, without payment (3:24). Redemption ἀπολύτρωσις · apolytrōsis Release by ransom, deliverance from slavery (3:24). Propitiation, mercy seat ἱλαστήριον · hilastērion The golden lid of the ark, sprinkled with blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:15). Paul says God set forth Christ as the hilastērion (3:25). Boasting καύχησις · kauchēsis Glorying or confidence.

Faith excludes it (3:27), because it receives rather than earns. Seal σφραγίς · sphragis A mark of ownership and confirmation. Paul calls circumcision a seal of the righteousness Abraham had by faith (4:11). Synergy συνεργία · synergia Working together. The Orthodox term for our free cooperation with God's grace, from Paul's own word in 1 Corinthians 3:9.

III. None Righteous (3:1–20) Paul ended chapter 2 by saying that the true Jew is one inwardly. So what advantage is there in being a Jew? "Much in every way," he answers. Israel was given the words of God, and God remains faithful even when His people are not. Romans 3:1-2 "What advantage then has the Jew, or what is the profit of circumcision? Much in every way! Chiefly because to them were committed the oracles of God." Orthodox reading: Israel's privilege was real, but it was a gift of God, not an achievement. St John Chrysostom Homily 6 on Romans (on 3:1) "...for to be called a Jew and to know His Will and to approve the things which are more excellent, was no well doing of their own, but came of the grace of God..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Then Paul draws his conclusion from chapters 1 and 2: Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin. He proves it with a chain of quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah. Romans 3:10-12 "As it is written: 'There is none righteous, no, not one; There is none who understands; There is none who seeks after God.

They have all turned aside; They have together become unprofitable; There is none who does good, no, not one.'" Orthodox reading: Paul gathers the prophets' laments over their own generation to show that no one, Jew or Gentile, can stand before God on his own record. Protestant reading: In Reformed teaching this passage is a chief proof of total depravity: fallen man, left to himself, is unable to seek God or do any spiritual good until God regenerates him. St John Chrysostom Homily 7 on Romans (on 3:9–18) "He had accused the Gentiles, he had accused the Jews; it came next in order to mention the righteousness which is by faith. For if the law of nature availed not, and the written Law was of no advantage, but both weighed down those that used them not aright, and made it plain that they were worthy of greater punishment, then after this the salvation which is by grace was necessary." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 7 on Romans (on 3:19) "So close is the relationship of the Old Testament with the New, since even the accusations and reproofs were

entirely with a view to this, that the door of faith might open brightly upon them that hear it." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Romans 3:20 "Therefore by the deeds of the law no flesh will be justified in His sight, for by the law is the knowledge of sin." Orthodox reading: The law shows sin up. It cannot remove it. St John Chrysostom Homily 7 on Romans (on 3:20) "For if you boast in the Law, he means, it puts you to the greater shame: it solemnly parades forth your sins before you." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Total Depravity? The Fathers and the Reformers agree on the main point: all have sinned, no one can justify himself before God, and salvation must come by grace. Where they differ is the condition of fallen man. Reformed theology holds that sin has so corrupted every part of human nature that, without regeneration, a person cannot even respond to God. The Orthodox hold that the image of God is wounded and darkened but not destroyed, and that the will, though weakened and unable to save itself, can still respond to God's grace when He calls.

Chrysostom reads Romans 3:10–18 as Paul's indictment of a whole world gone astray, not as a statement about the powers of the human will. The deeper roots of this question are on Romans 5 and Original Sin .

secs.h: 1. The law as a whole, especially its moral demands
secs.x: IV. What Are "the Works of the Law"? Paul says no one is justified "by the deeds of the law" (3:20, 28). Which deeds? The answer changes how the whole letter reads, and there are two main views. 1. The law as a whole, especially its moral demands St Augustine argued that Paul cannot mean only the ceremonies, because in the same verse he says "by the law is the knowledge of sin," and in Romans 7 the commandment that shows him sin is "You shall not covet": St Augustine of Hippo On the Spirit and the Letter 14 "And lest any one should suppose that, in the passage just quoted from him, the apostle had meant to say that none are justified by that law, which contains many precepts, under the figure of the ancient sacraments, and among them that circumcision of the flesh itself... he immediately adds what law he meant, and says, For by the law is the knowledge of sin.

secs.h: 1. The law as a whole, especially its moral demands
secs.x: He refers then to that law of which he afterwards declares, I had not known sin but by the law; for I had not known lust except the law had said, You shall not covet." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 3:28) "Why he names the works of the law, I have already explained; and I have also proved that it is quite absurd to confine them to ceremonies. Frigid also is the gloss, that works are to be taken for those which are outward, and done without the Spirit of Christ." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) 2. The law as what marked Israel apart Chrysostom, like many Greek Fathers, keeps returning to circumcision, sabbaths and the boast of the Jew who rested in the law.

secs.x: On 3:28 he says the point that troubled the Jews most was whether the uncircumcised could share the same blessings: St John Chrysostom Homily 7 on Romans (on 3:28) "For these two things were what confused the Jews; one, if it were possible for men, who with works were not saved, to be saved without them, and another, if it were just for the uncircumcised to enjoy the same blessings with those, who had during so long a period been nurtured in the Law; which last confused them more by far than the former." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 7 on Romans (on 3:28) "He does not say, a Jew, or one under the Law, but after leading forth his discourse into a large room, and opening the doors of faith to the world, he says a man, the name common to our race." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION In the late twentieth century a group of Protestant scholars, often called the New Perspective on Paul (E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T.

secs.x: Wright among them), argued for a version of this second reading: that "works of the law" refers chiefly to the badges of Jewish identity, and that Paul's main target was not people trying to earn salvation but the claim that Gentiles must become Jews to belong to God's people. Many Reformed and Lutheran scholars reject this, as Calvin rejected the earlier version. Notice that Chrysostom actually holds both questions together: whether people "who with works were not saved" could be saved without them, and whether the uncircumcised could share the blessings. The Orthodox reading does not need to choose. Paul excludes any work of the law as the ground of our acceptance, moral or ceremonial, and he does so precisely so that Jew and Gentile can come in by the same door. What he does not exclude is the life of love that faith brings forth in Christ, which he calls "faith working through love" (Galatians 5:6).

secs.h: V. The Righteousness of God Revealed (3:21–26)
secs.x: V. The Righteousness of God Revealed (3:21–26) Romans 3:21-22 "But now the righteousness of God apart from the law is revealed, being witnessed by the Law and the Prophets, even the righteousness of God, through faith in Jesus Christ, to all and on all who believe. For there is no difference;" Orthodox reading: God's righteousness comes apart from the law, yet the law and the prophets bear witness to it. It is given through faith to all who believe. Romans 3:23 "for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God," Orthodox reading: Sin is not only breaking rules. It is falling short of the glory for which we were made. Romans 3:24-25 "being justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation by His blood, through faith, to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance God had passed over the sins that were previously committed," Orthodox reading: Christ is the true mercy seat, the place where God meets His people and sin is covered by blood. This is God's own initiative and gift.

secs.h: V. The Righteousness of God Revealed (3:21–26)
secs.x: Protestant reading: Most Protestants read hilastērion as "propitiation": Christ's death turned away God's just wrath by bearing the penalty of sin in our place, the doctrine of penal substitution. Leviticus 16:15 "Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering, which is for the people, bring its blood inside the veil, do with that blood as he did with the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it on the mercy seat and before the mercy seat." Orthodox reading: The background of Paul's word. On the Day of Atonement the high priest sprinkled the blood on the mercy seat to cleanse the sanctuary and the people. Chrysostom notices that Paul's word points back to the sacrifices of the old covenant: St John Chrysostom Homily 7 on Romans (on 3:25) "For it was on this ground that he said, In His blood, to call to their minds those sheep and calves.

secs.h: V. The Righteousness of God Revealed (3:21–26)
secs.x: For if the sacrifices of things without reason, he means, cleared from sin, much more would this blood." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION And on "to demonstrate His righteousness" (3:26) he makes the point that will matter most on this page: God's righteousness is shown not only in His being righteous but in His making sinners righteous. St John Chrysostom Homily 7 on Romans (on 3:25–26) "So also is the declaring of His righteousness not only that He is Himself righteous, but that He does also make them that are filled with the putrefying sores of sin suddenly righteous... Doubt not then: for it is not of works, but of faith: and shun not the righteousness of God, for it is a blessing in two ways; because it is easy, and also open to all men." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Athanasius, a century before, explained the cross in a way that includes substitution, "in the stead of all," but sets it within the larger work of healing our nature from corruption: St Athanasius of Alexandria On the Incarnation 8 "...because all were under penalty of the corruption of
