secs.x: death He gave it over to death in the stead of all, and offered it to the Father... of His loving-kindness, to the end that, firstly, all being held to have died in Him, the law involving the ruin of men might be undone... and that, secondly, whereas men had turned toward corruption, He might turn them again toward incorruption, and quicken them from death by the appropriation of His body and by the grace of the Resurrection..." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Calvin reads 3:25 as reconciliation with an offended God, but notice what he says God hates and what He loves: John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 3:25) "God does not indeed hate in us his own workmanship, that is, as we are formed men; but he hates our uncleanness, which has extinguished the light of his image.

secs.h: V. The Righteousness of God Revealed (3:21–26)
secs.x: When the washing of Christ cleanses this away, he then loves and embraces us as his own pure workmanship." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 3:25) "And this definition or explanation again confirms what I have already often reminded you, that men are pronounced just, not because they are such in reality, but by imputation..." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Both sides agree that Christ's death is a true sacrifice for sin, that He died for us and in our place, and that this is entirely God's gift. The Orthodox do not deny that Christ bore our sins (Isaiah 53; 1 Peter 2:24). What they do not accept is a picture in which the Father must punish the Son before He can love us, or in which the cross is only a legal transaction. The Fathers speak of ransom, sacrifice, victory over death and healing together. How the traditions compare is set out on Theosis & Deification .

VI. Justified by Faith Apart from Works (3:27–31) Romans 3:27 "Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith." Orthodox reading: Faith leaves no room for boasting, because faith receives what God gives. Romans 3:28 "Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith apart from the deeds of the law." Orthodox reading: No one is justified by doing what the law commands. Justification comes by faith. Protestant reading: Luther and the Lutheran and Reformed confessions read this as justification by faith alone: faith is the only means by which the sinner receives Christ's righteousness, and works, though they must follow, add nothing to it. Romans 3:29-30 "Or is He the God of the Jews only? Is He not also the God of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also, since there is one God who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith." Orthodox reading: This is why Paul insists on faith: there is one God of Jews and Gentiles, and He justifies both the same way.

Chrysostom's comment on 3:27 is one that every Orthodox reader of Romans should know: St John Chrysostom Homily 7 on Romans (on 3:27) "But what is the law of faith? It is, being saved by grace. Here he shows God's power, in that He has not only saved, but has even justified, and led them to boasting, and this too without needing works, but looking for faith only." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Romans 3:31 "Do we then make void the law through faith? Certainly not! On the contrary, we establish the law." Orthodox reading: Faith does not abolish the law. It fulfils what the law was for. St John Chrysostom Homily 7 on Romans (on 3:31) "What was the object of the Law and what the scope of all its enactments? Why, to make man righteous. But this it had no power to do. For all, it says, have sinned: but faith when it came accomplished it.

For when a man is once a believer, he is straightway justified." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The Confessions Augsburg Confession (1530) Augsburg Confession, Article IV "Also they teach that men can not be justified before God by their own powers, merits, or works; but are justified freely for Christ's sake through faith, when they believe that they are received into favor, and their sins forgiven for Christ's sake, who by his death hath satisfied for our sins. This faith doth God impute for righteousness before him." Lutheran Confession VERBATIM · AUGSBURG CONFESSION, SCHAFF Westminster Confession (1646) Westminster Confession of Faith XI.2 "Faith, thus receiving and resting on Christ and his righteousness, is the alone instrument of justification; yet is it not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · WESTMINSTER CONFESSION, SCHAFF Read carefully, the Westminster Confession says what the Fathers say in one respect: faith "is not alone in the person

justified... but worketh by love." No serious Protestant teaches that a person can be saved by a faith that produces no change. The question is whether the love that faith produces has any part in our justification. For Westminster, none: faith alone is the instrument, and love is its companion. For the Fathers, faith is the door into a life in which God makes us righteous, and that life is part of what it is to be justified.

secs.h: VII. Was "Faith Alone" a Patristic Phrase?
secs.x: VII. Was "Faith Alone" a Patristic Phrase? Protestant writers often point out that some Fathers used the words "faith alone." This is true, and it should be acknowledged plainly. Chrysostom's "looking for faith only" on 3:27 is one example. Here are others: Origen Commentary on Romans III (on 3:27–28) Commenting on 3:27–28, Origen says that a person can be justified by faith alone, without works, and gives as his example the penitent thief, who was promised paradise though he had no opportunity to do good works afterwards. Elsewhere in the same commentary he insists that good works must follow as the fruit of justification. Early Witness PARAPHRASE St Basil the Great Homily 20, On Humility St Basil says that the perfect glorying in God is not to boast in one's own righteousness, but to know oneself lacking in true righteousness and justified by faith in Christ alone, as Paul gloried in despising his own righteousness and seeking the righteousness from God that is through faith (Philippians 3:8–9).

secs.h: VII. Was "Faith Alone" a Patristic Phrase?
secs.x: Church Father PARAPHRASE St John Chrysostom Homily 9 on Romans (on 5:2) "On His part, however, there be things varied and numerous and diverse. For He died for us, and farther reconciled us, and brought us to Himself, and gave us grace unspeakable. But we brought faith only as our contribution." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION So did the Fathers teach the Reformation doctrine? Look at what each of them says in the same breath. Chrysostom , who said "faith only" on 3:27, said on 2:7 that "it is not right to trust in faith only. For it is deeds also into which that tribunal will enquire" (see Romans 1–2 ). And in the very passage on 5:2 quoted above, he goes on to say that the grace to which faith brings us includes "the obtaining of all the blessings that come through Baptism." Origen's example is a man who came to faith with no time to do anything else. He is speaking of how a sinner enters salvation, not of a believer who goes on to refuse a life of love. Basil's point is humility: no one can boast before God of his own righteousness.

secs.h: VII. Was "Faith Alone" a Patristic Phrase?
secs.x: The same Basil wrote the Morals and the monastic Rules , two of the most demanding works on Christian obedience ever written. In other words, when the Fathers say "faith alone" they mean faith as opposed to works of the law done to earn God's favour, and faith as the way a sinner, however late, first comes to Christ. They never mean that justification is a legal verdict separate from the renewal of the person, or that the works of love done in Christ have no part in final salvation. That is why the same Fathers can say "faith only" and speak of judgement by works without contradicting themselves. The phrase is shared; the doctrine is not. More on this is on Sola Fide .

VIII. Abraham Believed God (4:1–8) Paul now turns to the father of Israel. If anyone could boast of works, it was Abraham. But Scripture says something else: Romans 4:2-3 "For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God. For what does the Scripture say? 'Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.'" Orthodox reading: Abraham's righteousness before God came by trusting God's promise, not by a record of deeds. Paul quotes Genesis 15:6. Romans 4:4-5 "Now to him who works, the wages are not counted as grace but as debt. But to him who does not work but believes on Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness," Orthodox reading: A wage is earned; a gift is received. God justifies the ungodly, those who have nothing to offer, when they believe.

Romans 4:6-8 "just as David also describes the blessedness of the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works: 'Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, And whose sins are covered; Blessed is the man to whom the Lord shall not impute sin.'" Orthodox reading: David's blessing in Psalm 32 is the blessing of forgiveness: sins covered and not counted. St John Chrysostom Homily 8 on Romans (on 4:5) "For reflect how great a thing it is to be persuaded and have full confidence that God is able on a sudden not to free a man who has lived in impiety from punishment only, but even to make him just, and to count him worthy of those immortal honors." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 8 on Romans (on 4:7–8) "For if he be blessed that by grace received forgiveness, much more is he that is made just, and that exhibits faith." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The earliest Fathers read Abraham the same way, while never separating his faith from his obedience: St Clement of Rome First Epistle of Clement 31 "For what reason was our

father Abraham blessed? Was it not because he wrought righteousness and truth through faith?" Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION St Cyril of Jerusalem Catechetical Lecture 5.5 "He was justified not only by works, but also by faith: for though he did many things well, yet he was never called the friend of God, except when he believed. Moreover, his every work was performed in faith." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 4:3) "For if there be any righteousness by the law or by works, it must be in men themselves; but by faith they derive from another what is wanting in themselves; and hence the righteousness of faith is rightly called imputative." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 4:3) "We hence conclude that the question is not, what men are in themselves, but how God regards them; not that purity of conscience and integrity of life are to be separated from the gratuitous favor of God; but that when the reason is asked, why God loves us and owns us as just, it is necessary that Christ
should come forth as one who clothes us with his own righteousness." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849)

IX. Accounted or Made Righteous? Here is the real point of division, and it is worth setting out carefully. Westminster Confession (1646) Westminster Confession of Faith XI.1 "Those whom God effectually calleth he also freely justifieth; not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous: not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ's sake alone..." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · WESTMINSTER CONFESSION, SCHAFF For the Reformed, then, justification is a verdict about the person, not a change in the person. God counts the believer righteous because Christ's righteousness is credited to him. The change, sanctification, really happens and always follows, but it is a different gift. Calvin's phrase on 3:25 is blunt: "not because they are such in reality, but by imputation." For Chrysostom, Paul's language of "accounting" describes God doing something real. God "is able on a sudden... even to make him just" (4:5).

God's righteousness is shown in that He makes "them that are filled with the putrefying sores of sin suddenly righteous" (3:26). And on 4:25, "for this cause He both died and rose again, that He might make us righteous." Augustine said the same in plain words: "what else does the phrase being justified signify than being made righteous" (On the Spirit and the Letter 45). The Fathers Justification is forgiveness and more: God makes the sinner righteous by uniting him to Christ in faith and baptism and giving him the Holy Spirit. Being counted righteous and being made righteous are one gift, though it grows over a lifetime. Reformed and Lutheran Justification is God's legal verdict: sins pardoned and Christ's righteousness credited to the believer. Renewal (sanctification) always follows, but it is distinct and is not the ground of our standing with God.

2 Corinthians 5:21 "For He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him." Orthodox reading: Paul does not say we are counted as the righteousness of God but that we "become" it, in Christ. The Fathers read this as a real exchange: He took what is ours so that we might share what is His. Protestant reading: Reformed readers see here the double imputation: our sin credited to Christ, His righteousness credited to us. Is there common ground? More than the debates suggest. Both sides say justification is God's free gift in Christ and not earned. Both say a justified person will be changed. Many Protestant theologians also speak of "union with Christ" as the root of both justification and sanctification, which brings them closer to the Fathers. The Orthodox worry about a purely legal justification is that it can make the change in the believer seem optional. The Protestant worry about the Orthodox view is that it can make our standing with God depend on how holy we have become.
The Orthodox answer is that our standing rests always on Christ, in whom we live, and that the holiness is His life in us, not ours apart from Him. That is theosis .

secs.h: X. Circumcision, the Seal of Faith (4:9–12)
secs.x: X. Circumcision, the Seal of Faith (4:9–12) Romans 4:9-10 "Does this blessedness then come upon the circumcised only, or upon the uncircumcised also? For we say that faith was accounted to Abraham for righteousness. How then was it accounted? While he was circumcised, or uncircumcised? Not while circumcised, but while uncircumcised." Orthodox reading: Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised. Faith came first. Romans 4:11 "And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while still uncircumcised, that he might be the father of all those who believe, though they are uncircumcised, that righteousness might be imputed to them also," Orthodox reading: Circumcision was a sign and seal of the righteousness he already had by faith, so that he could be the father of believers among the uncircumcised too. St John Chrysostom Homily 8 on Romans (on 4:10–11) "For he was uncircumcised, yet was not hindered from being justified. The circumcision therefore is behind the faith...

secs.h: X. Circumcision, the Seal of Faith (4:9–12)
secs.x: Nor is it behind faith only, but very far inferior to it, even so far as the sign is to the reality of which it is the sign; for instance, as the seal is to the soldier." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Irenaeus of Lyons Against Heresies IV.16.2 "And that man was not justified by these things, but that they were given as a sign to the people, this fact shows... that Abraham himself, without circumcision and without observance of Sabbaths, believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness; and he was called the friend of God." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Does this mean baptism, which Colossians 2:11–12 calls the circumcision of Christ, is also only an outward seal of something already complete? Baptists and many evangelicals argue so. The Reformed see baptism as a seal of the covenant, which is why they baptise infants as Israel circumcised them.

secs.h: X. Circumcision, the Seal of Faith (4:9–12)
secs.x: The Fathers saw a difference between the two: circumcision marked the flesh, while baptism is where God Himself does the inward circumcision of the heart, as Justin said: "we have received it through baptism." Abraham's faith came before the sign. In the new covenant, faith and baptism belong together (Mark 16:16; Acts 2:38), and for an adult believer the faith comes first and is completed in the font. This is the theme of Romans 6 .

secs.h: XI. The Faith of Abraham and the Resurrection (4:13–25)
secs.x: XI. The Faith of Abraham and the Resurrection (4:13–25) Romans 4:16 "Therefore it is of faith that it might be according to grace, so that the promise might be sure to all the seed, not only to those who are of the law, but also to those who are of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all" Orthodox reading: The promise rests on faith so that it can rest on grace, and so that it can be sure for all Abraham's children, Jew and Gentile. Romans 4:17 "As it is written, 'I have made you a father of many nations' in the presence of Him whom he believed—God, who gives life to the dead and calls those things which do not exist as though they did;" Orthodox reading: The God Abraham trusted is the God who raises the dead and creates out of nothing.

secs.h: XI. The Faith of Abraham and the Resurrection (4:13–25)
secs.x: St John Chrysostom Homily 8 on Romans (on 4:17) "For if He could quicken the dead and bring in those things that were not as though they were, then could He also make those who were not born of him to be his children." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 8 on Romans (on 4:17–18) "But after saying, that the gift of God was great and unspeakable, and having discoursed concerning His power, he shows farther that Abraham's faith was deserving of the gift, that you may not suppose him to have been honored without reason." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Romans 4:20-22 "He did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, and being fully convinced that what He had promised He was also able to perform. And therefore 'it was accounted to him for righteousness.'" Orthodox reading: Abraham's faith was not a single moment of assent. It was trust that held firm through years of waiting and gave glory to God.

secs.h: XI. The Faith of Abraham and the Resurrection (4:13–25)
secs.x: Romans 4:23-25 "Now it was not written for his sake alone that it was imputed to him, but also for us. It shall be imputed to us who believe in Him who raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was delivered up because of our offenses, and was raised because of our justification." Orthodox reading: The same faith is counted to us when we believe in the God who raised Jesus. Christ died for our sins and rose for our justification. St John Chrysostom Homily 9 on Romans (on 4:25) "For the purpose of His dying was not that He might hold us liable to punishment and in condemnation, but that He might do good unto us. For for this cause He both died and rose again, that He might make us righteous." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Notice that Paul ties justification to the resurrection, not only to the cross. Justification is not only the cancelling of a debt but entry into the risen life of Christ. This is why the Fathers connect it with baptism, where we die and rise with Him, and with the gift of the Spirit.

secs.h: XI. The Faith of Abraham and the Resurrection (4:13–25)
secs.x: Abraham's faith is the pattern: trust in the God who gives life to the dead.

XII. Paul and James No discussion of Romans 4 can avoid James 2, where the same verse from Genesis is used to make what sounds like the opposite point: James 2:21-24 "Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered Isaac his son on the altar? Do you see that faith was working together with his works, and by works faith was made perfect? And the Scripture was fulfilled which says, 'Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.' And he was called the friend of God. You see then that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only." Orthodox reading: James says Abraham's faith "was working together with his works," and was made perfect by them. Faith and works are not rivals but partners. Protestant reading: Most Protestants read James as speaking of how a true faith is shown to be real before others, not of how a sinner is accepted by God. John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 3:28) "What, James says, that man is not justified by faith alone, but also by works, does not at all militate against the preceding view.

The reconciling of the two views depends chiefly on the drift of the argument pursued by James. For the question with him is not, how men attain righteousness before God, but how they prove to others that they are justified, for his object was to confute hypocrites, who vainly boasted that they had faith." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) St Augustine of Hippo On Grace and Free Will 18 "Unintelligent persons, however, with regard to the apostle's statement: We conclude that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law, have thought him to mean that faith suffices to a man, even if he lead a bad life, and has no good works." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Augustine of Hippo On Grace and Free Will 18 "Therefore they possess not the faith by which the just man lives... the faith which works by love in such wise, that God recompenses it according to its works with eternal life." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The Fathers reconcile Paul and James simply.

Paul says no one is justified by works of the law done without faith, and that the sinner comes to God by faith, as Abraham did in Genesis 15. James says that the faith that justifies is a living faith that works, as Abraham's did in Genesis 22, and that a faith without works is dead. Both are true of the same Abraham, as St Cyril of Jerusalem said: "his every work was performed in faith." Calvin's reconciliation, that James speaks of proving faith to others, is a serious one, but James says faith was "made perfect" by works and that a man "is justified by works, and not by faith only" (2:24). The Fathers took him at his word.

XIII. Objections Answered "Romans 3:28 says faith apart from works. The Orthodox add works, so they preach another gospel." OO Response: Paul says "apart from the deeds of the law." The Orthodox agree that no one is justified by doing the works of the law, and that the sinner comes to God by faith, without any prior works. Chrysostom said exactly that on 3:27 and 3:31. What the Orthodox add is not works to earn salvation but the life that faith leads into: baptism, the Spirit, love and perseverance. Paul himself says "faith working through love" (Galatians 5:6) and that God "will render to each one according to his deeds" (2:6). Holding these together is not another gospel. It is the whole of Paul. "The Fathers said "faith alone," so they were Protestants before Protestantism." OO Response: Some Fathers did use the words, and Protestants are right to point it out. But the same Fathers taught baptismal regeneration, judgement by works, the real change of the believer, and the possibility of falling away.

They used "faith alone" to exclude boasting in works of the law and to show how a sinner first comes to Christ. Taking one phrase while leaving the rest of their teaching behind does not make them Protestants. It is better to let them speak for themselves, as this page tries to do. ""Accounted" in Romans 4 is accounting language. It can only mean a legal reckoning, not an inward change." OO Response: The word does mean to count or credit. The question is whether God's counting is like a human accountant recording a fact, or like God's word in creation, which makes what it says. When God counted Abraham's faith as righteousness, Chrysostom says, He was able "even to make him just." Paul himself, in the same chapter, describes God as the one who "calls those things which do not exist as though they did" (4:17). God's reckoning is creative. That is why the Fathers never separated being counted righteous from being made righteous.

"If justification is being made righteous, no one can be sure of it, since no one is perfectly righteous." OO Response: The Orthodox do not teach that we must become perfect before God accepts us. We are accepted in Christ from the moment of faith and baptism, as Chrysostom says, "straightway justified." The making righteous begins then and continues through life. Our confidence rests on Christ's faithfulness, not on measuring our own holiness. The Orthodox simply do not claim that a single moment guarantees the end regardless of how we live afterward. Paul himself warns believers not to be high-minded but to fear, and to continue in God's goodness (Romans 11:20–22). See Assurance of Salvation . "Romans 3:10 proves total depravity: no one seeks God unless God first regenerates him." OO Response: Paul is quoting Psalm 14 and others to show that all, Jew and Gentile, are under sin and cannot justify themselves. The Fathers fully agree. But the same Paul says in chapter 2 that God's kindness leads people to repentance and that some Gentiles do by nature what the law requires.

The Orthodox teach that no one can come to God without grace, but that God's grace goes out to all and that people can resist or receive it. Grace comes first; regeneration is given in baptism to those who respond in faith. Whether grace is irresistible is the question of Romans 9 .

XIV. FAQ Did Luther really add the word "alone" to Romans 3:28? Yes. His German New Testament of 1522 reads "allein durch den Glauben," by faith alone. In his Open Letter on Translating (1530) he argued that German idiom needed the word to convey Paul's meaning clearly, and that Paul's sense excludes all works. Critics, then and now, answer that a translator should not add a word that settles a disputed doctrine. The word is not in the Greek, and most modern English Protestant translations, including the NKJV, do not include it. Does the Orthodox Church believe in justification by faith? Yes, in the sense that the Fathers taught it: the sinner is justified freely, by God's grace, through faith in Christ, without the works of the law. What it does not accept is the Reformation definition of justification as a purely legal verdict separate from the renewal of the person, or the teaching that works done in Christ have no part in final salvation.

What is the Orthodox view of the atonement? The Fathers use many images together: sacrifice, ransom, victory over death and the devil, healing of our nature, and Christ dying in our place. They do not make any one image the key to all the others. The Orthodox reject the idea that the Father's anger needed to be satisfied by punishing the Son before He could love us, since the cross itself is the Father's love (John 3:16; Romans 5:8). Is this the same as the Catholic view? On justification as both forgiveness and inner renewal, the Orthodox and Roman Catholics are close, since both follow the Fathers. The Orthodox do not share the later Latin system of merit, temporal punishment and indulgences. See Roman Catholic Dogmas and Purgatory . What about the thief on the cross? Origen used him as an example of justification by faith alone, and rightly: he came to Christ at the end and was promised paradise. He shows that God receives the sinner who turns to Him in faith, however late. He does not show that someone who has years to live may refuse baptism and a life of love.

God binds us to His commandments, but He is not bound by them, and the Church leaves extraordinary cases to Him. What comes next? Having shown that we are justified by faith, Paul describes the peace with God that follows and then compares Adam and Christ. That is the subject of the next page, Romans 5: Adam and Ancestral Sin , where the Greek Fathers and Augustine part ways over Romans 5:12.

I. Introduction: Two Men Romans 5 turns on two men. Through Adam sin and death came into the world; through Christ grace and life came in "much more." Paul builds the whole chapter on the comparison: as the one, so the other, and yet not as the one, because the gift is far greater than the fall. The chapter has also been the ground of one of the deepest disagreements between East and West. From Romans 5:12, St Augustine drew the doctrine that all people sinned in Adam and are born guilty of his sin. The Reformers inherited and sharpened that teaching. The Greek Fathers, reading the same verse, spoke instead of an inheritance of death and corruption, out of which personal sin grows. Orthodox writers today often call this "ancestral sin" to mark the difference, though some Orthodox, including many Coptic teachers, use the phrase "original sin" as well. The words differ; what matters is what is meant. This page tries to set the question out fairly.

It shows what the Fathers on each side actually wrote, admits the texts that do not fit easy summaries (including a canon of the Council of Carthage), and then turns to what Paul cares about most: that where sin abounded, grace abounded much more. "For Christ has paid down far more than we owe, yea as much more as the illimitable ocean is than a little drop." St John Chrysostom, Homily 10 on Romans This page is part of Romans with the Fathers , a series of nine pages that read St Paul's letter to the Romans section by section with the Church Fathers, setting their reading beside the main Protestant readings. Use the bar at the top of the page to move between the sections of the letter. A Note on Quotations Every quotation marked VERBATIM has been checked word for word against a public domain translation: St John Chrysostom's thirty-two Homilies on Romans and the other Fathers in the Ante-Nicene and Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series, John Calvin's Commentary on Romans in John Owen's translation (1849), and the Reformation confessions in Philip Schaff's Creeds of Christendom .

Chrysostom's homilies follow J. B. Morris's translation as revised by W. H. Simcox, in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, volume 11. Where a work has no public domain English translation, its teaching is summarised and marked PARAPHRASE . Scripture follows the NKJV.

II. Glossary of Terms Peace εἰρήνη · eirēnē Not only the end of hostility but wholeness and right relationship with God (5:1). Reconcile καταλλάσσω · katallassō To change enmity into friendship. In Paul it is always we who are reconciled to God, and God who does the reconciling (5:10; 2 Corinthians 5:19). Offence, trespass παράπτωμα · paraptōma A false step, a fall. Adam's sin (5:15–18). Type, pattern τύπος · typos A figure that foreshadows something greater. Adam is "a type of Him who was to come" (5:14). Because, in that ἐφ᾽ ᾧ · eph᾽ hō The two words at the end of 5:12. Most translations render them "because"; the old Latin rendered them "in whom." Much depends on this phrase. Death θάνατος · thanatos In Romans 5 a power that "reigns" (5:14, 17), not only the end of bodily life but the whole condition of separation from the God who is life. Corruption φθορά · phthora Decay, the tendency of a creature made from nothing to fall back toward nothing (Athanasius). The Greek Fathers' key word for what we inherit.

Were made κατεστάθησαν · katestathēsan "Were made" or "were constituted" sinners (5:19). Whether this means made guilty, made liable to death, or made sinful in nature is part of the debate. Ancestral sin προπατορικὴ ἁμαρτία · propatorikē hamartia "The sin of the forefather." A term preferred by many Orthodox writers for Adam's sin and its consequences in us, to distinguish it from inherited guilt. Recapitulation ἀνακεφαλαίωσις · anakephalaiōsis "Summing up again under one head." St Irenaeus's word for Christ going back over Adam's path and undoing it (Ephesians 1:10).

III. Peace with God (5:1–5) Romans 5:1 "Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ," Orthodox reading: Justification brings peace with God. Peace is both a gift received and a state to be kept. Many of the oldest Greek manuscripts of Romans read not "we have peace" ( echomen ) but "let us have peace" ( echōmen ), a difference of one vowel. Modern critical editions usually print "we have," judging that it fits Paul's argument better, but "let us have" has very strong early support, and it is the text Chrysostom read and preached: St John Chrysostom Homily 9 on Romans (on 5:1) "For after having said much on the subject of faith, he had set it before righteousness which is by works, to prevent any one from supposing what he said was a ground for listlessness, he says, let us have peace, that is, let us sin no more, nor go back to our former estate.

For this is making war with God." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 9 on Romans (on 5:1) "For it is not the same thing to receive peace when there had been none, and to keep it when it has been given, since to acquire surely is harder than to keep. Yet nevertheless the more difficult has been made easy, and carried out into effect." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Romans 5:2 "through whom also we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God." Orthodox reading: Faith is the door into a standing in grace and a hope of glory. Romans 5:3-5 "And not only that, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces perseverance; and perseverance, character; and character, hope. Now hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who was given to us." Orthodox reading: Suffering, borne in faith, forms us. The guarantee of our hope is the love of God poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit.

St John Chrysostom Homily 9 on Romans (on 5:5) "Now had He not been willing to present us after our labors with great crowns, He would never have given us such mighty gifts before our labors. But now the warmth of His Love is hence made apparent, that it is not gradually and little by little that He honors us; but He has shed abroad the full fountain of His blessings, and this too before our struggles." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Whichever reading is original, both are true to Paul. Peace with God is a gift already given in Christ, and it is also a peace to be lived in and kept. The Orthodox emphasis on keeping what has been received is not a denial of the gift; it is the way the gift is honoured.

secs.h: IV. While We Were Still Sinners (5:6–11)
secs.x: IV. While We Were Still Sinners (5:6–11) Romans 5:6-8 "For when we were still without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly. For scarcely for a righteous man will one die; yet perhaps for a good man someone would even dare to die. But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." Orthodox reading: The cross is the proof of God's love, not the cause of it. Christ died for us while we were still His enemies. Romans 5:9-10 "Much more then, having now been justified by His blood, we shall be saved from wrath through Him. For if when we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved by His life." Orthodox reading: Reconciled by His death, we shall be saved by His life. Salvation is not finished at the cross; it continues in the risen life of Christ.

secs.h: IV. While We Were Still Sinners (5:6–11)
secs.x: St John Chrysostom Homily 9 on Romans (on 5:8) "For if for a virtuous man, no one would hastily choose to die, consider your Master's love, when it is not for virtuous men, but for sinners and enemies that He is seen to have been crucified..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Who needed to be reconciled to whom? Paul never says God was reconciled to us, only that we were reconciled to God (5:10) and that "God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself" (2 Corinthians 5:19). The Fathers took this seriously: the change was in us, not in God. Here Calvin, quoting St Augustine, agrees: John Calvin Institutes of the Christian Religion II.16.4 (quoting St Augustine) "For it was not after we were reconciled to him by the blood of his Son that he began to love us, but he loved us before the foundation of the world...

secs.h: IV. While We Were Still Sinners (5:6–11)
secs.x: Our being reconciled by the death of Christ must not be understood as if the Son reconciled us, in order that the Father, then hating, might begin to love us, but that we were reconciled to him already, loving, though at enmity with us because of sin." Reformer VERBATIM · BEVERIDGE TRANSLATION (1845) This is real common ground. Whatever else is said about wrath and propitiation, both traditions at their best confess that the Father's love is the source of the cross, not its result.

V. Death Through One Man (5:12–14) Romans 5:12 "Therefore, just as through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and thus death spread to all men, because all sinned—" Orthodox reading: Sin entered through Adam, and death through sin. Death then spread to all, and all have sinned. Romans 5:13-14 "For until the law sin was in the world, but sin is not imputed when there is no law. Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned according to the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a type of Him who was to come." Orthodox reading: Death reigned even over those who had not broken a commandment as Adam did. Something more than personal transgression was at work: the reign of death itself. Genesis 2:17 "but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die." Orthodox reading: The warning was death. Adam's sin brought it, and death is the inheritance that passed to all.

St John Chrysostom Homily 10 on Romans (on 5:12) "But what means, for that all have sinned? This; he having once fallen, even they that had not eaten of the tree did from him, all of them, become mortal." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 10 on Romans (on 5:13–14) "From whence it is clear, that it was not this sin, the transgression, that is, of the Law, but that of Adam's disobedience, which marred all things. Now what is the proof of this? The fact that even before the Law all died..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Athanasius explains what this death is. Man was made from nothing, and by nature would fall back toward nothing; it was his union with God that kept him from corruption.

When he turned from God, he began to return to what he came from: St Athanasius of Alexandria On the Incarnation 4–5 "For transgression of the commandment was turning them back to their natural state, so that just as they have had their being out of nothing, so also, as might be expected, they might look for corruption into nothing in the course of time." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Athanasius of Alexandria On the Incarnation 4 "For man is by nature mortal, inasmuch as he is made out of what is not; but by reason of his likeness to Him that is (and if he still preserved this likeness by keeping Him in his knowledge) he would stay his natural corruption, and remain incorrupt..." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION This is the Greek Fathers' picture: Adam's sin cut humanity off from the life of God, and what flowed to all his descendants was mortality and corruption. Death, in turn, becomes the soil in which sin grows, through fear, self-preservation and passion (Hebrews 2:14–15).

secs.h: VI. "Because All Sinned" or "In Whom All Sinned"?
secs.x: VI. "Because All Sinned" or "In Whom All Sinned"? The last words of 5:12 in Greek are eph᾽ hō pantes hēmarton . The old Latin translation, which St Augustine used, rendered them in quo omnes peccaverunt , "in whom all sinned," taking "whom" to be Adam. Augustine built much of his argument on this reading: St Augustine of Hippo Against Two Letters of the Pelagians IV.7 "...it remains that all men are understood to have sinned in that first man, because all men were in him when he sinned; and from him sin is derived by birth, and is not remitted save by being born again." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION To be fair to Augustine, two things should be said. First, he did look at the Greek: in the same chapter he discusses the gender of the Greek pronoun and argues from it. Second, he was not the first to read the verse this way.

secs.h: VI. "Because All Sinned" or "In Whom All Sinned"?
secs.x: He cites "the sainted Hilary," meaning a Latin commentary on Paul then thought to be by St Hilary and now known as Ambrosiaster, which had already said that all sinned in Adam "as it were in the mass." Still, most scholars today, Protestant and Catholic as well as Orthodox, agree that eph᾽ hō does not mean "in whom." Almost every modern English Bible, the NKJV included, translates it "because." Some take it as "with the result that," and some Orthodox theologians, notably John Meyendorff, have suggested it refers back to death: "death spread to all, because of which all sinned." On the usual reading, Paul says that death spread to all because all sinned , which leaves open how Adam's sin and ours are connected. Paul answers that in 5:19, and so must we. "Because all sinned" The Greek Fathers, and most modern translations. Death spread to all, and all have sinned in their own persons, under the reign of death that began with Adam. "In whom all sinned" Ambrosiaster and Augustine, followed by much of the Latin West.

secs.h: VI. "Because All Sinned" or "In Whom All Sinned"?
secs.x: All sinned in Adam, being present in him, and so share his guilt from birth. Whatever one concludes, it is not true that the doctrine of inherited guilt stands or falls with one Latin mistranslation. Augustine also argued from 5:18–19 ("judgment came to all men, resulting in condemnation"), from infant baptism, and from Psalm 51:5. Those arguments need answering on their own terms, and the next sections try to do that.

VII. What Do We Inherit from Adam? Romans 5:18-19 "Therefore, as through one man's offense judgment came to all men, resulting in condemnation, even so through one Man's righteous act the free gift came to all men, resulting in justification of life. For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so also by one Man's obedience many will be made righteous." Orthodox reading: Through Adam's disobedience the many were "made sinners"; through Christ's obedience the many will be "made righteous." The question is what "made sinners" means. Chrysostom raises the question himself, and answers it: St John Chrysostom Homily 10 on Romans (on 5:19) "For the fact that when he had sinned and become mortal, those who were of him should be so also, is nothing unlikely. But how would it follow that from his disobedience another would become a sinner? For at this rate a man of this sort will not even deserve punishment, if, that is, it was not from his own self that he became a sinner.

What then does the word sinners mean here? To me it seems to mean liable to punishment and condemned to death." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Cyril of Alexandria, the great Coptic Father, explained the same verse by speaking of our nature rather than our guilt: St Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Romans (on 5:18–19) Cyril says that human nature "fell sick" with sin through the disobedience of one man, Adam. The many were made sinners, he says, not because they transgressed together with Adam, for they did not yet exist, but because they share his nature, which fell under the law of sin. In Christ that nature is healed and made new. Coptic Pope & Church Father PARAPHRASE The Western Answer Calvin is often said to teach that we are guilty of Adam's act. His own words are more careful.

He grounds our condemnation in the corruption we inherit, which he calls truly sin: John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 5:12) "There are indeed some who contend, that we are so lost through Adam's sin, as though we perished through no fault of our own, but only, because he had sinned for us. But Paul distinctly affirms, that sin extends to all who suffer its punishment... But to sin in this case, is to become corrupt and vicious; for the natural depravity which we bring, from our mother's womb, though it brings not forth immediately its own fruits, is yet sin before God, and deserves his vengeance: and this is that sin which they call original." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) John Calvin Institutes of the Christian Religion II.1.8 "Original sin, then, may be defined a hereditary corruption and depravity of our nature, extending to all the parts of the soul, which first makes us obnoxious to the wrath of God, and then produces in us works which in Scripture are termed works of the flesh." Reformer VERBATIM · BEVERIDGE TRANSLATION (1845) Augsburg Confession (1530)

Augsburg Confession, Article II "Also they teach that, after Adam's fall, all men begotten after the common course of nature are born with sin; that is, without the fear of God, without trust in him, and with fleshly appetite; and that this disease, or original fault, is truly sin, condemning and bringing eternal death now also upon all that are not born again by baptism and the Holy Spirit." Lutheran Confession VERBATIM · AUGSBURG CONFESSION, SCHAFF Westminster Confession (1646) Westminster Confession of Faith VI.3 "They being the root of all mankind, the guilt of this sin was imputed, and the same death in sin and corrupted nature conveyed to all their posterity descending from them by ordinary generation." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · WESTMINSTER CONFESSION, SCHAFF The Greek Fathers We inherit mortality, corruption and a nature weakened and inclined to passion. We are not guilty of Adam's personal act. Each person becomes guilty by his own sins, which grow in the soil of death. Augustine All sinned in Adam.

We inherit both his guilt and a corrupted nature, so that even infants are under condemnation until baptised. Reformed and Lutheran We inherit a corruption of our whole nature that is itself truly sin and deserves God's wrath. Westminster adds that Adam's guilt is also imputed to all his descendants. Notice where the real line falls. Everyone agrees that we inherit death and a damaged nature. The question is whether that inheritance is itself guilt before God. Ezekiel 18:20 says, "The son shall not bear the guilt of the father." The Greek Fathers read Romans 5 in the light of that principle; the Western tradition read it as an exception to it. Calvin's own reasoning stands between the two: he denies that we are condemned for Adam's act as such, but holds that the corruption we inherit is already sin. The fuller treatment is on Original Sin .

VIII. Adam and Christ (5:15–21) Romans 5:15 "But the free gift is not like the offense. For if by the one man's offense many died, much more the grace of God and the gift by the grace of the one Man, Jesus Christ, abounded to many." Orthodox reading: The gift is not a mirror image of the fall. It is far greater. Romans 5:17 "For if by the one man's offense death reigned through the one, much more those who receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness will reign in life through the One, Jesus Christ." Orthodox reading: Those who receive grace do not merely escape death; they will reign in life. St John Chrysostom Homily 10 on Romans (on 5:17) "For we were at once freed from punishment, and put off all iniquity, and were also born again from above and rose again with the old man buried, and were redeemed, justified, led up to adoption, sanctified, made brothers of the Only-begotten, and joint heirs and of one Body with Him, and counted for His Flesh, and even as a Body with the Head, so were we united unto Him!" Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John

Chrysostom Homily 10 on Romans (on 5:17) "For Christ has paid down far more than we owe, yea as much more as the illimitable ocean is than a little drop." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Irenaeus, writing around AD 180, made this comparison the centre of his theology. Christ went back over the path of Adam and undid it, obedience for disobedience, the tree of the cross for the tree of Eden, and Mary's faith for Eve's unbelief: St Irenaeus of Lyons Against Heresies V.16.3 "...He clearly shows forth God Himself, whom indeed we had offended in the first Adam, when he did not perform His commandment. In the second Adam, however, we are reconciled, being made obedient even unto death." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION St Irenaeus of Lyons Against Heresies III.22.4 "And thus also it was that the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by the obedience of Mary.

For what the virgin Eve had bound fast through unbelief, this did the virgin Mary set free through faith." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 "For since by man came death, by Man also came the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ all shall be made alive." Orthodox reading: Paul's other Adam and Christ passage. In Adam all die; in Christ all shall be made alive. The contrast is death and resurrection. Romans 5:20-21 "Moreover the law entered that the offense might abound. But where sin abounded, grace abounded much more, so that as sin reigned in death, even so grace might reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." Orthodox reading: The law made sin plain and even increased it, but grace overflowed beyond it. For the Fathers, Romans 5 is above all good news about Christ. Whatever we inherit from Adam, what we can receive from Christ is "much more." That is why they could speak honestly about the wound without despair: the one who heals is greater than the one who wounded.

IX. Infants, Baptism and Original Sin If infants are not guilty of Adam's sin, why does the Church baptise them, and why does the Creed say "one baptism for the remission of sins"? This is the strongest argument on Augustine's side, and Orthodox readers should face it honestly. In 418 a council at Carthage, led by African bishops including Augustine, condemned the Pelagians in a series of canons. One of them reads: Council of Carthage (418) African Code, Canon 110 "Likewise it seemed good that whosoever denies that infants newly from their mother's wombs should be baptized, or says that baptism is for remission of sins, but that they derive from Adam no original sin, which needs to be removed by the laver of regeneration... let him be anathema." Regional Council VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION These canons were later received into the canon law of the Byzantine Church through the Council in Trullo (692), a council the Oriental Orthodox do not recognise.

Eastern Orthodox writers usually explain the canon by saying that what infants "derive from Adam" and what baptism removes is the inherited condition of death, corruption and separation from God, rather than personal guilt. That explanation is not forced: the canon's target was the Pelagian claim that infants inherit nothing at all from Adam, a claim every Orthodox tradition also rejects. St John Chrysostom, preaching to people about to be baptised, gave the Greek answer to the question directly: St John Chrysostom Baptismal Instruction 3.6 (quoted by Augustine, Against Julian I.6) Chrysostom says that the Church baptises infants although they have no sins, so that they may receive what baptism gives besides forgiveness: holiness, righteousness, adoption, inheritance, brotherhood with Christ, and becoming members of His body and temples of the Holy Spirit. Church Father PARAPHRASE Augustine knew this passage and argued that Chrysostom meant only that infants have no sins of their own. The editors of the Oxford translation of Chrysostom's homilies on Romans took the same view.

Both readings are possible; what is clear is that Chrysostom treats infant baptism as the gift of new life in Christ, not chiefly as the removal of guilt. Infants Who Die Unbaptised The difference shows most clearly here. Augustine concluded that unbaptised infants are condemned, though with the mildest punishment: St Augustine of Hippo Enchiridion 93 "And, of course, the mildest punishment of all will fall upon those who have added no actual sin, to the original sin they brought with them..." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Gregory the Theologian, speaking of those who could not receive baptism "on account of infancy, or some perfectly involuntary circumstance," reached a different conclusion: St Gregory of Nazianzus Oration 40, On Holy Baptism 23 "...the third will be neither glorified nor punished by the righteous Judge, as unsealed and yet not wicked, but persons who have suffered rather than done wrong." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Calvin, for his part, said that infants "bring their condemnation with them from their mother's womb," though he

also taught that the children of believers are within the covenant. The Orthodox Church does not teach that infants who die unbaptised are condemned. She commends them to the mercy of God, baptises infants because she wants them to have the life of Christ from the start, and does not claim to know more than God has revealed.

X. Death as a Mercy One striking teaching of the Fathers on Romans 5 is that death, though the wage of sin, is also a mercy. God did not want sin to become immortal in us. St Irenaeus of Lyons Against Heresies III.23.6 "...because He pitied him, [and did not desire] that he should continue a sinner for ever, nor that the sin which surrounded him should be immortal, and evil interminable and irremediable. But He set a bound to his [state of] sin, by interposing death, and thus causing sin to cease..." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Chrysostom, asked why all should become mortal through one man, says that the question is best answered by looking at what God has done with death: St John Chrysostom Homily 10 on Romans (on 5:19) "That we are so far from taking any harm from this death and condemnation, if we be sober-minded, that we are the gainers even by having become mortal, first, because it is not an immortal body in which we sin; secondly, because we get numberless grounds for being religious." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 10 on

Romans (on 5:19) "For it is from hence that the crowns of the martyrs come, and the rewards of the Apostles." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION This is why Orthodox funeral hymns can be full of sorrow and full of hope at once. Death is an enemy, the last enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), but Christ has turned it into a passage. "By death He trampled down death" is sung at every Pascha.

XI. Objections Answered "Romans 5:12 says all sinned in Adam. The Orthodox simply deny the text." OO Response: The Greek says death spread to all "because all sinned" ( eph᾽ hō ). The rendering "in whom" comes from the old Latin, and almost all modern Bibles, including Protestant ones, translate "because." The Orthodox are reading the text as most scholars now read it. That said, the Orthodox do not deny that Adam's sin affects us all. Paul says through one man's offence many died and many were made sinners. The disagreement is about how: by inheriting guilt, or by inheriting death and a wounded nature out of which we all sin. "If we do not inherit Adam's guilt, we do not need a Saviour until we sin personally." OO Response: We need a Saviour from death and corruption as much as from guilt. Paul's argument in Romans 5 is about the reign of death (5:14, 17, 21), and Christ came to destroy "him who had the power of death" (Hebrews 2:14). Every human being is born under that reign. And every human being who lives long enough does in fact sin (3:23).

The Orthodox have never taught that anyone could live without sin and so without Christ. The Theotokos herself called God "my Saviour" (Luke 1:47). "Psalm 51:5 proves that infants are born guilty." OO Response: David says he was brought forth in iniquity and conceived in sin. The Fathers read this as describing the sinful condition into which every human being is born, and some as referring to the circumstances of conception in a fallen world. A poetic confession of how deep sin goes is not a doctrinal statement about the legal guilt of newborns. Ezekiel 18:20 is a doctrinal statement, and it says the son does not bear the father's guilt. "Infant baptism "for the remission of sins" only makes sense if infants are guilty." OO Response: Baptism is far more than forgiveness. It is new birth, union with Christ's death and resurrection, adoption and the gift of the Spirit. Chrysostom says infants are baptised to receive all of these.

And what baptism remits in an infant is the inheritance from Adam, the separation from God and the reign of death, which every Orthodox tradition holds is real. Whether to call that inheritance "sin" is partly a question of words. Whether to call it personal guilt is the real question, and there the Greek Fathers say no. "The Orthodox view is just Pelagianism." OO Response: Pelagius taught that Adam harmed us only by bad example and that a person can live without sin by his own powers. The Orthodox reject both. We inherit death and corruption, our nature is wounded, and no one is saved without grace. The Council of Ephesus in 431, which the Oriental Orthodox honour as the third Ecumenical Council, confirmed the condemnation of Celestius, Pelagius's leading follower. Rejecting inherited guilt is not the same as rejecting the fall.

XII. FAQ Do the Orthodox use the term "original sin"? Some do and some do not. Many Eastern Orthodox writers prefer "ancestral sin" to avoid the Augustinian idea of inherited guilt. Coptic and other Oriental Orthodox teaching often uses "original sin," and baptises for its remission. What matters is the meaning, and on the central point the Orthodox are agreed: Adam's fall brought death and corruption on the whole race, and Christ alone delivers us from it. What about the Immaculate Conception? The Roman Catholic doctrine that Mary was preserved from original sin from her conception assumes the Augustinian view that original sin includes inherited guilt. Since the Orthodox do not hold that infants inherit Adam's guilt, the doctrine is not needed, and the Orthodox do not accept it. They honour the Theotokos as all-holy because of her lifelong cooperation with grace. See Mary: Theotokos & Perpetual Virginity . Was there a real Adam? Paul treats Adam as a real man and the beginning of the human story, and so did the Fathers.

How Genesis relates to modern science is discussed on Creation & Evolution . Whatever position one takes there, the theological point of Romans 5 stands: humanity is one, and it fell away from God and needed a new head in Christ. Why did Augustine see things so differently? Partly the Latin text, partly the fight with Pelagius, who taught that people could live without sin by their own effort. Against that, Augustine stressed the depth of the fall and the absolute need of grace, and the Church agreed with him on that. The Greek Fathers, who were fighting different battles, especially against fatalism and the Manichees, stressed free will and the goodness of human nature. Both were defending real truths. What comes next? If grace abounds where sin abounded, should we go on sinning? Paul's answer is baptism: we died with Christ and rose with Him. That is Romans 6 .
