I. Introduction: Grace Is Not a Licence At the end of Romans 5 Paul said something daring: "where sin abounded, grace abounded much more." The obvious objection follows at once. If more sin means more grace, why not keep sinning? Paul's answer is one of the great baptismal passages of the New Testament. You cannot go on living in sin, he says, because you died to it. When? In baptism, where you were buried with Christ and raised with Him to walk in newness of life. Romans 6 is therefore where the question of what baptism is becomes unavoidable. Is it the place where God unites us to Christ's death and resurrection, or a sign that this has already happened by faith, or a public testimony of an inward change? Every major Christian tradition has an answer, and the answers differ more here than almost anywhere else. The Orthodox answer is the Fathers' answer, and it is the oldest. This page sets it out alongside Luther, Calvin, the Westminster Confession and the Baptist confessions, each in their own words.

Some Protestants, it turns out, say more about baptism than many of their followers today realise. "For Baptism is the Cross. What the Cross then, and Burial, is to Christ, that Baptism has been to us..." St John Chrysostom, Homily 10 on Romans This page is part of Romans with the Fathers , a series of nine pages that read St Paul's letter to the Romans section by section with the Church Fathers, setting their reading beside the main Protestant readings. Use the bar at the top of the page to move between the sections of the letter. A Note on Quotations Every quotation marked VERBATIM has been checked word for word against a public domain translation: St John Chrysostom's thirty-two Homilies on Romans and the other Fathers in the Ante-Nicene and Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series, John Calvin's Commentary on Romans in John Owen's translation (1849), and the Reformation confessions in Philip Schaff's Creeds of Christendom . Chrysostom's homilies follow J. B. Morris's translation as revised by W. H. Simcox, in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, volume 11.
Where a work has no public domain English translation, its teaching is summarised and marked PARAPHRASE . Scripture follows the NKJV.

II. Glossary of Terms Baptise βαπτίζω · baptizō To dip, plunge or immerse. Used of washing as well as of the Christian sacrament. Buried with συνθάπτω · synthaptō To be buried together with. Paul's word for what happens to us in baptism (6:4; Colossians 2:12). United, planted together σύμφυτος · symphytos Grown together, as a graft grows into a tree (6:5). The older English Bible has "planted together." Old man ὁ παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος · ho palaios anthrōpos The old self, the whole person as ruled by sin, crucified with Christ (6:6). Freed, justified δεδικαίωται · dedikaiōtai "He who has died has been freed from sin" (6:7). The Greek is the verb "justify," showing that for Paul justification includes liberation from sin's power. Reckon λογίζομαι · logizomai The same word as in Romans 4: count it so. Here, count yourselves dead to sin and alive to God (6:11). Instruments, weapons ὅπλα · hopla Tools or arms. Our bodily members can be weapons for sin or for righteousness (6:13). Holiness, sanctification ἁγιασμός · hagiasmos The process and fruit of being made holy (6:19, 22).
Wages ὀψώνια · opsōnia A soldier's ration pay. Sin pays its soldiers in death (6:23). Gift χάρισμα · charisma A free gift of grace. Eternal life is not wages but gift (6:23).

secs.h: III. Shall We Continue in Sin? (6:1–2)
secs.x: III. Shall We Continue in Sin? (6:1–2) Romans 6:1-2 "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? Certainly not! How shall we who died to sin live any longer in it?" Orthodox reading: Grace is not permission. The one who has died to sin cannot keep living in it. St John Chrysostom Homily 10 on Romans (on 6:1) "Since then he showed the greatness of the grace by the greatness of the sins it healed, and owing to this it seemed in the eyes of the unthinking to be an encouragement to sin (for if the reason, they would say, why greater grace was shown, was because we had done great sins, let us not give over sinning, that grace may be more displayed still), now that they might not say this or suspect it, see how he turns the objection back again." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION It is worth noticing that Paul had to answer this objection at all. A gospel of salvation by keeping the law would never be accused of encouraging sin. Paul's gospel was accused of it because it really did announce free grace to sinners.

secs.h: III. Shall We Continue in Sin? (6:1–2)
secs.x: The Orthodox, who stress the life of holiness, need to remember this; Protestants, who stress free grace, need to remember Paul's answer. Both are in the same chapter.

secs.h: IV. Buried with Him in Baptism (6:3–5)
secs.x: IV. Buried with Him in Baptism (6:3–5) Romans 6:3-4 "Or do you not know that as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? Therefore we were buried with Him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." Orthodox reading: Baptism unites us to Christ's death and burial, so that we may share His resurrection life now and walk in it. Romans 6:5-7 "For if we have been united together in the likeness of His death, certainly we also shall be in the likeness of His resurrection, knowing this, that our old man was crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be done away with, that we should no longer be slaves of sin. For he who has died has been freed from sin." Orthodox reading: We have been grown together with Him in a death like His. The old self was crucified so that sin's power over us might be broken. St John Chrysostom Homily 10 on Romans (on 6:3–4) "What does being baptized into His Death mean? That it is with a view to our dying as He did.

secs.h: IV. Buried with Him in Baptism (6:3–5)
secs.x: For Baptism is the Cross. What the Cross then, and Burial, is to Christ, that Baptism has been to us, even if not in the same respects. For He died Himself and was buried in the Flesh, but we have done both to sin." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 10 on Romans (on 6:4) "For both the one and the other is a death, but not of the same subject; since the one is of the Flesh, that of Christ; the other of sin, which is our own. As then that is real, so is this. But if it be real, then what is of our part again must be contributed." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 10 on Romans (on 6:4) "When then the fornicator becomes chaste, the covetous man merciful, the harsh subdued, even here a resurrection has taken place, the prelude to the other." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Two things stand out in Chrysostom. First, the death in baptism is "real," as real in its own way as Christ's death on the cross.

secs.h: IV. Buried with Him in Baptism (6:3–5)
secs.x: Second, because it is real, "what is of our part again must be contributed." Baptism is God's act, and it calls for a life that matches it. That is the Orthodox view of baptism in two sentences.

V. What Does Baptism Do? Here are the main Christian answers, each in its own words. Luther Martin Luther Small Catechism (1529), On Baptism: "What does Baptism give?" "It worketh forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives everlasting salvation to all who believe, as the Word and promise of God declare." Reformer VERBATIM · LUTHER'S SMALL CATECHISM, SCHAFF Calvin John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 6:3) "...for it is beyond any question, that we put on Christ in baptism, and that we are baptized for this end, that we may be one with him." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 6:4) "...the death of Christ is efficacious to destroy and demolish the depravity of our flesh, and his resurrection, to effect the renovation of a better nature, and that by baptism we are admitted into a participation of this grace...

for we never have naked and empty symbols, except when our ingratitude and wickedness hinder the working of divine beneficence." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Westminster The Westminster Confession calls baptism "a sacrament of the New Testament," and goes on: Westminster Confession (1646) Westminster Confession of Faith XXVIII.1 "...ordained by Jesus Christ, not only for the solemn admission of the party baptized into the visible Church, but also to be unto him a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, of his ingrafting into Christ, of regeneration, of remission of sins, and of his giving up unto God, through Jesus Christ, to walk in newness of life..." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · WESTMINSTER CONFESSION, SCHAFF Westminster Confession (1646) Westminster Confession of Faith XXVIII.5–6 "Although it be a great sin to contemn or neglect this ordinance, yet grace and salvation are not so inseparably annexed unto it, as that no person can be regenerated or saved without it, or that all that are baptized are undoubtedly regenerated...

The efficacy of baptism is not tied to that moment of time wherein it is administered..." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · WESTMINSTER CONFESSION, SCHAFF The Baptists New Hampshire Baptist Confession (1833) New Hampshire Baptist Confession XIV "We believe that Christian Baptism is the immersion in water of a believer, into the name of the Father, and Son, and Holy Ghost; to show forth, in a solemn and beautiful emblem, our faith in the crucified, buried, and risen Saviour, with its effect in our death to sin and resurrection to a new life..." Baptist Confession VERBATIM · BAPTIST CONFESSION, SCHAFF Many Baptist and evangelical readers also argue that the "baptism" of Romans 6:3 is not water baptism at all but the baptism of the Spirit, by which every believer is joined to Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13). On that reading Romans 6 says nothing about the water. Orthodox Baptism is where God unites the believer to Christ's death and resurrection, forgives sins, gives new birth and the Holy Spirit (given in chrismation immediately after).

It is God's act, received in faith, and it must be lived out. Lutheran Baptism works forgiveness and new birth through the Word joined to the water, received by faith. Infants are baptised and regenerated. Reformed Baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant, and God really confers the grace it signifies on the elect, though not always at the moment of baptism and not to all who are baptised. Baptist and many evangelicals Baptism is an act of obedience and a public emblem of a salvation already received by faith. It is for believers only, by immersion. Read side by side, the Orthodox view has more in common with Luther, and even with Calvin's comment on Romans 6, than with the purely symbolic view that is now common in evangelical churches. The symbolic view has a harder time with Paul's language. Paul does not say baptism shows that we died with Christ; he says we were buried with Him "through baptism." More on this is on Infant Baptism and Salvation .

secs.h: VI. The Fathers on the Font
secs.x: VI. The Fathers on the Font From the first generation after the apostles, the Church spoke of baptism as the place of new birth. There is no early Christian writer who treats it as a mere symbol. Epistle of Barnabas Epistle of Barnabas 11 "This means, that we indeed descend into the water full of sins and defilement, but come up, bearing fruit in our heart, having the fear [of God] and trust in Jesus in our spirit." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION St Justin Martyr First Apology 61 "Then they are brought by us where there is water, and are regenerated in the same manner in which we were ourselves regenerated. For, in the name of God, the Father and Lord of the universe, and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, they then receive the washing with water.

secs.h: VI. The Fathers on the Font
secs.x: For Christ also said, Unless you be born again, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION The Mystagogical Lectures, given to the newly baptised in Jerusalem in the fourth century and traditionally ascribed to St Cyril of Jerusalem (some scholars think they are by his successor John), explain Romans 6 to people who had just come up from the water: St Cyril of Jerusalem Mystagogical Lecture 2.4 "And at the self-same moment you were both dying and being born; and that Water of salvation was at once your grave and your mother." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Cyril of Jerusalem Mystagogical Lecture 2.5 "O strange and inconceivable thing! We did not really die, we were not really buried, we were not really crucified and raised again; but our imitation was in a figure, and our salvation in reality.

secs.h: VI. The Fathers on the Font
secs.x: Christ was actually crucified, and actually buried, and truly rose again; and all these things He has freely bestowed upon us, that we, sharing His sufferings by imitation, might gain salvation in reality." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Cyril of Jerusalem Mystagogical Lecture 2.6 "Let no one then suppose that Baptism is merely the grace of remission of sins, or further, that of adoption; as John's was a baptism conferring only remission of sins: whereas we know full well, that as it purges our sins, and ministers to us the gift of the Holy Ghost, so also it is the counterpart of the sufferings of Christ." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Titus 3:5-7 "not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, whom He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, that having been justified by His grace we should become heirs according to the hope of eternal life." Orthodox reading: Saved not by works of righteousness we have done, but by God's

secs.h: VI. The Fathers on the Font
secs.x: mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. Acts 22:16 "And now why are you waiting? Arise and be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord." Orthodox reading: Ananias to Paul himself: be baptised and wash away your sins. Notice that Titus 3:5 puts "not by works" and "the washing of regeneration" side by side. For the Fathers there was no tension. Baptism is not a work we do to earn salvation; it is the place where God, in mercy, does the saving work. That is why baptism and "faith alone" were never set against each other in the early Church.

VII. Three Immersions The Coptic Church, like all the Orthodox Churches, baptises by three full immersions in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Fathers saw in this the three days of Christ in the tomb, and the burial of Romans 6:4 made visible. St Basil the Great On the Holy Spirit 15.35 "...the water receiving the body as in a tomb figures death, while the Spirit pours in the quickening power, renewing our souls from the deadness of sin unto their original life. This then is what it is to be born again of water and of the Spirit, the being made dead being effected in the water, while our life is wrought in us through the Spirit. In three immersions, then, and with three invocations, the great mystery of baptism is performed..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Cyril of Jerusalem Mystagogical Lecture 2.4 "...and you made that saving confession, and descended three times into the water, and ascended again; here also hinting by a symbol at the three days burial of Christ." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Is immersion required? The earliest

church order outside the New Testament, the Didache (late first or early second century), prefers running water and immersion but allows pouring when that is impossible: The Didache Didache 7 "...baptize into the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in living water. But if you have not living water, baptize into other water; and if you can not in cold, in warm. But if you have not either, pour out water thrice upon the head into the name of Father and Son and Holy Spirit." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION The Orthodox keep full immersion as the normal form, because it shows what Paul describes, while recognising that in real necessity, such as grave illness, the Church has always allowed exceptions. Here the Orthodox and the Baptists agree on the form, while disagreeing about who may be baptised and what baptism does. The Westminster Confession, by contrast, says that "dipping of the person into the water is not necessary."

VIII. The Old Man Crucified (6:6–11) Romans 6:8-11 "Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Him, knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, dies no more. Death no longer has dominion over Him. For the death that He died, He died to sin once for all; but the life that He lives, He lives to God. Likewise you also, reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord." Orthodox reading: Christ died to sin once and lives to God. In Him, we are to count ourselves dead to sin and alive to God. St John Chrysostom Homily 11 on Romans (on 6:6) "And he does not say is crucified, but is crucified with Him, so bringing baptism near to the Cross." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 11 on Romans (on 6:6) "...that the body of sin might be destroyed, not giving that name to this body of ours, but to all iniquity.

For as he calls the whole sum of wickedness the old man, thus again the wickedness which is made up of the different parts of iniquity he calls the body of that man." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 11 on Romans (on 6:7) "This he says of every man, that as he that is dead is henceforth freed from sinning, lying as a dead body, so must he that has come up from baptism, since he has died there once..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION In 6:7 Paul uses the verb "justify": literally, "he who has died has been justified from sin." Every English Bible translates it "freed," because that is what it means here. It is a small but important sign that for Paul justification is not only a verdict but a liberation, a point the Fathers never lost and that was discussed on Romans 3–4 . St John Chrysostom Homily 11 on Romans (on 6:11) "He well says, reckon, because there is no setting that, which he is speaking of, before the eyes as yet." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION

secs.h: IX. Not Under Law but Under Grace (6:12–14)
secs.x: IX. Not Under Law but Under Grace (6:12–14) Romans 6:12-14 "Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts. And do not present your members as instruments of unrighteousness to sin, but present yourselves to God as being alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God. For sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under law but under grace." Orthodox reading: Because we are under grace, sin no longer rules us. So we must not let it reign, but offer our bodies to God as instruments of righteousness. St John Chrysostom Homily 11 on Romans (on 6:12) "He does not say, let not the flesh live or act, but, let not sin reign, for He came not to destroy our nature, but to set our free choice aright." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 11 on Romans (on 6:14) "It is this; that our body, before Christ's coming, was an easy prey to the assaults of sin. For after death a great swarm of passions entered also. And for this cause it was not lightsome for running the race of virtue.

secs.h: IX. Not Under Law but Under Grace (6:12–14)
secs.x: For there was no Spirit present to assist, nor any baptism of power to mortify." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION This is the difference grace makes, in the Fathers' reading. The law told people what to do but gave no power to do it. Grace, given in baptism and by the Spirit, gives the power. "Under grace" does not mean free from God's commandments; it means freed to keep them. The body, which Paul does not despise, becomes an instrument of righteousness, which is one reason the Orthodox fast, bow, make the sign of the cross and pray with the body. See Fasting .

X. Slaves of Righteousness (6:15–22) Romans 6:15-18 "What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law but under grace? Certainly not! Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves slaves to obey, you are that one's slaves whom you obey, whether of sin leading to death, or of obedience leading to righteousness? But God be thanked that though you were slaves of sin, yet you obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine to which you were delivered. And having been set free from sin, you became slaves of righteousness." Orthodox reading: Everyone serves someone. Set free from sin, we have become slaves of righteousness, by obeying from the heart the teaching handed on to us. Romans 6:19 "I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members as slaves of uncleanness, and of lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves of righteousness for holiness." Orthodox reading: Paul calls for the same energy in holiness that was once given to sin.

Paul says they "obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine to which you were delivered" (6:17). The Greek speaks of a "pattern of teaching" into which they were handed over, the tradition received at baptism. For the Fathers this was the baptismal creed and catechesis, which is why the Church still teaches catechumens before baptism and has them confess the faith at the font. Freedom in Christ is not freedom from all masters, but freedom to serve the right one. Many Protestants rightly stress that sanctification is the fruit of justification. The Orthodox agree, and would add only that the two are not separate gifts but one life. Paul ends the paragraph: "you have your fruit to holiness, and the end, everlasting life" (6:22). Holiness is the road on which eternal life is reached.

secs.h: XI. The Wages and the Gift (6:23)
secs.x: XI. The Wages and the Gift (6:23) Romans 6:22-23 "But now having been set free from sin, and having become slaves of God, you have your fruit to holiness, and the end, everlasting life. For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." Orthodox reading: Sin pays wages, and they are death. God pays no wages; He gives eternal life as a gift in Christ. St John Chrysostom Homily 12 on Romans (on 6:23) "After speaking of the wages of sin, in the case of the blessings, he has not kept to the same order... for he does not say, the wages of good deeds, but the gift of God; to show, that it was not of themselves that they were freed, nor was it a due they received, neither yet a return, nor a recompense of labors, but by grace all these things came about." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 12 on Romans (on 6:23) "That these things then might not both make them rather listless, he inserted the part about strictness of life, using every opportunity of rousing the hearer to the practice of virtue." Church Father

secs.h: XI. The Wages and the Gift (6:23)
secs.x: VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Chrysostom holds the two together as always. Eternal life is a pure gift, "nor a recompense of labors." And because it is such a gift, Paul surrounds it with calls to holiness, so that no one treats it carelessly. This verse is a good place for Orthodox and Protestant readers to stand together: no one earns eternal life, and no one who has received it is free to despise it.

XII. Objections Answered "Romans 6 is about Spirit baptism, not water baptism." OO Response: Paul's readers had all been baptised in water, and he reminds them of it: "do you not know that as many of us as were baptized..." The early Church, from Barnabas and Justin to Cyril and Chrysostom, read Romans 6 as speaking of the font. No early writer separated a "Spirit baptism" from water baptism here. Water and Spirit belong together in the New Testament: "born of water and the Spirit" (John 3:5), "be baptized... and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:38). St Basil explains how: in the water the old life dies, and through the Spirit the new life is given. "If baptism saves, then salvation is by a work." OO Response: Baptism is not something we do for God but something God does to us. No one baptises himself.

Paul puts it in the passive: we "were baptized," we "were buried." Titus 3:5 calls it the washing of regeneration in the same breath as "not by works of righteousness which we have done." Luther made the same point against those who called baptism a human work: it is God's word and promise joined to the water, received by faith. "The thief on the cross was saved without baptism." OO Response: He was, and the Church has never denied it. He lived before Christian baptism was commanded (Matthew 28:19), and he confessed Christ at the moment of his death. The Fathers also recognised the "baptism of blood" of martyrs who died before they could be baptised, as St Cyril of Jerusalem says: "except only Martyrs, who even without the water receive the kingdom." God is not bound by the sacraments He has given, but we are. An exception God makes for one who could not be baptised does not give anyone who can be baptised a reason to refuse it.

"Many baptised people live as if nothing happened, so baptism cannot really do anything." OO Response: Paul wrote Romans 6 precisely because baptised people were in danger of going on in sin. A real gift can be neglected. Chrysostom: "As then that is real, so is this. But if it be real, then what is of our part again must be contributed." Calvin made a similar point: Scripture speaks of what baptism really is when it is rightly received, and we never have "naked and empty symbols, except when our ingratitude and wickedness hinder the working of divine beneficence." A gift ignored is still a gift. "Mark 16:16 is not even in the oldest manuscripts." OO Response: That is true: the longer ending of Mark (16:9–20) is missing from the two oldest complete Greek manuscripts, though it was known in the second century and is read in the Church. But the teaching of Mark 16:16 does not depend on it. John 3:5, Acts 2:38, Acts 22:16, Romans 6:3–4, Galatians 3:27, Titus 3:5 and 1 Peter 3:21 all say the same.

XIII. FAQ Why are infants baptised if Romans 6 talks about faith and walking in newness of life? Because baptism is God's gift, and God gives His gifts to children as well as adults, as He gave circumcision to infants in the old covenant. Children baptised in the Church are raised to walk in the life they received. The question is treated fully on Infant Baptism and touched on in Romans 5 . Can a person be baptised twice? No. Baptism is a death and resurrection with Christ, and Christ "dies no more" (6:9). The Creed confesses "one baptism." Someone who falls away and returns is restored through repentance and confession, not rebaptised. What is chrismation, and how does it relate to Romans 6? In the Orthodox Churches the newly baptised are immediately anointed with holy chrism (myron) for the gift of the Holy Spirit, and receive Holy Communion. Romans 6 speaks of dying and rising with Christ; Romans 8 speaks of the Spirit who dwells in us. In Orthodox practice the two are given together, as in Acts 2:38.

Does Romans 6 teach that Christians can live without sin? It teaches that sin no longer has the right to rule us and that we are given the power to resist it. It does not teach that Christians never sin; Paul's own struggle in Romans 7 and his warnings throughout show otherwise. The Orthodox life of repentance is the daily return to what baptism began. What comes next? If we are not under law but under grace, was the law bad? And why does Paul then describe the agony of wanting good and doing evil? That is Romans 7 .

XIV. pages.t: Romans 7: The Law & the Divided Self

secs.x: I. Introduction: The Most Personal Chapter Romans 7 is the most personal chapter Paul ever wrote, and perhaps the most argued over. "For what I will to do, that I do not practice; but what I hate, that I do... O wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?" Almost every Christian recognises himself in these words. The question is whether Paul meant them to describe the Christian. St John Chrysostom, and most of the Greek Fathers, read the chapter as a portrait of humanity under the law and before grace: a person who knows the good and delights in it, but has no power to do it until Christ comes. St Augustine read it that way too, at first, and then changed his mind and took it as the struggle of a mature Christian. Luther and Calvin followed the later Augustine, and the idea that the believer is "at once righteous and a sinner" grew partly from this chapter. The question is not academic.

It shapes how a Christian understands his own struggle with sin: as the normal and permanent state of the believer in this life, or as something that grace in Christ, given in Romans 8, really overcomes. This page lays out the readings fairly, including an Egyptian desert father who offers a third view, and shows why the Orthodox answer holds both the honesty of the struggle and the reality of the victory. "For I delight in it, and consent to it, and flee for refuge to it, yet still it had not the power of saving one who had fled to it. But Christ saved even one that fled from Him." St John Chrysostom, Homily 13 on Romans This page is part of Romans with the Fathers , a series of nine pages that read St Paul's letter to the Romans section by section with the Church Fathers, setting their reading beside the main Protestant readings. Use the bar at the top of the page to move between the sections of the letter.

A Note on Quotations Every quotation marked VERBATIM has been checked word for word against a public domain translation: St John Chrysostom's thirty-two Homilies on Romans and the other Fathers in the Ante-Nicene and Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series, John Calvin's Commentary on Romans in John Owen's translation (1849), and the Reformation confessions in Philip Schaff's Creeds of Christendom . Chrysostom's homilies follow J. B. Morris's translation as revised by W. H. Simcox, in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, volume 11. Where a work has no public domain English translation, its teaching is summarised and marked PARAPHRASE . Scripture follows the NKJV.

II. Glossary of Terms Law νόμος · nomos Usually the law of Moses, but in 7:21–25 Paul also speaks of a "law" in the sense of a ruling principle: "the law of sin" and "the law of my mind." Commandment ἐντολή · entolē A single command, here "You shall not covet" (7:7). Flesh σάρξ · sarx Not the body as such, but human nature as weak, mortal and open to sin. "In the flesh" means living apart from the Spirit (7:5). Carnal, fleshly σάρκινος · sarkinos Made of flesh, weak. "I am carnal, sold under sin" (7:14). Spiritual πνευματικός · pneumatikos Of the Spirit, from God. "The law is spiritual" (7:14). Desire, lust ἐπιθυμία · epithymia Strong desire, here wrong desire, coveting (7:7–8). Passions παθήματα · pathēmata "The sinful passions" (7:5). In the Orthodox ascetic tradition, the passions are disordered desires that the Christian struggles to heal. Inward man ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος · ho esō anthrōpos The inner self, mind and heart, which delights in God's law (7:22). Mind νοῦς · nous The mind or understanding.
In Orthodox spirituality, the nous is the eye of the soul, the place of prayer and the knowledge of God. Wretched ταλαίπωρος · talaipōros Miserable, distressed. "O wretched man that I am!" (7:24).

secs.h: III. Dead to the Law, Married to Christ (7:1–6)
secs.x: III. Dead to the Law, Married to Christ (7:1–6) Romans 7:1-3 "Or do you not know, brethren (for I speak to those who know the law), that the law has dominion over a man as long as he lives? For the woman who has a husband is bound by the law to her husband as long as he lives. But if the husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. So then if, while her husband lives, she marries another man, she will be called an adulteress; but if her husband dies, she is free from that law, so that she is no adulteress, though she has married another man." Orthodox reading: A law binds only while a person lives. When a husband dies, his wife is free to marry another. Romans 7:4 "Therefore, my brethren, you also have become dead to the law through the body of Christ, that you may be married to another—to Him who was raised from the dead, that we should bear fruit to God." Orthodox reading: Through Christ's body we died to the law, so that we might belong to another, the risen Christ, and bear fruit for God.

secs.h: III. Dead to the Law, Married to Christ (7:1–6)
secs.x: Romans 7:5-6 "For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions which were aroused by the law were at work in our members to bear fruit to death. But now we have been delivered from the law, having died to what we were held by, so that we should serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter." Orthodox reading: The law could stir up sinful passions but not heal them. Now we serve in the newness of the Spirit, not the oldness of the letter. Paul's image is a marriage. We were once bound to the law; through baptism into Christ's death (6:3–4), we died to it, and now we belong to Christ. The point is not that God's commandments no longer matter. The point is that we are no longer trying to be righteous by the law's power, which was never able to give life, but are joined to the living Christ, whose Spirit bears fruit in us. Chrysostom notices how careful Paul is not to insult the law even here. In the illustration it is the husband who dies, but in the application Paul says it is we who died to the law. He spares the law the indignity of being called dead.

IV. Is the Law Sin? (7:7–13) Romans 7:7 "What shall we say then? Is the law sin? Certainly not! On the contrary, I would not have known sin except through the law. For I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, 'You shall not covet.'" Orthodox reading: The law is not sin. It shows sin up for what it is. "You shall not covet" revealed the coveting already in the heart. Romans 7:9-11 "I was alive once without the law, but when the commandment came, sin revived and I died. And the commandment, which was to bring life, I found to bring death. For sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it killed me." Orthodox reading: Sin used the good commandment as a beachhead, and deceived and killed. Romans 7:12 "Therefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good." Orthodox reading: The law is holy, and the commandment holy, just and good.

St John Chrysostom Homily 13 on Romans (on 7:14) "For by calling it spiritual, he shows it to be a teacher of virtue and hostile to vice; for this is what being spiritual means, leading off from sin of every kind. And this the Law did do, by frightening, admonishing, chastening, correcting, recommending every kind of virtue. Whence then, was sin produced, if the teacher was so admirable? It was from the listlessness of its disciples." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Here Orthodox and Protestants stand together. The law of God is good. The fault lies in us, not in the commandment. Both traditions have had to resist people who despised the Old Testament or set Christ against the law, from Marcion in the second century onward. Jesus came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17). Where they differ in emphasis is the law's role after conversion. Lutheran theology especially stresses the law's work of showing sin and driving us to Christ. Reformed theology gives special weight to a "third use" of the law as a guide for the believer's life.
The Orthodox would say that the commandments, written now on the heart by the Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33), are the shape of the life of love, and are kept not by our own strength but by grace.

secs.h: V. The Flesh Is Not Evil
secs.x: V. The Flesh Is Not Evil Romans 7:18-20 "For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh) nothing good dwells; for to will is present with me, but how to perform what is good I do not find. For the good that I will to do, I do not do; but the evil I will not to do, that I practice. Now if I do what I will not to do, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me." Orthodox reading: "In my flesh nothing good dwells." Paul is describing what human nature can do left to itself, not condemning the body God made. In Chrysostom's day the Manichees taught that matter and the body were evil, the creation of an evil god. They loved Romans 7. Chrysostom answered them: St John Chrysostom Homily 13 on Romans (on 7:18) "For the fact that no good thing dwells in it, does not show that it is evil itself.

secs.h: V. The Flesh Is Not Evil
secs.x: Now we admit, that the flesh is not so great as the soul, and is inferior to it, yet not contrary, or opposed to it, or evil; but that it is beneath the soul, as a harp beneath a harper, and as a ship under the pilot." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 13 on Romans (on 7:23) "But such doctrines as these are not the Church's, for it is the sin only that she condemns; and both the Laws which God has given, both that of nature and that of Moses, she says are hostile to this, and not to the flesh; for the flesh she denies to be sin, for it is a work of God's, and one very useful too in order to virtue, if we live soberly." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 13 on Romans (on 7:14) "For in themselves they were not sin, but, when their extravagancy was unbridled, it wrought this effect.

secs.h: V. The Flesh Is Not Evil
secs.x: Thus (that I may take one of them and examine it as a specimen) desire is not sin: but when it has run into extravagance, being not minded to keep within the laws of marriage, but springing even upon other men's wives; then the thing henceforward becomes adultery, yet not by reason of the desire, but by reason of its exorbitancy." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION This is an important point of difference with the Augustinian and Reformation tradition. Augustine taught that concupiscence, disordered desire, remains in the baptised and can be called sin, because it comes from sin and inclines to it, though its guilt is taken away. The Lutheran and Reformed confessions go further: the Westminster Confession calls the remaining corruption and "all the motions thereof... truly and properly sin." Chrysostom says that the natural desires God gave are not sin; sin is their disorder and excess, when the will consents. The Orthodox ascetic tradition, which distinguishes carefully between a passing thought, consent and action, follows Chrysostom.

secs.h: 1. Humanity under the law: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: VI. Who Is the Wretched Man? (7:14–25) Romans 7:14 "For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin." Orthodox reading: "I am carnal, sold under sin." Paul now speaks in the present tense. Romans 7:15 "For what I am doing, I do not understand. For what I will to do, that I do not practice; but what I hate, that I do." Orthodox reading: Knowing the good and willing it, yet not doing it. Romans 7:22-23 "For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man. But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members." Orthodox reading: Delight in God's law in the inward man, and yet another law at war in the members. Romans 7:24-25 "O wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? I thank God—through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, with the mind I myself serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin." Orthodox reading: The cry for deliverance, and the answer: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ. 1.

secs.h: 1. Humanity under the law: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: Humanity under the law: St John Chrysostom Chrysostom says that with the words "but I am carnal" Paul begins "giving us a sketch now of man, as comporting himself in the Law, and before the Law." The "I" is Paul speaking for all who lived without the grace of Christ: St John Chrysostom Homily 13 on Romans (on 7:14) "For when he says, sold under sin, he means it not of those who were under the Law only, but of those who had lived before the Law also, and of men from the very first." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 13 on Romans (on 7:24) "Do you notice what a great thraldom that of vice is, in that it overcomes even a mind that delighted in the Law? For no one can rejoin, he means, that I hate the Law and abhor it, and so sin overcomes me. For I delight in it, and consent to it, and flee for refuge to it, yet still it had not the power of saving one who had fled to it. But Christ saved even one that fled from Him. See what a vast advantage grace has!" Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION 2.

secs.h: 1. Humanity under the law: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: The mature Christian: St Augustine (later), Luther, Calvin Augustine tells us himself that he changed his mind: St Augustine of Hippo Against Two Letters of the Pelagians I.22 "And it had once appeared to me also that the apostle was in this argument of his describing a man under the law. But afterwards I was constrained to give up the idea by those words where he says, Now, then, it is no more I that do it. For to this belongs what he says subsequently also: There is, therefore, now no condemnation to them that are in Christ Jesus." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Augustine of Hippo Against Two Letters of the Pelagians I.22 "...since this very delight in good, by which, moreover, he does not consent to evil, not from fear of penalty, but from love of righteousness...

secs.h: 1. Humanity under the law: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: can only be attributed to grace." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 7:15) "He now comes to a more particular case, that of a man already regenerated; in whom both the things which he had in view appear more clearly..." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Martin Luther Lectures on Romans (1515–1516) Luther reads Romans 7 as Paul speaking as a Christian, and finds in it the condition of every believer in this life: at the same time righteous and a sinner (simul iustus et peccator). He is righteous in God's sight because of Christ, and a sinner in himself, because the flesh still fights against the Spirit until death.

secs.h: 1. Humanity under the law: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: Reformer PARAPHRASE Westminster Confession (1646) Westminster Confession of Faith XIII.2 "This sanctification is throughout in the whole man, yet imperfect in this life; there abideth still some remnants of corruption in every part, whence ariseth a continual and irreconcilable war, the flesh lusting against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · WESTMINSTER CONFESSION, SCHAFF 3. The saints and their thoughts: Abba Theonas in Egypt St John Cassian, who learned the monastic life in the Egyptian desert, records a conference with Abba Theonas that takes a third path. Theonas agrees with Augustine that the passage describes holy people, not gross sinners, but he says the "evil" the saints cannot escape is not adultery or theft but the wandering of the mind away from God in prayer: St John Cassian (Abba Theonas) Conferences XXIII.1 "...these passages on the contrary plainly show that they cannot possibly fit the person of sinners, but that what is said can only apply to those that are perfect, and that it only suits the chastity of those who follow

secs.h: 1. Humanity under the law: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: the good example of the Apostles." Desert Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Cassian (Abba Theonas) Conferences XXIII.10 "For they feel that they cannot perform the good that they would, but are ever falling into the evil which they would not, and which they hate, i.e., wandering thoughts and care for carnal things." Desert Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Chrysostom and the Greek Fathers The "I" is humanity under the law and before grace, knowing the good but powerless to do it. Romans 8 describes the Christian, set free by the Spirit. Later Augustine, Luther, Calvin The "I" is the mature Christian, still fighting the remnants of sin. The believer is righteous in Christ and yet a sinner in himself until death. Abba Theonas (Cassian) The "I" is the saint, who no longer falls into grave sin but cannot yet hold his mind on God without distraction, and longs for perfect union with Him. Modern scholars are still divided. Since W. G. Kümmel's study of 1929, many have read the "I" as a rhetorical figure for humanity or Israel under the law, close to Chrysostom.

secs.h: 1. Humanity under the law: St John Chrysostom
secs.x: Others, such as C. E. B. Cranfield and James Dunn, defend the Christian reading. The strongest argument for the Christian view is the present tense and the delight in God's law. The strongest argument against it is that the man of 7:14 is "sold under sin," while the Christian of 6:18 has been "set free from sin," and that 8:2 says the Spirit "has made me free from the law of sin and death," using the very phrase of 7:23.

VII. Free Will in Romans 7 Does "what I will to do, that I do not practice" mean the will is enslaved and cannot choose? Chrysostom is careful to say no: St John Chrysostom Homily 13 on Romans (on 7:15) "Whence it appears that he says, that I would not, not as denying free will, or as adducing any constrained necessity. For if it was not willingly, but by compulsion, that we sinned, then the punishments that took place before would not be justifiable." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 13 on Romans (on 7:19–20) "Now the essence of the soul and body and of that choice are not the same, for the two first are God's works, and the other is a motion from ourselves towards whatever we please to direct it.

For willing is indeed natural, and is from God: but willing on this wise is our own, and from our own mind." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Calvin agrees that sin is voluntary and not compelled, but draws a stronger conclusion about the natural man: John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 7:14) "Compulsion I always except, for we sin spontaneously, as it would be no sin, were it not voluntary. But we are so given up to sin, that we can do willingly nothing but sin; for the corruption which bears rule within us thus drives us onward." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Both reject the idea that we sin under compulsion. The difference is whether fallen man can do anything but sin. Chrysostom's man in Romans 7 still "delights" in the good and hates the evil; his will is weak and overpowered, but not dead. Calvin's natural man "can do willingly nothing but sin." The Orthodox stand with Chrysostom: the will is wounded and cannot save itself, but it can still turn toward God when grace calls, and grace does not override it but heals it.
This is the ground of the discussion of Romans 9.

secs.h: VIII. The Struggle and the Victory
secs.x: VIII. The Struggle and the Victory Galatians 5:16-17 "I say then: Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, so that you do not do the things that you wish." Orthodox reading: The flesh and the Spirit are at war, in the Christian too. But the command is to walk in the Spirit, and the promise is that we will not fulfil the desires of the flesh. 1 John 1:8-9 "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." Orthodox reading: No Christian is sinless. But confession brings real forgiveness and real cleansing. Romans 8:1-2 "There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit.

secs.h: VIII. The Struggle and the Victory
secs.x: For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death." Orthodox reading: The answer to Romans 7 comes at once: no condemnation in Christ, and freedom from the law of sin and death through the Spirit. Whatever one decides about the "I" of Romans 7, every tradition agrees on two things. Christians still struggle with sin, and the answer is Christ. The difference is in what one expects of that struggle. The Orthodox tradition does not pretend the struggle ends at baptism. The Philokalia, the great collection of Orthodox writings on prayer, is largely about the war with thoughts and passions that Abba Theonas described. But it never treats defeat as normal. Its whole aim is healing: the passions can be quieted, the mind can be gathered in prayer, and the saints are living proof that grace really transforms.

secs.h: VIII. The Struggle and the Victory
secs.x: That is why Chrysostom insists that Romans 8, not Romans 7, is the picture of the Christian life: "the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free." The concern Orthodox readers have about "at once righteous and a sinner" is not that it is too honest about sin, but that, taken as a permanent description, it can make the victory of Romans 8 seem out of reach. The concern Protestants have about the Orthodox view is that it can make Christians anxious about their progress. Both concerns are worth hearing. The Orthodox answer is the Jesus Prayer: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner," prayed by people who are being made saints.

IX. Objections Answered "Paul uses the present tense, so he must be describing his life as an apostle." OO Response: Paul also uses the past tense in 7:7–13 ("I was alive once without the law") of a time he cannot literally remember, and Augustine himself first read the passage as describing humanity under the law. The present tense makes the picture vivid; it does not settle who is speaking. And the description does not fit what Paul says of Christians elsewhere. The Christian is "set free from sin" (6:18); the man of Romans 7 is "sold under sin" (7:14). The Holy Spirit, named some twenty times in Romans 8, is not named once in 7:14–25. "The Orthodox view leads to perfectionism, the idea that Christians can stop sinning." OO Response: The Orthodox pray "have mercy on me, a sinner" every day and go to confession for life. Abba Theonas, a saint of the Egyptian desert, insisted that even the holiest are not without sin. The Church does not teach sinless perfection in this life.

What she teaches is that grace really changes us, so that sin no longer rules (6:14) and the saints grow in holiness. That is not perfectionism; it is Romans 6 and 8. "If concupiscence is not sin, the Orthodox take sin too lightly." OO Response: Chrysostom says desire becomes sin "by reason of its exorbitancy," when it breaks out of God's order. The Orthodox ascetic writers are severe about thoughts and desires, teaching that a thought welcomed and entertained already defiles the heart (Matthew 5:28). The difference is that they do not call the bare natural desire, which God created, sin in itself. That protects the goodness of creation and the body, which Romans 7 is often misused to attack. "Augustine changed his mind after deeper study, so his later view should prevail." OO Response: Augustine changed his mind during the Pelagian controversy, when he needed to show that even the holiest Christians depend wholly on grace. That was a real truth, and the Orthodox affirm it.

But Chrysostom and the Greek tradition read Paul in his own language and never adopted the later Augustinian reading. A change of mind in the heat of controversy is not automatically the better reading, and Augustine's own first view remains a witness on the other side.

X. FAQ Was Paul himself a struggling sinner after his conversion? Paul calls himself the chief of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15) and says he disciplines his body lest he be disqualified (1 Corinthians 9:27). He knew struggle. But he also says, "I have fought the good fight" (2 Timothy 4:7) and "imitate me, just as I also imitate Christ" (1 Corinthians 11:1). The Fathers saw in him both humility and real holiness. How should an Orthodox Christian use Romans 7 in prayer? As the cry of every person who has tried to be good by his own strength and failed, and as the doorway to Romans 8. The right response to "O wretched man that I am!" is not despair but "I thank God, through Jesus Christ our Lord," followed by prayer, repentance, confession and the Eucharist, through which the Spirit gives life. What about the law today? Do Christians keep the law of Moses? Christians are not bound by the ceremonial law of Moses, such as circumcision and the food laws (Acts 15). The moral law, summed up in love of God and neighbour, is fulfilled in us by the Spirit (Romans 8:4; 13:8–10).

See Sabbath & the Lord's Day . What comes next? "There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus." Romans 8 is the answer to Romans 7: life in the Spirit, adoption, the groaning of creation and the love from which nothing can separate us. That is Romans 8 .
