I. Introduction: The Summit of Romans Romans 8 has been called the summit of the letter, and for good reason. It begins with "no condemnation" and ends with "nothing can separate us." In between, Paul speaks of the Holy Spirit more than in any other chapter he wrote: the Spirit who frees, dwells, gives life, makes us sons, prays in us and will raise our bodies. The whole creation waits, groaning, for what the Spirit is doing in the children of God. This chapter is the answer to Romans 7. The man who cried "O wretched man that I am!" now hears that the law of the Spirit of life has set him free. For the Orthodox, Romans 8 is the charter of the Christian life as the life of the Spirit, the life that the Fathers called theosis : becoming by grace what Christ is by nature. The chapter also contains two passages that divide Christians. Verses 29–30, the "golden chain" of foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification and glory, are a foundation of the Reformed doctrine of election. Verses 35–39, "nothing can separate us," are the classic text for the perseverance of the saints.

This page gives the Reformed reading in Calvin's and Westminster's words, and the Fathers' reading in theirs. "For what the Only-begotten was by Nature, this they also have become by grace." St John Chrysostom, Homily 15 on Romans This page is part of Romans with the Fathers , a series of nine pages that read St Paul's letter to the Romans section by section with the Church Fathers, setting their reading beside the main Protestant readings. Use the bar at the top of the page to move between the sections of the letter. A Note on Quotations Every quotation marked VERBATIM has been checked word for word against a public domain translation: St John Chrysostom's thirty-two Homilies on Romans and the other Fathers in the Ante-Nicene and Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series, John Calvin's Commentary on Romans in John Owen's translation (1849), and the Reformation confessions in Philip Schaff's Creeds of Christendom . Chrysostom's homilies follow J. B. Morris's translation as revised by W. H. Simcox, in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, volume 11.
Where a work has no public domain English translation, its teaching is summarised and marked PARAPHRASE . Scripture follows the NKJV.

II. Glossary of Terms Condemnation κατάκριμα · katakrima The sentence of judgement. "There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus" (8:1). Spirit πνεῦμα · pneuma In Romans 8, chiefly the Holy Spirit, named about twenty times, the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ (8:9). Righteous requirement δικαίωμα · dikaiōma What the law rightly demands. It is "fulfilled in us" who walk by the Spirit (8:4). Adoption υἱοθεσία · huiothesia Being made a son. We become by grace children of the Father in the Son (8:15, 23). Abba ἀββά · abba Aramaic for "Father," the word Christ used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), now on the lips of the baptised (8:15). Glorify δοξάζω · doxazō To share in God's glory. The goal of the whole chain of 8:30. Futility, vanity ματαιότης · mataiotēs Emptiness, frustration. Creation was subjected to it because of human sin (8:20). Corruption φθορά · phthora Decay and death. Creation will be freed from its bondage (8:21). Foreknow προγινώσκω · proginōskō To know beforehand.

Whether this means God's foreseeing or His loving choice is a key question (8:29). Predestine προορίζω · proorizō To mark out beforehand. Here, to be conformed to the image of the Son (8:29). Theosis θέωσις · theōsis Deification: sharing by grace in God's own life (2 Peter 1:4), the goal of salvation in Orthodox teaching.

III. No Condemnation (8:1–4) Romans 8:1-2 "There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death." Orthodox reading: In Christ there is no condemnation, because the Spirit has done what the law could not: set us free from the law of sin and death. Romans 8:3-4 "For what the law could not do in that it was weak through the flesh, God did by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, on account of sin: He condemned sin in the flesh, that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit." Orthodox reading: God condemned sin in the flesh of His Son, so that the law's righteous requirement might be fulfilled in us, not only counted to us.

St John Chrysostom Homily 13 on Romans (on 8:1) "Then as the fact that many fall into sin even after baptism presented a difficulty, he consequently hastened to meet it, and says not merely to them that are in Christ Jesus, but adds, who walk not after the flesh; so showing that all afterward comes of our listlessness. For now we have the power of walking not after the flesh, but then it was a difficult task." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 13 on Romans (on 8:4) "What means this word, righteousness? Why, the end, the scope, the well-doing. For what was its design, and what did it enjoin? To be without sin. This then is made good to us now through Christ. And the making a stand against it, and the getting the better of it, came from Him. But it is for us to enjoy the victory." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION "Fulfilled in us" is the key phrase. Many Protestants read 8:4 as the law fulfilled for us by Christ and credited to us. Chrysostom reads it as the law's aim, a life free from sin, now made possible in us by Christ and the Spirit.

Both are true in their way: Christ fulfilled the law, and the Spirit fulfils it in those who walk by Him. The Orthodox insist on the second as much as the first. Chrysostom's reading of 8:1 also answers a pastoral question. If Christians still sin after baptism, is there condemnation after all? He says the "no condemnation" belongs to those "who walk not after the flesh," and that the power to walk so is now given. Sin after baptism comes not from a lack of grace but from neglect of it, and it is healed by repentance.

secs.h: IV. The Spirit Who Dwells in You (8:5–13)
secs.x: IV. The Spirit Who Dwells in You (8:5–13) Romans 8:9-11 "But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. Now if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not His. And if Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit who dwells in you." Orthodox reading: To belong to Christ is to have His Spirit. The same Spirit who raised Jesus will give life to our mortal bodies. Romans 8:12-13 "Therefore, brethren, we are debtors—not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live." Orthodox reading: A warning to believers: living by the flesh leads to death; putting to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit leads to life.

secs.h: IV. The Spirit Who Dwells in You (8:5–13)
secs.x: Romans 8:9 is a striking verse for the doctrine of the Trinity: the same Spirit is called "the Spirit of God" and "the Spirit of Christ," and having the Spirit is the same as Christ being in you (8:10). St Basil built his defence of the Spirit's divinity partly on texts like this. In the Orthodox Church the newly baptised are anointed with holy chrism for the gift of the Spirit, so that from the beginning of their Christian life Romans 8:9 is true of them. Verse 11 also shows that salvation includes the body. The Spirit who dwells in us now is the pledge that our bodies will be raised. That is why the Church honours the bodies of the saints and why Orthodox spirituality is never merely "spiritual" in the sense of ignoring the body. Verse 13 deserves notice. It is addressed to "brethren," believers, and it is conditional: "if you live according to the flesh you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live." The Spirit does the work; we cooperate with Him in putting sin to death. That is synergy in a single verse.

secs.h: V. Sons and Heirs: Adoption and Theosis (8:14–17)
secs.x: V. Sons and Heirs: Adoption and Theosis (8:14–17) Romans 8:14-17 "For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption by whom we cry out, 'Abba, Father.' The Spirit Himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God, and if children, then heirs—heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with Him, that we may also be glorified together." Orthodox reading: By the Spirit we are made sons of God and cry "Abba, Father." We are heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if we suffer with Him. St John Chrysostom Homily 14 on Romans (on 8:15) "Now what is this? That we cry, Abba, Father. And how great this is, the initiated know... being with good reason bidden to use this word first in the Prayer of the initiated." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 14 on Romans (on 8:15) "But we all, priests and laymen, rulers and ruled, are ordered to pray herein.

secs.h: V. Sons and Heirs: Adoption and Theosis (8:14–17)
secs.x: And this is the first language we give utterance to, after those marvellous throes, and that strange and unusual mode of labor." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Chrysostom is describing the ancient practice: the Lord's Prayer was taught to catechumens just before baptism, and the first time they prayed "Our Father" with the faithful was right after it, the "marvellous throes" of new birth. To call God Father is the privilege of the baptised. The Fathers saw in adoption the heart of salvation. The eternal Son became a son of man so that we might become sons of God: St Irenaeus of Lyons Against Heresies III.19.1 "For it was for this end that the Word of God was made man, and He who was the Son of God became the Son of man, that man, having been taken into the Word, and receiving the adoption, might become the son of God.

secs.h: V. Sons and Heirs: Adoption and Theosis (8:14–17)
secs.x: For by no other means could we have attained to incorruptibility and immortality, unless we had been united to incorruptibility and immortality." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION St Athanasius of Alexandria On the Incarnation 54 "For He was made man that we might be made God; and He manifested Himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father..." Coptic Pope & Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Basil the Great On the Holy Spirit 9.23 "...abiding in God, the being made like to God, and, highest of all, the being made God." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION 2 Peter 1:4 "by which have been given to us exceedingly great and precious promises, that through these you may be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust." Orthodox reading: Partakers of the divine nature: the scriptural root of the Fathers' language of deification. "Made God" does not mean we become God by nature or cease to be creatures.

secs.h: V. Sons and Heirs: Adoption and Theosis (8:14–17)
secs.x: It means sharing by grace in the life, glory and incorruption of God, as iron in the fire glows with the fire's heat without becoming fire. Many Protestants are uneasy with the language, but the substance is in Romans 8 itself: sons of God, heirs of God, conformed to the image of the Son, glorified. See Theosis & Deification . Note also the condition in 8:17: "if indeed we suffer with Him, that we may also be glorified together." Glory comes by way of the cross. That is why the Orthodox life includes fasting, ascetic struggle and patience in suffering, not as a way of earning adoption, but as the path the adopted children walk with their Brother.

VI. The Groaning Creation (8:18–25) Romans 8:18 "For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." Orthodox reading: Present sufferings are nothing compared with the coming glory. Romans 8:19-21 "For the earnest expectation of the creation eagerly waits for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it in hope; because the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God." Orthodox reading: Creation was subjected to futility because of human sin, and it waits to be set free into the glorious liberty of God's children. Romans 8:22-23 "For we know that the whole creation groans and labors with birth pangs together until now.

Not only that, but we also who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, eagerly waiting for the adoption, the redemption of our body." Orthodox reading: Creation groans like a woman in labour, and so do we, waiting for the redemption of our bodies. St John Chrysostom Homily 14 on Romans (on 8:20) "What is the meaning of, the creation was made subject to vanity? Why that it became corruptible. For what cause, and on what account? On account of you, O man. For since you have taken a body mortal and liable to suffering, the earth too has received a curse, and brought forth thorns and thistles." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 14 on Romans (on 8:21) "For neither do they that dwell therein, mankind, that is, undergo such an one, but a temporary one, and through it they are changed into an incorruptible state, and so therefore will the creature be." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St Irenaeus of Lyons Against Heresies V.32.1 "It is fitting, therefore, that the creation itself, being restored to its primeval

condition, should without restraint be under the dominion of the righteous; and the apostle has made this plain in the Epistle to the Romans..." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Revelation 21:5 "Then He who sat on the throne said, 'Behold, I make all things new.' And He said to me, 'Write, for these words are true and faithful.'" Orthodox reading: The end of the story is not escape from creation but its renewal. Here Orthodox and most Protestants agree: salvation is not only of souls but of the whole creation, and the Christian hope is the resurrection of the body in a renewed world, not a disembodied heaven. The Orthodox express this in the blessing of water at Theophany, of fields, homes and food, and in the icons, where matter shows forth grace. Creation is waiting for us to become what God made us to be.

secs.h: VII. The Spirit Who Prays in Us (8:26–27)
secs.x: VII. The Spirit Who Prays in Us (8:26–27) Romans 8:26-27 "Likewise the Spirit also helps in our weaknesses. For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit Himself makes intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. Now He who searches the hearts knows what the mind of the Spirit is, because He makes intercession for the saints according to the will of God." Orthodox reading: We do not know how to pray as we should, but the Spirit intercedes for us according to God's will. St John Chrysostom Homily 14 on Romans (on 8:26) "God did in those days give to all that were baptized certain excellent gifts, and the name that these had was spirits... And with all these there was also a gift of prayer, which also was called a spirit, and he that had this prayed for all the people. For since we are ignorant of much that is profitable for us and ask things that are not profitable, the gift of prayer came into some particular person of that day..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Chrysostom connects 8:26 with the spiritual gifts of the apostolic age.

secs.h: VII. The Spirit Who Prays in Us (8:26–27)
secs.x: Later Orthodox writers, especially in the tradition of prayer of the heart, saw in it the work of the Spirit in every Christian who prays: the aim of prayer is that the Spirit Himself should pray in us, so that our own words give way to His "groanings which cannot be uttered." St Seraphim of Sarov famously said that the goal of the Christian life is the acquisition of the Holy Spirit. Romans 8 is where that teaching begins.

secs.h: VIII. All Things Work Together for Good (8:28)
secs.x: VIII. All Things Work Together for Good (8:28) Romans 8:28 "And we know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are the called according to His purpose." Orthodox reading: God works all things, even suffering, for the good of those who love Him and are called according to His purpose. Whose purpose? Most translations add "His," and Calvin understood it as God's eternal purpose of election. Chrysostom, reading the Greek "according to purpose," took it to include the purpose of those who are called, their willing response: St John Chrysostom Homily 15 on Romans (on 8:28) "The purpose he here mentions, however, that he might not ascribe everything to the calling; since in this way both Greeks and Jews would be sure to cavil. For if the calling alone were sufficient, how came it that all were not saved? Hence he says, that it is not the calling alone, but the purpose of those called too, that works the salvation. For the calling was not forced upon them, nor compulsory.

secs.h: VIII. All Things Work Together for Good (8:28)
secs.x: All then were called, but all did not obey the call." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 8:28) "The word purpose distinctly excludes whatever is imagined to be adduced mutually by men; as though Paul had denied, that the causes of our election are to be sought anywhere else, except in the secret good pleasure of God..." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Calvin also notes that 8:28 is chiefly about suffering: God turns the afflictions of His people to their salvation. Chrysostom says the same. On that, there is no disagreement. The disagreement is whether God's calling is a call that all may answer, so that the difference between the saved and the lost lies partly in their response, or a call that is effective only in those God has chosen, so that the difference lies in God's choice alone.

IX. Foreknew, Predestined, Called (8:29–30) Romans 8:29-30 "For whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, that He might be the firstborn among many brethren. Moreover whom He predestined, these He also called; whom He called, these He also justified; and whom He justified, these He also glorified." Orthodox reading: God's plan reaches from eternity to glory: foreknown, predestined to be conformed to the Son, called, justified, glorified. St John Chrysostom Homily 15 on Romans (on 8:29) "See what superb honor! For what the Only-begotten was by Nature, this they also have become by grace." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 15 on Romans (on 8:30) "Now He justified them by the regeneration of the laver.

And whom He justified, them He also glorified by the gift, by the adoption." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION For Calvin, "foreknew" means far more than foresight: John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 8:29) "But the foreknowledge of God, which Paul mentions, is not a bare prescience, as some unwise persons absurdly imagine, but the adoption by which he had always distinguished his children from the reprobate." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) St John of Damascus, summing up the Greek Fathers, distinguishes what God foreknows from what He predetermines: St John of Damascus Exposition of the Orthodox Faith II.30 "We ought to understand that while God knows all things beforehand, yet He does not predetermine all things. For He knows beforehand those things that are in our power, but He does not predetermine them.

For it is not His will that there should be wickedness nor does He choose to compel virtue." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John of Damascus Exposition of the Orthodox Faith II.30 "Bear in mind, too, that virtue is a gift from God implanted in our nature, and that He Himself is the source and cause of all good, and without His co-operation and help we cannot will or do any good thing." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The Fathers God foreknows who will respond to His call and predestines them to be conformed to His Son. His call goes to all; it is not forced. Every good comes from His grace, but His grace does not compel. Reformed "Foreknew" means God's prior loving choice of particular people. Those He chose He will certainly call, justify and glorify. The cause of election is God's good pleasure alone, not anything foreseen in us. Notice two things. First, Paul's goal in 8:29 is conformity to Christ, the image of the Son, which is what the Fathers mean by theosis.

Predestination in Romans 8 is predestination to holiness and glory, not a bare decree about destinations. Second, Chrysostom reads "justified" in 8:30 as baptism, "the regeneration of the laver," which connects this chain to Romans 6 . The full argument over election is the subject of Romans 9 .

X. Nothing Can Separate Us (8:31–39) Romans 8:31-32 "What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all, how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things?" Orthodox reading: If God gave His own Son, He will give us all things with Him. Romans 8:33-34 "Who shall bring a charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, and furthermore is also risen, who is even at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us." Orthodox reading: No one can accuse or condemn those whom God justifies and for whom Christ intercedes. Romans 8:35-37 "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written: 'For Your sake we are killed all day long; We are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.' Yet in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us." Orthodox reading: No suffering can separate us from Christ's love.

In all these things we are more than conquerors. Romans 8:38-39 "For I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor depth, nor any other created thing, shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Orthodox reading: Nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ. For Reformed Christians this is the great text of assurance and the perseverance of the saints: John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 8:38) "This declaration is clearly against the schoolmen, who idly talk and say, that no one is certain of final perseverance, except through the gift of special revelation, which they make to be very rare. By such a dogma the whole faith is destroyed, which is certainly nothing, except it extends to death and beyond death.

But we, on the contrary, ought to feel confident, that he who has begun in us a good work, will carry it on until the day of the Lord Jesus." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Westminster Confession (1646) Westminster Confession of Faith XVII.1 "They whom God hath accepted in his Beloved, effectually called and sanctified by his Spirit, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace; but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · WESTMINSTER CONFESSION, SCHAFF Chrysostom reads the passage as a hymn of love, and notices that Paul lists only things outside us: St John Chrysostom Homily 15 on Romans (on 8:35) "For he does not mention the things that we are daily getting taken by, love of money and desire of glory and the thraldom of anger, but things that are far more enthralling than these, and of power to put a force upon nature itself..." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 15 on Romans (on 8:38–39) "These are great things here mentioned.

But the reason we do not enter into them is, because we have not so great love." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 15 on Romans (on 8:39) "...even if there were any other creation as great as the visible, and as great as the intelligible, none of them could part me from that love." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION The Orthodox read these verses with great joy and great confidence. No power in heaven or earth, no suffering, no demon, nothing outside us can tear us from God's love. That is real assurance. What the Orthodox do not draw from the passage is the doctrine that a believer cannot himself turn away. Paul's list is of external forces; he does not say "nor our own will." Elsewhere he warns believers that they can fall (Romans 11:20–22; 1 Corinthians 10:12; Galatians 5:4), and in this very chapter he says "if you live according to the flesh you will die" (8:13). God will never let go of us; we must not let go of Him. See Assurance of Salvation .

XI. Objections Answered ""No condemnation" means a Christian can never be condemned, whatever he does." OO Response: Paul says no condemnation "to those who are in Christ Jesus," and describes them as those who "do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit" (8:4; the text Chrysostom read, followed by the NKJV, has the same words in 8:1 as well). The same chapter warns believers that living by the flesh leads to death (8:13). The promise is total and true for all who abide in Christ. It is not a guarantee for someone who abandons Him. Chrysostom: "all afterward comes of our listlessness." "The golden chain of 8:30 proves that everyone called is certainly glorified, so salvation cannot be lost." OO Response: The chain describes God's purpose and how it unfolds for those who love Him (8:28). It is written to encourage believers in suffering, not to answer whether a believer can fall away, a question Paul answers elsewhere (Romans 11:22). Chrysostom, who read the chain as joyfully as any Calvinist, also said that the call is "not forced upon them, nor compulsory.

All then were called, but all did not obey the call." God's part is certain; ours is real. ""Made God" is pagan language. Christians never become divine." OO Response: The Fathers do not mean that we become God by nature, which would be blasphemy. They mean what Peter calls being "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4) and what Paul calls being "conformed to the image of His Son" (8:29) and "glorified" (8:30). St Athanasius, who said "He was made man that we might be made God," was also the great defender of the absolute difference between the uncreated God and every creature. He saw no contradiction, because deification is a gift of grace to a creature, not a change of nature. "Predestination means God has already decided who will be saved, so our choices do not matter." OO Response: Paul says God predestined believers "to be conformed to the image of His Son." That is a destiny of holiness that we must walk into, as 8:13 and 8:17 show.

St John of Damascus: God "knows beforehand those things that are in our power, but He does not predetermine them." God's foreknowledge does not cause our choices any more than our knowing that the sun will rise causes it to rise. And God's will is that all be saved (1 Timothy 2:4). Our choices matter because God made them matter.

XII. FAQ Why do the Orthodox give the Spirit right after baptism? Because Romans 8:9 says that anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ is not His. In Acts the apostles laid hands on the baptised to give the Spirit (Acts 8:14–17). The Church continues this in chrismation, anointing every newly baptised person, infants included, with the holy myron. Does "all things work together for good" mean bad things will not happen to Christians? No. Paul lists tribulation, persecution, famine and the sword in the same chapter (8:35). The promise is that God uses even these for the good of those who love Him, conforming them to Christ. The martyrs are the proof. What does Romans 8 say about animals and the environment? That the whole creation suffers because of human sin and will share in the freedom of God's children. Christians are not owners of the world but stewards of something God intends to renew. The Fathers saw the saints, at peace with wild animals, as a foretaste of that renewal. Is Romans 8 the end of Paul's argument? It is the end of his account of salvation in Christ.
But it raises a question. If God's purpose cannot fail, why have so many of Israel, God's chosen people, not believed? That question fills chapters 9 to 11, beginning with Romans 9 .

I. Introduction: The Most Misread Chapter Few chapters of the Bible have been read with more fear than Romans 9. "Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated." "He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills He hardens." "Does not the potter have power over the clay?" From these verses St Augustine in his later years, and after him John Calvin and the Synod of Dort, drew the doctrine that God, before the world began, chose some people for eternal life and passed over the rest, without regard to anything He foresaw in them. Many sincere Christians have read Romans 9 and concluded that their eternal destiny was fixed before they were born. The Orthodox Church reads the chapter differently, and so did the Church before Augustine. That reading does not make God smaller. It takes seriously that Romans 9 is the first part of a single argument running to the end of chapter 11, that it is about God's dealings with Israel and the nations, that Paul himself says why Israel stumbled, and that the image of the potter has a history in Scripture.

The most important part of that history is the prophet Jeremiah's visit to the potter's house, where God explained the image Himself. This page sets out both readings in full, gives the Reformed position in the words of Calvin, Westminster and Dort, shows that Protestants themselves have never agreed on it, and then makes the case from Jeremiah 18, St Paul's own words in 2 Timothy, and the Fathers. It also says honestly where the case is strong and where it needs care. "As then Pharaoh became a vessel of wrath by his own lawlessness, so did these become vessels of mercy by their own readiness to obey." St John Chrysostom, Homily 16 on Romans This page is part of Romans with the Fathers , a series of nine pages that read St Paul's letter to the Romans section by section with the Church Fathers, setting their reading beside the main Protestant readings. Use the bar at the top of the page to move between the sections of the letter.

A Note on Quotations Every quotation marked VERBATIM has been checked word for word against a public domain translation: St John Chrysostom's thirty-two Homilies on Romans and the other Fathers in the Ante-Nicene and Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series, John Calvin's Commentary on Romans in John Owen's translation (1849), and the Reformation confessions in Philip Schaff's Creeds of Christendom . Chrysostom's homilies follow J. B. Morris's translation as revised by W. H. Simcox, in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, volume 11. Wisdom 15:7, which is not in the NKJV, is quoted from the Douay-Rheims. Where a work has no public domain English translation, its teaching is summarised and marked PARAPHRASE . Scripture follows the NKJV.

II. Glossary of Terms Election ἐκλογή · eklogē Choosing. In Romans 9:11, God's choice of Jacob's line over Esau's. Purpose πρόθεσις · prothesis A plan set forth beforehand (9:11; 8:28). Hated ἐμίσησα · emisēsa "I hated" (9:13, quoting Malachi 1:3). In Hebrew idiom, to love one and "hate" another often means to choose or prefer one over the other (Genesis 29:30–31; Luke 14:26). Harden σκληρύνω · sklērynō To make hard or stubborn (9:18). Used of Pharaoh, who is also said to have hardened his own heart. Potter κεραμεύς · kerameus The craftsman who shapes clay (9:21). The image comes from Isaiah, Jeremiah and Wisdom. Lump φύραμα · phyrama A batch of kneaded clay or dough (9:21; 11:16). Vessel σκεῦος · skeuos A pot or container, and by extension a person as God's instrument (9:21–23; 2 Timothy 2:20–21; Acts 9:15). Prepared, fitted κατηρτισμένα · katērtismena "Vessels of wrath prepared for destruction" (9:22). A perfect participle with no stated agent: Paul does not say who fitted them.

Prepared beforehand προητοίμασεν · proētoimasen "Vessels of mercy, which He had prepared beforehand for glory" (9:23). Here God is the stated subject. The difference from 9:22 is noticed by many commentators. Longsuffering μακροθυμία · makrothymia Patience that holds back anger. God "endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath" (9:22), the same patience that leads to repentance (2:4).

secs.h: III. Paul's Grief and Paul's Question (9:1–9)
secs.x: III. Paul's Grief and Paul's Question (9:1–9) Romans 9:1-3 "I tell the truth in Christ, I am not lying, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual grief in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my countrymen according to the flesh," Orthodox reading: Paul begins not with a theory of predestination but with grief. He would be cut off himself if it would save his people. Romans 9:4-5 "who are Israelites, to whom pertain the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service of God, and the promises; of whom are the fathers and from whom, according to the flesh, Christ came, who is over all, the eternally blessed God. Amen." Orthodox reading: Israel's privileges were real, and from them came Christ, "who is over all, the eternally blessed God." Romans 9:6-8 "But it is not that the word of God has taken no effect.

secs.h: III. Paul's Grief and Paul's Question (9:1–9)
secs.x: For they are not all Israel who are of Israel, nor are they all children because they are the seed of Abraham; but, 'In Isaac your seed shall be called.' That is, those who are the children of the flesh, these are not the children of God; but the children of the promise are counted as the seed." Orthodox reading: The question of Romans 9 is whether God's word to Israel has failed. Paul answers that the true Israel has always been the children of the promise. Everything in Romans 9 must be read in the light of this question. Paul has just said that nothing can separate God's people from His love (8:39). But most of Israel, God's own people, have not believed in their Messiah. Has God's promise failed? Romans 9 to 11 is one answer in three parts, and it ends not with a fixed number of the elect and the reprobate but with "God has committed them all to disobedience, that He might have mercy on all" (11:32). Chrysostom saw the shape of the argument clearly.

secs.h: III. Paul's Grief and Paul's Question (9:1–9)
secs.x: Paul is answering a Jewish objection, and he answers it by showing that God has always chosen freely within Abraham's family, and is free now to show mercy to Gentiles who believe: St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (on 9:6–8) "Now if all have sinned, how come some to be saved, and some to perish? It is because all were not minded to come to Him, since for His part all were saved, for all were called." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (on 9:8–9) "Thus are we also gendered by the words of God. Since in the pool of water it is the words of God which generate and fashion us. For it is by being baptized into the Name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost that we are gendered. And this birth is not of nature, but of the promise of God." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION

IV. Jacob and Esau (9:10–13) Romans 9:10-13 "And not only this, but when Rebecca also had conceived by one man, even by our father Isaac (for the children not yet being born, nor having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works but of Him who calls), it was said to her, 'The older shall serve the younger.' As it is written, 'Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated.'" Orthodox reading: Before the twins were born or had done anything, God chose the younger to carry the promise. Election is God's free gift, not a wage for works. Genesis 25:23 "And the Lord said to her: 'Two nations are in your womb, Two peoples shall be separated from your body; One people shall be stronger than the other, And the older shall serve the younger.'" Orthodox reading: What God told Rebecca was about two nations: the people descended from Esau would serve the people descended from Jacob. Malachi 1:2-3 "'I have loved you,' says the Lord. 'Yet you say, 'In what way have You loved us?' Was not Esau Jacob's brother?' Says the Lord.

'Yet Jacob I have loved; But Esau I have hated, And laid waste his mountains and his heritage For the jackals of the wilderness.'" Orthodox reading: Malachi, writing more than a thousand years after the twins, speaks of the nation of Edom and its land. Three things about these verses are often missed. First, they are about peoples and roles in history. Genesis 25:23 speaks of "two nations" and "two peoples," and the promise was that "the older shall serve the younger," a matter of which line would carry the promise to Christ. Malachi speaks of Edom's mountains laid waste. Neither passage says anything about Esau's soul or his eternal destiny. Even Calvin, who reads the verses as pointing to eternal election, admits that in Malachi "earthly blessings are there recorded" and that the Lord "rejected the Edomites, the progeny of Esau." John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 9:13) "I therefore chose you for my people, that I might show the same kindness to the seed of Jacob; but I rejected the Edomites, the progeny of Esau...

Now, though earthly blessings are there recorded, which God had conferred on the Israelites, it is not yet right to view them but as symbols of his benevolence..." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) Second, "hated" is Hebrew idiom for choosing one over another. When Jacob "loved Rachel more than Leah," Scripture immediately says Leah was "unloved," literally "hated" (Genesis 29:30–31). Christ says no one can be His disciple who does not "hate" his father and mother (Luke 14:26), which Matthew renders "loves father or mother more than Me" (Matthew 10:37). Genesis 29:30-31 "Then Jacob also went in to Rachel, and he also loved Rachel more than Leah. And he served with Laban still another seven years. When the Lord saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb; but Rachel was barren." Orthodox reading: Leah was not the object of Jacob's malice; she was simply not chosen as Rachel was. Deuteronomy 23:7 "You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother.

You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were an alien in his land." Orthodox reading: God's law forbade Israel to abhor the Edomites: "he is your brother." Esau's descendants were not the objects of divine loathing. Genesis 33:9 "But Esau said, 'I have enough, my brother; keep what you have for yourself.'" Orthodox reading: Esau himself was blessed with plenty and forgave his brother. His story in Genesis is not the story of a man cursed by God. Third, Paul's point is that the choice was not earned. "Not of works but of Him who calls." The Orthodox agree completely: no one is chosen because of merit. Chrysostom adds that God, unlike us, does not need to wait for the outcome to know a person's character: St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (on 9:11–13) "With what intent then did God say this? Because He does not wait, as man does, to see from the issue of their acts the good and him who is not so, but even before these He knows which is the wicked and which not such." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Reformed readers object that this makes election depend on foreseen

character, which Paul's "not of works" excludes. That is a fair objection to a crude version of the view. But foreknowing how a person will freely respond to grace is not the same as rewarding his works. Faith is not a work that earns (4:4–5), and the Fathers never said God chose anyone because they deserved it. They said God's choices are not arbitrary, because He knows the heart.

V. Mercy and Pharaoh's Heart (9:14–18) Romans 9:14-16 "What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? Certainly not! For He says to Moses, 'I will have mercy on whomever I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whomever I will have compassion.' So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy." Orthodox reading: God's mercy is His to give. No one can claim it by willing or running. Exodus 33:19 "Then He said, 'I will make all My goodness pass before you, and I will proclaim the name of the Lord before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion.'" Orthodox reading: The words were spoken to Moses after the golden calf, when all Israel had sinned and God chose to show mercy. They are a revelation of God's goodness, not of arbitrary choice. St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (on 9:15) "For it is not yours to know, O Moses, he means, which are deserving of My love toward man, but leave this to Me.

But if Moses had no right to know, much less have we." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs" (9:16). St Gregory the Theologian explains how the Fathers read this verse: not as denying our will, but as denying that our will is enough on its own: St Gregory of Nazianzus Oration 37.13 "For it is necessary both that we should be our own masters and also that our salvation should be of God. This is why He says not of him that wills; that is, not of him that wills only, nor of him that runs only, but also of God. That shows mercy. Next; since to will also is from God, he has attributed the whole to God with reason." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (on 9:16) "Because when he says, it is not of him that wills, nor of him that runs, he does not deprive us of free-will, but shows that all is not one's own, for that it requires grace from above.

For it is binding on us to will, and also to run: but to confide not in our own labors, but in the love of God toward man." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Who Hardened Pharaoh? Romans 9:17-18 "For the Scripture says to the Pharaoh, 'For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may show My power in you, and that My name may be declared in all the earth.' Therefore He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills He hardens." Orthodox reading: God raised Pharaoh up to show His power, and He hardens whom He wills. Exodus 4:21 "And the Lord said to Moses, 'When you go back to Egypt, see that you do all those wonders before Pharaoh which I have put in your hand. But I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go." Orthodox reading: God foretold that He would harden Pharaoh's heart. Exodus 8:15 "But when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he hardened his heart and did not heed them, as the Lord had said." Orthodox reading: Yet Exodus also says, again and again, that Pharaoh hardened his own heart.

Exodus 9:12 "But the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh; and he did not heed them, just as the Lord had spoken to Moses." Orthodox reading: Only after Pharaoh had hardened himself through the earlier plagues does the text say that the Lord hardened him. The Fathers explained the two statements with a famous image. The same sun that melts wax hardens mud. The sun does not change; the material does. So God's same goodness, shown to Pharaoh in sign after sign, softened some Egyptians who left with Israel and hardened the man who refused it. Origen De Principiis III.1.11 "Now it is not incorrect to say that the sun, by one and the same power of its heat, melts wax indeed, but dries up and hardens mud: not that its power operates one way upon mud, and in another way upon wax; but that the qualities of mud and wax are different, although according to nature they are one thing, both being from the earth.

In this way, then, one and the same working upon the part of God, which was administered by Moses in signs and wonders, made manifest the hardness of Pharaoh, which he had conceived in the intensity of his wickedness..." Early Writer (not a saint) VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION St Irenaeus of Lyons Against Heresies IV.29.1 "For one and the same God [that blesses others] inflicts blindness upon those who do not believe, but who set Him at naught; just as the sun, which is a creature of His, [acts with regard] to those who, by reason of any weakness of the eyes cannot behold his light..." Early Witness VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Origen was a great biblical scholar, but some of his speculations, especially about the pre-existence of souls, were rejected by the Church; Pope Theophilus of Alexandria condemned them around AD 400. He is quoted here only where his reading agrees with the Fathers the Church received.

secs.h: What Chrysostom Says the Image Means
secs.x: VI. The Potter and the Clay (9:19–24) Romans 9:19-21 "You will say to me then, 'Why does He still find fault? For who has resisted His will?' But indeed, O man, who are you to reply against God? Will the thing formed say to him who formed it, 'Why have you made me like this?' Does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?" Orthodox reading: The objector asks why God finds fault if no one can resist Him. Paul answers that the creature has no standing to put its Maker in the dock. Romans 9:22-24 "What if God, wanting to show His wrath and to make His power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, and that He might make known the riches of His glory on the vessels of mercy, which He had prepared beforehand for glory, even us whom He called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles?" Orthodox reading: God endured the vessels of wrath with great patience, and made known His glory to vessels of mercy, called from Jews and Gentiles alike.

secs.h: What Chrysostom Says the Image Means
secs.x: Paul's words echo several Old Testament passages. Isaiah twice rebukes the clay for questioning the potter (Isaiah 29:16; 45:9). The Wisdom of Solomon, which the Orthodox Churches read as Scripture, describes a potter making clean and common vessels "of the same clay," the very phrase Paul uses: Isaiah 45:9 "Woe to him who strives with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth! Shall the clay say to him who forms it, 'What are you making?' Or shall your handiwork say, 'He has no hands'?" Orthodox reading: Isaiah's rebuke was aimed at Israelites who questioned how God chose to save them, through the Persian king Cyrus. "The potter also tempering soft earth, with labour fashioneth every vessel for our service, and of the same clay he maketh both vessels that are for clean uses, and likewise such as serve to the contrary: but what is the use of these vessels, the potter is the judge." Wisdom 15:7 (Douay-Rheims) What Chrysostom Says the Image Means St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (on 9:20–21) "Here it is not to do away with free-will that he says this,

secs.h: What Chrysostom Says the Image Means
secs.x: but to show, up to what point we ought to obey God. For in respect of calling God to account, we ought to be as little disposed to it as the clay is." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (on 9:21) "...do not suppose that this is said by Paul as an account of the creation, nor as implying a necessity over the will, but to illustrate the sovereignty and difference of dispensations; for if we do not take it in this way, various incongruities will follow, for if here he were speaking about the will, and those who are good and those not so, He will be Himself the Maker of these, and man will be free from all responsibility." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (on 9:21) "And yet not even is it on the potter that the honor and the dishonor of the things made of the lump depends, but upon the use made by those that handle them, so here also it depends on the free choice." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Vessels of Wrath and Vessels of Mercy Look closely at 9:22–23.

secs.h: What Chrysostom Says the Image Means
secs.x: Of the vessels of mercy Paul says God "prepared [them] beforehand for glory." Of the vessels of wrath he says only that they were "prepared for destruction," with no agent named, and he says God "endured [them] with much longsuffering." Why would God patiently endure vessels He had Himself made for destruction? Chrysostom answers: St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (on 9:22) "Pharaoh was a vessel of wrath, that is, a man who by his own hard-heartedness had kindled the wrath of God. For after enjoying much long-suffering, he became no better, but remained unimproved. Wherefore he calls him not only a vessel of wrath, but also one fitted for destruction. That is, fully fitted indeed, but by his own proper self." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (on 9:22) "Yet still, though God knew this, He endured him with much long-suffering, being willing to bring him to repentance.

secs.h: What Chrysostom Says the Image Means
secs.x: For had He not willed this, then He would not have been thus long-suffering." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (on 9:23–24) "As then Pharaoh became a vessel of wrath by his own lawlessness, so did these become vessels of mercy by their own readiness to obey. For though the more part is of God, still they also have contributed themselves some little. Whence he does not say either, vessels of well-doing, or vessels of boldness, but vessels of mercy, to show that the whole is of God." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Calvin reads the same verses as a statement of God's sovereign decree: John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 9:20) "It is indeed evident that no cause is adduced higher than the will of God." Reformer VERBATIM · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849) John Calvin Commentary on Romans (on 9:22) "There are vessels prepared for destruction, that is, given up and appointed to destruction: they are also vessels of wrath, that is, made and formed for this end, that they may be examples of God's vengeance and displeasure." Reformer VERBATIM

secs.x: · OWEN TRANSLATION (1849)

VII. The Potter's House: Jeremiah 18 When Paul asks, "Does not the potter have power over the clay?" he is using an image that God had already explained at length through the prophet Jeremiah. The nineteenth-century English editors of Chrysostom's homilies printed a note at this very verse: "Read Jer. xviii. 1–10." It is good advice. Here is what Jeremiah saw. Jeremiah 18:1-4 "The word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: 'Arise and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause you to hear My words.' Then I went down to the potter's house, and there he was, making something at the wheel. And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter; so he made it again into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to make." Orthodox reading: The vessel was spoiled in the potter's hand, and the potter remade it into another vessel. The potter is fully in charge, and what he does responds to the condition of the clay.

Jeremiah 18:5-6 "Then the word of the Lord came to me, saying: 'O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter?' says the Lord. 'Look, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel!" Orthodox reading: God applies the image to His people: as the clay is in the potter's hand, so is Israel in His. Jeremiah 18:7-8 "The instant I speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, to pull down, and to destroy it, if that nation against whom I have spoken turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I thought to bring upon it." Orthodox reading: If a nation God has threatened turns from its evil, God relents of the disaster. Jeremiah 18:9-10 "And the instant I speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it, if it does evil in My sight so that it does not obey My voice, then I will relent concerning the good with which I said I would benefit it." Orthodox reading: And if a nation God has promised to build does evil, God relents of the good He said He would do for it.

Jeremiah 18:11-12 "'Now therefore, speak to the men of Judah and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying, 'Thus says the Lord: 'Behold, I am fashioning a disaster and devising a plan against you. Return now every one from his evil way, and make your ways and your doings good.''' And they said, 'That is hopeless! So we will walk according to our own plans, and we will every one obey the dictates of his evil heart.'" Orthodox reading: The potter appeals to the clay: "Return now." The people answer, "That is hopeless! So we will walk according to our own plans." What the Potter's House Teaches 1. God really is the potter. Nothing in Jeremiah weakens God's sovereignty. "As the clay is in the potter's hand, so are you in My hand." He does with the vessel "as it seemed good to the potter to make." The Orthodox do not deny one word of Romans 9:20–21. 2. The spoiling comes from the clay, not the potter. The vessel was "marred in the hand of the potter." No potter sets out to ruin his own work.

When God's people are spoiled, it is because they have refused His hands: "we will walk according to our own plans" (18:12). 3. Our turning really changes how God shapes us. This is the heart of the passage. God says plainly that if a nation turns from evil, He relents of the disaster, and if a nation turns to evil, He relents even of the good He intended (18:8, 10). The potter does not shape us without regard to what we do. Our sin and our repentance genuinely change what He makes of us. 4. And what He makes is always good. The potter is never the problem. Whether He builds or pulls down, remakes or reshapes, He acts in goodness, and even His threats are calls to return: "Return now every one from his evil way" (18:11). A vessel remade after being spoiled is not a lesser work of God. It is the same goodness responding to a different clay. This is exactly what Paul says in Romans 9:22: God "endured with much longsuffering" even the vessels of wrath, and in 2:4, that His longsuffering is meant to lead to repentance.

Read with Jeremiah, Paul's question "Does not the potter have power over the clay?" does not mean "God fixes each person's destiny regardless of anything in them." It means "God has every right to remake Israel, to set aside those who refuse Him and to form a new people from Jews and Gentiles who believe." That is exactly the subject of Romans 9 to 11. A Note on the Fathers In fairness, none of the Fathers in the public domain translations consulted for this page quotes Jeremiah 18 when commenting on Romans 9. The connection rests on Scripture itself: Jeremiah 18 is the Old Testament's own explanation of the potter image. But the conclusion the Fathers drew from Romans 9 is the same as Jeremiah's, and two of them reached it by linking Romans 9 to another of Paul's own vessel passages, as the next section shows.

VIII. Vessels That Change: 2 Timothy 2 and Romans 9–11 Paul uses the image of honourable and dishonourable vessels in one other place, and there he says what makes the difference: 2 Timothy 2:20-21 "But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay, some for honor and some for dishonor. Therefore if anyone cleanses himself from the latter, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful for the Master, prepared for every good work." Orthodox reading: In a great house there are vessels for honour and dishonour, and "if anyone cleanses himself" he will be a vessel for honour. The same apostle, the same image, and the outcome depends on the vessel's response.

St John of Damascus, who summed up the teaching of the Greek Fathers in the eighth century, puts the two passages side by side: St John of Damascus Exposition of the Orthodox Faith IV.19 "It is to be observed that it is the custom in the Holy Scripture to speak of God's permission as His energy, as when the apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans, Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour and another unto dishonour? And for this reason, that He Himself makes this or that. For He is Himself alone the Maker of all things; yet it is not He Himself that fashions noble or ignoble things, but the personal choice of each one." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION St John of Damascus Exposition of the Orthodox Faith IV.19 "And it is evident that the purification must be voluntary: for if a man, he says, purge himself.

And the consequent antistrophe responds, If a man purge not himself he will be a vessel to dishonour, unmeet for the master's use and fit only to be broken in pieces." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION Origen, five centuries earlier, had made the same connection: Origen De Principiis III.1.21 "He, accordingly, who purges himself, is made a vessel unto honour, while he who has disdained to cleanse himself from his impurity is made a vessel unto dishonour... For God the Creator makes a certain vessel unto honour, and other vessels to dishonour; but that vessel which has cleansed itself from all impurity He makes a vessel unto honour, while that which has stained itself with the filth of vice He makes a vessel unto dishonour." Early Writer (not a saint) VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Origen De Principiis III.1.22 "...we are not to suppose either that those things which are in our own power can be done without the help of God, or that those which are in God's hand can be brought to completion without the intervention of our acts, and desires, and intention..." Early Writer (not a

saint) VERBATIM · ANF TRANSLATION Inside Romans Itself The same logic runs through Romans 9 to 11. Vessels change: Romans 9:25-26 "As He says also in Hosea: 'I will call them My people, who were not My people, And her beloved, who was not beloved.' 'And it shall come to pass in the place where it was said to them, 'You are not My people,' There they shall be called sons of the living God.'" Orthodox reading: Those who were "not My people" become "My people." Paul applies Hosea to Gentiles who believe. Vessels of dishonour are remade. Romans 11:22-23 "Therefore consider the goodness and severity of God: on those who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness, if you continue in His goodness. Otherwise you also will be cut off. And they also, if they do not continue in unbelief, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again." Orthodox reading: Branches broken off for unbelief can be grafted in again "if they do not continue in unbelief," and branches that stand can be cut off if they do not continue in God's goodness. That is Jeremiah 18 in Paul's own words.

The potter's freedom is complete, and He uses it to respond to the clay: cutting off for unbelief, grafting in through faith, and always longing that the spoiled vessel return. This is why the Orthodox say that Romans 9, read to the end of Romans 11, teaches the opposite of a fixed decree of reprobation.

secs.h: How a Reformed Reader Would Answer Jeremiah 18
secs.x: IX. The Reformed Reading in Its Own Words It would be unfair to answer the Reformed position without first letting it speak. Its roots are in the later Augustine: St Augustine of Hippo Enchiridion 99 "He has mercy of His great goodness, He hardens without any injustice; so that neither can he that is pardoned glory in any merit of his own, nor he that is condemned complain of anything but his own demerit. For it is grace alone that separates the redeemed from the lost, all having been involved in one common perdition through their common origin." Church Father (Latin) VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION John Calvin Institutes of the Christian Religion III.21.5 "By predestination we mean the eternal decree of God, by which he determined with himself whatever he wished to happen with regard to every man.

secs.h: How a Reformed Reader Would Answer Jeremiah 18
secs.x: All are not created on equal terms, but some are preordained to eternal life, others to eternal damnation; and, accordingly, as each has been created for one or other of these ends, we say that he has been predestinated to life or to death." Reformer VERBATIM · BEVERIDGE TRANSLATION (1845) John Calvin Institutes of the Christian Religion III.23.7 "The decree, I admit, is, dreadful; and yet it is impossible to deny that God foreknew what the end of man was to be before he made him, and foreknew, because he had so ordained by his decree." Reformer VERBATIM · BEVERIDGE TRANSLATION (1845) Canons of Dort (1619) Canons of Dort, First Head, Article 6 "That some receive the gift of faith from God, and others do not receive it, proceeds from God's eternal decree...

secs.h: How a Reformed Reader Would Answer Jeremiah 18
secs.x: According to which decree he graciously softens the hearts of the elect, however obstinate, and inclines them to believe; while he leaves the non-elect in his just judgment to their own wickedness and obduracy." Synod of Dort (1619) VERBATIM · CANONS OF DORT, SCHAFF Canons of Dort (1619) Canons of Dort, First Head, Article 15 "...whom God, out of his sovereign, most just, irreprehensible and unchangeable good pleasure, hath decreed to leave in the common misery into which they have willfully plunged themselves, and not to bestow upon them saving faith and the grace of conversion... And this is the decree of reprobation which by no means makes God the author of sin (the very thought of which is blasphemy), but declares him to be an awful, irreprehensible, and righteous judge and avenger." Synod of Dort (1619) VERBATIM · CANONS OF DORT, SCHAFF Westminster Confession (1646) Westminster Confession of Faith III.5 "Those of mankind that are predestinated unto life, God, before the foundation of the world was laid, according to his eternal and immutable purpose, and the secret counsel and

secs.h: How a Reformed Reader Would Answer Jeremiah 18
secs.x: good pleasure of his will, hath chosen in Christ, unto everlasting glory, out of his mere free grace and love, without any foresight of faith or good works, or perseverance in either of them, or any other thing in the creature, as conditions, or causes moving him thereunto; and all to the praise of his glorious grace." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · WESTMINSTER CONFESSION, SCHAFF Westminster Confession (1646) Westminster Confession of Faith III.7 "The rest of mankind God was pleased, according to the unsearchable counsel of his own will, whereby he extendeth or withholdeth mercy as he pleaseth, for the glory of his sovereign power over his creatures, to pass by, and to ordain them to dishonor and wrath for their sin, to the praise of his glorious justice." Reformed Confession VERBATIM · WESTMINSTER CONFESSION, SCHAFF Three things deserve to be said in the Reformed tradition's favour. It insists that no one is saved by his own merit, which is true. It insists that God is not the author of sin and that the lost are condemned "for their sin," which is also true.

secs.h: How a Reformed Reader Would Answer Jeremiah 18
secs.x: And Calvin was honest enough to call the decree "dreadful." The Reformed are not cruel people who enjoy the thought of reprobation; they believe Scripture compels it. How a Reformed Reader Would Answer Jeremiah 18 A careful Calvinist would reply to the potter's house in four ways. First, Jeremiah 18 is about nations and earthly judgements, not the eternal salvation of individuals. Second, the potter's freedom is the point of both passages: "as it seemed good to the potter." Third, repentance is itself God's gift: "Restore me, and I will return" (Jeremiah 31:18); "God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life" (Acts 11:18). So even when the clay turns, it is because the potter turned it, and Dort says exactly this. Fourth, Paul in Romans 9:20 is silencing the objector, not explaining God's reasons. Jeremiah 31:18 "I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself: 'You have chastised me, and I was chastised, Like an untrained bull; Restore me, and I will return, For You are the Lord my God." Orthodox reading: The penitent asks God to restore him so that he can return.

secs.h: How a Reformed Reader Would Answer Jeremiah 18
secs.x: Repentance is a gift. The Orthodox Response To the first: Romans 9 is also about nations. Paul's examples are Jacob and Esau, of whom God said "two nations are in your womb," Edom in Malachi, and Israel and the Gentiles throughout. If Jeremiah 18 cannot speak to individuals because it concerns nations, the same is true of Romans 9's own examples. And Paul applies Jeremiah's logic to individuals when he says branches will be grafted in again "if they do not continue in unbelief" (11:23). To the second: agreed. God is the potter and is free. The question is how He uses His freedom, and Jeremiah 18 is God's own answer: He uses it in response to the clay. To the third: the Orthodox agree that repentance is a gift of grace. St Gregory says "even to wish well needs help from God." But Scripture also shows that grace can be refused: "You always resist the Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:51); "I wanted to gather your children... but you were not willing" (Matthew 23:37).

secs.h: How a Reformed Reader Would Answer Jeremiah 18
secs.x: In Jeremiah 18 itself the potter calls, "Return now," and the clay says, "We will walk according to our own plans." If the potter's call were irresistible, that answer could not be given. To the fourth: Paul does silence the proud objector, as Chrysostom says. But he then gives an answer (9:22–24), and the answer is about God's longsuffering and mercy. And at the end of the chapter he gives the reason Israel stumbled, which is a human reason (9:32).

X. Protestants Divided The Reformed doctrine of unconditional election and reprobation is not "the Protestant view." Protestants have argued about it since the beginning, and two major Protestant traditions reject important parts of it. The Lutherans The Lutheran Formula of Concord (1577) teaches that election to salvation is wholly of grace, but it refuses to say that God destines anyone to damnation, and it condemns the following teachings outright: Formula of Concord (1577) Formula of Concord, Epitome XI, Negative "That God is unwilling that all men should repent and believe the Gospel... That when God calls us to him, he does not earnestly wish that all men should come to him... All these dogmas are false, horrid, and blasphemous, and by them all consolation is utterly taken away from godly minds..." Lutheran Confession VERBATIM · FORMULA OF CONCORD, SCHAFF Formula of Concord (1577) Formula of Concord, Epitome XI.3 "For sin arises from the devil, and from the depraved and evil will of man.

Nor is this foreknowledge of God the cause why men perish, for this they ought to impute to themselves." Lutheran Confession VERBATIM · FORMULA OF CONCORD, SCHAFF The Arminians and Methodists In 1610 the Dutch followers of Jacobus Arminius set out five articles that the Synod of Dort later rejected. On grace, they said: The Remonstrance (1610) Remonstrance, Article IV "That this grace of God is the beginning, continuance, and accomplishment of all good, even to this extent, that the regenerate man himself, without prevenient or assisting, awakening, following and cooperative grace, can neither think, will, nor do good, nor withstand any temptations to evil; so that all good deeds or movements, that can be conceived, must be ascribed to the grace of God in Christ.

But as respects the mode of the operation of this grace, it is not irresistible, inasmuch as it is written concerning many, that they have resisted the Holy Ghost." Arminian Articles (1610) VERBATIM · REMONSTRANCE, SCHAFF John Wesley and the Methodist movement took the same side, and today most Pentecostal, Methodist, Wesleyan and many Baptist Christians reject unconditional reprobation. The Orthodox did not arrive at their view by joining one side of a Protestant argument; they held it a thousand years before that argument began. But it is worth knowing that on Romans 9 the Orthodox stand much closer to most of the world's Protestants than to Geneva and Dort.

XI. Why Israel Stumbled (9:30–33) Romans 9:30-32 "What shall we say then? That Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness of faith; but Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, has not attained to the law of righteousness. Why? Because they did not seek it by faith, but as it were, by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumbling stone." Orthodox reading: Paul's own conclusion: Israel did not attain righteousness "because they did not seek it by faith, but as it were, by the works of the law." Romans 9:33 "As it is written: 'Behold, I lay in Zion a stumbling stone and rock of offense, And whoever believes on Him will not be put to shame.'" Orthodox reading: Christ is the stone. Those who believe on Him will not be put to shame. This is the most neglected verse in the debate.

After all the talk of Jacob and Esau, Pharaoh and the potter, Paul gives the reason Israel stumbled, and it is not "because God passed them over." It is "because they did not seek it by faith." The cause is in the clay's response to the potter, exactly as in Jeremiah 18. St John Chrysostom Homily 16 on Romans (summing up Romans 9) "I, however, have a good reason to give you why the Gentiles were justified and you were cast out. And what is the reason? It is that they are of faith, you of the works of the Law. And it is owing to this obstinacy of yours that you have in every way... been given up." Church Father VERBATIM · NPNF TRANSLATION And the story does not end there. In Romans 10 Paul says God has stretched out His hands "all day long" to a disobedient people (10:21), and in Romans 11 he says that "God has committed them all to disobedience, that He might have mercy on all" (11:32). The potter has not given up on the clay. See Romans 10–11 .

secs.h: XII. How Strong Is the Potter Argument?
secs.x: XII. How Strong Is the Potter Argument? An honest page should say where its own argument is strong and where it needs care. Where it is strong. Jeremiah 18 is not a stray verse. It is the Old Testament's fullest use of the potter image, and God Himself interprets it there. It shows that "the potter has power over the clay" and "the potter responds to the clay" are not opposites in Scripture's own mind. Paul's other vessel passage (2 Timothy 2:21) says the same, and the Fathers read Romans 9 through it. Romans 9:22 (longsuffering), 9:25–26 (not My people become My people), 9:32 (they did not seek it by faith) and 11:23 (if they do not continue in unbelief) all fit Jeremiah's picture and fit poorly with a fixed decree. Where it needs care. First, Jeremiah 18 does speak of nations, and a Calvinist can say God's conditional dealings in history sit on top of a deeper, unconditional decree.

secs.h: XII. How Strong Is the Potter Argument?
secs.x: The best answer to that is not Jeremiah alone but the character of God revealed everywhere: He "desires all men to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:4), is "not willing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9), and has "no pleasure... that the wicked should die" (Ezekiel 18:23). Scripture does speak of "secret things" that belong to God (Deuteronomy 29:29), but it never presents a hidden will of God that contradicts His revealed desire for the salvation of all. Second, Chrysostom himself warns that Paul uses the potter image for one purpose, to silence presumptuous questioning, and that we should not press every detail of it. That warning applies to everyone. It is a reason not to build a doctrine of reprobation on the image, and also a reason to let God's own explanation of the image in Jeremiah guide how we read it. Ezekiel 18:23 "Do I have any pleasure at all that the wicked should die?' says the Lord God, 'and not that he should turn from his ways and live?" Orthodox reading: God's revealed heart toward the wicked: He wants them to turn and live.

secs.h: XII. How Strong Is the Potter Argument?
secs.x: 2 Peter 3:9 "The Lord is not slack concerning His promise, as some count slackness, but is longsuffering toward us, not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance." Orthodox reading: God's longsuffering is aimed at repentance, for all. Taken together, the argument is a strong one. It does not depend on clever reasoning but on letting Scripture interpret Scripture: the potter of Romans 9 is the potter of Jeremiah 18, and both are the God who is "longsuffering toward us."

XIII. Objections Answered "Romans 9:11 says election is "not of works," so it cannot depend on anything foreseen in us." OO Response: The Orthodox agree that election is not earned by works. But Paul's contrast in Romans is between works and faith, not between works and nothing. In 9:30–32 he says the Gentiles attained righteousness by faith and Israel did not attain it because they sought it by works. Faith is not a work that earns (4:4–5). God's foreknowledge of who will receive His grace in faith does not make His choice a reward for merit. It makes it the choice of a God who knows hearts. Chrysostom: God "does not wait, as man does, to see from the issue of their acts" who is good. ""Who has resisted His will?" Paul does not deny the objector's premise, so he must agree that no one can resist God." OO Response: Paul answers the objector's tone, not his premise: "who are you to reply against God?" He then explains that God endured the vessels of wrath with great patience, which would make no sense if their resistance were impossible or unreal.

Elsewhere Scripture plainly says God's will for salvation is resisted: "You always resist the Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:51); "you were not willing" (Matthew 23:37). The Remonstrants quoted the same verse against Dort. "God hardened Pharaoh's heart. That proves He hardens whom He chooses regardless of their response." OO Response: Exodus says both that God hardened Pharaoh and that Pharaoh hardened himself, and the first plagues describe Pharaoh hardening his own heart before the text says God did. The Fathers explained this with the sun that melts wax and hardens clay: God's same goodness meets different hearts. Chrysostom adds that God endured Pharaoh "with much long-suffering, being willing to bring him to repentance." Hardening in Scripture is God's judgement on a heart that has refused Him, giving it over to what it chose (Romans 1:24). "Jeremiah 18 is about nations, not individual salvation, so it does not apply." OO Response: Romans 9 is also about nations: Jacob and Esau are "two nations," Malachi speaks of Edom, and Paul's whole subject is Israel and the Gentiles.

Whatever applies to Jeremiah 18 here applies equally to Romans 9. And Paul does apply the same logic to individuals, in 2 Timothy 2:21 ("if anyone cleanses himself") and in Romans 11:23 ("if they do not continue in unbelief"). "If salvation depends on our response, then we save ourselves and can boast." OO Response: No. Every good thing in us, including the will to respond, is God's gift. St Gregory: "since to will also is from God, he has attributed the whole to God with reason." Chrysostom: Paul says "vessels of mercy" "to show that the whole is of God." Receiving a gift is not earning it. A beggar who opens his hand for bread does not boast of having fed himself. What the Orthodox deny is not that grace is everything, but that grace forces anyone.

XIV. FAQ Does the Orthodox Church believe in predestination? Yes, in the sense of Romans 8:29: God foreknew and predestined His people to be conformed to the image of His Son. St John of Damascus says God "knows all things beforehand, yet He does not predetermine all things." What the Orthodox reject is the idea that God unconditionally decreed some people to be lost, or that His grace is irresistible. Was Esau damned? Scripture does not say so. Romans 9 and Malachi speak of God's choice of Jacob's line and of the nation of Edom. Hebrews 12:16–17 warns against Esau's profane choice of selling his birthright, a warning about what he did, not a statement that he was created for destruction. Esau's eternal state is left to God. Why did Augustine read Romans 9 the way he did? In his early writings Augustine read Romans 9 much as the Greek Fathers did. Around AD 396, in his reply to Simplicianus, he changed his mind, and his later struggle with Pelagius pushed him further. Much of the Latin West followed him, and Calvin built on him.

The Greek and Oriental Churches never adopted his later view. If I struggle with sin, does that mean I am a vessel of wrath? No. The very fact that you care is a sign of grace at work. Jeremiah's potter remade the spoiled vessel. Paul says vessels can be cleansed for honour (2 Timothy 2:21). No Orthodox Christian should ever conclude that God has decided against him. The door of repentance is open until the last breath. What comes next? Paul turns from God's freedom to Israel's responsibility and to the hope of the nations: "faith comes by hearing," the remnant, and the olive tree. That is Romans 10–11 .
