The Question The critic's case usually rests on three claims: that Scripture regulates slavery rather than condemning it; that revered Fathers accepted it; and that the medieval Papacy practised it. Each contains a grain of fact wrapped in a distortion. Slavery was the universal condition of the ancient world — historians estimate that perhaps a fifth to a third of the population of classical Athens and Roman Italy were slaves — and no book written into that world could pretend it did not exist. The question is not whether the Bible mentions slavery, but what it did to it: whether it left the institution as it found it, or planted principles that would one day destroy it.

What Christianity introduced Master and slave share one human nature made in God’s image Both are equally brothers in Christ, equal at the altar and the Judgment Man-stealing (the slave trade) is condemned as a capital crime Manumission — freeing slaves — is praised as a holy, God-pleasing act Slavery is called a fruit of sin, not part of God’s created order What the ancient world assumed Some men are “slaves by nature,” fit only to be owned (Aristotle) A slave was a “living tool,” property with no rights before the law Masters could often kill, brand, or maim slaves with little legal check Enslaving the conquered was the normal reward of war Slavery was hereditary, and the institution itself beyond question (even where individual slaves were often freed, as in Rome) The distortion in the popular charge is to read the Bible as if it invented or commanded slavery, when in fact it inherited a world drowning in it and began, quietly and then openly, to dissolve its foundations. The sections below follow that work from Sinai to abolition.

Scripture & the Ancient World The slavery of Israel's neighbours — Egypt, Assyria, Babylon — was chattel slavery: human beings owned as property, bought and sold. Debt bondage had limits there too (Hammurabi's code released debt slaves after three years, §117), but the same code made helping a runaway slave escape a capital crime (§§15–16), the reverse of Deuteronomy 23:15–16 below. The Law of Moses did not create this system; it constrained it, and for fellow Hebrews replaced it almost entirely with a system closer to indentured or contract labour, bounded by time and dignity. Honesty requires adding the harder half: the same Law allowed Israelites to buy slaves from the surrounding nations and to keep them, and their children, permanently as property (Leviticus 25:44–46), and it treated a master who beat a slave who survived more leniently than other assailants (Exodus 21:20–21). Christians have to read these texts in the light of Christ, as the Fathers did, not pretend they are absent.

A Hebrew who sold himself out of debt was to be released, debt-free, in the seventh year: “When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing.” Exodus 21:2 (ESV) “And when you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty-handed. You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your winepress.” Deuteronomy 15:13–14 (ESV) Every fiftieth year, the Jubilee, cancelled debts and returned people to their families and land (Leviticus 25). Most decisively, the Law struck at the very root of the slave trade — the stealing of persons to sell — making it a capital crime: “Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death.” Exodus 21:16 (ESV) This single command, taken seriously, makes the Atlantic slave trade impossible: every link in that chain — the raid, the sale, the possession — was a capital crime under Moses.

The Law also forbade returning a runaway slave to his master, the reverse of most ancient slave codes and of the American fugitive slave laws: “You shall not give up to his master a slave who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you… you shall not wrong him.” Deuteronomy 23:15–16 (ESV) And beneath the statutes lay a conviction that would in time undo slavery altogether — that master and slave share one Maker who sees no rank between them. Job states it plainly: “If I have rejected the cause of my manservant or my maidservant… what then shall I do when God rises up? … Did not he who made me in the womb make him? And did not one fashion us in the womb?” Job 31:13–15 (ESV) The same Law bound liberty into the very calendar of Israel. Every fiftieth year, freedom was to be proclaimed to all: “And you shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants.

It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan.” Leviticus 25:10 (ESV) The reason given is that Israel belongs to God alone, and what is God's cannot be another man's chattel: “For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves.” Leviticus 25:42 (ESV) And the memory of their own bondage in Egypt was made the ground of mercy toward every servant: “You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the Lord your God redeemed you; therefore I command you this today.” Deuteronomy 15:15 (ESV) The prophets carried this further still, until liberation of the oppressed became the very worship God desires: “Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?” Isaiah 58:6 (ESV) And Amos names the traffic in human beings among the sins for which the nation is judged: “…because they sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals.” Amos

2:6 (ESV) The Law of Moses was not the last word — its provisions were a floor beneath a hard-hearted age, not the summit of God's will (cf. Matthew 19:8). But measured against Hammurabi, Egypt, and Assyria, it was a revolution in mercy, and it carried within it the seeds of slavery's undoing.

Greece, Rome & the New Testament The world of the Apostles was the Roman Empire, where slavery was total. Slaves may have numbered a fifth or more of Italy's population; they worked the mines and fields, staffed the households, and had no standing in law. Aristotle had taught that some people are “slaves by nature,” and Roman law treated the slave as a res , a thing. Christianity possessed no armies and no legislature; it could not overturn Rome's economy by decree. What it did instead was subvert the idea on which the whole system rested — that the slave was less than a man. Saint Paul declares that in Christ the deepest human divisions, slavery among them, are abolished at the level where they matter most: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Galatians 3:28 (ESV) He tells slaves who can gain their freedom to take it, and warns believers against selling themselves into bondage: “Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it.

(But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)… You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men.” 1 Corinthians 7:21–23 (ESV) He lists slave-traders — literally “men-stealers” — among the worst of sinners, alongside murderers, echoing the death penalty of Exodus: “…the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient… enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine.” 1 Timothy 1:9–10 (ESV) The clearest picture is the little letter to Philemon. Paul sends back the runaway slave Onesimus — but asks the master, with all his apostolic weight, to receive him no longer as a slave: “…no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother … both in the flesh and in the Lord. So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me.” Philemon 16–17 (ESV) This liberating word did not begin with Paul.

Christ opened his own ministry by claiming Isaiah's proclamation of release as his mission: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed.” Luke 4:18 (ESV) The Apostles then turned the ancient hierarchy on its head, warning masters that they stand under the same Lord and the same judgment as their slaves: “Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him.” Ephesians 6:9 (ESV) “Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.” Colossians 4:1 (ESV) Saint James cries out against those who grow rich by defrauding their labourers, declaring that the very wages withheld accuse them before God: “Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have

reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.” James 5:4 (ESV) And at the end of the Bible, the traffic in human beings is numbered among the merchandise of doomed Babylon — the last item in her cargo, named for what it truly is: “…cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.” Revelation 18:13 (ESV) A master who must greet his slave as he would greet the Apostle Paul — as a brother, an equal, a son — no longer really has a slave at all. This is how the Gospel worked on slavery: not by a slogan of revolt, which would have drowned the young Church in blood and left the institution intact, but by dissolving from within the belief that made slavery thinkable.

Voices of the Fathers Far from “defending” slavery, the greatest Fathers — and above all the Oriental Fathers of Egypt and Cappadocia — attacked it at the root. The most radical condemnation of slavery to survive from the ancient world came not from a philosopher but from a Cappadocian bishop, a Father shared by all the ancient churches. Saint Gregory of Nyssa (d. c. 394), preaching in Cappadocia, gives what historians often describe as the earliest surviving condemnation of slavery itself as sinful — not merely its abuses, but the ownership of any human being: St Gregory of Nyssa (d. c. 394) “‘I got me slaves and slave-girls,’ he says… You condemn man to slavery, when his nature is free and possesses free will, and you legislate in competition with God, overturning his law for the human species. … What did you find in existence worth as much as this human nature? … How many obols did you reckon the equivalent of the likeness of God? … God said, Let us make man in our own image and likeness.” Homily 4 on Ecclesiastes (trans.

Hall & Moriarty) Direct quote He grounds the argument where Scripture does — in the image of God and the redemption of Christ, who freed the whole race from bondage and would never re-enslave it: St Gregory of Nyssa (d. c. 394) “God would not therefore reduce the human race to slavery, since he himself, when we had been enslaved to sin, spontaneously recalled us to freedom. But if God does not enslave what is free, who is he that sets his own power above God’s?” Homily 4 on Ecclesiastes (trans. Hall & Moriarty) Direct quote Saint John Chrysostom (d. 407), Archbishop of Constantinople and son of Antioch, taught that slavery is no part of God's order but a consequence of sin, and that in Christ it is emptied of meaning: St John Chrysostom (d. 407) “Slavery is the fruit of covetousness, of degradation, of savagery; since Noah, we know, had no servant, nor had Abel, nor Seth, no, nor they who came after them. The thing was the fruit of sin.” Homily 22 on Ephesians ( NPNF 1st ser., vol. 13 ) Direct quote St John Chrysostom (d.

407) “He is a brother, or rather he has become a brother, he enjoys the same privileges, he belongs to the same body. Yea, more, he is the brother, not of his own master only, but also of the Son of God.” Homily 22 on Ephesians ( NPNF 1st ser., vol. 13 ) Direct quote Saint Gregory the Great (d. 604), Pope of Rome, wrote into his official grant of freedom for two slaves a theology of manumission that treats liberty as man's original and proper state: St Gregory the Great, Pope of Rome (d. 604) “…it is a salutary deed if men, whom nature originally produced free, and whom the law of nations has subjected to the yoke of slavery, be restored by the benefit of manumission to the liberty in which they were born.” Register of Letters VI.12 (trans. NPNF 2nd ser., vol. 12 ) Direct quote These are not fringe voices. Gregory of Nyssa is a Father of the Second Ecumenical Council; Chrysostom is among the most beloved teachers of the whole Church, East and West; Gregory the Great is a Doctor of the Church.

When the critic says “the Fathers supported slavery,” these are the very Fathers he must answer. Nor do they stand alone. From the earliest days the Church taught, in an unbroken chorus stretching across every century and both East and West, that master and slave are equals before God, that redeeming captives is the highest charity, and that man was never meant to own man. The witnesses below are arranged in order of time. The Didache (1st–2nd c.) “You shall not enjoin anything in your bitterness upon your bondman or maidservant, who hope in the same God, lest ever they shall fear not God who is over both; for he comes not to call according to the outward appearance, but unto them whom the Spirit has prepared.” Didache 4 ( ANF vol. 7 ) Direct quote St Clement of Alexandria (d. c. 215) “Domestics, too, are to be treated like ourselves; for they are human beings, as we are. For God is the same to free and bond, if you consider.” The Instructor (Paedagogus) III.12 ( ANF vol. 2 ) Direct quote St Cyprian of Carthage (d.

258) “The captivity of our brethren must be reckoned as our captivity… Christ is to be contemplated in our captive brethren, and He is to be redeemed from the peril of captivity who redeemed us from the peril of death.” Epistle 59, to the Numidian Bishops ( ANF vol. 5 ) Direct quote St Basil the Great (d. 379) “Among men no one is a slave by nature… even though one man be called master and another servant, nevertheless, both in view of our mutual equality of rank and as chattels of our Creator, we are all fellow slaves.” On the Holy Spirit XX.51 ( NPNF 2nd ser., vol. 8 ) Direct quote St Gregory of Nyssa (d. c. 394) “You are condemning to slavery human beings whose nature is free and characterised by free will… Have you forgotten the limits of your authority? Your rule is limited to control of irrational creatures… How then do you… exalt yourself against a nature which is free, counting people like you among four-footed or footless creatures?” Homily 4 on Ecclesiastes (trans. Maguire) Direct quote St Ambrose of Milan (d.

397) “The highest kind of liberality is to redeem captives, to save them from the hands of their enemies, to snatch men from death, and, most of all, women from shame.” On the Duties of the Clergy II.15 ( NPNF 2nd ser., vol. 10 ) Direct quote The Apostolic Constitutions (4th c.) “Such sums of money as are collected from them in the manner aforesaid, appoint to be laid out in the redemption of the saints, the deliverance of slaves, and of captives, and of prisoners, and of those that have been abused, and of those that have been condemned by tyrants.” Apostolic Constitutions IV.9 ( ANF vol. 7 ) Direct quote St Augustine of Hippo (d. 430) “He did not intend that His rational creature, who was made in His image, should have dominion over anything but the irrational creation — not man over man, but man over the beasts.” City of God XIX.15 ( NPNF 1st ser., vol. 2 ) Direct quote St Augustine of Hippo (d.

430) “The prime cause, then, of slavery is sin, which brings man under the dominion of his fellow… by nature, as God first created us, no one is the slave either of man or of sin.” In fairness, Augustine goes on in the same chapter to call slavery a just penalty in a fallen world and to urge slaves to serve faithfully; he did not call for its abolition. City of God XIX.15 ( NPNF 1st ser., vol. 2 ) Direct quote St Patrick of Ireland (d. c. 461) “You betray the members of Christ as if in a brothel” (tr. Liam de Paor). Patrick, himself once a slave, wrote against a British chieftain whose soldiers had seized newly baptized Irish converts. Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus Direct quote

secs.h: “But the Fathers and Popes owned slaves…”
secs.x: “But the Fathers and Popes owned slaves…” Honesty requires facing the hardest form of the charge, not the easiest. Some Christians did own slaves, some Fathers did counsel slaves to obey, and some medieval Popes did sanction enslavement. None of this is hidden here. Didn’t Paul and the Fathers tell slaves to obey their masters? Yes — and in a world where slave revolts (like Spartacus’) ended in mass crucifixion, telling powerless people to remain peaceful was pastoral realism, not approval of the system. In the same breath Paul tells masters to stop threatening and to remember they too have a Master in heaven who shows “no partiality” (Ephesians 6:9), tells slaves to take freedom if they can get it (1 Corinthians 7:21), and asks one master to receive his slave as a brother (Philemon 16). Counselling patience to the weak while dismantling the ideology of the strong is not an endorsement of slavery; it is the only strategy available to a movement with no political power.

secs.h: “But the Fathers and Popes owned slaves…”
secs.x: Did the Church Fathers really accept slavery as normal? Some, writing pastorally, addressed slaves and masters as they found them, and Church institutions, including monasteries, themselves held slaves for centuries. Apart from Gregory of Nyssa, even the Fathers quoted on this page did not call for the institution to be abolished. But the Church's leading theologians went far beyond their era: Gregory of Nyssa condemned slave-owning as rebellion against God, Chrysostom called it the fruit of sin, and Gregory the Great treated freedom as man's birthright. Few comparable voices exist in Greek or Roman literature (the Jewish Essenes, as Philo describes them, also refused to own slaves). The trajectory of patristic thought is unmistakably against slavery, not for it — which is why, over the long run, slavery receded where that mind took hold. Didn’t the Popes authorise slavery and the slave trade? The record of the Renaissance Papacy is genuinely mixed and, at its worst, shameful.

secs.h: “But the Fathers and Popes owned slaves…”
secs.x: In Dum Diversas (1452) Pope Nicholas V granted Portugal leave to subdue “the Saracens and pagans and any other unbelievers and enemies of Christ” and “to reduce their persons into perpetual servitude.” Issued as Portugal was raiding the West African coast, it gave papal cover to the Portuguese slave trade there, and Romanus Pontifex (1455) confirmed it. Yet the same office also produced the opposite: in Sublimis Deus (1537) Pope Paul III declared that the native peoples of the Americas “are by no means to be deprived of their liberty… even though they be outside the faith,” are “truly men,” and must not be enslaved. In 1839 Pope Gregory XVI, in In Supremo Apostolatus , condemned the slave trade outright and forbade any Catholic to defend it. The Papacy's failures are real; they are also the failures of one particular Western jurisdiction, entangled in the politics of Portugal, Spain, and the Papal States — and even there the Church's own conscience kept rising against the practice.

secs.h: “But the Fathers and Popes owned slaves…”
secs.x: What does this have to do with the Oriental Orthodox? Less than with the Western churches, but not nothing. The Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian, and Indian Churches were never part of the Papal apparatus that issued those bulls, held no colonial empires, and ran no Atlantic trade. Honesty requires one exception: the Christian empire of Ethiopia kept slavery and a slave trade, often enslaving peoples of its southern and western borderlands, until Haile Selassie decreed gradual emancipation in the 1920s and finally abolished slavery in 1942. Even so, for most of the second millennium most Oriental Christians were not slave- owners but slave- victims , living under Islamic rule and subject to the raids, tributes, and levies described below. To indict “the Church” for the Atlantic trade is to name a very specific Western chapter — and to pass over in silence the Eastern Christians who bore the lash rather than held it.

How Christianity Ended Slavery Slavery is as old as civilisation and was found on every continent. What has to be explained is not its existence but its abolition as a moral cause: the movement that ended slavery across whole civilisations arose in Christendom, driven overwhelmingly by Christians appealing to Christian principles. The pattern begins early. As the Church grew, freeing slaves became an act of piety; manumissions were performed in church before the bishop, and wealthy Christians freed slaves by the thousands as works of mercy. Chattel slavery in the medieval Christian West gradually gave way to serfdom and then to free labour, until by the High Middle Ages chattel slavery had largely vanished from northwestern Europe. It did not vanish everywhere: around the Mediterranean, Christian Spain, Italy and the merchant republics of Venice and Genoa kept slaves and traded them, including Muslims and Orthodox Christians from the Black Sea. When slavery revived through the Atlantic trade, it was again Christians who led the fight to destroy it.

The English abolition movement was founded and carried by devout believers — the Evangelical William Wilberforce, the former slave-trader John Newton who wrote “Amazing Grace,” the Quakers, and countless clergy — who argued from the image of God and the brotherhood of man that no Christian could hold another. Their campaign ended the British slave trade in 1807 and slavery across the Empire in 1833. In America the abolitionist cause was likewise saturated with Christian preaching and Scripture. Honesty requires adding that slaveholders also quoted the Bible, and American churches split over slavery (the Southern Baptists separated in 1845); the abolitionists won the argument from Scripture, but they had to fight other Christians to do it. The abolitionists were doing consciously and politically what Gregory of Nyssa had done theologically fourteen centuries earlier: measuring slavery against the image of God in man and the freedom Christ purchased, and finding it condemned. No other civilisation produced a comparable abolition movement from within.
The idea that every human being bears God's image and is a brother for whom Christ died — the specifically Christian idea — is the ground on which slavery was finally judged and abolished.

The Islamic Slave Trade The Atlantic trade is rightly remembered with horror. Less remembered — though far longer in duration, and ended largely under outside pressure (Tunisia's abolition of 1846 was an early exception) — is the Islamic slave trade, under which the Oriental Christians themselves lived and suffered. Any honest history of slavery must include it. Beginning in the seventh century and continuing into the twentieth, the trans-Saharan, Red Sea, and Indian Ocean slave routes carried an estimated ten to eighteen million Africans into the Muslim world over some thirteen centuries — a traffic that ran far longer than the roughly four centuries of the Atlantic trade. Europeans, too, were seized: by one historian's estimate (Robert Davis), the Barbary corsairs of North Africa enslaved on the order of a million Christians from Mediterranean coasts and ships between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries. Two features stand out.

First, male captives were frequently castrated to serve as eunuchs, a mutilation with a mortality so high that the surviving numbers represent a fraction of those taken. Second, under the Ottoman devshirme or “blood tax,” Christian families in the Balkans and Anatolia were forced to surrender their sons — boys taken from Orthodox homes, converted to Islam, and raised as Janissary soldiers or palace servants. For the Christians of the East, slavery was not a distant institution to be studied but a standing threat under which whole communities lived for a thousand years. None of this excuses the sins of Western Christians in the Atlantic trade. It does correct a lopsided picture — one in which slavery is imagined as a peculiarly Christian or Western crime, when in truth Christian civilisation was the first to abolish it, and Christian peoples were among its most enduring victims.

The Oriental Christian Witness The Oriental Orthodox — the Copts of Egypt, the Ethiopians, the Syriacs, the Armenians, and the Malankara Christians of India — stand at a particular angle to this whole history, and it is a witness worth naming. They share with all the ancient churches the most uncompromising ancient opponent of slavery, Saint Gregory of Nyssa, and the great Egyptian and Antiochene teachers of the equal brotherhood of slave and free. Apart from the long survival of slavery in Christian Ethiopia, they never held a colonial empire, ran no Atlantic trade, and issued no bulls of enslavement; the failures of the medieval Western Papacy are simply not theirs to answer for. And for the greater part of the last fourteen centuries they lived not as masters but as a subject people under Islamic rule, exposed to the raids, the child-levies, and the slave markets described above. This is why the history matters for Oriental Christians in particular.

The charge that “Christianity upheld slavery” collapses the whole Church into one Western chapter and then reads even that chapter selectively. The fuller truth is that the faith which the world accuses of chaining men is the faith that first called them all brothers — and the Oriental Churches, which for most of their history bore the chains rather than forged them, are a living witness to it.

Frequently Asked Questions If slavery is wrong, why didn’t God simply forbid it outright? God’s way with a fallen world is often to plant a principle and let it grow, rather than to impose a rule an age cannot yet bear (cf. Matthew 19:8 on divorce). Scripture forbids the slave trade outright — man-stealing was a capital crime — and then sows the deeper seed, the image of God and the brotherhood of all in Christ, which in time uprooted the institution itself. A bare prohibition dropped into the ancient economy would have been ignored; a new vision of the human person reshaped civilisation. Was biblical “slavery” the same as Atlantic slavery? No. For Hebrews it was closer to indentured or contract labour: time-limited, debt-based, released with generous provision, and protected by law. It was not race-based and not permanent for fellow Israelites (though foreign slaves could be held permanently, Leviticus 25:44–46), and — crucially — could not be fed by kidnapping, since man-stealing carried the death penalty.

The Atlantic system, built on the mass abduction of a targeted race for perpetual, hereditary bondage, is precisely what the Law of Moses made a capital crime. Doesn’t the very existence of slave laws prove God endorsed it? Regulation is not endorsement. Law meets people where they are in order to move them somewhere better: the Mosaic code took the brutal chattel slavery of the ancient Near East and, for Israel, hedged it with sabbaths, jubilees, release years, and protections unknown to any neighbouring nation — while forbidding the trade that fed it. The direction of the Law is toward freedom, not away from it. Why bring up the Islamic slave trade — isn’t that changing the subject? It is part of the same subject: the honest history of human bondage. The popular charge singles out Christianity while passing over the longest slave trade in history, under which Eastern Christians were themselves victims. Naming it is not deflection; it is refusing a double standard and restoring the whole picture — in which Christian civilisation is the one that produced abolition.

Glossary Chattel slavery The ownership of human beings as permanent, saleable property with no rights — the system of Egypt, Rome, and the Atlantic trade. Indentured / bond service Time-limited labour to repay a debt, ending in release — closer to the Hebrew servitude regulated by the Law of Moses. Man-stealing Kidnapping a person to enslave or sell. A capital crime in the Law (Exodus 21:16) and condemned by Paul (1 Timothy 1:10). Manumission The formal freeing of a slave. In the Church it became an act of piety, often performed before a bishop. Jubilee The fiftieth year in Israel (Leviticus 25) when debts were cancelled, servants freed, and land restored to families. Devshirme The Ottoman “blood tax”: the forced levy of Christian boys, converted to Islam and raised as soldiers or servants. Barbary corsairs North African raiders who, by one estimate, enslaved on the order of a million European Christians from the 16th–18th centuries. Abolitionism The movement to end slavery, which arose within Christendom, led by believers appealing to the image of God in man.

I. Introduction Sola fide — "faith alone" — is the material principle of the Protestant Reformation. First systematically articulated by Martin Luther (1483–1546) as the article by which the Church stands or falls, it holds that a sinner is justified (declared righteous before God) by faith alone, apart from any works, merits, or sacramental participation. For Luther and subsequent Protestants, the Roman Catholic emphasis on works, merit, and sacraments obscured and undermined the pure grace of God. The Oriental Orthodox tradition — never part of Western Christendom, never subject to the corruptions that provoked the Reformation, and never carrying the baggage of medieval Scholastic theology — approaches this question from a completely different angle. The Oriental Orthodox fully agree that salvation is by God's grace alone and that no human being can earn or merit salvation. But the Oriental Orthodox insist that sola fide as the Reformers defined it is not the teaching of the New Testament, not the teaching of the Church Fathers, and not the teaching of the pre-Reformation Church.

The debate is not: grace vs. works. Both sides affirm grace. The debate is: what is faith? How does faith relate to love, obedience, and the sacraments? Is justification a declaration or a transformation? And what does the whole New Testament — not just Paul's letters in isolation — actually teach about how sinners come to be right with God?

secs.h: II. What Did Paul Mean by "Works of the Law"?
secs.x: II. What Did Paul Mean by "Works of the Law"? The key to understanding Paul's doctrine of justification is identifying what he means by "works of the law" ( erga nomou ) — the works he says do not justify. Luther and the Reformation understood this as "moral effort" or "good deeds" generally. Modern New Testament scholarship has largely corrected this reading. The "works of the law" in Paul's context are the specifically Jewish identity markers — circumcision, dietary laws, Sabbath observance, purity codes — that divided Jews from Gentiles and that some Jewish Christians were requiring Gentile converts to perform in order to be fully accepted. Galatians 2:11–16 CTX "We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ." The immediate context is the dispute over whether Gentile Christians must live like Jews (v.14) — specifically regarding table fellowship and dietary laws (vv.11–13).

secs.h: II. What Did Paul Mean by "Works of the Law"?
secs.x: The "works of the law" Paul rejects are the Jewish boundary markers that Peter was imposing on Gentiles, not moral effort in general. This is confirmed by the specific examples Paul uses throughout Galatians: circumcision (5:2–6), dietary laws, calendar observances (4:10). Romans 3:28–30 CTX "For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law. Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also?" The question "is God the God of Jews only?" immediately after the justification statement confirms that the issue is Jewish/Gentile inclusion — the ethnic boundary markers of the Mosaic law — not moral effort in general. Paul's point is that Gentiles can be right with God through faith in Christ without becoming Jews. This is the liberating gospel of Galatians: Gentiles do not need to be circumcised to be saved. Ephesians 2:8–10 CTX "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.

secs.h: II. What Did Paul Mean by "Works of the Law"?
secs.x: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them." Paul's most famous grace-faith-not-works statement is immediately followed by: "created for good works, which God prepared that we should walk in them." The rejection of "works" as the basis of salvation does not eliminate good works as the fruit and purpose of salvation. The Oriental Orthodox reading: we are not saved by works, but we are saved for works. Works are the necessary outcome of genuine saving faith, not the basis of it. Philippians 3:6–9 CTX "As to righteousness under the law, blameless. But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ… that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law." Paul's personal testimony: his pre-Christian "righteousness under the law" was the specific Jewish covenantal status he held as a Pharisee — circumcised, of the tribe of Benjamin, a persecutor of the Church. This is not general moral effort but Jewish covenantal identity.

secs.h: II. What Did Paul Mean by "Works of the Law"?
secs.x: What he counts as loss is his Jewish status-righteousness; what he gains is union with Christ — a very different category from moral effort as such.

secs.h: III. The Oriental Orthodox Understanding of Justification
secs.x: III. The Oriental Orthodox Understanding of Justification The Oriental Orthodox tradition, rooted in the Alexandrian and Antiochene theological schools, understands salvation not primarily as a legal transaction (guilty person declared righteous by a judge) but as a healing and transformative participation in the divine nature. These are not mutually exclusive categories, but they produce very different theological emphases. Protestant Sola Fide Justification is a forensic (legal) declaration: God declares the sinner righteous on the basis of Christ's imputed righteousness, received by faith alone. Justification is a single, complete, instantaneous event — a change of legal status, not of moral character. Sanctification (actual moral transformation) is separate from and subsequent to justification. Oriental Orthodox View Salvation (theosis/divinization) is a dynamic process of healing and union with God, not merely a legal declaration. Christ does not merely provide a legal cover for sin; he heals, transforms, and divinizes human nature.

secs.h: III. The Oriental Orthodox Understanding of Justification
secs.x: Faith is not merely intellectual assent or trust but a living, active, loving union with Christ — inseparable from love (Galatians 5:6: "faith working through love"). The Oriental Orthodox are not Pelagians or semi-Pelagians — they do not teach that humans earn salvation by their own moral effort. The entire tradition from Cyril of Alexandria to the present insists that salvation is from first to last God's gracious gift. But they equally insist that God's grace is not merely declaratory — it actually changes the one who receives it. A faith that leaves the believer unchanged is not saving faith.

secs.h: IV. James 2 — The Apostolic Rebuke of Sola Fide
secs.x: IV. James 2 — The Apostolic Rebuke of Sola Fide The most direct New Testament critique of "faith alone" is James 2:14–26 — a passage so uncomfortable for Luther that he famously called the Epistle of James "a right strawy epistle" and questioned its canonicity. The Oriental Orthodox, whose canon was not determined by the Reformation, receive James as fully authoritative Scripture. James 2:14 OO "What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?" James explicitly asks: can "faith" without works save? The Greek implies the expected answer is "no." This is not a hypothetical; James is addressing an actual error — a claim to have faith that is not accompanied by works. The Oriental Orthodox reading: such a faith is not genuine saving faith; it is a dead intellectual assent. James 2:17 OO "So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead." "Faith by itself" — kath heautēn , "alone" — is dead. This is as close to a direct denial of sola fide as Scripture gets.

secs.h: IV. James 2 — The Apostolic Rebuke of Sola Fide
secs.x: A faith that stands alone, without works, is not merely weak or immature — it is dead. Dead things do not save. James 2:19 OO "You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe — and shudder!" Demons have correct theological beliefs and even an appropriate emotional response (fear/shuddering) — yet they are not saved. This demolishes any definition of "faith" that is merely intellectual or emotional. Saving faith must be something more than right belief about God. It must include trust, love, and obedience — the active orientation of the whole person toward God. James 2:24 OO "You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone." The only place in the entire Bible where "faith alone" appears — and it denies it. James 2:24 is the single verse where the exact phrase "faith alone" ( pisteos monon ) occurs in Scripture, and it says justification is NOT by faith alone. This is the verse the Reformation had to explain away; the Oriental Orthodox receive it at face value.

secs.h: IV. James 2 — The Apostolic Rebuke of Sola Fide
secs.x: James 2:26 OO "For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead." James's concluding analogy: a faith without works is like a body without a spirit — technically the right thing, but dead, inert, incapable of saving action. Works are to faith what the spirit is to the body — not an add-on but the animating principle that makes faith alive and effective. This is the Oriental Orthodox understanding: works are faith in action.

secs.h: V. Faith and Works Together — The Whole New Testament
secs.x: V. Faith and Works Together — The Whole New Testament Galatians 5:6 OO "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love." Paul's own definition of the operative faith: "faith working through love" ( pistis di agapēs energoumenē ). The faith that matters in Christ is not solitary, inert belief but faith that is energized and expressed through love. This is the Oriental Orthodox "synergy" — not human effort supplementing divine grace, but human love as the natural and necessary expression of genuine faith in God who is love. Matthew 25:31–46 OO "For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink… 'Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.'" Christ's description of the Last Judgment makes concrete works of mercy the criterion of entry into the kingdom — not a profession of faith, not correct doctrine.

secs.h: V. Faith and Works Together — The Whole New Testament
secs.x: The Oriental Orthodox do not read this as works-based salvation; they read it as Christ defining what genuine faith in him actually looks like in practice. Those who truly know Christ naturally serve him in the poor and suffering. 1 John 3:14 OO "We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death." John gives the criterion for knowing one has "passed out of death into life" — love for the brothers. Not a doctrine of imputation, not a moment of faith-decision, but the ongoing practice of love. This is typical of John's theology: genuine relationship with God always manifests in concrete love. The one who claims faith but does not love "abides in death" — unchanged, unsaved.

secs.h: V. Faith and Works Together — The Whole New Testament
secs.x: Revelation 20:12–13 OO "And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done… And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one of them, according to what they had done." The final judgment in Revelation is explicitly according to "what they had done" — deeds, works, actions. Not doctrine alone. Not faith-statement alone. The whole life of the person stands before God. The Oriental Orthodox reading: genuine faith produces a whole life of faithful response to God that will stand at the judgment — not because it earns merit, but because it is the authentic expression of the saving union with Christ. Romans 2:6–7 CTX "He will render to each one according to his works: to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life." Paul himself — in the very letter that contains his doctrine of justification by faith — says God renders to each according to works and gives eternal life to those who patiently do well.

secs.h: V. Faith and Works Together — The Whole New Testament
secs.x: The Reformation reading creates a tension within Paul's own letter that the Oriental Orthodox reading — where faith and works are inseparable — does not face.

secs.h: VI. Theosis and Synergy — The Eastern Alternative
secs.x: VI. Theosis and Synergy — The Eastern Alternative The Oriental Orthodox tradition offers a different framework for understanding salvation — not the legal/forensic framework of Western theology (whether Catholic merit or Protestant imputation), but the participatory/transformative framework of the Eastern tradition: theosis (deification) and synergy (cooperation). Theosis — St. Athanasius (c. AD 296–373): "He was made man that we might be made God" (On the Incarnation 54, NPNF). The goal of salvation is not merely legal pardon but genuine transformation — the believer becoming, by grace, a participant in the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). This is not pantheism; the Creator-creature distinction is never abolished. But it is genuine transformation: the human person is healed, renewed, and elevated into an increasingly intimate union with God. Synergy — God and the human person cooperate in salvation — not as equals, but as the infinite God graciously working with and through finite human freedom.

secs.h: VI. Theosis and Synergy — The Eastern Alternative
secs.x: God's grace enables, initiates, and sustains every step; human cooperation is itself a gift of grace. St. Paul: "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me" (1 Cor 15:10). Paul works and the grace of God works — inseparably. In this framework, the question is not "faith alone vs. works" but "is the believer genuinely united with Christ?" A genuine union with Christ necessarily produces love, obedience, and good works — not as meritorious achievements but as the natural outpouring of a life actually transformed by the living God.

secs.h: VII. The Church Fathers on Faith and Salvation
secs.x: VII. The Church Fathers on Faith and Salvation St. Clement of Rome (c. AD 35–99) 1 Clement, Chapter 31 — c. AD 96 "Let us cleave then to His blessing, and consider what are the means of possessing it. Let us think over the things which have taken place from the beginning. For what reason was our father Abraham blessed? Was it not because he wrought righteousness and truth through faith?" Significance: Clement describes Abraham's faith as inseparable from "righteousness and truth" — it is a faith that acts, not a purely interior disposition. This integration of faith and righteous action characterizes the entire patristic tradition and stands against any separation of "faith" from its behavioral expression. St. John Chrysostom (c. AD 347–407) Homily 4 on 1 Timothy; Homily 1 on Ephesians — c.

secs.h: VII. The Church Fathers on Faith and Salvation
secs.x: AD 390s "What then was it that was thought incredible? That those who were enemies, and sinners, neither justified by the law, nor by works, should immediately through faith alone be advanced to the highest favor." … "That you may not then, when you hear that He has chosen us, imagine that faith alone is sufficient, he proceeds to add life and conduct." VERBATIM — NPNF Significance: Chrysostom uses the phrase "faith alone" himself: sinners are justified apart from the works of the law, by faith. Yet in the same breath he refuses to let "faith alone" mean that a holy life is optional. Justification is the free gift; "life and conduct" are what that gift is for. Protestants rightly point to the first passage; the Orthodox insist it be read with the second. St. Basil the Great (c. AD 330–379) On Faith — c. AD 375 Summary: For Basil, faith is not bare assent of the mind but a living trust that shapes the whole person, thought, desire, and action. Whoever truly believes in Christ does what Christ commanded, and a faith that produces no obedience and love is not yet the faith that saves.

secs.h: VII. The Church Fathers on Faith and Salvation
secs.x: SUMMARY Significance: Basil's definition of faith as a holistic orientation of the whole person — encompassing mind, will, and action — reflects the Eastern patristic consensus. "Faith" in the Eastern tradition is not a category of the intellect alone but of the entire human person in relationship with God. A faith that leaves the will and actions unchanged has not yet reached the living God. St. Cyril of Alexandria (c. AD 376–444) Commentary on John 6:29 — c. AD 425 Summary: Cyril reads "this is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent" as not excluding all work, but as showing that the work God requires and approves is faith in Christ, a faith that then expresses itself in love and obedience. SUMMARY Significance: Cyril reads John 6:29 — "this is the work of God, that you believe" — as the integration of faith and action: believing IS the supreme work, not an alternative to works. His commentary shows the Eastern patristic pattern: faith and obedience are not competing categories but unified aspects of the single human response to God in Christ.

secs.h: VIII. Protestant vs. Oriental Orthodox — A Comparison
secs.x: VIII. Protestant vs. Oriental Orthodox — A Comparison Protestant Sola Fide Justification: Forensic declaration — God declares the sinner righteous. A change of legal status. Righteousness: Imputed (Christ's righteousness credited to the believer's account). Faith: Primarily trust/confidence in Christ's atoning work. Works: Evidence of salvation, but not part of justification. Good works follow but do not contribute to justification. Sacraments: Signs and seals of grace already received, or memorials. Do not confer grace in themselves (most Protestant views). Oriental Orthodox Salvation: Theosis — healing and transformation into participation in the divine nature. More than a legal declaration. Righteousness: Both imputed AND imparted — Christ's righteousness is given to us and genuinely transforms us. Faith: The whole person's living union with Christ — includes trust, love, and obedience (Gal 5:6). Works: The necessary and natural expression of genuine faith — not meritorious but inevitable in the truly saved.

secs.h: VIII. Protestant vs. Oriental Orthodox — A Comparison
secs.x: Sacraments: Real means of grace — vehicles by which the risen Christ acts in and transforms the believer.

IX. Protestant Objections Objection: James and Paul contradict each other — they must be harmonized in favor of Paul The Claim Paul and James use the same example (Abraham, Genesis 15:6) and reach apparently opposite conclusions. Paul says Abraham was justified by faith before his circumcision (Romans 4); James says Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac (James 2:21–23). These must be harmonized — James must be speaking of the demonstration of pre-existing justification, not a separate justification event. Response The Oriental Orthodox read Paul and James as complementary — addressing different errors, not contradicting each other. Paul addresses the error of thinking that Jewish identity markers (circumcision, dietary laws) are required for Gentile salvation. James addresses the opposite error of thinking that correct theological belief with no behavioral change constitutes saving faith. Both are right: Gentile Mosaic observance is not required for salvation, AND faith without works is dead.

The apparent contradiction dissolves when we recognize they are fighting different battles. Chrysostom, the greatest patristic commentator on both letters, sees no contradiction. Nor does any pre-Reformation Father. Objection: Adding works to faith makes salvation dependent on human effort and undermines grace The Claim Any role for works in salvation introduces human merit and undermines the total sufficiency of Christ's atoning work. Grace plus anything equals works-salvation. The Oriental Orthodox position makes salvation insecure — how do you know you have done enough? Response This objection conflates two different claims: (1) works as the basis of salvation (Pelagianism — rejected by the Oriental Orthodox), and (2) works as the necessary expression and fruit of genuine saving faith (the Orthodox position). The Oriental Orthodox do not teach that anyone earns or deserves salvation by their works.

They teach that genuine saving faith — the living union with God that the Holy Spirit creates in the believer — necessarily manifests in love and good works, just as a living body necessarily breathes. As for assurance: the Oriental Orthodox do not seek assurance in a past moment of faith-decision but in the ongoing life of repentance, sacramental grace, and love — the "patient well-doing" that Paul himself describes (Romans 2:7). Assurance is not a certificate issued at conversion; it is the fruit of a life increasingly conformed to Christ.

X. Frequently Asked Questions Q: Do the Oriental Orthodox teach that anyone can earn their way to heaven? Absolutely not. The Oriental Orthodox consistently and emphatically teach that salvation is entirely God's gift — from first to last, unearned and undeserved. No human being can place God in their debt. What the Oriental Orthodox reject is not the priority of grace but the Reformation definition of faith as something that stands alone, separate from love and obedience. In Eastern theology, "faith" without love and obedience is not yet faith in the full saving sense — not because love and obedience earn anything, but because genuine saving faith in a living God necessarily transforms the one who has it.

Q: What did Luther mean by adding "alone" to Romans 3:28 in his German translation? Luther's famous 1522 translation of Romans 3:28 added the word "allein" (alone) — "we are justified by faith alone, apart from works of the law" — even though the Greek does not contain the word "alone." Luther defended this addition as necessary for clear German expression of Paul's meaning (Open Letter on Translating, 1530). In fairness, he was not the first to use the phrase: the Catholic scholar Joseph Fitzmyer lists earlier writers, from Origen and Ambrosiaster to Thomas Aquinas, who spoke of justification by faith alone, though they usually meant faith apart from the works of the Mosaic law, not faith set against love and obedience. The Oriental Orthodox point out that: (1) the word is not there; (2) the only place "faith alone" actually appears in the Bible (James 2:24) explicitly denies it; (3) Luther's addition reveals his theological presuppositions driving his translation, not the text driving his theology.

This is not a minor textual note — it is the foundational text of the Reformation, and the word that defines the doctrine is not in the original. In fairness to Luther, the phrase "faith alone" was not his invention: Fathers such as Chrysostom used it (see the card above), though they did not mean by it what the Reformers meant. Q: Is the Oriental Orthodox view the same as the Roman Catholic view on justification? There is significant overlap — both traditions reject sola fide as defined by the Reformers, both affirm the role of sacraments in salvation, and both affirm the necessity of charity/love as intrinsic to saving faith. However, there are also differences: Catholic theology developed in a Scholastic, Aristotelian framework that is foreign to Eastern theology. The Catholic doctrine of merit (meritum de condigno and meritum de congruo), purgatory, indulgences, and the specific Scholastic categories of justification have no place in Oriental Orthodox theology.

The Eastern tradition speaks of theosis, synergy, and the uncreated energies of God — categories that do not map neatly onto either the Protestant or Catholic Western frameworks. The Oriental Orthodox are not crypto-Catholics; they are a genuinely distinct theological tradition.
