I. Introduction Sola Scriptura — "Scripture alone" — is the formal principle of the Protestant Reformation. Articulated by Martin Luther at the Diet of Worms (1521) — "my conscience is captive to the Word of God" — it holds that Scripture alone is the supreme and sufficient authority for Christian doctrine and practice. No tradition, council, pope, or bishop may bind the Christian conscience unless what they teach can be verified by Scripture. The Oriental Orthodox tradition, rooted in the Alexandrian, Antiochene, and Armenian theological schools and representing the faith of the ancient Eastern churches that were never part of Western Christendom, rejects sola scriptura — not because it denigrates Scripture, but because it believes sola scriptura misunderstands the relationship between Scripture, Tradition, and the Church. For the Oriental Orthodox, Scripture is not opposed to Tradition — Scripture is part of Tradition. The biblical texts were written within the Church, for the Church, and were recognized by the Church.

The same Spirit who inspired the authors of Scripture also guides the Church in interpreting it. Scripture and Tradition are not two separate sources of authority competing for supremacy; they are two expressions of the single apostolic deposit of faith.

secs.h: II. What Is Sola Scriptura? — The Protestant Claim
secs.x: II. What Is Sola Scriptura? — The Protestant Claim It is important to distinguish the strong and weak forms of sola scriptura as articulated within Protestantism itself: Strong Sola Scriptura: Scripture is the only authority for Christian doctrine. Tradition, councils, and creeds have no independent authority — they are useful only insofar as they accurately reflect Scripture, and every Christian may judge for themselves whether they do. This is the position of many Baptist and evangelical traditions. Weak Sola Scriptura (Prima Scriptura): Scripture is the supreme authority, but tradition, councils, and creeds have derivative authority as witnesses to the correct interpretation of Scripture. This is the position of Reformed and Lutheran confessional Protestantism. The Westminster Confession, the Augsburg Confession, etc. have real authority — but always subject to correction by Scripture. Both forms, the Oriental Orthodox argue, face fatal problems — the "canon problem" and the "interpretation problem" — which ultimately undermine themselves.

secs.h: III. The Oriental Orthodox View — Scripture Within Tradition
secs.x: III. The Oriental Orthodox View — Scripture Within Tradition The Oriental Orthodox do not place Tradition alongside or above Scripture as a separate, competing authority. Rather, they understand Scripture as the written core of the one apostolic Tradition. The Tradition encompasses: the Scriptures themselves, the Creeds and councils, the liturgical life of the Church, the writings of the Fathers, and the ongoing life of the Spirit in the Body of Christ. St. Basil the Great (c. AD 330–379) articulated the standard Eastern position: "Of the beliefs and practices whether generally accepted or publicly enjoined which are preserved in the Church some we possess derived from written teaching; others we have received delivered to us in a mystery by the tradition of the apostles; and both of these in relation to true religion have the same force." ( On the Holy Spirit , ch. 27) The apostolic Tradition was transmitted in two modes from the beginning: written (the letters of Paul, the Gospels, etc.) and oral (the preaching, the liturgy, the sacramental practice).

secs.h: III. The Oriental Orthodox View — Scripture Within Tradition
secs.x: These were not two separate streams but two aspects of the one apostolic deposit. The Church — guided by the Holy Spirit — recognized the written texts as Scripture precisely because they recognized them as faithful expressions of the same apostolic faith they already held and practiced.

IV. Scripture Commands Tradition Remarkably, the Bible itself explicitly commands Christians to hold to tradition — not Scripture alone. This is rarely noted in Protestant discussions of sola scriptura . 2 Thessalonians 2:15 OO "So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter." Paul explicitly commands holding to traditions transmitted both in writing ("our letter") AND orally ("our spoken word"). The two modes of transmission — written and oral — are placed on equal footing. Paul does not say "hold only to our letters"; he says hold to everything we taught you, by whatever means. This directly contradicts sola scriptura : Paul himself insists that his oral tradition carries the same authority as his written letters. 2 Timothy 2:2 OO "And what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also." The apostolic teaching is transmitted through a chain of persons — from Paul to Timothy to faithful men to others.

This is the living oral tradition of the Church. Paul does not say "write it all down and give everyone a Bible." He describes a human, ecclesial chain of transmission that is distinct from (though consistent with) the written texts. 1 Corinthians 11:2 OO "Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you." Paul commends the Corinthians for maintaining the traditions as he delivered them — this is the language of formal transmission ( paradosis/paralambanō ), the same technical language used throughout the Eastern tradition for the handing-on of the apostolic deposit. The traditions Paul delivered were both oral and sacramental, not merely written. John 21:25 CTX "Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written." John explicitly acknowledges that the written Gospels do not capture the totality of Jesus' teaching and actions.

The Church possesses more than what was written down — and this "more" is the living tradition: the liturgy, the sacramental practices, the oral teachings preserved in the episcopal succession. Scripture itself points beyond itself to a living, unwritten tradition. 2 John 1:12 CTX "Though I have much to write to you, I would rather not use paper and ink. Instead I hope to come to you and talk face to face, so that our joy may be complete." The Apostle John deliberately withholds teaching from the written letter, preferring to transmit it face-to-face. This is not laziness — it reflects the apostolic conviction that the full deposit of faith is communicated through personal presence and oral instruction, not only through writing. The preference for personal, living transmission over the written text is an implicit critique of sola scriptura's exclusive focus on the written word.

secs.h: V. The Canon Problem — Scripture Cannot Define Itself
secs.x: V. The Canon Problem — Scripture Cannot Define Itself The most fundamental problem with sola scriptura is the canon problem: sola scriptura requires knowing which books are Scripture — but Scripture itself does not contain a list of its own books. The 27-book New Testament canon was determined not by the New Testament but by the Church, through a gradual process of discernment, conciliar discussion, and episcopal consensus that culminated in the late 4th century. The key councils that defined the New Testament canon were: the Council of Laodicea (c. AD 360), the Synod of Hippo (AD 393), and the Third Council of Carthage (AD 397). The bishops who made these determinations were the same bishops who practiced and defended the full sacramental, episcopal, creedal tradition of the Church — the tradition that Protestants reject as non-binding. This creates an irresolvable inconsistency for sola scriptura : the Protestant accepts the canon on the authority of the Church's tradition, then rejects the Church's tradition as non-binding because "Scripture alone" is the authority.

secs.h: V. The Canon Problem — Scripture Cannot Define Itself
secs.x: But which Scripture? The Scripture the Church defined. The Protestant accepts the product of the tradition while rejecting the tradition that produced it. In fairness, classical Protestants answer that they do not reject tradition, only its claim to be infallible. On their view the Church did not make the canon but recognised books that already carried the marks of apostolic authority, as a witness recognises a voice; the Church's judgment was faithful, but it was a judgment under Scripture, not over it. The Orthodox reply is that the same Church, with the same authority and in the same centuries, also recognised the liturgy, the episcopate and the creeds, and that it is arbitrary to trust its discernment in the one case and not the others. Furthermore, different Christian traditions have different canons: the Protestant canon (66 books), the Catholic canon (73 books), the Eastern Orthodox canon (varies, generally larger), and the Oriental Orthodox canon (the Ethiopian Church has 81 books — the largest canon in Christendom).

secs.h: V. The Canon Problem — Scripture Cannot Define Itself
secs.x: If Scripture alone were sufficient, we would expect agreement on which books constitute Scripture. Instead we find centuries of disagreement resolved only by — the Church's tradition.

secs.h: VI. The Interpretation Problem — Scripture Cannot Interpret Itself
secs.x: VI. The Interpretation Problem — Scripture Cannot Interpret Itself Even granting agreement on the canon, sola scriptura faces a second fatal problem: Scripture requires interpretation, and interpreters disagree. If Scripture alone is the supreme and sufficient authority, and individual Christians read it and reach different conclusions, who adjudicates? Classical Protestantism does not answer "every man for himself": Lutherans and Reformed read Scripture within their confessions and the ancient creeds, and hold that Scripture interprets Scripture, its clear passages governing the obscure. But when confessions themselves disagree, there is no authority above them except the reader's judgment of Scripture. The result is visible in history: from the single principle of sola scriptura in 1521, Protestantism has divided into a great many separate bodies, each claiming to follow Scripture and disagreeing with the others on the nature of Baptism, the Eucharist, church government, predestination, and other issues.

secs.h: VI. The Interpretation Problem — Scripture Cannot Interpret Itself
secs.x: (The often-quoted figure of 30,000 or more counts every independent body in every country, Catholic and Orthodox ones included, so it overstates doctrinal division; the real number of distinct Protestant traditions is far smaller, but the disagreements among them are real and lasting.) That is the historical result of applying sola scriptura over five centuries. The Oriental Orthodox approach is different: the authoritative interpretation of Scripture belongs to the Church — specifically to the bishops in council as the successors of the Apostles. The Ecumenical Councils (Nicaea, Ephesus, etc.) did not impose meanings on Scripture from outside; they articulated the Church's consistent, received understanding of Scripture against heretical novelties. The Council of Nicaea did not invent the Trinity; it defended the apostolic understanding of Christ against Arius's novel interpretation.

secs.h: The Argument from Silence — and What Counts as Legitimate Development
secs.x: The Argument from Silence — and What Counts as Legitimate Development The most common instrument the skeptic reaches for is the argument from silence : "the New Testament does not mention this practice, therefore it is a later invention" — or, more strongly, "if Scripture does not command it, it is forbidden." Behind this lies an unstated rule, sometimes called the regulative principle : that whatever the Bible does not explicitly authorize is prohibited. Before answering any single doctrine, the rule itself must be examined — because the rule is found nowhere in Scripture . No verse says "only what is written may be believed or practised." By its own standard, then, the principle disqualifies itself: it is an extra-biblical tradition used to forbid extra-biblical tradition. Scripture, in fact, denies its own exhaustiveness.

secs.h: The Argument from Silence — and What Counts as Legitimate Development
secs.x: John tells us plainly that "there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books" (John 21:25), and that the signs recorded were only "not written in this book" (John 20:30). Paul commands the Thessalonians to "hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle " (2 Thessalonians 2:15) — placing spoken apostolic teaching alongside the letter. He praises the Corinthians for keeping "the ordinances, as I delivered them to you" (1 Corinthians 11:2) and leaves the rest to be "set in order when I come" (1 Corinthians 11:34), and he charges Timothy to entrust the deposit "to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:2). The apostolic deposit is, by the New Testament's own testimony, larger than the New Testament. The principle also collapses under its own selective use.

secs.h: The Argument from Silence — and What Counts as Legitimate Development
secs.x: The New Testament contains no list of which books belong in it, gives no complete order of a Sunday service, and nowhere commands that the canon be closed, yet every Protestant holds a closed canon and an ordered service. (The doctrine of the Trinity is a different case: Protestants rightly answer that it is taught in Scripture even though the word is not, and the Orthodox agree.) If silence proved absence, these would fall first. In practice the argument from silence is wielded against the ancient churches and quietly suspended for the modern believer's own commitments. Where the Burden of Proof Lies For a practice already present in the first centuries, continuity is the natural default and rupture is what must be demonstrated.

secs.h: The Argument from Silence — and What Counts as Legitimate Development
secs.x: When a belief or practice is found everywhere in the ancient world at once — Greek, Latin, Syriac, and Coptic churches alike — with no record of its introduction, no name attached to its invention, and no controversy over its origin, the economical explanation is that it was received from the beginning, not that every church on earth silently and simultaneously adopted the same novelty without anyone noticing. A genuine innovation leaves fingerprints: a date, a promoter, and opponents. Infant baptism, prayers for the departed, and the threefold ministry of bishop-priest-deacon leave no such fingerprints; they are simply there, universally, as far back as the record goes. Legitimate Development Is Not Corruption This does not mean every later formulation is apostolic. The faith was delivered whole and "once for all" (Jude 3), but its articulation sharpens as heresy forces precision. The word homoousios ("of one essence") is not in the Bible, yet Nicaea (325) used it to defend the biblical Christ against Arius.

secs.h: The Argument from Silence — and What Counts as Legitimate Development
secs.x: Theotokos was formally defined in 431; the canon list was settled only in the late fourth century. None of these added a new revelation — each defended the original against a novelty. Vincent of Lérins (cited above) supplied the criterion in AD 434: authentic development grows "in the same doctrine, in the same sense, and in the same meaning," as an infant grows into an adult — the same being matured, not a different creature substituted — and is measured by what has been held "everywhere, always, by all" That criterion cuts in both directions, and this is decisive. It is precisely why the Oriental Orthodox can affirm the developed definitions of Nicaea and Ephesus yet reject later Roman additions such as papal infallibility (1870) or the Immaculate Conception (1854). The test is never "is it later?" but "is it the same seed grown, or a new seed planted?" A doctrine that can be traced in continuity through the undivided Church is development; a doctrine that surfaces at a datable moment as a new article of faith, against the ancient consensus, is innovation.

secs.h: The Argument from Silence — and What Counts as Legitimate Development
secs.x: Silence in the text was never the enemy of the apostolic faith — rupture in the received tradition is.

secs.h: VII. The Church Fathers on Scripture and Tradition
secs.x: VII. The Church Fathers on Scripture and Tradition St. Basil the Great (c. AD 330–379) On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 27 — c. AD 375 "Of the beliefs and practices whether generally accepted or publicly enjoined which are preserved in the Church, some we possess derived from written teaching; others we have received delivered to us in a mystery by the tradition of the apostles; and both of these in relation to true religion have the same force." Significance: Basil is the defining Eastern statement on Scripture and Tradition. "Both have the same force" — written and oral apostolic tradition carry equal authority for piety. Basil then gives specific examples of apostolic traditions not found in Scripture: signing with the cross, facing east in prayer, the epiclesis over the Eucharist. These practices, he insists, are apostolic tradition with full authority even without written documentation. St. Irenaeus of Lyons (c. AD 130–202) Against Heresies, Book III, Chapter 4 — c.

secs.h: VII. The Church Fathers on Scripture and Tradition
secs.x: AD 180 "For how should it be if the apostles themselves had not left us writings? Would it not be necessary, [in that case,] to follow the course of the tradition which they handed down to those to whom they did commit the Churches? To which course many nations of those barbarians who believe in Christ do assent, having salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit, without paper or ink, and, carefully preserving the ancient tradition." Significance: Irenaeus imagines a Church without written Scripture and asks: would such a Church be without authority? His answer is no — the apostolic tradition in the Church would be sufficient. He points to actual barbarian peoples who received the faith orally without written Scripture and held it faithfully. Scripture is the written deposit of the apostolic tradition; it is not the only form of that deposit. St. Vincent of Lérins (died c. AD 445) Commonitory, Chapter 2 — c.

secs.h: VII. The Church Fathers on Scripture and Tradition
secs.x: AD 434 "Since the canon of Scripture is complete, and sufficient of itself for everything, and more than sufficient, what need is there to join with it the authority of the Church's interpretation? For this reason — because, owing to the depth of Holy Scripture, all do not accept it in one and the same sense, but one understands its words in one way, another in another." Significance: Vincent articulates precisely the "interpretation problem" of sola scriptura 1,100 years before the Reformation. He acknowledges Scripture's sufficiency in principle — but insists that the Church's interpretive tradition is necessary in practice precisely because individuals read Scripture differently. His famous "Vincentian canon" — what has been believed "everywhere, always, by all" — is the antidote to individualistic interpretation. St. John Chrysostom (c. AD 347–407) Homily 4 on 2 Thessalonians — c. AD 400 "Hence it is manifest, that they did not deliver all things by Epistle, but many things also unwritten, and in like manner both the one and the other are worthy of credit.

secs.h: VII. The Church Fathers on Scripture and Tradition
secs.x: Therefore let us think the tradition of the Church also worthy of credit. It is a tradition, seek no farther." Significance: Chrysostom — commenting on 2 Thessalonians 2:15, Paul's command to hold traditions delivered orally — explicitly states that unwritten tradition is worthy of belief. His conclusion, "It is a tradition, seek no farther," is a direct affirmation of the authority of oral apostolic tradition independent of its written documentation. This is the universal Eastern patristic position.

secs.h: VIII. What Is Sacred Tradition? — A Clarification
secs.x: VIII. What Is Sacred Tradition? — A Clarification A common Protestant misunderstanding is that "Tradition" in the Oriental Orthodox sense means human customs, clerical traditions, or later additions to the original faith. This misunderstands what the Eastern tradition means by Paradosis (the Tradition). Sacred Tradition in the Oriental Orthodox sense encompasses: The Holy Scriptures themselves — The written texts are part of the Tradition, not separate from it. The Ecumenical Councils — The definitions of Nicaea (325), Constantinople (381), Ephesus (431), and the Oriental Orthodox councils, which articulate the apostolic faith. The Creeds — The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed as the summary of apostolic faith, prayed by the whole Church at every Eucharist. The Liturgy — The Divine Liturgy of St. Basil, St. Cyril (St. Mark), and the other ancient Eucharistic prayers, which embody and transmit the faith in worship.

secs.h: VIII. What Is Sacred Tradition? — A Clarification
secs.x: The Church Fathers — The theological writings of the Fathers, who represent the accumulated wisdom of the apostolic succession in interpreting Scripture and defending the faith. The ascetic and sacramental life — The lived practice of prayer, fasting, the sacraments, and the pursuit of theosis that has been handed down through generations. Sacred Tradition is not a static set of texts alongside the Bible but the living, breathing life of the Church guided by the Holy Spirit — the same Spirit who inspired the Scriptures in the first place. To place Scripture against Tradition is to place the Spirit against himself.

IX. Protestant Objections Objection: Jesus condemned "the traditions of men" in Mark 7 — tradition corrupts Scripture The Claim Jesus explicitly rebuked the Pharisees for "teaching as doctrines the commandments of men" (Mark 7:7) and for "making void the word of God by your tradition" (Mark 7:13). This shows that human tradition is dangerous and should not be given authority alongside Scripture. Response The Oriental Orthodox fully agree that human tradition can corrupt the word of God — and this is precisely why the Oriental Orthodox insist on apostolic tradition, not arbitrary human customs. The Pharisaic traditions Jesus condemned were post-biblical oral rulings that contradicted the plain sense of Scripture. The apostolic tradition that the Oriental Orthodox affirm — the liturgy, the Creeds, the councils — does not contradict Scripture; it is the context in which Scripture was received, preserved, and correctly understood.

Furthermore, Paul in the same breath condemns Gnostic/pagan "philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition" (Colossians 2:8) while commanding fidelity to apostolic tradition (2 Thess 2:15). The distinction Jesus and Paul both draw is between apostolic/divine tradition and human tradition — not between Scripture and all tradition. Objection: 2 Timothy 3:16–17 says Scripture makes us "complete, equipped for every good work" — so it is sufficient The Claim "All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work" (2 Tim 3:16–17). Scripture is sufficient — it makes us "complete." Response This passage establishes the divine inspiration and profitability of Scripture — which the Oriental Orthodox fully affirm. But "complete, equipped for every good work" does not mean "Scripture alone is the only authority." A well-equipped soldier is equipped for every battle — but this doesn't mean a compass, a map, and fellow soldiers are useless.

Paul tells Timothy that Scripture equips him for good works; he also tells Timothy to hold to the traditions (2 Tim 1:13–14), to guard the deposit entrusted to him (2 Tim 1:14), to entrust what he heard to faithful men (2 Tim 2:2), and to follow the pattern of sound words (2 Tim 1:13). The same letter that contains 3:16–17 commands traditional transmission of the apostolic deposit — the very thing sola scriptura denies. Furthermore, "the Scriptures" Timothy knew from childhood (3:15) were primarily the Old Testament — not the full New Testament canon, which was not yet determined. Objection: The Church Fathers also held to Scripture's supremacy — they are not evidence for Tradition as an independent authority The Claim When Irenaeus, Basil, or Chrysostom appeal to tradition, they mean Scripture — they always tested tradition by Scripture, and never placed tradition as an authority equal to or above Scripture. They were proto-Protestants who would have agreed with sola scriptura. Response This claim does not survive a reading of the Fathers.

Basil explicitly states that written and oral apostolic tradition "have the same force" — not that oral tradition derives its authority from Scripture. Chrysostom says "it is a tradition, seek no farther" without appealing to a scriptural warrant. Irenaeus appeals to the succession of bishops as his primary argument against Gnostic heresy — not to Scripture alone, because the Gnostics also claimed to follow Scripture (their own versions of it). The Fathers did not test tradition by Scripture; they used Scripture and tradition together as the two modes of the single apostolic deposit. To claim the Fathers for sola scriptura requires either ignoring their actual statements or drastically reinterpreting them.

X. FAQ Q: Does the Oriental Orthodox Church add to Scripture? No. The Oriental Orthodox Church adds nothing to Scripture — it receives and transmits the apostolic deposit of which Scripture is the written center. The Creeds, councils, and patristic writings do not supplement Scripture with new revelation; they articulate and defend the meaning of Scripture against error. The Nicene Creed does not add to John 1:1 ("the Word was God") — it clarifies what "God" means in that context against the Arian denial of Christ's full divinity. This is not addition; it is faithful interpretation. Q: How does the Oriental Orthodox Church handle apparent contradictions between Scripture and Tradition? The Oriental Orthodox do not experience Scripture and Tradition as competing authorities that can contradict each other — they are two modes of the one apostolic deposit. An apparent contradiction between Scripture and a patristic teaching signals either a misinterpretation of Scripture, a misinterpretation of the Father, or a later addition to "tradition" that is not genuinely apostolic.

The criterion for authentic tradition is precisely the Vincentian canon: what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. A practice or teaching that emerges in the 5th century without earlier attestation does not qualify as apostolic tradition simply because a Church claims it. Q: If tradition is authoritative, how do you avoid traditionalism — repeating errors just because they are old? This is a genuine concern and the Oriental Orthodox take it seriously. The safeguard is the breadth and universality of the criterion: genuine apostolic tradition is attested across multiple independent churches, in multiple languages, from the earliest centuries. A local practice or a single Father's opinion does not constitute Tradition in the binding sense. What is held "everywhere, always, by all" (Vincent of Lérins) — the Nicene faith, the seven sacraments, the apostolic succession — is binding. What is held locally or recently has proportionally less authority. This is why the Oriental Orthodox appeal to Ecumenical Councils, not merely to their own patriarchal decisions.

I. Introduction — A Different Framework 01 The spiritual gifts (Greek: charismata ) are one of the most contested areas of Protestant theology today. Pentecostals and Charismatics insist that speaking in tongues is the initial evidence of Spirit baptism, that prophecy continues as a regular congregational phenomenon, and that healing miracles should be a normal feature of Christian life. Cessationists — many Reformed and Baptist — argue that the miraculous gifts ceased with the apostolic age. Between these two poles, a vast middle ground of Protestant evangelicalism is perpetually unsettled. The Oriental Orthodox tradition offers a different framework entirely — one grounded in Scripture, in the continuous Patristic witness, and in eighteen centuries of lived experience. The OO neither denies the charismata nor misidentifies them. Its key convictions are: The gifts of the Spirit are real and continue. The Holy Spirit has never withdrawn his gifts from the Church.

The charismata described in 1 Corinthians 12, Romans 12, and Ephesians 4 are genuine expressions of the Spirit's life in the Body of Christ, present in every generation. The gifts are given for the building up of the Church, not for personal experience. The purpose of the charismata is the oikodomē — the edification — of the whole Body (1 Cor 14:12). Gifts are not badges of spiritual achievement or evidence of a "second blessing." The primary channels of the Spirit's charismata are the sacramental life and the holy persons of each generation. The gifts are not primarily expressed in charismatic worship services but in the healing sacrament of unction, the prophetic ministry of holy elders (startsy / abba), the miraculous works of the saints, and the teaching office of the bishops. Discernment is essential. Not every spiritual manifestation is from the Holy Spirit. The Fathers developed an elaborate theology of diakrisis (discernment) to distinguish authentic charismata from diabolical counterfeits and self-deception.

II. Glossary 02 Charisma (pl. Charismata) Greek: χάρισμα — gift of grace A gift freely given by the Holy Spirit to a member of the Body of Christ for the benefit of the whole Church. From charis (grace) — a charisma is a grace-gift, unearned and undeserved, given for service. Pneumatika Greek: πνευματικά — spiritual things The broader term Paul uses in 1 Cor 12:1 — "spiritual gifts" or "spiritual matters." Encompasses the entire range of the Spirit's manifestations in the community, including charismata proper. Glossolalia Greek: γλωσσολαλία — tongue-speaking The gift of tongues. In the OO reading: the Spirit-given ability to speak in a human language unknown to the speaker — for the purpose of proclamation to those of that language. Not ecstatic utterance or a private prayer language. Prophecy (Propheteia) Greek: προφητεία — speaking forth Spirit-inspired proclamation of God's word — not necessarily future prediction.

In the OO tradition, prophecy continues in the Church through the teaching of holy elders, the decrees of councils, and occasional direct divine communication to holy persons. Cessationism Protestant theological position The view that miraculous gifts (tongues, healing, prophecy, miracles) ceased with the death of the last apostle or the closing of the NT canon. Held by most Reformed and Baptist theologians. Rejected by the OO tradition. Diakrisis Greek: διάκρισις — discernment, judgment The gift and practice of discerning spirits — distinguishing what is truly from the Holy Spirit from what is from evil spirits, human self-deception, or psychological phenomena. Central to the OO ascetic tradition. Nepsis Greek: νῆψις — sobriety, watchfulness The spiritual discipline of watchful sobriety — the opposite of spiritual enthusiasm or emotionalism. Essential to OO discernment of spiritual phenomena. The Philokalia is largely devoted to neptic (watchful) spirituality.

Prelest Slavonic: прельсть — spiritual deception Spiritual delusion — the condition of one who mistakes demonic or self-generated spiritual experiences for genuine gifts of the Holy Spirit. A major concern of the OO ascetic tradition. Many false "spiritual gifts" are understood as prelest.

secs.h: III. The Gift Lists in Scripture — A Unified Picture
secs.x: III. The Gift Lists in Scripture — A Unified Picture 03 The New Testament contains four major lists of spiritual gifts, each with a different emphasis. Together they provide a comprehensive picture of how the Spirit equips the Body of Christ: 1 Corinthians 12:8–10 Word of wisdom · Word of knowledge · Faith · Gifts of healing · Miracles · Prophecy · Discernment of spirits · Tongues · Interpretation of tongues OO: The "sign gifts" — supernatural manifestations for the edification of the assembly 1 Corinthians 12:28 Apostles · Prophets · Teachers · Miracles · Gifts of healing · Helps · Administration · Tongues OO: Gifts within the ordered life of the Church — apostolic, prophetic, and diaconal Romans 12:6–8 Prophecy · Service · Teaching · Exhortation · Giving · Leadership · Mercy OO: The "service gifts" — ministry-oriented charismata for the practical life of the community Ephesians 4:11 Apostles · Prophets · Evangelists · Pastors · Teachers OO: The ordained ministry gifts — given for the equipping of the saints and the building up of the Body Context: Given "until we all attain to the

secs.h: III. The Gift Lists in Scripture — A Unified Picture
secs.x: unity of the faith" — ongoing, not temporary The OO reads these four lists as complementary, not competing. Together they show that the Spirit gives gifts across a wide spectrum — from the spectacular (miracles, tongues) to the ordinary (mercy, administration). No single gift is the mark of Spirit-fullness. The Pentecostal insistence that tongues is the necessary evidence of Spirit baptism has no scriptural basis — Paul explicitly states "not all speak in tongues" (1 Cor 12:30) and places tongues last in the list.

secs.h: IV. Tongues & Interpretation — The Most Contested Gift
secs.x: IV. Tongues & Interpretation — The Most Contested Gift 04 △ OO Position: The gift of tongues is real but widely misidentified The Oriental Orthodox affirm the biblical gift of tongues but understand it as the Spirit-given ability to speak in a genuine human language for the purpose of proclamation — as at Pentecost. Private "prayer tongues" as ecstatic utterance is not the biblical gift. Acts 2:4–11 "And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance... each one was hearing them speak in his own language... 'we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.'" OO: The Pentecost tongues were real human languages — each hearer understood in their native dialect. This is the paradigm for the gift.

secs.h: IV. Tongues & Interpretation — The Most Contested Gift
secs.x: Charismatic: Tongues is ecstatic language — Acts 2 is one expression; 1 Cor 14 is another (private prayer) 1 Corinthians 14:2 "For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit." Charismatic: Proof of a private prayer language beyond human understanding OO: "No one understands him" = no one present happens to speak that language. The point is it is unintelligible without an interpreter — not that it is inherently supernatural babble. 1 Corinthians 14:19 "Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue." OO: Paul subordinates tongues to intelligible edification — a corrective to Corinthian enthusiasm 1 Corinthians 14:27–28 "If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church." OO: Strict regulation — tongues requires interpretation or silence.

secs.h: IV. Tongues & Interpretation — The Most Contested Gift
secs.x: Not the centerpiece of worship but its most regulated element. The OO Interpretation The gift of tongues in the OO reading is the miraculous ability to speak in a human language one has not naturally learned — given by the Spirit for the proclamation of the Gospel to peoples of other tongues. This is the clear reading of Acts 2 (where each hearer understood in their own language) and the common reading of the Fathers. The idea of a "private prayer language" — an ecstatic utterance that bypasses the mind and communicates directly with God beyond human language — has no Patristic support and is a modern Pentecostal innovation (originating c. 1900–1906 at Azusa Street). Interpretation of Tongues: The companion gift — the Spirit-given ability to translate what is spoken in an unknown language so the congregation can benefit. Without this gift present, Paul commands silence.

secs.h: IV. Tongues & Interpretation — The Most Contested Gift
secs.x: The OO tradition has no liturgical practice of tongues-speaking in services — because the liturgical languages of the OO (Coptic, Ge'ez, Syriac, Armenian) are themselves ancient, sacred tongues through which the Spirit has spoken for millennia. John Chrysostom c. AD 390 — Homilies on 1 Corinthians "This whole place is very obscure: but the obscurity is produced by our ignorance of the facts referred to and by their cessation, being such as then used to occur but now no longer take place." — Chrysostom acknowledges the diminishing of the spectacular manifestations while affirming the gifts in principle. Augustine of Hippo c. AD 406 — Homilies on 1 John "In the earliest times, the Holy Ghost fell upon them that believed: and they spoke with tongues, which they had not learned, as the Spirit gave them utterance. These were signs adapted to the time. For there behooved to be that betokening of the Holy Spirit... That thing was done for a betokening, and it passed away."

secs.h: V. Prophecy — The Living Voice of the Spirit
secs.x: V. Prophecy — The Living Voice of the Spirit 05 ✓ OO Position: Prophecy continues in the Church — primarily through holy persons, councils, and Scripture The Oriental Orthodox affirm that the prophetic gift of the Holy Spirit continues in every generation. It is not primarily expressed as spontaneous congregational declarations but through the prophetic ministry of holy elders, the authoritative teaching of bishops in council, and the lived witness of the saints. 1 Corinthians 14:1 "Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy." OO: Prophecy is the most desirable gift — because it edifies the whole assembly. The OO tradition has always honored prophetic voices. 1 Corinthians 14:3 "On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation." OO: Prophecy is defined by its fruit — edification, encouragement, consolation. It is primarily pastoral, not sensational.

secs.h: V. Prophecy — The Living Voice of the Spirit
secs.x: Acts 2:17–18 "And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy... even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy." OO: The prophetic gift is poured out on all flesh in the age of the Church — it does not cease Context: Peter quotes Joel 2 at Pentecost — the "last days" are the entire Church age 1 Thessalonians 5:19–21 "Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good." OO: Three commands — don't suppress, don't despise, but test. The OO tradition tests through discernment (diakrisis). Prophecy in the OO Tradition The OO tradition has always had prophetic figures — holy persons whose words carried the weight of divine insight. The Desert Fathers were frequently asked to give a "word" (Greek: logos ) — a brief, Spirit-inspired utterance of guidance and truth. The great abbots of Egypt, Syria, and Ethiopia were consulted as prophetic figures.

secs.h: V. Prophecy — The Living Voice of the Spirit
secs.x: The Coptic Pope's formal teaching, the decrees of synods, and the witness of canonized saints all partake of the prophetic function of the Spirit in the Church. This is not "open microphone" congregational prophecy — it is the sober, tested, communal exercise of the gift within the ordered life of the Body.

VI. Gifts of Healing 06 ✓ OO Position: Healing is among the most abundantly attested gifts in the OO tradition — primarily through Holy Unction, the prayers of the saints, and holy relics James 5:14–15 "Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up." OO: This is the biblical institution of Holy Unction — the sacrament of healing given to the Church for all ages Prot: A description of elder-prayer, not a sacrament; fulfilled in the apostolic age Mark 16:17–18 "And these signs will accompany those who believe... they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover." OO: Christ's promise — healing accompanies faith in every generation (from the longer ending of Mark, which the Church has always read as Scripture) The Oriental Orthodox tradition does not organize healing crusades or healing services in the Pentecostal manner.

It has instead a rich, sacramental theology of healing: Holy Unction (the anointing of the sick) is administered by the Church's ordained priests as a means of healing for both body and soul. The healing prayers of the saints — both living and departed — are also understood as a channel of the Spirit's healing power. The OO hagiographic literature is replete with authenticated healing miracles, from the Coptic Desert Fathers through the Ethiopian saints to modern figures such as Fr. Bishoy Kamel of Alexandria (1931–1979) and Pope Kyrillos VI. Chrysostom taught that the gifts of healing were given not for the glory of the healer, but to build up faith and lead the one healed to God. — summarizing St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew

VII. Miracles & Signs 07 ✓ OO Position: Miracles and signs continue — primarily through the saints and the sacraments, tested by the Church John 14:12 "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father." OO: Christ's own promise — the works of the Spirit continue through believers Cessationist: "Greater works" = greater scope of evangelism, not more spectacular miracles Acts 19:11–12 "And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them." OO: The biblical basis for the healing power of relics — objects associated with holy persons carry the Spirit's power The OO miracle tradition is not the theatrical, stage-managed world of televangelist healing crusades. It is the quiet, tested, communally-verified world of the saints.

Miracles in the OO tradition are typically associated with: the relics of saints (their bodies and associated objects), icons (especially weeping or myrrh-streaming icons), the prayers of holy elders, and the sacraments. The Coptic, Ethiopian, and Syriac churches have extensive documented traditions of miracles — including apparitions of the Virgin Mary at Zeitoun, Egypt (1968–1971), witnessed by hundreds of thousands including non-Christians and atheists. These are not claimed uncritically — the Church carefully investigates before acknowledging them.

VIII. Discernment of Spirits 08 ✓ OO Position: Discernment of spirits is one of the most vital gifts — and one of the most developed in the OO ascetic tradition 1 John 4:1 "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world." OO: The command to test spirits — essential, because not all spiritual phenomena are divine 1 Corinthians 12:10 "...to another the ability to distinguish between spirits..." OO: Diakrisis pneumaton — discernment of spirits is a distinct spiritual gift, not merely natural wisdom 2 Corinthians 11:14 "And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light." OO: The demonic can mimic spiritual gifts — making discernment indispensable The Eastern Christian ascetic tradition, rooted in the Egyptian desert that the Oriental Orthodox share, has developed one of the richest theologies of discernment in Christianity.

The Philokalia (an 18th-century collection of writings by Desert and Byzantine Fathers, treasured above all in Eastern Orthodoxy), the Ladder of Divine Ascent (John Climacus), the Sayings of the Desert Fathers — all are substantially concerned with the discernment of spirits. The key principles: genuine spiritual gifts produce humility, not pride; they conform to Scripture and tradition; they are submitted to the judgment of a spiritual father; they bear the fruit of love, peace, and holiness. Manifestations that produce excitement, pride, spiritual superiority, or independence from the Church's authority are deeply suspect. The Orthodox ascetic concept known by the Slavonic word prelest (spiritual delusion) is directly relevant here. Many of what the Charismatic movement presents as gifts of the Spirit — frenzied "manifestations," uncontrolled laughter, "slaying in the Spirit," fortune-telling "words of knowledge" — the OO Fathers would identify as spiritual self-deception at best and demonic at worst.

secs.h: IX. Word of Wisdom & Word of Knowledge
secs.x: IX. Word of Wisdom & Word of Knowledge 09 Word of Wisdom Greek: logos sophias — utterance of wisdom Spirit-given insight to apply divine truth rightly to a concrete situation. The practical, pastoral wisdom that enables a holy elder, a bishop, or a gifted teacher to speak the right word at the right time for the edification of souls. OO Reading Primarily manifested in the abbots of the desert tradition, holy elders (startsy), and bishops whose pastoral counsel carries divine authority beyond their natural capacity. Charismatic Reading Often used as a designation for prophetic revelation about a person's situation — "God is showing me a word of wisdom about your marriage..." 🔍 Word of Knowledge Greek: logos gnōseōs — utterance of knowledge Spirit-given knowledge of a fact or situation that could not be known through natural means — distinct from general wisdom. In the OO tradition, associated with the gift of "reading hearts" (kardiognōsia) found in holy persons.

secs.h: IX. Word of Wisdom & Word of Knowledge
secs.x: OO Reading Attested throughout the Desert Father literature — holy elders who knew the state of a person's soul before they spoke, or who revealed sins the penitent had concealed. Charismatic Reading Used in healing contexts — "I sense someone here has pain in their left knee" — as a form of diagnostic revelation. 1 Corinthians 12:8 "For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit." OO: Both gifts are "utterances" (logoi) — spoken wisdom and spoken knowledge, not mere inner states

X. The Gift of Faith 10 1 Corinthians 12:9 "...to another faith by the same Spirit..." OO: This is not saving faith (which all believers have) but a supernatural measure of trust — enabling the believer to act with confidence in God's power in impossible situations Matthew 17:20 "For truly, I say to you, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, 'Move from here to there,' and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you." OO: The charismatic gift of faith — operative trust in God's power that enables extraordinary acts of prayer and intercession The OO tradition associates the gift of faith especially with the martyrs — who faced death with supernatural peace and confidence — and with the great monastic founders, who built communities and churches in impossible circumstances on the strength of this gift. It is not the "name it and claim it" faith of prosperity theology; it is the faith that moves mountains by aligning itself with God's will, not by asserting human desire.

XI. Teaching, Exhortation & Evangelism 11 Teaching (Didaskalia) Greek: διδασκαλία The Spirit-given ability to expound, explain, and apply Scripture and the Tradition with clarity and power. The primary charism of the bishop and the catechist. In the OO tradition, teaching is inseparable from the Church's liturgy and the Patristic inheritance — it is never solo interpretation. Exhortation (Paraklēsis) Greek: παράκλησις — encouragement, comfort The gift of speaking words of encouragement, comfort, and moral exhortation that move people to action and fidelity. The same word used of the Holy Spirit as "the Paraclete" (John 14:16) — exhortation partakes of the Spirit's own ministry. Evangelism (Euangelizomenos) Greek: εὐαγγελιστής — herald of good news The Ephesians 4:11 gift — Spirit-given ability to proclaim the Gospel effectively to the unconverted. Not all are evangelists (Eph 4:11 distinguishes evangelists from pastors and teachers), but the gift is essential for the Church's mission.
The great OO missionary saints — Frumentius of Ethiopia, Gregory the Illuminator of Armenia, Thomas in India — exemplify this gift.

XII. Helps, Giving, Leadership & Mercy 12 The Romans 12 gifts are often overlooked in discussions of spiritual gifts because they are less spectacular than tongues and miracles. But for the OO tradition, these are the gifts that constitute the daily texture of the Spirit's life in the Church — and they are no less supernatural for being less dramatic. Helps / Service Greek: antilēmpsis (1 Cor 12:28); diakonia (Rom 12:7) The gift of practical assistance — supporting others' ministries, meeting practical needs with supernatural effectiveness. The deaconal gift. In the OO tradition, the diaconate is precisely the institutionalization of this charism within the ordained ministry. Giving Greek: metadidous — sharing The Spirit-given impulse and ability to give generously and effectively. Not simply donating money but knowing where, when, and how much to give in a way that transforms situations. The OO tradition's emphasis on almsgiving as a spiritual discipline is the communal expression of this gift.

Leadership / Administration Greek: proistamenos (Rom 12:8); kubernēsis (1 Cor 12:28) The gift of governing and directing the community with wisdom. Kubernēsis is the navigator's art — steering a ship through complex waters. In the OO tradition, this is the gift of the bishop and abbot — those who govern the Church and the monastery with the Spirit's wisdom. Mercy Greek: eleon — compassionate action The Spirit-given capacity to show compassion with cheerfulness — particularly to those who are suffering, marginalized, or difficult. The gift of the hospital-founder, the prison visitor, the stranger-welcomer. Abundantly attested in OO monastic and social history.

secs.h: XIII. Cessationism vs. Continuationism — The OO Position
secs.x: XIII. Cessationism vs. Continuationism — The OO Position 13 The debate between cessationism and continuationism — whether miraculous gifts ceased after the apostolic age — is a distinctively Protestant debate. The Oriental Orthodox tradition stands outside it: it has never taught cessationism (though Fathers such as Chrysostom and Augustine noted that tongues and similar signs had become rare), and it has never needed the modern Pentecostal-Charismatic corrective to cessationism, because it never lost the genuine gifts in the first place. 1 Corinthians 13:8–10 "Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease... when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away." Cessationist: "The perfect" = the completed NT canon — gifts ceased when Scripture was finished OO: "The perfect" = the eschaton — the fullness of the Kingdom at Christ's return. Until then, the gifts continue.

secs.h: XIII. Cessationism vs. Continuationism — The OO Position
secs.x: Context: v.12 — "then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known" — this is the beatific vision, not the canon Ephesians 4:11–13 "And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers... until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood..." OO: The gifts are given "until" full maturity and unity — which has not been reached. They continue. Cessationist: "Apostles and prophets" in the foundational sense ceased — ongoing offices remain The OO position is unambiguously continuationist — but it is a sober, patristic, sacramental continuationism , not the emotionally-driven, experience-centered continuationism of the Charismatic movement. The gifts have never ceased in the Church; they have been exercised in every generation — primarily through the sacraments, the holy persons recognized by the Church, and the ordinary faithful in their various callings. Irenaeus of Lyon c.

secs.h: XIII. Cessationism vs. Continuationism — The OO Position
secs.x: AD 185 "Those who are in truth His disciples, receiving grace from Him, do in His name perform [miracles], so as to promote the welfare of other men, according to the gift which each one has received from Him... Others still, heal the sick by laying their hands upon them, and they are made whole. Yea, moreover, as I have said, the dead even have been raised up." Origen of Alexandria c. AD 248 "And some give evidence of their having received through this faith a marvellous power by the cures which they perform, invoking no other name over those who need their help than that of the God of all things, and of Jesus, along with a mention of His history." (Against Celsus III.24) Cyril of Jerusalem c. AD 350 "For He employs the tongue of one man for wisdom; the soul of another He enlightens by Prophecy; to another He gives power to drive away devils; to another He gives to interpret the divine Scriptures." (Catechetical Lecture 16.12)

secs.h: XIV. The Charismatic Movement — An OO Assessment
secs.x: XIV. The Charismatic Movement — An OO Assessment 14 The Charismatic and Pentecostal movements — born in the early 20th century and now representing over 600 million Christians — claim to have recovered the apostolic gifts. The Oriental Orthodox tradition, which never lost them, assesses the movement with a mixture of recognition and serious concern. What the OO Affirms The genuine desire for a living, Spirit-filled Christianity, not a dead formalism The recognition that the gifts of the Spirit are real and continue The emphasis on prayer, fasting, and expectation of God's action Authentic healings and genuine conversions that have occurred in these movements What the OO Critiques Tongues as evidence of Spirit baptism — no biblical or Patristic support. "Not all speak in tongues" (1 Cor 12:30). This teaching has no precedent before 1901. Absence of discernment — the movement largely lacks the sophisticated diakrisis of the Patristic tradition. Emotional excitement is often mistaken for spiritual gift.

secs.h: XIV. The Charismatic Movement — An OO Assessment
secs.x: Prelest / spiritual delusion — many Charismatic manifestations (uncontrolled laughter, "Toronto blessing," "slaying in the Spirit") have no Scriptural or Patristic basis and bear the marks of prelest. Individualism — gifts are exercised outside the ordered life of the Church, without submission to apostolic authority. Paul's instructions require order and submission (1 Cor 14:32–33). Prosperity gospel — the perversion of the gift of faith into a technique for obtaining wealth, health, and success is a heresy the Fathers would have condemned without hesitation. "The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace." — 1 Corinthians 14:32–33

secs.h: XV. The Gifts in the OO Tradition — Where Are They?
secs.x: XV. The Gifts in the OO Tradition — Where Are They? 15 If the gifts continue, where are they in the Oriental Orthodox churches? The OO tradition has never organized healing rallies or tongues-speaking services — yet it has produced an extraordinary abundance of spiritual gifts across every generation. Here is where the discerning eye finds them: In the sacraments: Healing in Holy Unction; prophecy in the authoritative teaching of bishops; wisdom in Confession; discernment in the spiritual father's counsel; all gifts mediated through the living Body of Christ. In the saints: Every generation of the OO churches has produced holy persons credited with gifts of healing, prophecy, knowledge, miracles, and discernment — from Anthony the Great and Pachomius to Yared of Ethiopia, Gregory the Illuminator of Armenia, and modern figures like Pope Kyrillos VI of Alexandria (1902–1971), whose documented miracles of healing and prophecy are attested by thousands.

secs.h: XV. The Gifts in the OO Tradition — Where Are They?
secs.x: In the monasteries: The desert tradition — Coptic, Syrian, Ethiopian, Armenian — has always been the primary locus of the charismatic life in the OO churches. The monastery is not a flight from the world but the spiritual powerhouse that sustains the entire Church's life in the Spirit. In the faithful: The daily practice of the Agpeya (Coptic Hours), fasting, almsgiving, and holy living among ordinary OO Christians is itself an expression of the Spirit's gifts of faith, mercy, and service — unpretentious, sustained, and real.

XVI. Protestant Objections & Orthodox Responses 16 Objection 1 (Cessationist): The miraculous gifts ceased with the apostles — 1 Corinthians 13:10 says they pass away when "the perfect" comes, meaning the completed canon. When the NT was completed, the foundation was laid. Miraculous gifts were scaffolding — now removed since the building is done. Orthodox Response "The perfect" in 1 Corinthians 13:10–12 cannot mean the completed canon. Paul describes it as the state in which "I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known" — complete, face-to-face knowledge of God. This is the beatific vision, the eschaton, not the closing of the biblical canon. Moreover, the Patristic witnesses — Irenaeus (c. 185), Origen (c. 248), Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 350) — all describe miraculous gifts as operative in their own times, long after the apostles. If gifts ceased with the last apostle (d. c. 100), cessationists must explain these reports away, as B. B. Warfield tried to do.

In fairness, cessationists can appeal to some Fathers: Chrysostom and Augustine both said that the spectacular signs of the apostolic age, such as tongues, no longer occurred in their day (see the cards below). But neither taught that the Spirit's gifts as such had ended; both recorded miracles in their own time (Augustine's City of God XXII.8 is a long catalogue of them). Full cessationism took shape in the Reformation, with Calvin, and was given its classic modern form by B. B. Warfield ( Counterfeit Miracles , 1918). Objection 2 (Charismatic): The OO church has lost the gifts by relying on ritual rather than Spirit-led worship. Liturgy quenches the Spirit. The OO's formal, liturgical worship suppresses genuine Spirit-manifestation. Real Spirit-filled churches are spontaneous and free. Orthodox Response This objection assumes the Holy Spirit operates primarily through emotional spontaneity — an assumption nowhere found in Scripture. The Spirit filled the highly ordered Temple worship.

The four living creatures of Revelation 4 repeat "Holy, holy, holy" in a perfectly fixed liturgical pattern — and this is the highest worship in the universe. The OO church has produced an extraordinary stream of spiritual gifts across two millennia, centered precisely in its sacramental and liturgical life. The gifts are not absent — they are where they have always been: in the sacraments, in the saints, in the ordered Body of Christ. The Charismatic movement, by contrast, is 120 years old and already showing the signs of spiritual inflation and doctrinal confusion that the Fathers predicted when gifts are divorced from the ordered Church. Objection 3: Speaking in tongues is the sign that you have been baptized in the Holy Spirit — this is what Acts shows. Acts 2, Acts 10, and Acts 19 all show tongues accompanying the outpouring of the Spirit — establishing a pattern that tongues signals Spirit baptism.

Orthodox Response Acts records three instances of tongues at Pentecost — and several conversions and Spirit-fillings where no tongues are mentioned (Acts 8:17; Acts 9:17–18; Acts 16:15; Acts 16:33). If tongues were the universal sign, why does Paul say "not all speak in tongues" (1 Cor 12:30)? Paul explicitly denies that any single gift is the universal mark of Spirit-baptism — instead listing the variety of gifts given to different members (1 Cor 12:4–11). The three Acts passages are historically unique occasions: Pentecost (founding of the Jewish church), Cornelius (founding of the Gentile church), and Ephesus (correction of an incomplete baptism). They are not a repeatable pattern for every conversion — any more than the earthquake at Paul's prison (Acts 16:26) means earthquakes should accompany every church service.

XVII. Frequently Asked Questions 17 Can an OO Christian speak in tongues? If God grants the genuine gift — the miraculous ability to speak in a human language one has not learned — yes. The OO affirms the reality of the gift. What the OO does not affirm is the Pentecostal doctrine that a specific form of ecstatic utterance is the necessary mark of Spirit-baptism, or that all Christians should seek and expect this gift. The OO Christian who genuinely receives a miraculous linguistic gift would be expected to use it in submission to the Church's pastoral authority, not as a personal spiritual experience pursued for its own sake. Does the OO church have healing services? Not in the Pentecostal sense. The OO form of healing service is the sacrament of Holy Unction — a solemn liturgical rite administered by priests, in which the sick person is anointed with blessed oil and the Church's prayers are offered for their healing. In the Coptic Church, Unction of the sick is administered communally on the last Friday of Great Lent, as well as for individual sick people.

This is not a prayer rally or a healing crusade — it is the sacramental healing ministry of the Church as instituted by the apostles (James 5:14–15). What is the OO view of Pentecostalism? The OO views Pentecostalism with a mixture of sympathy and serious concern. The desire for a living, experiential faith is entirely understandable — and in many Protestant churches, cessationism has produced a dry, intellectualized Christianity that genuinely lacks the Spirit's evident presence. Pentecostalism is, in part, a reaction to this failure. However, the Pentecostal solution — making tongues the necessary sign, encouraging unordered congregational manifestations, and divorcing charismatic experience from the apostolic and sacramental life of the Church — creates new and serious problems. The OO tradition believes the answer to dead formalism is not chaotic enthusiasm but genuine ascetic life, sacramental depth, and patient submission to the Church's patristic wisdom.

Are the gifts of the Spirit ranked in order of importance? Paul does rank the gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:28 ("first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues") — placing tongues last. And in 1 Corinthians 14:1 he urges the Corinthians to "earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy" — elevating prophecy above tongues in the congregational context. The OO tradition reads this as: the gifts that build up the community (prophecy, teaching, wisdom) are more desirable than the gifts that are unintelligible without interpretation (tongues). Charity — love — is above all gifts (1 Cor 13:1–3). The gift of love, expressed in a life of holiness and service, surpasses any spectacular charism.

XVIII. Primary Sources & Further Reading 18 Scripture 1 Corinthians 12–14 — the central Pauline treatment of spiritual gifts Romans 12:6–8 — the service gifts Ephesians 4:11–13 — the ministry gifts 1 Peter 4:10–11 — gifts as stewardship Patristic Sources Irenaeus — Against Heresies II.32 (c. AD 185) Origen — Against Celsus I.46; III.24 (c. AD 248) Cyril of Jerusalem — Catechetical Lectures XVI–XVII (c. AD 350) John Chrysostom — Homilies on 1 Corinthians XXIX–XXXVI (c. AD 390) John Climacus — The Ladder of Divine Ascent — discernment (c. AD 600) The Philokalia — esp. writings of Evagrius, Makarios, Hesychios — nepsis and diakrisis Sayings of the Desert Fathers — the charismatic holy elders of Egypt Modern OO and Scholarly Works Thomas Hopko — The Spirit of God Sergius Bulgakov — The Comforter (1936) D.A. Carson — Showing the Spirit (1987) — irenic cessationist critique Gordon Fee — God's Empowering Presence (1994) — continuationist exegesis Mark Cartledge — Charismatic Glossolalia (2002)

pages.t: Twenty Questions on God and Christ

secs.x: Enda Mariam Cathedral Eritrean Orthodox · Asmara In the Orthodox Church a lamp is never merely decoration. It burns before the icons, in the sanctuary, and in the homes of the faithful as a confession: that Christ is “the true Light which gives light to every man coming into the world” (John 1:9) , and that His Church is set on a lampstand to give light to all (Matthew 5:15) . This series takes up twenty questions — some sounding simple, all of them deep — and answers them from the Holy Scriptures and the writings of the Church Fathers, in the faith of the Apostles handed down through the One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic Church, and treasured in the Oriental Orthodox communion of Alexandria, Antioch, Armenia, Ethiopia, Eritrea, and India. The Fathers warn us to approach these mysteries with reverence. St. Gregory the Theologian said that it belongs “not to every one, my friends, … to philosophize about God,” and “not before every audience, nor at all times” (Oration 27.3), for the subject is holy ground.

We do not answer these questions to satisfy curiosity, but so that, knowing God more truly, we may love and worship Him more fully. Read slowly. Where the answer reaches a mystery, the right response is not frustration but doxology. ☩ Part I On God and the Holy Trinity 1 How can God be one and three at the same time? 2 What is the Trinity? 3 Why doesn’t the Bible use the word “Trinity”? 4 Is Jesus God, or the Son of God? 5 Is the Holy Spirit a person or merely a force? 6 How can Jesus be both fully God and fully man? 7 Why did God create humanity? 8 Why does God allow evil and suffering? 9 Does God know the future? 10 Does God change His mind? ☩ Part II On Christ and His Saving Work 1 Why did Jesus have to die on the Cross? 2 What exactly did Jesus accomplish through His death? 3 Did Jesus descend into Hades after His death? 4 Why did Jesus rise from the dead? 5 Is Jesus the only way to salvation? 6 Could Jesus have sinned? 7 What happened during Christ’s earthly ministry? 8 What does it mean that Jesus is seated at the Father’s right hand? 9 Why is Christ called the “Second Adam”?

10 When will Jesus return? ✦ ☩ ✦ Part I On God and the Holy Trinity “Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory.” — Isaiah 6:3 Part I · Question 1 How can God be one and three at the same time? God is one in essence and three in persons. He is not one and three in the same respect — that would be a contradiction. He is one in what He is, and three in who He is. The objection usually runs: “One cannot equal three; the Trinity is a logical contradiction.” But a contradiction only exists when something is affirmed and denied in the same respect . The Church has never said God is one person and three persons, or one essence and three essences. She confesses that God is one in ousia (essence, being, nature) and three in hypostasis (person, concrete subsistence). The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three gods, nor three parts of God, nor three masks worn by one person, but three persons who each fully possess the one undivided divine essence. There is exactly one “What” and exactly three “Whos.” St.

Basil the Great, writing in the fourth century against those who confused these terms, explained the distinction with a precision the Church has used ever since: “The distinction between ousia and hypostasis is the same as that between the general and the particular; as, for instance, between the animal and the particular man. Wherefore, in the case of the Godhead, we confess one essence or substance so as not to give a variant definition of existence, but we confess a particular hypostasis, in order that our conception of Father, Son and Holy Spirit may be without confusion and clear.” St. Basil the Great, Letter 236.6 Both truths — the oneness and the threeness — are pressed upon us by Scripture itself, and the Church refuses to surrender either one. The oneness of God is the bedrock confession of Israel: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one!” Deuteronomy 6:4 “I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God besides Me.” Isaiah 45:5 Yet the same Scriptures present three who are each fully God, each personally distinct, acting and speaking to one another.

At the Lord’s baptism in the Jordan — the feast the Coptic and Syriac churches call Theophany, “the appearing of God” — the three are manifest at once: the Son standing in the water, the Spirit descending as a dove, the Father’s voice from heaven (Matthew 3:16–17) . And the risen Christ commands baptism “in the name [singular] of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19) — one name, one divine being; three named, three persons. Why is this not a contradiction, even if it remains a mystery? Because “one” and “three” answer different questions. Consider how impoverished the alternative is: a god who is a solitary monad has no one to love until he creates. Love would then be an acquired property, not his eternal nature. But St. John dares to say “God is love” (1 John 4:8) — love is what God eternally is, which is only possible if within the one God there is eternally Lover, Beloved, and the Spirit of love; the Father loving the Son “before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24) .

The Fathers also insist that the three persons are not three separated centers each owning a third of divinity. They mutually indwell one another — what later theology calls perichoresis — as the Lord said, “I am in the Father, and the Father in Me” (John 14:10) . Hence every divine act is the single act of all three: the Father creates through the Son in the Spirit; the Father saves through the Son in the Spirit. There is one will, one power, one glory, one worship. St. Gregory the Theologian (Gregory of Nazianzus), whom the Church gave the rare title “the Theologian” precisely for his teaching on the Trinity, described the experience of contemplating this mystery — not as a puzzle to be solved, but as light too bright to divide: “No sooner do I conceive of the One than I am illumined by the splendour of the Three; no sooner do I distinguish Them than I am carried back to the One. When I think of any One of the Three I think of Him as the Whole... When I contemplate the Three together, I see but one torch, and cannot divide or measure out the undivided light.” St.

Gregory the Theologian, Oration 40.41, On Holy Baptism Notice his image: one torch . The lamp of this series is a fitting emblem — flame, light, and heat are distinguishable yet inseparable, a single burning. Every analogy limps (the persons are not “parts” or “aspects”), and the Fathers used analogies only as ladders to be kicked away. The final word is worship: the seraphim do not explain God; they cry “Holy, Holy, Holy” — thrice holy, one Lord (Isaiah 6:3) . ↑ Back to contents Part I · Question 2 What is the Trinity? The Trinity is the one true God as He has revealed Himself: one God in three co-equal, co-eternal persons — the Father unbegotten, the Son eternally begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit eternally proceeding from the Father. The doctrine of the Trinity is not a theory bolted onto the Gospel; it is the Gospel’s grammar. To say “God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son” (John 3:16) already requires a Father who gives and a Son who is given. To say the Father and the Son send “another Helper...

the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17) requires a third. The Trinity is simply the Church saying back to God, carefully, what God has shown of Himself in the history of salvation. The classic summary is the Creed of Nicaea–Constantinople (AD 325/381), which every Oriental Orthodox liturgy confesses to this day: “We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth and of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only begotten Son of God, begotten of his Father before all worlds, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten not made, being of one substance with the Father, by whom all things were made… And [we believe] in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and Giver-of-Life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified, who spoke by the prophets.” The Nicene–Constantinopolitan Creed (NPNF translation) Three things in that confession deserve unpacking.

The persons are distinguished only by how they relate The Father is unbegotten — the fountainhead (the Fathers call Him the arche , the source) of the Godhead. The Son is begotten of the Father eternally — not created, not adopted, but begotten as light is begotten of fire, “Light of Light.” The Spirit proceeds from the Father (John 15:26) . (The Oriental Orthodox, with the original creed, confess the procession from the Father alone, without the later Latin addition “and the Son.”) These relations — unbegottenness, begottenness, procession — are the only distinctions among the persons. In everything else — power, glory, eternity, will, divinity — they are absolutely equal and identical. “Begotten” does not mean “made” or “younger” Human begetting happens in time, so a human son is younger than his father. But God is beyond time. The Father was never without His Son, for the Son is His eternal Word and Wisdom — and God was never wordless or without wisdom. As the Scripture says of the Son: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1) .

St. Athanasius of Alexandria, the great champion of Nicaea, hammered this point against the Arians, who claimed “there was once when the Son was not”: “For if the Son was not before His generation, Truth was not always in God, which it were a sin to say; for, since the Father was, there was ever in Him the Truth, which is the Son…” St. Athanasius, Against the Arians I.20 (NPNF) The Trinity is the object of worship, not merely of study St. Athanasius also gave what may be the most compact patristic definition we possess, in his letters to Serapion on the Holy Spirit: Summary: Athanasius describes the Trinity as holy and perfect, confessed as God in Father, Son and Holy Spirit, with nothing foreign or external mixed into it. It is consistent in itself and indivisible in nature, and its activity is one: the Father does all things through the Word in the Holy Spirit. In this way the unity of the Trinity is kept, and one God is preached in the Church, who is over all, through all and in all. Summary of St.

Athanasius, Letters to Serapion 1.28 Notice the shape of that sentence: from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. That is the shape of every blessing that descends to us, and of all prayer that ascends from us — we pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. The Trinity is not an abstract diagram; it is the living God into whose own life we are baptized (Matthew 28:19) , and the apostolic benediction places us inside it: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14) . ↑ Back to contents Part I · Question 3 Why doesn’t the Bible explicitly use the word “Trinity”? Because “Trinity” is the Church’s technical name for a reality the Bible everywhere reveals. The word is absent; the thing itself is on nearly every page of the New Testament. This question has more force in the asking than in the answering. The Bible also never uses the words “Bible,” “incarnation,” “monotheism,” or “omniscience” — yet no one doubts these are biblical realities.

Doctrine is not a word-search; it is the faithful summary of what Scripture teaches. The word “Trinity” ( Trias in Greek, trinitas in Latin) was coined precisely because the Church needed a single name for the threefold pattern stamped on the whole apostolic faith. And the word is ancient — far older than many assume. The first surviving use is by St. Theophilus, bishop of Antioch, around AD 180, barely three generations after the apostles: “The three days which were before the luminaries are types of the Trinity ( Triados ): of God, and His Word, and His Wisdom.” St. Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus 2.15 (c. AD 180) A generation later Tertullian of Carthage used the Latin trinitas and gave the West its working vocabulary of “one substance, three persons.” These men were not innovating; they were labeling. The label stuck because the data demanded it. The data the word summarizes Three lines of biblical evidence converge. First , Scripture insists there is exactly one God (Deuteronomy 6:4; Isaiah 44:6; 1 Corinthians 8:4) .

Second , Scripture presents three distinct persons who speak to and of one another — the Father who sends, the Son who is sent and prays to the Father, the Spirit who is “another Helper” (John 14:16) , not the Son returned. Third , Scripture ascribes full deity to each: to the Father everywhere; to the Son — “the Word was God” (John 1:1) , “my Lord and my God!” (John 20:28) ; to the Spirit — lying to the Holy Spirit is lying “not to men but to God” (Acts 5:3–4) . Hold all three lines without cutting any, and the Trinity is the only possible conclusion. Every heresy in history is the result of cutting one of the three threads. The threefold pattern is woven even into the most practical texts, where the apostles were not “doing theology” at all but blessing, baptizing, and praying: “Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Matthew 28:19 “There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. There are differences of ministries, but the same Lord.

And there are diversities of activities, but it is the same God who works all in all.” 1 Corinthians 12:4–6 Notice: “in the name ” — singular — “of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Not “in the names,” as of three gods; not “in the name of God, Jesus, and a force,” mixing Creator and creature. The grammar of baptism is already trinitarian grammar. The earliest Church manual, the Didache (first century), already commands baptism with this same threefold name, and every catechumen in Alexandria, Antioch, and Armenia was baptized into it centuries before the councils.
