Scripture and Holy Tradition are not rivals The deeper issue beneath this question is the relationship of Scripture to the Church. The Orthodox answer: the Bible is the supreme written treasure of the Church’s living Tradition, not a rival to it. The same apostolic community that wrote and canonized these books also baptized, worshipped, and confessed in the threefold name — and when wolves arose teaching that the Son was a creature, that same community defined its faith at Nicaea. As St.

Paul commands: “Stand fast and hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or our epistle” (2 Thessalonians 2:15) . The word “Trinity” is one such tradition of words — a fence built by the shepherds around a treasure the Scriptures had already delivered. St. Athanasius put it with characteristic bluntness when accused of using the unbiblical word homoousios (“of one essence”) at Nicaea: the words are new, he said, but the sense is everywhere in Scripture; the bishops “were again compelled on their part to collect the sense of the Scriptures” into a word the heretics could not twist. So with “Trinity”: a new word for the oldest of realities — the Name into which we were baptized. ↑ Back to contents Part I · Question 4 Is Jesus God, or the Son of God? Both — and the “or” is the mistake. He is the Son of God precisely because He is God the Son: begotten of the Father’s own essence, and therefore everything the Father is. The question assumes that “Son of God” is a lesser title — that a son must be junior, derivative, or created.

In human experience that is true; in God it is not. Among men, a son is younger than his father because human nature is bound to time. But the divine Son is begotten eternally , outside time altogether, as radiance is begotten of light. The very point of the title “Son” is not inferiority but identity of nature : a human son is human; the divine Son is divine. The Jews of Jesus’ day understood this instantly — when He called God His own Father, they took up stones, “because You, being a Man, make Yourself God” (John 10:33; cf. John 5:18) . They grasped what modern doubters miss: “Son of God,” claimed in the unique sense Jesus claimed it, is a claim to deity. The Scriptural witness that the Son is God “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God...

And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.” John 1:1, 14 “Jesus said to them, ‘Most assuredly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I AM.’” John 8:58 — claiming the divine Name of Exodus 3:14 “And Thomas answered and said to Him, ‘My Lord and my God!’” John 20:28 — and Jesus accepts the worship rather than correcting it To these add: “in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily” (Colossians 2:9) ; the Son is “the brightness of His glory and the express image of His person,” who “upholds all things by the word of His power” (Hebrews 1:3) ; of the Son the Father Himself says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (Hebrews 1:8) ; He is “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13) ; “the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End... the Almighty” (Revelation 1:8; 22:13) .

He forgives sins, which “only God” can do (Mark 2:5–7) ; He receives worship, which angels and apostles refuse (Matthew 28:17; Revelation 22:8–9) ; He created all things (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16) . Why the Church fought for one word In the fourth century the priest Arius taught that the Son was the first and greatest creature — godlike, but made. The Church’s answer at the Council of Nicaea (AD 325), led above all by the deacon (later Pope) Athanasius of Alexandria, was the word homoousios : the Son is “of one essence with the Father.” Not similar to God — what the Father is, the Son is . Athanasius saw with total clarity that the Gospel itself was at stake: a creature, however exalted, cannot save creatures. Only God can join us to God. “Whence the Word of God came in His own person, that, as He was the Image of the Father, He might be able to create afresh the man after the image… For He was made man that we might be made God; and He manifested Himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father.” St.

Athanasius, On the Incarnation 13, 54 (NPNF) That famous sentence — “He was made man that we might be made god” — does not mean we become deities by nature; it means that because the Son is truly God, His incarnation can lift us into real participation in the divine life, “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4) . If Jesus were only “a son of God” in some honorary sense, Christianity would collapse into the veneration of a hero. Because He is God the Son, the Cross is God’s own love poured out (Romans 5:8) , and union with Christ is union with God. “The Father is greater than I”? Texts where the Son obeys, prays, or says “My Father is greater than I” (John 14:28) describe either His voluntary self-emptying in the flesh — He took “the form of a bondservant” (Philippians 2:6–7) , and a servant’s words befit the servant’s form — or the Father’s place as fountainhead within the Trinity, a priority of origin , never of essence, glory, or power.

The Fathers read all such verses by a simple rule: Scripture speaks of the one Christ sometimes according to His divinity, sometimes according to His humanity, and confusing the two registers creates every christological error. He is at once David’s Son and David’s Lord (Matthew 22:42–45) — and the question “God, or Son of God?” is answered by the centurion at the Cross and the Church in every liturgy: truly, this is the Son of God; truly, this is our Lord and our God. ↑ Back to contents Part I · Question 5 Is the Holy Spirit a person or merely a force? A person — the third person of the Holy Trinity, “the Lord, the Giver of Life,” worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son. A force cannot be grieved, cannot speak, cannot will, and cannot be lied to. The teaching that the Spirit is an impersonal power — God’s “energy,” like electricity — is an ancient error (the fourth-century Pneumatomachi , “Spirit-fighters,” taught a version of it) revived by modern sects.

Scripture refutes it on every page where the Spirit appears, because Scripture consistently ascribes to the Spirit the three marks of personhood: mind, will, and affections — and, beyond personhood, the marks of deity itself. The Spirit acts as only a person can He speaks in the first person and issues commands : “the Holy Spirit said, ‘Now separate to Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them’” (Acts 13:2) . He teaches and reminds (John 14:26) , testifies (John 15:26) , intercedes for us with groanings (Romans 8:26) , searches the depths of God and knows His thoughts (1 Corinthians 2:10–11) . He wills : He distributes gifts “to each one individually as He wills ” (1 Corinthians 12:11) — a force is wielded; it does not choose. He forbids : the Spirit “did not permit” Paul to enter Bithynia (Acts 16:6–7) . And he can be personally wronged: “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30) ; Ananias lied to Him (Acts 5:3) ; blasphemy against Him is the one unforgivable sin (Matthew 12:31–32) . One cannot grieve gravity or lie to lightning.

The Spirit is not only personal but divine “But Peter said, ‘Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit...? You have not lied to men but to God.’” Acts 5:3–4 — to lie to the Spirit is to lie to God He is eternal (Hebrews 9:14) , omnipresent — “Where can I go from Your Spirit?” (Psalm 139:7) — omniscient (1 Corinthians 2:10–11) , the agent of creation who “was hovering over the face of the waters” (Genesis 1:2) , the inspirer of all prophecy (2 Peter 1:21) , and the one who raises the dead (Romans 8:11) . He is named in one breath and one name with the Father and the Son in baptism (Matthew 28:19) and benediction (2 Corinthians 13:14) — unthinkable if He were a creature or an energy. Our bodies are His temple (1 Corinthians 6:19) , and a temple belongs to God alone. The witness of the Fathers The classic patristic treatise on this question is St. Basil the Great’s On the Holy Spirit (AD 375), written when some hesitated to glorify the Spirit with the Father and the Son.

Basil’s argument is devastating in its simplicity: examine what the Spirit does — sanctifies, gives life, deifies, makes sons of God — and ask whether a creature or a force could do it. “Through the Holy Spirit comes our restoration to paradise, our ascension into the kingdom of heaven, our return to the adoption of sons, our liberty to call God our Father, our being made partakers of the grace of Christ, our being called children of light, our sharing in eternal glory… If such is the earnest, what the perfection?” St. Basil the Great, On the Holy Spirit 15.36 “Shining upon those that are cleansed from every spot, He makes them spiritual by fellowship with Himself. Just as when a sunbeam falls on bright and transparent bodies they themselves become brilliant too, and shed forth a fresh brightness from themselves, so souls wherein the Spirit dwells, illuminated by the Spirit, themselves become spiritual, and send forth their grace to others.” St.

Basil the Great, On the Holy Spirit 9.23 The Council of Constantinople (AD 381) — the second of the three great councils the Oriental Orthodox Churches receive — enshrined this faith in the creed: the Spirit is “the Lord and Giver-of-Life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified.” Worshipped — not used; glorified — not harnessed. The practical stakes are enormous. If the Spirit is a force, the Christian life is a technique for tapping power. Because He is a person, the Christian life is a communion : He indwells us (John 14:17) , prays in us (Romans 8:26) , transforms us “from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18) , and pours the love of God into our hearts (Romans 5:5) . Every sacrament of the Church — baptism, chrismation (the seal of the Spirit), the Eucharist over which the priest invokes the Spirit’s descent in the epiclesis — is fellowship with Him. We do not use the Spirit; we worship Him, and He sanctifies us.

↑ Back to contents Part I · Question 6 How can Jesus be both fully God and fully man? Because the eternal Son, without ceasing to be God, truly made our complete humanity His own in the womb of the Virgin. From the union there is one Christ, one person, one incarnate nature of God the Word — His divinity never parted from His humanity for a single moment, nor a twinkling of an eye. This is the mystery the Apostle calls “great” — “God was manifested in the flesh” (1 Timothy 3:16) — and it is the heart of the Oriental Orthodox faith, defended at the Council of Ephesus (AD 431) under St. Cyril the Great, Pope of Alexandria. The question “how can one person be both?” is best answered by first ruling out the wrong answers, for each was tried and condemned. What the Church rejects Not a mixture. Christ is not a hybrid, a demigod, half-God and half-man.

Divinity and humanity are not diluted into some third thing, as the heretic Eutyches implied when he suggested the humanity was swallowed up “like a drop of honey in the sea.” The Oriental Orthodox Churches explicitly condemn Eutyches: Christ’s humanity is real, complete, and consubstantial with ours — body, rational soul, mind, and will. He hungered (Matthew 4:2) , thirsted (John 19:28) , wept (John 11:35) , grew (Luke 2:52) , and died. Not a partnership. Nor is Christ two persons glued together — the divine Word merely indwelling the man Jesus, as Nestorius taught, so that Mary bore “the man” but not God. Against this St. Cyril insisted that the one who lay in the manger and the one who upholds the universe are the same one . Therefore the Virgin is rightly called Theotokos — “Birth-giver of God” — for the one she bore according to the flesh is God the Word. There are not two Sons, one divine and one human; there is one Lord Jesus Christ.

What the Church confesses “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” John 1:14 — He did not enter a man; He became man “Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but made Himself of no reputation, taking the form of a bondservant, and coming in the likeness of men.” Philippians 2:5–7 — one subject, two “forms”: He who is God took what is ours St. Cyril gave the Oriental Orthodox Churches their treasured formula: mia physis tou Theou Logou sesarkōmenē — “one incarnate nature of God the Word.” The word “one” here does not deny that Christ is fully divine and fully human; it denies that He is divisible. As soul and body unite into one living man without the soul becoming flesh or the flesh becoming soul, so — incomparably more perfectly — divinity and humanity are united in the one Christ without confusion and without separation. After the union, we do not count two; we worship one Emmanuel who is at once entirely God and entirely man.

“For we do not say that the nature of the Word was changed and became flesh, or that it was converted into a whole man consisting of soul and body; but rather that the Word having personally united to himself flesh animated by a rational soul, did in an ineffable and inconceivable manner become man… because the two natures being brought together in a true union, there is of both one Christ and one Son; for the difference of the natures is not taken away by the union, but rather the divinity and the humanity make perfect for us the one Lord Jesus Christ by their ineffable and inexpressible union.” St. Cyril of Alexandria, Second Letter to Nestorius (NPNF) St. Severus of Antioch, the great Syriac Orthodox teacher (d. 538), guarded the same faith after Chalcedon: Emmanuel is one, he wrote, “one nature incarnate of God the Word,” the difference of the elements from which He is composed never dissolved, yet never permitting a count of “two” that would split the single Christ into two acting subjects.

Every act of Christ — touching the leper, sleeping in the boat, raising Lazarus, dying on the Cross — is the act of one divine person acting through His own complete humanity. This is why we may say the astonishing things Scripture says: that they “crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8) , and that God purchased the Church “with His own blood” (Acts 20:28) . The Word truly suffered — in the flesh , His own flesh — while His divine nature remained impassible. The Coptic Liturgy of St. Basil places this confession on the lips of every communicant before the chalice: Summary: The priest confesses that this is the life-giving Body which the only-begotten Son, our Lord, God and Saviour Jesus Christ, took from the holy Theotokos, and which He made one with His divinity without mingling, without confusion and without alteration, and that His divinity never parted from His humanity for a single moment, nor the twinkling of an eye. Summary of the Confession before Communion, Coptic Liturgy of St. Basil (English translations vary) Long before the controversies, St.

Ignatius of Antioch — a disciple of the apostles, martyred c. AD 107 — had already confessed the paradox in a single breath: “There is one Physician who is possessed both of flesh and spirit; both made and not made; God existing in flesh; true life in death; both of Mary and of God; first passible and then impassible, even Jesus Christ our Lord.” St. Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Ephesians 7 (ANF) Why it must be so is the Gospel itself: only God can save, and only what is assumed is healed. As St. Gregory the Theologian said, “that which He has not assumed He has not healed.” Had Christ lacked a human mind, our minds would be unredeemed; had He been less than God, His sacrifice could not carry infinite weight. He is the bridge with both ends anchored: fully God, so that in Him we touch God; fully man, so that God touches us. The “how” exceeds our comprehension — the Fathers call it ineffable — but the “that” is our salvation, and before it the Church does not calculate; she kneels.

↑ Back to contents Part I · Question 7 Why did God create humanity? Not out of need — God lacks nothing — but out of the overflow of His goodness and love: to create persons in His own image who could freely know Him, love Him, share His life, and grow into His likeness forever. Begin with what the answer is not . God did not create us because He was lonely, bored, or incomplete. The Holy Trinity is eternally complete in itself: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit dwell in perfect mutual love and glory “before the foundation of the world” (John 17:5, 24) . As Paul preached in Athens, God is not “worshiped with men’s hands, as though He needed anything, since He gives to all life, breath, and all things” (Acts 17:25) . This is, paradoxically, the most liberating truth about our existence: we are not God’s servants hired to meet a deficiency. We exist because love, by its nature, is generous — goodness diffuses itself. Creation is grace from its first syllable.

“For God is good, or rather is essentially the source of goodness: nor could one that is good be niggardly of anything: whence, grudging existence to none, He has made all things out of nothing by His own Word, Jesus Christ our Lord. And among these, having taken special pity, above all things on earth, upon the race of men…” St. Athanasius, On the Incarnation 3 (NPNF) In the image, toward the likeness “Then God said, ‘Let Us make man in Our image, according to Our likeness’... So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.” Genesis 1:26–27 Two details here shaped all patristic thought. First, the plural — “Let Us make” — which the Fathers heard as the eternal counsel of the Trinity: humanity is created by a communion of persons, for communion.

Second, the pairing of “image” and “likeness.” Many Fathers distinguished them: the image is what every human being indelibly possesses — reason, freedom, personhood, the capacity for God; the likeness is the destination — actually becoming like God in holiness and love, by free cooperation with grace. We were created not as finished products but as royal seeds, made to grow. Man was placed in the world as priest and king of creation: to “tend and keep” the garden (Genesis 2:15) , to name the creatures, and to gather the praise of mute creation into articulate thanksgiving — which is why the Church’s central act is called the Eucharist , “thanksgiving.” The Psalmist marvels at this vocation: “What is man that You are mindful of him...? For You have made him a little lower than the angels, and You have crowned him with glory and honor. You have made him to have dominion over the works of Your hands.” Psalm 8:4–6 Created for communion — and for glory St.

Irenaeus of Lyons (2nd century), the disciple of Polycarp who was the disciple of John, gave the most celebrated one-line answer to this question ever written: “The glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God. For if the manifestation of God which is made by means of the creation, affords life to all living in the earth, much more does that revelation of the Father which comes through the Word, give life to those who see God.” St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 4.20.7 God’s glory is not enhanced by us as a king is enriched by taxes; His glory is displayed in us as a fire is displayed in what it kindles. We glorify God the way a healthy tree glorifies the gardener — by flourishing, by becoming fully alive in Him. And the destiny is staggering: not mere moral improvement but theosis , deification by grace — real participation in God’s own life.

“Beloved, now we are children of God; and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be, but we know that when He is revealed, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2) ; we are called to be “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4) . Here the doctrine of creation joins hands with the Incarnation. The Fathers taught that Adam was made according to the Image of God — and the Image of God is the Son (Colossians 1:15) . Humanity was, from the first, shaped toward Christ; the Incarnation is not merely an emergency repair but the crown of God’s eternal purpose: “He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world... having predestined us to adoption as sons by Jesus Christ to Himself, according to the good pleasure of His will” (Ephesians 1:4–5) . Why did God create you? So that, in Christ and by the Spirit, you might become by grace what the Son is by nature — a child of God, alive forever in the light of His face. Anything less is too small an answer for the Scriptures we have been given.

↑ Back to contents Part I · Question 8 Why does God allow evil and suffering? God did not create evil and is never its author. He created free persons capable of love, and love’s freedom can be refused; evil is that refusal and its wreckage. God permits it for a time rather than abolish freedom — and He has answered it, not from a distance, but from inside it, on the Cross. This is the oldest wound in the human heart, and the Church refuses both cheap answers. She will not say evil is an illusion, and she will not say God wills it. The Orthodox answer has four movements: what evil is , where it came from , why God permits it, and what God has done about it. Evil is not a thing God made Everything God made is good: “God saw everything that He had made, and indeed it was very good” (Genesis 1:31) . Evil is therefore not a substance, not a creature, not a rival power — it is a corruption , a parasite on the good, as rust is on iron and blindness is in an eye. St.

Basil the Great preached an entire homily on precisely this question, with a title that is itself a creed: That God Is Not the Author of Evils . “Evil is not a living animated essence; it is the condition of the soul opposed to virtue, developed in the careless on account of their falling away from good. Do not then go beyond yourself to seek for evil, and imagine that there is an original nature of wickedness. Each of us, let us acknowledge it, is the first author of his own vice.” St. Basil the Great, Hexaemeron 2.4–5 (NPNF) It entered through freedom God created angels and men free, because He wanted sons, not machines. Love that cannot be withheld is not love; obedience that cannot be refused is not obedience. The devil fell first, by pride; then man, tempted, freely turned from the source of life — and turning from Life, found death: “through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin” (Romans 5:12) .

Much of the world’s anguish flows from this double fountain: moral evil from misused freedom (wars, cruelty, betrayal), and the groaning of a creation “subjected to futility” (Romans 8:20–22) — disease, decay, death — the shockwave of the Fall through a world whose appointed king had defected. God permits what He does not will , because to annihilate the possibility of evil tonight He would have to annihilate freedom — and with it, love, virtue, repentance, and every soul still on its way home. The patience of God is not indifference; “the Lord is... longsuffering toward us, not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9) . God bends evil to good without approving it Scripture shows a God so sovereign that He weaves even wickedness into His providence — without ever becoming its author. Joseph, sold by his brothers, tells them: “you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good... to save many people alive” (Genesis 50:20) .

The supreme case is the Cross itself: the worst crime in history — the murder of the incarnate God “by lawless hands” — was at the same time “the determined purpose and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23) , becoming the salvation of the world. Hence the apostle’s promise, not that all things are good, but that “all things work together for good to those who love God” (Romans 8:28) . God’s answer is not an argument but Himself Job demanded an explanation and received instead a theophany — God Himself, speaking from the whirlwind — and it sufficed: “I have heard of You by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees You” (Job 42:5) . The Gospel goes further: God did not send an answer; He came. The Word took flesh that can be scourged, a brow that can be pierced, a mother who can weep at His feet. Whatever you suffer, you cannot say God does not understand: He was betrayed by a friend, abandoned by His companions, tortured by the state, and died young, in agony, unjustly — “a Man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3) . And by dying He detonated death from within.

The Cross is God absorbing the worst evil can do and returning resurrection. “And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; there shall be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying. There shall be no more pain, for the former things have passed away.” Revelation 21:4 This is the final movement: evil has an expiration date. The permission is temporary; the victory is accomplished and awaits only its unveiling. St. Paul, who was flogged, stoned, and shipwrecked, did the arithmetic from inside the suffering: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18) . The martyrs of the Oriental Orthodox Churches — from the era of Diocletian, by which the Copts date their calendar of the martyrs, to those of our own century — did not go to their deaths holding a tidy syllogism. They went holding Christ.

In the end, the problem of evil is answered the way the Church answers everything: by pointing to the Lamb standing as though slain (Revelation 5:6) — wounds glorified, death undone — and by the cry that closes the Bible: “Even so, come, Lord Jesus.” ↑ Back to contents Part I · Question 9 Does God know the future? Yes — perfectly, eternally, and in every detail. But God’s foreknowledge does not cause our choices; He knows them because we will freely make them, not the other way round. Scripture stakes God’s very identity on this. When the Lord, through Isaiah, puts the idols of the nations on trial, the test He sets is precisely knowledge of the future — only the true God possesses it: “Remember the former things of old, for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like Me, declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times things that are not yet done, saying, ‘My counsel shall stand, and I will do all My pleasure.’” Isaiah 46:9–10 The Bible’s entire prophetic architecture rests on this.

Centuries in advance, God names Cyrus the deliverer (Isaiah 44:28–45:1) , foretells the Messiah’s birthplace (Micah 5:2) , His pierced hands and divided garments (Psalm 22:16–18) , His silent suffering and grave with the rich (Isaiah 53) . Jesus tells His disciples the future precisely so that fulfilled prophecy will anchor their faith: “Now I tell you before it comes, that when it does come to pass, you may believe that I am He” (John 13:19) . He foreknows Peter’s three denials down to the rooster’s crow (Matthew 26:34) and Judas’s betrayal from the beginning (John 6:64) . The Psalmist extends this knowledge to every unlived day of every life: “Your eyes saw my substance, being yet unformed. And in Your book they all were written, the days fashioned for me, when as yet there were none of them” (Psalm 139:16) . “Known to God from eternity are all His works” (Acts 15:18) . How God knows: eternity, not prediction God does not “foresee” the future the way a forecaster extrapolates from the present, and He does not wait for time to deliver information.

God is not in time at all; He is the Creator of time. “One day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day” (2 Peter 3:8) ; He is the one “who is and who was and who is to come” (Revelation 1:8) , inhabiting eternity (Isaiah 57:15) . All of history — what to us is past, present, and future — is present to God in a single, undivided act of knowing, as a man on a mountain sees in one glance the whole road that travelers below walk step by step. The Fathers therefore speak less of God’s “foreknowledge” than of His eternal knowledge , which only looks like “fore-” from our position inside time. Does this destroy our freedom? No — and here the Fathers are unanimous and emphatic. Knowledge is not compulsion. I may know my friend so well that I am certain how he will choose; my knowledge does not cause his choice. God’s knowledge is infinitely more perfect, but the logic holds: He knows our free acts as free acts . The order of dependence runs from our choosing to His knowing, not from His knowing to our choosing. St.

John Chrysostom, preaching on Judas, insisted that Christ’s foreknowledge of the betrayal in no way forced Judas’s hand — the Lord even washed his feet and warned him, leaving his freedom intact to the last hour. As the Fathers put it in a formula the whole Church inherited: God foreknows all things, but He does not predetermine all things. He foreknows our sins without willing them; He foreknows our repentance and crowns it as truly ours. Summary: For Chrysostom, God's foreknowledge is not the cause of our sinning. He does not compel virtue, and the wickedness of the wicked does not come from Him; knowing all things beforehand, He waits for the free movement of each person, and what we choose He knows from eternity. A summary of St. John Chrysostom’s consistent teaching on foreknowledge and freedom (cf.

Homilies on Romans 16; Homilies on Matthew) This is why Scripture can hold, without strain, both “the determined purpose and foreknowledge of God” and “you have taken by lawless hands” in a single verse about the Cross (Acts 2:23) : God’s plan and man’s freedom interlock without canceling each other. And the pastoral fruit is immense. Because God knows the future, no tomorrow can ambush Him; “your Father knows the things you have need of before you ask Him” (Matthew 6:8) . Because His knowledge does not coerce, your repentance today is real, your prayers matter, and your future — known to God — is still, in time, genuinely yours to live. The believer walks forward into a future that is dark to him but lit, end to end, before the eyes of his Father. ↑ Back to contents Part I · Question 10 Does God change His mind? No — God’s nature, character, and eternal purpose are utterly unchangeable. When Scripture says God “relented,” it describes, in human language, the unchanging God responding differently to people who have changed. The repentance is ours; the consistency is His.

The question arises from an apparent contradiction in Scripture. On one side stand the great immutability texts: “God is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should repent. Has He said, and will He not do? Or has He spoken, and will He not make it good?” Numbers 23:19 “For I am the LORD, I do not change; therefore you are not consumed, O sons of Jacob.” ... “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and comes down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning.” Malachi 3:6; James 1:17 On the other side, the narratives: God “was sorry that He had made man” before the flood (Genesis 6:6) ; He “relented” from destroying Israel when Moses interceded (Exodus 32:14) ; He spared Nineveh after Jonah’s preaching (Jonah 3:10) ; He added fifteen years to Hezekiah’s life after announcing his death (2 Kings 20:1–6) . Does the Bible contradict itself? The Fathers answer: no — these are two registers of language about the one unchanging God. Divine condescension: God speaks baby-talk to us St.

John Chrysostom built much of his exegesis on the principle of synkatabasis — God’s loving “condescension,” His stooping down to speak our language, as a father lisps to his infant. Scripture gives God hands, eyes, nostrils, wings; no one imagines the infinite Spirit has feathers. “Repentance” language belongs to the same family: it describes how God’s unchanging action appears from within the human story . When a city repents, the same unchanging holiness that threatened judgment now embraces it — not because God moved, but because the city did. The sun does not change when a man steps from a cellar into daylight; yet to him, everything has changed. Summary: Chrysostom warns that when Scripture speaks of God's fury and anger, we should understand nothing human by these words. They are words of condescension: God is far removed from such passions, and speaks this way to bring the matter home to hearers who could not otherwise grasp it. Summary of St.

John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis (on divine condescension) God’s warnings are doors, not verdicts Here is the deeper resolution: many of God’s announcements are not unconditional decrees but conditional summonses — and God Himself published the condition as a standing rule of His governance: “The instant I speak concerning a nation... to pluck up, to pull down, and to destroy it, if that nation against whom I have spoken turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I thought to bring upon it.” Jeremiah 18:7–8 Read in this light, Nineveh is not God changing His mind but God keeping His word. The threat “forty days and Nineveh shall be overthrown” carried, as all such threats do, the implicit clause of Jeremiah 18 — which Jonah knew perfectly well, and resented: “I know that You are a gracious and merciful God... One who relents from doing harm” (Jonah 4:2) . The “change” was the whole point of the warning.

A doctor who says “without surgery you will die,” and then cancels the funeral when the patient accepts surgery, has not been inconsistent; he has been faithful to one unchanging purpose — the patient’s life. Why immutability is good news Far from making God cold or distant, His changelessness is the anchor of every promise. A god who changes his mind might one day change it about you: about mercy, about the Cross, about the value of your repentance. But “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Hebrews 13:8) ; “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29) ; His covenant love “endures forever” — the refrain of Psalm 136, twenty-six times. Precisely because God cannot change, prayer and repentance are not attempts to alter Him but the appointed means by which we step into the path of His unchanging mercy. The prodigal’s father did not become loving when the son returned; the love was waiting the whole time, scanning the road (Luke 15:20) . God’s “relenting” is what His eternal, immovable love looks like when, at last, we come home.

↑ Back to contents ✦ ☩ ✦ Part II On Christ and His Saving Work “He was wounded for our transgressions... and by His stripes we are healed.” — Isaiah 53:5 Part II · Question 1 Why did Jesus have to die on the Cross? Because sin had bound humanity to death, and only the death of the incarnate God could untie the knot — satisfying God’s truthfulness, conquering death from within, and revealing a love that argument alone could never reveal. The “had to” must be understood rightly. Nothing outside God compelled Him; the Cross was freely chosen: “No one takes My life from Me, but I lay it down of Myself” (John 10:18) . The necessity lies in what God had said and in what man had become. St. Athanasius, in On the Incarnation — the single most important patristic book on this question — frames it as what he calls the divine dilemma . The divine dilemma God had warned Adam truthfully: “in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die” (Genesis 2:17) . Man ate; death entered and began unmaking the creature made for incorruption. Now, says Athanasius, consider God’s position.

It would be unworthy of God’s truthfulness to simply cancel the sentence — God would be a liar, and His word would mean nothing. Yet it would be unworthy of God’s goodness to watch the creatures He made in His own image disintegrate into nothingness. Mere repentance could not solve it, for repentance might cover the guilt of sin but could not heal the corruption — the death already metastasizing in human nature. Something more radical was required: “For the Word, perceiving that no otherwise could the corruption of men be undone save by death as a necessary condition, while it was impossible for the Word to suffer death, being immortal, and Son of the Father; to this end He takes to Himself a body capable of death, that it, by partaking of the Word Who is above all, might be worthy to die in the stead of all, and might, because of the Word which had come to dwell in it, remain incorruptible, and that thenceforth corruption might be stayed from all by the Grace of the Resurrection.” St.

Athanasius, On the Incarnation 9 (NPNF) This is why the Word became flesh at all: the immortal One acquired, in the Virgin’s womb, a mortality He could offer. He took a body precisely so that He would have something to die with — and someone to die as : one of us, our kinsman, our representative, the Second Adam standing where the first fell. What love required But the Cross is not bare bookkeeping. Scripture insists the deepest “why” is love: “God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son” (John 3:16) ; “God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8) ; He “loved me and gave Himself for me” (Galatians 2:20) . The prophet had seen it seven centuries before, in the most precise prophecy in the Old Testament: “He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement for our peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray...

and the LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all.” Isaiah 53:5–6 And the death had to be this death — public, on a cross, not private illness or old age. Athanasius answers even that detail: the Lord came to bear the curse, and “cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Galatians 3:13; Deuteronomy 21:23) ; He died lifted up between heaven and earth, arms stretched out, “that He might draw all peoples to Myself” (John 12:32) — one hand, the Fathers loved to say, reaching to the Jews and the other to the Gentiles. He died before witnesses so that the resurrection would have witnesses; a death no one saw could be doubted, but Rome itself certified this one. Death destroyed by death Finally — and this is the note the Oriental Orthodox liturgies sound loudest — He died in order to invade death. Human death is the soul’s separation from the body; but this dead body was still the body of God the Word , and this human soul, descending to the realm of the dead, was still the soul of God the Word .

Death swallowed Him as bait and was caught on the hook of His divinity; it took in Life Himself, and burst. “Inasmuch then as the children have partaken of flesh and blood, He Himself likewise shared in the same, that through death He might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil , and release those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” (Hebrews 2:14–15) . The Cross, which Rome designed as the advertisement of terror, became the instrument by which the fear of death itself was abolished. That is why the Church does not mourn before the Cross but venerates it, and why every Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopian believer signs himself with it: it is not the trophy of death over Jesus, but of Jesus over death. ↑ Back to contents Part II · Question 2 What exactly did Jesus accomplish through His death? A single, many-sided victory: He offered the perfect sacrifice for sin, paid our debt, conquered death and the devil, reconciled us to the Father, healed human nature itself, and opened paradise.

Scripture uses many images because no one image can hold it all. Ask the New Testament what the Cross accomplished and it answers in a chorus of metaphors drawn from the temple, the law-court, the slave-market, the battlefield, and the sickbed. The Orthodox instinct is to keep all of them, refusing to reduce the mystery to any single theory. Consider the principal strands. Sacrifice: the Lamb of God Every lamb slain from Abel to the last Passover before A.D. 33 was a shadow pointing to one morning outside Jerusalem. “Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29) . The Epistle to the Hebrews works this out in detail: the blood of bulls and goats could never actually remove sin (Hebrews 10:4) ; they were annual reminders, IOUs awaiting payment. Christ is at once the true High Priest and the true offering, entering “with His own blood… the Most Holy Place once for all, having obtained eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12) . “So Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many” (Hebrews 9:28) .

This is why the Eucharist stands at the center of Orthodox worship: it is the Church’s participation, until He comes, in that one unrepeatable sacrifice. Ransom and redemption: the price of freedom “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45) . We were slaves — to sin, to corruption, to the fear of death — and a price was paid that we could never raise: “you were not redeemed with corruptible things, like silver or gold... but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot” (1 Peter 1:18–19) . He also bore, in our place, the curse pronounced by the law: “Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13) ; God “made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him” (2 Corinthians 5:21) . The innocent stood in for the guilty — “the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18) . Victory: death trampled, the devil disarmed The note the early Church sang most loudly is conquest.

On the Cross, what looked like defeat was ambush: “Having disarmed principalities and powers, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them in it” (Colossians 2:15) . Death, the “last enemy” (1 Corinthians 15:26) , took into itself the Author of life and was ruptured from the inside. The ancient taunt became the Church’s Paschal shout: “O Death, where is your sting? O Hades, where is your victory?” (1 Corinthians 15:55; Hosea 13:14) . “For of old, before the divine sojourn of the Saviour took place, even to the saints death was terrible, and all wept for the dead as though they perished. But now that the Saviour has raised His body, death is no longer terrible; for all who believe in Christ tread him under as nought, and choose rather to die than to deny their faith in Christ. For they verily know that when they die they are not destroyed, but actually [begin to] live, and become incorruptible through the Resurrection.” St.

Athanasius, On the Incarnation 27 (NPNF) Reconciliation and healing: the nature restored Sin was not only a debt; it was an estrangement and a disease. The Cross addresses both. Estrangement: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not imputing their trespasses to them” (2 Corinthians 5:19) ; “having made peace through the blood of His cross” (Colossians 1:20) — the veil of the temple tearing top to bottom at the moment of His death (Matthew 27:51) , God’s own declaration that the way into His presence stood open. Disease: “by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5) . The Fathers loved the medical register: Christ assumed our wounded nature and carried it through death into incorruption, so that human nature itself — not merely our legal record — is renewed in Him. St. Ephrem the Syrian, the harp of the Spirit, sang of the wondrous exchange: the Lord took from us our weakness and gave us His glory; He took our manhood and gave us His divinity’s riches. In his own image, He gave us divinity and we gave Him humanity. And St.

Irenaeus compressed the whole economy into one line: “…who did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself” (Against Heresies 5, preface). One Cross, then, and a cascade of effects: sins forgiven, the debt cancelled — “having wiped out the handwriting of requirements that was against us... having nailed it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14) — death gutted, Satan disarmed, the Father’s house reopened, human nature healed, paradise unlocked. The first soul to walk through that reopened gate was a crucified thief, promised it by the dying Lord Himself: “Assuredly, I say to you, today you will be with Me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43) . What did Jesus accomplish through His death? Nothing less than the unmaking of the Fall. ↑ Back to contents Part II · Question 3 Did Jesus descend into Hades after His death? Yes.

While His body lay in the tomb — never separated from His divinity — His human soul, united to His divinity, descended into Hades, proclaimed His victory, shattered its gates, and led out the righteous who had died in hope from Adam onward. The descent into Hades (the “Harrowing of Hell”) is not a pious legend; it is apostolic doctrine, woven into the New Testament, the ancient creeds, and above all the Paschal worship of the Orthodox Churches. Hades (Hebrew Sheol ) in Scripture is not the lake of fire; it is the realm of the dead — the shadowed prison where all the departed, even the righteous, were held under death’s dominion before Christ (cf. Psalm 6:5; Isaiah 38:18) .

The Scriptural witness “For Christ also suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive by the Spirit, by whom also He went and preached to the spirits in prison.” 1 Peter 3:18–19 “Now this, ‘He ascended’ — what does it mean but that He also first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is also the One who ascended far above all the heavens, that He might fill all things.” Ephesians 4:9–10 Add to these: “For this reason the gospel was preached also to those who are dead” (1 Peter 4:6) ; Peter’s Pentecost sermon applying Psalm 16 to Christ — “You will not leave My soul in Hades, nor will You allow Your Holy One to see corruption” (Acts 2:27, 31) ; the Lord’s own sign of Jonah, “three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40) ; and the risen Christ’s declaration: “I am He who lives, and was dead... And I have the keys of Hades and of Death” (Revelation 1:18) . One does not hold the keys of a prison one has not entered and conquered.

Matthew even records the firstfruits of the harrowing: at the Lord’s death and resurrection “the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised” (Matthew 27:52–53) . What happened there The Fathers are careful: Christ descended not as a captive but as a conqueror. His soul was not dragged to Hades as ours were; He entered as Lord, and Hades’ ancient machinery — built to hold sinners — seized the one sinless Man and, in seizing Him, seized God. St. John Chrysostom’s Paschal homily, read aloud in churches at every Pascha, exults in the catastrophe this caused: “It took a body and, face to face, met God! It took earth and encountered heaven! It took what it saw but crumbled before what it had not seen! ‘O death, where is thy sting? O hades, where is thy victory?’ Christ is risen, and you are overthrown! Christ is risen, and the demons are fallen! Christ is risen, and the angels rejoice! Christ is risen, and life reigns! Christ is risen, and not one dead remains in a tomb!” St.

John Chrysostom, Paschal Homily (translation as published by OrthodoxWiki) St. Ephrem the Syrian devoted whole hymn-cycles (the Nisibene Hymns) to this drama, personifying Death and Satan as they lament their ruin — Death wailing that, having swallowed the One, it is forced to vomit out the many. The icon of the Resurrection in the Orthodox tradition depicts not Christ stepping from the tomb (no one witnessed that moment) but precisely this: Christ standing on the shattered, cross-shaped gates of Hades, grasping Adam and Eve by the wrists — not their hands, for salvation is His grip, not their grasp — hauling our first parents, and in them all humanity, out of the grave. The Coptic Church confesses it tersely in the liturgy’s commemorations, and the universal Paschal hymn of the East compresses it to a single line: Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and upon those in the tombs bestowing life.

Why it matters First, it answers the question of the righteous dead: what of Abel, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, the prophets — those who died in faith before the Cross? “These all died in faith, not having received the promises” (Hebrews 11:13, 39–40) . The descent is the Gospel reaching backward: Christ’s salvation is not limited by chronology; He is “the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world” (Revelation 13:8) , and the first beneficiaries of His Cross were the dead of forty centuries. Second, it transforms the meaning of every Christian’s death. Hades has been gutted; for those in Christ, death is no longer a prison but a passage — “absent from the body... present with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8) . There is no depth where He has not gone before us: “If I make my bed in hell, behold, You are there” (Psalm 139:8) . The lamp of this series burns even there: the Light descended into the deepest darkness ever known, and the darkness could not overcome it (John 1:5) .

↑ Back to contents Part II · Question 4 Why did Jesus rise from the dead? Because death had no rightful hold on the Sinless One — “it was not possible that He should be held by it.” He rose to vindicate His sacrifice, to destroy death as a power, to become the firstfruits of our own resurrection, and to begin the new creation in His own glorified body. The first thing to say is that the resurrection was not optional — not a happy epilogue appended to the real work of the Cross. Cross and Resurrection are one indivisible act, two faces of one victory. St. Paul stakes the entire faith on it: “if Christ is not risen, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins!” (1 Corinthians 15:17) . A dead savior saves no one. Peter, preaching at Pentecost, gives the deepest reason it happened: “...whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of death, because it was not possible that He should be held by it.” Acts 2:24 Not possible. Death’s legal claim runs only over sinners — “the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23) — and over creatures. Christ was neither: sinless, and the Author of life.

Death seized Him by the only foothold it had, His freely-assumed mortal flesh; but having taken in the Life Himself, it could no more retain Him than night can retain the sunrise. The resurrection is simply who He is, asserting itself: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25) . Vindication: the Father’s “Amen” to the Son The resurrection is God’s public verdict on Jesus of Nazareth. The Sanhedrin judged Him a blasphemer; Rome judged Him a criminal; the resurrection reversed both courts: He was “declared to be the Son of God with power... by the resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:4) . And it is the verdict on His work as much as His person: He “was delivered up because of our offenses, and was raised because of our justification ” (Romans 4:25) . The risen Christ is the Father’s receipt that the offering of Good Friday was accepted in full. This is why the apostles, in Acts, preach the resurrection more than anything else — sermon after sermon hammering one note: you killed Him, God raised Him, and we are witnesses (Acts 2:32; 3:15; 5:30–32; 10:39–41) .

The Church was not founded on an idea but on an empty tomb and five hundred eyewitnesses (1 Corinthians 15:6) , most of whom went to their deaths rather than retract. Firstfruits: our resurrection has already begun “But now Christ is risen from the dead, and has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For since by man came death, by Man also came the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ all shall be made alive.” 1 Corinthians 15:20–22 “Firstfruits” is harvest language: the first sheaf is not a different crop from the rest; it is the same harvest, arriving first and guaranteeing the remainder. Christ did not rise as a private miracle but as the head of a body — what happened to Him on the third day is what will happen to all who are His. And note what rose: not a ghost (“Handle Me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see I have” Luke 24:39 ), not a resuscitated corpse like Lazarus, who died again — but the same body, glorified and deathless, still bearing the wounds (John 20:27) yet no longer subject to corruption.

Our hope, accordingly, is not the soul’s escape from the body but the body’s redemption (Romans 8:23) : He “will transform our lowly body that it may be conformed to His glorious body” (Philippians 3:21) . “For now that the Saviour works so great things among men, and day by day is invisibly persuading so great a multitude from every side, both from them that dwell in Greece and in foreign lands, to come over to His faith, and all to obey His teaching, will any one still hold his mind in doubt whether a Resurrection has been accomplished by the Saviour, and whether Christ is alive, or rather is Himself the Life? Or is it like a dead man to be pricking the consciences of men…?” St. Athanasius, On the Incarnation 30 (NPNF) Athanasius adds his famous image: now that death has been conquered, Christians mock it — believers “tread him under as nought,” and even children and women who once trembled at it hasten toward martyrdom as toward life. A defeated tyrant, he says, is laughed at by the very citizens who once paid him tribute.

The resurrection turned the human race’s oldest terror into a defeated and derided enemy. Finally, the resurrection inaugurates the new creation. It happened “on the first day of the week” (John 20:1) — the eighth day, as the Fathers call it, the first morning of the world to come — and in a garden, where the new Adam was mistaken for “the gardener” (John 20:15) by no accident of narrative: the world’s true Gardener had returned to His ruined garden to replant it. Every Sunday liturgy, every baptism (“buried with Him... raised with Him,” Colossians 2:12 ), every lamp lit at Pascha announces the same fact: the future resurrection has already broken into the middle of history, and its name is Jesus. ↑ Back to contents Part II · Question 5 Is Jesus the only way to salvation? Yes. Salvation is union with God, and only God incarnate can unite humanity to God. There is no other mediator, no other sacrifice, no other name. What God in His mercy does with those who never heard of Him is His judgment to make — but He has shown us the Way, and commanded us to walk it and proclaim it.

The claim is not the Church’s invention; it is the Lord’s own, spoken on the night before His death, and the apostles’ unanimous preaching at the risk — and cost — of their lives: “Jesus said to him, ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.’” John 14:6 “Nor is there salvation in any other, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” Acts 4:12 — Peter, on trial before the Sanhedrin To these add: “there is one God and one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:5–6) ; “he who does not believe the Son shall not see life” (John 3:36) ; “I am the door. If anyone enters by Me, he will be saved” (John 10:9) . Note the definite articles: the way, the door, one mediator. The New Testament does not present Jesus as a way among ways but as the single bridge over an otherwise unbridgeable chasm. Why it could not be otherwise This exclusivity is not arbitrary narrowness; it follows from what salvation is .

If salvation were merely information, many teachers could deliver it. If it were merely moral effort, many paths could host it. But salvation, as the previous questions have shown, is nothing less than the healing of a death-infected nature and the union of man with God — and that required God Himself to become man, die our death, and rise. No prophet, sage, or founder of a religion did this, claimed to do it, or could do it. Buddha pointed to a path; Muhammad claimed to relay a message; philosophers refined ethics. Christ alone said “I am the resurrection” and walked out of His grave. As St. Athanasius argued, only the One through whom we were created could recreate us; a creature cannot save creatures, for only the Maker can remake what He made. The uniqueness of the Way is simply the uniqueness of the Incarnation. There is one God-man; therefore there is one bridge; therefore there is one way — not because God is stingy, but because only one such bridge ever existed or needed to exist, and God paid for it with His own blood (Acts 20:28) .

The way is walked in His Body, the Church The Orthodox faith adds what modern individualism forgets: Christ is not received as a private opinion but as a life entered. He instituted baptism as the gateway — “unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5) ; “he who believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16) — and the Eucharist as the sustenance: “unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you have no life in you” (John 6:53) . The Way, therefore, is concrete: faith, baptism, the sacramental life, repentance, and love within the Body He founded. St. Cyprian of Carthage stated the ancient consensus without embarrassment: “He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother” (On the Unity of the Church 6). The ark is one; the flood is real; the door stands open. What about those who never heard? Here the Church speaks with care.

Scripture affirms both that God “desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4) and that “the Judge of all the earth” will “do right” (Genesis 18:25) ; that those without the law will be judged by what they had (Romans 2:12–16) ; and that Christ’s descent into Hades carried His salvation even to those who died before His coming. Whatever mercy God extends beyond the visible boundaries of the Church is extended through Christ — there is no salvation that bypasses the Cross — and it is His to give, not ours to presume or to preach. We are not the judges of the unevangelized; we are the messengers to them. The command we received is not “speculate” but “go”: “Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations” (Matthew 28:19) . The question to ask is rarely “what about the man on the distant island?” and almost always “what about me, who has heard?” To us who have seen the Light, the word stands: “How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?” (Hebrews 2:3) . ↑ Back to contents Part II · Question 6 Could Jesus have sinned? No.

His temptations were utterly real — pressed on Him from outside with a force we will never know — but the one tempted was the divine person of God the Word, and God cannot sin. He is not merely the man who happened never to sin; He is the One who could not, and that is our security, not a diminishment of His humanity. The question must honor two facts Scripture states with equal force. First, the temptations were genuine: “For we do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but was in all points tempted as we are, yet without sin.” Hebrews 4:15 Second, the tempted One is God, and “God cannot be tempted by evil” (James 1:13) in the sense of being susceptible to it; He is “the Holy One” (Acts 3:14) , and “in Him there is no sin” (1 John 3:5) . The resolution lies where all christological questions are resolved: in the unity of His person . Actions and possibilities belong to persons, not to natures floating free. The question “could Jesus have sinned?” means “could the person acting through that human nature have sinned?” — and the person is God the Word.

Sin is precisely the creature’s turning away from God; for the incarnate Word to sin, God would have to turn away from God — an absolute impossibility. As the Oriental Orthodox confession insists, His humanity was never for one moment a separate, independent agent that might have gone its own way; from the instant of conception it was the Word’s own humanity, inseparably united to His divinity. A humanity that could sin “on its own” would imply exactly the two-subjects error of Nestorius that the Council of Ephesus condemned. Then were the temptations theater? No — and this is the crucial pastoral point. The reality of a temptation does not depend on the possibility of failure; it depends on the reality of the assault and of the felt cost of resisting. Christ truly hungered in the wilderness when the tempter came (Matthew 4:1–11) ; truly recoiled in Gethsemane — “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death... let this cup pass from Me” (Matthew 26:38–39) — sweating as it were great drops of blood (Luke 22:44) .

His human will genuinely shrank from the Cross as every human will shrinks from death, and genuinely, freely submitted: “nevertheless, not My will, but Yours, be done.” The Fathers observed, moreover, that the sinless One experienced temptation’s full force in a way sinners never do: we capitulate early; He endured the entire weight to the end. The man who resists ten minutes and yields knows less of temptation’s power than the man who withstands the whole siege. C. S. Lewis’s modern image only restates the ancients: only the man who never gives in knows how strong the wind really blows. Why His impeccability matters for us Some fear that if Christ could not sin, He cannot really sympathize with us. Scripture says the opposite: His sympathy rests on what He experienced (hunger, weariness, grief, dread, the tempter’s whisper), not on a capacity for evil. A physician need not be susceptible to a disease to know its symptoms perfectly and cure it. Indeed, His impeccability is the very ground of our hope, in at least three ways.

First, the certainty of salvation : had the outcome in the wilderness or the garden hung in doubt, the entire economy of salvation hung with it — creation’s redemption balanced on a coin-flip. God does not gamble with His promise; “the Scriptures must be fulfilled” (Mark 14:49) . Second, the spotless sacrifice : only “a lamb without blemish and without spot” (1 Peter 1:19) could be offered for the sins of the world; a savior who merely happened not to sin would leave us with a salvation that merely happened. Third, the healing of our nature : Christ took our humanity precisely to render it sin-proof in Himself — to drive the serpent’s venom out of the bloodstream of the race. In Him human nature has already arrived where grace is leading us: the inability to fall that the saints will enjoy in glory is not the loss of freedom but its perfection — freedom finally immune to slavery. Summary: Athanasius and Cyril teach that the Lord hungered, thirsted, grew weary, feared and was troubled in prayer because He permitted His own flesh to suffer what belongs to it.

This showed that He bore a true body and not a phantom, and by making our passions His own He broke their tyranny in Himself. Summary of the teaching of St. Athanasius and St. Cyril on the Lord’s blameless passions (cf. Against the Arians 3.54–57; Cyril, Commentary on John) So the believer under temptation looks to Christ and finds not a fellow gambler who got lucky, but a conqueror who has already broken the enemy’s line — and who now, as the sympathizing High Priest, “is able to aid those who are tempted,” because “He Himself has suffered, being tempted” (Hebrews 2:18) . We are not following an example merely; we are grafted into a victory. ↑ Back to contents Part II · Question 7 What happened during Christ’s earthly ministry? For roughly three years the incarnate God walked through our life and rewrote it from within: sanctifying our waters in His baptism, reversing Adam’s defeat in the wilderness, teaching as the Truth in person, healing as the Kingdom breaking in, founding His Church, and instituting the mysteries by which we share His life.

Peter gave the shortest summary ever preached: “God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with Him” (Acts 10:38) . But the Fathers saw beneath the surface of those three years a deliberate architecture: St. Irenaeus called it recapitulation — Christ passing through every stage and station of human life as the new head of the race, undoing at each point what was done amiss in Adam, sanctifying each stage by inhabiting it. “He became what we are,” and in becoming it, healed it. Trace the major stations. The Baptism: the waters sanctified The Sinless One had no sins to wash; the Jordan did not cleanse Him — He cleansed the Jordan. By descending into the water, the Lord sanctified water itself as the womb of the new birth, and the heavens opened to reveal the Trinity: the Son in the river, the Spirit descending as a dove, the Father’s voice — “This is My beloved Son” (Matthew 3:16–17) . The Coptic and all Eastern churches keep this as the great feast of Theophany .

Every baptismal font in the world flows from the Jordan of that morning. The Temptation: Adam’s test, retaken and passed Adam, in a garden of plenty, fed and comfortable, fell at the first whisper. Christ, in a desert, after forty days’ hunger, threw back all three assaults — appetite, spectacle, and power — answering each from Scripture (Matthew 4:1–11) . The first round of the ancient duel was thus refought and won; the strong man’s house had been entered, and his binding had begun (Matthew 12:29) . The Teaching: not a scribe, but the Word “The people were astonished at His teaching, for He taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes” (Matthew 7:28–29) . Prophets said, “Thus says the LORD”; Jesus said, “But I say to you” (Matthew 5:22) — and “heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will by no means pass away” (Matthew 24:35) . The Sermon on the Mount, the parables, the Last Supper discourses — this is not religious advice but the self-disclosure of the Truth in person, the Lawgiver standing on the mountain interpreting His own Law.

The Miracles: the Kingdom arriving in deeds The miracles are not advertisements; they are the thing itself arriving — creation’s ruin running backward wherever its Maker walked. Blind eyes (light restored), lepers (the unclean made clean by a touch that should have defiled and instead healed), storms silenced by a word the disciples recognized with terror as the prerogative of the Creator — “Who can this be, that even the wind and the sea obey Him!” (Mark 4:41; cf. Psalm 107:29) — and the dead raised: Jairus’s daughter, the widow’s son, and Lazarus four days in the tomb (John 11) , dress rehearsals for the third day. “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28) . The Transfiguration: glory unveiled before the Cross On the mountain He drew back, for a moment, the veil of His flesh: “His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as the light,” with Moses and Elijah — the Law and the Prophets — in attendance, and the Father’s voice again: “This is My beloved Son... Hear Him!” (Matthew 17:1–5) .

The disciples were shown, days before Golgotha, that the coming Passion would be voluntary: no one crucifies that glory against its will. The Foundation: a Church and her mysteries He left behind no book, but a community with His life in it : twelve apostles deliberately echoing the twelve tribes, given authority to bind and loose (Matthew 16:18–19; 18:18) , a new commandment of love (John 13:34) , the promise of the Spirit to guide them into all truth (John 16:13) , and on the night of His betrayal, the mystery of mysteries: “Take, eat; this is My body... this is My blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (Matthew 26:26–28) . The whole sacramental life of the Orthodox Church — baptism, Eucharist, priesthood, absolution (John 20:22–23) — was planted in those three years. “For He came to save all through means of Himself — all, I say, who through Him are born again to God — infants, and children, and boys, and youths, and old men.

He therefore passed through every age, becoming an infant for infants, thus sanctifying infants; a child for children, thus sanctifying those who are of this age… So likewise He was an old man for old men, that He might be a perfect Master for all…” St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.4 (ANF) St. John closes his Gospel admitting the impossibility of a full inventory: “there are also many other things that Jesus did, which if they were written one by one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books” (John 21:25) . But the shape is clear: the ministry was not a prelude to the real work; it was the Physician making His rounds through the whole ward of human existence — birth, childhood, labor, friendship, grief, temptation, prayer — leaving each one sanctified, before ascending the Cross to heal the last enemy of all.

↑ Back to contents Part II · Question 8 What does it mean that Jesus is seated at the Father’s right hand? Not a location but an enthronement: the crucified and risen Man now reigns with the full authority, honor, and power of God — His finished work accepted, His humanity glorified, His intercession unceasing, His return awaited. God is spirit (John 4:24) ; He has no literal right hand, and heaven is not furnished with chairs. “The right hand” is the Bible’s idiom of supreme honor and executive power — the position of the vizier, the crown prince, the one through whom the king acts. The image comes above all from the most-quoted Old Testament verse in the entire New Testament: “The LORD said to my Lord, ‘Sit at My right hand, till I make Your enemies Your footstool.’” Psalm 110:1 — cited or echoed over twenty times in the New Testament Jesus Himself used this Psalm to silence His questioners (how is the Messiah merely David’s son, if David calls Him “my Lord”? Matthew 22:41–46 ), and at His trial He claimed it as His own destiny: “hereafter you will see the Son of Man sitting at

the right hand of the Power, and coming on the clouds of heaven” (Matthew 26:64) — the claim for which the high priest tore his robes. After the resurrection, the apostles proclaim it as accomplished fact: He “was received up into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19) ; God “raised Him from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly places, far above all principality and power and might and dominion” (Ephesians 1:20–21) . Unpack what the session means, strand by strand. The work is finished The priests of the old covenant never sat down on duty — there were no seats in the tabernacle’s holy place — “every priest stands ministering daily and offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But this Man, after He had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:11–12) . The sitting is the visible form of “It is finished” (John 19:30) : nothing remains to be added to the sacrifice — not by Him, and not by us.

Our humanity is enthroned Mark this carefully: what ascended and sat down is not the bare divine Word — He never left the Father’s side as God — but the Word in our flesh . A human body, born of the Virgin, scarred by Roman nails, now occupies the throne of the universe. The session is humanity’s coronation: in Christ our nature has been carried higher than the cherubim. Daniel saw it in advance: “One like the Son of Man... came to the Ancient of Days... Then to Him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve Him” (Daniel 7:13–14) . And astonishingly, His enthronement is the pledge of ours: God “raised us up together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6) ; “to him who overcomes I will grant to sit with Me on My throne” (Revelation 3:21) . He reigns now — and intercedes now The session is not retirement but government: “He must reign till He has put all enemies under His feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25) ; “All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18) .

History since the Ascension is not drifting; it is being subdued. And at the center of that reign is a priestly heart: “He is also able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through Him, since He always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25) ; “if anyone sins, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1) . Every prayer of the Church ascends “through Christ our Lord” because He is, at this hour, our Forerunner within the veil (Hebrews 6:20) — the wounds He shows the Father are the permanent liturgy of our forgiveness. The first Christian to see it was the first martyr. As the stones fell, Stephen looked up: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!” (Acts 7:56) — standing, the Fathers noted, as if risen from the throne to welcome His witness home. That is the session in one image: absolute sovereignty, leaning toward us. The creed of the Church places it between two certainties — “and ascended into heaven, and sits at the Right Hand of the Father.

And he shall come again with glory…” The throne is occupied; the footstool is filling; the King is coming back. ↑ Back to contents Part II · Question 9 Why is Christ called the “Second Adam”? Because as Adam stood at the head of the old humanity and dragged it into sin and death, Christ stands at the head of a new humanity and carries it into righteousness and life. Point by point — tree for tree, garden for garden, disobedience for obedience — He retraced Adam’s steps and reversed them. The title is St. Paul’s. Twice he sets the two heads of humanity side by side and runs the comparison like a ledger: “For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ all shall be made alive... And so it is written, ‘The first man Adam became a living being.’ The last Adam became a life-giving spirit... The first man was of the earth, made of dust; the second Man is the Lord from heaven.” 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45, 47 “For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so also by one Man’s obedience many will be made righteous...

For if by the one man’s offense death reigned through the one, much more those who receive abundance of grace... will reign in life through the One, Jesus Christ.” Romans 5:19, 17 Behind the title lies a profound anthropology: human beings are not isolated units but a single organism with a head. What the head does, the body inherits. From Adam we inherited a nature wounded by corruption and tilted toward death — not by imitating him but by being born of him. The Gospel’s logic is the same in reverse: from Christ we inherit healed nature and immortal life — not by imitating Him only, but by being born of Him , “born again” (John 3:3) by water and the Spirit, grafted into Him as branches into a vine (John 15:5) . Salvation is a change of head. The great reversal, point by point St. Irenaeus, in the second century, traced the symmetry with wonder, calling it recapitulation — and the Fathers after him filled in the details like artists completing a diptych.

Adam was tempted in a garden of abundance and fell; Christ was tempted in a desert of hunger and stood — and then, completing the pattern, agonized in another garden, Gethsemane, where “not My will but Yours” untied the knot of “my will, not Yours” tied at Eden. Through a tree death entered; on a tree death was slain — “who Himself bore our sins in His own body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24) . Adam stretched out his hand to seize forbidden fruit; Christ stretched out His hands to the nails. Adam’s disobedience was crowned with fig leaves of shame; Christ’s obedience was crowned with thorns — the very sign of the curse on the ground (Genesis 3:18) pressed onto the brow of the One bearing it away. Eve, a virgin, listened to the serpent and brought forth death; Mary, a virgin, listened to the angel — “let it be to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38) — and brought forth Life. St.

Irenaeus states this last parallel explicitly: “the knot of Eve’s disobedience was loosed by the obedience of Mary” (Against Heresies 3.22.4) — which is why the Orthodox honor the Theotokos as the New Eve, mother of all the truly living. Even the geography of redemption preaches it. Adam, having sinned, slept and was opened that Eve might be formed from his side; Christ, having finished His work, slept on the Cross and His side was opened (John 19:34) — and from the blood and water the Fathers saw the Church, His bride, born: the water of baptism, the blood of the Eucharist. An ancient tradition cherished in the East even places Golgotha — “the place of the skull” — over the grave of Adam, which is why Orthodox icons of the Crucifixion paint a skull beneath the Cross: the blood of the Second Adam running down to baptize the bones of the first.

“He has therefore, in His work of recapitulation, summed up all things, both waging war against our enemy, and crushing him who had at the beginning led us away captives in Adam… For as by the disobedience of the one man who was originally moulded from virgin soil, the many were made sinners, and forfeited life; so was it necessary that, by the obedience of one man, who was originally born from a virgin, many should be justified and receive salvation.” St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.21.1; 3.18.7 (ANF) What the title means for us “Second Adam” is finally a word about belonging. Every human being lives under one of the two heads; there is no third. In the first Adam we receive what he had to give: a magnificent, mortally wounded nature — “as we have borne the image of the man of dust” (1 Corinthians 15:49) . In Christ we receive what He has to give: forgiveness, the Spirit, incorruption — “we shall also bear the image of the heavenly Man.” Baptism is the transfer of headship: dying with the old Adam, rising in the New (Romans 6:3–5) .

And the destiny of the new race exceeds even Eden, for the Second Adam cannot fall: He does not return us to the garden gate to try again, but carries us where the first Adam never arrived — to the throne. The Fathers dared to put it this way: God did not merely repair Adam; in Christ, He finished him. ↑ Back to contents Part II · Question 10 When will Jesus return? No one knows — by the Lord’s own design and declaration. He will return visibly, gloriously, and suddenly, to raise the dead and judge the living and the dead. The Church is not given a date; she is given a command: watch, and keep your lamp burning. On this question the Lord Himself drew the line, and drew it absolutely: “But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but My Father only...

Therefore you also be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.” Matthew 24:36, 44 And again, in His final recorded conversation before the Ascension, when the disciples asked the question one last time: “It is not for you to know times or seasons which the Father has put in His own authority” (Acts 1:7) .
